policy.titleEn: An AI Accord, a New Czar and an Autonomous Warfare Command
policy.titleZh: 一项人工智能协议、一位新负责人与一个自主作战司令部
policy.summaryZh: 本周，科技高管在白宫与总统特朗普、众议院议长迈克·约翰逊及政府高级官员会面。OpenAI、Anthropic、谷歌、Meta、xAI和英伟达签署了自愿性的《前沿责任联合承诺》，承诺实施严格的内部控制和外部监督与治理，该协议被《连线》杂志称为“花哨的拉钩承诺”。特朗普发布行政命令《开启超级智能时代》，指示联邦政府使用“超级智能”一词取代“人工智能”，并任命国家情报总监杰伊·克莱顿领导新的“超级智能特别工作组”，负责制定应对超级智能威胁社会的计划，同时防止过度监管和监管俘获，该工作组将在120天内提交报告。联邦贸易委员会对OpenAI和Anthropic等人工智能公司展开广泛调查，考虑对消费者的潜在伤害，包括不公平和欺骗性行为以及“恶意”人工智能代理的威胁。国防部长皮特·赫格塞斯在匡蒂科发表讲话，宣布成立四星级的自主作战司令部，以“加速超级智能、机器人和自主系统时代”跨军种发展。参议院国土安全小组委员会就“恶意”人工智能代理举行听证会，聚焦于OpenAI代理未经授权访问Hugging Face系统的事件以及与中国的“竞赛”。加州总检察长罗伯·邦塔就Hugging Face黑客事件向OpenAI发出调查传票；欧洲尽管华盛顿反对，仍继续推动全球人工智能规则；法国对Palantir和Anduril在北约机密网络中的角色提出质疑；澳大利亚准备就OpenAI代理入侵政府系统举行参议院听证会。
policy.bodyText:
An AI Accord, a New Czar and an Autonomous Warfare Command Justin Hendrix / Oct 4, 2026 The Tech Policy Press newsletter is published every Sunday.   Subscribe here to receive it in your email inbox .

President Donald Trump holds a press conference on the North Lawn of the White House with Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, and other tech leaders on September 29, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Leyden/NurPhoto via AP)

Republish

Good morning!

This week, tech executives met at the White House with President Donald Trump , House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), and senior Trump administration officials. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia signed a voluntary “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities” to commit to robust internal controls and external monitoring and governance, an accord Wired dubbed “a fancy pinky-swear.”

Photos of Trump, Johnson, Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and other officials on the White House lawn with Elon Musk , Mark Zuckerberg , Dario Amodei , Jensen Huang , Sundar Pichai , Greg Brockman and others offered another indelible image of this administration’s relationship with the tech industry, and capped a week of other developments:

Trump issued an executive order “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,” instructing the federal government to use the term rather than “artificial intelligence,” which the president has criticized as suggesting the technology is “fake” for more than a year. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead a new “Super Intelligence Task Force” that will be tasked to “develop plans for responding to SI-enabled threats to our society, while preventing overregulation and regulatory capture that would stifle innovation and competition,” according to the Wall Street Journal . The task force will issue a report in 120 days. The FTC opened a “ broad investigation ” into AI firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic to consider potential harms to consumers, including unfair and deceptive practices and the threat of “rogue” AI agents. In a “State of the Force” address to junior officers and enlisted leaders at Quantico, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command (AutoWarCom) to “supercharge the era of SI, robotics and autonomous systems” across the armed services . On Capitol Hill, senators queried witnesses in a Homeland Security subcommittee hearing on “rogue” AI agents centered on the Hugging Face incident, in which OpenAI agents accessed Hugging Face systems without authorization, and the “race” with China. Yuqing Liu was in the room for Tech Policy Press. (The phrase “superintelligence” was used at least nine times, by my count, just as it was by executives throughout the week — for instance, Jensen Huang referred to data centers as “superintelligence factories” on stage with Elon Musk .)

There were many other developments on AI governance in the US and beyond this week. California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI over the Hugging Face hack; Europe signaled a continued push for global AI rules despite Washington’s opposition; France is challenging Palantir and Anduril’s role in NATO classified networks; and Australia is preparing for a Senate hearing with OpenAI’s chief strategy officer on the intrusion of the company’s agents into Australian government systems.

Tech Policy Press staff, fellows and contributors covered the global discourse on AI in a variety of ways this week. (And yes, the Tech Policy Press style desk has confirmed we will continue to prefer the term, flawed as it is, to SI — see a relevant post from contributing editor Amber Sinha below.) Read on for more on this subject, and many more!

A chance to hear your voice on the Tech Policy Press podcast This week, I’ll be at Georgetown for an exciting conference hosted by The Privacy Center at Georgetown Law called “ Life After Data: the conference on de-datafication .” The event and the sessions at it are offered as a provocation to “imagine a future in which digital data is no longer the currency mediating all of our social, economic and political systems, structures and practices. How might we get there from here?”

I answered one of the calls, and will give a short, speculative talk on the topic “Why, How, and When to Abandon the Internet.” With corporate and government surveillance, AI agents and machine-generated slop increasingly overrunning the web, I reckon it’s worth engaging in some thought experiments about what might come next. To help me think it through, I’m inviting Tech Policy Press’ global audience to send voice memos explaining in their own voices how they would answer the provocation, and I plan to use a selection of these submissions in the podcast.

If you are interested in participating, consider responding to one of these questions:

What would have to break, or be built, before people would be willing to leave the current internet behind? Who would lead such a movement, and who would stand in its way? What from today’s internet and the platforms that define it is worth saving, and what should be left behind? What would a better, more sustainable and pro-democratic network look like, and how would we build it? We’re looking for short memos, one to two minutes long. Send yours as an attachment or a link to contributions@techpolicy.press . At the start of your memo, please state your name and any relevant affiliation. We won’t be able to use every submission, but we’re grateful for every one we receive.

Want to be involved in these kinds of speculative conversations that encourage us to imagine different possible futures? With The Privacy Center, we’re looking for ideas upstream of tech policy that point to a more just, equitable, sustainable and democratic future in more than one way. On Oct. 22, The Privacy Center and Tech Policy Press will launch “The Edge Dialogues,” a new series of conversations, with special guest Dr. Alondra Nelson . You can register here .

AI governance Daniel Stone , executive director of Diffusion.Au, examines the OpenAI agent incident in Australia: “84 days, almost three months, from the first access to the warning being raised.” He calls for enforceable rules, prompt notice, access to logs and a way to recover costs. On the Tech Policy Press podcast , I talk with Data & Society’s Maia Woluchem and Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes and People’s Tech Project’s Hannah Sassaman about “The AI Factory,” a new report on data centers, power and resistance in Pennsylvania. AI transparency means different things to investors, regulators, civil society and safety researchers. Dunstan Allison-Hope , independent consultant on just and sustainable business, and Sam Wallace , head of corporate governance, risk, and responsible practice at the Partnership on AI, on why that distinction should shape what companies disclose and to whom. The term artificial intelligence (and yes, the term “super intelligence” too) actively distorts our cognitive understanding , misdirects public concern, and derails legal and policy frameworks, says Tech Policy Press contributing editor Amber Sinha . Effective technology policy requires that we discard this language and build enforceable, democratic guardrails grounded in reality, he argues. Tech Policy Press rounds up what non-Western governments said about AI at the UN last week, from calls for a greater role in shaping the rules to warnings that slowing AI must not deepen the digital divide. Ramsha Jahangir and Justin Hendrix report. Chinese AI models like DeepSeek and Qwen are gaining ground with developers in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, not because of geopolitics, but because they are cheaper and more flexible. The Information Society Law Center’s Ninsiima Melissa on the strategic consequences that follow. Russia’s new AI law borrows the vocabulary of contemporary AI regulation but uses it to combine industrial policy with technological control , write Dmitry Kuteynikov , a lawyer focused on AI governance and digital regulation, and Lyubov Popovets , a data journalist. “Russia’s answer to the AI race is to build at the frontier but to own the checkpoint,” they write. Does AI training count as scientific research? The answer may be decided by MEPs negotiating the EU’s Digital Omnibus, writes Stephen Wyber , director of external affairs at the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions. Changing AI providers is like unwinding an ecosystem, says Tom Smith of the Royal Air Force College. He argues that the most important question for universities isn’t which model to choose today, but how to preserve free choice in the future. Our content delivered to your inbox. Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy

Subscribe

Loading...

Thank you! You have successfully joined our subscriber list.

Tech and elections Days before Brazil’s election, Meta briefly blocked President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ’s campaign page from running political ads and removed an Instagram profile behind a viral video on Flávio Bolsonaro . Both decisions were reversed, but raised public concerns about the role of platforms in moderating election-related discourse. Brazilian journalist Laís Martins reports. Taiwan’s deepfake law was designed to protect elections. It has never once been used. Eddy Yen-Ting Lin , Lloyd M. Robbins Doctor of Juridical Science Fellow at UC Berkeley School of Law, breaks down three fatal flaws — and draws lessons for others. “A deepfake election law worthy of a democracy should neither rely entirely on ‘more speech’ nor chill free expression,” he writes. A public scandal involving the mishandling of voter records by the Election Commission of India highlights the fallacy of depending on a centralized system for the friction and realities of human democracy , writes Tech Policy Press contributing editor Amber Sinha . On the Tech Policy Press podcast, I spoke with UNC’s Daniel Kreiss and Lorcan Neill about their new paper , “Militant Platform Democracy: A Framework for Democracy-Worthy Platform Policies.” Listen to our conversation here . Child online safety The EU KIDS Act arrived without an impact assessment . Asha Allen , director and secretary general of the CDT Europe Office, writes that a law with far-reaching fundamental rights implications cannot be shaped outside democratic due process. Is KOSA the “social reckoning” we’re looking for? Not quite, argues Karolina Mackiewicz , policy fellow at George Washington University’s Institute for Data, Democracy & Politics: “A true social reckoning calls for standards that prioritize safety over engagement, without sacrificing anyone’s privacy, agency, or free expression.” “Adults are harmed when their data is leaked, but kids suffer more,” writes Logan Kolas , director of technology policy at the American Consumer Institute, arguing that age verification laws meant to protect children could put America “on a collision course” with its newly discovered AI-augmented cybersecurity reality . Platform regulation and accountability The remedies in the Google ad tech case “stopped well short of actually preventing future abuses of monopoly power,” writes Public Knowledge’s Patrick Gallaher , who argues the ruling shows the need for the bipartisan AMERICA Act. Most state attorneys general released Meta from Cambridge Analytica-related claims as part of the child safety settlement. New Mexico wasn’t part of that deal, and a jury there just found 26 of 29 past statements about Cambridge Analytica , hate speech and misinformation willfully deceptive. I wrote about the jury’s findings. Australia’s draft Digital Duty of Care is “a welcome and necessary reform,” but its public pitch as an off switch for “the algorithm” misses the point, write Daniel Angus and Jean Burgess of the Queensland University of Technology and Amanda Third of Western Sydney University. Brazil’s platform rules have focused on harms from commercial platforms. João Alexandre Peschanski of Wikimedia Brasil, Amalia Toledo of the Wikimedia Foundation, and Elise Silva of the University of Pittsburgh argue digital public goods like Wikipedia need their own legal category . Who bears the burden? Grab drivers in Vietnam called for a two-day app boycott last month over commission rates. Tech Policy Press fellow Lam Le reports on what it reveals about the changing politics of platform work in Southeast Asia. Economic violence against women through the use of digital IDs is a growing, rarely recognized problem in Denmark and across Europe, reports investigative journalist Polina Bachlakova . “Across the European Union, one in five women experiences some form of economic violence, yet only nine European countries specifically criminalize it. Denmark is not one of them,” she reports. September in review In their September roundup, Maria Buza and Şeymanur Yönt Gökcen of Digital Policy Alert track G20 developments in content moderation, AI, competition and data governance, including the European Commission’s proposed KIDS Act and Ireland’s €403 million fine against Google. The September US tech policy roundup, from Rachel Lau and Shirley Frame of Freedman Consulting and Ashley Faler and me at Tech Policy Press, tracks everything from Trump’s order on using the term “super intelligence” to AI safety pledges, stalled bills in Congress, state action, key court rulings and more . “Someone has to care” “Someone has to care to make things happen,” Francine Berman writes in Better Tech , new from MIT Press. Reviewing the book, data scientist Nathan Sanders says readers will come away newly equipped with specific ideas to make change. Competition in the cloud To get ahead of EU mandates and alleviate pressure from the Federal Trade Commission, the biggest cloud service providers started offering fee exemptions for customers looking to exit their cloud. It has had little practical effect on competition, argue Luke Hogg and Sophia Bulla of the Foundation for American Innovation. “At best, eliminating egress fees is benignly unproductive in the effort to improve competition in the cloud,” they write. Recognition for work on data centers We’re excited to share that two collaborative projects to which Tech Policy Press contributed have received recognition this year:

An investigation led by Investigate Europe into how Big Tech embedded secrecy provisions into EU law to shield data center environmental data from public scrutiny has been shortlisted for the 2026 Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for Journalism . Tech Policy Press was a media partner on the project, alongside The Guardian, Le Monde and El País. “Dark Side of the Boom” — a collaboration across 14 outlets and 11 countries tracing the water, energy and community costs of data centers, AI infrastructure and crypto mining across Asia — took home the 2026 SOPA Award for Excellence in Reporting on the Environment and a citation for journalistic innovation from the 2026 Osborn Elliott Prize for Excellence in Journalism on Asia . Tech Policy Press contributed reporting on data centers in India to the project. We’re grateful to all the partners who made this work possible.

I wish you the best for the week ahead!

-Justin

policy.titleZh: 宾夕法尼亚州：数据中心政治的摇摆州案例研究
policy.summaryZh: 数据与社会（Data & Society）发布新报告《AI工厂：宾夕法尼亚州晚期工业中的数据中心、电力与抵抗》，基于在该州一年半的田野调查，探讨支持者如何借该州工业历史推销数据中心，以及为何许多社区拒绝行业与政客的承诺。宾州成为全美数据中心政治斗争的缩影，类似冲突也在其他州上演。州长乔什·夏皮罗曾宣布亚马逊将投资200亿美元建设两个数据中心，并加速审批，但遭到费城、匹兹堡、哈里斯堡、伊利及农村地区的广泛抵制。反对者关注水电资源优先权、就业稀少（费城规划委员会估计每5000平方英尺仅一个岗位）、电网负荷及电价上涨，以及对AI对儿童、家庭和民主影响的担忧。行业依赖工业怀旧等叙事，但这些叙事与宾州现状脱节。
policy.bodyText:
Pennsylvania is a Swing-State Case Study for Data Center Politics Justin Hendrix / Oct 4, 2026 Subscribe to the   Tech Policy Press   podcast via your favorite service here.

Republish

Pennsylvania offers a particular case study in which to consider the political battle over data centers that is playing out across the United States and beyond. A new report from Data & Society, "The AI Factory: Data Centers, Power, and Resistance in Late Industrial Pennsylvania," draws on a year and a half of fieldwork across the state. It examines how boosters sell data centers by invoking Pennsylvania's industrial past, and why so many communities aren't buying the promises made by industry and politicians.

I spoke with Data & Society's Maia Woluchem and Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes and with organizer Hannah Sassaman about the findings.

What follows is a lightly edited transcript of the discussion.

A "No Data Center" yard sign is seen in Allenwood, Pennsylvania on July 7, 2026. The sign is in opposition to a proposed 300-megawatt data center at nearby Great Stream Commons industrial park in Gregg Township. (Photo by Paul Weaver/Sipa via AP Images)

Maia Woluchem:

My name is Maia Woluchem. I am the program director of the Trustworthy Infrastructures team at Data & Society.

Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes:

I'm Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes, and I'm a postdoctoral fellow on Maia's team, the Trustworthy Infrastructures team at Data & Society.

Hannah Sassaman:

I'm Hannah Sassaman. I'm the executive director at People's Tech Project. We're based in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

Justin Hendrix:

And we're going to turn our eyes to Pennsylvania during this conversation and catch up a little bit about what's happening there, but also look at the results of this report that Data & Society has just put out called the AI Factory: Data Centers, Power, and Resistance in Late Industrial Pennsylvania []. I feel like I've been following this project for some time, been kind of around it, had the opportunity, Maia, to talk to you of course, and have you on the podcast even in recent months as we've been studying this issue alongside you. But I want to just start off by asking you about the title, where it comes from. I know you've borrowed this from an activist, The AI Factory, what does this phrase mean to you?

Maia Woluchem:

Yeah, it was such a great turn of phrase that came up in one of our early interviews with an organizer who's been doing incredible work around the state. But yeah, the thrust of the report was really trying to connect data centers to this long history of industrial re-imagination in Pennsylvania. It is a state that has meant so much to the country and to the global economy for its contributions and coal and steel and iron and many other things. And that idea of the factory is still really present in this conversation around AI. We were very lucky that one of our interviewees really made that connection. I believe that full quote was something like, "This here is an AI factory. It is as extractive as mining instead of mining for coal or mining for tokens." And I think that has really played out in many of the interviews that we had over the two years that we were crossing the state.

I think when a lot of boosters come to town and they sort of pull on these ideas of industrialization to try to win favor for this idea around data centers and AI, what it pulls on for people is this deep history mining of steel. And for many people that is not so much about the future, but that's about the past. And that's about, in some ways, some very traumatic experiences of the past.

Justin Hendrix:

And this might be a place to bring in Hannah too, but I think of Pennsylvania as a place that is contested. I often feel like it's the number one swing state whenever we talk about American politics. And as you say, it is somehow stuck between past and present. There's so much history and so much runs through the state, but maybe bring us up to speed. What's the picture right now when it comes to data centers in Pennsylvania? What does that look like?

Hannah Sassaman:

Well, I'm sure Maia and Ana can add a lot more, but I think just building on what you laid out, there was a storied announcement, I believe last year from our governor, Governor Josh Shapiro. He's in the middle of running for reelection for his second term. And the announcement was, I think he did it in the middle of the Lehigh Valley, which is a traditional sort of eastern side of the state, industrial part of the state, like Allentown and places like that. And he was ready to say that they were going to bring $20 billion worth of investment from Amazon into the state, building starting with two data centers, I believe one in Salem Township and then the other basically on the other side of the river from Trenton. And that was supposed to be the harbinger of tons and tons of data center development.

And he was also fast tracking permitting. He was making it possible for many different communities to try to get these data centers. And these were often in places where there had been brutal disinvestment over decades and generations. I believe the Salem Township one is in an area where the last sort of major hospital had closed a couple of years before, for example. So that's an interesting sense of the contradiction. But I think to answer your question directly, there is a robust, organic, deeply activating, incredibly diverse resistance to this kind of development in big cities like Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, in smaller cities and towns like Harrisburg, like Erie, and in the more rural counties of the Commonwealth, because there is a lot of clarity about in relationship to the union beauty that built the infrastructure of the working class of the state about what these data centers actually offer and promise.

What they offer and promise isn't much. In most places, they're situated near water that would be prioritized for the data center rather than prioritized for communities. The jobs that they offer are only in relationship to the construction jobs during the building, but after they're up, there was an estimate done by the Philadelphia Planning Commission, and we can talk in more detail about the organizing, the beautiful diverse resistance to data centers in my city. But the Philadelphia Planning Commission found that for every 5,000 square feet, there would only be one job. And then there's obviously a deep impact on everyone across the Commonwealth that relies on a variety of the electrical grid and infrastructure. They've already been impacted not just from data centers built in Pennsylvania, but also in Virginia, also in Maryland in the PJM territory where there's been about a decade of data center mass boom expansion starting and centering in Virginia that's impacting the electrical rates of our residents.

Here in Philadelphia in the southeastern part of the state, the PECO, which is the major sort of electrical company had to grant an amnesty basically of $10 million last year, and I think they're doing something similar this year for community members who just couldn't afford their electrical bills. So they literally had to offer charity for those bills. And so what we're finding is that the promises that the governor, the promises that Amazon, the promises that Microsoft, which is actually trying to reopen Three Mile Island, the big nuclear reactor site, which was the cause of the biggest natural nuclear, not natural, biggest nuclear meltdown disaster in United States history, what they're finding is deep resistance, not just to the electrical costs, not just to the lies about development, not just to the water damage, but also around what's happening inside those buildings. There's a lot of deep concern about what AI is doing to our kids, AI is doing to our families, AI is doing to our democracy.

Ana Carolina de Assis Nunes:

Our report as well, of course we are talking about Pennsylvania, but in the report, Pennsylvania kind of emerged as a microcosmo of America because this data center fight is happening in other states as well. And in the second part of our report, we explore in depth how industries in Pennsylvania, but in other parts of the US as well, they're trying to really convince folks to welcome them into their spaces by leveraging nostalgia, by trying to tell stories of a different industrial era, by trying to appeal to especially blue collar families. Oh, remember the good times when you had a stable job as in a factory is exactly what Hannah is saying. And then when the data center is in place, yeah, we are seeing other reports about the employment numbers and there are not too many. And just to highlight this fact that we focus in Pennsylvania, but also because Pennsylvania allows us to tell a bigger story about the country, there's a new report by the Data Center Watch that came out about the second quarter of 2026.

So there are a lot of projects that have been blocked. But there are new reports showing too that beyond Pennsylvania, this is happening in different parts of the US. And when Pennsylvania merges a microcosm of this larger opposition data center, we can also see that these strategies used in Pennsylvania and in different states are pretty similar in terms of appealing to this industrial past in terms to say that data centers and AI kind of a continuation of this golden days of American industrial as well.

Justin Hendrix:

And so you went and spent a lot of time there, Maia, I understand multiple weeks, traipsing across different parts of Pennsylvania that have three different regions that you targeted doing what you do, ethnography, talking to people, studying this phenomenon with this particular social sciences approach. Let me just ask you a little bit about the kind of myths that you heard that were being relied on, some of the kind of messages that the industry is trying to reach people with. What did you hear as you listened for what the industry is trying to tell people of Pennsylvania?

Maia Woluchem:

It's true. We were out in crossing the state from the week right after the presidential elections. It was quite a fascinating time to still be there as everybody still had their signs in their windows and confetti on the ground in some places all the way up until 2026. So we saw really some significant swings, but also some really huge sign points in the sort of development of this data center narrative. We were in town just about every time that Trump was in Pennsylvania. We followed a bunch of industry conferences. We got to get into a few of them to see how the sell developed over time. What we found is exactly what's sort of been noted here that we say in the report that they're relying on three big buckets of ideas. There are many under them, but the first is this idea of industrial nostalgia, and they pull on that in some ways that are really dissonant with the ways that Pennsylvania understands itself now.

We understand Pennsylvania as this purple state, this sort of blue collar imagination that arrives every election season. But in that time since de-industrialization, the biggest unions in the state are those that do care work. They're municipal workers. They're not necessarily the builders and construction workers that are being pulled on for this kind of industrial build. However, they are the ones that are showing up on the stage all the time through the narratives that Trump, Shapiro, and many other sort of industrial leaders are naming when they talk about what data centers could mean. So that vision, that very thinness that that nostalgia is a really, really key part of that sort of myth making around the state. The second is that it's not necessarily unique to Pennsylvania, but I think there are some local flavors that the vision of AI today has taken on such a profoundly nationalistic turn.

We are in this AI race, we're supposedly trying to beat China, whatever that might mean to those who are designing that kind of narrative. But that one is distinctly pulling on this history in Pennsylvania that is around war. So many of those industries that we think of when we talk about that industrial nostalgia were really building a war effort. They were building the tanks that were showing up in World War II, the steel showed up in all of those war efforts. And so trying to pull people into that nationalism at this particular time is a bit of a faulty argument. We have a quote in the piece from a journalist that we spoke to who had gone to one of those community meetings where this kind of idea of war was showing up all the time in the AI argument. And they had spoken to a veteran who showed up at that municipal meeting and that veteran is saying, "Well, I actually was in war, so what is it that they're talking about?

These aren't necessarily soldiers that we're sending away. That is not the kind of rhetoric that is going to convince me to say I'm going to give up all my water and my land. What fight are we trying to win here?" But then the last one that really fits really neatly into a bunch of these is this pull on the unions. And this is a bit of a tricky one, as has been noted, some of the labor numbers that we're seeing for data centers are really, really thin. However, we did speak to a bunch of folks from the building trades as part of our work who would say, even if this is a bubble, we have a really precious moment of time to expand our ranks, to expand our apprenticeship programs, to really take advantage of this moment, even if it's going to be really short-lived.

And we see that this alignment between nationalism, industrialism and labor is kind of crafting this narrative around what AI is supposed to mean to Pennsylvania. But all of those things, I think they kind of misread the moment that we can't talk about those things and we're also in a bigger crisis of our own. I often think back to this election time that we were leaving in or that we first started this trip in, in which we're having real debates about immigration, about healthcare, about education. And in the past two years that we have been on the road, those things have been really pulled apart for Pennsylvanians. I'm a graduate of the University of Pittsburgh and is a public university. news.summaryZh: 北卡罗来纳州一家联邦法院驳回了RealPage提出的驳回反垄断诉讼的动议，允许各州执法机构对其提起的诉讼继续推进。此前，RealPage已与联邦政府达成和解，但法院的裁决表明，联邦层面的和解并不必然终结各州层面的反垄断风险。该案的核心指控是，RealPage提供的软件被房东用于协调或影响租金设定，从而非法抬高公寓价格。法院保留各州诉讼，为住房市场中算法定价工具的监管保留了重要的执法途径。
news.bodyText:
N.C. Federal Court Lets States’ Antitrust Case Against RealPage Move Forward

by Bruno Queiroz

A federal court in North Carolina has declined to dismiss antitrust claims brought by state enforcers against RealPage, allowing a closely watched challenge to rental-pricing software to proceed even after the company reached a settlement with the federal government. The ruling is a notable reminder that federal resolution does not necessarily end parallel state antitrust exposure.

The case centers on allegations that RealPage supplied software used by landlords to coordinate or influence rent-setting in ways that unlawfully inflated apartment prices. By keeping the states’ claims alive, the court preserved a significant avenue of enforcement in the broader scrutiny of algorithmic pricing tools in the housing market.

For legal professionals, the decision matters on several levels. First, it underscores the layered nature of antitrust enforcement. Companies facing investigations or litigation over pricing technology may view a federal settlement as a major milestone, but state attorneys general can continue to pursue their own theories, remedies, and injunctive demands. That dynamic raises the stakes for settlement strategy, particularly where conduct touches consumers across multiple jurisdictions.

Second, the ruling adds to the growing body of litigation testing how traditional antitrust principles apply to software-driven pricing recommendations. Plaintiffs have increasingly argued that algorithmic tools can facilitate coordinated pricing behavior even without a traditional cartel structure. Businesses that deploy revenue-management, market-optimization, or pricing analytics products should expect continued scrutiny not only of what the software does, but also of how customers use it and what information flows through the platform.

The North Carolina action is part of a wider litigation landscape surrounding RealPage. Docket Alarm users tracking this dispute may also want to monitor UNITED STATES OF AMERICA et al v. REALPAGE, INC. , the federal enforcement case in the Middle District of North Carolina, as well as the appellate proceeding In re: Realpage Inc, Rental Software Antitrust Litigation in the Sixth Circuit.

For litigators, the decision is a useful marker in pleading-stage antitrust battles involving platform and software defendants. For in-house counsel and compliance teams, it is another signal to revisit antitrust risk assessments around pricing tools, data-sharing practices, marketing representations, and customer guidance. In the housing sector especially, where public enforcement interest remains high, the RealPage litigation continues to serve as a bellwether for how courts and regulators will approach algorithmic rent-setting claims.

news.titleEn: Former Allen & Overy senior partner Wim Dejonghe co-founds native AI firm
news.titleZh: 前安理国际律师事务所高级合伙人Wim Dejonghe联合创立原生AI律所Falcon
news.summaryZh: 前安理国际律师事务所全球高级合伙人Wim Dejonghe与比利时HR科技公司Mbrella的创始人及前富瑞斯律师Rémy Bonnaffé共同创立了Falcon，这是一家以AI为核心、采用固定费用定价的新型律所，而非按小时收费。该律所瞄准欧洲每年约490亿欧元的市场，为中小企业提供商业法律支持，成本和时间仅为传统律所的一小部分。Falcon初期专注于高量商业合同，包括保密协议、数据处理协议、主服务协议及客户和供应商合同。客户通过Slack或Microsoft Teams等聊天应用提交合同，每份审查由合格律师签署并当天返还。创始团队包括Mbrella创始人Amaury Gérard、Quinten Vandermeulen和David Nguyen，以及前富瑞斯律师Rémy Bonnaffé。Falcon的理念源于三人建立和出售Mbrella的经验，当时商业合同成为时间消耗，外包给传统律所可能花费3000至4000欧元且耗时数天或数周。他们决定利用AI减少常规法律工作的时间和成本，同时保留律师参与。传统法律行业需要类似新银行式的变革，AI改变了法律工作速度，但传统模式仍按时间收费，这种矛盾在按小时计费模式下难以解决，因此Falcon从零开始围绕更快交付和固定费用定价构建，并确保每项工作由合格律师负责。每次合作始于45分钟的电话沟通，以了解客户业务、交易类型和法律风险，然后建立支持合同审查的剧本。比利时增长最快的消费品牌之一Loop Earplugs是其早期客户。AI使事实性和重复性任务易于自动化，但法律经验和建议仍需处于每项决策的中心。Falcon从比利时起步，英国从一开始就是关键市场，伦敦被确定为其下一个欧洲中心之一。
news.bodyHtml:
Wim Dejonghe, former global senior partner of Allen & Overy, has teamed up with the technology entrepreneurs behind Belgium HR-tech scaleup Mbrella and a former Freshfields lawyer to co-found Falcon, an AI-native law firm built around AI and flat-fee pricing rather than the billable hour.

The new law firm is targeting an estimated €49 billion-a-year European market, offering small and medium-sized businesses commercial legal support at “a fraction of the cost” and time of a traditional law firm. Falcon will initially focus on high-volume commercial contracts, including NDAs, data processing agreements, master service agreements and customer and supplier contracts. Clients submit contracts through chat apps such as Slack or Microsoft Teams, with every review signed off by a qualified lawyer and returned the same day.

Advertisement

The founding team includes technology entrepreneurs and Mbrella founders, Amaury Gérard, Quinten Vandermeulen and David Nguyen, alongside former Freshfields lawyer Rémy Bonnaffé. The idea for Falcon grew out of the trio’s experience building and selling Mbrella. As Mbrella scaled and began signing larger customers, the teams says that commercial contracts became an increasing drain on their time, while outsourcing relatively straightforward work to traditional law firms could cost €3,000–€4,000 and take days or weeks. They set out to build a law firm that could use AI to cut the time and cost of routine legal work without taking the lawyer out of the process.

“The traditional legal sector is due its neo-bank moment. AI has changed how quickly legal work can be done, but the traditional model still rewards firms for the time that work takes. That tension is very difficult to solve from inside a billable-hour model.  Falcon has been built from scratch around faster delivery and flat-fee pricing, while keeping a qualified lawyer accountable for every piece of work. That’s why I had to be involved”, said Dejonghe.

Advertisement

 Each engagement starts with an intake call of 45 minutes to understand how the customer’s business works, what deals they do, and what legal risk means for them. It then builds a playbook to support the legal contract review. Loop Earplugs, one of Belgium’s fastest-growing consumer brands, is one of its early customers.

“AI has shifted the dimensions of contract negotiations. It has made factual and repetitive tasks easy to automate. But it’s not a one and done solution. Legal experience and advice still need to sit at the centre of every decision”, said Rémy Bonnaffé, a former Freshfields lawyer and co-founder and Chief Legal Officer at Falcon. “Our new AI-native neo law firm strips out the hours spent on repetitive work without removing the lawyer out of the legal advice.”

Falcon is launching from Belgium, with the UK a key market from the outset and London identified as one of its next European hubs.

news.titleEn: Beacon Collective: Strategic conversations the legal sector needs to have right now
news.titleZh: Beacon Collective：法律行业当下亟需的战略对话
news.summaryZh: Beacon Collective上周举办的法律科技领袖聚会，其讨论的坦诚与活跃令人耳目一新。在Elena Folkes创办的这一查塔姆宫规则活动上，与会高级代表并未聚焦产品发布或转型承诺，而是深入探讨了人工智能与律所商业模式、法律培训、治理、风险及客户期望碰撞时产生的问题。会后，剑桥大学出版社与考评部总法律顾问Catie Sheret及Weightmans合伙人、前首席技术官Stuart Whittle分别接受了采访，指出了法律行业正在应对的一系列战略问题，尽管许多答案仍不明朗。会议凸显的一个主题是，律所与客户围绕AI应用的讨论日趋成熟，但也存在紧张关系。最令人印象深刻的是听到了私执业律师与客户之间关于AI使用场景及权衡的坦诚对话。一些律所与客户的关系良好，对话诚实，风险讨论也开诚布公，这本质上是一切的关键。如果客户要求更低价格，就必须接受律师监督减少带来的更多风险。她呼吁将这种对话扩展为更广泛的讨论和合理的框架。法律培训可能是行业最大的未决挑战，会议期间反复提及。初级律师的培养是重大关切，尤其是如果AI减少了传统上提供法律场景和客户问题接触机会的重复性工作。她质疑基于模拟的学习能否完全替代多年的实际经验。她提到，自己的团队规模虽不算小，但不足以建立培训项目。
news.bodyHtml:
We speak with Cambridge University Press GC Catie Sheret and Weightmans partner and former CTO Stuart Whittle – see video interview below

One of the refreshing things about Beacon Collective’s gathering of legal tech leaders last week was that the conversations were often candid and almost always unruly.

Advertisement

While much of the legal technology market remains preoccupied with product announcements and promises of transformation, senior delegates at the Chatham House event founded by Elena Folkes spent much of their time discussing what happens when AI collides with law firm business models, legal training, governance, risk and client expectations.

Following the event, I spoke separately with attendees Catie Sheret, general counsel at Cambridge University Press & Assessment, and Stuart Whittle, partner and former CTO at Weightmans, to reflect on what stood out. They highlighted a series of strategic questions that the legal profession is grappling with – although admittedly, answers are in many cases still elusive.

Advertisement

One of the themes to emerge at the conference was the growing maturity of but also tensions within discussions between law firms and clients around AI adoption.

According to Sheret, the most striking aspect of the event was hearing genuinely open conversations between private practice lawyers and clients about where AI can and should be used, and what trade-offs it creates.

“What surprised me was just how open and transparent it sounds like some of the profession is being, in terms of private practice conversations with clients about how and where to use AI,” Sheret observed. “I thought that was really refreshing because I’m in quite a lot of conversations around ‘we need to tell law firms how to use AI and this is what we want and we want lower prices.’ That’s just not going to help anybody. That’s such a destructive way of approaching it. I don’t agree with that at all. I could hear that there are clearly some great relationships and very honest conversations going on and an honest discussion about risk, which is basically what this all comes down to.

“If you want it cheaper, then you’re going to have to take more risk about there not being so much lawyer oversight.”

She added: “My take away building on that was how do we turn that into more of a broader discussion and sensible framework for how we do this.”

Legal training, meanwhile, may be the profession’s biggest unresolved challenge, and it was a topic that repeatedly surfaced throughout discussions at the conference.

Sheret observed that junior-lawyer development is a major concern, particularly if AI reduces opportunities for repetitive work that traditionally provided exposure to legal scenarios and client issues. She questioned whether simulation-based learning alone can replace years of real-world experience.

“We have a reasonably large team, but not large enough for us to build a training program,” she said.

Whittle argues that the traditional training model was not especially effective to begin with. Rather than lamenting the loss of repetitive tasks, he suggested there is an opportunity to create more deliberate, contextual learning experiences that integrate legal knowledge, technology skills, communication and client service. Effective lawyers, he argued, require far more than black-letter law expertise. You can watch Whittle’s video interview below for more reflections on that and many other topics raised at the conference.

What struck me most about the reflections from Beacon Collective was that the biggest takeaways were not technological. The most valuable discussions focus on difficult strategic questions: how lawyers will be trained, how risk will be shared, how legal services will be priced, how governance will operate and whether the profession’s longstanding business models are finally approaching a tipping point. Well done to Folkes and all of the speakers and attendees for a lively debate that shows at the end of the day, we all (myself included) love the sound of our own voice.

See below my video interview with Whittle for more insights into the conference discussions.

caroline@legaltechnology.com

news.titleEn: Freedom, AI and security: Are law firms able to enable innovation without losing control?
news.titleZh: 自由、AI与安全：律师事务所能否在推动创新的同时不失去控制？
news.summaryZh: 律师如今期望能够随时随地工作、即时获取信息、无缝协作，并利用AI工具提高工作效率。然而，对于负责保护律所的安全团队而言，这种自由带来了截然不同的挑战。敏感客户信息现在已远超传统网络边界被访问，AI在数据治理、所有权和风险方面引发了新的问题。同时，安全负责人面临压力，既要提供更强的保护，又不能妨碍生产力。Legal IT Insider联合BlueFort Security和iboss将于10月22日举办深入讨论，探讨各组织应对新挑战的最佳实践方法。讨论将聚焦领先法律机构如何重新思考安全策略，以适应用户、应用和数据无处不在的世界。AI的采用速度远超治理，因此关键在于如何重新掌控治理，讨论将涉及传统安全、数据主权以及零信任的局限性。许多公司和律所并不清楚什么是可能的，这是大问题，强调不应盲目跟风。主要讨论点包括：确保律师在办公室、家中或客户处都能获得一致保护的安全远程工作；在保护敏感客户和企业信息的同时支持AI计划的安全采用与治理；超越传统安全，减少复杂性和淘汰为旧边界设计的基础设施；数据主权与控制，了解敏感数据的处理、存储和保护地点；零信任实践，控制用户、应用和数据所在位置的访问；以及从已完成转型的法律组织获取实际经验，了解哪些做法有效、哪些无效以及他们会采取哪些不同措施。
news.bodyHtml:
Lawyers today expect the freedom to work from anywhere, access information instantly, collaborate seamlessly and take advantage of AI-powered tools that help them work faster and smarter.

For the security teams responsible for protecting the firm, that freedom brings a very different challenge.

Advertisement

Sensitive client information is now accessed far beyond the traditional network perimeter. AI is creating new questions around data governance, ownership and risk. At the same time, security leaders are under pressure to deliver stronger protection without creating barriers to productivity.

Join Legal IT Insider, BlueFort Security and iboss on 22 October for an in-depth discussion on the best practice approaches that organisations are taking to rise to new challenges. How are leading legal organisations rethinking security for a world where users, applications and data can be anywhere?

Advertisement

We’ll be joined by Bluefort chief technology officer Josh Neame, who says: “Adoption is hugely outpacing any kind of governance right now, so it’s a case of how do you claw the governance back? We’ll be looking at legacy security, data sovereignty, and the limitations of zero trust – don’t berate me for saying this, but it’s a wishy-washy term.”

We’ll also be joined by Simon Eappariello, SVP EMEA and APJ at iboss (who many years ago was systems manager at Richards Butler) who says: “A lot of companies and firms don’t know what is and isn’t possible. That’s the big problem. What is achievable? Things are moving so fast and it’s important not to just jump on the bandwagon.”

Key discussion points
– Secure work from anywhere: delivering consistent protection whether lawyers are in the office, at home or with clients.
– Safe AI adoption and governance: enabling AI initiatives while protecting sensitive client and corporate information.
– Moving beyond legacy security: reducing complexity and eliminating infrastructure designed for yesterday’s perimeter.
– Data sovereignty and control: understanding where sensitive data is processed, stored and protected.
– Zero Trust in practice: controlling access wherever users, applications and data reside.
– Practical lessons from legal organisations that have already made this transition and learn what worked, what didn’t, and what they would do differently.

Thursday 22nd October 2026
3:00pm – 3:45pm BST
Reserve Your Free Spot HERE

news.titleEn: Relativity CEO Says 2028 Server Deadline Stands; Will Prioritize Partnering with Frontier Labs Over Legal AI Companies
news.titleZh: Relativity CEO称2028年服务器迁移截止日期不变；将优先与前沿实验室合作而非法律AI公司
news.summaryZh: 公司坚持要求所有新案件自2028年1月1日起托管在云端，并警告未合作的伙伴：“要知道我们会从你身上碾过去。”这一表态是在芝加哥Relativity Fest最后一天的媒体简报会上作出的，他与7月被任命为总裁的Chris Brown共同回答了记者提问。当被问及公司是否坚持2025年1月宣布的截止日期时，Saunders迅速回答“是的”。他解释，政策并非终止Server的生命，而是确保自1月1日起没有净新案件进入Server。Saunders本周早些时候在面向数百名合作伙伴的简报会上传达了相同信息。他将合作伙伴分为三类：第一类“高度一致”，已将新工作区和数据迁移至云端，采用公司AI能力并与Relativity合作服务终端客户；另一极端是“不一致”的伙伴，其商业模式基于购买Server作为资本支出并随时间折旧；中间是“混合型”伙伴。忽视截止日期的伙伴是在服务自己的利益而非终端客户，并指出Relativity从云端赚取的利润远低于Server，但重要的是自我颠覆以适应市场和业务发展方向。对于犹豫不决的伙伴，Relativity已预算“积分、资金和努力”帮助其从资本支出模式转向运营支出模式。他强调“一致的伙伴将获胜，不一致的伙伴——我们谈谈吧”。
news.bodyHtml:
Relativity is holding firm on its plan to require that all new matters be hosted in the cloud beginning Jan. 1, 2028, CEO Phil Saunders said Thursday, and he had a blunt message for partners who are not on board: “Know we’re going to run through you.”

Saunders made the comments during a media briefing on the last day of Relativity Fest in Chicago, where he and Chris Brown, who was named president in July, took questions from reporters.

Asked by me whether the company is sticking to the deadline it announced in January 2025 to require that all new matters be hosted on its cloud platform rather than its legacy Relativity Server, Saunders quickly answered, “Yes.”

“The policy is not to end the life of Server,” he said. “The policy is to make sure that no net new matter is going to Server effective Jan. 1.”

Three Buckets of Partners

Saunders said he delivered the same message earlier in the week at a briefing for several hundred of the company’s partners – the companies and consultants who are central to distributing and implementing Relativity for legal, investigative and compliance teams.

He described partners as falling into three buckets. The first are “super duper aligned,” already sending new workspaces and data to the cloud, adopting the company’s AI capabilities, and collaborating with Relativity on the end customer.

At the other extreme, he said, there are some that are “just not aligned.” He attributed that to business models built around buying Server as a capital expense and depreciating it over time.

In between are those “we would politely call hybrids,” doing some of both. “We don’t blame them for that,” he said, noting that many of their customers remain on Server.

Saunders said partners that ignore the deadline are serving their own pockets, not the end customer. He said that even Relativity earns less from the cloud.

“We make a lot less money on Relativity aiR than we do on Server, like a lot less,” he said. “But it doesn’t matter. It’s about disrupting yourself to service where the market and business is going.”

For partners on the fence, he said, Relativity has budgeted “credits and money and effort” to help them move from a capital-expense to an operating-expense model.

“The aligned partners are going to win,” he said, “and the non-aligned partners – let’s talk about it.”

Saunders said that as of the end of June, nearly 84% of the company’s annual recurring revenue was in Relativity aiR, the name the company recently gave its cloud platform, formerly RelativityOne.

When it announced the deadline in January 2025, the company put the figure at more than 75%. 

Frontier Labs Before Harvey and Legora

Saunders also said Relativity is prioritizing partnerships with the frontier AI labs over integrations with legal AI companies such as Harvey and Legora.

A reporter at the briefing, Stephanie Wilkins, director of content at Legaltech Hub, brought up the fact that at last year’s briefing, Saunders said he was in conversations with the founders of both companies. Those conversations continue, he replied, but the priority lies elsewhere.

“Our strategy, at least at this point, is to spend a lot of time with the frontier models,” he said, citing Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. “It doesn’t mean that we wouldn’t consider Harvey or Legora, but prioritization is probably at the frontier labs at this point.”

His reasoning is that corporate customers tell Relativity they run more than one frontier model, often alongside Harvey, Legora or both, and that the frontier labs are the surest to endure.

“I don’t think Harvey and Legora are going away anytime soon,” he said. “I think these are real valuable, high-performing companies.”

But he said Relativity expects there will be at least one frontier model “on the desktop of every law firm, of every company on the planet that we serve.”

Brown added that has been the plan all along. “That really has been our intent, to go to the frontier models, frontier labs first,” he said.

In 2027, Brown said, Relativity will make matter intelligence available through its MCP connector, so that an authorized user working in a tool such as Claude could query a matter as they would inside Relativity.

Saunders said the first job, however, is getting claiR, the company’s conversational AI interface, right as a native experience.

“If we don’t get that right, how we surface it up in other locations won’t matter,” he said. “It’ll be just a mediocre offering.” 

Gavel Integration Coming This Year

Asked about the integration of Gavel, the document automation company Relativity acquired in June, Brown said it will enter the company’s advanced access program this year.

“Gavel’s going into advanced access momentarily,” he said. “I can’t give you a date specifically, but it’ll be this year.”

Brown described the goal as keeping work product connected to the evidence. A lawyer who builds a deposition outline tied to specific documents should be able to open it in Word, share it with collaborators and have redlines sync back, he said.

He suggested the approach could extend beyond Word to Excel and other tools, and said customers have asked him about trial preparation.

Saunders said Gavel’s chief technology officer, Pierre Martin, “has taken on a much bigger role here at Relativity.”

“It’s more than just good tech,” Saunders said. “It’s good people.”

‘Not Out Here to Flip This Company’

Although a company spokesperson opened the briefing by saying executives could not discuss Relativity’s confidential IPO filing, Saunders addressed it anyway.

He said the company publicly confirmed the filing only because Bloomberg had reported it, and that the announcement did not signal the company is for sale.

“We’re not out here to flip this company,” he said. “We’re out here to build a really great company.”

He said there is no concrete timeline. “The market is a really unstable thing, and maybe one day when that settles out, something will happen,” he said.

Saunders said that Silver Lake continues to own the largest share of the company, although still a minority investor. Founder Andrew Sieja and investor ICONIQ each own nearly 25%, and every employee holds equity.

Other News from the Briefing

Among other news that came out of the briefing:

  • R&D spending. Saunders said Relativity reinvests more than $200 million a year in research and development, which he said is a greater percentage of revenue than most companies. “Probably not allowed to say this, but we’re over budget this year and the board says keep on going,” he said. The spending goes, in order, to the core platform, aiR and claiR.
  • Where it won’t go. Asked where the company draws its boundaries, Saunders said, “We’re not interested in being the Swiss Army knife for law.” Transactional law, he said, is probably not an area where Relativity will spend much time.
  • Legal authority. Brown said Relativity is exploring bringing outside sources such as regulations and legal research into the platform to add context to matter work, but has not settled on an approach.
  • KPMG. Brown confirmed that KPMG is the first Big Four firm in the claiR advanced access program. Saunders said KPMG represents Relativity’s platform in 22 countries.
  • Singapore. Brown said the company expects to announce an opening in Singapore next month.

news.titleEn: Startup Corner: Notorio – One place to organise your legal business
news.titleZh: 创业角：Notorio——一站式管理你的法律业务
news.summaryZh: 由Leonardo Lupiano和Rhet Porter创立的Notorio，瞄准法律科技市场的一个空白，提供一个平台，帮助创始人组织和管理公司的法律基础设施。从合规和企业记录到股权表管理和AI辅助指导，这家初创公司旨在成为企业的一站式中心，特别是那些在美国建立业务的国际创始人。经营一家公司会产生大量法律事务，如公司文件、所有权记录、合规截止日期、协议等重要信息，往往分散在收件箱、文件夹和电子表格中。Notorio为创始人提供一个集中管理法律事务的地方，并让他们知道哪些事项需要关注。Notorio是一个以创始人为先的法律科技平台，用于管理公司的法律基础设施。它将结构化公司数据、文件管理、合规工作流、股权表和所有权信息、自动化以及AI驱动的审查和指导整合在一个环境中。其理念是，当这些功能共享相同的公司数据时，它们能更好地协同工作。Notorio不是将文件、所有权变更或合规义务视为孤立事件，而是将这些信息在公司内部连接起来，帮助创始人了解现有内容、可能缺失的内容以及下一步需要采取的行动。Notorio于2025年6月由Leonardo Lupiano创立，Rhet S. Porter随后不久加入并成为联合创始人。两人是在一家初创孵化器工作时认识的，在那里他们接触了早期公司以及创始人成长过程中面临的挑战。
news.bodyHtml:
Founded by Leonardo Lupiano and Rhet Porter, Notorio is targeting a gap in the legal tech market with a platform that helps founders organise and manage their company’s legal infrastructure. From compliance and corporate records to cap table management and AI-assisted guidance, the startup aims to become a one-stop hub for businesses, particularly international founders establishing a presence in the United States.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Running a company creates a surprising amount of legal housekeeping. Corporate documents, ownership records, compliance deadlines, agreements and other important information often end up spread across inboxes, folders and spreadsheets.

Advertisement

Notorio gives founders one place to keep the legal side of their business organized and know what needs their attention.

And to a techy?

Notorio is a founder-first legal technology platform for managing a company’s legal infrastructure.

Advertisement

It combines structured company data, document management, compliance workflows, cap table and ownership information, automation, and AI-powered review and guidance in one environment.

The idea is that these functions work better when they share the same company data. Instead of treating a document, ownership change or compliance obligation as an isolated event, Notorio can connect that information across the company and help the founder understand what is there, what may be missing and what needs to happen next.

When were you founded?

June 2025.

By who?

Notorio was founded by Leonardo Lupiano in June 2025. Rhet S. Porter became involved shortly afterward and joined as co-founder.

The two had met while working at a startup incubator, where they were exposed to early-stage companies and the challenges founders face as they grow.

 

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Leonardo Lupiano and Rhet S. Porter, co-founders.

Leonardo founded Notorio after working in the startup ecosystem and seeing how fragmented the legal and corporate side of running a company could become. He has a background in startups, business and technology and is currently attending law school, where his interest in legal technology and corporate law has continued to shape the platform.

Rhet became involved shortly after Notorio was founded. He has a background in finance and has built and operated companies across multiple industries, including construction and education.

They are supported by a board that includes attorneys, founders and business leaders with experience across law, technology and entrepreneurship.

Who are your target clients?

Founders and business owners.

A lot of legal technology is built for the lawyer. Notorio approaches the relationship from the other side, focusing on the person actually running the company and trying to keep its legal infrastructure in order.

The platform has a particular focus on international founders who want to enter the U.S. market or establish a credible U.S. presence as they take their companies global.

Creating the entity is the easy part. After that comes ownership, corporate records, compliance, agreements, filings and the ongoing work of maintaining a real U.S. business. For a founder doing that from another country, the process can become fragmented very quickly.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Start with the legal infrastructure every company needs, then become more valuable as the company grows.

A founder may initially come to Notorio to organize corporate records or manage compliance. As the business develops, the same platform can support ownership and cap table management, governance, documents, compliance workflows and other recurring legal and administrative needs.

A major part of that growth strategy is deeper AI integration throughout the platform. Rather than treating AI as a standalone chatbot that generates or reviews agreements, Notorio is being designed to work with a company’s actual records and workflows. That includes helping founders review documents, identify missing information, understand compliance obligations, manage corporate records and work with cap table and ownership data more intelligently.

International expansion is also an important part of the strategy. Notorio aims to become a natural starting point for foreign founders building a serious presence in the United States.

Partnerships are another important distribution channel, particularly with startup incubators, accelerators, universities, professional organizations and other institutions that already support founders. The goal is to put Notorio in front of businesses at the stage when they are beginning to formalize their legal and corporate infrastructure.

Key achievements?

Building traction in legal tech without outside capital.

Notorio has grown from an idea founded by Leonardo Lupiano into a working legal technology platform with paying customers, with Rhet Porter joining shortly after its founding as co-founder. Together, they have built and iterated on the core platform themselves, allowing Notorio to stay lean and develop the product without raising outside capital to fund engineering.

Notorio has also started gaining recognition within the legal technology industry. In September 2026, Law360 published a Legal Tech Talks feature by Leonardo discussing Notorio’s origins and the challenges of building and evaluating legal technology.

Have you received investment?

No outside investment.

Notorio has been funded by its co-founders and supported by customer revenue. Building the platform in-house has allowed the company to stay lean and continue developing the product without relying on external capital.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

Yes, but the underlying problem has stayed the same.

The original idea was much closer to incorporation services. While exploring that market, the founders realized that incorporation is a relatively small moment in the life of a company. The harder problem is everything that comes after it.

Companies have to maintain corporate records, track ownership, manage documents, meet compliance obligations and keep their legal information organized for years. That shifted Notorio from helping create a company to helping manage the legal infrastructure behind one.

That realization became the foundation for the platform Notorio is building today.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Trust and clarity.

Legal technology has historically been built primarily around lawyers and law firms. Notorio approaches the problem from the business owner’s perspective, which means making sophisticated corporate and legal processes understandable and useful to founders who may not have legal training.

The challenge is giving founders better tools to stay organized, understand what requires attention and manage more of their company’s legal infrastructure without creating the impression that technology replaces professional legal advice.

As AI becomes more capable, that balance becomes even more important. The opportunity is to use technology to make founders better informed and better prepared while preserving the role of attorneys where legal judgment is needed.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company? 

Leonardo is originally from São Paulo, Brazil, and moved to the United States before founding Notorio. Rhet grew up in rural Utah, giving the company two very different founder perspectives.

Leonardo’s experience building a career and starting a company in a new country gave him firsthand exposure to some of the practical challenges founders face when trying to establish themselves in the U.S. That perspective helped shape Notorio’s focus on international founders and its goal of making it easier for entrepreneurs from abroad to build and manage a credible U.S. business presence.

news.titleEn: ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 finds DDoS leads incident counts while ransomware stays most impactful in the short term
news.titleZh: ENISA 2026年威胁态势报告：DDoS攻击数量居首，勒索软件短期影响最大
news.summaryZh: 欧盟网络安全局（ENISA）于9月22日发布《ENISA威胁态势2026》报告，分析了2025年全年记录的8257起事件。分布式拒绝服务（DDoS）攻击占事件总数的51.3%，但短期影响最大的威胁来自以勒索软件为首的财务动机攻击。ENISA警告，网络依赖关系扩大了攻击面，供应链、第三方供应商和云环境中的妥协在2025年持续引发大规模、高影响事件。报告将大部分事件描述为低影响且短暂，而真正导致泄露通知和法律保留的暴露往往集中在较小的财务动机类别中。意识形态驱动的事件占57.3%，财务动机占29.3%，网络间谍占5.9%。其中，亲俄组织NoName057(16)占意识形态活动的48%，但经独立第三方可用性检查，仅23.8%的声明得到证实，部分声明可能旨在夸大运营影响。报告还提到，网络间谍是长期更具影响力的威胁，且间谍活动通常在发生后六个月至四年以上才被曝光。由于收集范围扩大，事件数量从上一版的4875起增至8257起，并非直接可比。2026年人工智能可能使更多攻击阶段自动化，并提醒引用时应以报告原文为准，而非新闻稿中的数字。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: Ransomware and supplier compromises, not the DDoS attacks that make up most of the count, are where the ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 places the short-term impact, while cyberespionage remains the agency’s longer-term concern. The EU cybersecurity agency analyzed 8,257 incidents from 2025 and found financially motivated attacks remained the most impactful threat in the short term, and its review of ransomware techniques likely confirms a tilt toward data theft and extortion.

For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery professionals, that shift makes data maps, retention schedules and vendor contracts part of incident response, and ENISA’s caution that forum breach listings could not be verified bears directly on notification decisions. The report also arrives as Cyber Resilience Act reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities takes hold. One practical point: several figures in ENISA’s Sept. 22 press release differ from the report, so the report is the version to cite.

Watch for whether ENISA’s expectation that AI will likely enable more stages of attacks in 2026 shows up in incident data.

News Analysis – Cybersecurity Beat

ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 finds DDoS leads incident counts while ransomware stays most impactful in the short term

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

Distributed denial-of-service attacks made up just over half of the 8,257 incidents the EU cybersecurity agency ENISA analyzed for 2025, but its newest threat report says the activity with the most impact came from elsewhere.

Financially motivated attacks, ransomware above all, remained the most impactful threat to organizations in the short term, the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity said in the ENISA Threat Landscape 2026, published Sept. 22. The agency’s announcement led with a related warning: cyber dependencies “expand the attack surface,” it said, and require “a new level of vigilance.” The report ties those dependencies to supply chains, third-party providers and cloud environments, whose compromise kept producing large-scale, impactful incidents during 2025.

That pairing matters for cybersecurity, information governance and eDiscovery practitioners, because it separates the activity that fills the charts from the activity ENISA ties to disruption and data loss. ENISA describes most of that volume as low-impact and short-lived. The exposure that reaches breach notices and legal holds tends to sit in the smaller financially motivated categories, the ones ENISA ranks as most impactful in the short term. Before anyone repeats the report’s totals, though, its own caveats deserve a close read.

What 8,257 incidents can and cannot tell you

ENISA built the 101-page report from incidents recorded between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2025, drawing mainly on open sources plus anonymized data from EU member states and from participants in the agency’s Cyber Partnership Programme. This edition moved to a calendar year, so its period overlaps the previous edition by six months. ENISA also widened the cybercrime activity it tracks, including data breaches and fraud, and said that change affected the numbers without substantially changing the trends or rankings.

Those design choices matter for anyone tempted to compare totals across years. The 2025 edition analyzed 4,875 incidents from July 2024 through June 2025, according to ENISA’s publication listing. Because collection expanded between editions, the rise to 8,257 is not a like-for-like measure of more attacks. ENISA calls the report a snapshot of prevailing trends, and it warns that espionage campaigns typically come to light six months to over four years after they occur. Heavier reporting on a threat, the agency added, can reflect audience interest rather than a faster tempo of activity.

Noise at volume, impact elsewhere

Those caveats shape how the headline split should be read. By ENISA’s classification of assessed objectives, ideology-driven activity accounted for 57.3 percent of incidents, financially motivated activity for 29.3 percent and cyberespionage for 5.9 percent. DDoS led incident types at 51.3 percent, followed by unauthorized access at 39.5 percent. ENISA said the ideology-driven claims, though the most numerous, produced no large-scale impact, and its methodology section calls cyberespionage “a more impactful threat in the long term.”

The agency counted 4,709 claims by hacktivists against EU member states, and over 89 percent of them involved DDoS. The pro-Russia group NoName057(16) alone accounted for 48 percent of ideology-driven activity. ENISA’s own analysis tempers those totals. When the agency examined NoName057(16) activity from July through November 2025, only 23.8 percent of the claims it assessed held up against independent third-party availability checks. ENISA said the gap suggests some claims “may have served an influence objective by inflating perceptions of operational impact.”

Public administration remained the most targeted sector at 31.8 percent of recorded events, and ideology-driven DDoS made up 81.8 percent of incidents in that sector. Essential and important entities under the NIS2 Directive represented 73 percent of recorded events, which ENISA, an agency that publishes NIS2 implementation guidance, said confirms the relevance of the directive’s approach. Member-state reporting under NIS2 paints a somewhat different picture. Of the 1,954 events member states had reported under the directive as of July 14, 2026, the top five sectors for 2025 included health and digital infrastructure, a gap ENISA traced to differences in scope, thresholds and reporting conditions.

Claimed attacks on operational technology deserve the same skepticism. Such claims rose from 37 in the third quarter to 124 in the fourth, yet most named neither the techniques used nor the affected entities. ENISA assesses that these claims will likely keep rising while confirmed incidents with operational impact will likely remain stable.

Why ENISA sees ransomware tilting toward data theft

The short-term impact, by ENISA’s account, sits in those financially motivated categories. Ransomware made up 47.3 percent of financially motivated claims, data breaches 36 percent and fraud and impersonation 13.3 percent. Manufacturing absorbed the largest share of ransomware claims at 25.2 percent, and Germany led member states in ransomware claims at 26.5 percent. Qilin, SafePay, Akira, INC Ransom and Hunters International were the most active operators in the EU.

The technique data is where information governance teams should look hardest. In ENISA’s analysis of publicly reported techniques used by the most active operators, exfiltration over command-and-control channels represented 73.3 percent, while data encryption for impact represented 13.7 percent. ENISA said the split likely confirms a wider move away from encryption and toward data exfiltration and extortion. When an attack steals before it locks, every unmapped file share and over-retained mailbox becomes potential notification exposure, so data maps and retention schedules belong in incident planning rather than only in compliance binders.

The report also describes Qilin adding a “call lawyer” feature that mimics legal escalation to pressure victims. ENISA said the tactic carries extra weight in the EU, where incident-reporting rules and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) duties likely push victims toward paying to protect their reputations. Thirty-three EU organizations were identified as targets of repeat victimization, with ransomware accounting for 44 percent of that activity and data breaches for 40 percent. ENISA judged it likely that some of that activity was operationally linked, and that a lack of restoration practices after incident response enabled the repeated targeting.

Breach claims need verification before they drive decisions. ENISA’s data breach analysis rests on listings offering stolen data on criminal forums, and the agency said it could not verify whether those listings were authentic or current. The forum darkforums.st alone accounted for 58 percent of those claims. Legal and privacy teams weighing notification obligations after a forum listing should confirm what data, if any, actually left their environment before treating the listing as fact.

When the supplier becomes the way in

That verification burden grows when the breach happens at someone else’s company. Cybercriminals went after third-party providers more often, ENISA said, highly likely as a way to make their attacks more efficient, and adversaries compromised software, repositories and browser extensions. The report flags a rise in compromised libraries and npm packages, citing the Shai-Hulud campaign, and notes that ENISA issued a technical advisory on using package managers securely in March 2026.

The examples are concrete. In September 2025, according to the report, a ransomware incident affecting U.S.-based Collins Aerospace’s passenger-processing software disrupted automated check-in at several airports in the EU, among them Brussels and Berlin. A ransomware attack on a Swedish IT supplier affected about 200 municipalities and regional authorities. The report traces the data-theft group ShinyHunters across the full attack chain. It typically got in by phoning staff while posing as IT support to collect single sign-on credentials and multifactor codes, and its activity reached Salesforce, Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Slack and Google BigQuery environments.

For legal and compliance teams, that pattern argues for an inventory of which vendors hold which data and under what access, plus contract terms that require prompt notice when a supplier is compromised. Revoking stale OAuth tokens and limiting standing access between software-as-a-service platforms costs little next to an exfiltration that runs through a trusted integration.

Where ENISA expects AI to go next

Attackers in 2025 relied mostly on off-the-shelf consumer AI tools to sharpen skills they already had, according to the report, not to gain breakthrough capabilities. ENISA expects that to change. The agency assessed it is likely that 2026 will bring more stages of the attack chain enabled directly by AI, possibly including experiments with human-out-of-the-loop proofs of concept. It also warned that AI applications are becoming targets themselves, particularly those that can reach files, credentials, browser sessions or development environments.

AI use is already measurable in information manipulation. The European External Action Service, whose data ENISA used for its foreign information manipulation chapter, detected 540 incidents in 2025, and 27 percent involved AI-related techniques, with such cases rising from 41 in 2024 to 147.

Read the release with the report open

Practitioners who cite ENISA’s figures should take them from the report rather than the announcement. In its analysis by threat categories, the Sept. 22 release says cybercrime covered 36 percent of total events and lists ransomware deployment at 40 percent “of all analysed events,” followed by data breaches at 31 percent and fraud and impersonation at 19 percent. The report’s cybercrime chapter and its charts put cybercrime at 29.3 percent of events and give ransomware, data breaches and fraud as 47.3, 36 and 13.3 percent of financially motivated claims. The release also says state-nexus groups mostly carried out intrusion operations, at 87 percent, where the report’s corresponding sentence gives unauthorized access at 81.7 percent. The release does not explain the differences, and elsewhere it says almost 30 percent of incidents were financially motivated, consistent with the report.

Other headline figures line up. Over 48,000 new vulnerabilities received Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers in 2025, a 22 percent increase from the year before, and in November 2025 ENISA became a root within the CVE program, the system that assigns those identifiers. In unauthorized-access incidents where ENISA could identify an intrusion vector, 60.4 percent involved exploiting a vulnerability. That figure rests on a narrow base. The report puts the incidents with an identifiable vector at 5.2 percent, so the share describes the cases ENISA could see into rather than all unauthorized access.

The vulnerability numbers arrive as a new reporting duty takes hold. Since Sept. 11, 2026, manufacturers have been required under the Cyber Resilience Act to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting the security of their products. Those notifications go through a single reporting platform to the computer security incident response team in the member state where the manufacturer has its main establishment. The information reaches ENISA at the same time unless particularly exceptional circumstances apply, according to the European Commission.

“The analysis highlights how threats become more interconnected and how threat groups spread their impact across the larger map of digital services and infrastructures,” ENISA Executive Director Juhan Lepassaar said in the release.

If ENISA is right that the chances to reach many victims through a single supplier compromise are likely to grow, how many legal and governance teams could say today which of their vendors would be first to tell them?
