news.titleEn: Clio buys Learned Hand as judiciary strategy takes shape
news.titleZh: Clio收购Learned Hand，司法领域战略布局成形
news.summaryZh: 法律科技公司Clio于9月30日宣布收购Learned Hand，这是一家专门为法官和法院开发技术的人工智能公司。此次收购标志着Clio首次直接进军司法领域，此前该公司在8月聘请了Casetext联合创始人Pablo Arredondo担任司法部门高级副总裁，并在9月聘请了前密歇根州最高法院首席法官Bridget Mary McCormack担任司法部门总经理。AI正在改变整个法律体系中法律工作的速度和规模，但只有法院能够跟上，这种进步才有意义；如果律师和诉讼当事人速度大幅加快，而法官和法院团队仍受制于同样的能力，瓶颈就会转移到法院。Clio花了近二十年时间构建连接法律体系的技术、法律数据和基础设施，Learned Hand使其能够将这一基础直接带入司法部门，帮助建立更强大、更现代、更有韧性的法院。Learned Hand为法官和书记员构建了一个AI工作空间，可连接法院案件管理系统，帮助他们了解案件、处理文件和争议问题、进行法律研究，并准备符合各案件程序要求的庭审备忘录和命令草稿。Learned Hand的技术已被美国多家法院使用，包括全国最大的审判法院洛杉矶县高等法院。他们创建Learned Hand是因为法官和书记员需要围绕司法工作现实构建的技术，特别是在案件数量和复杂性持续增长的情况下；他们有幸与法官一起构建技术，并了解技术如何在法庭上赢得一席之地。此次收购将Learned Hand与Clio的法律和法院数据相结合，Learned Hand将成为Clio司法业务的一部分，并构成其法院产品的基础。Clio表示将继续支持Learned Hand现有的部署和试点，同时投资于其技术和团队。
news.bodyHtml:
Clio today (30 September) announced the acquisition of Learned Hand, an AI company building technology specifically for judges and courts. The acquisition marks Clio’s first direct expansion into the judiciary, following the hire in August of Pablo Arredondo, co-founder of Casetext, as senior vice president, judiciary and in September of former Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Bridget Mary McCormack as general manager, judiciary.

“AI is changing the pace and volume of legal work across the entire system, but that progress only matters if the courts can keep up,” said Jack Newton, CEO and founder of Clio. “If lawyers and litigants can move dramatically faster while judges and court teams remain constrained by the same capacity, the bottleneck simply shifts to the courts. We have spent nearly two decades building the technology, legal data, and infrastructure that connect the legal system. Learned Hand gives us the opportunity to bring that foundation directly into the judiciary and help build courts that are as capable, modern, and resilient as the legal system around them increasingly demands.”

Learned Hand has built an AI workspace for judges and clerks that connects with court case management systems and helps them understand the matters before them, work through filings and disputed issues, conduct legal research, and prepare bench memoranda and draft orders tailored to the procedural requirements of each matter.

Learned Hand’s technology is already being used by courts across the United States, including the Superior Court of Los Angeles County, the nation’s largest trial court.

Advertisement

“We started Learned Hand because judges and clerks needed technology built around the realities of judicial work, especially as the volume and complexity of matters continued to grow,” said Klapper. “We’ve had the privilege of building alongside judges and learning what it takes for technology to earn a place in the courtroom. With Clio, we can take everything we’ve learned and built for the judiciary at a scale this opportunity deserves.”

The acquisition brings Learned Hand together with Clio’s legal and court data. Learned Hand will become part of Clio’s judiciary business and form the foundation of its products for courts. Clio says that it will continue supporting Learned Hand’s existing deployments and pilots while investing in its technology and team.

news.titleEn: The Board Director’s Playbook—Responsible Director Use of Artificial Intelligence
news.titleZh: 董事会董事手册——董事负责任地使用人工智能
news.summaryZh: 人工智能正从企业运营进入董事会，帮助董事研究、起草、总结和检验假设，但这种便利带来治理成本：一次提示可能泄露重大非公开信息和受特权保护的通信，而流畅但实质错误的回答可能影响董事会决策。本手册聚焦董事自身对AI的使用，而非管理层的企业AI项目，为董事提供知情、安全、可审查和坦诚的实用框架。AI已成为日常治理工作的一部分，包括准备会议、组织尽职调查、检验假设、比较情景、起草问题和审查公开信息。它能提高效率，但也增加受托责任、保密、披露、特权、网络安全和记录保存风险，因为提示本身可能包含公司须保护的信息。基本原则是：AI可辅助董事准备，但不能替代董事的判断、保密义务或充分知悉的责任。特拉华州法律将公司业务和事务置于董事会指导下（8 Del. C. § 141(a)），并在满足法定条件时保护对公司记录和适当信息、意见、报告或陈述的善意依赖（8 Del. C. § 141(e)）。目标不是禁止有用工具，而是将其视为受控的董事会工具，而非保密顾问、独立专家、法律顾问替代品或隐形董事会成员。以下假设案例说明董事使用AI最常见的风险：Sam是特拉华州公司ABC（纽交所上市）的独立董事，ABC正评估收购一家竞争对手，该交易尚未公开。董事会审查包括竞争对手身份、估值和融资假设、管理层预测、谈判状态、尽职调查结果和潜在时间等详细信息，这些信息属保密且包含重大非公开信息。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from the enterprise into the boardroom — helping directors research, draft, summarize, and test assumptions. That convenience carries a governance cost: a single prompt can expose material nonpublic information and privileged communications, and a fluent answer that is materially wrong can influence board decision-making. This playbook focuses on directors’ own use of AI, not management’s enterprise AI program, and provides directors with a practical framework for use that is informed, secure, reviewable, and candid. AI is now part of ordinary governance work: preparing for meetings, organizing diligence, testing assumptions, comparing scenarios, drafting questions, and reviewing public information. It can increase efficiency, but it also adds fiduciary, confidentiality, disclosure, privilege, cybersecurity, and recordkeeping risk because the prompt itself may contain information the company must protect. The governing principle is simple: AI may assist a director’s preparation, but it cannot replace the director’s judgment, confidentiality obligations, or duty to become adequately informed. Delaware law places the corporation’s business and affairs under the board’s direction, 8 Del. C. § 141(a), and protects good-faith reliance on corporate records and appropriate information, opinions, reports, or statements when the statutory conditions in 8 Del. C. § 141(e) are met. The objective is not to ban useful tools but to treat them as controlled boardroom instruments — not confidential advisers, independent experts, substitutes for counsel, or invisible board members. The following hypothetical illustrates the most common risks posed by a director’s use of AI: Sam is an independent director of ABC, Inc., a Delaware corporation listed on the NYSE. ABC is evaluating a proposed acquisition of a competitor that is not yet public. The board is reviewing detailed information about the proposed acquisition, including the competitor’s identity, valuation and financing assumptions, management projections, negotiation status, diligence findings, and potential timing. The information is confidential and includes material nonpublic information about ABC and the proposed acquisition. While riding in an Uber to the board meeting, Sam wants to use AI to test his thinking before the discussion. The company-approved AI platform is unavailable on his phone, so he uses a personal ChatGPT account instead. He enters detailed information about ABC and the proposed acquisition — including the competitor’s identity, valuation, financing, projections, diligence, negotiations, and timing — and asks ChatGPT to identify the principal risks, assess whether the proposed acquisition appears justified, and recommend how he should approach the discussion. ChatGPT returns a confident but materially flawed analysis. It overlooks an important diligence concern, accepts a key transaction assumption without support, and gives Sam an overly reassuring conclusion about the proposed acquisition. Sam then quotes that conclusion during the board discussion without disclosing that it was AI-generated. During the board meeting, the board is informed of an anonymous complaint submitted through ABC’s whistleblower hotline alleging a material misstatement in ABC’s last earnings release. The board’s discussion includes speculation about the facts and who may be responsible. During the meeting, Sam utilizes an AI program to listen to the discussion and generate a summary after the meeting. After the meeting, Sam also uses ABC’s approved AI platform to generate an analysis of the relative strengths and weaknesses of ABC’s legal position based on the board’s discussion. Sam may believe he acted efficiently and in ABC’s interests. His conduct nevertheless creates three distinct, overlapping risks. First, he disclosed confidential information about the proposed acquisition to a personal ChatGPT account outside ABC’s controls. Second, he allowed a materially flawed AI output to influence the board process without verifying its assumptions or reliability. Third, he created exposure by entering and generating sensitive information about legal risk into an AI Platform that will be discoverable in litigation and by regulators, including the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Department of Justice (DOJ). The first risk implicates confidentiality, cybersecurity, and disclosure controls; the second implicates an informed and candid board process; and the third implicates privilege and discovery. The sections that follow address those risks in that order and then translate the lessons into policy and oversight rules. Sam’s disclosure of detailed information about ABC’s proposed acquisition into a personal ChatGPT account was not merely an informal use of a device. It placed ABC’s confidential information outside the approved platform and may have exposed it to retention, human access, model training, subprocessors, or a security incident. That creates confidentiality, contractual, cybersecurity, and disclosure-controls risk. ABC should assess the incident under its disclosure controls and procedures, including Exchange Act Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e), and under its incident-response process.

news.titleEn: Shanghai First Intermediate People’s Court Holds AI Voice-Cloning Platform Liable, Shifts Burden of Proof on Training Data
news.titleZh: 上海一中院判决AI语音克隆平台担责，将训练数据举证责任转移
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月29日，上海市第一中级人民法院对上海首例AI合成语音侵害自然人声音权案作出终审判决，确立了一项针对生成式AI训练数据不透明的侵权证明框架。原告王某为实名认证配音演员，在应用程序上发布作品并获取收入。2025年1月，她发现某公司A在互联网推广活动中使用了疑似AI合成其声音的音频，但从未授权。王某对争议音频进行公证并起诉，要求停止使用并索赔30万元。公司A承认音频由其AI系统生成，但声称因前员工离职无法核实训练材料来源。为完成举证，王某提交了司法声学比对报告，分析28项共振峰指标，其中24项偏差低于10%，总体相似度达90%。一审法院认定侵权成立，判决赔偿5万元。双方上诉后，二审法院驳回上诉，维持原判。二审法院明确，未经同意将自然人声音作为训练语料，生成可识别为该自然人的合成声音，即构成声音权侵权，无论算法如何。在举证责任上，原告只需证明被告获取其声音的合理途径及合成声音与原告声音高度相似，此后举证责任转移至被告，因其对训练数据具有排他控制权。公司A未能证明合法来源，承担不利后果。法院将分析焦点从训练数据转向输出可识别性，以应对生成式AI的“黑箱”问题。在损害赔偿方面，法院采用两步法：先参考可比许可费，若无则综合考量使用时长、传播范围、过错程度等因素。本案中合成声音仅短暂用于流程提示，且王某知名度有限，故维持5万元赔偿。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On September 29, 2026, the Shanghai First Intermediate People’s Court issued a final ruling addressing what is described as Shanghai’s first case concerning natural-person voice-rights protection arising from AI-synthesized speech. The case centers on the intersection of generative AI training practices and personality rights, and its principal contribution is an evidentiary framework for proving infringement when a plaintiff has no visibility into how a generative model was trained. Note though that this case has not been marked as typical or guiding at the time of writing and therefore may have minimal precedential value. The plaintiff, Ms. Wang, is a real-name-verified voice actor who performs and publishes work on an app, earning income from that activity. In January 2025, she learned that Company A had used what appeared to be an AI-synthesized version of her voice in an internet promotional campaign. She had never worked with or authorized Company A. She notarized the disputed audio and filed suit seeking cessation of use and RMB 300,000 in damages. Company A admitted the audio was generated by its own AI system but claimed it could not verify the specific training material or source because a former employee involved in that work had since left the company. It denied prior knowledge of Wang’s identity as a voice actor and argued there was no direct evidence that its training data included her voice. To meet her burden, Wang submitted a forensic acoustic comparison between the notarized disputed audio and a live-sampled reference of her own voice, analyzed across 28 formant acoustic indicators. The comparison found 24 of 28 indicators had deviation under 10%, 16 of those under 5.36%, and an overall similarity of 90% between the two voices. The first-instance court found that Company A’s conduct constituted AI-generated voice infringement causing economic loss and awarded RMB 50,000. Both sides appealed; the Shanghai First Intermediate Court affirmed, dismissing both appeals. The appellate court’s reasoning rests on a core substantive rule directly addressed to generative AI: using a natural person’s voice as training corpus, without consent, to generate a synthetic voice that mimics that person’s timbre, intonation, and pronunciation style – such that the output is recognizable as that person – constitutes infringement of voice rights, regardless of the algorithmic method used to produce the output. The court was explicit that the legal question is not how the training or generation process works technically, but whether the personality interest embodied in the voice has been appropriated in a recognizable way. The court’s more significant holding concerns how this is to be proven, given the structural information asymmetry inherent in generative AI. The plaintiff’s burden is met by showing (a) a plausible channel by which the defendant could have obtained her voice for training – here, her work was publicly posted and thus accessible as potential training data – and (b) that the resulting synthetic voice is highly similar to her own such that ordinary members of the public would associate the two. Once that showing is made, the burden shifts to the defendant, as the party with exclusive control over training data, model logs, and data-sourcing records, to prove either the lawful origin of its training material or that it did not in fact use the plaintiff’s voice characteristics. Company A’s claim that records were unavailable due to staff turnover did not satisfy this burden, and it bore the adverse consequences of that failure of proof. The court framed this explicitly as a shift in analytical focus for generative AI personality-rights cases: away from requiring proof of what specific data trained the model (something plaintiffs structurally cannot access) and toward whether the output is recognizable as the plaintiff (something that can be established through forensic comparison of the generated content itself). This reframing is presented as a response to the “black box” problem of generative AI – where the training corpus, weights, and generation logic are opaque to anyone outside the entity operating the model. On damages, the court applied a two-step approach relevant to voice used as training data and later monetized: first, look to a comparable licensing fee for use of the plaintiff’s voice, if provable; absent that, weigh factors including duration of the infringing use, scope of dissemination, manner of use, degree of fault, resulting harm, and the proportional contribution of the personality element to commercial value. Here, the synthetic voice was used briefly as a process/notification prompt rather than as a core commercial asset, and Wang’s own public profile and market activity were modest, which the court treated as limiting the independent commercial value of her voice for damages purposes. The RMB 50,000 award was upheld on that basis. For comparison, the Beijing Internet Court’s April 2024 decision – reported as the first case nationwide on AI-generated voice personality-rights infringement – had already established that voice rights under Civil Code Article 1023 extend to AI-generated voice where the output is recognizable, and that authorization to use a sound recording (e.g., under copyright) does not itself confer authorization to use the underlying voice as material for AI training or synthesis. Beijing’s facts involved a traceable commercial chain from original recording to licensed data transfer to AI product, so the case did not need to resolve how a plaintiff proves unauthorized training use when that chain is not documented or disclosed. Shanghai’s ruling takes up that gap directly, and expressly ties its reasoning to Article 4 of the Supreme People’s Court’s September 2026 Opinions on AI-related disputes, suggesting this burden-shifting approach to training-data opacity is intended to have broader application in future generative AI personality-rights cases.

news.summaryZh: 第三巡回上诉法院就版权法、法律出版与人工智能交叉领域作出重要上诉裁决，确认汤森路透对罗斯智能公司的胜诉，认定罗斯侵犯了Westlaw的判例摘要，且不能以合理使用作为抗辩。该裁决对法律界意义重大，不仅限于这一长期争议。它强化了在公共法律材料基础上构建的编辑内容仍可获得实质性版权保护。虽然司法意见本身不受版权保护，但法律出版商对该法律体系进行组织、总结和添加编辑分析的方式可以受到保护。这一区别在法律研究市场一直很重要，在人工智能时代更加重要。
news.bodyText:
Third Circuit Backs Thomson Reuters in Pivotal AI Copyright Fight With Ross

by Bruno Queiroz

The Third Circuit has delivered one of the most important appellate rulings yet at the intersection of copyright law, legal publishing, and artificial intelligence. In affirming Thomson Reuters’ win against Ross Intelligence, the court left in place a ruling that Ross infringed Westlaw headnotes and could not shield its conduct under fair use.

For legal professionals, the decision is significant well beyond this long-running dispute. At a high level, it reinforces that editorial content built on top of public-law materials may still receive meaningful copyright protection. While judicial opinions themselves are not copyrightable, the way a legal publisher organizes, summarizes, and adds editorial analysis to that body of law can be. That distinction has always mattered in the legal-research market; it now matters even more in the AI era.

The litigation has been closely watched because Ross’s alleged use of Westlaw headnotes was tied to building an AI-driven legal research product. The appellate ruling therefore lands squarely in the broader debate over whether copyrighted materials can be used to train, improve, or structure AI tools without a license. By refusing to extend fair use here, the court gave content owners a stronger position in arguing that commercial AI development does not automatically transform protected works into permissible inputs.

The underlying Delaware case, Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH et al v. ROSS Intelligence Inc. , has served as a bellwether for how courts may treat “non-generative” AI uses of copyrighted works. Now, with the Third Circuit affirmance in Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH, et al v. Ross Intelligence Inc , litigators and in-house teams have appellate guidance to cite when assessing risk around training data, product development, and licensing strategy.

For law firms and legal departments, the practical takeaway is straightforward: AI procurement and development decisions increasingly require careful rights analysis, especially where a tool relies on third-party editorial content rather than raw public-domain materials. Compliance teams should pay close attention to vendor representations about training data and content provenance. In-house counsel evaluating AI partnerships or internal tools will want to revisit contract language, indemnity provisions, and usage restrictions in light of this ruling.

The opinion is also likely to shape competitive dynamics in legal research. Established publishers may view it as validation of the value of their proprietary enhancements, while AI entrants may face greater pressure to license content or redesign workflows around clearly noninfringing inputs. Either way, this is a decision that will be cited far beyond the legal-research industry.

news.summaryZh: Salesforce公司于2026年9月24日向美国专利审判和上诉委员会（PTAB）提交了IPR2026-00476号多方复审请求，开启新的专利挑战程序。该案件受到关注，因为企业软件公司正利用PTAB挑战可能影响核心平台、客户关系管理或云端业务工具的已授权专利。目前公开案卷仅显示申请人为Salesforce公司，被挑战的专利号、专利权人身份及引用的现有技术组合尚未公开，需待案卷更新。案件的关键问题可能包括依据美国法典第35编第102条或第103条提出的复审理由、现有技术的范围、本领域普通技术水平的界定，以及涉及数据库、工作流、消息传递、权限或分布式计算等术语的权利要求解释争议。专利权人可能提交初步回应，涉及酌情拒绝受理、真正利益相关方或现有技术弱点等论点。Salesforce是PTAB的常客，其申请策略反映成熟科技公司应对专利主张的风险管理方式。早期案卷活动可能揭示案件是否与平行地区法院诉讼相关，从而影响禁止反言、中止诉讼策略和和解筹码。若挑战的权利要求涉及广泛使用的企业软件功能，委员会的处理可能产生超出当事方的更广泛影响。内部法律顾问、诉讼律师和起诉团队应尽早关注此案，机构决定文件、专家声明和酌情拒绝受理的简报可能为现代软件专利挑战提供指导。
news.bodyText:
Salesforce Targets Patent in New PTAB Challenge, IPR2026-00476

by Bruno Queiroz

Salesforce, Inc. has launched a new inter partes review at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, filing IPR2026-00476 on September 24, 2026. The petition opens another closely watched PTAB dispute for technology and software-focused patent practitioners, particularly those tracking how enterprise software companies are using the Board to challenge issued patents that may affect core platform, customer relationship management, or cloud-based business tools.

At this stage, the public docket identifies the proceeding under the title Salesforce, Inc. , but practitioners will want to monitor the record for the challenged patent number, the patent owner’s identity, and the specific prior-art combinations asserted in the petition as those details become available through the docket. Those core facts will shape the significance of the case, including whether the challenged claims are directed to software functionality, data processing, user interfaces, networked systems, or other computer-implemented features commonly litigated in the enterprise technology space.

As with any PTAB petition, the key issues will likely center on the asserted grounds for review under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and/or 103, the scope of the prior art, and how the petitioner frames the level of ordinary skill in the art. If the challenged claims involve software or cloud architecture, claim construction disputes may also become important, particularly where terms related to databases, workflows, messaging, permissions, or distributed computing are at issue. The patent owner’s preliminary response, if filed, may also preview arguments on discretionary denial, real-party-in-interest issues, or substantive weaknesses in the prior-art case.

Why should patent counsel follow this matter now, even before institution? First, Salesforce is a major repeat PTAB participant, and its filing strategies often provide insight into how sophisticated technology companies are approaching risk management against patent assertions. Second, early docket activity can reveal whether the case is tied to parallel district court litigation, which in turn can affect estoppel, stay strategy, and settlement leverage. Third, if the petition targets claims that map onto widely used enterprise software functions, the Board’s treatment of the case could have implications beyond the immediate parties.

For in-house counsel, litigators, and prosecution teams advising software clients, this is the kind of proceeding worth putting on a watchlist early. Institution papers, expert declarations, and any discretionary-denial briefing may offer useful guidance on PTAB treatment of modern software patent challenges.

news.titleEn: Insurance When AI Agents Are the Decision-Makers
news.titleZh: 当AI代理成为决策者时的保险问题
news.summaryZh: 随着AI代理在医疗保健领域的应用增多，其错误决策引发的索赔将不可避免，风险经理需确定哪份保单响应。过去投保人可假设AI风险已包含在现有保险计划中，但市场正迅速变化，被保险人需主动确认。新威胁出现时，现有标准保单通常覆盖，如一般责任险承保“事件”，D&O险承保“不当行为”，在无特定除外条款时覆盖新风险，正如“静默网络风险”曾获保障，后行业才引入网络除外和专门产品。AI模式类似，但速度更快。AI是载体，伤害本质不变，如AI转录工具故障导致错误剂量、AI误读图表导致错误诊断，这些普通医疗索赔不因涉及AI而改变实质，无除外时应获保障。保险公司正快速行动，2026年1月ISO发布CGL生成式AI批单：CG 40 47排除A、B部分因生成式AI引起的身体伤害、财产损失及个人和广告伤害；CG 40 48仅排除B部分；CG 35 08适用于产品和完工操作。多家领先保险公司已采用。趋势超出CGL：Berkley引入“绝对”AI排除，拒绝承保任何“由任何个人或实体实际或涉嫌使用、部署或开发AI引起或归因于”的索赔；Philadelphia Insurance在技术E&O和网络风险表格中排除为第三方使用生成式AI创建的内容；Hamilton Select有职业责任批单排除涉及生成式AI的索赔。这些批单只是开端，随着AI采用激增，不警惕的被保险人可能在续保时发现风险被排除。但宽泛定义有双向影响：涵盖预测文本和临床软件的定义可能被视为模糊，而模糊性不利于保险公司。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The rising use of AI agents across healthcare will inevitably produce claims when those agents make the wrong call. The question that lands on the risk manager’s desk is which policy responds. Until recently, policyholders could reasonably assume that AI risks were folded into their existing insurance program. The market is moving quickly to change that, and insureds now need to confirm rather than assume. When a new threat vector emerges, existing standard forms often cover it. General liability policies broadly insure “occurrences.” D&O policies broadly insure “wrongful acts.” Those broad grants pick up new and unforeseen risks in the absence of a specific exclusion. That is how “silent cyber” coverage arose — cyber losses were covered because nothing excluded them. The industry eventually responded with the interlocking network of cyber exclusions and dedicated cyber products in place today. The same pattern is now repeating with AI on a much faster timeline. AI is the vector, but the underlying injuries are not new. An AI transcription tool malfunctions, and the wrong dosage is ordered. An AI agent misreads a chart, and the wrong diagnosis is recommended. These are ordinary healthcare claims that do not change in substance because AI was involved, and absent a specific exclusion they should remain covered. Insurers are working quickly to foreclose that argument. In January 2026, the Insurance Services Office, Inc. (ISO) published generative-AI endorsements for commercial general liability policies. CG 40 47 excludes bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising out of generative AI under both Coverage A and Coverage B. CG 40 48 excludes only Coverage B. CG 35 08 applies the exclusion to the products and completed operations coverage part. Many leading insurers have filed to adopt these forms. The trend extends well beyond CGL. Berkley has introduced an “absolute” AI exclusion denying coverage for any claim “arising out of, or attributable to” “any actual or alleged use, deployment, or development of Artificial Intelligence by any person or entity[.]” Philadelphia Insurance has drafted an exclusion to its Integrated Technology E&O and Cyber Risk Coverage Form carving out content created for a third party using “generative artificial intelligence” in the performance of services. Hamilton Select Insurance Co. has a professional liability endorsement excluding claims “based upon, arising out of, or in any way involving any actual or alleged use of generative artificial intelligence by the insured.” These forms are the leading edge rather than the whole of it, and as such endorsements proliferate alongside AI adoption, unwary insureds may find previously covered risks excluded at the next renewal. Breadth cuts both ways, however. Definitions written sweepingly enough to capture predictive text and long-standing clinical software invite the argument that the exclusion is ambiguous — and ambiguity is construed against the insurer. An AI-powered scribe hallucinates a critical note from a patient consult. The physician does not catch it, and the patient is fatally misdiagnosed. Which policies respond? This is the obvious first answer. These policies cover professional services rendered by the insured. If the physician read the AI-generated note and simply missed the hallucination, this is an ordinary malpractice claim and the professional liability policy should respond. But what if the human element drops out, and the hallucinated transcription auto-populates a prescription order or triggers autonomous triage in the emergency department? If direct human error is taken out of the equation, is it still a covered professional liability claim? Knowing the precise language of your policy is critical. An AI exclusion should not be discovered for the first time after a claim is made. Your CGL policy excludes professional services, so expect little help here. With the rise of the AI exclusions discussed above, these claims are now barred on two fronts. Cyber policies are built for security and privacy events — a data breach or a failure of network security — not isolated system failures like an AI hallucination. But cyber wordings vary far more than CGL forms. One policy may restrict these claims while a broader coverage grant responds, even if the insurer believes it was never intended for that kind of loss.

news.titleEn: Client Alert: Artificial Intelligence Broke the Software Contract: The New Battle Over Indemnities, Warranties, and Liability Caps
news.titleZh: 客户警报：人工智能打破软件合同平衡——赔偿、保证与责任上限的新博弈
news.summaryZh: 数十年来，软件合同遵循相对可预测的模式：客户力求获得广泛的知识产权赔偿、有意义的保证以及足够高的责任上限，以便在出现问题时获得实际救济；供应商则通过缩小义务、限制损害赔偿和尽可能排除风险来应对。双方经谈判找到折中方案后达成交易。人工智能打破了这一平衡，并非因为传统合同原则不再适用，而是因为这些原则大多围绕确定性软件制定。若软件产品发生故障，各方通常能清楚了解发生了什么、为何发生以及谁应负责，而人工智能系统并不总能提供同等程度的确定性。因此，当前技术交易中一些最具争议的谈判不再聚焦于功能或服务水平，而是集中于一个更根本的问题，答案日益取决于各方如何谈判赔偿、保证和责任限制条款。传统软件依据既定规则执行特定功能，若薪资系统算错税款或金融应用损坏数据，错误通常可追溯至编码问题、配置问题或操作失误。生成式人工智能的运作方式不同，相同提示可能产生不同回应，输出可能不准确、不完整、有偏见、具有误导性或完全虚构。多数供应商现公开承认，人工智能生成内容在依赖前应经人工审核。从技术角度看，这一免责声明可以理解，但从合同角度看则复杂得多。许多客户购买人工智能赋能产品，正是期望其协助决策、内容生成、分析、预测或提升运营效率。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! For decades, software contracts followed a relatively predictable pattern. Customers pushed for broad intellectual property (IP) indemnities, meaningful warranties, and liability caps large enough to provide a practical remedy if things went wrong. Vendors responded by narrowing obligations, limiting damages, and carving out as much risk as possible. The parties negotiated, found a middle ground, and closed the deal. Artificial intelligence (AI) has disrupted that balance. Not because traditional contract principles no longer apply; they do. The challenge is that many of those principles were developed around deterministic software. If a software product malfunctioned, the parties generally had a clear understanding of what happened, why it happened, and who was responsible. AI systems do not always provide the same level of certainty. As a result, some of the most contentious negotiations in technology transactions today are no longer focused on functionality or service levels. They are focused on a much more fundamental question: The answer increasingly depends on how the parties negotiate indemnities, warranties, and liability limitations. Traditional software is designed to perform specific functions according to defined rules. If a payroll system calculates taxes incorrectly or a financial application corrupts data, the error can generally be traced to a coding issue, configuration problem, or operational failure. Generative AI operates differently. The same prompt may produce different responses. Outputs may be inaccurate, incomplete, biased, misleading, or entirely fabricated. Most vendors now openly acknowledge that AI-generated content should be reviewed by humans before being relied upon. That disclaimer is understandable from a technical perspective, but it becomes much more complicated from a contracting perspective. Many customers purchase AI-enabled products precisely because they are expected to assist with decision-making, content generation, analysis, forecasting, or operational efficiency. If the customer is paying for those capabilities, it is reasonable to ask what happens when they fail.

news.titleEn: SB 5: Preparing for Connecticut’s Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency Act
news.titleZh: SB 5：为康涅狄格州《人工智能责任与透明度法案》做好准备
news.summaryZh: 康涅狄格州已颁布美国最广泛的州级人工智能法律之一，即《替代参议院法案第5号》（SB 5），于2026年5月27日由州长内德·拉蒙特签署成为《公共法案第26-15号》，立法者称之为《康涅狄格州人工智能责任与透明度法案》（CART法案）。合规义务自2026年10月1日起分阶段生效，直至2028年1月1日。该法涵盖五类人工智能活动：自动化就业决策工具、人工智能伴侣和聊天机器人、前沿模型开发者、生成式人工智能内容溯源，以及面向未成年人的社交媒体平台。使用“自动化就业相关决策技术”（AEDT）的雇主，若该技术于2027年10月1日或之后在州内使用，须遵守新的通知义务。AEDT指处理个人数据并利用计算生成输出（包括预测、推荐、分类、排名、评分等）且该输出是做出或实质性影响就业决策的重要因素的技术。自2027年1月1日起，运营人工智能伴侣或具有自然语言界面、能提供适应性类人响应并维持多轮交互的系统的运营商，须承担安全和披露义务。该法还适用于训练基础模型计算量超过10^26次的前沿开发者、月活跃用户超100万的生成式人工智能系统提供商，以及向18岁以下用户算法推荐内容的社交媒体平台运营商。该法案由州长、总检察长和主要起草人共同制定，作为对联邦层面人工智能监管停滞的回应。州长表示该州“不能再等待华盛顿特区采取行动”，并称该法“在保护儿童、确保工人公平待遇和促进创新之间取得了良好平衡”。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Connecticut has enacted one of the most wide-ranging state AI laws to date. Companies that develop or deploy automated tools affecting Connecticut employees, consumers, or minors should begin assessing whether the new law applies to them, since obligations start phasing in on October 1, 2026. Effective date: Staggered, beginning October 1, 2026, through January 1, 2028 After a year of stalled negotiations over a predecessor bill in 2025, Gov. Ned Lamont signed Substitute Senate Bill 5 into law on May 27, 2026, as Public Act No. 26-15. Legislators have referred to it as the Connecticut Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency Act, or the “CART Act.” Unlike Colorado’s recently narrowed approach to AI regulation (which we covered in a separate blog post), Connecticut chose breadth over simplicity — addressing five distinct categories of AI activity in a single bill: (1) automated employment decision tools, (2) AI companions and chatbots, (3) frontier model developers, (4) generative AI content provenance, and (5) social media platforms used by minors. The law’s reach depends on which provision of the CART Act is involved. Employers that use “automated employment-related decision technology” or “AEDT,” which is defined as “any technology that processes personal data and uses computation to generate any output, including, but not limited to, any prediction, recommendation, classification, ranking, score or other information, that is a substantial factor used to make or materially influence an employment-related decision,” must comply with new notice obligations once the AEDT is deployed in the state on or after October 1, 2027. A “substantial factor” is any output, including a “constraint, ranking, score, recommendation or classification, that meaningfully alters the outcome of an employment-related decision.” Separately, operators of “AI companions” or systems with a natural language interface that provide “adaptive, human-like responses to user inputs” and are “able to sustain a relationship across multiple interactions” face safety and disclosure obligations beginning January 1, 2027. The law also reaches “frontier developer[s]” that train foundation models using more than 10²⁶ computing operations, providers of generative AI systems with more than one million monthly users, and operators of social media platforms that algorithmically recommend content to users under age 18. The governor, attorney general, and lead author of SB 5 developed the bill jointly, which was framed as a state-level response to a stalled federal debate over AI regulation. In announcing the signing, Gov. Lamont said the state “can no longer wait for Washington, D.C. to do the right thing and enact protections over these digital tools that give parents more control — it is time for the states to take action,” adding that the law “strikes a good balance between protecting children, ensuring workers are being treated fairly, and promoting innovation.” Attorney General William Tong was more pointed, calling the law “a major bipartisan step towards reclaiming parental control over our kids’ exposure to dangerously addictive and deeply destructive social media platforms, and an important first step towards harnessing and containing the possibilities and risks of artificial intelligence.” Sen. James Maroney, the bill’s principal author, described it as legislation that “safeguards children from the dangers of unregulated AI chatbots, shields residents from potential bias in the hiring process,” and sets the state “toward becoming the most AI-literate workforce in America.” That last point is borne out by the bill. The law also establishes a “Connecticut AI Academy,” an AI regulatory sandbox program, and several workforce and small-business AI literacy initiatives, reflecting the Connecticut Legislature’s stated intent to pair new restrictions with investment in AI adoption. With the earliest obligations taking effect October 1, 2026, companies operating in Connecticut should take the following steps to ensure compliance: As the provisions of SB 5 go into effect, businesses touching Connecticut employees, consumers, or minors should treat it as an immediate compliance priority.

news.titleEn: Illinois Judge's Standing Order on AI Use Marks a Shift in Judicial Transparency
news.titleZh: 伊利诺伊州法官关于人工智能使用的常设命令标志着司法透明度的转变
news.summaryZh: 伊利诺伊州麦迪逊县第三司法巡回法院法官莎拉·史密斯于八月发布常设命令附录，说明法院如何使用人工智能，成为该州首批此类命令之一。此举旨在提高透明度，消除公众对司法系统中AI的疑虑，增强公众信心。只要律师和公众了解其使用方式及限制，透明度就能提升对司法机构的信任。根据其《关于负责任地使用人工智能的司法实践声明》，AI被视为“生产力工具”，仅用于行政和起草工作，如编辑和总结材料，司法裁决始终由“独立人类判断”作出，绝不委托给AI。此前，史密斯已要求律师在使用AI回答质询、总结客户记录或生成证据时向对方披露。这两项命令基于2025年1月伊利诺伊州最高法院AI政策，该政策不要求诉状中披露AI使用。史密斯希望命令实现三个目标：提高透明度、教育律师负责任地使用AI、减少对该技术的污名。她强调法官应视AI为“技术进步”，在明确界限内使用。史密斯主要使用Westlaw CoCounsel，该工具协助她研究法律、组织复杂案件，并通过判例法检验裁决的弱点。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As courts and attorneys navigate the integration of artificial intelligence into legal practice, Illinois Circuit Judge Sarah Smith has taken an unusual step: formally disclosing how she uses the technology in her courtroom. Smith, a judge in the 3rd Judicial Circuit in Madison County, issued a standing order addendum in August outlining how the court uses AI, making it one of the first known judicial orders of its kind in Illinois. With a growing number of judicial orders containing AI-generated citations, she viewed the order as a proactive way to increase transparency and eliminate “some of the suspicion” surrounding AI in the judiciary. Smith said the disclosure was intended to increase public confidence by explaining how she uses AI and the limits she places on it. “As long as the bar and the public see the transparency, and know the ways that I’m using it and the left and right limits, and how I’m using it, I think that transparency increases the confidence they have in the judiciary,” Smith said. Under Smith’s Statement of Judicial Practice Regarding the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI is treated as a “productivity tool” that can assist the court with administrative and drafting functions, such as editing written work and summarizing materials. The statement clarifies that judicial decisions remain the product of “independent human judgment” and are “never delegated to AI.” The addendum followed Smith’s initial standing order requiring attorneys to disclose to opposing counsel if they used AI for answering interrogatories, summarizing client records, or generating evidence. Both orders build on the January 2025 Illinois Supreme Court Policy on Artificial Intelligence, which does not require AI disclosure in a pleading. “If I’m asking attorneys to be this cognizant in my specific standing order on their use of it, how unfair is it for me to kind of have those expectations of them when they should have those very same expectations of me?” Smith said. She hoped the standing order would accomplish three things: increase transparency, educate members of the bar about responsible AI use, and reduce the stigma surrounding the technology. Smith emphasized the importance of educating members of the bar about the capabilities and risks of generative AI. Rather than ignoring these developments, Smith believes judges should treat AI as an “advancement in technology,” another tool to be used within clear boundaries. Smith primarily uses Westlaw CoCounsel, which was recently made available to her jurisdiction. The tool has assisted her with researching the law, organizing complex cases, and identifying weaknesses in holdings by testing those rulings against case law.

news.titleEn: ‘Zero Associates’ Firm Pierson Ferdinand Hits 300 Partners
news.titleZh: “零助理”律所Pierson Ferdinand合伙人规模达300人
news.summaryZh: 新型模式律所Pierson Ferdinand（简称PierFerd）宣布，其全球合伙人总数已突破300人。该所不设助理层级，而是依赖Harvey等AI平台承担大量基础工作。这一里程碑是在2024年1月成立后不到三年内达成的。该所采取“深思熟虑的战略”，持续吸纳全球顶尖律师。其业务覆盖商业诉讼、房地产、跨境交易、高管薪酬等大型律所常见领域。PierFerd始终专注于构建现代化、技术驱动的平台，以在各地域和各业务领域持续超越客户期望。自2024年创立以来，AI及其他技术已深度融入该所的业务与运营，助力其快速成长并为客户创造卓越成果。在Harvey的一篇博客文章中，PierFerd指出，多数律所依赖杠杆模式，即在合伙人之下堆积大量助理律师，而PierFerd彻底颠覆了这一模式，是一家纯合伙人制律所，刻意不设助理，也不进行初级培训。随着客户日益追求效率、价值以及与资深律师的直接沟通，该所模式提供了不同路径。该所提出的问题是：资深合伙人如何在牺牲速度、利润或质量的前提下，吸收传统上由初级律师处理的工作？其答案是，利用AI在很大程度上替代原本由初级律师执行的任务。市场上也存在其他以资深律师为主的“律所”，例如Gunnercooke，此类“分布式”律所之间的差异往往在于内部结构和利润分成机制。Gunnercooke已引入AI平台Legora，并得到其律师的广泛使用。
news.bodyText: Pierson Ferdinand, a new model law firm that has no associates and instead relies of AI platforms such as Harvey to do the heavy lifting, has now reached 300 partners globally. PierFerd, as it’s known, said that the 300 total has been hit ‘less than three years after launching in January 2024’. They added that the firm has a ‘deliberate strategy’ of bringing aboard top lawyers worldwide. Plus, they also handle all the Big Law work areas you’d expect: commercial litigation, real estate, cross-border transactions, executive compensation, and more. Co-Chairman Michael Pierson, commented: ‘PierFerd remains focused on building a modern, technology-enabled platform that consistently exceeds client expectations across practices and geographies for our global client base. ‘From our founding in 2024, AI and other technologies have been deeply embedded in our practices and operations, which has empowered us to grow so quickly and produce stellar results for our clients.’ — Advertisement — — In a Harvey blog post, PierFerd noted: ‘Most firms run on leverage: armies of associates stacked beneath partners. Pierson Ferdinand flipped that model on its head. It is a partner-only firm, with no associates and no junior training, by design. ‘As clients increasingly seek efficiency, value, and more direct engagement with experienced counsel, the firm’s model offered a different approach. That bold structure raised an equally bold question: how do experienced partners absorb the work juniors traditionally handle, without sacrificing speed, margin, or quality? ‘In place of junior staff, we use AI to largely replace the tasks that would have ordinarily been performed by more junior lawyers.’ Is this a big deal? Well, there are other ‘firms’ out there that are mostly senior lawyers, for example Gunnercooke. Often the difference between such ‘distributed’ firms are the intricacies of their internal structure and profit share systems. And in Gunnercooke’s case, they have brought aboard AI platform Legora, which now is used widely by the lawyers there.
news.relevanceReason: 文章核心是法律科技与AI在法律业务中的应用，重点描述了一家律所利用AI替代助理层级、实现业务运营的模式，属于法律AI在律所工作流程中的典型应用，符合本站主题。

news.titleEn: Clio Buys Learned Hand as Judiciary Strategy Expands
news.titleZh: Clio收购Learned Hand，司法领域战略持续扩张
news.summaryZh: 法律科技公司Clio宣布收购Learned Hand，后者是一家专注于为法官和法院提供人工智能支持的初创企业。此次收购是Clio在司法领域市场拓展战略的一部分，该战略此前已包括多项重要人事任命，例如聘请美国仲裁协会前首席执行官等高管。Learned Hand开发了一款专为法官和书记官设计的人工智能工作空间，能够与法院案件管理系统对接，帮助法官处理案件。该技术已被美国多家法院采用，其中包括全美最大的初审法院——洛杉矶县高等法院。人工智能正在改变整个法律体系的工作速度和案件量，但只有法院能够跟上这一进展，进步才有意义。如果律师和诉讼当事人能够大幅提速，而法官和法院团队仍受限于原有能力，瓶颈就会转移到法院。Clio近二十年来一直致力于构建连接法律体系的技术、法律数据和基础设施，收购Learned Hand将使其能够将这一基础直接带入司法系统，帮助建设更强大、更现代、更具韧性的法院。公司成立的初衷是为法官和书记官提供符合司法工作现实的技术，尤其是在案件数量和复杂性持续增长的背景下。公司有幸与法官合作，了解技术如何在法庭上赢得一席之地，现在借助Clio，可以将这些成果推广到更大规模。此外，Clio还聘请了Casetext联合创始人巴勃罗·阿雷东多担任司法领域高级副总裁，并聘请前密歇根州最高法院首席大法官、前美国仲裁协会首席执行官布里奇特·玛丽·麦科马克担任司法领域总经理。
news.bodyText: Clio has bought Learned Hand, an AI company focused on supporting judges and the courts. The move is part of its wider strategy to build within the judiciary segment of the market, which has included major hires, including the former CEO of the AAA. So, what is the company they’ve bought? Learned Hand has built ‘an AI workspace specifically for judges and clerks’ that connects with court case management systems and helps them: In short, if you’re a judge then it’s really a go-to tool for you. Learned Hand’s technology is already being used by courts across the US, including the Superior Court of Los Angeles County, the nation’s largest trial court, Clio noted. Jack Newton, Clio CEO, commented: ‘AI is changing the pace and volume of legal work across the entire system, but that progress only matters if the courts can keep up.’ ‘If lawyers and litigants can move dramatically faster while judges and court teams remain constrained by the same capacity, the bottleneck simply shifts to the courts. We have spent nearly two decades building the technology, legal data, and infrastructure that connect the legal system. ‘Learned Hand gives us the opportunity to bring that foundation directly into the judiciary and help build courts that are as capable, modern, and resilient as the legal system around them increasingly demands.’ Learned Hand CEO, Shlomo Klapper, added: ‘We started Learned Hand because judges and clerks needed technology built around the realities of judicial work, especially as the volume and complexity of matters continued to grow. ‘We’ve had the privilege of building alongside judges and learning what it takes for technology to earn a place in the courtroom. With Clio, we can take everything we’ve learned and built for the judiciary at a scale this opportunity deserves.’ And as noted, this is part of a strategic growth initiative that has also seen Clio hire Pablo Arredondo, co-founder of Casetext as Senior Vice President, Judiciary; and also former Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice Bridget Mary McCormack – who is also the former AAA CEO – and is joining as General Manager, Judiciary. More about Clio here.
news.relevanceReason: 该文章主要报道法律科技公司Clio收购专注于司法领域AI的Learned Hand，并涉及AI在法院工作流程中的应用，属于法律AI和司法技术范畴。

news.titleEn: The AI Value Gap: Why Your Investment Isn’t Paying Off
news.titleZh: AI价值差距：为何你的投资未见回报
news.summaryZh: 英国律师事务所的AI应用已从必然趋势转向价值兑现困境。该机构新报告《AI价值差距》提出尖锐问题：律所已普遍采用AI，但为何未见成效？Thomson Reuters《2026年未来专业人士》研究显示，91%的收费人员认为所在机构未能达到AI可实现的预期效果。问题并非投资不足：拥有清晰AI战略的律所获得可衡量回报的可能性是其他律所的四倍，但多数律所和法律部门仍无法说明实际回报，仅18%的机构系统化收集ROI指标。同时，多家美国大型律所在AI使用增长的同时，计费工时反而上升，承诺的时间节省去向不明。价值差距本质上是信心差距，责任在于领导层而非IT或人力资源部门。Thomson Reuters《杰出律师》调查发现，即使是最重度使用AI的合伙人，也仅有约三分之一与多数客户讨论过AI的影响。合伙人作为商业传导机制，若未亲自使用工具并具备可信的沟通能力，便无法向客户推销AI价值。此外，所有权问题引发犹豫：律所将AI系统基于合伙人的累积判断进行训练，但计费工时或利润分成均未对合伙人提供相应补偿。Kirkland & Ellis承诺投入5亿美元建设专有平台，被评论者解读为对所有权和控制权的考量，而非单纯追求效率。目前，部分律所正考虑将自身AI能力分拆为独立商业实体，即成为自己的NewMod，而非被其颠覆。
news.bodyText: By James Tuke, CEO, AI Futures Forum. It is late September 2026. Sixteen months ago, our first report established that AI adoption was becoming inevitable across UK law firms. Since then, we’ve tracked the story through a hardening client mandate (September 2025), a warning about the collapsing training pipeline in ‘Broken Ladder’ (January 2026), and the reckoning with the billable hour in May. At every stage, the story has been usage curves climbing, budgets growing and tools proliferating. That story has now changed. Our new report, ‘The AI Value Gap’, asks a more uncomfortable question: your firm has probably already adopted AI, so why isn’t it paying off? 91% and Falling Short Thomson Reuters’ 2026 Future of Professionals research found that 91% of fee earners believe their own organisations are falling short of what AI could realistically deliver. This is not a story about under-investment. Firms with a genuinely visible AI strategy are nearly four times more likely to see measurable return than those without one – and yet most firms and legal departments still cannot tell you what their return actually is. Only 18% collect ROI metrics in any systematic way. Meanwhile, in several major US firms, billable hours are rising even as AI use grows – and nobody has offered a convincing account of where the promised time savings went. It’s Not a Technology Problem The instinctive explanation is that the tools remain immature, or that governance hasn’t caught up. Both are true, but neither explains a gap this size. Our research points somewhere less comfortable: the value gap is a confidence gap, and it sits squarely with leadership, not IT or HR. The clearest evidence is uncomfortable reading for managing partners specifically. Thomson Reuters’ Stand-out Lawyers survey found that even among the heaviest partner users of AI, only around a third have discussed its impact with most of their clients. Partners are a firm’s commercial transmission mechanism – the people who set matter strategy and staffing expectations. A partner who hasn’t personally used the tools enough to talk about them credibly cannot sell that impact to a client, however good the firm’s official strategy claims to be. The Ownership Question There is a more self-interested reason for hesitation too. As firms train AI systems on their own partners’ accumulated judgement, a legitimate question of ownership arises: who benefits from the resulting asset? Neither the billable hour nor a profit share pays a partner for having supplied the raw material of a system that keeps generating value long after they’ve retired. Kirkland & Ellis’s decision to commit US$500 million to a proprietary platform was read by commentators as being about ownership and control, not efficiency. We are now seeing firms weigh spinning off their own AI capability as a separate commercial entity – in effect, becoming their own NewMod rather than being disrupted by one.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦法律行业AI应用的价值实现、投资回报、领导层责任及所有权问题，属于法律AI领域的核心议题。

research.titleEn: Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents
research.titleZh: 法律研究基准：衡量长时程法律研究代理的端到端可靠性
research.abstractEn: Legal research is a core and time-consuming legal workflow. Lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive workflow, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. We introduce \textbf{Legal Research Bench} (LRB), a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. We evaluate thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. We score agent responses through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. We also validate the LLM judge against expert attorneys ensuring that benchmark scores track attorney judgment. Agents remain far from reliable: among the models we tested, the strongest, Claude Opus 4.8, is fully correct on 42.9\% of questions. Performance also varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.
research.abstractZh: 法律研究是法律工作中核心且耗时的流程。律师必须识别具有约束力的权威依据，验证其仍然有效，协调法规与判例，并综合出有根据的答案。语言模型代理非常适合这种检索密集型工作流程，即使自动化其中一部分也将具有重要价值。但这一价值取决于可靠性：一个缺失的权威依据、过时的引注或错误的法律结论，都可能使原本看似合理的答案无法使用。我们引入了法律研究基准（LRB），这是一个包含413个由专家撰写的开放式美国法律研究问题的基准，每个问题都配有标准答案、支持性权威依据和二元评分标准。我们在一个配备网络搜索、判例法搜索、页面解析和检索工具的实验环境中评估了十三个前沿模型。我们通过带来源验证的全通过评分来对代理的回答进行评分，即只有当所有必需标准都得到满足且其引用的权威依据得到验证时，回答才算正确。我们还针对专家律师验证了LLM评判员，确保基准分数与律师的判断一致。代理远未达到可靠：在我们测试的模型中，最强的Claude Opus 4.8在42.9%的问题上完全正确。性能也因任务设置而有显著差异：全通过率在不同法律领域有所不同，并且在需要协调冲突权威依据的问题上较低。跨模型来看，更多的轮次、工具调用和推理成本并不能预测更高的准确性。

research.titleEn: ViLegalExpert: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Vietnamese Legal Retrieval and Question Answering from Real-World Consultations
research.titleZh: ViLegalExpert：面向真实咨询场景的大规模越南法律检索与问答基准
research.abstractEn: Trustworthy Legal AI requires systems that can answer legal questions while grounding their responses in authoritative sources. However, existing Vietnamese legal benchmarks provide limited coverage of real-world legal consultations. We introduce \textbf{ViLegalExpert}, a large-scale benchmark constructed from authentic citizen--lawyer consultations, containing over \textbf{172K} questions across \textbf{34 legal domains}, together with professional answers and expert-verified legal evidence. ViLegalExpert supports legal information retrieval, extractive QA, and abstractive QA. Experiments with representative retrieval methods and language models reveal substantial challenges in evidence retrieval and grounded answer generation. While pretrained models perform strongly on QA, hybrid retrieval achieves the best retrieval performance. These results demonstrate the difficulty of mapping naturally expressed legal questions to authoritative provisions and establish ViLegalExpert as a challenging benchmark for reliable Vietnamese Legal AI.
research.abstractZh: 可信赖的法律人工智能要求系统能够回答法律问题，同时将其回答基于权威来源。然而，现有的越南法律基准对真实世界法律咨询的覆盖有限。我们引入了 	extbf{ViLegalExpert}，一个基于真实公民与律师咨询构建的大规模基准，包含超过 	extbf{17.2万} 个问题，涵盖 	extbf{34个法律领域}，并配有专业回答和专家验证的法律证据。ViLegalExpert 支持法律信息检索、抽取式问答和生成式问答。使用代表性检索方法和语言模型进行的实验揭示了证据检索和基于证据的答案生成方面的重大挑战。虽然预训练模型在问答上表现强劲，但混合检索取得了最佳的检索性能。这些结果证明了将自然表达的法律问题映射到权威条款的难度，并将 ViLegalExpert 确立为评估可靠越南法律人工智能的一个具有挑战性的基准。

research.titleEn: LexReward: A Taxonomy-Driven Reward Framework for Legal Language Models
research.titleZh: LexReward：面向法律语言模型的基于分类学的奖励框架
research.abstractEn: Legal language models require reward signals that capture not only answer correctness but also the multidimensional quality of legal responses. Existing reward methods, however, often rely on coarse-grained holistic judgments, providing limited domain specificity and interpretability. We introduce LexReward, a taxonomy-driven framework for legal reward modeling. LexReward characterizes legal response quality along three complementary dimensions: Style, covering lexical and syntactic quality; Element, assessing legal subjects, facts, statutes, and decisions; and Chain, evaluating the order, completeness, correctness, and non-redundancy of legal reasoning. For each dimension, we develop rubrics that specify evaluation criteria and quality levels. The resulting rewards are used to construct pairwise preference data for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and reward-model training. Experiments show that the rubric-based rewards reliably distinguish legal responses of different quality and that DPO training on the preference data improves performance across all three dimensions. The learned reward models, LexRM, also support effective downstream optimization: each dimension-specific reward model improves policy performance in its corresponding dimension through reinforcement learning, without requiring reference answers at reward time. Dimension-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed taxonomy and reward construction.
research.abstractZh: 法律语言模型需要能够捕捉不仅答案正确性，还包括法律回答的多维质量的奖励信号。然而，现有的奖励方法通常依赖于粗粒度的整体判断，提供的领域特异性和可解释性有限。我们引入了LexReward，一个用于法律奖励建模的基于分类学的框架。LexReward沿着三个互补维度刻画法律回答质量：风格（Style），涵盖词汇和句法质量；要素（Element），评估法律主体、事实、法规和判决；以及链条（Chain），评估法律推理的顺序、完整性、正确性和非冗余性。对于每个维度，我们制定了详细说明评估标准和质量水平的评分标准。由此产生的奖励被用于构建用于直接偏好优化（DPO）和奖励模型训练的成对偏好数据。实验表明，基于评分标准的奖励能够可靠地区分不同质量的法律回答，并且在这些偏好数据上进行DPO训练可以提高所有三个维度的性能。学习到的奖励模型LexRM也支持有效的下游优化：每个特定维度的奖励模型通过强化学习在其对应维度上提升策略性能，而无需在奖励时提供参考答案。逐维度的分析进一步支持了所提出的分类学和奖励构建的有效性。

research.titleEn: JusticeAxis: Benchmarking Legal Judgment between Rigid Rule Application and Ungrounded Discretion
research.titleZh: JusticeAxis：刚性规则适用与无依据自由裁量之间的法律判决基准测试
research.abstractEn: A sound judgment applies the law to established facts and weighs the circumstances in which they arose. However, existing methods swing between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion, benchmarks score a label or a rubric, and the experience that would supply the balance stays unverified. We formalize legal judgment as a reference-anchored task, whose object is a single decision that stays tied to the statute and to the circumstances at once. We introduce JusticeAxis, 256 real-world criminal cases from 18 countries with audio, image, and text evidence, and three lawyer-written judgments for every case: the recorded one and one for each failure. We further propose JusticeAgent, a harness whose element agents establish the facts and whose judge agent applies the law under skills carrying experience of the circumstances. Skills are distilled from execution trajectories and admitted only under Bayesian credible bounds. Experiments show that failure turns direction with scale: open-weight backbones drift to unsupported grounds, frontier models to the statutory default. We further verify that JusticeAgent, as a simple yet effective plugin, carries a frozen open-weight backbone to commercial level. Project resources are available at https://github.com/beita6969/JusticeAxis.
research.abstractZh: 健全的判决应当将法律适用于已确认的事实，并权衡这些事实产生时的具体情况。然而，现有方法在僵化的法条匹配与无依据的自由裁量之间摇摆不定，基准测试仅对标签或评分标准进行评分，而能够提供平衡的经验却未得到验证。我们将法律判决形式化为一个以参考为锚定的任务，其目标是作出一个既与法条紧密相连又兼顾具体情况的单一判决。我们引入了JusticeAxis，包含来自18个国家的256个真实刑事案件，附带音频、图像和文本证据，并为每个案件提供三份由律师撰写的判决：一份是实际记录在案的判决，另外两份分别对应两种失败模式。我们进一步提出了JusticeAgent，一个框架，其要素代理负责确定事实，而法官代理在携带具体情况经验的技能指导下适用法律。这些技能从执行轨迹中提炼，并仅在贝叶斯可信界限内被采纳。实验表明，失败方向随规模而变化：开放权重的基础模型倾向于无依据的推理，而前沿模型则倾向于法条默认。我们还验证了JusticeAgent作为一个简单而有效的插件，能够将冻结的开放权重基础模型提升至商业水平。项目资源可在https://github.com/beita6969/JusticeAxis获取。

policy.titleEn: On Eve of Brazil Elections, Meta Content Moderation Decisions Raise Questions
policy.titleZh: 巴西大选前夕，Meta内容审核决定引发质疑
policy.summaryZh: 在巴西大选前夕，Meta的内容审核决定引发质疑。上周三，Meta短暂禁止巴西总统卢拉的竞选页面投放政治广告，称其“部分活动不符合我们的规则”，但未具体说明。卢拉所属的劳工党提出申诉后，限制被解除。卢拉正与参议员弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗竞选连任，后者是前总统雅伊尔·博尔索纳罗的长子，前总统因未遂政变服刑。同日，Meta下架了Instagram账号“Revelando Brasil”，该账号前一天发布了一段关于弗拉维奥与政治丑闻关联的病毒式解释视频，涉及一名因巴西史上最大金融欺诈案被调查的银行家。Meta仅称视频违反社区准则，未作具体说明。在公众抗议后，该账号于当日下午恢复，Meta致歉。这些决定发生在外部势力干预选举的报道背景下。与特朗普有关的右翼影响者付费推广弗拉维奥在Polymarket上领先的帖子；劳工党还要求选举法院调查与副总统万斯有关的保守派捐赠者团体Rockbridge的潜在参与。Meta的行动被许多人视为审查和外国干涉，尤其是在大选前12天。该视频在YouTube上的完整版未被删除，Instagram上的预告视频浏览量近2500万。非营利组织Ctrl+Z已要求联邦检察院调查Meta，并要求其说明删除账号的原因；联邦议员奥兰多·席尔瓦也提出类似要求。Meta在特朗普上台和扎克伯格改变内容审核政策后，此类行动增多，且缺乏对用户的解释。
policy.bodyText:
On Eve of Brazil Elections, Meta Content Moderation Decisions Raise Questions Laís Martins / Sep 30, 2026 A supporter of opposition presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro attends an Independence Day event the month before the general election in São Paulo, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Andre Penner)

Republish

Last Wednesday, Meta briefly disabled Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign page from running political ads. The company said the restriction occurred because “some of its activities don’t follow our rules”, but did not specify which activities, or which rules. Lula’s Workers’ Party lodged an appeal with the company, and the restriction has since been lifted.

Lula is running for reelection against Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is now serving a prison sentence for an attempted coup d’état. “In practice, this is not only about the incalculable damage to the candidate and the elections, but the favoritism of his political opponents in the electoral process,” wrote the Workers’ Party campaign in its appeal to Meta. Tech Policy Press reached out to Meta for comment on the incident, but received no response by the time of publication.

The restriction on Lula’s campaign page followed another concerning content moderation decision by Meta on the same day. Last Wednesday morning, Meta took down an Instagram profile that had just the day before published a viral explainer video about alleged connections between Flávio Bolsonaro and political scandals, including ties to a banker being investigated for the largest financial fraud in Brazilian history.

Revelando Brasil , which operates the Instagram profile that was taken down, is a project led by Calma Urgente , a weekly podcast hosted by journalists Alessandra Orofino, Bruno Torturra and Gregorio Duvivier, together with two other independent news organizations.

Meta gave no explanation for the takedown, stating simply that the video violated its community guidelines, according to Revelando Brasil . After hours of public outcry and backlash against the company, the profile came back online in the middle of the afternoon. In response to an earlier set of questions sent by Tech Policy Press about this incident, Meta said only that “after internal review, the account mentioned in the report was restored. We apologize for the inconvenience.”

These two moderation decisions involving high profile candidates come amid a flurry of other concerning news about potential foreign interference in the elections by outside actors. Last Tuesday, the newspaper Folha de S. Paulo reported that a group of right-wing influencers connected to United States President Donald Trump, including former Republican congressman Matt Gaetz, have been paying to promote posts showing Flávio Bolsonaro taking a lead in Polymarket bets. Although Polymarket is prohibited in Brazil, Bolsonaro and right-wing allies have been publicly pushing the predictions as proxy polls.

Two weeks ago, the Workers’ Party also requested an investigation from the Electoral Court on potential involvement of Rockbridge , a group of wealthy conservative donors co-founded by Vice President J.D. Vance, in Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign. On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump also asked allied countries to designate 24 criminal groups, including two Brazilian factions, as foreign terrorist groups, as Flávio Bolsonaro had petitioned Trump to do.

Cries of censorship The action against Lula’s campaign page prompted many of his supporters to raise concerns around censorship. And one of the removed Instagram video’s authors called Meta’s decision—just 12 days before Brazilians head to polls to choose their next president—a form of censorship . Others, like left-wing candidates running for Congress, called it an act of foreign interference in Brazil’s electoral process.

The video posted on Instagram was a short teaser, linking to the full 30-minute video hosted on YouTube, which had reached the top of the ‘Hype’ ranking in less than 24 hours and was not removed. As of Thursday morning, the two teaser videos on Instagram had nearly 25 million views.

“The video script was the result of rigorous work from journalists, researchers, fact-checkers and a legal department,” Bruno Torturra, the editor at Calma Urgente and Revelando , told Tech Policy Press. He added that the takedown was not preceded by any warnings, with a standard message sent after the profile had already been excluded.

“The video was not a campaign, it was not libel, not guesswork, it was a list of facts, all amply reported by the press and explained in an accessible format to everyone,” said Fábio Porchat, a comedian from the group Porta dos Fundos who featured in the explainer, on a separate Instagram video posted after the page came back online.

“We showed the narrow relationships that exist between politicians like Flávio Bolsonaro, Nikolas Ferreira, the Lagoinha Baptist Church, Daniel Vorcaro and the Supreme Court of Justice,” he said. “After lots of pressure, the page came back online, but we don’t know for how long.”

In May, The Intercept Brasil published a bombshell investigation about Bolsonaro’s connections to Vorcaro , a banker currently under investigation for what has been dubbed as the biggest financial fraud of the country’s history. Since then, other media outlets have published new stories connecting other politicians, including federal deputy Nikolas Ferreira and multiple Supreme Court Justices to the banker. Many of these connections can be traced back to Lagoinha , a baptist church in the state of Minas Gerais.

Immediately after the Revelando profile was taken down by Meta, there was outcry from Brazilian users, including artists, journalists , activists and left-wing politicians , with many calling Meta’s decision censorship. Many also raised questions about whether this episode can be considered foreign interference. The episode has sparked questions about sovereignty, freedom of expression, and the limits of big tech’s decisions amid electoral processes.

“Beyond the story told in the video, this case reveals another scandal: Meta’s arbitrary, opaque, and disproportionate power over the national media landscape”, said Torturra. “It also highlights a central issue for the State and society to consider: can we speak of freedom of expression on social media without algorithmic transparency? Is the press truly free when subject to unwritten rules? To codes over which we have absolutely no editorial control or influence? To the whims of nameless executives?” he added.

Torturra said the group is now working on a script for an upcoming video about platforms, digital sovereignty and the privatization of freedom of expression.

Investigation under consideration Last Wednesday afternoon, Ctrl+Z, a Brazilian nonprofit organization focused on big tech accountability, requested the Federal Prosecution Service to investigate Meta and demand the company detail the reasons behind the removal of the Instagram account. (Tatiana Dias, a program director at Ctrl+Z, is a fellow at Tech Policy Press.) The case was distributed to the Regional Prosecutor's Office for Citizens' Rights in São Paulo and a prosecutor has been assigned to it, according to confirmation from the press office.

“The removal of an established journalistic profile—with a track record, an audience, and editorial partnerships—without specifying the particular rule allegedly violated runs counter to the duty of transparency and due process that the Supreme Federal Court’s own jurisprudence has come to require of platforms, and it frustrates the right of the user and the public to know and contest the grounds for such a severe measure,” Ctrl+Z wrote in its request.

In addition to Ctrl+Z, federal deputy Orlando Silva, the former rapporteur of Brazil’s Fake News Bill , also requested the Federal Prosecution Service investigate Meta over its decision to shut down the profile.

Meta’s takedown of the Revelando Brasil profile is not an isolated event, explained Luã Cruz, director of strategic litigation at Ctrl+Z. Over the past few months, the organization has been tracking cases of censorship to newsrooms and individual journalists.

“We understand this is another action by Meta like others that have been happening, and more strongly after Trump took power, after Zuckerberg changed Meta’s content moderation policies, with the use of AI, and the lack of explanation to users who have their accounts taken down or banned,” said Cruz.

If this weren’t a case involving famous actors, with wide media coverage, it would likely fall “into the limbo,” like many other businesses, he pointed out.

“We can't have this ‘black box’ situation where content of such great importance goes offline—without us knowing why—and then comes back online—again, without us knowing why, or how it returned, what the decision or reason was, or what the process was that caused the account to be taken down and subsequently restored,” he added.

policy.summaryZh: 欧盟委员会主席冯德莱恩在2026年国情咨文中宣布《欧盟儿童法案》，旨在为未成年人创造更安全的网络环境。该提案回应了成员国和公众对网络骚扰、歧视等危害的关切，但数字权利界对其立法程序表示担忧。此前，《欧盟人工智能法案》通过后不久，欧盟便以快速程序推出AI综合法案，削弱了基本权利保护；《通用数据保护条例》中关于假名化等关键条款的解释也可能被修改。欧洲议会主席还启用紧急程序通过了俗称“聊天控制”的电子隐私减损措施，该框架曾因权利关切两次被否决。新法案同样缺乏影响评估和利益相关方磋商，违反了“更好监管”程序要求。法国宪法法院曾推翻类似法律，这更凸显了审慎评估的必要性。提案旨在将《数字服务法》第28条指南转化为“硬法”，但未充分借鉴指南制定过程中的广泛磋商。提案未采取全面禁止社交媒体，而是纳入安全设计措施，但包含广泛的年龄验证要求，依赖零知识证明，专家指出该技术并非万能。提案还设想通过应用程序进行家长监督，需确认监护关系，增加身份验证层级。从言论自由角度看，13岁以下儿童的权利可能受影响，13至15岁青少年的“迷你”账户受家长监控，引发自由表达担忧。总之，该提案虽有一些可取之处，但可能无意中损害儿童及所有网络用户的基本权利，立法捷径和快速程序不可接受。
policy.bodyText:
A Safer Internet Should Not Come with Democratic Shortcuts Asha Allen / Sep 30, 2026 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivers a speech at the annual State of the European Union at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, eastern France, Wednesday, Sept 16, 2026. (AP Photo/Pascal Bastien)

Republish

This year’s State of the European Union address by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen drew a bated breath for many in the digital rights community, as we awaited the announcement of the EU Kids Act , new legislation aimed at creating a safer online environment for minors.

The online space offers young people the chance for connection and exploration, but it also exposes them to significant risks of online harassment and discrimination , among other recognized harms. The proposal is a response to wide-reaching calls from Member States and the general public for more action to address these well-documented online harms, but the devil will be in the details.

As a new addition to the EU's digital rulebook, the proposal also arrives amidst growing institutional pushback against, and in some cases dismantling of, fundamental rights protections in some of the EU’s defining digital rules.

A worrying democratic backsliding on key digital files The ink was barely dry on the EU AI Act before the AI omnibus was introduced and pushed through the legislative process under an expedited procedure. The projected ‘tension’ between enforcing risk-based rules and championing innovation placed key fundamental rights protections first on the chopping block.

Civil society organizations successfully pushed back on the worst proposed changes, but many aspects were still watered down . The central pillar of data protection rules — the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — risks having key provisions on personal data be undermined through changes on how highly technical concepts such as pseudonymization should be interpreted and a wider mandate for AI-related data processing.

Most publicly, the European Parliament President enacted an urgent procedure to pass a vote on the lapsed e-privacy derogation , commonly known as Chat Control. The Parliament had previously voted down the framework twice because of the prevailing rights concerns many civil society groups have raised . This wave of procedural backsliding has led many to hold a pessimistic view of when and how best public interest advocates can continue to push to ensure that the EU’s evolving digital rules uphold our fundamental rights.

The concern is that, despite this welcome step forward in addressing online safety for minors, this new proposal falls into the same pattern of EU tech policies being shaped outside democratic due process. Amid the European Commission’s push for simplification of digital rules, procedural mechanisms to ensure transparent and multi-stakeholder engagement in policymaking are being undermined, and the adoption of the Act is no different.

Although debate on child safety online has been ongoing for months, and several member states have taken matters into their own hands by introducing a swathe of social media ban laws , it can be argued that the Commission had little choice but to propose the new KIDS Act.

The Commission President took the diligent step of establishing a special panel to develop a report with recommendations for EU action, informed by notable experts in the field. Despite many of the nuanced recommendations of the report being embedded throughout the proposal, this does not negate the lack of impact assessment and stakeholder consultation, which are essential requirements of the Better Regulation process .

Furthermore, the constitutional court's striking down of a similar law in France should have reinforced the need for diligent assessment and stakeholder engagement, not justified sidestepping these procedures.

This is all the more necessary given that the proposal explicitly aims to turn the Digital Services Act’s Article 28 Guidelines into ‘hard law’ through this new law, only strengthening the argument that the extensive consultation process that led to the development of the guidelines should have been mirrored in the knowledge that these non-binding measures are to become binding legal obligations. This embrace of procedural sidestepping is all the more concerning given the wide-ranging fundamental rights implications of the proposal.

Good intentions, but fundamental rights must be balanced For many civil society groups, the proposal has caused mixed reactions. On the surface, the fact that the European Commission is not proposing a blanket social media ban is appreciated. As conveyed by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights , bans and age restrictions are blunt legislative tools that fail to address the core issue of platform safety.

The proposal, which is highly complex, incorporates safety-by-design measures that many advocates have suggested as a more meaningful approach to addressing the online harms that not only young people, but all users and democracy at large, continue to face. Still, the draft proposal includes far-reaching age verification and age assurance requirements which undermine this more measured approach.

Advocates have long stressed the concerns for many existing age assurance tools, outlining a more privacy-preserving approach for lawmakers to consider. At the heart of the European Commission’s proposal is a reliance on the EU’s age verification scheme, with zero-knowledge proof presented as the privacy-preserving gold standard.

Experts have consistently highlighted , however, that zero-knowledge proof is not a silver-bullet solution and has its limitations . The proposal also envisages parental oversight via an app, which itself will require confirmation of guardianship, thereby adding another layer of ID verification for parents.

From a free expression perspective, there are questions as to whether the proposal respects the right to free expression and access to information for children under the age of 13, which are rights they maintain and should still safely enjoy . This runs alongside wider free expression concerns about an age-gated internet, especially for users from marginalized communities. For teens aged 13-15, ‘mini’ accounts with limited features are available, but parents can monitor account activity. Whether teens can freely enjoy these rights under the premise of parental monitoring is also a concern. Whether parents generally support this approach, given their preference for more personal choice, remains to be seen.

In short, the solution on the table, despite having some welcome aspects, may unintentionally undermine the fundamental rights of not only children, but all online users. Given this, concerns about legislative shortcuts and expedited procedures, where opportunities for public debate and expert consultation are reduced, are simply unacceptable; the issues this law aims to address and its potential impact are simply far too important.

Getting the process right: democratic oversight must come first As this law moves forward, public consultation and democratic scrutiny will need to be forefront. Children and young people, expert civil society and public interest technologists must be extensively consulted if this law is going to land where we hope it eventually will; as a complementary framework to laws like the Digital Services Act and the upcoming Digital Fairness Act, that truly protects all communities online.

Strengthening measures to ensure platforms meaningfully mitigate the harms they have thus far failed to address, while respecting the privacy and expression rights of children and all users, is critical. As the Commission President said , “Europe has the power to act, and it is we who decide our rules. ” The EU also has an obligation to establish these rules through an open, democratic process, informed by relevant expertise.
