policy.titleEn: Universities Need AI Infrastructure. They Don’t Need AI Lock-In
policy.titleZh: 大学需要AI基础设施，但不需要被AI锁定
policy.summaryZh: 大学正从讨论人工智能转向采购人工智能，但应避免被单一供应商锁定。英国大学联盟已呼吁让AI工具覆盖所有本科生，澳大利亚新南威尔士大学宣布为超过8万名学生和教职工提供ChatGPT Edu，这是亚太地区规模最大的高等教育AI部署之一。大学确实需要AI基础设施，但不应将AI采购视为普通软件购买，因为生成式AI正成为学生学习和教职工工作的计算层，采购决策可能逐渐演变为机构架构。联合国教科文组织在九月的数字学习周上，教育部长们呼吁AI系统应可审计、数据可移植，并考虑总拥有成本，声明支持互操作性、可移植性和开源系统。机构需要保留离开的能力，避免因工作流、知识积累和系统集成而形成依赖。新南威尔士大学在部署OpenAI产品的同时，也在开发多模型AI环境，以保持灵活性。大学应将机构AI环境与具体模型分离，通过机构治理层统一管理身份、数据访问和安全，同时允许不同模型在底层运行。AI系统越来越多地参与学生支持、研究、行政和评估，AI代理可能主动发起工作流，导致权力通过技术系统迁移，形成代码中介治理。因此，AI治理需超越原则，深入技术架构，要求可移植性、数据架构限制、AI网关和日志记录。作者建议先建立治理架构，再推广采用，并指出大学领导层最重要的AI决策不是选择哪个模型，而是是否构建能保留选择自由的机构架构。大学AI战略的真正考验不是2026年购买哪个模型，而是2030年是否仍能自由选择。
policy.bodyText:
Universities Need AI Infrastructure. They Don’t Need AI Lock-In Tom Smith / Sep 30, 2026 Gates of the Royal Airforce College in Cranwell, UK in 2011. Adapted from photo by Richard Croft (CC-BY-SA)

Republish

Universities are moving rapidly from debating artificial intelligence to buying it. That shift is understandable. Students already use generative AI extensively, employers increasingly expect graduates to understand it, and leaving access to the best systems dependent on who can afford which commercial subscriptions creates obvious problems of imbalance.

In the United Kingdom, Universities UK has now called for AI tools to be accessible to every undergraduate student. In Australia, UNSW Sydney has announced one of the largest higher education deployments in the Asia-Pacific region, providing ChatGPT Edu to more than 80,000 students and staff.

These initiatives point toward a future in which institutional access to AI becomes as normal as access to a learning management system, academic databases or university email.

Universities do need AI infrastructure. But they do not need AI lock-in.

That distinction is becoming urgent because universities risk treating AI procurement as though they were buying another piece of software. Generative AI is developing into something considerably more consequential: a computational layer through which students learn, academics research and professional staff increasingly perform institutional work.

A procurement decision can gradually become an institutional architecture.

Education’s emerging platform problem UNESCO put this problem unusually clearly on the international policy agenda in September. At its Digital Learning Week in Paris, education ministers called for AI systems used in education to be auditable, for data to remain portable and for education systems to consider the total costs of ownership before adopting AI. The resulting ministerial statement explicitly favors interoperability, portability, and open-source systems so that education systems retain the ability to change course.

The important principle can be expressed more simply: institutions need to be able to leave.

This is not an argument against commercial AI providers. Universities need access to capable systems, and institutionally managed versions of commercial products can provide significant advantages over consumer accounts in security, privacy, administration and equitable access.

The problem comes when access becomes dependence. Consider what happens over several years after a university selects a preferred AI platform. Staff develop workflows around it. Students learn through it. Bespoke assistants are created inside it. Institutional knowledge accumulates within it. Other university systems are connected to it. Eventually, AI agents may begin initiating actions across those systems.

At that point, changing providers is no longer comparable to replacing a software license. The institution must unwind an ecosystem. This is a familiar feature of platformization : the value of a platform increases as more activity takes place within it, while the cost of leaving rises at the same time.

Higher education has encountered versions of this problem before with learning management systems, cloud infrastructure, academic publishing and research analytics. AI potentially intensifies it because the technology is not simply storing information or providing access to content. Increasingly, it is mediating the work itself.

The relevant procurement question is therefore changing. It is no longer only, “which AI system offers the best capabilities today?” Universities also need to ask, “what architecture preserves our ability to choose differently tomorrow?”

The university should control the layer above the model UNSW offers an interesting glimpse of one possible answer. Alongside its large OpenAI deployment, the university says it is developing a multi-model AI environment in which students and staff can experiment with different AI systems as the technology evolves. That may ultimately prove more strategically important than the ChatGPT agreement itself.

The objective for universities should be to separate their institutional AI environment from any individual model operating within it.

An institutionally governed layer could establish common rules for identity, data access, security, privacy, and appropriate use while allowing different AI models to operate underneath. A university might use one model for particular research tasks, another for coding, and another for routine administrative work. Those choices could change as technology, cost, and evidence change.

Today’s leading model may not be tomorrow’s. Universities should be positioned to benefit from competition between providers rather than finding themselves locked into the winner of a procurement exercise conducted several years earlier.

This principle matters beyond higher education. Public institutions are under increasing pressure to adopt AI while a small number of companies control many of the most capable models and the cloud infrastructure on which they depend. Will Stronge, chief executive at the Autonomy Institute, has recently pushed the argument further, describing the AI systems through which students increasingly think and research as a form of “ cognitive infrastructure ” and arguing that questions of ownership and control therefore belong at the heart of educational policy.

Universities do not need to wait for publicly owned foundation models to act on that insight. The immediate policy challenge is to create conditions under which institutions can adopt commercial AI without surrendering technological agency. Interoperability and portability consequently become governance issues rather than technical preferences.

When platforms begin to exercise institutional authority There is a second reason universities should care about the architecture they are constructing: AI systems increasingly do more than generate text.

Universities are experimenting with AI in student support, research, administration, assessment, recruitment, and the identification of students considered at risk. The development of AI agents will push this further because systems will increasingly be capable not merely of recommending actions but of initiating workflows.

Imagine a university uses an AI-enabled system to identify students at risk of dropping out. Formally, the algorithm may make only a recommendation. A human member of staff retains responsibility for deciding whether intervention is required. But suppose staff accept the recommendation almost every time. Where does the decision actually sit?

The university can truthfully maintain that a human remains “in the loop” while the technical system increasingly determines which students attract institutional attention. Authority can migrate without any formal decision to transfer it.

The same process occurs through more mundane technical choices. A university regulation might give academics discretion over appropriate AI use in assessment, while the rule experienced by students is implemented through settings inside a learning management system: AI permitted here, prohibited there, one application accessible and another blocked.

Institutional policy is translated into permissions, defaults, interfaces, and automated workflows.

Policy becomes code This is code-mediated governance : institutional authority exercised partly through technical systems rather than exclusively through conventional rules and human decisions. That makes the question of who controls university AI infrastructure inseparable from the question of who governs the university. AI governance needs to move beyond AI principles. Many universities responded to generative AI by producing guidance. That was sensible when the principal institutional problem appeared to be how students and staff should use ChatGPT. It is increasingly inadequate when AI becomes infrastructure. Universities now need governance capable of answering a different set of questions. Which AI systems operate within the institution? What information can they access? Which other systems can they interact with? Which decisions do they inform? Who authorized those uses? Can their outputs be audited? When must a human intervene? What happens when a model changes? And what is the exit plan if a supplier no longer serves the institution’s interests?

These are not questions for an IT department alone. They involve procurement, academic governance, information security, data protection, research ethics, employment relations, student representation, and senior institutional leadership.

Nor can they be answered simply by creating another AI ethics committee. The governance has to reach the technical architecture itself. Procurement requirements can mandate portability. Data architecture can restrict what models can access. Institutional AI gateways can provide multiple models through common controls. Logging can make automated activity auditable. Governance processes can establish where human judgment must remain decisive.

In other words, principles have to become infrastructure.

Universities should also be cautious about allowing the urgency of AI adoption to reverse the appropriate sequence of governance. The pattern too often is: procure a system, distribute access, encourage experimentation, then work out how to govern what follows. The more sustainable sequence is governance architecture first, scalable adoption second.

The question is not which model wins None of this requires universities to become AI skeptics. The opposite may be true. Institutions with strong governance should be able to adopt AI more confidently because they know where responsibility lies and have reduced the consequences of any individual technology failing.

Universal access to capable AI could become an important part of higher education. Students should graduate understanding how to use these systems critically and professionally. Researchers should be able to exploit rapidly improving tools. Universities should seek productivity improvements in administration rather than preserving inefficient processes simply because they are familiar.

But technological ambition and institutional autonomy need not be opposites. The most important AI decision university leaders make over the next few years may therefore not be whether to choose ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot or whatever comes next; it will be whether they build an institutional architecture in which those remain choices.

The real test of a university’s AI strategy is not which model it buys in 2026. It is whether it will still be free to choose in 2030.

news.titleEn: Morae unveils Legal Intelligence Platform, starting with AI-powered Spend Intelligence
news.titleZh: Morae推出法律智能平台，首款AI驱动的支出智能模块上线
news.summaryZh: 9月29日，Morae公司正式发布其新的法律智能平台，首个模块为MorAI Spend Intelligence，该模块结合技术与托管服务，将企业法律管理、事务管理及律所账单数据整合至统一决策层。新平台旨在连接而非替代现有系统，通过整合不同法律技术栈，为法律团队提供基于全组织背景的决策支持。与竞争对手不同，公司提供易于采用的解决方案，而非复杂的拼图。智能是技术、AI与人工专业知识的结合，最后一英里由领域专家完成。法律部门通常缺乏跨系统洞察来评估费率上涨和复杂发票的合理性，公司通过结合账单训练的AI与专家人工审核，帮助法律领导者验证当前应支付的费用，并为未来支出做出数据驱动的决策。这种混合验证方法应对了法律团队在验证AI输出方面的挑战。早期部署中，一家全球保险公司的外部律师成本节省从8.5%翻倍至18%，并消除了14,000小时的人工发票审核时间。MorAI Spend Intelligence的目标市场为财富1000强和富时350强企业法律部门，其年度外部律师支出超过1000万美元，尤其聚焦保险、金融服务、医疗保健和技术行业。长期而言，公司旨在帮助企业法律团队和律所，Bashir认为律所和法律部门是同一枚硬币的两面。
news.bodyHtml:
Morae today (29 September) formally unveils a new Legal Intelligence Platform, with its first module – MorAI Spend Intelligence – providing a tech + managed services offering that connects ELM, matter management, and law firm billing data into a single decision layer.  

The new overarching platform unifies disconnected legal tech stacks into one decision layer. Rather than replacing systems of record, it sits above them and draws intelligence from them. Morae says that the cross-system intelligence allows legal teams to make decisions based on complete, organisation-wide context. Perhaps more importantly, by integrating with existing legal systems, the platform is designed to be live “in weeks,” avoiding lengthy replatforming or data migration projects. 

Advertisement

Speaking to Legal IT Insider ahead of the launch, Morae’s founder and CEO Shahzad Bashir (pictured above), said that the company’s mantra is to ‘connect not replace’ systems, observing: “Unlike some of our competitors, we’re not going to give you a 1000-piece jigsaw but a solution that will have ease of adoption.” He added: “The groundbreaking part is that Intelligence is technology plus AI plus human in the last mile. The last mile is our domain experts.” 

For its first verticalised spend module, by pairing billing-trained AI with expert review, Morae says that legal departments can leverage validated data to guide future strategy and budget decisions.  

Advertisement

“Legal departments routinely approve rate increases and complex invoices without the cross-system insights they need to know if those charges are reasonable,” said Peter Fisher (pictured above), chief product officer at Morae. “We’re combining billing-trained AI with expert human review so legal leaders can verify what they should pay today while making smarter, data-backed decisions about where to direct spend tomorrow.” 

The hybrid tech + human verification approach comes as legal teams struggle with the verification of AI outputs, which eat into efficiency gains. 

Morae reports that in an early deployment with a global insurance company, the hybrid model doubled outside counsel cost savings from 8.5% to 18% while eliminating 14,000 hours of manual invoice review. 

The target market for MorAI Spend Intelligence is Fortune 1000 and FTSE 350 corporate legal departments with $10M+ in annual outside counsel spend, particularly across insurance, financial services, healthcare, and technology verticals. 

The ambition longer term will be to help both corporate legal teams and law firms. Bashir said: “The very genesis of Morae was helping law firms and legal departments to work better together. There are companies that do one or other, or that do strategy or technology, that do processes or data. Our answer is that those distinctions have no meaning. We believe that law firms and legal departments are just a different side of the same coin.” 

We will be discussing the new offering in a webinar this week, sign up HERE

news.titleEn: Steno Doubles Down on World-Class Service Model, Adding LegalZoom Founder Brian Lee to Board
news.titleZh: Steno 加码世界级服务模式，引入 LegalZoom 创始人 Brian Lee 加入董事会
news.summaryZh: 洛杉矶，2026年9月29日——科技驱动的法庭记录与诉讼支持服务提供商 Steno 宣布，任命法律科技先驱 Brian Lee 为董事会成员。Brian Lee 是 LegalZoom 的创始 CEO，拥有数十年打造法律行业标杆企业的经验。Steno 的优势在于其混合模式，即提供白手套式礼宾服务，同时配备专为诉讼律师打造的 AI 和法律科技工具。Brian 在将 LegalZoom 从早期概念发展为行业标准的过程中展现了卓越能力，这将助力 Steno 扩大其作为顶级诉讼支持合作伙伴的版图。Brian Lee 在担任 LegalZoom 创始 CEO 期间，从零开始创建公司，以修复未能充分服务客户的传统法律体系，带领公司实现早期高速增长，营收突破3亿美元，并为其最终上市奠定基础，上市时市值达70亿美元。在诉讼支持领域，软件无法替代律师在庭审时所需的可靠性、高触达执行和信任，Steno 将服务视为核心优势而非附属品，他期待加入董事会，帮助领导团队将 Steno 的服务优先模式推广至整个法律行业。Brian Lee 的履历还包括联合创立 The Honest Company，并在三年内将其营收扩展至3亿美元，此外还联合创立了 ShoeDazzle 和与科比·布莱恩特共同创立的 Art of Sport，目前他担任 Arena Club 的 CEO。在商业投资之外，Lee 长期倡导创业发展。此次任命正值 Steno 快速发展时期，此前公司完成了由 Savano Capital Partners 领投的4900万美元 C 轮融资，并任命前 COO Prabhdeep Singh 为 CEO，Jon Hefler 为增长副总裁，Anjelica Garcia 为首席人力官，Jeff Herscott 为销售高级副总裁。这些领导层变动旨在加速 Steno 向 AmLaw 200 和企业法律市场的扩张，同时保持诉讼律师和法庭记录员所依赖的高触达、白手套体验。
news.bodyHtml:
Former LegalZoom CEO brings decades of category-defining legal services experience to support Steno as it solidifies its position as the leading tech-enabled court reporting and litigation support services provider in the USA. 

LOS ANGELES, September 29, 2026 – Steno, the leader in tech-enabled court reporting and litigation support services, today announced the appointment of legal tech pioneer Brian Lee to its Board of Directors. Lee’s addition reinforces Steno’s commitment to operating as both a world-class service provider and a top technology platform, ensuring law firms receive a seamless combination of high-touch service and specialized tools that are grounded in a deep understanding of litigation workflows.

“Steno’s strength is in its hybrid model: we deliver white-glove, concierge-level services alongside AI and legal tech tools built specifically for litigators,” said Prabhdeep Singh, Chief Executive Officer of Steno. “Brian understands how to build market-defining service companies in the legal sector better than anyone. His experience expanding LegalZoom from an early concept into an industry standard will be invaluable as we continue to scale our footprint as a top-tier litigation support partner.”

As founding CEO of LegalZoom, Lee created the company from scratch to fix a traditional legal system that failed to adequately serve clients. He guided LegalZoom through immense early growth, expanding revenue beyond $300 million and laying the foundation for its eventual public offering (NASDAQ: LZ) at a $7 billion market capitalization. 

“In litigation support, software alone cannot replace the reliability, high-touch execution, and trust that attorneys need when bringing a case to trial,” said Lee. “Steno stands out because it prioritizes the client experience, treating service as a core strength rather than an afterthought. I am thrilled to join the board and help Prabhdeep and the leadership team scale Steno’s service-first model across the legal industry.”

Lee’s background spans multiple successful ventures. Beyond LegalZoom, he co-founded consumer brands including The Honest Company (NASDAQ: HNST), which he scaled to $300 million in revenue within three years as CEO, ShoeDazzle, and Art of Sport, which he co-founded alongside Kobe Bryant. Brian currently serves as CEO of Arena Club. Outside of his commercial ventures, Lee serves as a longtime advocate for entrepreneurial development. 

Lee’s appointment follows a period of rapid momentum for Steno. Following a $49 million Series C funding round led by Savano Capital Partners, the company recently appointed former COO Prabhdeep Singh to Chief Executive Officer, Jon Hefler as Vice President of Growth, Anjelica Garcia as Chief People Officer, and Jeff Herscott as SVP, Head of Sales. Together, these leadership moves position Steno to accelerate its expansion into the AmLaw 200 and the enterprise legal markets, while maintaining the high-touch, white-glove experience that litigators and court reporters depend on.

About Steno

Steno is at the forefront of the court reporting and legal technology industries. Steno focuses on providing attorneys with innovative tools and options that overcome the technological and financial hurdles that arise when proving a case. As a partner in the pursuit of justice, Steno understands the unique challenges faced by legal professionals and is committed to delivering practical, impactful solutions. To learn more about Steno or to request information about its services, visit www.steno.com.

news.titleEn: Opus 2 Ingenuity™ transforms deposition designations with innovative use of agentic AI
news.titleZh: Opus 2 Ingenuity™ 以创新智能体AI革新证词指定流程
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月29日，领先法律软件与服务提供商Opus 2在纽约宣布推出AI驱动的证词指定工作流程，旨在简化诉讼团队处理这一传统上繁琐耗时的过程。该平台已提供业界最受信赖的笔录管理能力，支持数百种AI法律工作流，并提供摘要、分析和自然语言查询等功能。此次发布是对证词指定流程的全面革新，AI全程支持团队工作流，也是公司利用动态AI工作流构建器设计的首个“AI原生”工作流，由Opus 2 Ingenuity™智能体AI框架驱动，从案件智能中提取上下文，为理解、呈现、创建和基于洞察采取行动提供基础。工作流程为：律师启动后，AI代理结合相关议题分析笔录，标记最相关段落，立即呈现可能需数天才能找到的内容；律师审查标记，接受或拒绝，并可调整选择，确保每个决定由律师做出。批准的指定直接流入结构化案件记录，与议题关联，带时间戳，归属审查律师，并供案件所有用户访问。每个步骤（AI建议、律师审查、批准及后续编辑）均记录在审计跟踪中。该功能解决的核心问题是，提交和最终确定证词指定是美国庭审准备中最重要且劳动密集的过程之一。没有Opus 2，律师需阅读数百或数千页笔录，同时记住多个法律议题，并在严格截止日期前手动识别证明每一点的段落，工作可能持续数周，涉及多名法律专业人士。
news.bodyHtml:
AI-enabled workflow surfaces relevant transcript passages by issue, routes lawyer-approved designationsdirectly into the structured matter record, and provides a collaborative source of truth that updates in real time

 

New York – September 29, 2026 – Today, leading legal software and services provider Opus 2 announced an AI-enabled deposition designation workflow that streamlines the way litigation teams manage a traditionally tedious, time-consuming process—the latest advancement in the company’s continual push to deliver technology-driven innovation.

 Opus 2’s intelligent legal solution platform already offers the industry’s most-trusted transcript management capabilities, supports hundreds of legal workflows with AI, and delivers valuable AI featureslike summarization, analysis, and natural-language query for transcripts. This release, however, is a complete evolution of the deposition designation process, where AI supports the team’s workflow from start to finish. 

 The capability is also the first “AI-native” workflow designed using the company’s dynamic AI workflow builder. It’s powered by Opus 2 Ingenuity™, the company’s agentic AI framework, which supplies the deposition designation workflow with context drawn from matter intelligence. That intelligence provides a superior foundation for understanding, surfacing, creating, and acting on insights.

 

How it works

When a lawyer initiates the deposition designation workflow, an AI agent analyzes the transcript with the connected issues and flags passages with the highest relevance, immediately surfacing what might otherwise take days to find. Lawyers then review flagged passages, accept or reject them, and optionally adjust the selection, making every decision about what’s included.

 Approved designations flow directly into the structured matter record. They’re linked to the relevant issue, time-stamped, attributed to the reviewing lawyer, and accessible to every user on the case. Every step (AI suggestion, lawyer review, approval, and any subsequent edit) is captured in the audit trail.

 

The problem it solves

Submitting and finalizing deposition designations is one of the most consequential and labor-intensive processes in trial preparation in the United States. Without Opus 2, lawyers must read hundreds or thousands of transcript pages, hold multiple legal issues in mind at once, and manually identify the passages that prove each point under strict deadlines. This work can span weeks, with multiple legal professionals involved. 

 

Without a shared source of truth, conflicting or duplicative designations can persist until late in the process. Designations are also inherently iterative, where one party designates, the opposing party counter-designates or objects, and the record can cycle through several rounds before it’s set.

“For litigation teams preparing complex cases for trial, reviewing lengthy transcripts to identify testimony relevant to specific issues can take days or even weeks. Our deposition designation workflow uses AI to retrieve candidate passages by legal issue, then routes the designations an attorney approves straight into the structured case record; giving the whole team a live view of evidentiary coverage,” said Yael Hollander, Principal Product Manager at Opus 2.

“The difference is that we don’t treat this as a generic model analyzing a document in isolation. AI works within the context of the case, using the legal and factual issues the team has already identified to surface relevant testimony from the transcript. Every suggested designation is traceable to its source and tied to the issue it supports, becoming part of the structured case record once accepted. This reduces the manual effort involved, can surface relevant testimony that might otherwise be missed, and keeps the attorney in control of what ultimately becomes part of the record, which is non-negotiable in a legal context,” Hollander said.

Within the Opus 2 platform, every member of a legal team works together throughout the lifecycle of every case. They create case strategy, organize evidence, identify legal and factual issues, managedeadlines, prepare filings, track progress, and collaborate with clients. The matter intelligence this work generates, including the context and relationships between evidence, witnesses, events, facts, issues, and other valuable matter data, is what Opus 2 Ingenuity draws on, to deliver higher quality, more relevant,and cost-efficient AI outputs. 

“This is a clear demonstration of the power of Opus 2 Ingenuity, our agentic AI framework,” said Tiama Hanson-Drury, Chief Product and Technology Officer at Opus 2. “The workflow doesn’t just read transcripts; it draws on the matter intelligence already inside our platform, in this case the specific legal issues a team needs to prove or rebut to win, so the AI knows what it’s looking for. The result is smarter designations that lawyers can verify quickly and that connect automatically back into the shared case record, so every designation strengthens the single source of truth the whole team is working from.”

 

About Opus 2 


Founded in 2008, Opus 2 develops award-winning, AI-enabled software that solves the most pressing problems facing the practice of law. The company’s best-in-class solutions are essential to the commercial disputes ecosystem and trusted by the world’s most successful law firms for their critical matters. Those solutions are built on a flexible platform powered by its agentic AI framework, Opus 2 Ingenuity,™ that helps firms create intelligent legal solutions that win business, deepen client engagement, and simplify workflows firmwide. For more information, visit the Opus 2 website.

news.titleEn: Option, Not Pilots
news.titleZh: 选择权，而非试点项目
news.summaryZh: 律师事务所人工智能资本配置的策略。AI提案往往以试点项目形式逐一提交至执行委员会，如知识管理部门测试智能体研究工作流、公司业务部门实现自动化首轮尽职调查、业务发展部门利用工具识别交叉销售机会、IT部门寻求企业级平台，以及诉讼部门的多个项目。这些试点项目各有赞助者、预算和“试点”标签，单独看均合理，但批准过多试点等于在未进行组合讨论的情况下做出组合决策。问题在于试点可能成功却回答错误问题：它们问“能否让技术运作”，而应问“学到了什么以改变下一步投入”。文章主张将试点思维转为购买选择权：早期AI项目投入应视为购买决策相关信息，而非单纯能力或效率。原则是先用小额资本解决重大不确定性，再投入大额资本和机构能力。成功实验的标准是产生能改变后续决策的证据，而非仅证明工具能执行任务。若证据无法改变决策，则只是在为已做出的承诺收集支持。
news.bodyHtml:
Options, Not Pilots: The Mechanics of AI Capital Allocation

The AI proposals arrive at your executive committee one at a time. Knowledge Management wants to test an agentic research workflow. The corporate group wants automated first-pass diligence. Business Development has found a tool that promises to identify cross-selling opportunities from the firm’s relationship data. IT wants an enterprise platform rather than another collection of point solutions. The litigation group has three projects of its own. A few partners are already running experiments that nobody formally approved.

Each proposal sounds reasonable on its own. Each has an enthusiastic sponsor, a manageable initial budget, and some version of the same reassuring label: pilot. No single proposal requires you to make an existential bet on artificial intelligence. Approve enough pilots, however, and you have made a portfolio decision without ever having a portfolio discussion.

The problem with these pilots is not necessarily that the technology fails. Many will succeed. The problem is that they can succeed while answering the wrong question.

They ask: Can we make this technology work?

They should ask: What did we learn that changes what we should commit next?

In short, we need to stop thinking in terms of pilots and start buying options.

What Are You Actually Buying?

When you allocate $100,000 to an AI initiative, what are you actually purchasing? The conventional answer is capability, efficiency, or automation. Is it really? An early-stage AI project is usually an investment under considerable uncertainty. What you should be paying for is decision-relevant information.

Think of it as buying an option. You spend a relatively small amount today to learn enough to make a more consequential decision tomorrow. This is not a literal financial option, and nobody is going to calculate a Black-Scholes value for an agentic research workflow. The useful principle is simpler: spend small amounts of capital to resolve important uncertainties before spending large amounts of capital and institutional capacity on commitments that will be expensive to unwind.

That changes what counts as a successful experiment. It should not merely tell you whether a tool can perform a task. It should produce evidence capable of changing a consequential decision. The sequence is experiment → evidence → decision → commitment. If the evidence cannot plausibly change the decision, you are not buying much option value. You are gathering support for a commitment you have effectively already made.

Learning Before Commitment

That yields a governing principle for prudent AI capital allocation:

Learning Velocity > Commitment Velocity

Commitment is not measured only in dollars. A month-to-month software subscription might be easy to abandon. Connect the same tool to confidential firm data and the exposure changes. Rebuild a practice-group workflow around it and it changes again. Allow the old workflow to decay and the cost of retreat rises further. What began as a modest technology experiment can become an institutional dependency.

When commitment gets ahead of learning, assumptions harden into architecture before you have adequately tested them. On the other hand, when learning leads, evidence earns the next level of commitment. The objective is not maximum reversibility or minimum commitment. Some things can only be learned by making a real commitment, and delay has costs of its own. The objective is to make no more commitment than you need to resolve the next consequential uncertainty.

Cheap Experiments Should Make Us More Demanding

AI is making many experiments cheaper and easier to build. But cheap to build does not mean cheap to evaluate. KM expertise, IT integration time, information-security review, lawyer attention, clean data, workflow knowledge, training capacity, and executive attention remain scarce. Ten $25,000 pilots are not necessarily a cheap $250,000 portfolio if all ten depend on the same three people in KM and IT and compete for the attention of the same lawyers who must determine whether the results have real value.

So cheaper experimentation should not produce an indiscriminate explosion of pilots. It should let us put more of our important assumptions to the test before making expensive commitments.

This is where those early science classes become useful. An experiment designed only to prove something works is less useful than one designed to discover what might make the next investment a mistake. If an inexpensive experiment tells you that a proposed AI system works beautifully under one set of conditions but becomes unreliable under another, the experiment has bought information that can change what you do next.

Cheap experimentation should make ignorance harder to defend.

When Several Experiments Become One Bet

There is one more problem that does not appear on any individual pilot proposal. Five different groups can bring forward five genuinely different AI initiatives and still be making substantially the same underlying bet.

The KM project, corporate project, BD project, and litigation projects might all depend on the same foundation model, enterprise platform, retrieval architecture, or assumption that lawyers will reliably catch a certain category of error. Viewed project by project, you appear to be experimenting broadly. Viewed as a portfolio, you may be concentrating rapidly around a small number of untested assumptions.

So before approving the next commitment, look not only at the experiment in front of you but also across the table. What assumptions do these supposedly different experiments share? What scarce institutional capacity are they competing for? Where are you unintentionally climbing several commitment ladders at once?

The Option-Value Test

Before approving the next stage of an AI initiative, ask three questions.

1. The Uncertainty Question: What specific, consequential uncertainty are we paying to reduce?

2. The Cost-to-Learn Question: What is the smallest, cheapest, most reversible experiment that will meaningfully reduce that uncertainty?

3. The Pivot Question: What specific decision will change depending on what the evidence reveals?

The third question is the one most likely to expose a disguised implementation. If no plausible result will cause you to stop, redirect, narrow, expand, accelerate, or delay the commitment, the experiment is not functioning as an option. You are rehearsing a decision already made.

The purpose of an AI experiment is to acquire evidence that improves your ability to make the next consequential allocation decision about a specific AI use for the actual job to be done. Some experiments should move rapidly. Some should earn substantial institutional commitment. Others should end, not because they failed, but because they succeeded in telling you not to spend the next dollar there.

Prudent AI treats early AI investments as opportunities to buy information and preserve choices, not as down payments on predetermined implementations. Let evidence earn greater commitment while preserving the capacity to choose differently when it doesn’t.

Accelerate reversible learning. Pace irreversible commitment.

Dennis Kennedy – CC BY 4.0 license

news.titleEn: New Code, Old Rules: 9th Circuit Says GitHub Copilot’s Output Is Not a “Copy” Under the DMCA
news.titleZh: 新代码，旧规则：第九巡回法院称GitHub Copilot的输出不构成DMCA下的“复制品”
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月16日，美国第九巡回上诉法院在Doe诉GitHub案中，维持了地区法院对原告根据《数字千年版权法》（DMCA）第1202(b)条提出的索赔的驳回裁定。GitHub Copilot在生成代码时并未“移除或篡改”现有作品中的版权管理信息（CMI），因为其输出是全新作品，而非对存储作品的复制。原告是一组在GitHub公共仓库发布开源代码的程序员，他们指控Copilot和Codex有时会复制其代码，但未附上原始文件中的署名、版权声明或许可条款。原告将此定性为违反DMCA的CMI条款，而非普通版权侵权，可能是因为DMCA允许每项违规最高25,000美元的法定赔偿。原告提出了两种理论：一是“输入”理论，即GitHub和OpenAI在将代码输入训练数据前剥离了CMI；法院认为原告未纠正地区法院关于案件不涉及训练的陈述，因此放弃了该理论。二是“输出”理论，即Copilot在响应用户提示时复制代码但未附CMI；法院认为原告具有诉讼资格，但驳回了其实体主张。移除或篡改”是对已存在事物的积极行为，而Copilot根据统计模式生成新输出，并非检索存储文件，因此其输出从未包含CMI。法院还警告，若将实质性相似视为足以构成第1202(b)条索赔，将使DMCA的增强法定赔偿取代传统版权侵权索赔。该裁决未解决AI生成代码是否侵犯版权的问题，原告对GitHub的违约索赔仍在地区法院审理中。对于使用版权材料训练AI模型的公司，此案提示应记录模型生成输出的实际过程，而非仅记录训练数据。但该裁决并不免除版权侵权风险，法院明确区分了DMCA索赔与普通版权索赔。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! AI developers who train large language models on copyrighted code just cleared a significant legal hurdle. On September 16, 2026, the 9th Circuit affirmed dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claim in Doe v. GitHub, Inc. under Section 1202(b) of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, holding that Copilot does not “remove or alter” copyright management information from an existing work when it generates code, because it creates a new work rather than reproducing a stored one. A group of programmers who published open-source code on public GitHub repositories alleged that Copilot and Codex sometimes reproduce their code without the attribution, copyright notices, or license terms that accompany the original files. They framed this as a violation of the DMCA’s copyright management information (CMI) provisions rather than as ordinary copyright infringement, likely because the DMCA allows statutory damages of up to $25,000 per violation. The plaintiffs raised two distinct theories. Under the first, an “input” theory, GitHub and OpenAI supposedly stripped CMI from licensed code before feeding it into Copilot’s training data. The panel refused to consider this theory at all, finding that the plaintiffs had forfeited it by failing to correct the district court’s repeated statements that the case was not about training. That left the second theory, the “output” theory. Copilot allegedly reproduces near identical or identical copies of a programmer’s code in response to user prompts, without the CMI attached to the original. The 9th Circuit agreed the plaintiffs had standing to bring this claim, since they plausibly alleged a substantial risk that their code would eventually be reproduced this way. But standing only got them in the door. The court’s reasoning turns on what it means to “remove or alter” CMI. Judge Eric Miller’s opinion holds that both verbs describe an affirmative act performed on something that already exists. You cannot remove or alter CMI from a work unless there was a copy of that work, with its CMI attached, in the first place. Copilot, according to the complaint’s own description, does not retrieve and display stored files the way a search engine does. It identifies statistical patterns in the training data and generates a new output based on the most probable completion of a prompt. Because the resulting code is a newly created work rather than a reproduction of an existing one, the court held it never contained CMI to remove or alter in the first place. The opinion is careful to note that this is not a strict identicality requirement. Minor cosmetic edits will not save a defendant who otherwise reproduces a protected work wholesale and strips its CMI. What matters is whether the output can fairly be described as a copy of an existing work missing its CMI, or whether it is a new work that never had CMI attached to begin with. On the facts alleged here, the court placed Copilot’s output in the second category. The court also flagged the stakes of ruling otherwise. Treating ordinary substantial similarity between an AI output and a protectable work as enough to state a Section 1202(b) claim would let the DMCA’s enhanced statutory damages swallow traditional copyright infringement claims, which cap statutory damages at $30,000 per work rather than per violation. The panel declined to let a DMCA claim do that work. This decision does not resolve whether AI-generated code or other AI outputs infringe copyright. The panel expressly said it was not deciding that question, and the plaintiffs’ breach of contract claims against GitHub are still pending in the district court. What this decision does is close off one aggressive route to statutory damages against AI developers, at least within the 9th Circuit and at least on an output theory framed the way these plaintiffs framed it. For companies building or licensing generative AI tools that train on copyrighted or licensed material, the practical lesson is to document how a model actually generates its output, not just what it was trained on. The plaintiffs here lost in large part because their own complaint described Copilot’s process in terms that supported the court’s characterization of its output as a new work, so companies defending similar claims will want a clear, accurate technical record showing the model predicts likely completions rather than retrieving stored files. That said, this ruling is no shield against copyright infringement exposure generally. The court repeatedly distinguished the DMCA claim from a traditional copyright claim and noted that substantial similarity between an output and a protected work could still support an infringement theory, so that analysis remains a live risk entirely separate from CMI removal.

news.titleEn: LegalZoom Co-Founder Brian Lee Joins Steno Board
news.titleZh: LegalZoom联合创始人Brian Lee加入Steno董事会
news.summaryZh: Steno是一家提供法庭记录和AI驱动诉讼支持的先驱公司，近日宣布任命Brian Lee为其董事会成员。Lee于2000年共同创立了LegalZoom，该平台为消费者和小型企业提供负担得起的在线法律帮助，在当时被视为该领域的开创性企业。离开LegalZoom的全职岗位后，Lee成为连续创业者，在多家公司担任高级职位或共同创立公司，包括ShoeDazzle、The Honest Company、BAM Ventures、Art of Sport和Arena Club，其中部分公司有名人参与，如科比·布莱恩特。Lee引导LegalZoom经历了巨大的早期增长，收入超过3亿美元，并为其最终上市（纳斯达克：LZ）奠定了基础，上市时市值达70亿美元。Lee早年曾在Skadden律师事务所担任律师，如今重返法律界。此次任命之前，Steno在今年早些时候完成了4900万美元的C轮融资。在诉讼支持领域，软件本身无法取代律师在庭审时所需的可靠性、高触感执行和信任；Steno之所以突出，是因为它优先考虑客户体验，将服务视为核心优势而非事后考虑。他期待加入董事会，帮助首席执行官Prabhdeep和领导团队将Steno的服务优先模式扩展到整个法律行业。Steno的优势在于其混合模式，即提供白手套式礼宾级服务，同时配备专为诉讼律师打造的AI和法律科技工具。他认为Brian在构建法律行业市场定义型服务公司方面无人能及，其将LegalZoom从早期概念发展为行业标准的经验，对Steno继续扩大其顶级诉讼支持合作伙伴足迹将极具价值。
news.bodyText: AL doesn’t often do board roles, but this is a biggy, so…..Steno, the court reporting and AI-driven litigation support pioneer, has appointed Brian Lee to its Board of Directors. Lee co-founded LegalZoom in 2000 – which was then seen as a ground-breaking venture for this sector, as it provided consumers and small businesses with affordable online legal help. After leaving his full-time role at LegalZoom, Lee went on to become a serial entrepreneur, taking on senior positions at, and/or co-founding, several other companies that included: ShoeDazzle, The Honest Company, BAM Ventures, Art of Sport, and Arena Club – sometimes with celebrity involvement, such as with Kobe Bryant. Steno noted that Lee ‘guided LegalZoom through immense early growth, expanding revenue beyond $300 million and laying the foundation for its eventual public offering (NASDAQ: LZ) at a $7 billion market capitalization’. Now, Lee – who long ago worked as a lawyer at Skadden – has come back to the legal world. The move also follows Steno’s $49 million Series C funding round earlier this year. Lee commented: ‘In litigation support, software alone cannot replace the reliability, high-touch execution, and trust that attorneys need when bringing a case to trial. Steno stands out because it prioritizes the client experience, treating service as a core strength rather than an afterthought. I am thrilled to join the board and help Prabhdeep [the CEO] and the leadership team scale Steno’s service-first model across the legal industry.’ Prabhdeep Singh, Chief Executive Officer of Steno, added: ‘Steno’s strength is in its hybrid model: we deliver white-glove, concierge-level services alongside AI and legal tech tools built specifically for litigators. ‘Brian understands how to build market-defining service companies in the legal sector better than anyone. His experience expanding LegalZoom from an early concept into an industry standard will be invaluable as we continue to scale our footprint as a top-tier litigation support partner.’ More about Steno here. — Legal Innovators UK – Nov 4 and 5 / Legal Innovators New York – Nov 17 and 18 Cosmonauts have now opened Express Registration for Legal Innovators UK and New York. This means that if you are at a law firm or at an inhouse legal team you can now zoom directly to your tickets – which are complimentary as long as you qualify. news.titleEn: With August, A Company’s Agents Ask Lawyers For Help
news.titleZh: August推出新功能：企业AI代理可向律师寻求帮助
news.summaryZh: 法律AI平台August推出新功能“August for Agents”，允许公司内部的AI代理向律师请求帮助，这可能为律所带来更多业务。该功能呼应了Artificial Lawyer上Damien Charlotin提出的“Humans for AI”思想实验，即代理需要人类律师协助才能完全发挥作用。公司在采购、销售等业务中使用代理，这些代理常遇到关于签署、共享或批准内容的问题，新功能让代理在工作流程中直接向公司律师提问。对于某些公司，这可能是其选择的律所，也可能是内部法务团队。外部化查询适用于内部团队无法回答的问题，或公司尚未建立内部法务团队的情况。该功能并非替代律所，也不是让客户信任来自开放互联网的匿名法律答案，而是为客户选择的律所提供新的工作交付方式，比传统接收流程更快，但仍由律所定义和监督服务。例如，采购代理在续签供应商协议时发现客户数据处理限制，可将条款和拟议行动发送给公司律所运行的服务，若律所授权代理处理则立即回答，否则由律师审查批准。律所可构建“可重复法律工作包”，以服务形式提供，包含明确输入、范围和固定价格，并决定代理可使用的材料，August提供访问控制、支持来源和每次请求的记录，律所对建议负责。公司将实际工作交给代理，这些代理不断遇到只有律师才能回答的问题，通过August for Agents，客户代理可随时向其律所提问，律所通过其律师构建和监督的服务回答。若运行顺畅，这一举措将既适用于将请求转给内部团队的公司，也适用于没有自己律师的小公司。
news.bodyText: Legal AI platform, August, is launching a new feature that allows AI agents working inside a company to request help from lawyers – which could drive more work to law firms. It’s a novel take on the use of legal agents and echoes a recent thought experiment by Damien Charlotin in Artificial Lawyer titled ‘Humans for AI’ – see here – about how agents will need to call upon human lawyers to fully function. In this case, August – which offers a broad range of legal AI skills – explained that ‘companies now use agents for procurement, sales and other business work. Those agents regularly reach questions about what they can sign, share or approve. ‘August for Agents’ lets them put those questions to the company’s lawyers from inside the workflow’. August notes that for some companies this may be ‘their chosen firm’, but equally AL would say that this could be the inhouse legal team, if it’s a company with one. Naturally, externalising such queries would work when those issues where either ones that an inhouse team could not answer, or where a company is at a stage where they don’t have an inhouse legal group yet. As they explained: ‘August for Agents is designed around that allocation of responsibility. It is not a substitute law firm, and it does not ask a client to trust an anonymous legal answer from the open internet. It gives the client’s chosen firm a new way to deliver work: faster than a traditional intake process, but still within a service the firm defines and supervises.’ They then gave the following example: a procurement agent is renewing a supplier agreement and might find a restriction on how customer data may be processed. It can send the clause and the proposed action to a service run by the company’s law firm. The firm’s agent (via August) answers right away, if the firm has authorised it to handle that issue. Otherwise a lawyer at the firm reviews the question and signs off. — Advertisement — — August also said that law firms could build ‘packages of repeatable legal work as a service with defined inputs, a clear scope and a fixed price’. The law firm also then decides which materials the agents may use, and August provides access controls, supporting sources and a record of each request. Plus, the law firm stays responsible for the advice to the client, which is connecting to them via the agents. Thomas Bueler-Faudree, co-founder of August, commented: ‘Companies are handing real work to agents, and those agents keep hitting questions only a lawyer should answer. With August for Agents, a client’s agent can ask its own law firm at any time, and the firm answers through a service its lawyers built and supervise.’ Is this a big deal? Well, it’s a smart move, if it can be made to work smoothly. And as noted, it would function just as well for a company that can channel requests to their inhouse team, as well as smaller ones without their own lawyers, which are sending out legal requests to favoured external counsel.

news.titleEn: Ex-Freshfields Lawyers Launch New Model Firm
news.titleZh: 前富而德律师创办新型律所
news.summaryZh: 荷兰阿姆斯特丹新成立一家新型律所Driven Lawyers，由Jelle Drok和Arvid van Oorschot共同创立。Drok此前是富而德律师事务所的合伙人，van Oorschot曾是当地律所Vondst的合伙人，并在富而德工作超过六年。该律所专注于商事争议、知识产权法以及合同与责任法，致力于为企业预防和解决复杂的法律问题。他们宁愿成为构建AI的人，而不是开会讨论AI的人。这是一家将技术和AI尽可能全面融入工作与运营的律所，AI不仅是工具，更是工作方式的基础。该律所还推行固定收费模式，认为固定价格并非折扣，而是对流程深入理解后的逻辑结果。他们自主研发了技术平台Driven Drafter，这是创始人在过去一年中开发的软件平台，将知识以框架形式嵌入其中，律师通过与系统“切磋”来起草文件。该平台是一个受控环境，每项陈述都锚定于可直接验证的来源，从而负责任地代表客户部署AI，带来更高质量和更低成本。该系统的附加价值在于安全地将法律领域知识与经验同最佳AI相结合，律师因此既是开发者又是用户。
news.bodyText: We’ve seen new model law firms proliferate in the US and UK, and now here’s one in the Netherlands: Driven Lawyers, created by Jelle Drok and Arvid van Oorschot. Drok was a partner at Freshfields until recently, meanwhile van Oorschot was a partner at local firm Vondst and also spent over six years at Freshfields before that. The Amsterdam-based NewMod specialises in commercial disputes, intellectual property law, and contract and liability law. It focuses on preventing and resolving complex legal problems for businesses, they added. Co-founder Drok commented in terms of the firm’s raison d’être: ‘We’d rather be among the people building AI, than among the people holding meetings about it.’ They underlined that they are ‘a law firm in which technology and AI are integrated into the work and the operation as fully as possible – not merely as a tool, but as the very basis of the way of working’. And that’s very much in the new model spirit. They are also very much about fixed fees as well – again another key pillar of the new model movement. As they explain: ‘Every case has recognisable patterns, but also often unforeseen or unpredictable factors. We know that process inside out. Because we have automated part of the process, our analysis of the expected time involved is sharper. We rely on our experience to estimate the remaining steps, and we understand where the value lies for the client. ‘A fixed price is therefore not a discount offer. It is the logical consequence of a thorough understanding of the approach that leads to results.’ They have also built their own tech capabilities. For example, they added that the technical core of Driven Lawyers is the Driven Drafter, a software platform the founders have developed themselves over the past year. In it, they have embedded their knowledge in the form of frameworks, which they use to draft documents by ‘sparring’ with the system. It is a controlled environment in which every statement is anchored to a directly verifiable source. This allows AI to be deployed responsibly on behalf of clients. And that leads to higher quality and lower costs, they explained. Drok noted: ‘The added value of our system is that it safely combines our legal domain knowledge and experience with the best AI available.’ This meant, he added, that ‘the lawyers are therefore both developers and users’.
news.relevanceReason: 文章核心是新型律所将AI作为工作方式基础，并自主研发法律技术平台，属于法律AI与法律科技领域。

research.titleEn: LAURA: Knowledge Distillation for Interpretable Ambiguous Clause Identification in Legal Contracts
research.titleZh: LAURA：法律合同中可解释歧义条款识别的知识蒸馏
research.abstractEn: Legal contracts contain ambiguities that expose enterprises to financial and legal risks. Some ambiguities allow flexible interpretation without triggering disputes, while others lead to significant legal conflicts. This makes identification alone insufficient, and interpretable rationale analysis essential. We propose LAURA, a post-training framework for interpretable ambiguous clause identification. LAURA leverages knowledge distillation with an IRAC-Unlearning prompting technique to transfer knowledge from a teacher LLM to an open-weight student model (<=1B parameters), which is then trained using a joint objective combining classification and rationale generation losses. The framework supports both legal and non-legal stakeholders in making informed decisions about which ambiguities require further attention. Extensive experiments across 7 baselines and 7 open-weight models demonstrate that LAURA with Flan-T5 (250M) delivers state-of-the-art interpretability over all interpretable baselines while matching the identification performance of the best-performing opaque baseline.
research.abstractZh: 法律合同中的歧义使企业面临财务和法律风险。某些歧义允许灵活解释而不会引发争议，而其他歧义则可能导致重大法律冲突。这使得仅识别歧义是不够的，可解释的推理分析至关重要。我们提出了LAURA，一个用于可解释歧义条款识别的训练后框架。LAURA利用知识蒸馏和IRAC-取消提示技术，将知识从教师大语言模型转移到开放权重学生模型（参数不超过10亿），然后使用结合分类和推理生成损失的联合目标对该模型进行训练。该框架支持法律和非法律利益相关者就哪些歧义需要进一步关注做出明智决策。在7个基线和7个开放权重模型上的广泛实验表明，带有Flan-T5（250M）的LAURA在所有可解释基线上实现了最先进的可解释性，同时匹配了表现最佳的不透明基线的识别性能。

policy.titleEn: What Counts as Scientific Research? The EU’s Digital Omnibus Could Set the Definition
policy.titleZh: 什么算科学研究？欧盟数字综合法案或可定义其边界
policy.summaryZh: 欧盟《数字综合法案》的多数关注集中在隐私影响及130多个民间社会组织和工会的警告上，即该法案是欧盟迄今最大规模的数字权利倒退。但其中一段简短条文首次尝试在《通用数据保护条例》中写入“科学研究”的定义，其影响远超数据保护范畴。目前欧盟没有任何法律文书在操作性条款中定义研究，版权法在文本与数据挖掘例外及研究机构待遇中反复引用该概念却未作定义，欧盟委员会正在就统一研究版权例外征求意见，未来《欧洲研究区法案》也将需要定义支撑。2025年11月，欧盟委员会提出新第4(38)条，将研究定义为“亦可支持创新的任何研究，如技术开发和示范”，要求有助于现有科学知识或以新颖方式应用现有知识，旨在促进社会普遍知识和福祉增长，并遵守相关研究领域的伦理标准，且不排除研究同时追求商业利益。欧洲议会产业、研究与能源委员会和公民自由、司法与内政委员会共同负责该文件，报告人为欧洲人民党芬兰议员Aura Salla和社会民主党爱沙尼亚议员Marina Kaljurand，两人2026年6月的联合草案基本保留了委员会定义，但随后提出对立修正案：Salla遵循经合组织研发模板，Kaljurand删除商业利益条款并将研究限定为自主的公共利益工作。修正案沿五条断层线展开：是否应定义、AI开发测试是否算研究、研究还是研发、方法及意图立法问题、自主性与独立性。
policy.bodyText:
What Counts as Scientific Research? The EU’s Digital Omnibus Could Set the Definition Stephen Wyber / Sep 29, 2026 “ European Parliament ” by piotr iłowiecki , CC BY-SA 2.0

Republish

Most of the attention on the European Union's Digital Omnibus has gone to what it does to privacy, and to the warning from more than 130 civil society organizations and unions that it is the largest rollback of digital rights the Union has attempted. Less noticed is a short passage that would, for the first time, write a definition of "scientific research" into the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

That passage's impact extends well beyond data protection. No EU instrument currently defines research in its operative provisions. Copyright law relies on the idea repeatedly, in the exceptions for text and data mining and in the treatment of research organizations, without defining it, and the Commission is now consulting on a harmonized copyright exception for research that will need a definition to rest on. So will the forthcoming European Research Area (ERA) Act . A definition agreed in the GDPR could become an important reference point for EU legislation.

In this context, the Commission published its own proposal in November 2025, in the shape of a new Article 4(38) GDPR:

“any research which can also support innovation, such as technological development and demonstration. These actions shall contribute to existing scientific knowledge or apply existing knowledge in novel ways, be carried out with the aim of contributing to the growth of society´s general knowledge and wellbeing and adhere to ethical standards in the relevant research area. This does not exclude that the research may also aim to further a commercial interest.’” In the European Parliament, the file is shared between the Industry, Research and Energy (ITRE) and Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE) Committees, with Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) Aura Salla (European People's Party, Finland) and Marina Kaljurand (Socialists and Democrats, Estonia) as rapporteurs. Their June 2026 joint draft report left the Commission's definition largely in place.

Since then, the two MEPs have tabled opposing definitions : MEP Salla's follows the OECD template for research and development (R&D), while MEP Kaljurand's drops the commercial-interest sentence and confines research to autonomous, public-interest work. The argument is now in the amendments , tabled in large numbers, that the committees have to work through.

For the researchers, universities and libraries that Knowledge Rights 21 ( KR21 ) represents, the definition will help determine which activity carries the freedoms the GDPR attaches to research, and which does not.

The amendments fall along five fault lines.

1. Should there be a definition at all? Some MEPs would delete the definition outright on the grounds that this forms a basis for lighter obligations under GDPR, and so lower data protection. The concern is legitimate. However, removing the definition leaves regulators and courts to draw the boundary case by case, which is the uncertainty researchers already face. A clear statutory definition could provide greater legal certainty than leaving the boundary to case-by-case interpretation.

2. Does building and testing AI count as research? The Commission’s proposed definition says nothing about artificial intelligence (AI). Several amendments would change that by introducing explicit confirmation that developing, training, testing and validating AI systems can be scientific research where the general conditions are met.

Others (from far-left and far-right parties) actively state that the development, training or optimization of AI should be excluded.

None of this sits easily with what the Commission is saying elsewhere. When Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen launched the AI Continent Action Plan in April 2025, her first argument was talent: Europe, she said, has an "unparalleled pool" of it, and 30 percent more AI researchers than the United States. Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva has spent the same period making the case for science to choose Europe, with a Choose Europe for Science package now approaching 1 billion euros . In November, the two jointly launched RAISE , a virtual institute for AI in science.

The Commission is recruiting AI researchers to Europe and counting them as a strategic asset. That creates a potential tension between the Commission’s AI-in-science policy and a GDPR definition that could exclude core AI development, training or testing from “scientific research”.

3. Research, or research and development? The deepest split is over how far downstream the definition reaches. The Commission's text expressly includes activity that supports innovation, such as technological development and demonstration, and says research does not stop being research because it also serves a commercial interest. One group of amendments keeps that breadth: some actively confirm that privately funded research is covered, add a reference to competitiveness, or clarify that work inside a company, or feeding later commercial use, is still research.

MEP Axel Voss goes furthest, with a justification that research should be defined "by its purpose, methodology and contribution to knowledge, not by whether it is carried out by academia, public bodies or companies".

Others pull the other way, from the Greens through to ESN, removing the reference to innovation to keep the definition focused on core research.

This is the line KR21 has argued over for years . European copyright law already separates commercial from non-commercial research in a way that Europe's main competitors (US, China, Japan, Singapore) do not, and that separation makes collaboration between universities and companies harder than it needs to be. A GDPR definition that keeps commercial-facing research inside the boundary, as the Commission's does, is the sounder starting point.

4. Method, and the problem of legislating intention A separate group of amendments would write in tests for what type of research qualifies. Amendments from the S&D and the Greens would require research to be methodical and systematic; while two EPP amendments would make it "creative and systematic", documented and traceable, and point to the OECD's Frascati Manual , the standard reference for defining R&D.

There are also calls to obligate publishing, following peer review, with a view to ensuring that the results can subsequently be checked. Much of this tracks the joint opinion of the EU's two data-protection authorities, which asked for a systematic method, independent conduct and verifiable results. A linked set of proposals would judge research by intent, asking whether it is "genuinely intended" to produce such results.

Worth noting is what nobody disputes: the Commission's text already requires research to follow the ethical standards of its field, with amendments from various MEPs adding respect for participants' autonomy and consent. Those are the safeguards that protect people. The risk lies in tests that a regulator, or a rights holder, can use to second-guess whether a project is "genuine" enough: the kind of open-ended judgment that chills researchers and hands a lever to anyone with an interest in restricting access to their work. Objective, method-based criteria are workable. Subjective tests of intention are not.

5. Autonomy and independence A final theme, running through amendments from the S&D, Renew and the Greens group, is that research should be conducted autonomously and free from undue pressure.

A recital from the Renew group would permit commercial and private interests while asking that processing be kept "functionally separated from commercial monetization, tracking, or profiling.” Independence is a real principle of good research and worth stating.

Drawn too tightly, though, a functional-separation test could catch the ordinary public-private research that EU funding policy actively encourages. Such language should protect researchers from interference, not turn collaboration itself into a mark against the research claim.

What the committees should hold onto A workable definition is not hard to describe. It covers research that supports innovation and enables research centers to partner easily with start-ups, scale-ups and industry in general. It is explicit that developing and testing AI can count as research. It rests on objective, method-based criteria rather than judgments about a researcher's intent. And it treats independence as a protection for researchers rather than a disqualification of their partners.

That is close to what the Commission proposed: inclusion of development and innovation, an open definition of methods, a focus on overall goals, and adherence to ethical standards.

The reason to get it right is that the GDPR is not where this definition will stop. Once adopted, it could become a reference point the next time the EU legislates on research, on data, or on copyright, because no other instrument offers such a definition. The two committees are not only deciding how the data-protection rules treat science. They are writing down, for the rest of the body of EU law to borrow, what Europe means by research.

For now, the Omnibus is under negotiation in both the European Parliament and the Council (Member States), with the ambition of finalizing the dossier by the end of the year. Nonetheless, on a dossier with many potential political sticking points, sufficient consensus may still take longer to find.

policy.titleEn: AI Transparency Starts With the Audience
policy.titleZh: AI透明度始于受众
policy.summaryZh: 本文由邓斯坦·艾利森-霍普和萨姆·华莱士撰写，探讨AI公司应如何更具战略性地进行信息披露。萨姆·华莱士是人工智能合作组织（PAI）公司治理、风险与负责任实践负责人，该组织发布了本文讨论的披露建议草案。邓斯坦·艾利森-霍普是独立顾问，PAI是其客户之一。文章提到，Anthropic本月发布了最新威胁情报报告，概述了其破坏的现实威胁及趋势，包括马里监控约2500万张SIM卡的国内监控系统、中国的电子战和防空压制软件，以及也门的制导、导航和控制软件。Anthropic发布这些报告旨在帮助政府、网络安全团队和同行AI开发者识别和破坏类似威胁，并为基于证据的AI政策提供信息。随着AI进入更多行业，需要更战略性的披露方法，并提出三个关键因素：了解报告受众、关注实质性信息、应用高信息质量标准。不同受众需要不同信息，例如投资者关注财务风险，政府关注社会影响，民间社会组织关注人权影响。正式报告应遵循一致性、可比性、及时性、清晰性和准确性等原则。PAI今年早些时候发布了披露建议草案，目前正在征求意见。文章最后通过表格展示了不同报告类型对不同受众的用途，并呼吁采取更战略性的透明度方法。
policy.bodyText:
AI Transparency Starts With the Audience Dunstan Allison-Hope, Sam Wallace / Sep 29, 2026 Sam Wallace is Head of Corporate Governance, Risk, and Responsible Practice at Partnership on AI (PAI), which published the disclosure recommendations discussed in this article. Dunstan Allison-Hope is an independent consultant, and PAI is among his clients.

Shutterstock

Republish

Earlier this month, Anthropic published its latest Threat Intelligence Report , outlining real-world threats the company disrupted and the trends these cases reveal. These threats spanned topics including surveillance (such as a domestic surveillance system monitoring roughly 25 million SIM cards in Mali), cybersecurity and electronic warfare (such as developing software for electronic warfare and suppression of air defenses in China), and conventional weapons (such as developing guidance, navigation, and control software in Yemen).

Anthropic publishes Threat Intelligence Reports to help governments, cybersecurity teams, and peer AI developers identify and disrupt similar threats. The reports also inform evidence-based AI policy by grounding discussions in real-world cases and are part of Anthropic’s approach to corporate accountability.

Amid all the discussion about existential risk, reports like this remind us of the real near-term impacts and how they may evolve. As AI moves into more industries — from healthcare and education to infrastructure and aerospace — it creates new risks and opportunities. The concrete case studies offer far more specificity than “AI-will-kill-us-all” and show how addressing near-term risks also helps prepare for the long term.

Thus, while fascinating in their own right, these Threat Intelligence Reports underscore the need for a more strategic approach to AI-related disclosure, reporting, and transparency. What information about AI should companies publish, for whom, and what decisions might these reports inform? How can we move toward greater consistency and comparability of disclosure across the AI industry and over time, while remaining nimble amid AI's changing dynamics and impacts?

We have both spent decades addressing similar questions in sustainability/ESG reporting, where we have sought to enhance the quality of disclosures companies make on topics such as climate change, human rights, and community impacts. Based on this experience, we believe three key factors should shape a more strategic approach to reporting by AI companies.

One: Know the audience for the report Companies should publish reports so that report readers can make informed decisions. However, a challenge in reporting is that multiple audiences need different information to make different decisions.

For example, investors need information about risks and opportunities for a company’s financial position so that they can allocate capital and manage portfolios. Governments need information about the impacts of a company or technology on society and the economy so that they can make good policies and enforce regulation effectively. Civil society organizations need information about a company's impacts on people so they can advocate for human rights protection, social justice, and community well-being. AI researchers need information to inform AI safety and security strategies.

Not all of these needs will be satisfied in a single report; in AI, some readers are interested in the AI model, some in the overall AI system, and some in the corporation.

Two: Focus on material information that helps someone make a decision A core principle of financial and sustainability reporting standards is that all material information must be disclosed. In formal reporting, information is considered material if its omission, misstatement, or obscuring could reasonably be expected to influence the decisions of the report's primary users.

The challenge for companies is that what the report user considers material varies depending on the decisions they are trying to make and the reader's expertise.

For example, an AI system's performance against various benchmarks may be useful information to AI researchers or customers, but it's unlikely to mean much to investors or policymakers.

Companies often report on programs and practices they have in place. This can be useful, but more high-level information is more likely to be material. What are the real risks, and where do they concentrate in a company's operations and value chain? What is a company’s overall strategy, and how does it compare to its competitors? Who is ultimately responsible for risk management in the company’s management and board, and how is accountability structured?

Much of our work focuses on investors, and there’s a common assumption that investors only care about financial returns. Whether that's true or not, a company’s ability to navigate the AI age depends on a complex set of relationships with customers, governments, society, and natural resources.

The backlash against data centers is one example of how risks from public opinion and regulation can quickly snowball into major threats to the AI business. We can only expect more of this as AI revolutionizes additional industries and, inevitably, impacts stakeholders beyond businesses. We all deserve better information from companies about how they are navigating these complex issues.

Three: Apply high standards of information quality Formal reporting differs from other forms of communication because it should adhere to principles of information quality, such as consistency, comparability, and timeliness. Formal reporting on a regular schedule differs from publishing a blog post or long-form essay every so often, and AI companies should adopt several well-developed reporting principles when shaping their disclosure strategies. For example:

Comparability: Use of standardized topics and disclosure formats so readers can track performance over time and benchmark against other companies. Consistency: Use of uniform methodologies, reporting boundaries, and categories of information year over year. Timeliness: Disclosures should be made on a regular, predictable schedule so information is available when decisions are made. Clarity / Understandability: Information should be organized, clear, and accessible to its intended audience. Accuracy: Data and qualitative statements should be precise, rigorously calculated, and free from material error or misleading approximations. Bringing it together Transparency is often promoted as a core principle in responsible AI, but in practice its meaning and implications vary significantly by context. For example, transparency with individual users about their use of an AI application differs greatly from transparency with enterprise deployers about the risks of an AI system, and different again from corporate-level SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission) filings.

Earlier this year, Partnership on AI published draft Disclosure Recommendations to help companies identify material information about the impacts, risks, and opportunities associated with AI to include in their financial, sustainability, and other public reports. These draft Disclosure Recommendations are currently open for feedback and point to a broader question about what information is actually useful to the people making AI-related decisions.

Corporate disclosure is only one part of that question. System cards, regulator-required reports, and incident reports serve different purposes and audiences. A system card may help a technical audience understand model capabilities and limitations, while an incident report may help regulators, companies or researchers understand what went wrong and how to prevent recurrence. Treating all of these forms of disclosure simply as “transparency” can obscure these important differences.

The goal is not only greater transparency in the abstract, but more useful information for specific decisions. We have mapped these different forms of reporting according to their purpose, intended audience, and usefulness to that audience. As AI companies and their stakeholders rush into an agenda of increased transparency, we encourage a more strategic approach.

Which reports serve which audiences. Cells show whether each report type is a primary, relevant, or limited source of information for a given audience.

Report type Investors Material risks and opportunities for financial position Stakeholders Material impacts on people, society, and the environment Regulators Assuring compliance and developing policy Enterprise clients & developers Operational risk and performance of AI model/system Insurers Risk exposure Safety researchers Public good and infrastructure security

SEC filings (or equivalent) Company's financial performance and risks Primary Relevant Primary Limited Primary Limited

ESRS sustainability statements Company's sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities Primary Primary Primary Limited Relevant Limited

Model and system cards How an AI works, intended use cases, performance metrics, and limitations Relevant Relevant Primary Primary Primary Primary

Voluntary ESG/sustainability reports Company's sustainability impacts Relevant Primary Limited Limited Limited Limited

Voluntary AI reports Company's responsible AI governance, strategy, and risk management Relevant Primary Limited Relevant Limited Relevant

Transparency reports How user data is handled and content policy enforced Limited Primary Relevant Limited Limited Primary

Regulated reports Public reports required by specific regulations (e.g., DSA) Limited Relevant Primary Limited Relevant Relevant

Incident/threat reports Documented failures, malfunctions, or unintended harms Relevant Limited Primary Primary Primary Primary

ESRS: European Sustainability Reporting Standards .

policy.summaryZh: 欧盟数字战略平台发起一项定向咨询，旨在为欧洲创意与创新营造更好的版权环境。该咨询通过EUSurvey问卷形式进行，围绕潜在倡议收集利益相关方意见。问卷涵盖多个主题，包括版权与生成式人工智能、生成式AI作品的许可与版权及相关权利执法、AI生成的对表演者的模仿、时效性受版权保护内容的在线盗版、非欧盟国家国民录音制品在欧盟的使用、版权与研究等。咨询要求参与者填写身份信息，并针对各主题提供反馈。问卷还涉及对生成式AI相关版权问题的具体看法，如AI生成内容的法律责任、授权机制等。该咨询是欧盟数字战略的一部分，旨在评估现有版权框架是否适应人工智能等新技术发展，并为可能的立法或政策调整提供依据。咨询通过在线平台收集意见，参与者可提交书面回复。此次咨询反映了欧盟对版权制度现代化的关注，特别是在人工智能快速发展的背景下，如何平衡创作者权益、技术创新与公共利益。

news.titleEn: Exclusive: Legal tech leader David Lumsden joins Jalubro as advisor to the board
news.titleZh: 独家：法律科技领袖David Lumsden加入Jalubro担任董事会顾问
news.summaryZh: 英国法律转型咨询公司Jalubro任命法律科技领域资深高管David Lumsden为董事会顾问。Lumsden拥有三十余年企业建设与规模化发展经验，其职业生涯始于国际律师事务所Ashurst的CIO职位，随后担任Tikit Group首席执行官长达13年，推动公司发展直至被BT收购。2017年，他出任RAVN Systems CEO，带领公司完成被iManage收购的过渡。此后，他还担任过Enable Business Solutions及法律科技咨询公司Pinnacle的CEO。2024年Harbor收购Pinnacle后，Lumsden加入Harbor国际领导团队，担任区域运营与整合负责人直至2025年6月。此次任命正值Jalubro加速技术业务并推出新AI治理平台Ephiria之际。随着律所和法律团队采用Harvey、CoCounsel、Legora和Claude等AI工具，AI从辅助律师的副驾驶演变为能够跨系统和流程行动的智能体，组织面临如何治理和记录这些活动的挑战。Ephiria在该环境中提供独立控制层，在使用和执行点应用组织、客户和事务级政策，通过编辑在信息到达AI模型前保护敏感数据，并在行动前约束AI智能体的权限。Lumsden将为Jalubro领导层提供技术战略、国际增长和业务持续扩展方面的建议。Lumsden参与了过去三十年法律科技领域最重要企业的建设，很少有人能兼具他对律所和技术的理解以及建设科技企业的商业经验。Jalubro已是一家成熟企业，服务全球律所和企业法务团队，公司目标是开发更多自有技术，Lumsden的经验对扩展技术业务和实现国际抱负极具价值。Jalubro高级团队还包括首席客户与商务官Nick Morgan和首席运营官Andrew Murray。Lumsden表示期待与Jalubro团队合作，并指出随着律所采用更多AI工具并迈向智能体技术，拥有独立基础设施以维持控制将日益重要。
news.bodyHtml:
UK legal transformation consultancy Jalubro has appointed legal technology leader David Lumsden as advisor to the board, we can reveal. Lumsden, who brings with him more than three decades of experience of building and scaling businesses, joins as Jalubro enters a growth phase, having recently launched new AI governance platform Ephiria.

Lumsden is one of the UK legal technology sector’s most experienced executives. Having started in legal as the CIO of international law firm Ashurst, he then spent 13 years as CEO of Tikit Group, growing the business before its acquisition by BT. In 2017 he took over as CEO of RAVN Systems, helping the young company to navigate its acquisition by iManage. His subsequent roles include CEO of Enable Business Solutions and legal tech consultancy Pinnacle. Following Harbor’s acquisition of Pinnacle in 2024, Lumsden joined Harbor’s international leadership team, where he served as regional head of operations and integration until June 2025. 

Advertisement

Lumsden’s appointment comes as Jalubro accelerates its technology business and expands its proprietary technology offering with the launch of Ephiria. As law firms and legal teams adopt AI tools such as Harvey, CoCounsel, Legora and Claude, and AI evolves from copilots that assist lawyers to AI agents capable of acting across systems and workflows, organisations face a growing challenge around how that activity is governed and evidenced. Ephiria provides an independent control layer across that environment. It applies organisational, client and matter-level policy at the point of use and execution, protecting sensitive information before it reaches an AI model through redaction, and governing what AI agents are permitted to do before an action is taken. 

Lumsden will advise Jalubro’s leadership on its technology strategy, international growth and the continued scaling of the business. 

Advertisement

Arran Braganza, founder and CEO of Jalubro, said: “David has been involved in building some of the most important businesses in legal technology over the past three decades. There are very few people who combine his understanding of law firms and technology with the commercial experience of building and scaling technology businesses.”

He noted that Jalubro is already an established business, working with an impressive client base of law firms and corporate legal teams globally, commenting: “Our ambition is to build on that position by developing and delivering more of our own technology. David’s experience will be enormously valuable as we scale that side of the business and pursue that ambition internationally.” 

Jalubro’s senior team includes chief client & commercial officer Nick Morgan, who has previously held senior roles at the likes of Thomson Reuters and Xapien, and COO Andrew Murray, who has worked at companies including Harbor, Pinnacle and Thomson Reuters.

Speaking to Legal IT Insider about his new role, Lumsden said: “I’m really looking forward to working with the Jalubro team, which has such a long-established record in the legal technology sector and many years of experience.”

He added: “I’ve spent much of my career working with technology businesses at moments when the legal industry is undergoing significant change, and I believe we are entering one of those periods now. What particularly interests me about Jalubro is the combination of an established business, strong relationships across the legal market and a genuine ambition to build technology around where the industry is heading next. Ephiria is a good example of that. As firms adopt more AI tools and increasingly move towards agentic technology, having independent infrastructure that allows them to maintain control across that environment is going to become increasingly important.”
