news.titleEn: In A Marriage of Two ALSPs, Repario Acquires UnitedLex to Strengthen Its AI Offerings
news.titleZh: 两家ALSP联姻：Repario收购UnitedLex以强化其AI服务能力
news.summaryZh: 两家替代性法律服务提供商（ALSP）宣布合并，Repario收购了UnitedLex。Repario专注于电子取证和托管审查，而UnitedLex提供更广泛的服务，涵盖法律流程外包、法律运营、诉讼、知识产权、合同和技术。此次收购将自身灵活性与创新能力和UnitedLex的运营深度及跨国规模相结合，打造一家以技术为主导的法律服务公司，能够在企业级复杂法律工作流程中应用AI。人们对在法律中使用AI存在重大担忧，担心失去对数据的控制、对流程的可见性以及结果可靠性的信心，而客户应获得更高标准的法律服务，不应被迫做出这种取舍。UnitedLex自2018年起由CVC Capital Partners所有，Repario由JLL Partners所有。Repario历史上专注于电子取证、数字取证、托管审查、数据托管及相关咨询服务，而UnitedLex则专注于与企业客户合作，转型或运营其内部法律职能。合并后的公司将为客户提供结合法律专业知识与AI驱动工作流程的服务，使客户能够更快达成案件策略，成本可预测，AI可辩护。合并后的公司支持律师事务所、企业和政府机构，覆盖美国、墨西哥、印度、英国和欧盟。UnitedLex在2024年经历动荡，其CEO James Schellhase在任职仅一年后突然离职，由总法律顾问Renee Meisel接任，后来披露他成为旨在揭露儿童侵害者组织的目标。
news.bodyHtml:
In a marriage of two alternative legal services providers, Repario, a company with a focus on e-discovery and managed review, has acquired UnitedLex, a global company that provides a broader range of services spanning legal process outsourcing, legal operations, litigation, IP, contracts and technology.

Repario said that by blending its agility and innovation with the operational depth and multinational scale of UnitedLex, the acquisition will create a technology-led legal services company capable of applying AI across complex legal workflows at enterprise scale.

“There have been significant concerns that using AI in legal means giving up control of your data, visibility into the process, and confidence the results will hold up,” David Moran, chief executive officer of Repario, said in a statement. “Clients deserve a higher standard of legal service and shouldn’t have to make that trade.”

UnitedLex has been owned since 2018 by private equity company CVC Capital Partners. Repario is owned by the private equity firm JLL Partners.

Repario has historically focused on e-discovery, digital forensics, managed review, data hosting, and related advisory services, handling collections, processing, hosting, review, forensic work, incident response, and discovery workflows.

UnitedLex is a broader ALSP that has focused on working with enterprise customers to transform or operate their in-house legal functions and workflows.

For customers of the two companies, Repario said, the combination pairs legal expertise with AI-enabled workflows engineered around human review and accountability.

“Together, Repario and UnitedLex provide clients the ability to reach case strategy sooner, with costs they can predict and AI they can defend,” Moran said. “That is how we deliver better outcomes from a partner clients can trust.”

The combined company supports law firms, corporations, and government agencies from centers across the United States, Mexico, India, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.

UnitedLex went through a period of turmoil in 2024 due to the sudden departure of its CEO James Schellhase, who had been in that role just a year.

In fact, on Oct. 1, 2024, Schellhase was a guest on my LawNext podcast to discuss his first year, which was notable because he was only the company’s second CEO since its 2006 founding.

But just a week later, he was suddenly out of that job, replaced by the company’s general counsel Renee Meisel. It later was revealed that he had been the target of a group that aims to expose child predators.

Repario said that by blending its agility and innovation with the operational depth and multinational scale of UnitedLex, the acquisition will create a technology-led legal services company capable of applying AI across complex legal workflows at enterprise scale. “There have been significant concerns that using AI in legal means giving up control of your data, visibility into the process, and confidence the results will hold up,” David Moran, chief executive officer of Repario, said in a statement. “Clients deserve a higher standard of legal service and shouldn’t have to make that trade.” UnitedLex has been owned since 2018 by private equity company CVC Capital Partners. Repario is owned by the private equity firm JLL Partners. Repario has historically focused on e-discovery, digital forensics, managed review, data hosting, and related advisory services, handling collections, processing, hosting, review, forensic work, incident response, and discovery workflows. UnitedLex is a broader ALSP that has focused on working with enterprise customers to transform or operate their in-house legal functions and workflows. For customers of the two companies, Repario said, the combination pairs legal expertise with AI-enabled workflows engineered around human review and accountability. “Together, Repario and UnitedLex provide clients the ability to reach case strategy sooner, with costs they can predict and AI they can defend,” Moran said. “That is how we deliver better outcomes from a partner clients can trust.” The combined company supports law firms, corporations, and government agencies from centers across the United States, Mexico, India, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. UnitedLex went through a period of turmoil in 2024 due to the sudden departure of its CEO James Schellhase, who had been in that role just a year. In fact, on Oct. 1, 2024, Schellhase was a guest on my LawNext podcast to discuss his first year, which was notable because he was only the company’s second CEO since its 2006 founding. But just a week later, he was suddenly out of that job, replaced by the company’s general counsel Renee Meisel. It later was revealed that he had been the target of a group that aims to expose child predators.

news.titleEn: Exclusive: Alesis, a sovereign AI assistant for UK law firms, goes live
news.titleZh: 独家：面向英国律所的自主AI助手Alesis正式上线
news.summaryZh: 英国AI助手Alesis正式上线，其特点在于仅基于英格兰、威尔士、苏格兰及北爱尔兰法律，并对照原始来源“详尽”核查答案。所有数据均存储于英国，处理在英国及欧盟境内完成，与其他律所数据隔离，且不用于训练其他组织模型。Alesis可访问英国判例法、公司注册处及监察专员数据等英国来源数据，目前已被中小型律所及企业内部法务部门使用，包括一家大型养老金提供商。Alesis由专注于受监管行业AI的L25集团开发，未来数月将成为L25正在打造的AI原生案件管理系统的重要组成部分。L25联合创始人为Luke Roberts和Alex Clayton，两人曾在公共部门工作多年，包括在司法部任职，后转入私营部门咨询，为内部法务团队和律所提供案件管理建议，并帮助其摆脱现有系统。Roberts曾在律师监管局数字化转型项目中担任顾问。L25的投资方包括New South Law的老板，该律所是一家专业争议解决律所，在伯明翰、布里斯托尔和苏塞克斯设有办公室。L25已帮助行业利用AI达八年之久，包括与内阁办公室合作，使公务员能够轻松访问海量数据。Alesis是一款聊天机器人，类似Claude、ChatGPT或Gemini，但专为数据主权设计，数据不离开英国或欧盟（欧盟节点位于爱尔兰）。其采用军用或政府级安全标准，满足合规官所有要求。Alesis能理解英国法律环境，可实时查询公司注册处、国家档案馆、金融监察专员、养老金监察专员以及FCA、SRA、HMRC等政府机构数据。Alesis不会撒谎，不能捏造引文，也不会奉承，若用户出错会直接指出。
news.bodyHtml:
Alesis, an AI assistant grounded solely in the laws of England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and which checks its answers “exhaustively” against primary sources, has gone live, we can reveal.

Alesis’ selling point is that all information run through Alesis is held in the UK, processed in the UK and the EU, kept apart from every other firm, and never used as training data for other organisations. It can access UK case law, Companies House and ombudsman data, among other UK source data. It is already being used in SME law firms and by in-house departments, including a major pension provider.

Advertisement

Alesis is the brainchild of L25 Group, which specialises in AI for regulated sectors. In the coming months it will form a critical part of an AI-native case management system L25 is developing.

The co-founders of L25 are Luke Roberts and Alex Clayton, who both spent several years working in the public sector – including at the Ministry of Justice – before moving into consultancy in the private sector, advising in-house legal teams and law firms on case management and moving away from incumbent systems.

Advertisement

Roberts was a consultant to the Solicitors Regulation Authority during its digital transformation programme. L25’s investors include the owners of New South Law, a specialist disputes law firm with offices in Birmingham, Bristol and Sussex.

Speaking to Legal IT Insider, Roberts said that L25 has helped the industry to leverage AI for eight years, including working with the Cabinet Office on making millions of terabytes of data easily accessible to civil servants.

He observed: “The applicability of that is the same when you get to law firms that have a huge amount of data. Alesis is a chatbot. It is your Claude, your ChatGPT, your Gemini, whatever flavour you choose, but it’s specifically designed, one, for sovereignty. No data leaves the UK or the EU, depending on which inference you want or how clever you want it to be. But the EU location is Ireland, and so it’s still UK.

“It is designed with military grade or government grade security. It checks all the boxes that a compliance officer needs. Really importantly, it understands the UK landscape. So if you talk to it and you say L25, it will go and look at Companies House. It will read all the filings on Companies House, understand it. If you mention some case law, it will go to National Archives and find it. We keep that updated every single second of every single day, so it always have access to all of the information. All ombudsman are in there. So all of the Financial Ombudsman, the Pension Ombudsman, all the source books and guides from the FCA, the SRA, HMRC, every governmental body and any governmental data source that exists, we have as a first party connection.”

Roberts said that unlike other assistants, Alesis is explicitly designed to help lawyers do their job in the UK. “It has a great understanding of England and Wales laws. It has a good understanding of Scotland and Northern Ireland as best it can. It doesn’t lie. It cannot fabricate citations, it cannot make things up, and it’s not sycophantic. So unlike your consumer grade tools, if you are wrong, it will very happily tell you you’re wrong and why, and truly help you understand the complexity of what you’re in.”

Twenty five firms are using Alesis, representing 150 users, and they average six hours of use per user per day, with Roberts observing, “it’s a really sticky system and we’re not seeing any churn. Nobody is leaving and the feedback we’re getting is very, very good.”

Currently firms are in the 25-50 person range but there is interest from larger firms. Firms are able to connect to other systems, such as legal research providers, that they have a license for. Roberts says: “It just becomes another data source for it to go and grab,” although he adds: “We have parity in terms of the actual case law and assessment and the documents that underlie those judgments.”

In terms of why Alesis can’t hallucinate, Roberts says: “The architecture, how we built Alesis, is designed to be very, very hard.” Where other models have a goal to please, even if that means citing a case that doesn’t exist, Roberts said of Alesis “as soon as it thinks about a citation, it immediately has to go and read the full source copy and it’s only allowed to say things that are true. And then it provides a link to the citation, so you can go and check the original.”

He adds: “It will drop citation markers where you can click immediately and see it and it highlights the right relevant passage or clause. It does the same thing, not just against case law, but against ombudsman decisions, against handbooks from different years too. So if you’ve got a claim from 2022, it will go back in time to the right version of the handbook. Companies House, DVLA, all of these integration points with central government are all in it. It has to citation and fact check itself continuously.”

Alesis is funded by credit, not a subscription. On average, £25 currently lasts around 17 days.

Ben Parslow, managing director of New South Law, said: “Alesis is an exciting option for SME law firms that want to adopt AI but have concerns about its reliability and cost. Our experience is that Alesis acts as a very well-informed junior lawyer, whose work you still have to sign off but is of impressively high quality.”

L25 has applied to join the government’s new advisory AI Growth Lab for legal services to support its development of automated workflows. The lab is designed to accelerate the development of AI by helping innovators navigate regulatory frameworks.

news.titleEn: Exclusive: UnitedLex to be acquired by JLL-backed eDiscovery vendor Repario from CVC
news.titleZh: 独家：联合利信将被JLL支持的电子取证供应商Repario从CVC手中收购
news.summaryZh: 据公司内部消息人士透露，全球替代性法律服务提供商联合利信（UnitedLex）将被电子取证供应商Repario Data从私募股权巨头CVC手中收购。Repario由总部位于纽约、专注于收购中型企业的私募股权公司JLL支持。该交易预计将于今日（9月27日）宣布。联合利信已进行出售流程数月，这将使CVC得以退出其2018年的收购，当时该收购据报道推动了联合利信的大规模扩张，并被称为“迄今与任何法律服务提供商达成的最大交易之一”。近期动态包括加强其欧洲业务并推出AI咨询解决方案，但联合利信几年前因首席执行官James Schellhase突然离职而受到冲击，其职位由总法律顾问Renee Meisel接任。其英国收入从截至2022年12月的年度3050万英镑下降至截至2024年12月的年度940万英镑。然而，其整体收入来自北美、欧洲和亚太地区的全球业务。联合利信与瑞银一同被公司法律顾问协会评为2025年价值冠军。它拥有约2000名员工，对Repario而言代表增长机会，因为Repario不仅专注于电子取证和诉讼支持，还涉及合同审查、知识产权、网络安全和更广泛的法务运营管理。有趣的是，2024年Repario聘请了前联合利信副总裁兼公司法律顾问Eric Kelly担任其总法律顾问。我们已联系联合利信和Repario寻求评论和进一步信息。
news.bodyHtml:
Global alternative legal services provider UnitedLex is to be acquired from private equity giant CVC by eDiscovery provider Repario Data, according to our sources at the company. Repario is backed by private equity house JLL, which is based in New York and specialises in acquiring middle-market companies. The transaction is expected to be announced today (27 September). 

UnitedLex has been undergoing a sale process for some months, giving CVC an exit from its 2018 acquisition, reported at the time to be a driver of massive expansion for UnitedLex and said at the time to “represent one of the largest transactions to date with any legal services provider.” Recent developments include bolstering its European presence and launching AI Advisory Solutions, however UnitedLex was rocked a couple of years ago by the sudden departure of CEO James Schellhase, who was replaced by general counsel Renee Meisel. Its UK revenue is down from £30.5m in the year ending December 2022 to £9.4m in the year ending December 2024. However, it’s overall revenue is generated globally across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

Advertisement

UnitedLex, alongside UBS, was named a 2025 Value Champion by the Association of Corporate Counsel. It has an estimated 2,000 employees and represents a growth opportunity for Repario, given that it focuses not only on eDiscovery and litigation support but also contract review, IP, cyber security and legal operations management more broadly. Interestingly, in 2024, Repario hired former UnitedLex vice president and corporate counsel Eric Kelly as its general counsel. 

We have reached out to both UnitedLex and Repario for comment and further information.

news.titleEn: California SB 574 Puts Lawyer Use of Generative AI Under the Microscope
news.titleZh: 加州SB 574法案将律师使用生成式AI置于监管显微镜下
news.summaryZh: 加州批准SB 574法案，被视为今年法律行业最具影响力的进展之一。该法案旨在明确限制律师在法律工作中使用生成式AI，包括禁止将法律执业行为委托给AI工具、要求对AI生成内容进行核实，并对法庭文件提交施加披露相关限制。法案核心原则是：律师可以使用AI，但不能将专业判断外包给AI。此前多起AI生成虚假引文、不准确事实陈述及未经充分审查的AI辅助起草文件进入法庭提交物的事件，引发了司法界和律师协会的广泛关注。对诉讼律师而言，若法案按预期实施，将强化律师对诉状、动议、简报及支持性权威文件的准确性负全责，无论是否借助AI起草。核实义务可能影响律所工作流程，要求提交前进行更正式的审查程序，高量诉讼业务可能需新增内部控制，如引文核查、事实验证及律师监督记录。法务与合规团队亦需密切关注，许多法务部门正试点将生成式AI用于合同审查、内部调查、监管回应及外部律师管理。加州框架可能成为企业治理政策、供应商尽职调查标准及培训项目的模板，即使非加州运营的组织，若其律师在加州执业或出庭，也可能需适应此规则。更广泛而言，SB 574可能推动全国职业责任规则的下一阶段发展。目前法院和监管机构对AI采取零散方式，依赖常设命令、道德意见及现有能力、坦诚和监督义务。加州此举表明更直接的立法模式，明确律师不可委托的事项及必须独立确认的内容。
news.bodyText:
California SB 574 Puts Lawyer Use of Generative AI Under the Microscope

by Bruno Queiroz

California’s approval of SB 574 is emerging as one of the most consequential legal-industry developments of the year, even without a same-day court ruling attached to it. The bill would place clear limits on how lawyers use generative AI in legal work, including restricting delegation of legal practice to AI tools, requiring verification of AI-generated material, and imposing disclosure-related constraints in court filings.

At a high level, the measure reflects a simple but increasingly urgent principle: lawyers can use AI, but they cannot outsource professional judgment to it. That distinction has been at the center of growing judicial and bar-level concern after a series of well-publicized incidents involving fabricated citations, inaccurate factual assertions, and AI-assisted drafting that slipped into court submissions without adequate review.

For litigators, the practical implications are immediate. If enacted and implemented as expected, SB 574 would reinforce that attorneys remain fully responsible for the accuracy of pleadings, motions, briefs, and supporting authorities, regardless of whether an AI platform helped draft them. Verification obligations could also affect law firm workflows, requiring more formal review processes before filings are submitted. In high-volume litigation practices, that may mean new internal controls around cite-checking, factual validation, and documentation of attorney supervision.

In-house counsel and compliance teams should also pay close attention. Many legal departments are actively piloting generative AI for contract review, internal investigations, regulatory responses, and outside counsel management. A California framework that expressly addresses attorney use of AI could become a template for corporate governance policies, vendor diligence standards, and training programs. Even organizations operating outside California may find themselves adapting to its approach if their lawyers practice in the state or appear in California courts.

The broader significance is that SB 574 may help shape the next phase of professional-responsibility rules nationwide. Courts and regulators have so far taken a patchwork approach to AI, relying on standing orders, ethics opinions, and existing duties of competence, candor, and supervision. California’s move suggests a more direct legislative model—one that spells out what lawyers may not delegate and what must be independently confirmed.

That makes this more than a state policy story. It is a signal that the legal profession is entering a more regulated phase of AI adoption, where efficiency gains will be judged against core duties to clients, courts, and the integrity of the legal system. For legal professionals, the message is becoming harder to ignore: experimentation with AI may still be encouraged, but unverified reliance on it increasingly will not be tolerated.

news.summaryZh: 本期播客中，Andarzi创始人兼CEO Maryam Salehijam与主持人探讨了法律AI采用的核心问题：购买工具并非最难，难在确定要解决什么问题。她建议先观察工作流程，明确有用结果，再决定采用现有系统、新供应商或自建工具。许多法律团队付费使用AI平台却难以持续使用，她建议先检查已有工具并要求供应商提供更多培训，再考虑新增订阅，例如法律部门用ServiceNow处理案件受理。对话还涉及模型能力变化、按用量计费及将昂贵模型用于日常任务的高成本。关于AI投资回报，Salehijam认为除时间和金钱外，还应衡量员工满意度，因为重复性合同审查和文档工作占用了律师本应用于判断、业务和客户关系的时间。她建议在工作流程变更前后收集匿名反馈，以评估员工工作是否改善。讨论还涉及本地AI模型、数据安全及AI原生律所兴起。Salehijam主张根据任务和客户要求决策，包括与客户直接沟通信息处理方式，并指出小型和大型律所面临不同限制。关于“法律工程师”角色能否持续，她强调技术技能、资质和律师学习需求。她建议团队通过同伴实践、重复使用和工作成果学习，而非依赖短期证书，并警告领导者需考虑新工作流程所需的时间和精力。最后，她预测法律AI市场新进入者少于预期，更多律所和法律部门将考虑自建工作流程而非续订软件席位。
news.bodyHtml:
Law firms and legal departments face pressure to adopt AI, yet buying another tool does not answer the hardest question: Which problem needs solving? Dr. Maryam Salehijam, founder and CEO of Andarzi, joins TGIR hosts, Greg Lambert and Marlene Gebauer, to discuss how legal teams choose between existing systems, new vendors, and tools built for their own workflows. Her starting point is to observe the work, identify a useful outcome, and then decide what technology belongs in the process.

Salehijam describes legal teams paying for AI platforms while struggling to get consistent use from them. She urges organizations to examine tools they already own and ask vendors for more training before adding another subscription. A legal department’s use of ServiceNow for intake provides one example. The conversation also tackles shifting model capabilities, consumption pricing, and the cost of assigning an expensive model to a routine task.

What counts as a return on legal AI investment? Time and money matter, but Salehijam argues for measuring employee satisfaction as well. Repetitive contract review and document work consume attention lawyers would prefer to spend on judgment, business problems, and client relationships. She describes using anonymous feedback before and after a workflow change to learn whether people’s work has improved, while Greg raises the tension between hours saved and the billable hour.

The discussion turns to local AI models, data security, and the growing interest in AI-native law firms. Salehijam argues for decisions based on the task and the client’s requirements, including a direct conversation with clients about how their information should be handled. Greg presses her on whether smaller firms and large firms face different constraints. Marlene asks whether the emerging “legal engineer” role will endure, prompting a pointed exchange about technical skill, credentials, and what lawyers need to learn.

For teams putting AI into practice, Salehijam favors hands-on learning with peers, repeated use, and work product over a quick certificate. She also warns leaders to account for the time and effort a new workflow demands before promising immediate gains. In the closing questions, she reflects on a legal AI market with fewer new entrants than she expected and predicts more law firms and legal departments will ask whether owning a workflow serves them better than renewing another set of software seats.

Legal AI Strategy Beyond the Prompt: Maryam Salehijam on Adoption, ROI, and Building What Works

Law firms and legal departments face pressure to adopt AI, yet buying another tool does not answer the hardest question: Which problem needs solving? Dr. Maryam Salehijam, founder and CEO of Andarzi, joins Greg Lambert and Marlene Gebauer to discuss how legal teams choose between existing systems, new vendors, and tools built for their own workflows. Her starting point is to observe the work, identify a useful outcome, and then decide what technology belongs in the process.Salehijam describes legal teams paying for AI platforms while struggling to get consistent use from them. She urges organizations to examine tools they already own and ask vendors for more training before adding another subscription. A legal department’s use of ServiceNow for intake provides one example. The conversation also tackles shifting model capabilities, consumption pricing, and the cost of assigning an expensive model to a routine task.What counts as a return on legal AI investment? Time and money matter, but Salehijam argues for measuring employee satisfaction as well. Repetitive contract review and document work consume attention lawyers would prefer to spend on judgment, business problems, and client relationships. She describes using anonymous feedback before and after a workflow change to learn whether people’s work has improved, while Greg raises the tension between hours saved and the billable hour.The discussion turns to local AI models, data security, and the growing interest in AI-native law firms. Salehijam argues for decisions based on the task and the client’s requirements, including a direct conversation with clients about how their information should be handled. Greg presses her on whether smaller firms and large firms face different constraints. Marlene asks whether the emerging “legal engineer” role will endure, prompting a pointed exchange about technical skill, credentials, and what lawyers need to learn.For teams putting AI into practice, Salehijam favors hands-on learning with peers, repeated use, and work product over a quick certificate. She also warns leaders to account for the time and effort a new workflow demands before promising immediate gains. In the closing questions, she reflects on a legal AI market with fewer new entrants than she expected and predicts more law firms and legal departments will ask whether owning a workflow serves them better than renewing another set of software seats.LINKSAndarziDr. Maryam Salehijam on LinkedInAI Fluency for Legal Professionals on MavenHarveyLegoraServiceNow Legal Service DeliveryNotionAstra for LawListen on mobile platforms:  ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Apple Podcasts⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ |  ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Spotify⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ | ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠YouTube⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ | ⁠SubstackEmail: geekinreviewpodcast@gmail.comMusic: Jerry David DeCicca

Patlytics and the Patent AI Race: Paul Lee on Human Judgment and the AI Dividend

Paul Lee, co-founder and CEO of Patlytics, joins Greg Lambert to explain how an AI platform built specifically for intellectual property work is changing the patent lifecycle. Patlytics supports workflows spanning patent drafting, prior art analysis, office action responses, portfolio management, litigation readiness, and claim-chart preparation. Lee reports that the company now works with roughly 55 percent of the Am Law 100 and hundreds of corporations across technology, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and other patent-intensive industries.Lee traces Patlytics’ origins to his experience as a venture capitalist and more than 100 conversations with patent attorneys. Those interviews exposed a practice filled with expensive, labor-intensive processes, from drafting detailed patent specifications to constructing claim charts for litigation. His interest also grew from the Apple and Samsung patent battles, the IP expenses faced by venture-backed companies, and conversations with Patlytics co-founder Arthur Jen and former Latham & Watkins patent litigator Bob Steinberg.The conversation turns to Patlytics’ work involving USPTO patent examiners and the broader effect of placing AI on both sides of the examination process. While confidentiality limits the details Lee discusses, he identifies quality and the examination backlog as two areas where specialized technology offers meaningful assistance. He also contrasts Patlytics with broad legal AI platforms such as Harvey and Legora, arguing that patent professionals need tools designed for the precision, technical detail, and specialized workflows of IP practice.Human judgment stays central to Lee’s vision. Patent attorneys still own the work product, approve key decisions, and remain responsible when an AI-generated analysis falls short. At the same time, client expectations continue to rise. Clients want faster work, higher quality, and lower costs, while law firms need sustainable margins. Lee sees flat-fee arrangements and more predictable workflows as one route toward sharing the “AI dividend” between clients and their outside counsel. Judicaid: Bringing AI Mediation to Everyday Legal Problems

For millions of people, an everyday legal dispute never justifies the cost of a lawyer or a private mediator, no matter how much the outcome matters to them. Judge Victoria Wood saw that problem over and over during her years on the Napa County Superior Court bench. This week, Wood joins Judicaid Chief Strategy Officer Valerie Clemen to explain how those years led to Judicaid, an AI-assisted mediation platform built to help people resolve everyday disputes before time, expense, and emotion push them deeper into litigation.Wood traces Judicaid's origins to two problems she kept running into as a judge and mediator. Traditional settlement conferences arrive late in a case, after the parties have spent real money and dug into their positions. Then there are the lower-value landlord-tenant, contractor, neighbor, probate, and small-claims disputes where professional mediation rarely pencils out at all. Wood puts a number on the access problem. The State Bar of California's 2024 Justice Gap Study, released in 2025, found that Californians received no legal help, or inadequate help, for 85 percent of their civil legal problems. Judicaid aims at a slice of that gap by giving people an earlier and cheaper chance to communicate and negotiate.Clemen walks Greg Lambert and Marlene Gebauer through Judicaid's "shuttle-style" mediation process. Each participant talks privately with an AI mediator named Jude, so the two sides never have to speak to each other directly. Jude gathers each side's account of the dispute, identifies priorities and possible settlement terms, and moves between the participants while filtering out insults, anger, and inflammatory language. If the parties find common ground, the platform prepares a proposed settlement for review and electronic signature. Wood is careful about one boundary throughout the conversation. Jude is a facilitative mediator, and it stays away from evaluating legal rights. It will not decide who is legally correct, predict who will win, or give legal advice.The conversation then turns to Judicaid's pilot with Napa County Superior Court, and the role courts could play in expanding AI-assisted dispute resolution. In the court model, a court subscribes to the service and hands litigants' access through a QR code, with no integration into the court's technology systems. The pilot has already surfaced a behavioral lesson. Offering mediation as an optional service does not mean parties will use it, and Wood and Clemen see more potential where courts actively encourage or require litigants to attempt dispute resolution before proceeding. Language is another piece of the story, since Judicaid lets participants who speak different languages work through the same mediation without arranging multiple interpreters.Wood and Clemen also see mediation as just the starting point. The bigger ambition is a change in habits, where people reach for structured communication and settlement before a disagreement hardens into a lawsuit. Clemen boils that aspiration down to three words she hopes become part of the vocabulary of everyday disputes: "Just Judicate it."Listen on mobile platforms:  ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Apple Podcasts⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ |  ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Spotify⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ | ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠YouTube⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ | ⁠Substack⁠[Special Thanks to ⁠⁠Legal Technology Hub⁠⁠ for their sponsoring this episode.]Email: geekinreviewpodcast@gmail.comMusic: Jerry David DeCiccaLINKSJudicaidState Bar of California, California Justice Gap Study2024 California Justice Gap StudyNapa County Superior Court, Small Claims

AI might reduce the effort required for individual tasks while expanding the overall volume and ambition of legal representation.The shift holds major implications for the access-to-justice gap. Faster drafting, research, and document review would allow lawyers to serve more clients without sacrificing professional judgment. Anderson expects family law, immigration, bankruptcy, criminal defense, and employment litigation to experience some of the earliest growth. Motions, witnesses, and legal theories once abandoned over expense become economically viable, although courts face their own capacity crisis as more disputes and arguments enter the system.Rizner explains how Filevine’s legal AI platform, Lois, applies machine learning to one of legal research’s oldest problems: traditional citators often return different results. Lois combines citation graphs with semantic analysis to locate opinions discussing related legal doctrines even when no direct citation connects the cases. A panel of models then evaluates potential conflicts and produces a structured memo. The goal is richer legal analysis focused on the precise holding or proposition a lawyer needs, rather than a simple flag attached to an entire opinion.Accuracy still demands disciplined human review. Filevine organizes citation verification into three levels: confirming the cited case exists, determining whether the case supports the claimed proposition, and checking whether the authority is still good law. The conversation also examines Rizner’s research into how different large language models approach efficient breach of contract. OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic models produced dramatically different recommendations, revealing embedded legal and economic preferences beneath seemingly neutral answers.The guests also explore how AI changes legal drafting, law firm economics, and the billable hour. Filevine’s acquisition of Pincites, now Lois for Word, reflects Microsoft Word’s continuing role as the shared language of legal documents, redlines, formatting, and negotiations. Efficiency does not automatically eliminate hourly billing. Lawyers might instead use saved time to produce more thoroughly researched arguments, stronger contracts, and work product approaching senior-level depth. Firms still need incentives rewarding efficiency rather than treating faster work as lost revenue.Looking ahead, Anderson and Rizner predict a proliferation of frontier and open-source models tailored to firms, individual lawyers, and specific client relationships. Legal teams will increasingly pair proprietary knowledge with selected models to produce highly specialized analysis. Yet model choice introduces jurisprudential bias, accuracy risks, and serious training concerns for junior lawyers. What does legal AI value look like once speed stops serving as the headline metric? In this episode of The Geek in Review, Greg Lambert and Marlene Gebauer speak with Nikki Shaver, co-founder and CEO of Legal Technology Hub and a member of the inaugural Financial Times Law 50. Shaver argues that law firms need to move beyond time saved toward efficacy: stronger output, stronger client outcomes, and more effective legal advice.The conversation examines why the billable hour is far from finished yet no longer serves as the sole measure of legal value. Shaver compares hourly timekeeping to a taxi meter: useful for internal visibility, yet insufficient as the price signal for work transformed by AI. news.summaryZh: 瑞茜·威瑟斯彭公开表示拥抱AI是女权主义行为，并称女性“不想被落下”，随即遭到猛烈批评，她不得不澄清“没有人付钱给我”，自称只是“好奇的人”。这一事件折射出AI性别差距问题。研究显示，2026年Lean In调查中，33%男性每日使用AI工具，女性为27%；78%男性曾使用AI，女性为73%。女性比男性更可能担心使用AI被视为作弊（高32%）、感到威胁（高20%）、认为AI会更多取代女性工作（19%对8%）、质疑AI准确性（高29%）及提出伦理担忧（高38%）。男性更可能因使用AI获得赞扬（高27%）及被管理者鼓励使用（高23%）。伯克利哈斯商学院、斯坦福和哈佛商学院分析超14万用户的研究发现，女性使用生成式AI的可能性低约20%；ChatGPT女性用户占42%，Perplexity占42.4%，Claude仅占31.2%。肯尼亚研究中，即使提供直接支持，女性采用ChatGPT的可能性仍低13%。女性使用少导致训练数据代表性不足，形成自我强化循环。文章还提到，女性公开倡导AI会面临双重束缚，而男性高管类似言论却少受审视。AI系统偏见会影响招聘、医疗、法律研究等工具。Lean In警告，当前使用差距可能转化为未来机会差距。文章建议团队实验常态化、公平公开表扬、投资早期教育、领导层公开讨论参与度。对律所而言，支持女性律师建立AI权威是战略机遇。Conroy Creative Counsel近二十年来帮助律所构建思想领导力，由获奖营销顾问Karin Conroy领导，通过Counsel Cast播客、文章及The Authority Tour等活动，协助律师将专业知识转化为受认可的权威形象。
news.bodyHtml:
When Reese Witherspoon told her audience that embracing AI was a feminist act and that women “don’t want to be left behind,” she probably expected some pushback. What she got instead was a wave of criticism sharp enough that she felt compelled to clarify herself publicly: “no one is paying me,” she said, insisting she was just “a curious human” trying to understand the technology reshaping her industry.

It’s tempting to file this under celebrity news and move on. We’d argue the opposite: give Reese Witherspoon some peace, because the backlash aimed at her isn’t really about her. It’s a live, very public example of a gap researchers have been documenting for the past two years – the AI gender gap – and it says far more about how society reacts to women and technology than it does about one actress’s opinions on large language models.

What the Research Actually Shows

Strip away the celebrity angle and the pattern found across multiple studies is remarkably consistent. A 2026 survey from Lean In found that 33% of men use AI tools daily compared with 27% of women, and 78% of men report having used AI at all compared with 73% of women. On the surface, that looks like a modest usage gap. However, underneath it is a much more significant story about gender differences in how AI is experienced, not just adopted.

This is what the data suggests:

  • Women are 32% more likely than men to worry about being perceived as cheating when they use AI.
  • Women are 20% more likely to feel threatened by it, and nearly twice as likely as men to predict AI will cost more women their jobs than men (19% vs. 8%).
  • Women are 29% more likely to question AI’s accuracy and 38% more likely to raise ethical concerns about using it.
  • Men are 27% more likely to be praised for using AI at work, and 23% more likely to have a manager actively encourage them to use it.

Why The AI Gender Gap Persists

A separate study out of Berkeley’s Haas School of Business, Stanford, and Harvard Business School – one of the largest of its kind, analysing over 140,000 users – found women are roughly 20% less likely than men to use generative AI tools at all. The gap shows up tool by tool: women make up around 42% of ChatGPT’s web users, 42.4% of Perplexity’s, and just 31.2% of Claude’s. Even in a Kenya-based study where women were offered direct support, they remained 13% less likely to adopt ChatGPT than men in the same group – proof that access alone doesn’t answer a gap this deeply rooted in perception and confidence.

The researchers behind that study found something worth sitting with: as fewer women use these tools, the systems themselves get trained on data that under-represents women’s preferences and needs, which makes the tools less useful for women, which further discourages use.

It’s a self-reinforcing cycle, and most companies aren’t watching for it.

The Double Bind Reese Witherspoon Just Walked Into

This is where the backlash becomes genuinely instructive rather than just gossip. The same Lean In research found that women who do use AI are significantly more likely than men to fear being seen as taking a shortcut – as “cheating” rather than working smart. Witherspoon didn’t just use AI quietly; she said out loud that women should embrace it, and the response proved the exact fear the data describes. She was accused of promoting a technology that threatens the very creative industries – authors, writers, storytellers – that built her career.

Compare that to how male tech founders and executives talk about AI adoption in almost identical terms – urgency, competitive necessity, “get on board or get left behind” – and rarely face the same character-level scrutiny. That’s the double bind the research describes, playing out in real time on a public figure. Stay quiet about AI and risk falling behind on pay and job opportunities in a digital economy that increasingly rewards early fluency. Speak up about it, especially as a woman, and risk being cast as self-interested or complicit in something harmful. It is clearly evident here that men, on average, don’t carry the same reputational tax either way.

The Systems Problem: Why This Isn’t Just a Women’s Issue

There’s a broader risk hiding here underneath the personal one, and it affects more than the women currently opting out. Artificial Intelligence systems learn from the people who use them. If the group training today’s large language models skews male, the tools themselves start to reflect a narrower slice of the world – its concerns, its ideas, its priorities – and every consumer who touches those systems downstream inherits that bias, whether they realize it or not.

This is the part of the AI gender gap conversation that rarely makes it into the celebrity-news version of the story. It isn’t just about individual women missing out on productivity gains. It’s about a critical, formative moment in how these systems get built – being shaped by an incomplete picture of society. Because biased systems don’t stay contained to the group that built them – they shape hiring tools, healthcare tools, legal research tools, and every other application built on top of them. And that is a risk for everyone, not a niche concern for one demographic.

Why a Small Usage Gap Becomes a Big Career Gap

None of this stays contained to individual careers, either. Lean In’s researchers put it plainly: the usage gaps we’re seeing today could become significant opportunity gaps tomorrow. AI fluency is quickly becoming a proxy for productivity, and productivity is quickly becoming a proxy for who gets promoted, who gets invited into the room, and who gets recognised as a leader.

If fewer women use AI now – not because they lack the skills, but because they’ve absorbed a well-founded fear of judgment – then fewer women will be visible as the experts and decision-makers shaping how AI gets used across every industry, law included. That has knock-on effects for representation at every level: fewer women building the tools, fewer women in the leadership conversations, fewer women setting norms early, when norms are still being set. We wrote about this exact concern in Women in AI: Why the Future of Artificial Intelligence Needs More Female Leadership, Visibility and Recognition – the risk isn’t hypothetical, it’s already measurable, and the Witherspoon story is simply the moment it broke into mainstream conversation.

The Cost of Ignoring the AI Gender Gap

It’s easy for a company, or a firm, to treat this as someone else’s problem – a cultural footnote rather than a business risk. However, we believe that as workers across every sector are being asked to adopt AI tools faster than most organizations have built the culture to support it, and the firms that ignore the gender differences in how that adoption is landing will end up with a workforce split into two very different groups: one growing more confident and efficient by the month, and one quietly falling further behind out of fear rather than ability.

A few strategies actually move the needle, based on what the research has found:

  • Normalise Experimentation in Teams – Make it clear that trying an AI tool and getting an imperfect answer isn’t a performance issue – it’s how everyone, across every age and experience level, gets comfortable with new technology.
  • Give Credit Evenly and Publicly – If a smart use of AI earns a colleague praise, make sure that recognition isn’t quietly skewing toward men, even unintentionally.
  • Invest in Early Education, Not Just Access –The Kenya study proved that handing someone a tool isn’t the same as building their confidence with it. Training and mentorship close the gap that access alone can’t.
  • Talk About Participation Openly at the Leadership Level – If women are underrepresented in who’s using AI on your teams, that’s a pattern worth naming, not ignoring.

For law firms specifically, this is a strategic opportunity as much as a fairness issue. Firms that actively support their women lawyers and leaders in building visible, confident authority around AI – rather than leaving them to navigate the “cheating” stigma alone – will end up with a real competitive edge in a market where clients increasingly expect firms to understand the innovation reshaping their own industries.

Give Her Some Peace, We Say

The backlash against Reese Witherspoon was never really a referendum on her specific views about AI. It was a stress test of a bias that was already there, waiting for a high-profile woman to say the quiet part out loud. The more useful conversation isn’t whether she was right to talk about it – it’s why the reaction was so disproportionate, and what that tells us about the women in our own workplaces who are quietly deciding, right now, whether it’s safe to raise their hand and say they’re using AI too.

How Conroy Creative Counsel Can Help Your Law Firm

Closing the AI gender gap isn’t just a cultural conversation – for law firms, it’s part of a much larger opportunity to build visible, credible thought leadership in a rapidly changing digital landscape. Firms that support their women lawyers and leaders in speaking confidently about how they use AI, rather than staying silent to avoid scrutiny, are the ones who will be recognized as forward-thinking authorities in their practice areas.

For nearly two decades Conroy Creative Counsel has helped law firms build exactly that kind of authority. Led by award-winning legal marketing consultant, creative director, writer and podcast host Karin Conroy, our team works with firms and their leaders to turn genuine expertise into visibility that holds up under scrutiny. Through our Counsel Cast podcast series, speaking engagements, articles and initiatives such as The Authority Tour, we help attorneys build the kind of trusted, well-supported presence that gets noticed for the right reasons.

Whether that means developing a content and thought-leadership strategy that reflects how your firm is genuinely using AI, positioning your leaders as visible experts rather than reluctant adopters, or building an SEO, LinkedIn and content strategy that keeps your firm ahead of a rapidly shifting digital landscape, we help translate real expertise into recognized authority.

Connect With Us Today

If you are looking to strengthen your online presence and position your firm as a trusted authority in an evolving digital landscape, contact us today to discuss whether we are the right strategic marketing partner to help elevate your visibility, authority and long-term influence.

news.titleEn: D.C. Circuit Upholds the Anthropic Ban: What It Means for Federal Contractors
news.titleZh: 哥伦比亚特区巡回上诉法院维持对Anthropic的禁令：对联邦承包商的影响
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月25日，美国哥伦比亚特区巡回上诉法院就Anthropic PBC诉美国战争部案（案号26-1049）作出裁决，维持战争部根据2018年《联邦采购供应链安全法》（FASCSA）将Anthropic的Claude人工智能模型排除在供应链之外的决定。该裁决允许政府继续要求承包商在履行联邦合同时停止使用Anthropic产品。此案源于Anthropic持有2亿美元五角大楼合同，并成为首家在机密政府网络上部署模型的领先AI公司。Anthropic坚持两条红线：拒绝允许Claude用于大规模国内监控或全自主武器系统。2026年2月27日，特朗普总统和战争部长皮特·赫格塞斯宣布计划将Anthropic移出联邦供应链。3月3日，赫格塞斯正式认定Anthropic构成重大供应链风险，命令180天内移除所有产品。Anthropic在哥伦比亚特区巡回法院和加州北区地方法院提起诉讼。地方法院依据10 U.S.C. § 3252撤销了指定，但上诉法院以2比1多数意见推翻。Anthropic的模型训练嵌入限制功能构成FASCSA定义下的“操纵”，无需证明恶意意图。法院区分了FASCSA与第3252条，后者要求“对手”从事破坏或颠覆。该裁决影响重大，政府可将标准商业功能（如服务中断能力或软件更新）指定为供应链风险。法院还驳回了Anthropic关于正当程序和第一修正案的诉求，指出记录显示战争部因合同争议而非其倡导活动采取行动。Anthropic估值据报道已超过9000亿美元。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On September 25, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit issued its much-anticipated decision in Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War, No. 26-1049, upholding the Department of War’s (“DOW”) exclusion of Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence (“AI”) models from its supply chain under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (“FASCSA”), 41 U.S.C. § 4713. The ruling means the Government may continue its efforts to require contractors to cease the use of Anthropic as part of the performance of federal contracts. This post summarizes the decision and steps contractors should consider taking in response. As we covered in our prior blog post, the dispute between Anthropic and the federal government began with a contract disagreement over AI usage restrictions (Anthropic held a $200 million Pentagon contract and was the first frontier AI company to deploy models on classified government networks). Anthropic maintained two “red lines”: it refused to allow its Claude AI model to be used for mass domestic surveillance of Americans or in fully autonomous weapons systems. When the DOW demanded that Anthropic agree to “all lawful use” of its technology without these restrictions, Anthropic refused. On February 27, 2026, President Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced on social media their intention to remove Anthropic from the federal supply chain. On March 3, 2026, Secretary Hegseth issued a formal determination under FASCSA to take covered procurement actions against Anthropic, finding that the continued integration of Claude into DOW systems presented a “significant supply chain risk,” that removal was “necessary to protect national security,” and that no “less intrusive measures” were “reasonably available.” The Secretary also determined that an “urgent national security interest” required immediate action. The DOW’s Chief Information Officer then ordered removal of all Anthropic products from DOW systems within 180 days and prohibited contractors from using Anthropic products in DOW work. Anthropic filed suit challenging these designations in the D.C. Circuit (regarding the FASCSA designation) and the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (regarding the designation under a different statute, 10 U.S.C. § 3252). In Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War, No. 26-cv-01996 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 27, 2026), the district court set aside the DOW’s designation of Anthropic as a “supply chain risk,” finding that Section 3252’s definition of “supply chain risk”—which requires that “an adversary” engage in sabotage or subversion—did not encompass Anthropic’s good-faith enforcement of contractual usage restrictions. Writing for a 2-1 majority, Judge Katsas rejected each of Anthropic’s challenges. The central question was whether Anthropic’s conduct fell within FASCSA’s definition of “supply chain risk”—the risk that “any person” may “sabotage, maliciously introduce unwanted function, extract data, or otherwise manipulate” the design, integrity, or operation of covered information-technology products. The Court held that Anthropic’s model training, through which it embedded restrictions preventing Claude from performing certain tasks, constituted “manipulat[ing]” the design and operation of Claude within the statute’s plain meaning. The Court rejected Anthropic’s argument that the statute’s references to “sabotage” and “malicious” conduct imposed an overarching requirement of bad motive. Instead, the Court found that the word “manipulate” in both verb strings of the statutory definition does not uniformly connote bad intent. The Court emphasized that the statute focuses on what a supplier does to a product’s function, not why it does so. The Court distinguished FASCSA from the narrower Section 3252 at issue in the Northern District of California case. Under Section 3252, the term “supply chain risk” is limited to threats from an “adversary” who may “sabotage, maliciously introduce unwanted function, or otherwise subvert” covered systems—language that the Court held more clearly connotes hostile intent. The D.C. Circuit acknowledged that the Northern District reasonably concluded that Anthropic did not act with such bad motive but held that Section 4713’s broader language required no such showing. The breadth of the Court’s holding has significant implications for contractors. Under the Court’s holding, the Government could designate products as “supply chain risks” for standard commercial features. For example, the Government could designate a software-as-a-service provider a supply chain risk because it has the capability to cut off access for non-payment and therefore could “deny” the Government access under FASCSA. Similarly, an application developer who can push software updates is also a potential supply chain risk because such updates could “manipulate” the application under FASCSA. Having rejected Anthropic’s “bad motive” interpretation, the majority’s decision has handed the Government the authority to turn standard commercial features into potentially company-crippling vulnerabilities through a “supply chain risk” designation. The Court also upheld the Secretary’s finding that less intrusive measures were not reasonably available. Anthropic argued that the FASCSA designation “branded” it as a national-security threat, causing reputational harm beyond what ordinary contract termination would produce. The Court was skeptical, noting that Anthropic’s valuation had reportedly soared to over $900 billion since the exclusion. Regardless, the Court reasoned that articulating the same national security concerns through conventional contract termination would have been equally stigmatizing. The Court further credited the Secretary’s decision to make a “clean break” rather than undertake the delay, expense, and uncertainty of a granular, system-by-system review of Claude’s uses. The Court rejected Anthropic’s due process and First Amendment claims. On due process, the Court found that post-deprivation process was constitutionally sufficient given the Government’s legitimate need to act quickly. On the First Amendment, the Court found no causal connection between Anthropic’s protected advocacy regarding AI safety and the adverse action. The record showed that the DOW removed Anthropic from its supply chain because of a contractual dispute (i.e., Anthropic’s refusal to agree to an “all lawful uses” term), not because of the company’s public statements. The Court noted that the DOW had never retaliated against Anthropic during years of advocacy and had continued to pursue the commercial relationship even after Anthropic published articles calling for AI safety limits.
news.relevanceReason: 该文章主要涉及法院对AI公司Anthropic的联邦采购禁令的裁决，核心是AI在联邦合同中的使用限制及法律解释，属于法律AI领域。

news.titleEn: AI On The Loose: What the Latest Cyber Incidents Mean for Your Organization
news.titleZh: AI失控：最新网络事件对企业意味着什么
news.summaryZh: 近期涉及领先人工智能开发商的报告加剧了担忧，即AI代理可能超出预期边界运行，或被网络犯罪分子利用，发动更难预防和遏制的攻击。对于采用AI的组织而言，问题比任何单一模型或事件都更大：AI可能使威胁行为者以超越传统防御的速度识别漏洞、开发漏洞利用程序并在互联系统中移动。这并未使现有防护措施过时，多因素认证、端点检测与响应、加密等控制手段仍然至关重要。但组织可能需要重新评估在攻击变得更快、更具适应性且更难遏制的环境中，何为“合理防护措施”。Jackson Lewis隐私、数据与网络安全组的联合负责人Joe Lazzarotti和Damon Silver近期讨论了法律、隐私与安全团队如何应对。他们的核心信息是：预防仍然关键，但组织还需减少入侵者可获取的数据和访问权限，并准备在控制被突破时作出响应。许多安全程序围绕人类攻击者的速度和方法设计，AI可能改变这一格局。恶意行为者可能利用AI在压缩时间线上识别漏洞、调整代码并构建漏洞利用程序，可能先于补丁或其他防御措施。实际含义并非组织应放弃现有安全投资，而是领导者应评估控制措施是否针对AI驱动的威胁进行配置、监控和更新，以及组织能否识别、遏制并从中招入侵中恢复。组织两者都需要：预防支持合规并降低事件可能性，而准备则减少预防失败时的业务、法律和声誉后果。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! AI is accelerating cybersecurity threats. Learn how data minimization, incident response, data mapping, and vendor governance can help reduce risk. Recent reports involving leading artificial intelligence (AI) developers have heightened concern about whether AI agents can operate beyond their intended boundaries and/or be used by cyber criminals to perpetuate attacks that are more difficult to prevent and contain. For organizations adopting AI across business functions, the issue is larger than any single model or incident: AI may allow threat actors to identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and move through connected systems at a speed that outpaces traditional defenses. That does not make existing safeguards obsolete. Multifactor authentication, endpoint detection and response, encryption and other controls remain essential. But organizations may need to reassess what constitutes “reasonable safeguards” in an environment where attacks can become faster, more adaptive, and more difficult to contain. Co-leaders of Jackson Lewis’ Privacy, Data & Cybersecurity group, Joe Lazzarotti and Damon Silver, recently discussed how legal, privacy, and security teams can respond. Their central message: prevention remains critical, but organizations also need to reduce the data and access available to an intruder and prepare to respond when controls are overcome. Many security programs were designed around the speed and methods of human attackers. AI can change that equation. A malicious actor may use AI to identify a vulnerability, adapt code, and build an exploit on a compressed timeline, potentially before a patch or other defensive measure is available. The practical implication is not that organizations should abandon their existing security investments. Rather, leaders should evaluate whether controls are configured, monitored, and updated for AI-enabled threats—and whether the organization can identify, contain and recover from an intrusion that succeeds. Organizations need both. Prevention supports compliance and reduces the likelihood of an incident, while preparedness reduces the business, legal, and reputational consequences when prevention fails. The familiar assumption that a breach is a matter of “when,” not “if,” is becoming more important as AI accelerates—and tips the balance, unfavorably, in—the contest between attackers and defenders. Incident response plans should address decision-making authority, internal escalation, preservation of evidence, business continuity, communications, and potential notification obligations. Tabletop exercises can reveal whether the plan works under pressure and whether legal, privacy, security, HR, communications, and business leaders understand their roles. “Prevention remains critical, but preparedness determines how effectively an organization can contain disruption and meet its obligations when controls fail.” AI makes it easier to extract value from large datasets, creating a powerful incentive to collect and retain more information. That same footprint increases exposure. If an attacker gains access, a larger and more connected data environment can increase the number of affected individuals, the sensitivity of compromised information, operational disruption, and downstream litigation or regulatory risk.
news.relevanceReason: 该文章聚焦AI在网络安全中的角色，讨论AI驱动的威胁如何影响组织的法律、隐私和安全防护措施，属于法律技术领域，涉及AI在法律合规和风险管理中的应用。

news.titleEn: AI Is Forcing Law Firms To Get Serious About Matter Economics
news.titleZh: AI正迫使律师事务所认真对待案件经济学
news.summaryZh: AI正在改变法律工作的经济学，但律所在定价方面尚未跟上AI带来的变化。BigHand《2026年定价与预算趋势分析》报告显示，AI改变法律工作交付方式的速度快于律所改变定价方式的速度。报告发现，减少人工/重复性工作的比例从28%升至31%，但仅有29%的律所改变了AI增强工作的定价方式，只有20%的律所报告定价准确性或一致性有所提高。在如何反映AI驱动的效率方面，律所没有主导性方法：30%维持现有定价并将效率收益内部化，30%仍在评估，25%在客户允许使用AI时提供折扣。行业需要真正掌握案件经济学，即理解案件内部工作，以便为定价和资源配置提供依据。计时表不仅是计费记录，也是关于工作如何实际交付的最丰富证据来源之一。如果能够仔细阅读、一致结构化并分组为有意义的工作流，律所就能识别哪些过往案件与当前案件真正相似，这比让合伙人凭记忆估计或让定价团队基于不完善假设建模要好得多。AI在定价中的实际价值在于将混乱的案件历史转化为对可能工作量、工作阶段、人员配置和预算风险的清晰视图，为合伙人报价提供更坚实基础，也为客户提供更好体验，因为报价数字不太可能每周波动。
news.bodyText: By Stefan Ciesla, BigHand. AI is changing the economics of legal work. That much is clear. What is less clear is how law firms should price work when the inputs, effort, and delivery model are also shifting. There is a lot of noise around whether AI is saving lawyers time. It is an important question, although it is difficult to answer properly without knowing exactly what lawyers put into AI tools, what comes out, and how that changes the real work done on a matter. That level of analysis is important, but it is not the most immediate commercial issue for most firms. The more pressing question is simpler. If firms want to give clients greater certainty, why are so many still pricing matters through broad ranges and loose assumptions? The awkward gap between AI value and pricing BigHand’s 2026 Pricing and Budgeting Trends Analysis captures the tension well. The report finds that ‘AI is changing how legal work gets delivered faster than firms are changing how they price it.’ It also shows that operational progress is moving ahead of pricing maturity: ‘reduced manual/repetitive work has risen from 28% to 31% this year’, while ‘only 29% of firms have changed how they price AI-augmented work, and only 20% report any improvement in pricing accuracy or consistency.’ This is the hard bit. Delivering value and capturing value are different disciplines. A firm may use AI to complete certain work faster, then still struggle to decide who should benefit economically. The firm could keep the efficiency gain. The client could receive a lower fee. The fee could stay steady because the client is receiving better certainty or a stronger outcome. Each choice can be reasonable if it is deliberate and backed by evidence. At the moment, the market has not settled. Asked how they currently reflect AI-driven efficiencies in pricing, firms have no dominant approach: ‘30% are maintaining existing pricing while banking the efficiency gain internally, 30% are still evaluating what to do, and 25% are offering discounts when clients permit AI use.’ That should concentrate minds. Nobody has won the argument yet. Solving data problems solves pricing problems My view is that the industry needs to get a proper grip on matter economics. That means understanding the work inside a matter at a level that is useful for pricing and resourcing conversations. Timesheets are usually treated as a billing record. They are also one of the richest sources of evidence a firm has about how work was actually delivered. If that data can be read carefully, structured consistently and grouped into meaningful workstreams, firms can identify which past matters are genuinely similar to the one being scoped. That is a very different starting point from asking a partner to estimate from memory or asking a pricing team to build a model from imperfect assumptions. This is where AI becomes practically valuable in pricing. The useful application is the ability to turn messy matter history into a clearer view of likely effort, work phases, staffing patterns and budget risk. That gives partners a firmer basis for quoting. It also gives clients a better experience because the number they hear is less likely to drift every week.
news.relevanceReason: 文章聚焦AI对律所定价和案件经济学的影响，属于法律AI在法律工作流程中的应用，符合网站主题。

news.titleEn: Mitratech Buys BotDojo For Agent Orchestration
news.titleZh: Mitratech收购BotDojo以强化智能体编排能力
news.summaryZh: Mitratech Legal已收购专注于智能体编排的小型初创公司BotDojo，并将其整合进其ARIES AI产品线。BotDojo于2024年正式成立，团队规模估计不超过10人。此次收购对Mitratech而言，被视为其与其他AI平台之间数据集成的重要一步，尤其是通过其“双向”MCP连接，实现自身及其他公司智能体的互联互通。随着今年秋季双向MCP支持的上线，此次收购将使客户的记录系统能够原生兼容企业内日益普及的智能体AI平台。Mitratech还列出了BotDojo集成后所能提供的部分连接器。在充斥着AI包装器的市场中，自主智能体的有效性取决于其可访问的底层专有数据和工作流历史。每个法律团队都面临自建与购买的决策，此次收购提供了两全其美的方案：既有机构知识基础，又具备智能体AI的速度和适应性。此次收购不会改变Mitratech对ARIES的治理性和战略性愿景，反而会加速实现该愿景。此次并购交易规模估计较为“温和”，但值得注意的是，Mitratech是一家服务超过8000个法律团队的大型公司。关键点在于，Mitratech的数据及其智能体能力现在可以连接到客户可能正在使用的所有其他智能体系统。
news.bodyText: Mitratech Legal has bought BotDojo, a small startup focused on agent orchestration. It will become part of the far larger company’s ARIES AI offering, they said. BotDojo formally launched back in 2024 and is understood to be around 10 people or fewer. However, for Mitratech it’s seen as a major step forward for data integration between it and other AI platforms, in particular because of their ‘two-way’ MCP connections for its and other companies’ agents. The company said: ‘With two-way MCP support live this Fall, this acquisition makes the customer’s system of record natively interoperable with the agentic AI platforms becoming standard across enterprises.’ And here are some of its connectors: Mitratech set out that the integration of BotDojo means that it can now offer: And here’s a short video: Chris Iconos, CEO of Mitratech Legal, added: ‘In a market crowded with AI wrappers, an autonomous agent is only as effective as the underlying proprietary data and workflow history it can access. ‘Every legal team is facing build-versus-buy decisions right now, and this delivers the best of both worlds: a foundation of institutional knowledge with the speed and adaptability of agentic AI. This acquisition doesn’t change our governed, intentional vision for ARIES; it accelerates how quickly we can bring that vision to life.’ Is this a big deal? Well, the M&A deal would have been rather ‘moderate’ in scale, one would guess. But, it’s interesting to see how important this is to Mitratech – which is a large company that serves more than 8,000 legal teams. And the key point, which they focused on above, is that Mitratech data and its agentic capabilities can now connect to all the other agentic systems out there that their clients may be using. —
news.relevanceReason: 该新闻主要报道法律科技公司Mitratech收购AI智能体编排初创公司BotDojo，以增强其法律AI产品ARIES的集成能力，核心内容涉及法律AI技术及其在法律工作流程中的应用，符合网站主题。

news.titleEn: Disney Seeks Legal AI Chief Amid Inhouse Shakeup
news.titleZh: 迪士尼在法务部门重组中寻求法律AI负责人
news.summaryZh: 娱乐巨头迪士尼正经历一场法律AI变革。据Deadline上周报道，该公司拥有约1000名员工的法律与全球事务部门将面临重大调整，计划中包括“自动化工作流程”。同时，迪士尼正在招聘一位“AI赋能与法律工程总监”，负责“重新设计”这些法律工作流程，若工作地点在纽约，年薪最高可达26万美元。此外，迪士尼还任命了其首位公司层面的首席技术官Karandeep Anand，他此前是生成式AI平台Character.AI的首席执行官。迪士尼拥有规模庞大的法律部门，目前AI相关动态频繁。关于部门调整，Artificial Lawyer尚未独立证实Deadline的报道，但该报道已被好莱坞记者报等知名媒体跟进，且原文仍在线。Deadline的报道包含一份据称来自迪士尼首席法律与全球事务官Horacio Gutierrez的备忘录。法律与全球事务部门将比现在规模小得多，部分员工将受到决策影响。为此，该部门需考虑多种新工作模式，包括利用最新技术自动化某些工作流程、在适当情况下采用自助服务模式、引入替代性法律服务提供商、扩大共享服务，甚至外包。整体来看，备忘录暗示重大重组计划已提上日程，但未明确具体裁员人数。迪士尼招聘网站上的新职位描述显示，该总监将与律师、业务伙伴和技术团队合作，重新设计法律工作流程，实施技术驱动的解决方案，并创建可扩展的工作方式，以改善法律与全球事务部门的法律服务交付。
news.bodyText: Entertainment giant Disney is having a legal AI moment. Last week, Deadline reported that the company’s 1,000-strong Legal and Global Affairs group would face significant changes, with ‘automating workflows’ as part of the plan. At the same time, they’re looking for a Director of AI Enablement & Legal Engineering to ‘redesign’ those very same legal workflows – with a salary up to $260,000 if based in New York. Disney has also hired its first company-wide CTO, Karandeep Anand, who was previously CEO at Character.AI, a genAI platform for avatar generation. In short, there is a lot happening in relation to AI at Disney – a company with a very significant legal division. First the reported shakeup. AL has not independently confirmed the Deadline story, but it has been followed by other established sites such as the Hollywood Reporter and remains online. The Deadline story contains a memo reputedly from Horacio Gutierrez, Chief Legal and Global Affairs (LGA) Officer at Disney. The memo contains several key aspects. It states: ‘LGA will be a much smaller organization than it is today, and some of you will personally be affected by decisions we make in this process. ‘As a result, we’ll have to consider a whole range of new models for different workloads, including automating certain workflows by leveraging the latest technologies, moving to self-service models where appropriate, engaging alternative legal providers and others, and new expanded share services, even outsourcing.’ Overall, it reads as if Gutierrez had just spent some time with a group of legal ops consultants. And let’s highlight some of the key points: Now, whether any, or how many, lawyers will lose their jobs is not specifically set out, but anyone reading that memo would be left with little doubt that a major shakeup is planned. And that leads us directly onto the new high-powered legal AI role that has just been advertised on the Disney jobs site. When you look at the tasks they will focus on, one can immediately see the connection. Here’s an edited version of the job: ‘Director, AI Enablement & Legal Engineering [They] will partner with attorneys, business partners and technology teams to redesign legal workflows, implement technology-enabled solutions, and create scalable ways of working that improve how legal services are delivered across Legal & Global Affairs.
news.relevanceReason: 该文章主要聚焦于迪士尼法律部门采用AI技术进行工作流程自动化，并招聘法律AI相关高级职位，属于法律AI在法务部门的应用，符合网站主题。

news.titleEn: Arbitrators Embrace + Reject Legal AI
news.titleZh: 仲裁员对法律AI既接纳又排斥
news.summaryZh: 美国一项针对557名仲裁专业人士的调查显示，法律AI的应用情况存在显著分歧。部分AI用例颇受欢迎，但许多其他用例遭到回避。调查数据来自美国仲裁协会（AAA）与Jus Mundi。在AI使用方面，文件审查与整理获得相对较高的使用或潜在使用率，其次是法律研究，再次是案件管理与时间线追踪，但这三项领先用例的使用率均未超过51%。与此同时，58%的受访者明确表示不会主要使用AI协助起草裁决书，即仲裁中的最终“判决”；49%的受访者表示不会在证据听证中主要使用AI。令人意外的是，仅有11%的受访者表示会使用AI进行翻译，尽管目前已有专门针对律师翻译需求的公司及多家提供高质量通用翻译的服务商。这可能是因为在仲裁环境中，每个词都可能至关重要，仲裁员认为使用AI风险过高。总体而言，基于该调查，仲裁员对AI的使用相当保守，主要信任其在早期阶段（如审查与研究）的应用。在最关键的事项上，例如裁决书起草，对AI的热情极为有限，仅14%的受访者表示会主要使用AI。对准确性的疑虑可能是原因之一，但值得强调的是，最终裁决文件旨在体现专业仲裁员的个人判断，即他们主动希望该文件是“自己的思考”，而非通过AI重写争议的关键论点。在时间节省及其他收益方面，数据几乎呈对半分裂：43%的受访者报告显著节省时间，而37%认为AI使用没有重大益处。
news.bodyText: A survey of 557 arbitration professionals in the US has found strongly conflicting data about legal AI. While some use cases for AI seem popular, many others are shunned. Likewise, while 43% report significant time savings, 37% see no major benefits to AI use. First, let’s look at the AAA and Jus Mundi survey data for what arbitrators are using AI for, and what they prefer not to. As you can see in the table below, what gets a relatively high level of use, or potential use, is document review and organisation, followed by legal research, and then case management and timeline tracking. Although, none of those three leading examples are higher than 51%. Meanwhile, 58% explicitly said they would not primarily use AI to help with award drafting, i.e. the final ‘judgment’ in an arbitration, and 49% would also not primarily use AI in an evidentiary hearing. Surprisingly, only 11% said they’d use AI for translation – despite the fact that there are now companies focused just on that use case for lawyers, along with several others focused on good quality translation in general. Perhaps this is because in such an environment arbitrators feel it’s just too risky to use AI when every word could matter? The overall finding is that arbitrators are fairly conservative in their use of AI, at least based on this survey, trusting the technology primarily where the work is in the early stages, e.g. review and research. — Advertisement — — When it came to the most critical matters, e.g. the drafting of awards, then enthusiasm for AI is very limited, with only 14% out of the sample saying they’d use primarily AI. While doubts about accuracy are likely to be part of this, it’s worth underlining that the final award document is meant to represent the personal judgment of the professional arbitrators. I.e. they actively want that document to be their ‘own thoughts’, and not a rewrite via AI of the key arguments of the dispute. And now the time-savings and other benefits data. As you can see, it’s almost equally split between those who see benefits and those who don’t. The answer to this may be on several levels: Overall, AL would say that arbitration – of all legal work streams – is very much one based on human judgment. After all, it’s literally a case of asking respected experts their personal view in order to come to a solution to an often complex and previously intractable issue.
news.relevanceReason: 该文章聚焦于法律AI在仲裁领域的应用调查，涉及仲裁员对AI工具的使用态度、具体用例及收益评估，属于法律AI在司法/仲裁工作流中的应用范畴，符合网站主题。

news.titleEn: Harvey Launches Its First Ever TV Commercials
news.titleZh: Harvey 推出其史上首支电视广告
news.summaryZh: 法律AI平台Harvey推出其史上首支电视广告，将在ESPN、NBC、亚马逊、Netflix、HBO Max等频道播出，主题为“协议是法律职业的基石”。Harvey目前估值已超150亿美元。这是其首支电视广告，也是一项全新品牌活动，旨在致敬将共识转化为持久协议的律师。广告以“握手”这一最古老的协议形式为核心，突出律师在促成协议持久有效中展现的咨询与判断力。社会建立在协议之上，并通过达成新协议的能力向前发展；Harvey帮助律师更高效地工作，更快达成更好的协议，并将专业知识带给更多人，从而加速法律实践，推动社会进步。创作首支广告时希望立足于工作初衷及律师对社会的广泛影响，最终回归“握手”这一最简单的协议表达，其背后是帮助人们找到前进方向的对话、策略与判断。协议是法律职业的基石，该活动聚焦法律行业所能实现的价值，以及Harvey如何在全球范围内赋能这一工作。尽管此前已有法律科技公司投放电视广告，如LegalOn在日本、DISCO和LegalZoom在美国，但此类广告并不多见，部分原因是成本高昂。此举为与Legora及其他大型法律AI公司的竞争开辟新战线，此前竞争主要通过名人代言引人注目。此次广告未使用电影明星，而是传递“协议是基石”的信息。至于律师是否会看电视广告，答案是肯定的，就像所有人一样；而电视广告能否促进购买，可口可乐的成功案例或可参考。
news.bodyText: Harvey is launching its first ever TV commercials, which will run on ESPN, NBC, Amazon, Netflix, HBO Max and other channels. The theme is ‘agreements are foundational to the legal profession’. See a sample of the advert below. The fast-growing legal platform, which is now valued at well over $15 billion, told Artificial Lawyer: ‘This is our first TV commercial and a new brand campaign celebrating the lawyers who turn common ground into lasting agreements. Centered on the handshake, the oldest form of agreement, the campaign highlights the counsel and judgment lawyers bring to making agreements last.’ And they added that: ‘Society was built on agreements, and it moves forward through our ability to reach new ones: to resolve differences, compromise, and decide together what comes next. Harvey helps lawyers do that work more effectively, reach better agreements sooner, and bring their expertise to more people. As we accelerate the practice of law, we help move society forward.’ And here’s the campaign video. Chief Marketing Officer, Rachel Hepworth, commented: ‘When we set out to create Harvey’s first commercial, we wanted it to be grounded in why we do this work and the broader impact lawyers have on society. ‘We kept coming back to the handshake, the simplest expression of agreement. Behind it are the conversations, strategy, and judgment that help people find a way forward. This campaign lets us bring that story to a global audience while staying true to the lawyers at the heart of Harvey.’ While CEO, Winston Weinberg, added: ‘Agreements are foundational to the legal profession. This campaign focuses on what the legal industry makes possible, and how Harvey enables that work at a global scale.’ Is this a big deal? Well, although there have been legal tech TV campaigns before, for example, LegalOn has done commercials in Japan, while DISCO and LegalZoom also did TV ads in the US, there have not been that many. In part because they are rather expensive. This opens up a new front in the battle with Legora, and other large legal AI companies, which until recently has been notable via the use of celebrity endorsements. In this case, there are no movie stars, as yet, but rather the message above: that agreements are foundational. The next question is: do lawyers watch TV adverts? Well….yes. Just like everyone does. Does watching TV adverts make you buy things? Well……just ask Coca-Cola.

policy.titleEn: Eight Years On, Cambridge Analytica Scandal Catches Up With Meta in Santa Fe
policy.titleZh: 八年之后，剑桥分析丑闻在新墨西哥州圣塔菲追责Meta
policy.summaryZh: 9月28日，新墨西哥州圣塔菲陪审团裁定Meta（前身为Facebook）在剑桥分析数据隐私丑闻及仇恨言论、暴力和错误信息政策声明中误导公众，认定其29项公开声明中26项具有故意欺骗性，其中9项涉及其对剑桥分析丑闻的回应。扎克伯格和桑德伯格在审判前接受取证，州方在9月8日开始的审判中播放了视频。州检察官麦金质询扎克伯格关于内容审核，包括“交叉检查”名单；质询桑德伯格关于隐私信息、开发者调查及仇恨言论处理。陪审团依据两个数字计算违规：对11项媒体声明每项分配210万次违规，对15项公司渠道声明每项分配1,386,648次，总计43,899,720次。较大数字约等于新墨西哥州人口，较小数字反映该州2020年Facebook用户估计数。陪审团仅决定责任和违规次数，州法官马修将决定罚款金额。此前儿童安全案件中，法官维持3.75亿美元罚款并追加5.67亿美元基金。Meta发言人表示不同意判决并将继续辩护。该判决可能令其他州总检察长不满，他们多数在8月以约4.59亿美元和解了未来剑桥分析索赔，新墨西哥州未参与。佛罗里达州总检察长乌斯迈尔指责其他总检察长以“花生”价格和解，新墨西哥州裁决表明他可能正确。
policy.bodyText:
Eight Years On, Cambridge Analytica Scandal Catches Up With Meta in Santa Fe Justin Hendrix / Sep 28, 2026 Illustration from a screenshot of Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s July 14, 2026, deposition in New Mexico v Facebook .

Republish

On Friday, a jury in Santa Fe, New Mexico, found that Meta, formerly Facebook, misled the public in statements about the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal and its policies on hate speech, violence and misinformation. Jurors found 26 of 29 public claims by Facebook and its executives willfully deceptive, including nine concerning its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Both Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg were deposed ahead of the trial, and the state played the videos of the depositions for jurors during the trial, which started on Sept. 8 . State attorney Randi McGinn questioned Zuckerberg largely about content moderation, including the company’s "cross-check" list that gave high-profile users such as politicians and celebrities special review. She queried Sandberg on the company's messaging on privacy, the app developer investigation it promised after the Cambridge Analytica scandal, and its handling of hate speech and misinformation.

The jury relied on two figures to count violations, according to the verdict form . It assigned 2.1 million violations to each of 11 statements that appeared in major news outlets and 1,386,648 to each of 15 statements made through company channels, including its newsroom, executives' Facebook posts, earnings calls and a developer conference, for a total of 43,899,720. The Santa Fe New Mexican reported that the larger figure roughly equals New Mexico's population and the smaller one reflects an estimate of the state's Facebook users in 2020.

Unlike the jury in the state's child safety case against Meta, which set the penalty at the $5,000 maximum per violation, this jury decided only liability and the count. State District Judge Francis Mathew will determine how much Meta pays, Source New Mexico reported . In the earlier case, District Judge Bryan Biedscheid's Aug. 6 judgment kept the jury's $375 million penalty for 75,000 violations and ordered Meta to pay an additional $567 million into a fund to address harms to the state's youth.

"We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record," Meta spokesperson Alex Burgos said in an email to The Associated Press . "Meta's platforms are forums for free expression. We have a First Amendment right to manage those platforms in a way we believe best serves the interests of our community. This means prioritizing free speech, protecting our users' information and giving them control over their data."

The verdict may leave a bad taste in the mouths of other state attorneys general, most of whom released Meta from future Cambridge Analytica claims for about $459 million, a provision tucked into the company's $17 billion child safety settlement in August. New Mexico wasn't part of that deal.

"Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier accused the other AGs of settling for peanuts," said Daphne Keller, director of platform regulation at the Stanford Program in Law, Science & Technology. "New Mexico's stunning jury ruling suggests he may be right."
