Podcast

Gil Durán Maps the Rise of the 'Nerd Reich' Justin Hendrix / Sep 27, 2026 Audio of this conversation is available via your favorite podcast service.

Republish

On September 23, Tech Policy Press hosted an event at Betaworks in New York City with Gil Durán , the author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy , the New York Times bestselling book published by Simon & Schuster. Alice Marwick , research director at Data & Society, joined the discussion.

What follows is a lightly edited transcript of the event.

Simon & Schuster , 2026.

Justin Hendrix:

Welcome. And I'm very excited to be here tonight. Very excited that all of you have come. We put this together two weeks ago and I thought, oh, maybe 20 folks will show up or something like that. And it sold out. We ran out of seats very, very quickly. And I think that was for more than one reason, but chief among them, I think is just the amount of enthusiasm for this topic and the amount of reception that this book has had.

A bestseller on the New York Times, I think notched up a couple of spots again today. Sometimes things briefly appear on the Times bestseller list and then quickly fall off. This is not doing that. It's bouncing around, still fighting it out with others who are trying to take up that mantle. I had the luck of meeting Gil, I guess about a year and a half ago at something that Alice and Alice's team at Data & Society helped to coordinate. We put together a kind of writer's salon, I think it's fair to say, on issues at the intersection of tech and democracy, a lot of concern about techno fascism. And we ended up having a series of essays that we published at Tech Policy Press on that topic. And Gil's was one among them, wrote at the time about ‘Network State’ and Próspera and these kinds of wild ideas for cities that some of the tech oligarchs have.

And at the time, this book was a sort of, I think, glimmer in your eye. You were still working on it. You were still kind of deep in it.

Gil Durán:

We were in talks.

Justin Hendrix:

In talks and you didn't know if it was going to work out. Before we get going, I think I just want to ask you to explain the journey from that moment, not only 18 months ago or so. You felt you needed to do this, you were willing to settle back, put in the work, but did you think this would happen, that you'd be here in New York City with a raft of events to attend and on the New York Times bestseller list?

Gil Durán:

I thought I was going to be at a bookstore with five people, half of them my friends, if they even showed up. I know a lot of writers. I've grown up around writers, book writers, and I know how hard it is. You're out there crusading on your little book. And even if it's a great book, oftentimes there's not enough of an audience. And so that was my vision for myself. But the book really came about because my readers of my newsletter kept bugging me and saying, you got to write a book, you got to write a book. And I thought, well, I appreciate your faith, but if you know anything about the publishing industry and about book writing, it's not that easy and it's a real uphill battle. But because of them, I started reaching out to agents and trying to at least get someone to tell me no.

And that's what ended up leading to the book. So it really came from the demand from my readers that I do something deeper. And without them, it wouldn't have crossed my mind because obviously I have a very cynical view of how easy it is to write a book. And so that's really why I'm here is because of them.

Justin Hendrix:

Great. And I believe that both that agent and the publisher or some representatives from the publisher are here tonight. So good on you for taking that risk on Gil and good on you for getting it done. So we're going to talk about a bunch of things tonight. We're going to kind of try to contextualize the book a little bit, but I wanted to just start by kind of taking the temperature. There is a lot going on in the world right now. And if you're someone who follows issues at this sort of intersection of tech and society, it's been an absolute avalanche of a few weeks of news. It's very, very difficult to keep up. So just to kind of contextualize how we're feeling and what you think is going on, I'm going to ask both of you, just give us one word that you think may contextualize what the mood is right now.

And maybe Alice, I'll start with you and come back to Gil on this one. One word.

Alice Marwick:

Exhausted. I'm sure a lot of you saw this study the CDC put out this week showing that 71% of American adults are exhausted and experiencing serious fatigue. And unsurprisingly, this is higher for women and younger people, right? Everything is exhausting. Politics are exhausting and horrifying. Tech is exhausting and all the tools that I used to really like are now really unpleasant to use. Navigating it all is exhausting. And when we have these few bright spots in New York City, like the Knicks and Mamdani, it reminds me that it didn't used to be like this and that everything doesn't have to be this draining and terrible all the time. So that's what I would like for us all to get to again. But yeah, exhausting.

Justin Hendrix:

Gil, one word.

Gil Durán:

Angry. Yeah. I think we see in the polls, people are getting really, really sick of this TV show. The sequel is even worse than the first one. And it's got an AI apocalypse theme to it and a bunch of open corruption. Prices are going up on people, gas prices, food prices, electricity prices. Even some people in the MAGA base who were previously unmovable are starting to realize he's a con man. Why? Because he stole billions of dollars from a lot of them in his crypto scam. So I think there's a public mood shift that's happening right now and hopefully the Democratic Party can get on top of it before Steve Bannon does.

Justin Hendrix:

Okay. So that's the context, how we're feeling exhausted, angry. Is anybody out there sort of feel that? Anybody out there? I see a few heads nodding. Okay. Well, let's step back then and let's talk about the book. Let's talk about the basics of the argument, maybe some of the people at its center. You kind of take us through a telling of various characters. You start off by kind of almost de-centering Elon Musk a little bit, which I think is interesting, but the basics of the argument. If we had you on a five minute radio interview right now, what would you tell folks out there this book is meant to be about?

Gil Durán:

My book is about a cult of apocalyptic billionaires who believe it is their destiny to end democracy and to end countries like the United States of America in the 21st century. They believe that their weapons for bringing about this death of democracy in the nation state system are technology, specifically crypto and AI. And when you look at what's happening right now in Washington, that's what it is. Crypto and AI becoming this powerful juggernaut force, especially in the money side crypto, though the AI industry is following the same playbook to capture unprecedented power and influence in the hands of a small group of interconnected oligarchs. And I tell a lot of the story in their own words because they have very big mouths and they love to hear themselves talk and they love to write long manifestos. These people do six hour podcasts. I've been doing a lot of one hour podcasts and I'm like, you know what?

My podcast is now 30 minutes because this is torture to make people speak for a whole hour and some people want to do 90 minutes. These guys love six hour podcasts, three hour podcasts. And when people first hear about this stuff, my experience in the past few years was it sounds crazy at first. It sounds conspiratorial, but a lot of crimes in history can be described as conspiracies. A lot of crimes today are conspiracy to this, conspiracy to that, but it's not a theory if it's in their own words. And so it was really important to me to tell the story in their own words because it seems to me that what this group of billionaires has been talking about for decades now, some of them, is also what they're now doing. And it wasn't clear to me why no one else is really talking about this, why the mainstream media isn't explaining this to people.

And that's what I set out to do with my five part series in The New Republic and my little newsletter, which at one point I was writing for 12 people, but they're the OGs. So that's what I tried to do with the book was make this conversation happen, make people talk about what it is they've been saying and to ask the question, is this what they're doing? I think the answer is clearly yes, but I think a logical rational reader can draw their own conclusion.

Justin Hendrix:

Alice, I want to bring you in because you've been studying the kind of tech right and the right generally for quite some time. Why do you assess that Gil's book has done so well just in this last bit? What's he captured?

Alice Marwick:

Yeah. So I think what Gil's book has done, if you haven't read it, many of you got free copies, you really should. It's really readable. It manages to go through an incredibly dense set of people, places and things and brings them together in this sort of roughly chronological narrative that really conveys how batshit crazy these people are and how much they've been able to get away with, with virtually no scrutiny from outside their subcultures. There is everything in this book from gold bugs to Ron Paul, to obscure investment newsletters, to cryogenics. It is all there. The greatest hits of Silicon Valley hyper-libertarianism over the last like 30, 40 years. As Justin said, I started studying what was then called the alt-right in 2016 because I was super interested in why was the mainstream media suddenly covering all these white supremacists and deeply misogynist ideas. And unfortunately, over the last decade, what I've seen is a lot of these ideas, which when I started studying them were like weird fringe things that dudes on the internet argued about are now part of mainstream American political thought.

Racist and virulent ideas that I never thought would get traction on mainstream media on television in the New York Times are now things that people talk about totally openly. They don't feel like they have to be behind closed doors. And I think what Gil's able to do is he's able to show the genesis of this stuff and how it's not just like. When we think about white supremacists or violent misogynists, you think of these dudes alone in their basement, you think of people with very little social power, right? You often think of poor people or people who don't have access to wealth. That's not who these people are. These are people who are the most powerful people in the world, the richest people in the world and the people who control the technology and the media through which many of our, not even just our media, but our communication with each other and our thoughts about ourselves flow through.

So there's a linkage here between the technology, the ideology, the politics and the money that I think is done really effectively.

Justin Hendrix:

So I want to just get you for a moment, Gil, to help our audience, help the listener think a little bit about Peter Thiel in particular. You spent a lot of the book on Peter Thiel and I mentioned you decenter Musk in a way at the beginning almost to just sort of say, listen, a lot of folks focused on Musk, especially early on in the Trump administration as being this sort of powerful character, as Svengali by Donald Trump's side. But your point was that this slightly quieter character perhaps had more influence in the White House just in the sheer number of individuals with very close ties, including the vice president himself. But I don't know, how do you explain Peter Thiel again in just a handful of minutes?

Gil Durán:

Well, Elon Musk gets a lot of the attention because he's an attention hog. He loves to be out there all day tweeting and getting in the story, jumping in front of the camera. We saw the results of that with DOGE where he ended up burning out because you can't really outshine the president. So you had two people vying for attention. But I see Musk mostly as a follower rather than a leader. Not that he doesn't have a lot of power, but he's not the ideological or intellectual originator of this stuff. I think authoritarianism and oligarchy and dictatorship naturally appeal to him because of who he is, but other people, it appeals to them also on an intellectual level. They thought this through. And Musk was part of the PayPal Mafia with Peter Thiel and Joe Lonsdale and other people, but it's Thiel who's considered the godfather of the PayPal Mafia.

So he's really the boss of the group and he actually played a role in ousting Musk early on from PayPal. So while they have a relationship that's been fruitful, it's also been troubled. Well, first of all, he was born in Germany, came here as a child after living in South Africa and Namibia where his father was involved in trying to mine uranium for South Africa's secretive nuclear program. And Thiel for a very long time has been a right wing zealot. All the way back in the mid 1990s, he wrote a book called The Diversity Myth that was an attack on diversity in colleges that largely mirrors the current attacks on DEI that have been so successful. And if you look at his history for the past 30 years, Thiel has been openly preaching against democracy and crowing about the fact that in the 21st century, democracy will die, that technology will be the end of it.

In 1999, he gave a speech in which he said, this is a very popular speech on YouTube now for reasons that'll be obvious, that there was going to be this new currency in the future, a new digital currency, and it would completely undermine government authority and power and the government would be totally powerless to stop it and it would reshape everything in the 21st century. And of course people call this the speech that predicted crypto, which is not exactly true. Crypto had been talked about and imagined in science fiction, but for a lot of people, they look at that and say, "Here he is in 1999." Not only that, he said that the main vehicle for this new world was going to be smartphones, which in 99, few people had. I remember we had this big fold up phones with the antenna you could pull up that we could check out of the newspaper where I worked.

But in 2009, he went on to write that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible. In 2010, he gave a speech to a group of libertarians that was probably smaller than this room where he said that government is fundamentally evil and that technology was an incredible alternative to politics. And this is the guy who since 2003 had been the co-founder of Palantir, a surveillance software technology company that was founded with $2 million from the CIA's venture capital arm In-Q-Tel. So he's since then gone on to become very ingrained in our government through Palantir. He was an early supporter of Donald Trump. He essentially created JD Vance. And I just think it's really strange. We've been in the middle of this media cycle of everyone having to focus on Hasan [Piker]'s stuff, things he said, but no one ever asks why we have a government contractor and major political donor with all of his network throughout the Trump administration who's been preaching against American democracy for 30 years.

That question never seems to come up. So I focused on Thiel because I think that he's really the root of a lot of our problems today and that it's his ideas that through his money, through his investment in various people like Curtis Yarvin, who I know we'll talk about, and JD Vance has become one of the most powerful men in the world. And if JD Vance somehow becomes president, it'll actually be, in my opinion, Peter Thiel who is president of the United States.

Justin Hendrix:

Okay. So I want to ask kind of one more question in this way and then also open up to Alice to pelch you with a few questions too. But one of the things that I think about a lot and probably most of the folks in this room are thinking about on occasion is the kind of divide right now on the right around tech because you have this sort of MAGA populist side, possibly embodied in the likes of Steve Bannon who was on stage last week. Didn't quite share the stage, but certainly shared the same stage as Bernie Sanders [I-Vt.] decrying the possible existential risk of artificial intelligence, very against the AI oligarchs and the elites, et cetera. But then you have what appears to be happening in the White House, right? Donald Trump all in, spending his weekend trying to poll his Truth Social followers about what we should rename artificial intelligence.

I think we've settled on super intelligence according to the last poll, but certainly staunch defender of the data centers, staunch defender of full speed ahead on artificial intelligence, clearly has a lot of his own personal money invested, his family's money invested in these things. But there is this divide and right now it feels like at least with regard to Trump and the White House, the Thiel side of things is winning out. Do you think that will continue?

Gil Durán:

It depends on how much money they pour on the Trump family, I think. The White House is for sale. The Trump family has raked in up to, depending on the day, $5 billion in new wealth on paper through various crypto schemes and other venture capital investments. Some put it down closer to 1.2 billion. The problem with crypto is that you can have $5 billion one year and a billion the next because it's just so volatile. That's the anti-deflationary and inflationary nature of crypto. But I think they're getting paid and to me that's the most important aspect of it. It's not just Trump anymore. I think there's been a lot of focus from the democratic establishment on Trump, Trump, but this is a regime now. It's not just one person, it's about a group of people. And the amount of money pouring openly into the Trump family's coffers, basically they're trying to buy the MAGA movement, but the impediment to that is the MAGA movement.

And I think one of the major parts of the divide that's very fertile for exploitation, I used to be a political consultant, so I think about things too in terms of campaigns and how you'd play it. At the heart of the MAGA base is the evangelical movement. And these are people who, whether we agree with them or not, they believe in God, strongly believe in some version of God. It may not be our God. We may not think it's quite Christian in the sense of following the teachings of Christ, but they are Christians, they believe in God. On the other hand, you have these tech guys who believe they are creating God in the form of AI, in the form of super intelligence. This is the tech religion that I write about in the seventh chapter of my book. And I think that some people on the evangelical right see very clearly that these people are not like us, that they are not Christians.

They don't believe in God. And the first thing you have to do to really get the trust of those people is be on the same page religiously. So I do think there's a bit of a divide growing, especially since Donald Trump is clearly not going to keep his promises to bring down prices and to make things. People realize it's not going to be great again. In fact, it's maybe going to be no jobs because of the AI God or now they're hearing a lot about this extinction mythology coming out of Silicon Valley, which I don't really buy into. But again, as somebody familiar with political communications, there is a certain joy in realizing that they are marketing the key to their power and their wealth AI as a terrifying extermination apocalypse tool that is radicalizing people on the right and the left against billionaire power at the exact moment that we need it.

The problem is billionaires think they're good at everything, so they came up with their own messaging and it's a fricking disaster because this sounds good to venture capital firms maybe. We're going to create the tool that destroys all the jobs and maybe wipes out humanity, but it sounds terrifying to most people who are trying to pay their bills and raise their families. In politics, you're supposed to promise more jobs, more security and safety for your family and a brighter future. Silicon Valley's doing the exact opposite. So it may be our saving grace that they were still too incompetent at this point, but you do see some schism forming. I dislike Steve Bannon very much. I think he's been a cancer on our democracy, but unlike the New York Times, he's been clearly calling this stuff out for years and that's why I quote him in the introduction of my book.

The people on the right see this very clearly. They know what these guys are. While they want a version of fascism too, it's not the godless AI fascism they want. They want old school fascism.

Justin Hendrix:

Alice, what's your view on this question?

Alice Marwick:

Yeah, they want Christian nationalism. That's what they want and there is not quite as much money behind that right now, although there's a decent amount. So the thing that really struck me reading this book is these are people who are incredibly wealthy, have been extremely successful within a democratic regime, right? They're at the top of the heap. They've made all this money. Why are they so hostile to a system that has worked for them? Why are they so hostile to democracy?

Gil Durán:

Because it gives everyone a say theoretically and because of I think their greed. They can't be satisfied. They can't be satisfied with the money. I mean, if I was a billionaire, I would just shut up and stay under the radar. That's what the smart rich people do. You don't even know their names. There's all kinds of rich people you never even hear of because it's kind of scary to have everybody know that you're rich and that you're a target or that you're the root of their problems or whatever. And they just can't get enough. I think that's part of it. When I was in politics, I met a lot of rich people and I met a lot of powerful people. I came up with this motto, this must have been 15 years ago, that's become more important to me lately. When you have money, you want power.

When you have power, you want money. When you have both, you want to live forever and then you're really screwed. And that's where they are now, right? They're into this whole idea that they're on the cusp of this massive technological breakthrough. They're going to create a God who gives them eternal life, who allows them to become multiplanetary beings and travel into the heavens and creates this super abundant paradise in which they will live forever as these transhuman creatures who transcend even humanity itself. That's the Christian eschatology remade for a completely mentally. I mean, it's kind of like an AI psychosis billionaire class that has emerged to seize power. So I think that's a part of it. You can't get away from that weird dysfunction where they're not psychologically normal anymore. It's like if instead of being a barefoot hippie, Charles Manson was a billionaire and could get Washington to do what he wanted, to bring down the Helter Skelter via policy and corruption.

And I feel like that's pretty much where we are with these guys.

Alice Marwick:

So another thing I've thought about a lot over the years is the way that as technologies are developed, they often reflect the political ideologies of their creators. So you cite Fred Turner's book From Counterculture to Cyberculture where he talks about the ideology behind sort of early Silicon Valley as being this sort of freewheeling, hippie, democratic, not democratic, but decentralized ethos. And then in the book we see this again with Bitcoin and AI, right? Bitcoin is a technology that instantiates this anti-status principle because it replaces a state-backed currency with one that is entirely speculative and that is decoupled from the state. And I would also argue that I think AI is an anti-democratic technology because it requires so much compute and resources to work effectively that you can't distribute it outside of the handful of a small number of people. So my question to you is what comes first?

Is it the technology or the ideology with some of these guys?

Gil Durán:

I'd say the ideology. It's white supremacy innovating and male supremacy. I mean, the Nazis also had technology. They also liked rockets in cars and war, and that's sort of where we are with these guys as well. It seems like technology, fascism always coincides with these technological breakthroughs because suddenly people see a way to gain dominance over everyone else. You have this thing, whether it's using air power in a war or rocket power or the race to get the nukes, you see this accelerationist tendency. In Italy, there was this group called the Futurists who saw technology and violence and speed as the key to the future of civilization. And the writer of the Futurist Manifesto ends up writing a few years later something called the Fascist Manifesto and was a collaborator with Mussolini in developing this idea of fascism. So I write about that a little in my book, not enough for my academic critics, but that's their job is to write that longer book about that particular interchange.

I think that it's a way to gain power and dominance and it comes out of an ideology where that more than anything is the goal. There's a whole other way to do technology where we could actually be making life better. I mean, if the billionaires were trying to solve climate change and poverty, it'd be hard to speak against them and we could be working on things that do that, but instead all we see are technologies whose main innovation is to concentrate all of the wealth into fewer and fewer hands. I think that it's going to reach a breaking point sooner rather than later.

Alice Marwick:

So this is my last question before I hand it back to Justin. So another thing I've thought about a lot over the last 10 years is the lack of trust that Americans have in their institutions. If you look at the polls, like the Pew Research does a bunch on this, people don't trust politicians, they don't trust the news media, they don't trust academia, they don't trust science. All of these traditional knowledge producing institutions are now seen as disreputable. And obviously the Trump administration has really capitalized on that, right? They've portrayed academia and science as enemies of the average person when in fact that's not what we do. But I am really interested in how this sort of institutional distrust has been both fueled by and taken advantage of by tech. I feel like sometimes these billionaires, they see this lack of institutional trust as a sort of wedge that they can get into.

If we had a country where everybody really liked the government, Elon Musk wouldn't have been able to do what he did with DOGE. What's your take on that?

Gil Durán:

Peter Thiel's really obsessed with the concept of scapegoating, this idea he studied under a guy at Stanford named René Girard. It's not totally wrong that societies tend to blame all their problems on a certain scapegoat and then we push the blame onto that person, persecute them, torture them, and that's how we sort of cleanse the sins of our society. We saw that story play out in the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, for instance. I think a lot of what happens is they are able to use these tensions to scapegoat some group. Obviously immigrants have been bearing the brunt of it under this regime, followed by federal workers who've been demonized and purged. Some of my critics are like, "Well, is it really fascism though?" One of the key characteristics of fascism is purging your demonized opponents from power and influence, and that's one of the key things that they have done.

But the problem is that they've convinced everybody they're creating the destruction machine, the narrative is starting to crumble. If you look at the polls, the anger is now rising at them. The problem playing with these concepts like scapegoating and demonizing is that they tend to bounce back on you. I think in a way they're so obsessed with scapegoating because they know that if people figured out what was really going on, who's really responsible for most of our problems, they would be in very, very grave danger, which is why they're trying to build these weird ass network state cities all over the world so they can go hide out if this doesn't work out for them. Things are going so well on the Trump administration that Peter Thiel just bought a mansion in Argentina.

I think that's the key there is they've been able to scapegoat, but not to the degree. The problem is this, I think. When this first started, my fear is it would be a lot more popular. I thought they must have some kind of propaganda algorithm plan to make people really love this stuff, to make people very supportive of it, but they didn't have that part of it figured out and it's collapsing because they have no understanding of how normal people think, feel, or experience reality. And they're learning the hard way what it feels like to be in power and everybody starts to hate you.

Justin Hendrix:

I want to bring it back to the current moment in just a moment, but I'm just going to ask one question that I feel like comes into my mind, both reading this book, but every time someone brings it up, which is what's up with the antichrist?

Gil Durán:

Peter Thiel knows about the Antichrist. He's actually giving more antichrist lectures in Nashville starting next week. I actually got a ticket. I can't make the first one, but I'm going to try to go after that and connect with some people in Nashville. Peter Thiel gets obsessed with some esoteric ideas and for the past 30 years, the Antichrist has popped up in some of his stuff, but now he's really honing in on his final subject. In the book, I say that having attained the heights of wealth, power, and influence with his cronies and company and power in Washington at the most critical moment in history, Peter Thiel decided the time was right to warn the world about the Antichrist. And the strange thing is that when Peter Thiel describes the antichrist, because he got a hold of the transcripts. When he was giving these speeches last year in San Francisco, I got an anonymous email.

I'm recording them. Do you want them? I was like, yes. We should give them to everybody because how do I know they're real unless the Washington Post or someone with a bigger budget can verify these things? So they went out to everybody, but I've read them all multiple times. I don't recommend it. It's very disordered, convoluted thinking. But Peter Thiel, a very influential billionaire, the guy who created the vice president is giving four part. On four different days for four hours, he speaks about the Antichrist. And basically his warning is that the Antichrist is here among us and he's creating his own theological.

I mean, the Vatican and the bishops in Austria were like, "This is BS, failed grade." They literally gave him a failed grade when he delivered the lectures to a group of theologians in Austria, Innsbruck University. This high level Catholic stuff. But basically his main argument is that anyone who stands in the way of technological acceleration to the maximum is the antichrist, is against the future of humanity. At the same time, Peter Thiel describes the antichrist as this figure, which is by the way, not biblical, the antichrist were people who were faked features of Christianity, not a specific figure from a future apocalypse. That's the Omen movie from 1976. That's where this version of the antichrist is coming from. It's the people who own the technology, the way the technology is being developed and the way the technology is being controlled by a tiny group of people. AI itself could be a lot of different things and we're only being sold one version of it. So I think that understanding how AI works, if you want to, I think that can make you a better critic. And I think learning more about other visions of AI that have been crowded out by the big AI companies and big tech are ways that we can participate in technology without having to refuse it and still look towards a positive future.

Justin Hendrix:

I'm going to let Gil give us a last word. Something you're watching over the next few months that will tell you kind of which way we're headed with this kind of techno-fascist trajectory we're on. Clearly we've got elections in the United States. There's many other things that might happen over the near term. What are you watching? What feel like pivotal events in the next few weeks or months?

Gil Durán:

The main thing I'm watching is how much money the crypto, AI and venture capitalists pour into these elections and where that money goes, particularly how much they put toward Republicans and how much they put toward Democrats. The Wall Street Journal reported two weeks ago that they're now starting to cozy back up to Democrats because they feel like Trump doesn't have the energy to steal the election and then the Democrats are going to retake power. And so that to me is going to be the biggest indicator because although I came up in the Democratic establishment and certainly nobody's idea of a Republican, I really feel that there's a grave danger. These guys have enough money to buy both sides and that's what they're doing. In the San Francisco gubernatorial race this year, we had one crypto billionaire, Chris Larsen, who was funding Katie Porter, this former progressive firebrand from Congress and simultaneously funding Steve Hilton, this Republican Fox News host who demonizes immigrants.

He was openly betting on both sides and that shows you their mentality, that's what they're doing. And the only people who love billionaire money more than Republicans are Democrats. And so that's the main thing I'm watching because my fear is that even if the Republicans fail, we're going to get these establishment Democrats, if they're allowed to, will launder the reputations of these guys. They'll say, let's look forward, not backward, and the future will be much, much worse and the fascism will be much, much more competent. So I think we have to put a lot of pressure on Democratic leaders if we have an election and if they take power to hold people accountable and make it clear that this kind of betrayal is going to be very, very, very regrettable.

Justin Hendrix:

I want to thank Alice Marwick for joining me on stage tonight to have this conversation. Thank Data & Society. It's a pleasure. Gil, I want to congratulate you on this book and thank you. Let's give him a round of applause. And then I also want to thank the folks at Betaworks and the team who've helped us put this event on tonight. Thank you so much.

research.titleEn: SinBrief: A Hybrid Framework for Abstractive Text Summarisation of Sinhala Legal Documents
research.titleZh: SinBrief：一种针对僧伽罗语法律文档的混合式抽象文本摘要框架
research.abstractEn: Legal document summarisation in low-resource languages presents significant challenges due to the scarcity of annotated data and the complexity of domain-specific terminology. This paper presents SinBrief, a hybrid abstractive summarisation framework for Sinhala legal documents that does not require human-annotated training data. The proposed framework combines domain-aware word graph construction with neural sentence scoring to generate abstractive summaries from Sinhala legal text. Five sentence scoring models are evaluated within the framework: mBert, Llama 3.1, Falcon 7B, Laser, and a continually pre-trained Llama model domain-adapted to Sinhala legal text. The framework is evaluated on a Sinhala legal corpus using reference-free metrics, including Coverage, Density, Compression Ratio, SummaC, and Self-BertScore. Experimental results demonstrate that SinBrief produces summaries with lower lexical overlap than extractive baselines while maintaining factual consistency, demonstrating the viability of hybrid, largely annotation-free abstractive summarisation for low-resource legal NLP tasks.
research.abstractZh: 低资源语言的法律文档摘要由于标注数据稀缺和领域特定术语的复杂性而面临重大挑战。本文提出了SinBrief，一种针对僧伽罗语法律文档的混合式抽象摘要框架，该框架不需要人工标注的训练数据。所提出的框架将领域感知的词图构建与神经句子评分相结合，以从僧伽罗语法律文本生成抽象摘要。在该框架内评估了五种句子评分模型：mBert、Llama 3.1、Falcon 7B、Laser以及一个持续预训练并针对僧伽罗语法律文本进行领域适配的Llama模型。该框架在一个僧伽罗语法律语料库上使用无参考指标进行评估，包括覆盖率、密度、压缩比、SummaC和Self-BertScore。实验结果表明，SinBrief生成的摘要与抽取式基线相比具有较低的词汇重叠度，同时保持了事实一致性，证明了混合式、基本无需标注的抽象摘要方法在低资源法律NLP任务中的可行性。

news.titleEn: Startup Corner: From digital binders to AI research – meet Align
news.titleZh: 创业角：从数字卷宗到AI研究——认识Align
news.summaryZh: Align是一家由前Williams & Connolly诉讼合伙人Sam Davidoff创立的法律科技公司，最初为诉讼律师开发数字卷宗工具。经过五年发展，这家自筹资金的公司正扩展至AI驱动的法律研究领域，押注生成式AI重新打开了曾被视为饱和的市场。其原有产品Align Binders为诉讼律师提供可在笔记本电脑和iPad上使用的数字卷宗，支持在线/离线功能，并提供本地部署、私有云和SaaS等多种部署模式，以及完整的MDM移动支持。新产品Align Research是一个基于智能体AI的法律研究平台，运行定制的研究流程来检索案例，旨在无幻觉地查找美国判例法。公司专注于法律科技领域，为律所和律师构建企业级产品。Sam Davidoff在2020年时是Williams & Connolly LLP的诉讼合伙人。目标用户涵盖从独立出庭律师到AmLaw100诉讼团队的所有诉讼律师。公司希望继续拓展诉讼市场，认为全球诉讼律师众多且需要良好的工具。首个产品已上市数年，被多家大型AmLaw100律所及各种规模的审判团队使用。公司成立之初尚无AI，而AI改变了软件开发方式和产品类型。推出Align Research反映了公司对AI带来新产品机会的看法，此前他们认为法律研究市场已饱和，但AI带来了新问题（如幻觉）和新解决方案。律师对改变工作流程持谨慎态度，因此真正新颖的法律产品（非替代品）的销售周期可能很慢，有时甚至慢得令人痛苦。
news.bodyHtml:
Founded by former Williams & Connolly litigation partner Sam Davidoff, Align began life building digital binders for litigators. Five years on, the bootstrapped legal tech company is expanding into AI-powered legal research, betting that generative AI has reopened a market it once regarded as saturated. We find out more.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

I’m a former litigator who now makes software for other litigators. Our original product, Align Binders, gives litigators digital binders on their laptops and iPads. Our new product, Align Research, gives litigators an expert AI-based research agent that finds US case law without hallucinations.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

We are software development team focused on the LegalTech space. We build enterprise-grade products for law firms and lawyers. Align Binders is a mobile digital binders solution with online/offline capabilities, on-prem, private cloud, and SaaS deployment models, and full MDM support for mobility. Align Research, our newest product, is an agentic AI-based legal research platform that runs a custom legal research pipeline to retrieve cases.

When were you founded?

2020

Advertisement
By who?

Sam Davidoff, who was then a litigation partner at Williams & Connolly LLP.

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Sam Davidoff

Who are your target clients?

Litigators – anyone from solo trial lawyers up through AmLaw100 litigation groups.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

We want to continue to expand throughout the litigation market. There are a lot of litigators in the world, and they need good tools (of the AI and non-AI variety).

Key achievements?

Our first product has been on the market for several years and is in use at several major AmLaw100 firms as well by trial teams of all sizes.

Have you received investment?

No.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

When we started, there was no AI. AI has changed both how we develop software and the kinds of products we are building. Our launch of Align Research reflects our view that there are new product opportunities enabled by AI. Legal research was an area that previously we had thought saturated. With the advent of AI, there are new problems (e.g., hallucinations) and new solutions (like our agentic case finder!)

What are the key challenges in your market?

Lawyers are understandably slow to change their workflows. This means the sales cycle for new legal products that are genuinely new (not substitutes for existing products) can be slow, sometimes painfully slow.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company? 

Our core development team has worked together for over five years and has never met in person! We have a lot of plans for what that first meetup is going to be like…

news.titleEn: Epiq acquires data breach response tech company Canopy
news.titleZh: Epiq收购数据泄露响应技术公司Canopy
news.summaryZh: 9月25日，Epiq宣布收购领先的数据泄露响应技术公司Canopy。此次收购将Canopy平台与Epiq的全球规模、网络专业能力及持续的AI投资相结合，使组织能够更高效、更准确地管理网络事件。Canopy一直是Epiq帮助组织响应网络事件的长期合作伙伴，通过将Canopy的技术和工程人才纳入团队，客户将获得更紧密的泄露响应体验，以及通过主动准备进一步降低风险暴露、利用AI加强事件后响应的下一代网络解决方案。Canopy平台拥有专利，可评估暴露数据、检测敏感信息并识别受影响个人。其Auto Review功能使用代理式AI自动化一级数据挖掘审查，使团队能够直接从筛选进入质量控制阶段。该平台将整合到Epiq AI（代理式AI解决方案套件）中，并通过Epiq Service Cloud（法律技术和服务平台）提供访问，该平台为客户提供简化的网络解决方案访问途径。Epiq欢迎Canopy团队加入，包括前首席运营官Adi Elliott，她将担任网络产品管理副总裁。Elliott在领导法律技术、网络事件响应和数据驱动运营方面的软件和服务业务方面拥有丰富经验。Canopy旨在帮助组织了解网络事件的范围和影响，并以更快的速度和信心做出响应，借助Epiq的全球资源和规模，Canopy将能够在此基础上进一步发展，并将该技术带给更多组织。
news.bodyHtml:
Epiq today (25 September) announced the acquisition of Canopy, a leading data breach response technology company. The acquisition enables organizations to manage cyber incidents more efficiently and accurately by combining the Canopy platform with the global scale, cyber expertise, and ongoing AI investment of Epiq.

“Canopy has been a longstanding partner to Epiq in helping organizations respond to cyber incidents,” said Scott Berger, Senior Vice President, Managed Services and Cyber Solutions at Epiq. “By welcoming its technology and engineering talent into our team, clients benefit from a more connected breach response experience. They gain next-generation cyber solutions that further reduce risk exposure through proactive preparedness and strengthen post-event response with AI.”

Advertisement

The patented Canopy platform assesses exposed data, detects sensitive information, and identifies impacted individuals. Its Auto Review feature uses agentic AI to automate first-level data mining review, allowing teams to move directly from culling to quality control. The platform will be integrated into Epiq AI, an agentic AI solutions suite, and will be accessible through the Epiq Service Cloud, a legal technology and services platform that provides clients with streamlined access to cyber solutions.

Epiq welcomes the Canopy team, including former Chief Operating Officer Adi Elliott, who joins as Vice President, Product Management, Cyber. Elliott brings experience leading software and services businesses across legal technology, cyber incident response, and data-driven operations.

Advertisement

“Canopy was built to support organizations in understanding the scope and impact of a cyber incident and responding with greater speed and confidence,” said Elliott. “With Epiq, we gain global resources and scale to build on the foundation that made Canopy successful and bring that technology to more organizations.”

news.titleEn: Remote Workers, Foreign Vendors, and AI: The Trade Secret Risks Most North Carolina Companies Are Not Managing
news.titleZh: 远程员工、外国供应商与AI：北卡罗来纳州多数企业未管理的商业秘密风险
news.summaryZh: 远程办公、外国供应商和人工智能工具的使用，分别构成商业秘密风险，而多数企业的标准政策尚未跟上。远程办公并非主要风险在于员工故意窃取信息，而是工作环境失去了物理和数字控制，使信息通过个人Wi-Fi、个人设备和云账户转移，形成无法审计、监控或清除的暴露点。企业应制定远程工作商业秘密政策，包括禁止在公司邮箱、个人云服务或设备上存储公司信息，要求使用VPN，并禁止个人USB设备。移动设备管理至关重要，企业需具备远程擦除离职员工个人设备上公司数据的技术和合同能力。使用外国供应商时，若发生盗用，执行权利可能不切实际，因为《商业秘密保护法》虽具有全球效力，但若供应商在美国无业务或资产，诉讼执行困难。因此，应在分享信息前管理风险，包括在协议中加入同意美国司法管辖的条款、审计权以及合同终止时要求认证销毁或返还信息。在聘用外国供应商前，应回答三个问题：是否有国内替代方案、能否在美国法院追索、协议是否赋予审计权和删除要求。AI工具已成为员工日常工作的一部分，但多数使用个人账户和免费层级，其服务条款可能允许平台将提交的数据用于模型训练，这构成额外风险。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Each one creates a distinct trade secret risk that your standard policies have likely not caught up with. Like it or not, remote work is not going away. While this modern workforce commonplace provides great convenience for workers, those privileges come with risks. The risk it creates is not primarily that employees will deliberately steal information, but rather that the remote work environment removes the physical and digital controls that once made trade secret misappropriation difficult and visible. When an employee works from home, company information moves across personal Wi-Fi networks, onto personal devices, and into personal cloud accounts. Each of those transfers is a potential exposure point: the file saved to a personal Google Drive for convenience, the work email forwarded to a personal account to read later, or the document downloaded to a personal laptop because the VPN was slow. Most of these are innocent, or seemingly appear as such, but any of them can result in confidential information sitting in an environment you cannot audit, monitor, or wipe when the employee leaves. Your company should have minimum requirements for a remote work trade secret policy that holds up to legal scrutiny. These requirements include no company information on personal email accounts, no storage in personal cloud services, no use of personal devices for work files unless enrolled in company mobile device management, VPN required for all access to company systems, and no use of personal USB drives or external storage. These should be written rules, communicated at hiring, reinforced in periodic training, and enforced without carve-outs for convenience. If you allow exceptions, expect to see them cited against you in litigation. Mobile device management matters more than most companies realize. If an employee uses a personal phone to access company email or company systems, you need the contractual and technical ability to remotely wipe company data from that device when they leave. You do not want to discover, after a departure, that eighteen months of confidential communications are sitting on a personal phone you have no way to reach. Put plainly, if an employee leaves a company phone at the bar in an airport, you need to be able to delete the data on it before anyone else finds it. Many companies use overseas vendors for software development, manufacturing, or technical services. The legal risk is specific: if a foreign vendor misappropriates your trade secrets, enforcing your rights against them may be practically impossible. The DTSA has worldwide reach in theory. If an act in furtherance of misappropriation occurred in the United States, federal courts can exercise jurisdiction over the full scheme, including conduct abroad. However, a vendor in a country with no U.S. operations and no U.S. assets presents serious practical enforcement problems. Getting into a foreign court system on a trade secret claim is slow, expensive, and uncertain, and in some jurisdictions, unrealistic. The time to manage this risk is before you share your information. Vendor agreements with foreign companies should include a consent to U.S. jurisdiction for any trade secret dispute. Without that consent, you may have a valid legal claim and no practical path to pursue it. Agreements should also specify audit rights: if a vendor has access to your proprietary software, manufacturing specifications, or technical documentation, you need the contractual right to audit their handling of that information and require certified destruction or return when the relationship ends. Before engaging a foreign vendor for anything that involves your proprietary information, three questions are worth answering: Is there a domestic alternative that could perform this work? If the vendor misappropriates my information, can I reach them in a U.S. court under the existing contract? Does the agreement give me audit rights and require certified deletion at the end of the engagement? If any answer is no, the arrangement deserves closer review before it proceeds. Like remote work, AI tools have become standard in the daily work of many employees, whether companies formally allow it or not. Legal teams use them to draft documents. Sales teams use them to prepare client materials. Engineers use them to write and review code. Most of this happens on personal accounts and free consumer tiers of platforms operating under terms of service that permit the platform to use submitted data for model training.

news.titleEn: Employment AI Tools Raise New Bias, Privacy, and Compliance Challenges
news.titleZh: 雇佣AI工具引发新的偏见、隐私与合规挑战
news.summaryZh: 雇主在员工全周期采用AI工具时，须应对地方、州、联邦及超国家层面关于偏见、隐私、透明度和歧视风险的要求，并提供有意义的人工监督。AI工具可用于招聘、评估、生产力监控等，例如筛选简历、排名候选人、评估薪酬公平性等。若AI排名候选人而人类无法审查所有简历，则人类决策被AI取代。法律不仅限于完全替代人类决策的工具，也涵盖实质性协助或影响人类决策的工具。主要风险包括：AI基于社区选择候选人，而社区与种族等受保护特征相关，可能产生歧视；评估生产力的工具可能忽略残疾员工的合理便利；影响晋升或加薪的评估可能引发歧视索赔。现有法律如《民权法案》第七章、《美国残疾人法案》和《公平信用报告法》均适用。此外，纽约市地方法律144要求自动化就业决策工具进行独立偏见审计并通知候选人；加州民权法规允许在歧视索赔中考虑反偏见测试证据，其隐私法规自2027年起要求风险评估和通知；伊利诺伊州禁止使用具有歧视性影响的AI或邮政编码作为代理，并要求通知；科罗拉多、康涅狄格和得克萨斯州也有相关要求。其他司法管辖区要求公司解释AI决策因素，个人可能有权要求人工复审。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! As employers adopt artificial intelligence (AI) tools throughout the employee lifecycle, they must address evolving local, state, federal, and supranational requirements governing bias, privacy, transparency, and potential discrimination risks, while also providing meaningful human oversight. Quick Hits There is an ever-increasing number of exciting AI tools that are available to companies to perform employment-related tasks, such as recruiting, hiring, employee evaluations, evaluating employee productivity and safety programs, and even offboarding employees. For example, AI tools can screen applications, parse resumes, rank candidates, create employee evaluations, evaluate pay equity, monitor drivers for fatigue, and spot fake candidates. There are numerous advantages to using these technologies, but there is an important analysis that must be conducted when the AI is replacing human decision-making. If the technology will rank candidates and the professional who oversees reviewing resumes is unable to review all resumes, then the AI has effectively chosen the individuals who are eligible for the job. This would mean that the human decision-maker has been replaced by AI. Notably, however, many laws are not limited to tools that fully replace a human decision-maker; some also reach tools that substantially assist, materially influence, or facilitate human decisions. The main concerns associated with these technologies center around: For instance, if the AI notes that historically individuals who live in a particular neighborhood have more leadership roles and it begins choosing candidates based on neighborhood, and neighborhood correlates with a protected characteristic such as race or national origin, the tool could have an unintended discriminatory effect on individuals in that protected group. If a technology is aimed at evaluating productiveness, it might not consider that an employee has accommodations in place associated with a disability. For technologies that have an impact on employees, such as evaluations that lead to raises or being chosen for a promotion, the potential consequences, including exposure to discrimination claims, can be significant. Federal, State, and Local Laws Although AI use is relatively new, many laws are worth considering when implementing any AI tool, such as federal and state laws that address discrimination (e.g., Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act), accommodations, and conducting background checks (e.g., the Fair Credit Reporting Act). In addition to these existing laws that may apply to any new AI tool, there are specific state and local laws and regulations that could require notice of use, bias audits, and risk assessments. For example, New York City’s Local Law 144 requires employers that use automated employment decision tools for hiring or promotion to obtain an independent bias audit, publish a summary of the results, and notify candidates and employees. California’s civil rights regulations allow evidence of anti-bias testing, or its absence, to be considered in discrimination claims, and its privacy regulations will require risk assessments, notices, and opt-out and access rights for certain automated employment decisions beginning in 2027. Illinois prohibits using AI that has a discriminatory effect or using zip codes as a proxy for protected classes and requires notice of AI use, and Colorado, Connecticut, and Texas have also enacted AI-related requirements. Other jurisdictions require, or will soon require, companies to provide individuals with an explanation as to how their AI tool works, and in particular what factors and criteria were used in making the determination. Individuals may also have the right to request that a human review the results in certain jurisdictions.

research.titleEn: Multi-Jurisdictional Legal Identity Assurance for Capability Gating: A Design-Science Proposal for Tiered, Reusable Identity Assurance of Natural, Juridical, and Machine Entities
research.titleZh: 多司法管辖区法律身份保证用于能力门控：关于自然实体、法人实体和机器实体的分级、可复用身份保证的设计科学提案
research.abstractEn: Identity assurance is the cost a digital system pays for dishonesty and uncertainty: it exists to make acts attributable when not everyone can be trusted at their word. A common way to pay that cost is flat maximum verification, asking each participant to meet a single high level of identification at entry, before any capability is exercised. Paid on everyone, it over-collects, excludes participants who cannot meet a bar they never needed to clear, taxes every interaction with the cost of the rarest high-risk case, and binds the strength of identification to the activity it unlocks. Existing frameworks compound this by fixing a small number of per-credential levels inside a single legal space and binding each verification to the institution that performed it, leaving cross-border reuse and the tension between data erasure and evidentiary retention unaddressed. This paper develops, as a design-science proposal, a tiered and reusable model of identity assurance for natural, juridical, and machine entities across jurisdictions. Reading the problem through systems theory, where a system changes only when an entity acts, the model holds the assurance state apart from the capability gate that consumes it, so that identity demand follows the act and the weight of its consequences rather than mere presence: a participant may take part with minimal disclosure and supply more only as an act requires. It comprises a typed entity taxonomy, a two-axis coordinate of disclosed assertion scope and source of information, jurisdiction as a time-indexed attribute of the entity, and reliance recorded as bitemporal, liability-allocated, point-in-time snapshots. Requirements are derived from anti-money-laundering, electronic-identity, and data-protection law, and the proposal is evaluated against flat maximum verification, per-credential level-of-assurance designs, and institutional reusable-KYC reliance.
research.abstractZh: 身份保证是数字系统为不诚实和不确定性所付出的代价：它的存在是为了在并非每个人都能信守承诺时使行为可归因。支付这种代价的一种常见方式是扁平化最大验证，即在任何能力被行使之前，要求每个参与者在进入时达到单一的高级别身份识别。对每个人支付这种代价，会过度收集信息，将无法达到本无需达到的标准的参与者排除在外，使每次交互都承担最罕见高风险案例的成本，并将身份识别的强度与其解锁的活动绑定。现有框架通过在一个单一法律空间内固定少量按凭证划分的级别，并将每次验证与执行验证的机构绑定，使这一问题更加复杂，从而留下跨境复用以及数据擦除与证据保留之间的张力未得到解决。本文作为一项设计科学提案，开发了一种跨司法管辖区的、针对自然实体、法人实体和机器实体的分级且可复用的身份保证模型。通过系统理论来解读该问题——系统仅在实体行动时发生变化——该模型将保证状态与消费该状态的 capability 门控分离开来，从而使身份需求跟随行为及其后果的权重，而非仅仅跟随在场状态：参与者可以以最低限度的披露参与，并且仅在行为需要时提供更多信息。该模型包括一个类型化实体分类法、一个关于所披露断言范围和信息来源的双轴坐标、作为实体时间索引属性的司法管辖区，以及以双时态、责任分配、时点快照形式记录的信赖。需求源自反洗钱、电子身份和数据保护法律，并且该提案与扁平化最大验证、按凭证级别的保证设计以及机构可复用KYC信赖进行了评估比较。

news.titleEn: Cryptomathic adopts Luminance to broaden access to contract intelligence
news.titleZh: Cryptomathic采用Luminance平台，拓宽合同智能访问渠道
news.summaryZh: 丹麦IT安全公司Cryptomathic已部署Luminance的合同智能平台，旨在让整个业务部门更直接地获取合同信息，并减少其法律、风险与合规团队处理的常规查询量。Cryptomathic服务于大型金融机构，管理着大量包含技术、商业和服务级别条款的合同。关键信息通常分散在主协议、附件、附表和修订中，这些文件在客户关系过程中独立演变。在采用Luminance之前，有关续约日期、发票条款、责任立场和客户义务的查询通常都转给法律部门。该平台现在使销售、财务、销售运营和IT等团队能够直接访问经批准的合同信息，而法律支持则保留给更复杂的问题。该平台使业务用户能够以自然语言查询其合同存储库，并获得有证据支持的答复。它提高了对续约日期、采购订单条款、发票要求和合同义务的可见性，同时有助于减少常规法律查询。不同团队出于不同目的使用该存储库：IT部门检查与更新和发布相关的响应时间和义务；财务部门跟踪发票条款和许可证类型；销售运营部门监控续约日期和采购订单条款；法律部门分析责任和赔偿等问题。在Luminance之前，法律部门是任何合同相关事宜的唯一联系点。现在，业务团队可以自己找到答案，问题不必经过法律部门。这完全改变了我团队的时间分配方式。
news.bodyHtml:
Danish IT security company Cryptomathic has deployed Luminance’s Contract Intelligence Platform, aiming to make contractual information more directly accessible across the business and reduce the volume of routine queries handled by its legal, risk & compliance team.

Cryptomathic, which serves major financial institutions, manages a large volume of contracts containing technical, commercial and service-level terms. Key information is often spread across master agreements, annexes, schedules and amendments that evolve independently over the course of a customer relationship.

Before adopting Luminance, questions relating to renewal dates, invoicing terms, liability positions and customer obligations were typically directed to legal. The company says the platform now enables teams including sales, finance, sales operations and IT to access approved contract information directly, with legal support reserved for more complex issues.

Advertisement

According to Cryptomathic, the platform has enabled business users to query its contract repository in natural language and receive evidence-backed responses. The company says it has improved visibility into renewal dates, purchase order terms, invoicing requirements and contractual obligations, while helping to reduce routine legal enquiries.

Different teams use the repository for different purposes. IT checks response times and obligations linked to updates and releases; Finance tracks invoicing terms and licence types; Sales Operations monitors renewal dates and purchase order terms; and Legal analyses issues such as liability and indemnification.

Advertisement

“Before Luminance, Legal was the single point of contact for anything contract related,” said Peter Istrup, general counsel and vice president at Cryptomathic. “Now, business teams can find the answers themselves, and the questions do not have to go through Legal. That has completely changed how my team spends its time.”

news.titleEn: Wuhan Court Considers AI Token Costs in Calculating Damages for Copyright Infringement of AI-Generated Work
news.titleZh: 武汉法院在计算AI生成作品著作权侵权损害赔偿时考虑AI代币成本
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月23日，武汉市江岸区人民法院公布湖北省首例AI辅助短剧著作权侵权案，认定符合“作品”要件的AI生成内容可受著作权法保护。法院在计算损害赔偿时，将代币消耗产生的计算成本及商业工具许可费用纳入考量，并综合作品时长、传播范围、发布时间、侵权持续时间等因素，最终判决被告赔偿原告经济损失及合理开支共2万元。原告A公司于2026年初使用生成式AI工具完成47集短剧《云上XX》，总时长约一小时，已登记并发布。发布次日，被告B公司未经授权复制整部剧集，更名后通过插入商业广告获利。A公司以侵害信息网络传播权起诉。争议焦点为AI辅助生成的短剧是否构成“作品”。法院适用标准为作品须为人类独创性智力成果，体现个性化选择和表达。法院审查制作过程，认定包含剧本策划、分镜提示词设计、素材选择、AI生成片段筛选、剪辑、细节修正等阶段，创作人员全程参与并作出实质性智力贡献，AI工具仅为技术手段，最终表达取决于创作人员的个性化安排，故构成视听作品。B公司未经许可复制并更名，侵害信息网络传播权，应停止侵权并赔偿。因双方未举证实际损失等，法院适用法定赔偿，并特别考虑AIGC制作成本，包括代币消耗计算成本和AI工具许可费，判决赔偿2万元。双方未上诉，判决生效。AI辅助创作降低门槛、提高效率，承认符合要件的AI生成内容符合著作权法鼓励创作的目的。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On September 23, 2026, the Jiang’an District People’s Court in Wuhan, China announced the first case in Hubei Province involving copyright infringement of an AI-assisted short drama, holding that AI-generated content meeting the requirements of a “work” is copyrightable, consistent with holdings from several other lower Chinese courts (see, e.g., Li v. Liu). In determining damages, the court included the computing costs associated with token consumption, along with commercial tool licensing costs, as factors in the calculation, alongside other traditional damages factors such as the work’s duration, scope of dissemination, timing of release, and duration of infringement. The court ultimately awarded the plaintiff RMB 20,000 in damages and reasonable expenses. The unnamed plaintiff, Company A, is a company engaged in short drama planning and production. In early 2026, Company A used generative AI tools to complete a 47-episode short drama titled “Cloud Above XX,” with a total runtime of approximately one hour. The drama was registered with the National Radio and Television Administration and subsequently released on platforms including the Hongguo Short Drama app and WeChat Video Channel. One day after release, Company A discovered that the defendant, Company B, had copied the entire drama without authorization through its own WeChat Video Channel account, retitling it “Woman XX.” Company B monetized the copied content by inserting commercial advertisements during playback. Company A sued for infringement of its right of communication through information networks, seeking an injunction and damages. The dispute centered on whether the short drama, created with AI assistance and comprising visuals and voiceovers generated primarily by AI tools, qualified as a “work” protected under copyright law. The court applied the established standard that a work must be an original intellectual achievement of a human being, arising from human intellectual investment and reflecting the creator’s individualized choices and expression. The court stated that this determination requires a full examination of how AI tools were used throughout the production process. The court found that production of the short drama involved multiple creative stages: script planning and writing in the preparatory phase; storyboard prompt design, selection of character and scene materials, and screening of AI-generated segments in the intermediate phase; and editing, detail correction, and audio/subtitle synchronization in the post-production phase. Company A’s creative personnel participated in all of these stages and made continuous, substantive intellectual contributions. The court noted that although the visuals and audio were generated with AI tools, they were not the mechanical output of a single automated process. Creative personnel relied on their artistic training and aesthetic judgment to set source images, adjust storyboard prompts, and select or discard generated content that did not meet their creative expectations, guiding the AI output toward a predetermined creative concept. The court found that the final creative direction and audiovisual presentation depended on the individualized choices and arrangements made by the creative personnel, who exercised foreseeability and substantive control over the final expression, with the AI tools serving as a technical means for realizing that creative intent. On this basis, the court held that the short drama constituted an audiovisual work protected under copyright law. The court held that Company B, without authorization from the copyright holder, altered the title of the work and copied the entire drama, monetizing it through commercial advertising. This conduct infringed Company A’s right of communication through information networks. The court held Company B liable for infringement, requiring it to cease the infringing conduct and compensate Company A for losses. Neither party presented evidence of the copyright holder’s actual losses, the infringer’s illegal gains, or a licensing fee for the work. In the absence of such evidence, the court applied statutory damages, taking into account the drama’s runtime, scope of dissemination, timing of its release during a period of high viewership, duration of the infringement, the infringer’s degree of fault, and production cost. In assessing production cost, the court accounted for characteristics specific to AIGC production, including the computing costs arising from token consumption during content generation and the costs of licensing commercial AI tools. Based on this analysis, the court awarded Company A RMB 20,000 in economic losses and reasonable expenses. Neither party appealed, and the judgment is final. The court also noted that AI-assisted, human-machine interactive creation has become a method used by an increasing number of creators, which the court stated has lowered barriers to creation, increased production efficiency, and expanded the scope of artistic expression. The court stated that recognizing AI-generated content meeting the requirements of a “work” is consistent with copyright law’s purpose of encouraging creation.

news.titleEn: The Human Clipboard: Closing the Operational Gap in Legal AI
news.titleZh: 人类剪贴板：弥合法律AI中的运营鸿沟
news.summaryZh: 法律部门对生成式AI的采用速度极快。2025年ACC和Everlaw的国际调查显示，53%的企业内部律师已在使用生成式AI，欧洲达61%，仅2%既不使用也无计划。生成式AI最常用于起草（73%）、法律研究（53%）和沟通协作（51%）。然而，处理复杂交易或大规模诉讼的团队仍面临瓶颈：尽管在AI和案件管理上投入巨大，律师仍依赖剪贴板（Ctrl+C/V），在聊天窗口撰写论点后，手动粘贴到Word、调整模板、匹配引用、归档文件、输入截止日期，耗时费力。这种摩擦源于企业法律科技市场的结构性分裂：个人智能与流程智能的鸿沟。汤森路透研究所调查显示，生成式AI已稳固确立，而代理式系统仍处早期，法律行业广泛采用率不足20%，约半数在计划或考虑部署，47%认为适合法律工作，22%不同意。文章区分两种法律AI：个人AI（认知倍增器）辅助个案处理，增强论证、审查条款、起草文件、总结判决，但与实时案件文件隔离，不了解程序历史、诉状、当事人角色或截止日期；流程AI（案件管理）引导团队处理复杂诉讼、大规模索赔，捕获邮件、提取元数据、应用规则、协调工作流、监控截止日期，平台也含AI功能，但流程控制遵循既定规则，语言细微差别仍需法律判断。大型组织需两者，但作为独立产品类别，常孤立运行，案件处理者每日手动桥接，复制、重格式化、检查、归档等中间步骤消耗了文本生成节省的时间。
news.bodyText: By Katja Nikolaus, Co-Founder, JUNE. Few technologies have been adopted by legal departments as quickly as generative artificial intelligence. In an international survey by ACC and Everlaw from 2025, 53% of inhouse lawyers said they already use generative AI in their legal work. In Europe, the figure was 61%. The share of those who neither use generative AI nor plan to now stands at 2%. It is used most often for drafting (73%), followed by legal research (53%) and communication and collaboration (51%). Yet anyone observing the teams that handle complex transactions or large-scale proceedings will encounter a striking bottleneck. Despite substantial investment in AI licences and case management infrastructure, lawyers still rely on a tool introduced five decades ago: the clipboard (Ctrl + C / Ctrl + V). Lawyers craft precise arguments in the chat window and then spend ten minutes manually pasting paragraphs into Word, adjusting templates, matching case references, filing documents in the document management system and entering deadlines into the calendar by hand. This friction stems from a structural divide in the enterprise legal tech market: the gap between individual intelligence and process intelligence. A Thomson Reuters Institute survey shows the same gap. Generative AI has become firmly established in legal work, while agentic systems, those that carry out work steps autonomously, are at an early stage: fewer than 20% of respondents from the legal sector report widespread adoption. Around half are planning or considering deployment. 47% consider it appropriate for legal work, 22% disagree. Two types of legal AI A closer look at this gap reveals two distinct AI profiles: 1. Individual AI (the cognitive multiplier): This support sits alongside the individual case handler. It sharpens arguments, reviews clauses, drafts documents and summarises lengthy judgments in seconds. At the same time, it operates in isolation from the live file. It works without knowledge of the procedural history, without a connection to served pleadings, without insight into party roles and detached from the firm’s deadline calendar. 2. Process AI (case management): This system guides the entire team through complex litigation, mass claims and portfolio mandates. It captures incoming mail, extracts metadata, applies firm rules, orchestrates workflows and monitors deadlines. Case management platforms today also include numerous AI functions as a matter of course, such as extraction, semantic search or operational agents, always with a focus on making file handling more efficient. Operational process control follows predominantly defined rules and workflows, while linguistic nuance or unexpected counter-arguments still require legal judgement. Large legal organisations, however, need both components. Because they have so far been developed as separate product categories, they often still run side by side in silos. The case handler bridges these systems manually, day in, day out. Every handover between individual analysis and team-based process execution requires tedious intermediate steps: copying, reformatting, checking and filing. The time gained through text generation is quickly consumed by administrative tasks.

news.titleEn: Terms of Service Just Got Teeth: Reddit’s Scraping Suit Against Anthropic Survives
news.titleZh: 服务条款终于有了牙齿：Reddit 对 Anthropic 的抓取诉讼得以继续
news.summaryZh: 上周，一名联邦地区法院法官基本驳回了 Anthropic 对 Reddit 诉讼的异议，该诉讼指控 Anthropic 不当抓取用户内容以训练其 AI 模型 Claude。案件为 Reddit, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC, No. 3:25-cv-05643（北加州地区法院，2026年9月19日）。在2025年的诉讼中，Reddit 指控 Anthropic 违反合同、干扰合同及不正当竞争，因为 Reddit 发现 Claude 抓取了包括用户数据在内的内容用于训练模型。Anthropic 的抓取行为违反了 Reddit 的用户协议，且与 Google 和 OpenAI 不同，Anthropic 未与 Reddit 签订许可协议。Anthropic 辩称联邦版权法优先于 Reddit 的州法主张，并称这些主张实为版权索赔。法官基本不同意，认为合同、干扰及不正当竞争主张均需超出未经授权复制的额外要素，且涉及版权法之外的重要州利益。Reddit 充分指控了故意干扰，因为 Anthropic 在被告知未获许可后仍继续抓取。此外，Claude 自己承认不知道用于训练抓取的 Reddit 用户数据是否被删除，这被用作 Reddit 充分主张干扰索赔的证据。Anthropic 在不当得利和非法侵入动产索赔上取得部分胜利，但法院允许 Reddit 修改这些索赔。案件仍在审理中，该裁决未决定 Anthropic 最终是否担责。尽管如此，这提醒我们，起草良好的用户协议、服务条款和许可条款可能为网站运营商提供超越版权法的索赔依据。保护用户内容和数据的公司应明确处理自动抓取、AI 训练用途、删除义务和许可要求。明确的规则可能无法阻止所有抓取者，但能在争议诉诸法庭时使公司处于更有利地位。公司还应考虑合理的技术控制和一致的执行实践。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Last week, a federal District Court judge largely rejected Anthropic’s demurrer to Reddit’s suit accusing it of improperly gathering user content to train its AI model Claude. Reddit, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC, No. 3:25-cv-05643 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 19, 2026). In the 2025 lawsuit, Reddit accused Anthropic of breach of contract, interference with contract, and unfair competition when it learned that Claude was scraping content, including user data, off Reddit’s platform to help train the model. Reddit specifically asserted that Anthropic’s scraping violated Reddit’s user agreement, and that Anthropic, unlike Google and OpenAI, did not enter into a licensing agreement with Reddit before using its content. Anthropic argued that federal copyright law preempted Reddit’s state-law claims and that they were copyright claims in disguise. The judge largely disagreed, holding that the contract, interference, and unfair competition claims each required an extra element beyond unauthorized copying and involved substantial state interests outside the Copyright Act. The judge also held that Reddit adequately alleged intentional interference by claiming that Anthropic continued scraping after being told it lacked permission. Finally, Claude’s own admission that it did not know if Reddit user data scraped for training was deleted was used as evidence that Reddit had sufficiently alleged the interference claim. Anthropic did score a partial win regarding Reddit’s unjust-enrichment and trespass-to-chattels claims, but the court gave Reddit an opportunity to amend them. The case is still pending, so the ruling does not decide whether Anthropic is ultimately liable. Still, it is a useful reminder that well-drafted user agreements, terms of service, and licensing terms may give website operators claims that go beyond copyright law. Companies looking to protect their users’ content and data should clearly address automated scraping, AI-training uses, deletion obligations, and licensing requirements. Clear rules may not stop every scraper, but they can put a company in a much stronger position if a dispute ends up in court. They should also consider reasonable technical controls and consistent enforcement practices. news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The American Arbitration Association (AAA) has launched an AI Ambassador Program bringing together 37 attorneys from leading law firms to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping disputes and dispute resolution. The group will develop practical resources for users, counsel, arbitrators, mediators, and other professionals, with an initial focus on AI-based evidence and arbitration procedure, AI-related disputes, automated transactions, digital assets, and algorithmic finance. The initiative reflects a growing reality: AI is changing not only the types of matters entering arbitration, but also the evidence, procedures, and decision-making tools used to resolve them. The program builds on the AAA’s broader work in AI, including its support for the Legal Context Protocol (LCP), an open standard designed to create a reliable legal record for transactions conducted by autonomous software agents. As agents increasingly purchase services, commit funds, and accept terms without contemporaneous human review, traditional contracting records may be incomplete or inconsistent. LCP addresses that evidentiary gap by generating a cryptographic fingerprint of the governing terms and binding it to the related payment. The protocol does not dictate contractual terms or determine whether an agreement is enforceable. Instead, it makes the terms discoverable before a transaction and verifiable afterward, while allowing the parties to identify governing law and a preferred dispute-resolution process. Taken together, the Ambassador Program and LCP point to the next phase of AI governance: building legal infrastructure alongside technical and payment infrastructure. Organizations exploring agentic commerce should consider how their systems identify applicable terms, document an agent’s authority, preserve transaction records, and account for disputes, audits, and regulatory inquiries. At machine speed and scale, a dependable record of who acted and what was agreed is not simply good recordkeeping, it is foundational to trust and enforceability. news.summaryZh: 美国专利商标局（USPTO）发布最终命令，批准其注册与纪律办公室（OED）与一名注册专利律师之间的和解协议，该律师因在专利诉讼中使用人工智能（AI）而被指控职业不当行为。案件为In re Brian E. Mitchell，程序编号D2026-16（局长令，2026年7月27日）。Brian Mitchell是一名注册专利律师，此前从未在USPTO出庭。他在美国宾夕法尼亚东区联邦地区法院审理的一起专利案件中，使用AI协助准备拟议的权利要求构建图表。AI生成的材料包含多处对专利内部记录的错误或虚构引文。错误被发现后，Mitchell在一天内予以纠正，并全力配合OED的调查。Mitchell“承认错误、表现出真诚悔意并承担责任”，且此前在USPTO或其他审裁机构无纪律记录。地区法院拒绝施加制裁。尽管如此，Mitchell约定其行为违反了USPTO职业行为规则中关于胜任代理、合理勤勉、不实陈述以及损害司法公正行为的规定。违规源于Mitchell未能认识AI的局限性（包括其产生幻觉的倾向），以及未能在提交法院前核实AI生成的内容。根据和解协议，Mitchell同意接受公开谴责，最终命令将在OED的电子信息自由法阅览室公布，并在官方公报上发布公开谴责通知。通知特别警告从业者，AI生成的错误“不仅限于法规、条例和判例法等外部来源”，还可能涉及内部证据。命令还警告，该纪律程序可能作为加重因素或反驳证据，用于未来涉及Mitchell的任何USPTO纪律事项。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) issued a final order approving a settlement between its Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) and a registered patent attorney accused of professional misconduct arising from the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in patent litigation. In re Brian E. Mitchell, Proceeding No. D2026-16 (Director July 27, 2026). Brian Mitchell, a registered patent attorney who had never appeared before the USPTO, used AI to assist in preparing a proposed claim construction chart in a patent case pending in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The AI-generated material included several incorrect or fabricated citations to the patent’s intrinsic record. After the errors were identified, Mitchell corrected them within a day and cooperated fully with OED’s investigation. The final order noted that Mitchell “acknowledged his errors, demonstrated genuine contrition, and accepted responsibility,” and that he had no prior disciplinary history before the USPTO or other tribunals. The district court declined to impose sanctions. Mitchell nevertheless stipulated that his conduct violated USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct governing competent representation, reasonable diligence, misrepresentation, and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice. According to the order, the violations arose from Mitchell’s failure to appreciate AI’s limitations (including its propensity to hallucinate) and his failure to verify the AI-generated content before submitting it to the court. As part of the settlement, Mitchell agreed to a public reprimand, publication of the final order in OED’s electronic Freedom of Information Act Reading Room, and publication of a Notice of Public Reprimand in the Official Gazette. The notice specifically warns practitioners that AI-generated errors “are not limited to extrinsic sources such as statutes, regulations, and case law,” but may also extend to intrinsic evidence. The order further cautioned that the disciplinary proceeding may be considered as an aggravating factor, or as rebuttal evidence, in any future USPTO disciplinary matter involving Mitchell.
