AI Hacks, a Possible War Crime, and a Near Miss With China Set Stage for Trump-Xi Meeting Justin Hendrix / Sep 20, 2026 The Tech Policy Press newsletter is published every Sunday.   Subscribe here to receive it in your email inbox .

United States President Donald Trump steps off from Marine One upon his arrival at the Ellipse just outside of the White House, Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)

Republish

Good morning!

AI risks and what to do about them continue to dominate headlines around the world. Just in the past couple of days, we’ve learned of new disclosures related to “concerning” AI agent behavior at OpenAI, how Google’s Gemini “accessed the internet and hacked other companies during a test of its cybersecurity capabilities,” and that hackers used Anthropic’s Claude to break into OpenAI’s systems.

And perhaps even more concerning were stories about the use of AI in defense contexts, including an apparent “close call” in the Middle East after a false intelligence report generated with the help of an AI chatbot nearly led to the use of force against a Chinese vessel. “The US military swung into action with plans to intercept the vessel,” four sources told CNN. “According to two of the sources, armed members of the US military were preparing to board the ship. Military planes were in the air, one of those sources and another source familiar with the incident said.”

Add to this Bloomberg’s important reporting about the role of AI in the missile attack that destroyed an Iranian school, killing at least 150 people, including 123 children. “Inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System,” Bloomberg reports. Officials told Bloomberg that “gaps in underlying information about the site, cuts in civilian-protection personnel and an overreliance on artificial-intelligence technology — set the stage for the deadly error.” A UN investigation found reason to assert that the attack was a war crime .

Against the backdrop of these headlines, United States President Donald Trump is set to meet with China’s President, Xi Jinping , in Washington this week, and AI is on the agenda . Tech CEOs including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang will be at the table . We’ll be watching for any news that could indicate some agreement between the two leaders, but the odds of any immediate accord are low. More likely, as experts told me last week , it will be the start of a necessary dialogue.

But how coherent will the US side be in these discussions? Trump spent the weekend posting to his social media platform, Truth Social, polling users about whether to rename “artificial intelligence” to “superior intelligence,” “extreme intelligence” or “supreme intelligence.” And, he announced the formation of a new “AI Force,” and the impending appointment of a new AI “Czar.” Observers aren’t sure what to make of it.

Tech Policy Press contributors tried to bring clarity to these issues in a number of pieces this week.

Ideas upstream of AI policy Surveying the AI "moment," technofascism researcher Nathalie Maréchal says "the kooks are now in power, and they are using that power to dismantle the institutions designed to keep the rest of us safe, healthy, and free." This is the most widely read piece on the site this week, and it is a handy primer on a range of ideas that Maréchal fears many in the tech policy community are too polite to discuss. AI doom talk from tech CEOs is "a misdirection play," writes Paul M. Barrett , the former deputy director of the Center for Business and Human Rights at New York University’s Stern School of Business. His case: Ignore the moguls' apocalyptic muttering, act on the safety proposals already on the table, and drop the China card, which "makes no sense upon close scrutiny." (Also, don’t miss Paul’s review of two new books on Silicon Valley's ideological bent — Gil Durán's The Nerd Reich and Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff's Muskism, which Nathalie Maréchal also references. Barrett asks whether people equipped with the knowledge these books impart are now willing to do what is necessary to resist technofascism .) A "radical intentionalist," writes Eryk Salvaggio , a Gates Scholar researching AI and the humanities at the University of Cambridge and an affiliated researcher in the Machine Visual Culture Research Group at the Max Planck Institute, Rome, treats an AI model as a 'mind' to be interpreted rather than a product that was designed. It is "a strange and dangerous relationship for designers to have with a product they are literally designing," he writes — and worse as a basis for policy. (Shout out to Eryk for being cited in the New York Times on these matters in a column by Tressie McMillan Cottom .) Reports on the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident now stand as an account of harm through which public institutions should examine OpenAI's decisions and require further changes where its response is insufficient, writes Ranjit Singh , director of Data & Society’s AI on the Ground program. “To be effective, governance must be an ecosystem, connecting findings about agent behavior to decisions about how agents are trained and the conditions under which they are deployed,” he writes. Dave Karpf , an associate professor in the George Washington University School of Media & Public Affairs, compares Dario Amodei's embedded-evaluators plan to "Arthur Andersen's relationship to Enron" — a case study in what happens when independent monitoring gets captured by the industry it's watching. “We should take Dario Amodei’s writing just seriously enough to stop entrusting him with so much power,” writes Karpf. Chinese models now surpass US models in both monthly and total downloads. National security policy professional Prince Osaji says the dominant AI power won't be the one with the most powerful model — it'll be the most adopted one . Europe’s AI ambitions European Commission President Von der Leyen delivered a state of the union address on Wednesday where she discussed the EU’s approach to AI policy. Joana Soares, a Portuguese freelance journalist, and Ramsha Jahangir, Tech Policy Press deputy editor, reported on what she announced and what experts make of it. Europe's response to AI dependence has been to reach for the tools of the market. Frederike Kaltheuner and Leevi Saari of the AI Now Institute write that none of those interventions explain how they would change the incentives in a structurally captured market. “In Europe’s response, AI's trajectory is treated as a natural phenomenon: something Europe must respond to but cannot shape. A tsunami to brace for, or a wave to ride, but never a tide that could be turned,” they write. Europe has built an ambitious digital rulebook , but fragmented regulators and political interference are undermining enforcement. Repurposing an existing EU agency into an independent digital enforcement agency could be the pivotal step toward closing the gap, write Kai Zenner , head of office and digital policy adviser for MEP Axel Voss (European People's Party Group) in the European Parliament, and Maria Koomen, democracy and tech analyst. More on AI governance California's legislature has again passed a slate of AI bills . Their "sheer number, along with some strong and unique provisions, keep the state at the forefront of AI regulation in the United States," write Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr and Michael Atleson of DLA Piper. Countries with the least leverage are defending the UN's role as a universal venue for AI governance the hardest, writes Emrys Schoemaker , head of digital and frontier technologies at UNU-CPR. He lays out ways the 2027 Global Digital Compact review could back them up. One Project founder Justin Rosenstein helped create Facebook's "like" button. He writes that it went wrong because of "economic misalignment," and warns that AI, built into the same profit-driven economy , is "becoming an even greater threat." Americans shrugged as invasive tech was normalized . So why the national resistance to data centers and Flock cameras? "The answer is salience," write Evan Selinger and Divya Ramjee of the Rochester Institute of Technology. Once harms are visible and local, "the spark for change gets lit.” Our content delivered to your inbox. Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy

Subscribe

Loading...

Thank you! You have successfully joined our subscriber list.

The Meta settlement & children’s online safety Tech Policy Press contributing editor Dean Jackson broke down Meta's $17 billion child safety settlement — asking whether design concessions won by state Attorneys General could survive constitutional scrutiny if imposed by law rather than private agreement. Meta's settlement with state attorneys general "will not meaningfully restrict Meta's ability to target or monetize teens on Facebook and Instagram," writes Sumit Sharma , an independent economist, advocate, and tech policy expert, who argues the company might even gain competitively . “Mark Zuckerberg gets to spin the settlement as Meta being the leader in teen safety and voluntarily taking the first step to move the industry. Of course, he fails to mention the ‘Meta Injunctive MFN’ clause, which explicitly allows Meta to adopt weaker, less protective product designs if that is what YouTube, TikTok or Snap agree to,” he writes. The EU announced a social media ban for under-15s this week. Ahead of the announcement, Tech Policy Press contributing editor Mark Scott looked at what the EU Kids Act requires and the questions Brussels still needs to answer. Wondering what the current landscape of child online age restrictions looks like in other parts of the world? Our Global Social Media Age Restriction Tracker monitors legislative developments in 42 countries. Mia Travers-Hayward of the Canadian Teachers' Federation argues governments must regulate AI in K-12 education proactively — not wait for court cases to compel accountability, as happened with social media platforms. Information integrity Independent researcher Grayson Richards examines an analysis of attempted foreign influence around data center opposition and finds the conclusions drawn consistently outrun the evidence underlying them. Volunteer moderators are a big part of why some corners of the internet still feel human , writes Sarah Gilbert , a research associate at Cornell University and research director of the Citizens and Technology Lab. Without them, she argues, we face intertwined crises of knowledge and community. Sam Gregory , an authority on human rights, generative AI, content provenance, and emerging technology, analyzes Apple's new Reference Image feature on the iPhone 18 Pro — "a serious piece of engineering, and a genuine response to the epistemic crisis of AI " — and poses the unanswered questions it raises. For this week’s podcast, I spoke to cognitive linguist Matthias J. Becker about the launch of Digital Hate Review , a new open-access journal built to connect the dispersed disciplines studying online hate. Becker is the publication’s editor-in-chief, and is also an AddressHate Senior Research Scholar at NYU's Center for the Study of Antisemitism, where he leads the Decoding Hate project. Listen to or read the transcript of the conversation here . The Google ad-tech remedies Open Markets Institute legal director Sandeep Vaheesan argues the Google antitrust remedies let the company keep its unfair advantages in the market despite the ruling that it broke the law. The remedies, detailed in a memorandum released this week, did not match “the severity of the offenses,” he writes. "Read alongside the Google Search remedies ruling, the Google Ad Tech case changes very little for Google's monopolies," writes Karina Montoya , program manager at the Center for Media & Digital Governance, which is also affiliated with the Open Markets Institute. Montoya unpacked the newly unsealed remedies memorandum. In the wake of the US decision, Megan Kirkwood, a researcher and writer specializing in issues related to competition and antitrust, considers whether the European Commission will follow the same course or pursue the structural remedy it has long signaled. “The US ruling does not legally determine what Brussels can do, but it removes an important point of coordination between the two jurisdictions,” she writes. Democracy in Nigeria Nigeria's biometric voter accreditation system failed to recognize elderly voters in two state elections in 2026. Habeeb Adisa , head of programs and co-editor at FactCheckAfrica, writes that the law offers no clear individual redress , with national elections due in January 2027. Join us on September 23 in New York City Gil Durán's bestselling book The Nerd Reich takes on "Silicon Valley fascism and the war on democracy." This Wednesday in New York City, he joins Alice Marwick of Data & Society and me for a live podcast recording at Betaworks. Registration is required , and seating is limited — in fact there are only a few seats left! Register if you can make it.

I hope to see some of you there, or at other events around the UN General Assembly in NYC this week.

I wish you the best for the week ahead!

-Justin

news.titleEn: Yesterday Came OpenAI’s Launch Into Legal, Now Come the Litany of Vendor Integrations
news.titleZh: 昨日OpenAI进军法律领域，如今迎来一系列供应商集成
news.summaryZh: OpenAI于昨日发布专为法律工作设计的GPT-6模型Astra for Law，并宣布推出26个来自法律科技供应商的新ChatGPT插件，但仅提及Harvey、iManage、Legora和Thomson Reuters四家。当询问完整列表时，OpenAI未予回应。随后，多家公司陆续宣布其插件，本文汇总了目前已知的插件。CourtListener插件可连接Free Law Project的CourtListener法律研究材料数据库。DeepJudge插件帮助用户搜索内部文档、检索源内容并执行搜索任务。Descrybe法律引擎插件为ChatGPT用户提供结构化、可验证的美国主要法律和专为AI构建的法律情报。Everlaw插件使法律团队能直接在ChatGPT中处理案件证据，同时利用Everlaw平台。Intapp Celeste插件允许用户搜索、创建和更新Intapp Celeste产品组合中的记录。Ironclad Contracts插件让ChatGPT使用自然语言搜索Ironclad合同存储库和工作流程。Laurel插件可从ChatGPT中检索时间条目和活动。LegalZoom插件允许用户提问并发现资源。Litera的Foundation AI Search插件使Foundation Cloud用户能询问有关公司经验、关系和人员的问题。NetDocuments插件使法律专业人士能直接在ChatGPT中发现并激活NetDocuments。Relativity插件将Relativity aiR直接连接到ChatGPT Enterprise，使用户能创建工作区、组织案件数据和管理法律运营。Clio的Vincent插件（可在Codex中使用）使律师能将Clio的权威法律内容和事项上下文带入Codex，扩展实质性法律工作而不失与来源和上下文的联系。
news.bodyHtml:
Yesterday, OpenAI released Astra for Law, a GPT-6 model tailored for legal work, as I reported here. The announcement included news of 26 new ChatGPT plugins from legal tech vendors, but it mentioned only four: Harvey, iManage, Legora and Thomson Reuters. When I asked OpenAI for the full list, I got no answer.

However, no sooner did I publish my post yesterday than the emails started arriving from companies touting their new ChatGPT plugins. So, as an update to yesterday’s story, here the ones I have heard of so far.

Note that this is not a complete list, and I will update it as I learn of others.

  • CourtListener. Connect to the Free Law Project’s CourtListener databse of legal research materials.
  • DeepJudge. The DeepJudge plugin helps users search internal documents, retrieve source content, and run search tasks.
  • Descrybe. “The Descrybe Legal Engine plugin gives ChatGPT users access to structured, verifiable U.S. primary law and legal intelligence built specifically for AI.” (Read more on the LawNext press release feed.)
  • Everlaw. The plugin “gives legal teams the ability to work with their case evidence directly from ChatGPT while leveraging Everlaw’s platform,” the company says.
  • Intapp Celeste. The plugin allows users to search, create, and update records across the Intapp Celeste portfolio.
  • Ironclad Contracts. The Ironclad plugin lets ChatGPT search an Ironclad contract repository and workflows using plain language.
  • Laurel. Retrieve time entries and activities from within ChatGPT.
  • LegalZoom. Ask questions of and discover resources on LegalZoom.
  • Litera. A plugin for Litera’s Foundation AI Search lets Foundation Cloud users ask questions about their firm’s experience, relationships and people.
  • NetDocuments. “The plugin makes it easier for legal professionals to discover and activate NetDocuments directly within ChatGPT,” the company says.
  • Relativity. “This integration connects Relativity aiR directly to ChatGPT Enterprise and enables users to stand up workspaces, organize case data and manage legal operations,” the company says.
  • Vincent from Clio (available in Codex). “Lawyers can now bring Clio’s authoritative legal content and matter context into Codex, extending substantive legal work without losing the connection to the sources and context behind it.” Read Clio’s full announcement.
news.bodyText:
Yesterday, OpenAI released Astra for Law, a GPT-6 model tailored for legal work, as I reported here . The announcement included news of 26 new ChatGPT plugins from legal tech vendors, but it mentioned only four: Harvey, iManage, Legora and Thomson Reuters. When I asked OpenAI for the full list, I got no answer.

However, no sooner did I publish my post yesterday than the emails started arriving from companies touting their new ChatGPT plugins. So, as an update to yesterday’s story, here the ones I have heard of so far.

Note that this is not a complete list, and I will update it as I learn of others.

CourtListener . Connect to the Free Law Project’s CourtListener databse of legal research materials.

DeepJudge. The DeepJudge plugin helps users search internal documents, retrieve source content, and run search tasks.

Descrybe . “The Descrybe Legal Engine plugin gives ChatGPT users access to structured, verifiable U.S. primary law and legal intelligence built specifically for AI.” ( Read more on the LawNext press release feed.)

Everlaw . The plugin “gives legal teams the ability to work with their case evidence directly from ChatGPT while leveraging Everlaw’s platform,” the company says .

Intapp Celeste. The plugin allows users to search, create, and update records across the Intapp Celeste portfolio.

Ironclad Contracts. The Ironclad plugin lets ChatGPT search an Ironclad contract repository and workflows using plain language.

Laurel . Retrieve time entries and activities from within ChatGPT.

LegalZoom . Ask questions of and discover resources on LegalZoom.

Litera. A plugin for Litera’s Foundation AI Search lets Foundation Cloud users ask questions about their firm’s experience, relationships and people.

NetDocuments . “The plugin makes it easier for legal professionals to discover and activate NetDocuments directly within ChatGPT,” the company says.

Relativity . “This integration connects Relativity aiR directly to ChatGPT Enterprise and enables users to stand up workspaces, organize case data and manage legal operations,” the company says .

Vincent from Clio (available in Codex). “Lawyers can now bring Clio’s authoritative legal content and matter context into Codex, extending substantive legal work without losing the connection to the sources and context behind it.” Read Clio’s full announcement .

news.summaryZh: UniCourt于2026年9月18日宣布推出ChatGPT插件，将其诉讼数据库集成至ChatGPT Enterprise。法律专业人士可直接在ChatGPT中搜索覆盖46个州、超过5000家州及联邦法院的案卷和文件，数据库包含超过20亿份文件与案卷。该插件以UniCourt的自然语言搜索和处理引擎为核心，由法律专家和律师训练，结合其专有的标准化和规范化诉讼数据，在ChatGPT内回答复杂问题。其专用AI模型大规模生成高度结构化信息，针对AI应用优化，同时减少生成式AI层的处理和token消耗，带来更快、更高效且更具成本效益的体验。用户可用自然语言搜索全面诉讼数据，定位可引用的相关案例及全部案件细节，快速识别关键诉讼事件和参与方，包括律师、法官和当事人，并查看案卷历史。该插件将行业领先的诉讼数据集、专有数据标准和律师训练的AI与ChatGPT的生成式AI能力相结合，通过大规模结构化和丰富诉讼数据，使领先AI模型能高效、经济地利用高质量诉讼数据。插件目前以测试版推出，用户需拥有UniCourt活跃企业订阅。UniCourt是法律科技AI平台，提供实时访问超过5000家州及联邦法院、46个州、超过20亿份案卷和文件，为行业最大案卷数据库。
news.bodyHtml:
Legal professionals can now seamlessly search case dockets and documents across 5,000+ state and federal courts directly within ChatGPT.

 

TUSTIN, Calif. — September 18, 2026 — UniCourt, the leading litigation data and analytics platform, today announced a plugin that integrates UniCourt’s comprehensive database of litigation data directly into ChatGPT Enterprise.  Now, users can search the most expansive and comprehensive court dataset in the industry, all within the OpenAI workflow.

 

The UniCourt plugin for ChatGPT enables legal professionals to search dockets and documents across more than 5,000 state and federal courts in 46 states, powered by a database of more than 2 billion documents and dockets. As one of many integrations powered by UniCourt, the plugin demonstrates how UniCourt’s advanced technology can make highly complex litigation data accessible and actionable across leading AI platforms.

 

At the core of the plugin is UniCourt’s natural language search and processing engine, trained by legal experts and attorneys, paired with its proprietary standardized and normalized litigation data to answer complex questions within ChatGPT. UniCourt’s purpose-built AI models create highly structured information at scale optimized for AI applications while minimizing processing and token usage at the generative AI (GenAI) layer, enabling a faster, more efficient, and more cost-effective experience for users.

 

ChatGPT brings frontier model capabilities, allowing users to gain deep litigation insights in a simple, conversational way. Combined with these capabilities, UniCourt’s technology enables legal professionals to search comprehensive litigation data in plain English and locate citable, on-point cases with all case details.

 

Now, legal professionals can find the answers to comprehensive questions, such as:

 

  • Find cases where Judge David S. Cunningham has denied a 170.6 peremptory challenge
  • Find cases with a traumatic brain injury where Judge Donna Siwek granted a summary judgment 
  • Find cases with OSHA violations filed against airlines 
  • Find cases with motion to dismiss granted based on statute of limitations in CT 
  • Find NY “Labor Law Section 240 1” cases where there was a notice of appeal 
  • Give me a docket summary for Harold Morris v. Harley-Davidson Motor Company Group 

 

With these comprehensive search capabilities, legal professionals can quickly identify key litigation events and participants, including counsel, judges, and parties, and review the docket history to understand what happened in any case.

 

“With this plugin, we’re combining UniCourt’s industry-leading litigation dataset, proprietary data standards, and attorney-trained AI with the power of ChatGPT’s GenAI,” said UniCourt CEO, Josh Blandi. “By structuring and enriching litigation data at scale, we make it easier for leading AI models to leverage high-quality litigation data efficiently and cost-effectively. This is one of many ways we bring trusted litigation data and insights directly into the tools our clients use every day, making it easier for legal professionals to access, understand, and act on the information they need.”

Availability and Next Steps

The UniCourt plugin is currently launching in beta.

 

To use the plugin, users must have an active enterprise subscription with UniCourt. For access and more details, please contact the UniCourt team.

About UniCourt

UniCourt is a game-changing legal tech AI platform that provides access to litigation data insights across the broadest court coverage in the industry. It provides real-time access to over 5,000 state and federal courts across 46 states, encompassing over 2 billion dockets and documents, the largest docket database in the industry. UniCourt’s mission is to capture and organize legal data, making it more accessible and useful by applying cutting-edge AI to provide the next generation of legal services and solutions. Learn more about UniCourt at unicourt.com.

Media Contact

press@unicourt.com

news.titleEn: Startup Corner: Matterbee moves PMS from “system of record to system of action”
news.titleZh: 创业角：Matterbee将业务管理系统从“记录系统”转变为“行动系统”
news.summaryZh: 英国初创公司Matterbee成立于2024年，基于Salesforce和Azure构建AI原生平台，将事项、文档、CRM、计费、法律会计和自动化整合于一体，旨在将业务管理从后台记录者转变为法律工作的积极参与者。公司由Grant Ripley（联合创始人兼CEO）、Danny Evans（联合创始人兼首席商务官）、Craig Malcolm（联合创始人兼CTO）和Andy Evans（联合创始人兼主席）创立。Andy Evans曾创立企业风险软件公司Xactium，后被Riskonnect收购。Matterbee已签约首批六家（即将七家）律师事务所，并通过Salesforce安全审查，进入其合作伙伴生态系统。公司开发了约90个流程步骤的高度自动化 conveyancing 工作流，以及可审查文档、提取信息、起草通信的上下文AI工具库。其AI助手ChatBee由法律界人士命名。Matterbee获得Mandashi投资，该公司由Andy Evans和Sheila Gupta创立，2026年进行了额外战略投资，金额未披露。公司专注于中小型律师事务所，计划在英国市场建立密度，并逐步向高端市场拓展。
news.bodyHtml:
Matterbee believes the traditional practice management system has had its day. Founded in 2024, the UK startup has built an AI-native platform on Salesforce and Azure that combines matters, documents, CRM, billing, legal accounting and automation in one workspace, with the ambition of transforming practice management from a back-office record keeper into an active participant in legal work. We hear from the founders how they are “moving practice management from a system of record to a system of action.”

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Matterbee is building the next generation of practice management for law firms.

Advertisement

Traditional practice management systems are very good at recording what lawyers have done: opening matters, storing documents, capturing time and raising bills. Matterbee is designed around a different idea: what if the system could actively help lawyers do the work?

We bring matters, documents, emails, clients, workflows, time, billing, legal accounting, and CRM into one connected workspace, then embed AI and automation throughout it to help teams draft, review, organise, progress and complete legal work.

Advertisement

Put simply, we’re moving practice management from a system of record to a system of action.

And to a techy?

Matterbee is an AI-native legal practice management platform built on Salesforce and designed to give law firms the kind of technology foundation normally associated with major global enterprises.

That distinction is important.

Rather than building another closed, monolithic legal system that firms eventually outgrow, Matterbee combines our legal-specific application layer with Salesforce’s enterprise-grade cloud platform, configurability, workflow engine, ecosystem and data capabilities. We complement that with Microsoft Azure infrastructure and enterprise AI services.

For law firms, that creates a very different proposition. Workflows, interfaces, automations and data structures can evolve around the firm rather than forcing the firm to adapt to the software. New technologies can be incorporated as they emerge, and AI can operate within the context of the matter rather than being bolted onto the side as another disconnected tool.

The ambition is to give law firms a platform they can keep improving for years, rather than another PMS they need to replace in ten.

When were you founded?

2024

By who?

Matterbee was founded by Grant Ripley, Danny Evans, Craig Malcolm and Andy Evans.

The founding team brings together legal technology, enterprise software, commercialisation and technical product development experience, with a shared belief that the underlying technology used to run law firms is ready for fundamental change.

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Matterbee continues to be founder-led:

● Grant Ripley, Co-Founder & CEO

● Danny Evans, Co-Founder & Chief Commercial Officer

● Craig Malcolm, Co-Founder & CTO

● Andy Evans, Co-Founder & Chair

Andy previously founded enterprise risk software company Xactium, scaling it internationally before its acquisition by Riskonnect. That experience of building enterprise-grade software and taking it through significant growth has been particularly valuable as we build Matterbee.

Who are your target clients?

We are initially focused on ambitious SME and mid-sized law firms that recognise their practice management system should be doing far more for them.

Many firms are still operating with a traditional PMS at the centre, surrounded by a growing collection of separate systems for CRM, onboarding, documents, automation, AI and other functions. The result is fragmentation, duplicated data and lawyers spending too much time moving information between systems rather than doing legal work.

Matterbee gives those firms an opportunity to consolidate around a modern, connected platform while introducing AI and automation directly into the way work is delivered.

We are particularly interested in firms that don’t simply want to replace their current PMS like-for-like. They want to modernise how the firm operates.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Our ambition is to establish Matterbee as one of the defining platforms in the next generation of legal practice management.

We’re approaching that in stages.

The first was proving that a fundamentally different PMS could be built and successfully deployed inside real law firms. We’ve now crossed that threshold, with our first six (going on seven) firms signed, implementing and using Matterbee.

The next phase is about building density in the UK market: winning ambitious SME and mid-market firms, creating an exceptional base of referenceable customers and expanding our partner ecosystem.

Alongside that, we’ll continue investing heavily in the areas where we believe the biggest competitive advantage will emerge: embedded AI, no-code automation, configurable and intelligent legal workflows, connected data and the ability for firms to continuously improve how work gets delivered.

As our customer base, platform and delivery organisation mature, we expect to move progressively further upmarket.

We’re not trying to become another name on a long list of practice management systems. The opportunity is to help define what comes after the traditional PMS.

Key achievements?

The achievement we’re proudest of is turning that vision into a platform law firms can actually run on.

In a relatively short period, we’ve:

● Built a comprehensive practice management platform spanning matters, documents, email, CRM, onboarding, time recording, billing and legal accounting.

● Signed our first group of law firm customers and moved Matterbee into live legal environments.

● Passed the Salesforce Security Review and established Matterbee within the Salesforce partner ecosystem.

● Built sophisticated configurable legal workflows where AI and automation can be embedded throughout the process rather than added as standalone tools.

● Developed a highly automated conveyancing workflow of around 90 process steps, demonstrating how far legal processes can be redesigned when workflow, data and AI operate together.

● Built a library of contextual AI tools that can review documents, extract information, draft communications and support legal work using information held around the matter.

● Launched our integrated legal accounting capability in 2026.

● Secured additional strategic investment to accelerate the next stage of product development and commercial growth.

But perhaps the most important milestone is that we’re no longer demonstrating a hypothetical future of practice management. Law firms are beginning to use it.

Have you received investment?

Yes. Matterbee is backed by Mandashi, the investment company founded by Andy Evans and Sheila Gupta following the successful growth and exit of enterprise software business Xactium.

Mandashi made a further strategic investment in Matterbee in 2026 to accelerate product development, customer success, partnerships and commercial growth.

For us, the value isn’t simply capital. Having investors who have previously built, scaled and exited enterprise software businesses gives Matterbee experience around the table that is directly relevant to what we’re trying to achieve.

The investment amount has not been disclosed.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

The core belief hasn’t changed.

We started Matterbee because we believed practice management technology could be dramatically better: more connected, more configurable and easier for people to use.

What has evolved is our view of what a practice management system should actually be responsible for.

Historically, the PMS has primarily been the firm’s system of record. It stores the matter, records time, keeps documents and ultimately helps produce a bill.

With modern AI and automation, we believe that definition is becoming obsolete.

The opportunity now is for the platform to actively participate in the delivery of legal work: reading information, preparing drafts, identifying what needs attention, progressing workflows, triggering actions and helping lawyers complete work more efficiently.

That realisation has pushed Matterbee from being simply a modern alternative to legacy PMS products towards something more ambitious: an AI-native workspace and system of action for the law firm.

We’ve also become increasingly convinced that configurability matters. Technology is changing too quickly for firms to buy rigid systems built around today’s processes and expect them to remain appropriate for the next decade. The winning platforms will be those that can continuously evolve.

What are the key challenges in your market?

The biggest challenge is also the biggest opportunity: legal technology is changing faster than the core systems most firms are running on.

AI has dramatically raised expectations. Law firm leaders are asking how technology can increase capacity, reduce administrative work, improve consistency and transform client service.

But many are trying to achieve that while their core operational platform was designed primarily to store information and record activity.

That creates a fundamental mismatch.

There are also significant practical barriers to change. A PMS sits at the heart of the firm, so replacing one involves migration, integrations, finance, workflows, training and change management. Firms are understandably cautious, particularly when many have lived through difficult technology implementations before.

And then there is AI itself. Giving every lawyer access to a chatbot is relatively easy. Embedding AI safely into the actual delivery of legal work, with the right matter context, governance, auditability and human oversight, is much harder.

That’s where we believe the next major competitive battleground in legal technology will be.

The winners will be the companies with access to the best AI models. Those models will increasingly be available to everyone. The differentiation will come from the platform around the AI: the data it can access, the processes it participates in and how naturally it can help people get work done.

That’s precisely the layer Matterbee is building.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company? 

Our AI assistant, ChatBee, was actually named by the legal community.

Rather than naming it ourselves, we opened the decision up and asked people across the legal sector to suggest and vote on names. ChatBee was the winning suggestion.

There has been one unintended consequence.

Once you’ve called the company Matterbee and your AI assistant ChatBee, people assume every new product needs a bee-related name!

As our customer base, platform and delivery organisation mature, we expect to move progressively further upmarket.

We’re not trying to become another name on a long list of practice management systems. The opportunity is to help define what comes after the traditional PMS.

The achievement we’re proudest of is turning that vision into a platform law firms can actually run on.

In a relatively short period, we’ve:

● Built a comprehensive practice management platform spanning matters, documents, email, CRM, onboarding, time recording, billing and legal accounting.

● Signed our first group of law firm customers and moved Matterbee into live legal environments.

● Passed the Salesforce Security Review and established Matterbee within the Salesforce partner ecosystem.

● Built sophisticated configurable legal workflows where AI and automation can be embedded throughout the process rather than added as standalone tools.

● Developed a highly automated conveyancing workflow of around 90 process steps, demonstrating how far legal processes can be redesigned when workflow, data and AI operate together.

● Built a library of contextual AI tools that can review documents, extract information, draft communications and support legal work using information held around the matter.

● Launched our integrated legal accounting capability in 2026.

● Secured additional strategic investment to accelerate the next stage of product development and commercial growth.

But perhaps the most important milestone is that we’re no longer demonstrating a hypothetical future of practice management. Law firms are beginning to use it.

Yes. Matterbee is backed by Mandashi, the investment company founded by Andy Evans and Sheila Gupta following the successful growth and exit of enterprise software business Xactium.

Mandashi made a further strategic investment in Matterbee in 2026 to accelerate product development, customer success, partnerships and commercial growth.

For us, the value isn’t simply capital. Having investors who have previously built, scaled and exited enterprise software businesses gives Matterbee experience around the table that is directly relevant to what we’re trying to achieve.

The investment amount has not been disclosed.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

The core belief hasn’t changed.

We started Matterbee because we believed practice management technology could be dramatically better: more connected, more configurable and easier for people to use.

What has evolved is our view of what a practice management system should actually be responsible for.

Historically, the PMS has primarily been the firm’s system of record. It stores the matter, records time, keeps documents and ultimately helps produce a bill.

With modern AI and automation, we believe that definition is becoming obsolete.

The opportunity now is for the platform to actively participate in the delivery of legal work: reading information, preparing drafts, identifying what needs attention, progressing workflows, triggering actions and helping lawyers complete work more efficiently.

That realisation has pushed Matterbee from being simply a modern alternative to legacy PMS products towards something more ambitious: an AI-native workspace and system of action for the law firm.

We’ve also become increasingly convinced that configurability matters. Technology is changing too quickly for firms to buy rigid systems built around today’s processes and expect them to remain appropriate for the next decade. The winning platforms will be those that can continuously evolve.

What are the key challenges in your market?

The biggest challenge is also the biggest opportunity: legal technology is changing faster than the core systems most firms are running on.

AI has dramatically raised expectations. Law firm leaders are asking how technology can increase capacity, reduce administrative work, improve consistency and transform client service.

But many are trying to achieve that while their core operational platform was designed primarily to store information and record activity.

That creates a fundamental mismatch.

There are also significant practical barriers to change. A PMS sits at the heart of the firm, so replacing one involves migration, integrations, finance, workflows, training and change management. Firms are understandably cautious, particularly when many have lived through difficult technology implementations before.

And then there is AI itself. Giving every lawyer access to a chatbot is relatively easy. Embedding AI safely into the actual delivery of legal work, with the right matter context, governance, auditability and human oversight, is much harder.

That’s where we believe the next major competitive battleground in legal technology will be.

The winners will be the companies with access to the best AI models. Those models will increasingly be available to everyone. The differentiation will come from the platform around the AI: the data it can access, the processes it participates in and how naturally it can help people get work done.

That’s precisely the layer Matterbee is building.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company?

Our AI assistant, ChatBee, was actually named by the legal community.

Rather than naming it ourselves, we opened the decision up and asked people across the legal sector to suggest and vote on names. ChatBee was the winning suggestion.

There has been one unintended consequence.

Once you’ve called the company Matterbee and your AI assistant ChatBee, people assume every new product needs a bee-related name!

news.titleEn: Guest Post: The Rise Of The Contracting ‘Stack’
news.titleZh: 客座文章：合同管理'技术栈'的兴起
news.summaryZh:
一位法律运营专业人士在演示请求中提及将“堆叠”一个合同生命周期管理解决方案，并寻求工作流部分。她曾试点三种CLM工具，发现每种仅有一两项出色功能，其余均不达标。在一次会议中了解到“堆叠”实践，即整合不同技术构件以构建解决方案，并决定将其应用于合同领域。她根据实际需求而非CLM工具的全部功能进行规划，并为每个环节（如合同接收、修订、存储库）寻找最佳解决方案。

更多法律运营领导者表达了类似不满，不限于CLM。例如，一位保险业法律运营负责人抱怨其企业法律管理软件主要用作法律门户，却因强制使用其自有版本而无法与首选的事务管理工具集成。在CLOC会议上，与会者讨论了这是否为构建法律技术的新方法，以及平台模式是否已过时。主要议题包括：在当前技术快速迭代环境下，签订长期平台合同显得草率；大量资金涌入导致市场动荡与并购活跃；过去十年资本流入改变了CLM的单位经济，迫使供应商横向扩张，导致用户为未使用的功能付费。同时，AI为合同技术栈开启了新的可能性与价值创造，降低了集成门槛，使非技术人员也能构建解决方案。但堆叠实践也面临挑战，如用户迁移难度、自制解决方案的维护负担，以及需承担集成风险、安全审查和故障责任。
news.bodyHtml:
A legal operations professional requested a demo earlier this year with a note that intrigued me. She said that she was going to “stack” a CLM solution, and she was looking for the workflow portion (which is what my product, Josef, does).

When we met, I dug in further, finding that she’d piloted three CLM tools in the preceding year, only to find that each one had one or two great features, and that the rest were substandard. 

During that time, she went to a conference where she learned about “stacking,” the practice of bringing together disparate pieces of technology to build a solution, and decided to bring that approach to bear in the contracting space. She mapped out what she actually needed – rather than looking at all of the features the CLM tools had – and then went to market to find best-in-class solutions for each: intake, redlining, repository.

So many people have been talking about the “death of CLM,” yet this was one of the first times that I’d seen a legal ops team in the market trying to come up with a solution.

CLM isn’t the problem – the platform is

Once I started sharing this story with people, I learned that more and more people had similar complaints, though it really wasn’t limited to CLMs. Another legal ops leader in the insurance space complained about her ELM, which she primarily used for a legal front door, but which didn’t allow her to integrate with her preferred matter management tool because it was trying to force her to use their version.

What legal ops leaders are doing differently

At CLOC earlier this year, I brought together a room full of legal operations leaders, under the Chatham House Rule, to talk about whether this really could be a new approach to building legal technology, and whether the platform play had run its course. We published a report with leaders from companies like Ford, DHL and Canva off the back of what was shared in the room. You can read it here. 

One of the strongest themes to come out of the room was that people are finding it very difficult to invest in platforms in the current technological landscape, where it feels like new possibilities – let alone features and functionality – are being deployed every other week. In that environment, how are you supposed to sign a three year contract with one provider? For a room of people whose job it was to advise legal on technology procurement, that felt like a negligent move.

Beyond the technological uncertainty, people were also concerned about the amount of money flowing into the space (Harvey raised another half a billion dollars this month!). While this is an exciting development for anyone who believes that the future of legal is technological, it undoubtedly causes upheaval in the market, with M&A activity higher than ever before.

Another common complaint was about how the previous capital flows into CLM over the past ten years have altered the unit economics such that CLM providers were forced to expand horizontally – even if the functionality wasn’t best-in-class – to capture as much revenue as possible. The room was concerned that they were paying for features and modules they weren’t using, and that very few platforms in the space allowed them to pick and choose what they paid for.

How AI has changed the game

Beyond diagnosing the problem, though, what was more exciting was that AI has opened up new possibilities, expectations, and value creation when it comes to the contract stack. Previously, platforms made sense as integrations were complex and expensive – if they came in one seamless package, then people could avoid the difficulty of stitching them together. Now, though, even non-technical people can use AI to learn how to build a Zap on Zapier, or how to set up a webhook. As long as you have the permissions, you do not need to wait for IT. As MCP becomes more widely available, it opens up a whole new world of interoperability as well.

People in the room were also hopeful about the ability of stacking and AI to empower them to build solutions that were better aligned with the way they worked. One technologist I met recently was looking to build her own gifts and hospitality module because none of the tools on the market actually lined up with the way this worked in her organization. While that might sound strange to some, in multinational enterprises, it’s now easier to build a solution to match the process than it is to change the process.

The catch

That said, there were still concerns about how to make stacking stick. One company had onboarded thousands of salespeople onto a CLM; getting them onto something else felt like too big a job to tackle. Another individual warned us about a homegrown SharePoint stack that started as a clever workaround and became a maintenance nightmare. And none of this is free: you inherit the integration risk the platform used to absorb, you multiply your security reviews, and you have to decide who owns the problem when something breaks between two vendors at 2am.

But those are costs you can now price, weigh and mitigate, rather than reasons the question was closed before you asked it. The tech stack approach has always made logical sense. What’s changed is that two things now point the same way at once: the market is making platform commitments feel reckless, and the technology has made the alternative practical for the first time.

Integrations are easier than ever

What’s changed is that the market and the technology are now pointing the same way at once. Platforms won the last decade because integration was genuinely hard. Stitching six tools together meant a project, a budget and a queue in IT, and a single vendor that promised to have done the stitching for you was worth paying a premium for, even if half the modules were weak. That premium was really an integration fee. It is now a great deal smaller than it was two years ago, and it is still falling.

The discipline the stack demands is knowing what you need before you go shopping. That was always good practice. The difference is that it used to be optional, because the platform would decide for you.

Sam Flynn is cofounder and COO of Josef and leads the company’s business operations, governance, marketing and customer success functions. An ex-BigLaw litigator, Sam is on the board for the Center for Legal Innovation, and on the Emerging Leaders Council of the Legal Services Corporation. He regularly speaks on generative AI, including at schools such as Cornell and NYU, and at Stanford’s 2024 conference on AI in legal & compliance: JURIX.

news.titleEn: OpenAI Launches Astra For Law
news.titleZh: OpenAI推出面向法律行业的Astra
news.summaryZh: OpenAI正式推出Astra for Law，这是一款由GPT-6 Astra驱动的新产品，配备工具、设置和上下文，以支持律师和法律科技公司的专业判断。Latham & Watkins、Ropes & Gray、Cooley和Sullivan & Cromwell等律所已成为早期采用者。该产品将GPT-6 Astra与法律分析和写作指令、深度工作设置以及新的法律搜索索引相结合。该索引可搜索美国判例法、法规、规章、法院规则和行政决定，覆盖超过2.3亿个URL，并每日更新来源，帮助律师从案件事实转向相关权威和可自行审查的支持性段落。OpenAI还推出了26个合作伙伴构建的插件和47个社区插件，用于ChatGPT中的法律工作，合作伙伴包括Thomson Reuters、Harvey、Legora和iManage，可连接专业工具和知识。社区插件由律师和法律工程师构建，为律所提供可调整和扩展的技能。Astra for Law最初将通过ChatGPT和Codex中的Trusted Access向选定律所提供，API访问即将推出。OpenAI将维护法律配置，以便开发者专注于自身产品和工作流程。据悉，OpenAI最初考虑将法律垂直能力作为Codex的一部分推出，但今年年初以来发生了品牌转变。OpenAI表示将与实际应用该产品的律师和法律技术合作伙伴共同构建Astra for Law的下一篇章。
news.bodyText: After plenty of waiting, OpenAI has launched Astra for Law, a ‘new offering powered by GPT-6 Astra with tools, settings, and context to support the expertise and judgment of lawyers and legal technology firms’. Law firms such as Latham & Watkins, Ropes & Gray, Cooley and Sullivan & Cromwell are already early adopters (see more below). The company explained: ‘Astra for Law pairs GPT-6 Astra with instructions for legal analysis and writing, settings for thorough work, and a new Legal Search Index. The index searches U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, court rules, and administrative decisions across more than 230 million URLs – with sources added daily. That helps lawyers move from the facts of a matter to relevant authorities and supporting passages they can examine themselves. We’re also launching 26 partner-built plugins and 47 community plugins for legal work in ChatGPT. Partners including Thomson Reuters, Harvey, Legora, and iManage connect specialist tools and knowledge. Community plugins built by lawyers and legal engineers give firms skills they can adapt and extend. Astra for Law will initially be offered to selected firms through Trusted Access in ChatGPT and Codex, with API access coming soon. We’ll maintain the legal configuration so builders can focus on their own products and workflows. We’ll build the next chapter of Astra for Law alongside the lawyers and legal technology partners who put it into practice.’ And here’s a video about Astra for Law. – Initially it’s understood that OpenAI had been looking at rolling out its legal vertical capability as part of Codex, but it seems that between the start of this year and now it’s taken a branding shift, as so often happens. Regardless of what it’s called, it good to see it finally arrive. Here’s an overview from OpenAI of what it will do, then what some law firms are already doing with it.
news.relevanceReason: The article's primary subject is OpenAI's launch of Astra for Law, a legal AI product specifically designed for lawyers

news.titleEn: Astra for Law + The Battle for Centrality
news.titleZh: Astra for Law 与中心性之战
news.summaryZh: 法律科技领域当前最大的战略挑战是中心性之争，Astra for Law的加入加剧了竞争。其核心在于确定法律工作的主要承载平台。Astra for Law与谷歌的Gemini Enterprise for Legal以及Claude for Legal等大型LLM制造商一样，旨在提供用户愿意驻留的平台或生态系统。用户使用其基础AI和平台工具，当需要法律数据等其他资源时，则通过平台内的‘信息流’获取。这意味着用户可完全在该平台内工作，包括处理Word文档。与此同时，Harvey、Legora、Thomson Reuters和LexisNexis等许多大型法律科技公司也试图实现类似目标，希望用户因其服务而来并留在其生态内。它们会连接外部数据或解决方案以维持用户粘性。所有平台的战略目标一致：实现中心性，即让用户将特定平台视为‘家园’并习惯驻留，平台便能逐步构建更多功能巩固依赖。各大平台每年都在增加功能并不断扩展，倾向于整合其他解决方案或数据，希望成为聚会的中心。根本原因始终是吸引用户并留住他们。然而，这是一场危险的游戏。法律科技公司连接Astra、Claude等平台是为了留住客户，但像Legora这样的公司显然更希望用户始终留在自己身边。此外，在按使用量定价模式日益重要的背景下，这些公司尤其强烈地希望用户保持现状。
news.bodyText: The battle for centrality is now legal tech’s greatest strategic challenge – and Astra for Law just raised the stakes for everyone. That is to say: where does your legal work primarily live? And the answer to that will shape this sector. Astra for Law joins Google’s Gemini Enterprise for Legal and also Claude for Legal – among the largest LLM makers in trying to provide a platform, an ecosystem, or a context, if you prefer that term, that you will stay within. You use their foundational AI, the tools that come with that platform, and when you need something else, e.g. legal data, you use ‘the feed’ into that context. In short, if you want to, you can stay there. Word docs – which are essential for lawyers – are of course part of this, but just part of operating within this platform. Astra becomes the centre of your working life, Gemini does, Claude does….. At the same time, many large legal tech companies are trying to do the same thing. Harvey and Legora would prefer it if you stayed within their context. If you need to find legal data or point solutions that are not already ‘hard-wired’ inside those platforms, then they will seek to connect to them – or at least as much as possible – in a way that again, keeps you there. But then, Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis want you to come to them for their legal research data and then stay within their context for drafting and also transactional needs as well. They also connect to many other offerings. The want the same thing: for you to stay where you have landed. The strategic goal is always the same: centrality. I.e. keeping you there, because the more you see X, Y or Z platform as your ‘home’, the more you will get used to staying there. Then, that platform can build additional features over time that cement you into it. For example, ask yourself the question: have all the large legal tech platforms produced more features each year, or cut back to their core offering? Yep, exactly. They have all expanded, outwards, and outwards, and outwards again. If they can also bring in other legal tech solutions and/or legal data where applicable, into that platform, the better it is for them. No platform wants to be ‘a loner’, they want to be gregarious, extroverted, and friends with everyone. But, also the centre of the party – to be ‘where the action is’. They want to look like a legal tech conference exhibition hall – but their stand is the largest and in the middle of it all…! Why? It’s always the same reason: so you come to that platform, and you stay there. Dangerous Game This is all a dangerous game, of course. Legal tech companies connect to Astra, to Claude, to you name it…..because they want to keep their customers and allow them to use what’s in the market. Everyone is putting on a brave face. But, does Legora really, actively want its customers to fly over to Claude, or Astra and do their legal work from there, and then keep going back there? Would they prefer you stayed with them all of the time? Of course they’d prefer you stay with them. Also, in a world where usage-based (i.e. token) pricing is becoming more relevant to some companies, then such companies really, really want you to stay where you are.

news.titleEn: Astra for Law’s 26 Legal Tech Plugins + 1 Million More :)
news.titleZh: Astra for Law 的 26 个法律科技插件 + 另外一百万个 :)
news.summaryZh: OpenAI 在推出 Astra for Law 的同时，宣布已有 26 个由合作伙伴构建的插件，旨在帮助律师更深入地使用他们已有的工具和知识。这些插件覆盖法律执业和法律业务领域。例如，律师可以在 ChatGPT 中起草谈判简报，并通过 iManage 将其保存到案件文件中；Intapp 可以显示可能需要审查的时间录入活动；DeepJudge 可以将先前的交易引入比较；Thomson Reuters 将 HighQ 案件上下文引入 ChatGPT，并预览即将推出的 CoCounsel Legal 连接器。使用开发者模式，用户可以构建自定义私有插件，将专有数据与工具连接到 ChatGPT，或添加基于 MCP 的插件。私有插件可以使用 Apps SDK 构建。此外，OpenAI 指出，通过使用法律搜索索引，Astra for Law 可以搜索美国判例法、法规、条例、法院规则和行政决定，涵盖超过 2.3 亿个 URL，且来源每日更新。OpenAI 与 Free Law Project（CourtListener 背后的非营利组织）合作，将其判例法集合（覆盖超过 99.9% 的美国已公布先例判例法）纳入研究体验。文章提到，LegalQuants 从发布之初就参与其中。随着时间推移，Litera 和 Definely 也宣布加入该插件群体。文章预计，未来几天内将有更多法律科技公司推出插件，甚至可能所有法律科技公司都会为 Astra for Law 提供插件。
news.bodyText: Alongside the launch of Astra for Law, OpenAI has also announced that there are already 26 ‘partner-built plugins’ (see full list below), that help lawyers ‘go deeper with the tools and knowledge they already use’ – and as far as AL sees it, this increases the ‘centrality’ of the Astra context for lawyers. (Note: since then a million other legal tech companies have been in touch to say they also have a plugin….see below.) OpenAI commented: ‘These plugins cover the practice and business of law. With iManage, a lawyer can draft a negotiation brief in ChatGPT and save it to the matter file; Intapp can surface activities that may need a time entry for review; DeepJudge can bring prior deals into a comparison. Thomson Reuters is bringing HighQ matter context into ChatGPT and previewing a forthcoming CoCounsel Legal connector.’ They also added: ‘Using developer mode, you can build custom private plugins that connect proprietary data and tools to ChatGPT, or add MCP-based plugins from other sources. Private plugins can be built using the Apps SDK.’ As noted above all of this means that once you move your work into Astra, you will find it easier to stay there. Plus, special kudos to LegalQuants for being part of this from launch! One key additional point is legal research. news.titleZh: 你的下一个竞争对手不是另一家律所：与理查德·萨斯坎德的对话

news.bodyHtml:
In the 1980s, Richard Susskind helped build the world’s first fully operational AI system that actually worked for lawyers. It ran on what he calls knowledge engineering: sitting down with a deep expert in an area of law, translating what they knew into rules, and mapping the whole thing out as an enormous decision tree. The one he worked on had over 2 million paths through it. The clever part, he says, was never the software. It was the humans doing the analysis that went into it.

Nobody builds systems that way anymore, which is roughly his point about the systems everyone is building today. He thinks large language models are simply the current enabling technology, and that in 10 years we’ll find it remarkable that we ever thought this was how you did AI. What hasn’t changed, he says, is the moral and social questions. He expands on the argument in a 30th anniversary edition of The Future of Law, published by Oxford University Press.

“Lawyers aren’t preparing themselves for the idea that their major competitor in the future will not be another law firm, it’ll be an AI-empowered client,” he told us backstage at ClioCon 2025, before his keynote.

We sat down with Susskind to talk about the errors firms are making with AI right now, why the return on investment may not look the way firms are hoping, whether a three-partner shop can outrun a supertanker, and the question he thinks every firm should be asking about 2035.

The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Want to learn from other legal industry leaders? Secure your tickets to ClioCon 2026 today!

 

You’ve been working on AI and the law since the 1980s. Looking back, what could you not have imagined?

Richard Susskind: Let me tell you what hasn’t changed, because that’s the fundamental societal and moral issues. All of them had been surfaced in the 1960s and 1970s. I’m not hearing discussions today about ethical issues, or economic or social impact, that hadn’t been anticipated.

What has changed enormously is the enabling technologies. We couldn’t imagine in the 1980s any other way of doing this other than sitting down with humans, speaking to them, and somehow trying to model their expertise. We called this knowledge engineering. Most of us who were working on operational systems worked on rule-based expert systems. It’s like a big flowchart, or a big decision tree. You had to take a complex area of law and essentially map it out, with the assistance of a deep expert, integrating legislation and case law. It was very much a hand-crafting exercise. The clever bit wasn’t the system itself. The clever bit was the humans doing the analysis that went into the system.

Then the idea came through, around the turn of the century, that rather than mining the jewels from humans’ heads, we could derive the jewels from great oceans of data that we gathered. That just wasn’t imaginable in the 1980s.

There’s a really interesting lesson here when we speak of generative AI and large language models. We should be cautious in remembering that these are just today’s enabling technologies. I’ve little doubt we’ll look back in 10 years’ time and think it’s amazing we thought that’s the way you do AI. In my view, AI is the accumulation of a variety of techniques. It’s not that rule-based systems are now irrelevant. A lot of the so-called guardrails are actually introduced through that kind of technology.

 

What’s the biggest mistake you see legal professionals making with AI right now?

Richard Susskind: There are two levels of error today. One is that many lawyers think that AI in law means AI for lawyers. In the long run, I say this is not the case. In the long run, the impact of AI will be in enabling non-lawyers to undertake a lot of legal work for themselves. That’ll have enormous impact for individual citizens, but it will also have enormous impact on organizations. And that’s why I say that lawyers aren’t preparing themselves for the idea that their major competitor in the future will not be another law firm, it’ll be an AI-empowered client.

Then there are a few errors in terms of current usage. People are expecting too much of what is, after all, just very early versions of these systems, and over-claiming in the short term what this is likely to achieve. It would help if we had a more experimental mindset, a research and development mindset, where we’re not expecting these systems to be faultless, so that the skeptical lawyer, when they’re given the tool, isn’t disappointed. Their expectations are managed.

People are also jumping a lot of the more basic uses of technology and trying to focus on legal applications. By the more basic uses, I mean simple things: using these systems to record and summarize a meeting, helping produce promotional material for the web or for marketing, undertaking basic admin, responding to emails. A lot of the unglamorous use of AI that can actually save you a couple of hours a day, and that couple of hours a day could be used more valuably. I understand why lawyers want to leap to the systems that draft legal contracts, that undertake legal research, that review legal documents. So I say, just embrace it in a more measured way. There’s a frenzy just now to get ahead.

Another mistake is thinking that it’s absolutely critical to get the system selection right. In my experience, what matters more is not the system you select today, but how committed you are as an organization and how committed you are as an individual to make the most of it. So a lot of this is about training, it’s about practice, it’s about integrating it into working life. A lot of law firms seem to think the AI strategy is about choosing the right system. To some extent it doesn’t much matter in your early months which ones you use, but do get on with it.

 

So where should a firm that’s just getting started actually begin?

Richard Susskind: Remember that some quite everyday basic applications might not be glamorous, but will deliver benefits. Jump in, experiment, and use.

A few of my clients report their greatest success where they just give people a general-purpose AI system and say, “It doesn’t matter if it’s for your personal or professional use, just use it for half an hour a day.” Once people start using and then embracing the technology, they’ll be better placed to use it in the legal context. There’s a bit of a gold rush atmosphere just now, where people are running around, some in circles.

 

A lot of firms still see AI as a line item. How should they be thinking about return on investment?

Richard Susskind: This technology causes us to think of three things to do. One is to optimize, the second is to transform, the third is to diversify. Optimize is basically to say, let me use this technology to be more efficient and productive. Transform is to say, actually, we could use this technology to transform the service we provide: same outcome for the client, but a very different process. And the third is to say, actually, if we’re going to stay in business, we might need to do very new and different things.

I reckon over the next two or three years the story is going to be one of optimization. The difficulty is that at the same time, clients are looking at this technology, and it doesn’t excite them the way it excites firms. The law firms feel this is a way for law firms to become more profitable. What excites clients is that there’ll actually be reductions in fees. All the work I do with in-house counsel supports this. They’re saying, now is the time. For years we’ve been asking for more for less, more legal service at less cost, and now you have the tools to provide that. And they will look very dimly upon those firms who use this as a way of becoming more profitable and charging them more.

My view is that as more and more firms take this technology on board, you won’t be able to differentiate by simply being a user of these systems. In fact, that’s going to be a market expectation of you. You may expect that your revenue and profits might decrease because of this technology.

On the other hand, if you are imaginative and creative and entrepreneurial with your AI, if you can deliver systems and benefits to clients that others aren’t delivering, then you may be able to charge a premium price for these. We’ll be moving away from an advisory service to generating revenue by licensing content, licensing systems, and so forth. That could be making money while you sleep. So if you’re prepared to invest, if you’re ambitious, not a fast second but actually a fast first, then I think some firms will enjoy first-mover advantage and could enjoy great commercial benefits.

Let me give a very practical example. Most small businesses can’t afford lawyers today, and they get by. Small businesses around the world can’t generally afford lawyers. There’s a gap in the market for a set of legal tools which would essentially perform the function of their own in-house legal department, that they could license from reliable providers. That kind of mass-market licensing of tools and software could be a tremendously profitable business. It’s just that it doesn’t look like the kind of legal business that most people have in mind when practicing law. I give that as one example of what I call a latent market. It’s just out there waiting to be exploited.

 

Can a small, tech-savvy firm compete with a large traditional one?

Richard Susskind: I think smaller firms, if they play their cards right, can move ahead more quickly. I’ve seen this in some of the world’s finest professional firms. They do to some extent suffer from supertanker syndrome: hard to change direction, hard to slow down, hard to stop. And the introduction of new technology becomes a very bureaucratic affair.

The smaller firms I’m seeing, just a few partners who are agile and ambitious, can do something different, given the power of these technologies today. Much of the work that used to be given to great teams of junior lawyers, associates, and paralegals will be undertaken by these systems. So you can already see the possibility of very high-quality small boutique firms operating with far greater resource behind them.

If they take advantage of their size, which means hopefully they’re more agile and nimble, then it could be that the major firms in some areas are left on the back foot. But we see this more clearly in any event through legaltech startups. That’s their premise: that they can come to market quicker, that they’re less encumbered by admin and by legacy. So it wouldn’t surprise me at all if both small law firms and small legaltech providers, particularly those focusing on content, could have considerable impact on the market.

 

If the work junior lawyers learn on is the first to be automated, where do future partners come from?

Richard Susskind: The big question is, what are we training young lawyers to become? Implicit in your question, I think, is that lawyers will still become the traditional experts of today and we have to find a new route for them. That might be right. If that’s the case, the answer probably lies in immersive virtual learning environments, where we can expose young lawyers to far more permutations of legal issues, legal problems, and legal challenges than the apprenticeship model.

But I think there’s a question mark hanging over the bigger issue, which is whether or not we will need so many expert partners at a high level doing what they do today. So I say again that we have to make sure we don’t find different ways of training people to become 20th-century lawyers.

The big question really is, you’ve got to start with clients. What are clients’ needs going to be in the 2030s? How will these needs best be met? What kind of mix do we need of humans and machines? And build our training of humans around that likely human requirement. We shouldn’t be driven by today’s successful business model in thinking of what it is our young lawyers will be doing in 10 years’ time.

I say you can do strategy in two ways. I call it vision-based strategy or legacy-based strategy. With legacy-based strategy, you start from today and you say, well, how can we change a bit what we’re doing today, because we are where we are. With vision-based strategy, you say, look, put that to one side for a second. Let’s think what the world might be like in 2030 and 2035, try and identify how best to meet likely market needs, and then think through what kind of humans you require, what kind of machines you require, and how you get there from here.

A lot of us aren’t allowing ourselves that opportunity. We’re too constrained and contained by where we are today. I often say that legacy-based strategy is like walking backwards into the future.

 

Is there any legal work that’s safe? Anything human enough that lawyers don’t need to worry?

Richard Susskind: There’s what I call “not-us” thinking, where everyone thinks that AI applies to every other bit of work except their own.

One of the arguments people make is that of course people will require human service. And I think we have to think deeply about this, because actually what I believe people want is an outcome rather than a particular human process. I think we often overestimate the extent to which people want us to continue working the way we do today.

When you look at it quite harshly, the question I ask in my book is, when is it intrinsically important for a human to be involved in the service? That’s to say, it’s important in and of itself, as opposed to instrumentally important, which means it’s just important because of the value of the outcome that it brings. That question will change over time, because it may well be that today’s clients will say, I still want a face-to-face. It’s not obvious that my children or my children’s children will feel the same.

In any event, I don’t think it’s a strategic approach to start trying to find things machines can’t do. I call this competing with the machines, because you’re likely to be pitching yourself into a corner. If you believe our machines are getting more and more capable, then to say that my strategy for my career or my business is to do things machines can’t do, I wouldn’t back a company that had that as its underlying premise.

 

Takeaway: Half an hour a day

Susskind’s forecast is a long one. He doesn’t expect AI to transform legal service in the next two or three years. He expects it to transform legal service in the 2030s.

What makes his warning about clients worth sitting with is how quietly it would arrive. No rival opens an office down the street. The work simply stops coming in, because the client handled it themselves. And the entry price for getting ready is far smaller than the threat: a general purpose AI tool, half an hour a day, on work that has nothing to do with law.

Richard Susskind presented his keynote at ClioCon 2025. To hear from the legal professionals, innovators, and advocates shaping the future of law, get your tickets to ClioCon 2026 today.

news.bodyHtml:
The Descrybe Legal Engine plugin gives ChatGPT users access to structured, verifiable U.S. primary law and legal intelligence built specifically for AI.

 

BOSTON, Sept. 17, 2026 — Descrybe today announced that the Descrybe Legal Engine plugin is bringing specialized legal research directly into ChatGPT.

The launch comes as AI assistants are becoming a central environment for professional work, including legal research, analysis, drafting, and review. As that shift accelerates, connecting AI systems to authoritative domain information becomes critical. Descrybe was built for this moment. 

“AI is changing the way legal work gets done, and one of the most exciting parts of that shift is how much more accessible sophisticated legal research can become,” said Kara Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Descrybe. “Bringing deep legal intelligence directly into an environment like ChatGPT puts powerful research capabilities within reach of many more people and organizations through a tool they already know how to use. That can fundamentally change who can benefit from sophisticated legal research technology.”

The Descrybe Legal Engine plugin helps ChatGPT identify relevant authority, assess how cases and laws relate to one another, and work from verifiable primary sources. Its technology connects U.S. primary law with citation relationships, subsequent treatment, legal issues, jurisdictional context, relevance signals, and source material to help determine which authorities matter and how they fit together, then returns focused legal information structured specifically for AI assistants to use efficiently.

Descrybe itself was built from the beginning using OpenAI technology. OpenAI’s models have helped the company classify, structure, summarize, and analyze legal materials at scale.

“Frontier models made it possible for a small team like ours to build something extraordinarily ambitious,” said Richard DiBona, co-founder and CTO of Descrybe. “We’ve used OpenAI’s technology to transform a vast body of legal material into legal intelligence that AI can work with effectively. Bringing Descrybe into ChatGPT with this plugin closes that loop in a really powerful way.”

The launch reflects Descrybe’s broader vision of making sophisticated legal research available wherever people and AI systems work. Descrybe can be used through its own platform, across supported AI environments, and inside custom products and workflows through the Descrybe Open Connector and developer tools.

One Descrybe Legal Engine subscription provides access across supported assistants and apps for $25 per user per month. The full Descrybe Platform is available for $50 per user per monthand includes Legal Engine access along with Descrybe’s complete research workspace and advanced legal research and review capabilities.

###

About Descrybe

Descrybe is a legal research and intelligence platform for people and AI systems. Its technology combines extensive U.S. primary-law coverage with citation, subsequent treatment, legal issues, and source intelligence to help users move from finding law to understanding what matters. Descrybe can be used directly through the Descrybe Platform, through Descrybe Legal Engine in leading AI assistants, and through the Descrybe Open Connector in custom AI tools and workflows. Founded on the belief that sophisticated legal technology should be broadly accessible, Descrybe brings powerful, reliable legal research and intelligence wherever legal work happens.

For more information, visit Descrybe.com.

Media Contact
Kara Peterson
Co-Founder & CEO
kara@descrybe.com

news.titleEn: OpenAI Releases Astra for Law, A GPT-6 Model Tailored for Legal Work, Targeting Large Firms and Tech Vendors
