news.bodyText:
Calling it the “intelligence foundation” of its platform, Casepoint today launched Casepoint IQ, a suite of tools within a single AI framework that spans the company’s products for e-discovery, legal holds, FOIA and investigations.

The company says that Casepoint IQ pulls together all of its AI capabilities – including new semi- and fully autonomous agents, its generative AI assistants, its pre-existing CaseAssist machine learning and predictive coding, and its Model Context Protocol (MCP) server – under one framework with a shared governance and audit layer.

Alongside the framework, the company is introducing its first two AI agents to customers, one for relevance determination and one for issue coding, with more to come as the product is further developed.

Casepoint IQ is live now in the platform and generally available to all customers. The two agents are currently in what Casepoint describes as an alpha release, in use by a handful of customers, with a beta version due out before the year ends.

An interesting aspect of today’s announcement is how the company is melding its new generative AI tools with the technology-assisted review (TAR) tools that have been part of the platform for at least a decade.

Rather than introduce Casepoint IQ as a separate product alongside those existing tools, the company is treating agentic AI, assistive AI and its older predictive coding as points on a single continuum, with the same permissions, logging and human-approval controls applied across the board.

And both the relevance-determination and issue-coding agents carry forward the sampling, precision-and-recall measurement and QA validation conventions that would be familiar to anyone who has previously used TAR for review.

“We’ve always believed intelligence should be built at the platform level, not confined to individual products,” said Vishal Rajpara , Casepoint’s founder and chief technology officer, in a statement. “Casepoint IQ offers the foundation where an innovation developed for one workflow can create value across the entire platform.”

In a press briefing Monday, CEO Paul Colangelo described Casepoint IQ as a single framework that extends across four sets of capabilities:

IQ Agents. Colangelo described these agents as “purpose-built” to move legal, government and compliance work “from analysis to determination.” While the agents currently operate on a semi-autonomous level requiring human-in-the-loop oversight, the company plans to introduce additional levels that will allow the agents to operate with greater autonomy.

IQ Assist. This is Casepoint’s embedded gen AI. It is designed to help users find, understand and classify information through natural language search, summarization and workflow-specific assistance. During the media briefing, Chief Product Officer Pete Feinberg said there are now more than a dozen assistive AI tools across Casepoint’s e-discovery, FOIA, legal hold and file store applications.

CaseAssist. This is Casepoint’s machine learning and predictive coding technology, which Colangelo said has been in the platform for more than a decade. It prioritizes documents for relevance, helps identify potential privilege, and produces precision and recall reporting that Colangelo said helps teams validate results and support defensibility.

Casepoint MCP Server. Colangelo described this as a standardized connection that links approved external AI models and agents to the Casepoint platform, with authentication, permissions and audit logging applied to every transaction and no custom integration required.

For practitioners, Casepoint says this new framework offers three practical benefits.

First, it enables customers to add agentic capabilities within the platform they already use, without having to adopt separate tools, credentials or governance models. As new agents are developed, customers can add them to the same platform.

That platform is authorized under FedRAMP High and DOD Impact Level 5 and 6 standards. For customers, that means that adding new agentic workflows will not tigger a new vendor risk assessment, a separate security review, or new credentials to manage, Casepoint says.

Second, the company says that every AI-driven decision within the framework is permissions-aware, logged and traceable to the source, and that human-in-the-loop governance applies across the board, ensuring that every AI-driven decision is transparent and defensible.

In the briefing, Rajpara said that an agent “is never going to create the document, redact the document, produce a document to [the] other side,” and that human-led decision-making is built into the foundation.

Third, the company says organizations that prefer to use their own approved AI models or agents can connect them through the MCP server rather than being limited to the models Casepoint provides.

“Our customers have been clear: they want AI to take on more of the heavy-lifting work, but they still want visibility into, and control over how decisions are made, and have the final approvals,” Colangelo said in the release.

In the media briefing, Feinberg provided a demonstration of the relevance determination agent.

In the current alpha version, a user can run only a single agent per project. The beta version, coming later this year, will allow multiple agents to be chained into a workflow. An agentic workflow, for example, might proceed from relevance determination, then issue coding, then privilege review, then PII identification, and then redaction.

For the demo, Feinberg used a synthetic data set of roughly 10,000 documents that Casepoint built so it would have a gold standard to measure against, rather than relying on the Enron or Jeb Bush data sets that are often used for such purposes.

Based on the demo, the agent runs through five stages:

Setting the context. Rather than requiring users to write a prompt from scratch, the setup offers an “AI fast track” in which the user can load case documents. Feinberg added the complaint, the requests for production and a review protocol. Based on those documents, the system then extracted a case overview, key players, key terminology and a relevance definition, which the user can review and edit. Alternatively, a user can reuse the context from a prior project.

Choosing an autonomy level. During setup, the user selects how much autonomy the agent will have. The alpha launches at what Casepoint calls level two, in which the LLM proposes what it will do and the user reviews and confirms before execution. As it develops additional agents, the company will set the permitted autonomy on an agent-by-agent basis.

Iterative tuning. The agent selects a sample of 50 documents from the review set, predicts whether each is relevant, and writes a rationale for each prediction. A human then reviews each of the 50 documents. If the human’s decisions disagree with the AI’s, the system proposes refinements to the context based on the human’s feedback. Feinberg said the software enforces minimum quality thresholds of 90% recall and 80% precision. If the sample does not meet those thresholds, the user must adjust the context and run another 50-document sample.

AI review. Once the thresholds are met, the agent reviews the full set. For the set of 10,000 documents used in the demo, Feinberg said it took about an hour, and a results screen reported time saved (190 hours, 4 minutes), estimated cost savings ($11,911, calculated at a review rate of 50 documents per hour and $50 per hour), corpus richness (13%) and AI review time (58 minutes). The agent assigns each document a predicted likelihood of relevance and routes documents into tiers for not relevant, likely not relevant, borderline, likely relevant and highly relevant. Feinberg said this scoring was intentionally carried over from TAR. “We’ve kind of blurred the lines, if you will, between our history with machine learning and TAR, where the world has gotten used to and comfortable with the idea of this kind of 0 to 1 score by document and these plotted histograms,” he said.

Post-run QC. The final stage is a validation step in which the software draws a random sample and a human reviews each one against the agent’s decision. The system then calculates final recall, precision, elusion and F1 scores, with confidence intervals, that Feinberg said can be reported to opposing counsel or the court.

During the briefing, a reporter asked Feinberg about a “credits consumed” figure on one of the demo screens. He said the agent currently displays raw token consumption and that the beta will convert tokens to credits.

Ultimately, Casepoint intends to offer unmetered use to its largest customers and, for smaller subscriptions, an allocated number of credits with metering and overage charges, “not terribly dissimilar” to what competitors are doing.

Asked whether Casepoint plans to add more agents or mainly to chain the existing two, Feinberg said “both.” He said that eight other agents are in active development, including agents to identify privileged material, find PII and redact documents, and that the company is “not done” developing assistive AI tools.

news.titleEn: Harvey Raises Another $550M At A $15.5B Valuation
news.titleZh: Harvey再融资5.5亿美元，估值达155亿美元
news.summaryZh: 法律人工智能公司Harvey于今日宣布，已再次筹集5.5亿美元资金，公司估值达到155亿美元。本轮融资由Diffusion和Lightspeed联合领投。自2022年成立以来，Harvey累计融资总额已超过15亿美元。参与本轮投资的其他机构包括Sequoia、Kleiner Perkins、a16z、Coatue、Conviction、Elad Gil、Evantic、GIC、Goldman Sachs Alternatives、Whale Rock、WndrCo、Sapphire及Verified Capital。公司年度经常性收入已突破4亿美元，服务客户超过3000家，其中包括前100大律所中的80%、财富500强企业中的20%以及财富10强企业中的半数。本轮融资是在推出其首个后训练开放权重模型Tenet以及发布法律智能体基准Harvey LAB之后进行的。本轮融资所得资金将投入“人力和算力这两项最重要的资源”。公司正在产品、工程、研究和市场推广等岗位积极招聘，以拓展新垂直领域，并为合同、诉讼、交易和合规构建更专业的产品。在算力方面，公司将大力投资于其技术框架和自有模型训练。Tenet的发布只是一个开始，“本轮融资使我们能够扩大后续模型代际所需的算力和数据规模”。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal AI company Harvey said today that it has raised another $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed.

By my calculations, that puts the total amount Harvey has raised since its 2022 launch at north of $1.5 billion.

Other investors participating in this round were Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, a16z, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Whale Rock, WndrCo, Sapphire and Verified Capital.

On LinkedIn, cofounder Winston Weinberg wrote that the company has now crossed $400 million in annual recurring revenue and serves more than 3,000 customers, including 80% of the top 100 law firms, 20% of the Fortune 500, and half of the Fortune 10.

The company noted that the raise follows the introduction of Tenet, its first post-trained open-weight model, and the launch of Harvey LAB, the Legal Agent Benchmark. 

Weinberg said the capital from this round is being invested “into our two most important resources: people and compute.”

He said that the company is hiring aggressively across product, engineering, research, and go-to-market roles as it expands into new verticals and builds more specialized products for contracting, litigation, deals and compliance.

With regard to compute, he said that the company will be investing heavily in both its harness and its own model training.

He said the launch of Tenet was just the start, “and this round lets us scale the compute and data behind the generations that follow.”

news.titleEn: Intapp launches a network to help law firms recover revenue lost between pricing and collections
news.titleZh: Intapp推出网络，帮助律所挽回定价与收款之间流失的收入
news.summaryZh: Intapp（NASDAQ: INTA）在ILTACON 2026上宣布推出Intapp Profitability Network，这是一个经认证的合作伙伴生态系统，连接律所从定价、人员配置、工时记录、预账单到收款的全流程。该网络基于Intapp Time with Celeste和Intapp Billstream构建，首批六家创始合作伙伴为Capacity、Engage AI Solutions、Legora、Lexpipe、Oddr和Zebraworks。Intapp将此类AI称为“Firm AI”，即面向律所自身业务而非个人或工作成果的AI。该网络旨在解决多数律所各阶段系统与团队割裂、数据洞察在交接中丢失、发现利润流失时为时已晚的问题，使律所首次将盈利能力视为从首次定价决策到最终收款的不间断链条。每个集成都经过Intapp产品与研发团队对安全性、API兼容性和功能质量的认证，涉及工时记录或预账单的工作流由Intapp Time with Celeste治理执行，合作伙伴负责提议、分析和推荐，Intapp负责治理、存储并作为记录平台。Celeste作为专家AI协作者，运行跨阶段代理剧本，可在交付期间发现预算偏差、标记定价差异，并将实现结果与定价决策关联。创始合作伙伴各自提供认证专长：Capacity利用Intapp Time with Celeste的利用率和计费表现数据进行人员与事项匹配；Engage AI Solutions连接Intapp Intake and Terms确保业务约定书准确；Legora集成Intapp Walls和Intapp Time，使AI工作流遵守保密和道德墙边界并结构化记录工时；Lexpipe连接Intapp Time with Celeste，将历史事项成本数据转化为定价模型和固定费用基线；Oddr从Intapp Billstream获取完整账单背景以支持收款；Zebraworks连接工时、账单和收款，提供端到端实现分析。该网络现已可用，创始合作伙伴集成将在秋季通过Intapp认证计划后全面上市。
news.bodyHtml:
The Intapp Profitability Network connects Intapp Time with Celeste with certified products from Capacity, Engage AI Solutions, Legora, Lexpipe, Oddr, and Zebraworks, showing firm leaders where margin is made and lost across every matter

PALO ALTO, Calif. — September 9, 2026 — Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA), the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries, today announced the Intapp Profitability Network, a certified partner ecosystem that connects every stage of how a law firm earns and collects on a matter — from pricing and staffing through time capture, prebilling, and collections. Introduced at ILTACON 2026, the network launches with six founding partners: Capacity, Engage AI Solutions, Legora, Lexpipe, Oddr, and Zebraworks.

AI is now part of every firm’s strategy. The next question is what that means for firm profitability. The answer runs through the matter — from the moment a firm prices an engagement to the last dollar collected. At every stage of the lifecycle — pricing, staffing, time capture, prebilling, invoicing, collections — profitability can improve or erode.

But most firms manage each stage in separate systems with separate teams, with no shared view of what’s happening across the chain. Data clarity and insights are lost at every handoff. By the time a firm can see where margin leaked, it’s too late to recover it. The Intapp Profitability Network changes that.

Intapp calls this Firm AI — the category of AI aimed not at the individual or the work product, but at the business of the firm itself. Horizontal assistants speed up everyday tasks. Practice AI helps produce the work product. Firm AI runs the business behind both. Profitability is where that difference shows up on the income statement.

The network connects the full chain. For the first time, firms can see profitability as an unbroken chain, from the first pricing decision to the final dollar collected. Built on Intapp Time with Celeste and Intapp Billstream, the network links specialist partner capabilities into one governed system, not a collection of disconnected point tools that each see only part of the picture.

  • The network runs on the firm’s own economics. Every firm can buy a pricing tool. What sets a firm apart is what its own matters actually cost to deliver — by phase, timekeeper, matter type, and AI tool usage. As clients begin asking how technology was applied to their work, that transparency becomes both a trust requirement and a pricing input. Intapp Time with Celeste captures that history, and the Profitability Network puts it to work in scoping, staffing, and repricing decisions.
  • Every integration is certified. Intapp’s product and R&D teams review each network integration for security, API compatibility, and functional quality before it ships, with ongoing review as APIs evolve. For any workflow that touches timekeeping or prebilling, governed execution routes through Intapp Time with Celeste. Partners propose, analyze, and recommend, while Intapp governs, stores, and remains the platform of record.
  • Intapp Celeste orchestrates it. Celeste, an expert AI coworker, runs agentic playbooks that span chain stages — surfacing budget drift during delivery before it becomes an unrecoverable write-down, flagging pricing variance, and connecting realization outcomes back to the pricing decisions that shaped them.

Founding network partners

The founding partners bring certified expertise to the stages of the chain that sit beyond Intapp’s core platform. 

  • Capacity
    Resourcing and staffing optimization
    In a value-pricing model, staffing determines margin. The right timekeeper on the right matter is the difference between a profitable fixed fee and an underwater one. Capacity matches people to matters using utilization and billing performance data from Intapp Time with Celeste — not availability alone.
  • Engage AI Solutions
    Engagement letter accuracy from scoping through signature
    Engage AI Solutions connects to Intapp Intake and Terms so engagement letters reflect what was actually scoped and negotiated. Intake and Terms also natively integrate with DocuSign, giving risk professionals visibility and control throughout execution — not just at signature.
  • Legora
    Governed AI legal workflows with structured time capture
    Legora integrates Intapp Walls so AI workflows respect confidentiality and ethical wall boundaries. It also connects to Intapp Time, so any work lawyers do in Legora becomes a structured time entry rather than unbilled effort.
  • Lexpipe
    Pricing intelligence and matter scoping analytics
    Lexpipe connects to Intapp Time with Celeste, turning historical matter cost data into pricing models and fixed-fee baselines. Firms can scope new engagements against what comparable matters actually cost to deliver.
  • Oddr
    Collections with full billing context from Intapp Billstream
    Milestone fees, holdbacks, and success components create collections complexity that AR data alone can’t navigate. Oddr gives collections teams the context to understand why an invoice is disputed or delayed.
  • Zebraworks
    End-to-end realization analytics
    Zebraworks connects worked hours through billing to cash collected across every fee arrangement type. It answers the question managing partners increasingly ask: Are our value-priced matters actually more profitable than our hourly ones, and which clients, matter types, and fee structures should we price differently next time?

Availability

The Intapp Profitability Network is available now. Founding partner integrations will reach general availability throughout the fall, following completion of the Intapp certification program. Firms interested in connecting Intapp Time with Celeste and Billstream to network partners can contact their Intapp account team or visit intapp.com/partners/profitability-network/.

Supporting quote

Ken Houseman, Vice President and General Manager, Intapp Time

“Firm profitability has always been a chain problem, not a billing problem. Intapp Time with Celeste and Billstream govern the core of that chain; the network extends it, connecting the specialist capabilities that complete each stage in one system firms can rely on. The shift toward value pricing isn’t a trend firms can watch from a distance and address later — it’s a structural change driven by AI on both sides of the client relationship. The firms that compete on value in the next decade are the ones building their data infrastructure now.”

By applying Firm AI to core processes and data, Intapp helps partners, dealmakers, and advisors drive firm growth, manage compliance, and improve profitability. news.titleEn: Harvey Raises $550m at $15.5bn Val, Buys Guardrails AI
news.titleZh: Harvey以155亿美元估值融资5.5亿美元，收购Guardrails AI
news.summaryZh:
Harvey宣布完成5.5亿美元融资，估值达155亿美元，由Diffusion和Lightspeed Venture Partners联合领投。该公司同时收购了总部位于旧金山的AI安全平台Guardrails AI，后者专注于智能体的AI安全。Guardrails是AI可靠性与模拟基础设施领域的先驱，创建了首个开源AI护栏，帮助团队发现智能体偏离预期行为之处并实时管理智能体风险。Guardrails联合创始人Shreya Rajpal和Zayd Simjee及其团队将加入Harvey的产品与工程组织。这是Harvey在2026年的第四次收购。

本轮融资紧随Harvey推出首个后训练开放权重模型以及Harvey LAB法律智能体基准之后，将加速Harvey帮助律师事务所、内部法务团队和专业服务公司大规模构建并拥有自身智能能力的努力。现有投资者Sequoia、Kleiner Perkins、a16z、Coatue、Conviction、Elad Gil、Evantic、GIC、Goldman Sachs Alternatives、Verified Capital和WNDR参投，新投资者包括Diffusion、Lightspeed、Sapphire Ventures和Whale Rock。企业利用AI加速竞争优势的机遇前所未有，Harvey希望成为法律团队在全球的合作伙伴，并计划招聘和发展业内最佳团队，支持客户度过下一波AI转型。目前80%的Am Law 100律师事务所使用Harvey，众多全球领先的内部法务团队也在使用，包括财富10强中的五家。
news.bodyHtml:
Harvey has announced a $550m funding round at a $15.5B valuation, co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners. It has also bought San Francisco-based Guardrails AI, an AI security platform for agents.

Guardrails is a pioneer of AI reliability and simulation infrastructure, they said. They created the first open-source AI guardrails that help teams find where their agents stray from intended behaviour and manage agent risk in real time. Guardrails’ co-founders, Shreya Rajpal and Zayd Simjee, and their team will join Harvey’s product and engineering organization. This marks Harvey’s fourth acquisition of 2026.

The latest raise follows the introduction of Harvey’s first post-trained open-weight model and the launch of Harvey LAB, the Legal Agent Benchmark. It will accelerate Harvey’s efforts to help law firms, in-house legal teams, and professional services firms build and own their intelligence at scale, they said.

Existing investors Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, a16z, Coatue, Conviction, Elad Gil, Evantic, GIC, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Verified Capital, and WNDR participated in the round. New investors include Diffusion, Lightspeed, Sapphire Ventures, and Whale Rock.

Harvey co-founders Winston Weinberg and Gabe Pereyra said together: ‘The opportunity for companies to accelerate their competitive advantage with AI has never been higher. Harvey wants to be the global partner legal teams turn to for this work, and we plan to hire and develop the best team in the space to support our clients through the next wave of AI transformation.’

They added that 80% of Am Law 100 law firms now use Harvey alongside many of the world’s leading in-house legal teams, including five of the Fortune 10.

Congrats to the Harvey team.

More AL comment soon.—

Legal Innovators New York – Nov 17 and 18

See you at Legal Innovators New York – Nov 17 and 18 – join us at the intersection of legal AI and the business of law in New York for the most important legal innovation event of the year! Day One: law firms, Day Two: inhouse. Top speakers from across the legal AI world, leading law firms, and major companies. All for one purpose: to describe and explore the frontier of legal technology. See you there!

news.titleEn: ILTACON 2026: Highlights From The Event
news.titleZh: ILTACON 2026：活动亮点回顾
news.summaryZh: 上周，作者在盖洛德酒店参加了ILTACON，该会议吸引了5700名参会者，创下历史最大规模，所有房间售罄。本周的关键词是“上下文”：NetDocuments推出了Legal Context Graph，iManage围绕Context Fabric重建了平台，Harvey则不再谈论提示词，而是谈论事项、记忆和偏好。这些变化表明，AI的卖点已从“更智能的模型”转向“真正了解律所的模型”。然而，许多中型律所尚无法接受这一理念，因为这要求数据足够干净和结构化。技术部分容易，数据整理才是难点。治理方面，Intapp产品团队指出，随着智能体开始执行实际工作，治理难度会增加。参会者反映，律所并未看到预期的效率提升，因为仍需人工核查AI工作。首席产品官Triona Buckley将此称为“验证税”，这正在削弱律所最初申请预算时的投资回报率论证。智能体AI无处不在，MCP协议在供应商对话中频繁出现，iManage用它来在Thomson Reuters CoCounsel中呈现内容，NetDocuments则保持工具中立。智能体层的好坏取决于底层基础。购买工具本身并非转型，真正的转型在于前后的工作。律所购买AI工具的速度快于重新设计工作流程的速度，这导致价值流失。Actionstep Intelligence的开发注重在用户熟悉的平台内引入AI，以减少变革阻力。
news.bodyHtml:
It was a little over a week ago that I was at the Gaylord watching 5,700 people try to find their way through that hotel again. It never gets easier no matter how many years you’ve been going. It set the record as the biggest ILTACON yet, selling out every room. Some booths were so big they had their own zip codes.

Now that I am back at my desk and have had time to reflect, here’s what I actually took away from it.

Context is the new pitch

The word of the week was context. NetDocuments has Legal Context Graph. iManage rebuilt its whole platform around Context Fabric. Harvey has stopped talking about prompts and started talking about matters, memory, and preferences. The pitch has changed. The conversation isn’t “here’s a smarter model” anymore, it’s “here’s a model that actually knows your firm.”

This message resonates. It’s also one most mid-market firms aren’t in a position to accept yet, because it assumes your data is clean and structured enough to feed it.

I heard more than one CIO say the technology part is easy! Getting the data right is the hard part. I’ve been saying some version of that for quite some time now. It’s nice to hear it from those down in the trenches day after day.

Governance and the verification tax

Governance had a different tone this year, too. Intapp’s product team said that governance gets harder, not easier, as agents start doing real work instead of just answering questions. That tracks, because the more autonomy you hand a tool, the more you need to know what it’s doing on your behalf. The most interesting insights all week came from attendees. Firms aren’t seeing the efficiency gains they expected from AI, because someone still has to check the work. Triona Buckley, our Chief Product Officer, calls it the verification tax. It’s real, and it’s wrecking the ROI case a lot of firms used to get budget approved for this tech in the first place. You can’t fix governance by buying a better tool. You fix it by knowing what the agent touched, who reviewed it, and whether it correctly actioned on ten tasks, or just moved the work around for someone to clean up later

Agents are only as good as what’s underneath them

Agentic AI was everywhere, too.  All of it sounds great in a demo.

MCP came up in many vendor conversation I had, usually described as the thing that finally lets these tools talk to each other instead of living in their own silos. iManage is using it to surface content inside Thomson Reuters CoCounsel. NetDocuments is staying tool-agnostic on purpose so firms aren’t locked into one AI vendor’s roadmap.

My thoughts?  The agent layer is only as good as what’s underneath it. An agent that can act on your behalf is a bigger deal than a chatbot that answers questions, and it needs the bigger foundation under it to be trustworthy.

Buying the tool isn’t the transformation

The reality is a firm can purchase every tool on the exhibit floor and still not change how it does the work. What I kept hearing, in sessions and in hallway conversations, was firms deploying AI the way they’d deploy a new practice management or billing system, without asking what problem it’s trying to solve or who’s supposed to change their process because of it. Buying the tool isn’t the transformation, it’s all the work that comes before and after.

Once again there were discussions about moving off the billable hour. You can’t have a serious value-pricing conversation if you don’t have the operational visibility to know what work costs. Change management remains the hard part and a big part of the transformation story. Here’s the active version:

Firms are purchasing AI tools faster than they’re redesigning workflows or deciding where humans need to stay in the loop, which is where they’re losing a lot of the promised value. While we were developing Actionstep Intelligence we were very deliberate to bring AI to our customers within a platform they already know, use and trust. This helps to reduce friction around change since the users don’t have to change the way the work or learn a new tool. 

Is bigger better?

The parties were bigger and the booths looked like small buildings. There was a lot of money spent on being seen this year. I hope there is budget left to make technology that delivers results! I guess we’ll find out next year. See you back in Nashville next Summer.

research.titleEn: GANDR: Claim Auditing for Verifiable Legal Answer Generation
research.titleZh: GANDR：面向可验证法律答案生成的声明审计
research.abstractEn: In high-stakes domains such as legal practice, a language-model answer is only useful to the extent that a reader can verify each claim against the source the system cites. Current grounded-generation pipelines score the answer as a whole, so a correct conclusion can rest on fabricated or loosely matched citations and still score well. Closing this gap requires both a system built for per-claim verification and an evaluation that measures it. We introduce GANDR (Grounded ANswer DRafter), a two-agent system in which a Drafter writes an answer in a structured legal-reasoning format and a separate Critic, with the same view as a human verifier, audits each claim against its cited source and emits a per-claim audit trace on every round. We pair it with a strict correctness criterion requiring every citation to resolve to a passage the retriever returned. On a 185-item legal benchmark where all six systems share one backbone, one retrieval surface, and one citation instruction, GANDR ranks first on every primary metric, reaching 70.8% strict accuracy and leading the strongest baseline by 11.3 points (p<0.01). Reverting the protocol-anchored commit rule lowers strict accuracy by 22.7 points, and the strict lead stays positive on three further backbones, at +3.2 to +6.5 points. This lead traces to the Drafter configuration and the protocol-anchored commit, not to rewriting. Against two law-trained annotators the audit flags under-supported claims at F1 0.84 as a binary detector, while its four-way verdict labels agree only weakly and are advisory. Code is available upon request.
research.abstractZh: 在法律实践等高风险领域，语言模型给出的答案只有在读者能够对照系统引用的来源核实每一项声明时才有用。当前基于依据的生成流程对整个答案进行评分，因此一个正确的结论可能建立在捏造或松散匹配的引用之上，却仍能获得高分。要弥合这一差距，既需要一个为逐项声明验证而构建的系统，也需要一种能够衡量它的评估方法。我们提出 GANDR（Grounded ANswer DRafter，基于依据的答案起草器），这是一个双智能体系统：起草器以结构化法律推理格式撰写答案，而一个独立的批评者——与人类验证者拥有相同视角——对照所引来源审计每一项声明，并在每一轮输出逐项声明的审计轨迹。我们为其配以严格正确性标准，要求每一条引用都必须解析到检索器返回的段落。在一个包含 185 个条目的法律基准上，所有六个系统共享同一骨干模型、同一检索面和同一引用指令，GANDR 在每一项主要指标上均排名第一，达到 70.8% 的严格准确率，并以 11.3 个百分点的优势领先最强基线（p<0.01）。将协议锚定的提交规则回退会使严格准确率下降 22.7 个百分点，而严格准确率的领先优势在另外三个骨干模型上仍保持为正，为 +3.2 至 +6.5 个百分点。这一领先优势源于起草器配置和协议锚定的提交，而非改写。对照两位受过法律训练的标注者，该审计作为二元检测器以 F1 0.84 标记出支持不足的声明，而其四类判定标签仅呈现弱一致性，且仅供参考。代码可应请求提供。

research.titleEn: LexAgentHallu: A Hierarchical Benchmark for Profiling Hallucinations in Legal Agents
research.titleZh: LexAgentHallu：面向法律智能体幻觉画像的分层基准
research.abstractEn: As large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-augmented legal agents, they introduce agentic hallucinations where tool-call and reasoning errors cascade into fabricated holdings and miscited authority. However, existing legal benchmarks evaluate only single-turn QA with outcome-level metrics, while agentic hallucination benchmarks lack legal-specific diagnostic capability. Neither answers to what extent and how a legal agent hallucinates along its trajectory. To address these limitations, we introduce LexAgentHallu, a legal agentic hallucination benchmark designed to evaluate to what extent and how legal agents fail along multi-step trajectories. Built through a four-stage expert-in-the-loop pipeline, LexAgentHallu contains 3414 instances across 17 legal categories and 6 task types. Each instance is annotated under a dual-layer hallucination taxonomy of 7 high-level categories and 27 fine-grained subclasses, covering both substantive errors and agent-procedural failures. We further design fine-grained metrics that quantify to what extent and localize how each failure occurs along an agent's execution path. Our evaluation across 18 proprietary and open-source agents uncovers a Right-Answer-Wrong-Reason effect and reveals that hallucination subclasses cluster rather than scatter, forming distinct agentic framework, legal task, and category profiles. These findings, invisible to outcome-level evaluation, validate the diagnostic power of LexAgentHallu for evaluating agentic hallucination in law.
research.abstractZh: 随着大语言模型日益被部署为工具增强的法律智能体，它们引入了智能体幻觉，即工具调用和推理错误级联为捏造的裁判要旨和错误引用的权威依据。然而，现有的法律基准仅使用结果层面的指标评估单轮问答，而智能体幻觉基准缺乏法律特定的诊断能力。两者都无法回答法律智能体在其轨迹上以何种程度以及如何产生幻觉。为解决这些局限，我们提出了LexAgentHallu，一个法律智能体幻觉基准，旨在评估法律智能体在多步轨迹上以何种程度以及如何失败。通过四阶段专家在环流程构建，LexAgentHallu包含跨17个法律类别和6种任务类型的3414个实例。每个实例都按照包含7个高层类别和27个细粒度子类的双层幻觉分类法进行标注，涵盖实质性错误和智能体程序性失败。我们进一步设计了细粒度指标，以量化失败程度并定位智能体执行路径上每次失败的发生方式。我们对18个专有和开源智能体的评估揭示了“答案正确但推理错误”效应，并发现幻觉子类呈聚集而非分散分布，形成不同的智能体框架、法律任务和类别画像。这些在结果层面评估中不可见的发现，验证了LexAgentHallu在评估法律领域智能体幻觉方面的诊断能力。

policy.summaryZh: 2024年起，国产人工智能大模型井喷式发展，“AI幻觉”“AI换脸”“AI语音克隆”等纠纷不断涌现。最高法于2025年成立《意见》起草组，经调研并听取地方法院、行业代表、专家学者及相关部门意见后形成送审稿，审判委员会逐条审阅并深入研究讨论，最终制定《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》，于9月7日正式施行，是第一部较为全面的关于涉人工智能纠纷案件法律适用的司法文件。《意见》明确裁判规则、强化权益保障、促进产业发展，依法规制“AI换脸拟声”“网络开盒”、算法歧视、“AI幻觉”“AI伪造证据”、AI生成内容侵犯知识产权等滥用人工智能侵害公民人格尊严、私人生活安宁、财产安全等合法权益的行为。第八条明确依法适用人格权侵害禁令制度；起草组按照审委会要求，在送审稿第四条基础上增加了针对利用人工智能技术处理死者姓名、肖像等侵害死者人格利益行为的相关内容。在责任认定方面，第三条规定法律没有明确规定适用无过错责任或者过错推定责任时，人民法院应依照过错责任原则认定侵权责任；第七条规定审慎认定生成式人工智能服务提供者的侵权责任；第六条规定认定人工智能训练是否侵害个人信息权益的标准及“合理范围”的考量因素。对显而易见的侵权情形，不排除适用民法典第一千一百九十七条认定生产者、服务提供者侵权责任。
policy.bodyText:
2024年起，国产人工智能大模型井喷式发展，以前所未有的速度渗透进人们的工作和生活。与此同时，“AI幻觉”“AI换脸”“AI语音克隆”等带来的纠纷不断涌现。这些强大的工具，正在挑战人们的合法权益。
技术是否“无责”？如何让使用者敢使用，让创新者愿创新？
近日，《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》（以下简称《意见》）正式发布，明确裁判规则、强化权益保障、促进产业发展。在此之前，最高法审判委员会围绕《意见》送审稿召开会议，逐条逐字审阅文本，就司法审判实践和涉人工智能纠纷案件审理的难点堵点深入研究、充分讨论。
《意见》的制定与出台遵循着怎样的思路？我国最高审判机关的最高审判组织对人工智能飞速发展过程中出现的法律问题有着怎样的观点，作出了怎样的回应？
拒绝“野蛮生长”
——供给裁判规则，引领行为规范
数据显示，2025年我国人工智能核心产业规模已突破1.2万亿元，预计到“十五五”末，相关产业规模将突破10万亿元。
高歌猛进的人工智能技术究竟“路在何方”？
“人工智能技术发展越是一日千里，向上向善、造福人类的方向越要正确锚定，监管治理的尺度越要精准把握，防范失控的措施越要及时完善。”习近平总书记的论述高屋建瓴。
每一次科技革命都离不开规范化引领、法治化保障。党中央高度重视人工智能健康发展，习近平总书记在不同场合多次强调要确保人工智能安全、可靠、可控。“十五五”规划纲要则明确，要“完善人工智能领域法律法规、政策制度、应用规范、伦理准则”。
在这样的背景下，最高法于2025年即成立《意见》起草组，在对涉人工智能政策文件和法律法规深入研究的基础上，围绕司法实践中涉人工智能重点难点问题开展系统、深入调研，逐一梳理法答网涉人工智能高频咨询问题、人民法院案例库有关入库案例裁判规则，追踪分析域外涉人工智能立法司法实践，广泛、充分听取地方法院、行业代表、专家学者以及相关政府部门的意见，经过反复修改完善后，形成《意见》送审稿。
审委会对《意见》送审稿总体认可，认为《意见》送审稿贯彻落实以习近平同志为核心的党中央关于加快高水平科技自立自强，引领发展新质生产力重大决策部署，严格遵循法律规定，坚持问题导向，立足审判实践，“对于进一步明确裁判规则、强化当事人权益保障、促进行业健康发展、服务保障创新驱动发展重大战略实施，具有积极意义”。
针对当前“AI换脸拟声”、“网络开盒”、算法歧视、“AI幻觉”、“AI伪造证据”、AI生成内容侵犯知识产权等滥用人工智能技术侵害公民人格尊严、私人生活安宁、财产安全等合法权益的行为，《意见》依法予以规制。
比如，当前利用人工智能技术“换脸”“偷声”等侵害人格权益的行为多发，侵权手段多样、隐蔽，而当事人却面临举证难、投诉渠道缺失、诉讼成本高等维权难题。对此，《意见》在第八条专门明确“依法适用人格权侵害禁令制度”，规定了这一制度在人工智能领域的细化适用，以解决传统事后诉讼难以及时高效维护当事人合法权益的问题。
围绕“AI复活逝者”这一热议话题，《意见》起草组则按照审委会要求，在送审稿第四条基础上增加了针对利用人工智能技术处理死者姓名、肖像等侵害死者人格利益行为的相关内容，使《意见》对人格权益保护的范围更加全面。
“《意见》制定出来就是要解决问题的。”有审委会委员直言。
此外，在供给裁判规则的同时，《意见》也注重行为规范引领，通过厘清各方主体的权利、义务和责任，引导和推动市场主体加强风险内控与规范管理，防范化解人工智能技术误用、滥用带来的风险。
值得注意的是，《意见》起草组考虑到人工智能仍然处在发展初期，司法实践不足，因此对于人工智能生成内容的可版权性、训练数据的合理使用等暂时看不清、拿不准，难以形成共识的问题作了留白处理。
“留白处理”不等于“无法可依”。会上，《意见》起草组汇报时表示，关于“留白处理”的问题，预备先以参考案例、法答网问答等形式加强对下指导，进一步积累经验，待条件成熟时再通过适当方式作出明确规定。审委会对这一做法予以了充分肯定。
《意见》第二十二条也明确了加强审判监督指导的路径，其中一个要求就是“充分运用人民法院案例库，加强案例指导工作，促推法律适用统一和人工智能治理规则的完善”。
技术不是“免责牌”
——人工智能提供者需承担更多社会责任
“司法人员要考虑保护广大使用者的合法权益，规范行业发展，遏制人工智能开发者、提供者等的获利冲动，促使他们对产品、服务的安全性承担更多社会责任。”
关于如何平衡保护当事人合法权益与人工智能行业发展，审委会态度十分明确。
比如，人工智能大模型训练离不开大规模训练数据，其中不可避免地涉及个人信息。如何处理由此产生的纠纷？尽管我国个人信息保护法对处理个人信息作出了约束，但条文所强调的“合理的范围”一直是司法实践中的难点，如何在司法实践中把握好这一要求？
“《意见》作为规范性文件，要为司法实践提供更加清晰的操作规则，引导人工智能企业和法院在对待公民个人信息时更加谨慎负责。”有审委会委员指出。
《意见》第六条不仅规定了人民法院认定人工智能训练是否侵害个人信息权益的标准，也对法院认定“合理范围”作出了指引，考量因素包括处理个人信息的目的与模型功能的必要性和适当性、所涉个人信息的类型、敏感程度及对个人权益的潜在影响、个人公开信息时的场景及可合理预期的使用范围等。
随着人工智能越来越多地深入民众工作和生活，“AI幻觉”侵权以及利用生成式人工智能侵权早已不再是冷门话题。无论是判决生成式人工智能服务提供者不担责的全国首例“AI幻觉”侵权案，还是判决担责的“AI幻觉”编造罪名案，都曾引起社会广泛关注和讨论。
技术有责还是无责？人工智能开发者、产品和服务提供者在什么情况下担责？怎样才能既依法保护使用者合法权益又不影响创新者的积极性？
《意见》起草组认为，人工智能应用场景广泛、案件类型多样，对不同应用场景下的人工智能侵权应依照法律规定使用不同归责原则，“这是贯彻实施民法典规定的必然要求”。而另一方面，生成式人工智能侵权与传统网络侵权在主体、价值、情境等本质特征上具有高度相似性，人工智能服务提供者的责任具备类推适用“避风港原则”（网络服务提供者在接获权利人发出的有效通知后应当采取必要措施）的正当性、合理性基础。
基于这样的考量，《意见》不仅通过第三条明确在法律没有明确规定适用无过错责任或者过错推定责任的时候，人民法院应当依照过错责任原则认定行为人是否承担侵权责任，并在第七条规定“审慎认定生成式人工智能服务提供者的侵权责任”。
行业发展初期，出于鼓励新技术发展的目的，固然需要为人工智能生产者、服务提供者卸去不必要的枷锁，但是，他们是否能因此“高枕无忧”？当他们对显而易见的侵权可能性视而不见的时候，人民法院又当如何作出判断？
“企业不能只获利不担责。”审委会对此态度明确，“在司法实践中，如果出现相关情形，人民法院将不排除适用民法典第一千一百九十七条，认定人工智能生产者、服务提供者侵权责任。”
根据民法典该条规定，网络服务提供者知道或者应当知道网络用户利用其网络服务侵害他人民事权益，未采取必要措施的，与该网络用户承担连带责任。该规定体现了“避风港原则”的例外——“红旗原则”，即当侵权事实像“红旗”一样显著时，网络服务提供者即使未收到权利人通知，也应采取删除或屏蔽措施，否则需承担连带责任。
尽管《意见》并未制定“红旗原则”相关的单独条文，但《意见》起草组成员专门围绕理解与适用《意见》撰文刊发，其中就这一问题作出回应，及时传递出最高审判机关维护人工智能健康发展的明确立场。
全面保护、筑牢底线
——强调依法惩治，完善程序规则
人工智能为生产生活带来高效与便利，也为违法犯罪提供了工具。
今年全国两会期间，最高法研究室主任周加海在接受媒体采访时表示，用AI技术炮制虚假信息、实施“AI换脸”等“深度伪造”行为日益增多，并逐渐被用于网络侮辱、诽谤等违法犯罪活动，引起了人民群众广泛关注。这类案件事实查明难、责任链条长、法律适用边界模糊，给司法带来极大挑战。
作为一部主要围绕民事纠纷展开的规则指引，《意见》也兼顾了对涉人工智能刑事案件的法律适用要求。《意见》送审稿在“基本原则”章节即开门见山亮明了“坚决依法严惩”的态度。
尽管如此，审委会仍在审议时专门强调，要更加旗帜鲜明地传递人民法院依法惩治利用人工智能实施犯罪活动的立场。
对此，修改后的《意见》专门增加了第二十条。根据该规定，行为人利用人工智能实施各类犯罪的，比如行为人激活辅助驾驶功能后利用私自安装的配件逃避辅助驾驶系统监测导致道路交通事故，构成犯罪的，将被依法追究刑事责任。
值得注意的是，《意见》一方面对于故意利用人工智能实施危害国家安全、侵犯公民权益、扰乱社会秩序等犯罪行为的，要求坚决依法严惩；另一方面对于在人工智能研发、应用中的创新性行为，则明确要依法审慎处理，恪守罪刑法定、罪责刑相适应原则。这也是人民法院在涉人工智能纠纷领域全面准确贯彻宽严相济刑事政策的体现。
程序正义是结果正义的前提和保障。针对《意见》送审稿关于涉人工智能案件程序规则的部分，审委会委员们讨论得十分细致，使《意见》更具可操作性。
比如，针对涉人工智能案件技术性、专业性强等特点，《意见》第十七条经修改完善后，增加了人民法院为查明事实“应当”履行的职责——应当依法加强诉讼引导和释明，引导当事人围绕争议事实及时全面地完成举证；对于涉及人工智能专业技术问题的，应当依法充分发挥人民陪审员、鉴定人、专家辅助人以及技术调查官的作用，辅助查明案件事实。
此外，《意见》还进一步整合了涉人工智能案件证据审查的相关内容，以使体系更加合理、完善。
9月7日，《意见》正式施行，作为第一部较为全面的关于涉人工智能纠纷案件法律适用的司法文件，其为人工智能开发者、提供者和使用者划清法治“红线”和底线，为技术探索和产业创新预留必要发展空间，从司法角度为行业从“野蛮生长”进一步向“有序繁荣”转变提供了助推力。
（ 记者 姜佩杉 ）

news.titleEn: Richmond Vona Opens Claims Across 8 Insurance Carriers with a 100% Success Rate Using Lexafide
news.titleZh: Richmond Vona借助Lexafide在8家保险公司成功开立索赔，成功率100%
news.summaryZh: 总部位于加利福尼亚州帕洛阿尔托的Lexafide公司，是一家专为律师事务所打造的AI语音代理平台。该公司于2026年9月8日宣布，其与纽约州布法罗的人身伤害律师事务所Richmond Vona, LLC合作部署的成果已对外公布。在过去一个月中，Lexafide的AI代理代表Richmond Vona在八家保险公司（包括State Farm、Progressive和GEICO）成功开立了11起新的机动车事故索赔，成功率达到100%，并正确完成了每家保险公司的受理流程，且在每个案例中都获得了索赔编号。此外，这些AI代理还充当Richmond Vona现有索赔案件的跟进者，记录了23项针对PIP账目和IME报告的跟进请求，并逐一追踪至解决。与Lexafide的合作展示了人身伤害业务中深思熟虑的自动化实践，即技术围绕团队实际工作方式构建。随着业务从索赔开立扩展到PIP和IME报告请求，他们看到了在机动车事故索赔全生命周期中提升效率的切实机会。Lexafide持续扩大其在原告方及人身伤害律师事务所中的影响力，其中索赔开立和跟进代理是新客户最常见的切入点。
news.bodyHtml:
The Buffalo-based personal injury firm is using Lexafide’s AI voice agents to open new motor vehicle accident claims and follow up on PIP and IME requests on existing cases

 

[Palo Alto, CA] — [9/8/2026] — Lexafide, an AI voice agent platform built for law firms, today announced results from its deployment with Richmond Vona, LLC, a personal injury firm based in Buffalo, New York, with offices across Western New York. Over the past month, Lexafide’s agents opened 11 new motor vehicle accident claims on Richmond Vona’s behalf across eight carriers — including State Farm, Progressive, and GEICO — with a 100% success rate, correctly navigating each carrier’s own intake process and securing a claim number in every case. The agents are also acting as chasers on Richmond Vona’s existing claims, logging 23 follow-up requests for PIP ledgers and IME reports and tracking each through to resolution.

“Our work with Lexafide shows what thoughtful automation can look like in a personal injury practice: technology built around the way our team actually works. As we continue to expand from claims establishment into PIP and IME report requests, we see a real opportunity to improve efficiency across the MVC claims lifecycle.” said Lizzie DePalma, Operations Lead. 

Lexafide continues to expand its footprint among plaintiff and personal injury firms, with claims-opening and chaser agents among the most common entry points for new clients.
news.bodyText:
The Buffalo-based personal injury firm is using Lexafide’s AI voice agents to open new motor vehicle accident claims and follow up on PIP and IME requests on existing cases

[Palo Alto, CA] — [9/8/2026] — Lexafide, an AI voice agent platform built for law firms, today announced results from its deployment with Richmond Vona, LLC, a personal injury firm based in Buffalo, New York, with offices across Western New York. Over the past month, Lexafide’s agents opened 11 new motor vehicle accident claims on Richmond Vona’s behalf across eight carriers — including State Farm, Progressive, and GEICO — with a 100% success rate, correctly navigating each carrier’s own intake process and securing a claim number in every case. The agents are also acting as chasers on Richmond Vona’s existing claims, logging 23 follow-up requests for PIP ledgers and IME reports and tracking each through to resolution.

“Our work with Lexafide shows what thoughtful automation can look like in a personal injury practice: technology built around the way our team actually works. As we continue to expand from claims establishment into PIP and IME report requests, we see a real opportunity to improve efficiency across the MVC claims lifecycle.” said Lizzie DePalma, Operations Lead.

news.titleZh: OpenAI GPT-6 Astra：法律界需要了解的内容及早期反应

news.bodyHtml:
OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Astra, its latest frontier model, promising a significant step forward in computer use and complex, multi-step professional work. For the legal sector, early reactions suggest that the important development may be less about Astra producing a better individual answer and more about its ability to stay on track, understand the intended outcome and execute a workflow with significantly less human prompting. One early user tells us: “With a bit of iteration I think output is already better than a senior associate and many partners.” One big question, though, is whether you need it.

What’s available

Advertisement

Astra was launched on 3 September and OpenAI describes it as its “most intelligent and aligned model” to date. The model is initially being rolled out to a limited number of organisations, with OpenAI saying that access will expand to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure and AWS Bedrock. Astra usage is included within existing ChatGPT subscription allowances, with additional credits available to purchase. Enterprise administrators have to enable Astra, with access off by default at launch. 

From answering questions to completing work 

Advertisement

One of the potentially important distinctions for legal is Astra’s ability to maintain its understanding of the objective throughout a complex task. 

OpenAI says previous models could sometimes treat steering instructions as a new goal and lose sight of earlier requirements. Astra is designed to incorporate new instructions and change direction without losing the broader task. It is also designed to use context to fill routine gaps while asking questions where missing information could materially affect the outcome. 

That tallies with the initial experience of legal technology adviser Natalie Foster (pictured above) of consultancy Legally Fond, founder of digital law firm Inspire Legal Group. 

Foster told Legal IT Insider: “It’s vastly different from 5.6 in my view. The things that stood out immediately are there seems to be a much stronger route to an outcome rather than having to constantly replenish prompts.” 

Foster tested Astra on a complex property transaction example involving multiple documents and issues including mines and mineral rights. 

“I gave it a complex example and it followed it throughout,” she said.  

The significant difference for Foster is that, arguably, there is less margin for human error via incorrect prompts. It leads to the prospect, Foster says, of firms being able to draft a prompt policy that is signed off by your COLP and with less margin for deviation. 

She also observed a change in how Astra deals with gaps in information. Previous models could review documents and identify what’s missing, but Astra goes further. “With Astra already we’re seeing if you ask it to review a document and tell it what is missing, it will give you unprompted documents to plug the gap and suggest ways to change relevant systems so you can plug gaps going forward. 

“There’s an evolution where it is supporting you improving future tasks, not just isolated tasks.” 

OpenAI’s own early legal testing supports the suggestion that this is where the advance may lie. Niko Grupen, head of applied research at Harvey, said Astra represented “a significant quality improvement” over GPT-5.6 Sol on complex legal tasks, including distinguishing documents from established records, identifying unsupported assumptions and turning gaps into drafting positions. 

The junior lawyer question gets more urgent 

The advance also raises a familiar but increasingly pressing question about how junior lawyers learn. 

Foster said: “We’re now moving to the level of agentic AI that removes junior training. We knew it was going to happen.” 

The twists and turns of legal matters have traditionally helped juniors “cut their teeth on files”, she observed. Her concern is that the technology is progressing more quickly than anticipated towards a model where the human brain is no longer being trained through the process of checking and balancing work. 

That question becomes more pertinent if early assessments of Astra’s legal output prove representative. 

Greater autonomy means greater governance 

There is another side to increased agency: how much authority should firms actually give these systems? 

OpenAI has made alignment a central part of the Astra launch. In one evaluation, conducted without production safeguards, GPT-5.6 Sol went beyond its authorised target 48% of the time when confronted with a difficult or impossible task. Astra did so in 0% of cases. OpenAI says this demonstrates improved understanding of user intent and the ability to delegate tasks with greater confidence in the model’s judgement. 

Foster sees delegated authority becoming a critical governance issue as models increasingly interact with applications and organisational systems. 

“Whatever you’re going to do, you’re going to have to do the authority and audit piece,” she said. 

OpenAI has itself introduced additional safety monitoring around Astra. Where monitoring detects a potential case in which an agent may have incorrectly interpreted instructions, a conversation can be paused or stopped so that the user can review what is happening before deciding whether it should proceed. 

The frontier model race 

Matthew Letts, founder of Codified Strategy and a restructuring lawyer, raises a different question: whether firms should automatically assume that every workload needs the latest frontier model, cautioning against becoming distracted by the “one-upmanship” of frontier AI. He also sounds a warning around assessing your supply chain risk, given the amount of investment in the space. 

While lawyers might assume they need the latest models, Letts says that “90% of work can be done on models that are run locally. You don’t need Fable or Astra to do what they are doing.” 

Localisation potentially gives organisations greater control over both their infrastructure and their costs. That matters as legal AI vendors increasingly experiment with consumption-based pricing and as firms become dependent on a relatively small number of underlying model providers. 

Letts compares this to concentration risk in a supply chain, observing: “If you have a vendor in your supply chain that goes bust, how long to stand up another?” He draws a parallel with the collapse of Carillion, which created a domino effect among companies dependent on it. 

So what should legal take away? 

It is extremely early days for GPT-6 Astra, and benchmark results and enthusiastic first impressions need to be distinguished from sustained performance on live legal matters. 

But the initial legal feedback points to a potentially important shift. The question is becoming less whether a general-purpose model can produce a convincing legal answer and more whether it can understand the intended outcome, remain oriented over a long task, identify what needs doing next and increasingly carry out that work itself. 

That significantly changes both the risk and the productivity equation.

The Empty Chair: Why Practicing Attorneys Need to Be in the Room Where Legal Technology Is Built | Reflections from a Transactional Attorney at ILTACON 2026

By

Danial Manzoor

posted

5 days ago

Like

The first thing you notice at ILTACON is the energy. Thousands of legal technology professionals, IT leaders, knowledge management specialists, innovation officers, and vendor partners filling session halls and demo floors with an urgency that is unmistakable. These are people who have spent years building the infrastructure that modern law firms run on, and in 2026, with AI reshaping every layer of that infrastructure, the stakes feel higher than ever. The work on display was extraordinary, agents that query document management systems in real time, no-code platforms that let non-developers build workflow automations in minutes, connector protocols that promise to unify the fragmented systems law firms have lived with for decades. Walking the floor, I felt like I was seeing the future of legal practice taking shape in real time.

And then came a moment that reframed everything.

During a panel on AI adoption featuring professionals from K&L Gates, Harvey, Stradley Ronon, and Morrison Foerster, Ryan Sammi, Harvey’s Head of Product Innovation and a former M&A lawyer paused the discussion and asked the audience a simple question: “Stand up if you are a full-time practicing attorney.” The room stayed seated. Sammi shared that out of more than one hundred people he had spoken with at the conference, he had found maybe exactly one full-time practicing attorney and even that person spent roughly twenty percent of their time on innovation work rather than client matters. I was one of the few people standing. In that moment, what had been a feeling became a data point. The preeminent conference on legal technology innovation and the people the tools are being built for were almost entirely absent from the conversation.

THE GAP

I want to be precise about what I am saying here, because it matters. This is not a criticism of ILTACON or the people who attend it. ILTACON was one of the most impressive professional events I have ever experienced. The knowledge management teams, IT professionals, innovation leaders, and vendor partners in that room are doing essential, difficult work. Without them, none of the tools I use every day on live transactions would exist. Their expertise is foundational, and I have enormous respect for what they do.

But the conference also revealed a structural gap in our industry that I believe we need to address. The panel described it as a “partnership model” the idea that successful AI adoption requires a partnership between two roles: the “influencer,” typically a senior attorney with deep domain knowledge, institutional voice, and commercial outcomes to drive, and the “translator,” the innovation or technology professional who executes on AI initiatives and bridges the gap between the technology and the practice. When the influencer half of that partnership is absent from the rooms where the tools are being demonstrated, debated, and shaped, the conversation is incomplete.

Tracy Meyer of K&L Gates offered a framework during the panel that has stayed with me. She described three levels of engagement: the “user,” who adopts AI for personal productivity; the “translator,” who shares what works with their practice group and helps colleagues adopt; and the “influencer,” who shapes firm strategy and gets pulled into client conversations about the firm’s capabilities. Her key insight: “No one promotes you to translator, you assume the role.” That resonated deeply. The path from user to influencer is not a career track. It is a choice.

The goal is not to say the room was wrong. The goal is to say the room would be even more powerful with more practitioners in it. I see my role as a connector between these worlds, a practicing attorney who can speak the language of both the deal and the technology, not as a critic of either side.

WHAT I SAW

The gap matters because the tools I saw at ILTACON are not theoretical. They are solving problems I encounter every week on live transactions. Let me ground this in specifics.

In one session, a presenter built a fully functional AI agent live on stage in approximately twenty minutes using Microsoft Copilot Studio. The agent walked an attorney through a structured client intake conversation, asked follow-up questions to fill information gaps, flagged risk levels based on the responses, and drafted a summary email with next steps directly into the attorney’s Outlook inbox. No code was required. The scenario it was built around will feel familiar to any transactional lawyer: an M&A senior associate who lost a prospective client because the intake process sat for two business days while the attorney was pulled into other matters. A competing firm got back to the client faster and won the work. That is not a hypothetical. It is a scenario I have lived, and it is exactly the kind of friction I am building agents to eliminate.

In another demonstration, an AI agent connected to iManage and a SharePoint-based experience database fielded a conversational query about prior deal history on a roughly six-hundred-million-dollar acquisition. The agent searched across unstructured data, term sheets, voice memos, fact sheets, internal briefings, and returned a comprehensive answer identifying prior similar deals, internal subject-matter experts, key negotiating issues, and risk factors. Work that would take an associate hours of searching and asking around was completed in minutes. Perhaps more importantly, the agent could write back to the experience database, logging the attorney’s own matter experience and insights for future colleagues to find. The connector technology enabling this, called Model Context Protocol, or MCP, lets AI agents interact directly with systems of record like iManage and NetDocuments. Presenters urged firms to demand MCP access from their vendors: “It’s your data.”

The AI adoption panel surfaced another shift that resonated with my daily practice. Clients are no longer asking whether their outside counsel uses AI. They are asking what AI is doing on their specific deal. Sammi observed that AI is not simply cutting billable hours, it is force-multiplying the total volume of legal work. More transactions, more financings, more regulatory demands, more in-house teams returning to outside counsel. The attorneys who can speak specifically to how AI supports their deal process are the ones being pulled into pitches and client conversations.

The change management sessions reinforced something I have observed firsthand: training must be tailored to specific practice workflows. One panelist noted that demonstrating a transaction management tool to a room full of litigators “falls completely deaf.” Technical readiness and people readiness are two fundamentally different challenges, and firms that treat them as the same thing are stalling their own adoption.

I want to acknowledge something important: my notes represent only a fraction of what ILTACON offered. The conference was vast, with tracks spanning cybersecurity, litigation technology, knowledge management, records governance, and much more. What I captured was filtered through a transactional deal lawyer’s lens, and there was far more happening than any single attendee could absorb. The breadth and depth of the programming is one of the things that makes ILTACON exceptional.

WHAT I TOOK HOME

I am not someone who evaluates these tools from the outside. I am a practicing transactional attorney who builds and deploys AI workflow agents on live M&A transactions, real estate deals, venture capital financings, and commercial contracts every day. I practice across General Corporate, Mergers and Acquisitions, Real Estate, Emerging Companies and Venture Capital, Data Privacy and Cybersecurity, Commercial Contracts and Procurement, and Healthcare and Life Sciences. The tools I build are not experiments, they are part of how I practice law.

ILTACON validated what I experience in practice every day: the tools are ready. The attorneys who engage with them are finding real, measurable competitive advantage, faster response times, deeper institutional knowledge, more consistent work product, and the capacity to handle volume without sacrificing quality. But those attorneys also need to be in the rooms where the tools are shaped. They need to be contributing their daily reality, their pain points, their workflow knowledge, so that the technology community can build with the practitioner’s perspective, not just for it. The partnership model the panel described only works when both partners show up.

LOOKING AHEAD

I believe the bridge between practicing attorneys and the legal technology community is one of the most important things our industry can build right now, and I want to be part of building it.

If you are a practicing attorney and you have been watching the legal technology conversation from the sidelines, consider this your invitation to step into the room. The people there want you there. The conversations are richer when practitioners are at the table. And the tools they are building, the tools we use every day, will be better for it.

Danial Manzoor is a practicing attorney at Michael Best & Friedrich, LLP focusing on General Corporate, Mergers and Acquisitions, Real Estate, Emerging Companies and Venture Capital, Data Privacy and Cybersecurity, Commercial Contracts and Procurement, and Healthcare and Life Sciences.

Chamelio举例说明代理可执行的指令：合同等待签署超过五天时通知；每周报告已签署协议数量、未完成事项及卡点；监控客户合同里程碑，触发时准备修订并发送审批；监控法规变化并告知影响；确保续约协议提前60天审查。代理可观察Chamelio及连接系统中的信息、推理含义、创建文档、启动工作流、请求批准、更新数据、通知相关人员并根据法律团队定义的指令决定下一步。Agent Hub改变了法律团队与软件的关系，可委托责任并期望系统持续推进，AI的真正承诺是彻底卸下律师的工作负担。
news.bodyHtml:
Legal intelligence platform, Chamelio, has launched Agent Hub, which lets inhouse lawyers use a suite of ‘always-on AI agents’ that can work independently, monitor what is happening inside the business, and act when needed.

The approach means that lawyers don’t need to always manually ‘log in, open a matter, run a workflow, or ask an AI a question’ for an agent to roll into action. They are set to run whenever they are needed, with their activities controlled through a central hub, hence the ‘Agent Hub’.

As they explained: ‘Legal teams can now create agents with ongoing responsibilities, much like you would assign work to a member of your team.’

Chamelio added that this means inhouse lawyers can expand what they are able to do, but without having to hire more staff.

The company provided several examples of instructions an always-on agent could be set up to follow:

  • Tell me if a contract has been waiting for signature for more than five days.
  • Every week, tell me how many agreements were signed, what is still outstanding, and where something appears stuck.
  • Watch for this customer hitting its contractual milestone. When it happens, prepare the amendment and send it to me for approval.
  • Monitor this regulation and tell me when something changes that affects our obligations.
  • Make sure every agreement coming up for renewal is reviewed 60 days in advance.

Once organised, the agents will go and do what they are told to do – and as noted: without someone having to trigger each and every action.

Moreover, they noted that you can get the agents to do things such as ‘observe information across Chamelio and connected systems, reason about what it means, create documents, initiate workflows, request approvals, update data, notify the right people, and determine the next step based on instructions defined by the legal team’.

In short, this goes a very long way beyond the early days of legal AI where lawyers made a prompt, got back an answer, and resumed their work without any other assistance from the AI tools on their desktop.

Alex Zilberman, CEO and co-founder of Chamelio, commented: ‘Legal technology has spent decades giving legal teams better tools. We think the next step is giving them actual capacity.

‘Agent Hub changes the relationship between legal teams and their software. Instead of logging into a system to do the work, you can delegate a responsibility and expect the system to keep it moving. That’s a fundamentally different model for how a legal department can operate.’

And picking up on the point about staffing and inhouse workloads, he added: ‘The real promise of AI isn’t helping lawyers do the same work a little faster. It’s taking work off their plate entirely.’

More here about Chamelio.

–

Also don’t miss the upcoming Chamelio and AL Webinar – On Wednesday, September 16, 4 PM BST, 11 AM ET, 8 AM PT, Chamelio and Artificial Lawyer will be holding a live webinar to explore the increasingly important topic: ‘Why is the Legal AI ROI Conversation Still Broken?’ And where we will also come up with some answers to solve this challenge! 

RSVP here.

Speakers include: 

Overview:

​Every legal team can tell you what they spent on their tech stack. Almost none can tell you what it actually bought them.

​That’s not for lack of trying. Legal leaders have spent years bolting together dashboards, contract counts, and ‘time saved; estimates to prove the function is more than a cost center. But most of these metrics were never built to measure impact – they were built to justify a purchase. Counting signed contracts or logged hours tells you activity happened. It doesn’t tell you whether legal moved the business forward, reduced risk, or got out of anyone’s way.

​This session digs into why that gap exists and why it’s gotten more urgent as legal teams adopt AI. When the tools change but the measurement stays the same, leaders end up defending spend with numbers that don’t hold up in a budget conversation, and legal keeps getting treated like overhead instead of a function that drives outcomes.

​We’ll break down:

  • ​Why traditional legal ops metrics (contract volume, turnaround time, tool logins) measure motion, not value
  • ​What ‘impact’ actually looks like when legal is proactive instead of reactive, fewer bottlenecks, faster deal velocity, risk caught before it’s expensive
  • ​How to build a data narrative that connects legal’s work to business outcomes leadership already cares about
  • ​What changes about ROI measurement once AI is doing part of the work and how to avoid just automating the same broken metrics

RSVP here to reserve your place.

—

news.titleEn: Lexroom Acquires French + Bulgarian Companies
news.titleZh: Lexroom收购法国与保加利亚公司
news.summaryZh: 意大利领先的法律AI公司Lexroom宣布收购法国法律科技初创公司Query Juriste和保加利亚公司Praven Intelekt，这是该公司首次进行并购交易。此前，Lexroom在今年夏天完成了5000万美元的B轮融资，并已扩展至德国和西班牙市场。此次收购标志着Lexroom欧洲增长战略进入新阶段，通过有机增长与并购相结合，将其AI操作系统扩展至大陆法系市场，业务覆盖包括意大利在内的五个欧洲市场。两家公司的创始人和团队将加入Lexroom，继续开发各自市场，Query Juriste和Praven Intelekt品牌将逐步过渡至Lexroom。这些收购是欧洲扩张的重要里程碑，并强调公司计划结合自身技术、规模和资本与本地专业知识，构建欧洲法律AI领域的定义性平台。Lexroom的平台基于专有的认证法律来源基础设施，旨在跨多个司法管辖区提供可靠、可验证的AI输出。Query Juriste拥有近300家客户和约1000名付费用户，其法律研究平台连接超过500万份法国和欧洲法律文件。Praven Intelekt在保加利亚拥有超过900家客户，提供法律研究数据连接以及起草等功能。欧盟法律科技初创公司进行并购较为罕见，但Legora和Noxtua等公司也有类似扩张。
news.bodyHtml:
Italy’s leading legal AI company, Lexroom – which raised $50m in a Series B round this summer – has acquired French legal tech startup Query Juriste, and also Bulgarian Praven Intelekt, in its first ever inorganic deals.

Following its expansion into Germany and Spain, this move ‘marks a new phase in Lexroom’s European growth strategy, combining organic growth and M&A to scale its AI operating system across Civil Law markets, bringing its footprint to five European markets, including Italy,’ they said.

The founders and teams of both companies will join Lexroom and continue to develop their respective markets, while the Query Juriste and Praven Intelekt brands will gradually transition to Lexroom, they added.

Paolo Fois, co-founder and CEO of Lexroom, commented: ‘These acquisitions are a major milestone in our European expansion, and only the beginning. Over the past year we’ve met dozens of founders building toward a mission close to ours – Query Juriste and Praven Intelekt stood out immediately: exceptional teams, real traction, and products built with the same conviction we started Lexroom with.

‘It doesn’t make sense to reinvent the wheel market by market. When we find founders who’ve already built something great, the smartest move is to combine Lexroom’s technology, scale and capital with local expertise and hustle. That’s how you build the category-defining platform for legal AI in Europe.’

And as to Lexroom itself, the company said it has built its platform around a ‘proprietary infrastructure of certified legal sources, structured to deliver reliable, verifiable AI output across multiple jurisdictions’.

Hence, Query Juriste and Praven Intelekt extend this approach into two more EU markets, ‘adding local technology, expertise and established customer bases’, they concluded.

Query Juriste brings nearly 300 customers and around 1,000 paying users, together with a legal research platform connected to more than five million French and European legal documents. In Bulgaria, Praven Intelekt counts more than 900 customers, also with a connection to legal research data, and also provides drafting and other skils.

Looks like they are on their way to building a truly pan-European company.

Is this a big deal?

Yep. It’s quite rare for EU-based legal tech startups to go on an M&A binge. Legora – with its huge cash pile – has done several deals across Europe, and Noxtua from Germany has also expanded inorganically. But, such moves are usually the exception, not the rule.

Overall, Lexroom is sending out a very confident and ambitious message to the market. Congrats to them.

More about Lexroom here.

news.titleEn: Merrill – The NewMod For Litigation Work
news.titleZh: Merrill——诉讼工作的新型模式
news.summaryZh: Merrill是一家由Rick Merrill与LegalMation创始人James Lee和Thomas Suh共同创立的AI原生诉讼辩护律师事务所，专注于为财富1000强企业处理高量、重复性诉讼。该公司采用科技公司与律师事务所结合的MSO结构，总部位于加州，旨在通过AI技术与经验丰富的律师高效结合，以显著低于传统律所的价格提供法律服务。公司提供固定费用，并自建技术栈，利用处理案件积累的数据改进定价模型和工作流程，从而可能随着规模增长降低费用。Merrill计划最终扩展至美国10个州，未来几年内可能发展到100名律师，并正在考虑融资。其创始人Rick Merrill曾运营诉讼分析初创公司Gavelytics，该背景有助于管理大量案件中的变异性。传统律所难以转向降低收费的模式，而Merrill正是利用这一市场空白，成为原告律师行业AI工具的自然对立面。
news.bodyHtml:
‘Companies are very frustrated because there’s been no alternative,’ says Rick Merrill, co-founder of NewMod firm Merrill. Traditional law firms remain expensive and hourly-based, yet corporates with a high volume of litigation matters can’t rely on ALSPs or an AI tool alone either.

Merrill, which has been formed alongside James Lee and Thomas Suh, the creators of LegalMation, aims to address this litigation defence need and do so with significantly lower prices by tapping AI and deploying experienced lawyers in a highly efficient combination. (Note: LegalMation remains a separate business.)

‘We’re going to do even better work, but for less money. That’s not a message that really anyone leads with, in large part because it hasn’t been possible,’ Merrill told Artificial Lawyer in an AL TV in-depth interview, (see below).

He noted that they offer fixed fees for handling high volume claims that companies have to deal with. They have their own tech stack and will use data they collect on handling those matters to improve their price model and workflows. That means that they could actually reduce their fees as they grow.   

Merrill – whose experience running litigation analytics startup Gavelytics feeds into this work – underlined that in most traditional law firms if you announced to your fellow partners you were reducing what you charged clients, then you would not last long.

— Advertisement —

—

Whereas, in a NewMod, using AI on the basis that it allows work to be handled by its lawyers more rapidly, there is no billable time, and so there is no barrier to sharing the benefits of efficiency.

Merrill – the NewMod, which uses an MSO structure of a tech company and a law firm, and is based in California – wants to launch eventually across 10 US states and grow rapidly, perhaps to 100 lawyers in the next few years. They’re also looking at taking funding, which would go into the tech part of the MSO.

The focus on litigation represents a new growth market for NewMods, given that many are focused on startups and handling their corporate needs. It also comes at a time when AI itself is leading – at least in some parts of the economy – to an increase in claims brought by individuals who feel empowered by AI tools. Meanwhile, a growing number of startups are seeking to help the plaintiff law firm sector improve their efficiency and bring cases against large corporates.

And this comes at a time when despite plenty of discussions about the end of the billable hour, rates are going up in leaps and bounds, and as noted above, Merrill believes that many inhouse legal teams have had enough when it comes to paying the current fees for legal matters that are not ‘bet the company’. Moreover, as said: now there is an alternative.

In fact, Merrill is totally frank about pricing. I.e. this is all about the cost. If a NewMod can handle the same matters, with the same or better net outcome for the client, but at a far lower price, then that is their compelling USP. Why would a GC not use a NewMod if that is the case?

All of this reminds AL of the famous Jeff Bezos comment: ‘Your [profit] margin is my opportunity.’ And NewMods – which deliver the benefits of AI unhindered by the need to accumulate billable time via manual labour – are there for this in a way we have not seen before.  

To watch the video inside the page, please press Play, or you can go directly to the AL TV Channel to watch over 230 other interviews and product walk throughs.

news.bodyText:
‘Companies are very frustrated because there’s been no alternative,’ says Rick Merrill , co-founder of NewMod firm Merrill. Traditional law firms remain expensive and hourly-based, yet corporates with a high volume of litigation matters can’t rely on ALSPs or an AI tool alone either.

Merrill , which has been formed alongside James Lee and Thomas Suh , the creators of LegalMation, aims to address this litigation defence need and do so with significantly lower prices by tapping AI and deploying experienced lawyers in a highly efficient combination. (Note: LegalMation remains a separate business.)

‘ We’re going to do even better work, but for less money . That’s not a message that really anyone leads with, in large part because it hasn’t been possible,’ Merrill told Artificial Lawyer in an AL TV in-depth interview, (see below).

He noted that they offer fixed fees for handling high volume claims that companies have to deal with. They have their own tech stack and will use data they collect on handling those matters to improve their price model and workflows. That means that they could actually reduce their fees as they grow .

Merrill – whose experience running litigation analytics startup Gavelytics feeds into this work – underlined that in most traditional law firms if you announced to your fellow partners you were reducing what you charged clients, then you would not last long.

Whereas, in a NewMod, using AI on the basis that it allows work to be handled by its lawyers more rapidly, there is no billable time, and so there is no barrier to sharing the benefits of efficiency.

Merrill – the NewMod, which uses an MSO structure of a tech company and a law firm, and is based in California – wants to launch eventually across 10 US states and grow rapidly, perhaps to 100 lawyers in the next few years. They’re also looking at taking funding, which would go into the tech part of the MSO.

The focus on litigation represents a new growth market for NewMods, given that many are focused on startups and handling their corporate needs. It also comes at a time when AI itself is leading – at least in some parts of the economy – to an increase in claims brought by individuals who feel empowered by AI tools. Meanwhile, a growing number of startups are seeking to help the plaintiff law firm sector improve their efficiency and bring cases against large corporates.

And this comes at a time when despite plenty of discussions about the end of the billable hour, rates are going up in leaps and bounds, and as noted above, Merrill believes that many inhouse legal teams have had enough when it comes to paying the current fees for legal matters that are not ‘bet the company’. Moreover, as said: now there is an alternative.

In fact, Merrill is totally frank about pricing. I.e. this is all about the cost. If a NewMod can handle the same matters, with the same or better net outcome for the client, but at a far lower price, then that is their compelling USP. Why would a GC not use a NewMod if that is the case?

All of this reminds AL of the famous Jeff Bezos comment: ‘Your [profit] margin is my opportunity.’ And NewMods – which deliver the benefits of AI unhindered by the need to accumulate billable time via manual labour – are there for this in a way we have not seen before.

news.titleEn: Optimizing Use of AI in the Provision of Business Legal Services
news.titleZh: 优化人工智能在商业法律服务中的应用
news.summaryZh:
作者最初因多年经验、快速打字能力和客户服务心态而未采用生成式人工智能工具，并非出于对AI幻觉等常见担忧。基于大语言模型的定制软件应用具有实用性，但律师如何使用它们至关重要。作者曾撰写博客讨论是否希望律师使用AI、AI对总法律顾问处理常规合同的影响，以及与依赖AI的对手方合作的技巧。本文聚焦商业律师如何优化AI使用，以更高效率提供更好的客户服务。

AI工具必须合乎道德地使用，但律师在使用中可能犯错，某些错误可能跨越道德准则，尤其是胜任义务。作者发现生成式AI可在多方面支持商业律师执业：客户常自行使用AI，且往往未使用保护律师-客户特权的定制软件，这有助于律师理解客户如何生成问题。优化AI使用意味着了解AI在何处支持律师，并帮助客户认识到AI目前无法替代律师。作者接受这一说法：AI不会取代律师，但懂得正确使用AI的律师将比不使用的律师更优秀。作者对因AI在艺术中的使用而厌恶AI的人表示同情，但请认识公共领域法则，且好的AI工具本就基于供律师使用的材料训练。然而工具并非生而平等，作者未推荐任何产品，但测试发现各工具各有优劣。在输入机密信息前，必须阅读应用的预期用途、条款条件和用户协议。律师必须注意不要使用可能损害律师-客户特权或以其他不道德方式使用的工具。AI发展迅速，所有观察可能随时间改变。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! I was slow to adopt any generative AI tool usage, not because of the usual reasons (AI hallucinations and word salad), but because I didn’t need it. Years of experience, a fast typing speed, and a client service mentality had gotten me where I am today, so I saw no reason to pivot to a tool that had serious application questions. Now I do. Tailored software applications using large language models (LLMs), commonly referred to as generative AI, have utility, but how an attorney uses them makes all the difference. I’ve written blogs about whether or not you want your lawyer using AI, the implications for GCs on routine contracts, and tips for working with counter-parties who rely upon AI. This blog, however, is focused specifically on how a business attorney can optimize the use of AI to provide better client service with increased efficiency. First, a word on ethics and mistakes – a topic I haven’t written on before because there is a wealth of material out there, including guidance by the American Bar Association. Clearly the tools must be used ethically, but there are numerous ways that attorneys can make mistakes using them, some of which can cross ethical guidelines (especially the duty of competence). With that caveat, here are some of the ways I have found that generative AI can support a business attorney’s practice: Clients are often doing this anyway, frequently not with software tailored to protect the attorney client privilege (another area of concern), and it will help an attorney to understand how the client is generating their questions. Optimizing AI usage really means knowing where it supports the attorney and helping clients to recognize that AI (at this stage anyway) would do a very poor job of replacing an attorney. That said, I’ve come to accept the adage that AI won’t replace attorneys, but attorneys who know how to properly utilize AI will be better attorneys than those who do not. For those who despise AI because of its usage in art, I’m sympathetic to that, but please recognize the law of public domain, and the good AI tools are trained on materials intended for attorneys’ use anyway (like template databanks or analytics that would have been licensed to attorneys regardless of whether they were using an LLM). However, not all tools are created equal. I’m not going to endorse a product in this blog, but I’ve been testing some, and found that each tool does some things better than another tool and some things not as well. It’s important to read not only the application’s intended use, but also its terms and conditions and user agreements, before entering confidential information. Attorneys must take care not to employ tools that can impair the attorney-client privilege or otherwise be used unethically. Of course, AI is evolving quickly so all of these observations could change as do the times. More Upcoming Events

news.titleEn: AI Is Making Us Dumber. Can We Design it Not To?
news.titleZh: AI正让我们变笨。我们能设计出避免这种情况的AI吗？
news.summaryZh:
当前大多数AI工具如同答案贩卖机，输入提示即可获得精炼回复。然而，法律培训长期建立在近乎相反的互动模式上，即苏格拉底式教学法。该方法不直接提供答案，而是通过提问、挑战、改变事实来引导学生思考结论的稳固性，其设计中的挫败感旨在让学生学习规则、理解其局限并最终掌握关键问题。

AI日益让我们无需思考即可获得答案，这引发了担忧：当AI原生的专业人士从未学会思考时会发生什么？一项关于“谷歌效应”的里程碑研究发现，当人们预期信息能通过电脑获取时，他们记住的信息内容更少，而更多记住的是信息位置。生成式AI比谷歌更进一步，它不仅查找信息，还似乎为我们进行推理，在我们构建问题、形成初步理论或积累足够知识以识别缺失内容之前就给出结论。微软研究人员对319名知识工作者进行的调查显示，使用AI导致批判性思维、记忆力、创造力和元认知水平下降。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Most AI tools today operate like answer vending machines. Insert a prompt and out comes a polished response. But legal training has long been built around almost the opposite interaction. The Socratic method does not hand students the answer. It questions, challenges, changes a fact, and asks whether the conclusion still holds. The frustration is part of the design. Students learn the rule, its limits and, eventually, which questions matter in the first place. What would it look like for AI to borrow from that tradition? That question is becoming urgent. AI increasingly lets us get an answer without doing the thinking. What happens when AI-native professionals never learn to do the thinking in the first place? The temptation is obvious. It is in our nature to make thinking easier. We write things down, use calculators, and Google facts the moment we cannot recall them. This is not laziness. It is human nature. A landmark study of the “Google effect” found that when people expected information to remain available on a computer, they remembered less of the information and more about where to find it. That can be a good trade. Lawyers need not spend limited attention memorizing document locations or reconstructing project status from six email chains. But generative AI goes further than Google. It does not just find information. It appears to do the reasoning for us. It gives us the conclusion before we have framed the question, developed an initial theory, or learned enough to recognize what is missing. Microsoft researchers, including Advait Sarkar, surveyed 319 knowledge workers about their use of generative AI, and the results are striking. Use of AI resulted in lower levels of critical thinking, memory, creativity, and metacognition. The evidence is still emerging, but the warning signs are accumulating, and we should be sounding the alarm.
