news.titleEn: China’s Supreme People’s Court Issues First National Judicial Rules on AI Disputes — But Sidesteps Copyrightability of AI-Generated Works
news.titleZh: 中国最高人民法院发布首部人工智能纠纷司法规则——但回避AI生成作品的可版权性问题
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月7日，最高人民法院发布《关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》，共五部分24条，是中国最高司法机关首套涉AI司法裁判规则。意见以中国尚未制定专门AI立法为前提，指导下级法院将民法典、网络安全法、数据安全法、著作权法、反不正当竞争法、消费者权益保护法、个人信息保护法及民事诉讼法适用于涉AI民事和刑事案件。意见以专节规定知识产权：第12条规定AI生成内容侵犯著作权的责任，开发者主张不侵权须提供训练数据来源、训练过程记录和模型运行方式；第13条规定开源软件开发者、提供者与下游开发者之间的责任分配及免责；第14条涉及专利客体适格性、AI辅助发明中自然人作出创造性贡献时的发明人资格及充分公开；第15条规定AI技术开发、转让、许可、咨询和服务合同的违约标准；第16条将数据和数据集作为汇编作品、商业秘密或依据反不正当竞争法第13条予以保护。意见还规定AI训练和生成引发的人格权侵权，规制“AI换脸和声音克隆”及“AI复活逝者”，未经同意使用自然人声音作为训练语料生成可识别合成声音，或生成并发布可识别虚拟数字形象，构成对姓名、肖像或声音权的侵权（第4条）；AI聚合已公开信息进行“网络开盒”（第5条）；使用自行公开或合法公开个人信息训练属于“合理范围”的条件（第6条）。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On September 7, 2026, the Supreme People’s Court of the People’s Republic of China released the Opinions of the Supreme People’s Court on the Trial of Cases Involving Artificial Intelligence Disputes (最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见). The Opinions comprise five parts and 24 articles and are the first set of judicial adjudication rules concerning artificial intelligence issued by China’s highest judicial body. They are framed as guidance for lower courts applying existing law – the Civil Code, Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, Copyright Law, Anti-Unfair Competition Law, Consumer Protection Law, Personal Information Protection Law, and Civil Procedure Law – to AI-related civil and criminal disputes, on the express premise that China has not yet enacted dedicated AI legislation. Substantively, the Opinions devote a full section to intellectual property, addressing infringement liability for AI-generated content that infringes copyright, including the burden on developers asserting non-infringement to produce training data sources, training process records, and model operation modes (Article XII); liability allocation among open-source software developers, providers, and downstream developers, with express provision for appropriate liability exemptions (Article XIII); patent subject-matter eligibility, inventorship where a natural person makes a creative contribution to the substantive features of an AI-assisted invention, and sufficiency of disclosure (Article XIV); breach standards for AI technology development, transfer, licensing, consulting, and service contracts (Article XV); and protection of data and datasets as compilation works, trade secrets, or under Article 13 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law (Article XVI). Beyond IP, the Opinions address personality-rights infringement arising from AI training and generation, regulating “AI face-swapping and voice cloning” and “AI resurrection of the deceased”—using a natural person’s voice as training corpus to generate an identifiable synthetic voice, or generating and publishing an identifiable virtual digital likeness, without consent gives rise to liability for infringement of name, portrait, or voice rights (Article IV) – along with “network doxing” conducted by AI aggregation of published information (Article V) and the conditions under which training on self-published or lawfully published personal information falls within a “reasonable scope” (Article VI). The Opinions also set out liability rules for road traffic accidents involving autonomous vehicles and vehicles with driver-assist functions, including product-liability claims against manufacturers and sellers for vehicle defects, concurrent liability where a defect and driver fault combine to cause the same harm, liability for false or misleading advertising of automation level and performance, and the court’s authority to order data controllers to produce autonomous-driving and driver-assist records needed to establish accident causation (Article XI). Absent from the Opinions, however, is any direct rule on the copyrightability of AI-generated works themselves – that is, whether content generated with AI constitutes a “work” protected under the Copyright Law. The omission stands out because the Beijing Internet Court had already addressed the question. In its set of eight Typical Cases Involving Artificial Intelligence (涉人工智能典型案例) released September 10, 2025, Case I (Li v. Liu) held that a Stable Diffusion output was a copyrightable work of fine art and that the user who selected the model, entered prompts and reverse prompts, set generation parameters, and made the final selection was the author—reasoning that an AI model cannot itself be an author because Chinese copyright law limits authorship to natural persons, legal persons, and unincorporated organizations. Case VII similarly held that virtual digital human images reflecting a production team’s aesthetic choices as to line, color, and character design constitute protected works of art. Neither copyright decision was designated a typical case by the SPC; the SPC designations went instead to the Beijing Internet Court’s personality-rights rulings—Case II (Yin), extending voice rights to AI-synthesized voices identifiable by timbre, intonation, and pronunciation style, and Case VIII (He), extending personality rights to a natural person’s AI-generated virtual image and selected as a “Typical Civil Case on the Judicial Protection of Personality Rights after the Promulgation of the Civil Code.” The SPC then removed the issue from that court’s docket altogether: on October 10, 2025, it released the Provisions of the Supreme People’s Court on the Jurisdiction of Internet Courts (最高人民法院关于互联网法院案件管辖的规定), effective November 1, 2025, which amended the 2018 Provisions to strip Internet Courts of jurisdiction over “copyright or neighboring rights disputes involving works first published online” and “disputes arising from infringement of copyright or neighboring rights in works published or disseminated online,” on the stated rationale that Internet Courts should hear “new, cutting-edge, and complex online cases” while “general and traditional online cases are heard by other local courts.” Between the Opinions’ silence, the absence of SPC endorsement for the Beijing rulings that reached the issue, and the reassignment of online copyright disputes away from the court that developed the jurisprudence, the copyrightability of AI-generated output remains unresolved at the national level. A translation of the Opinions on Adjudicating Disputes Involving Artificial Intelligence in Accordance with the Law follows. The original text is available here (Chinese only). In order to fully implement the spirit of the 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China and its subsequent plenary sessions, to serve and safeguard the accelerated development of new productive forces through strict and impartial justice, and to guide people’s courts at all levels in adjudicating cases involving artificial intelligence disputes in accordance with the law, the following opinions are put forward based on relevant laws such as the Civil Code of the People’s Republic of China, the Cybersecurity Law of the People’s Republic of China, the Data Security Law of the People’s Republic of China, the Copyright Law of the People’s Republic of China, the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People’s Republic of China, the Consumer Rights Protection Law of the People’s Republic of China, the Personal Information Protection Law of the People’s Republic of China, and the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China, and in light of the actual work of the people’s courts. I. General Requirements (I) Guiding Principles Guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, we will thoroughly implement Xi Jinping’s thought on the rule of law, earnestly implement General Secretary Xi Jinping’s important thought on building a strong cyber power, deeply recognize that artificial intelligence is an important driving force for the new round of technological revolution and industrial transformation, adhere to the principle of giving equal importance to development and security, and combine the promotion of innovation with governance according to law. We will adjudicate cases involving artificial intelligence disputes fairly and impartially in accordance with the law, promote the improvement of the safety, reliability, controllability, and fairness of artificial intelligence technology applications, and provide strong judicial services and guarantees for comprehensively advancing the construction of a strong country and the great cause of national rejuvenation through Chinese-style modernization. (II) Basic Principles Upholding a people-centered approach, we will leverage the guiding role of judicial decisions to actively promote artificial intelligence in enhancing people’s well-being and effectively strengthen judicial protection of people’s rights and interests in the digital age. We will actively and steadily explore and improve judicial rules and mechanisms in the field of artificial intelligence, including those related to algorithm ethics and rules. We will make full use of existing legal provisions to properly address the rule conflicts, social risks, and ethical challenges brought about by the development of artificial intelligence technology. We will promote the improvement of the corporate social responsibility system for artificial intelligence enterprises, focus on preventing and eliminating algorithmic discrimination, legally protect individuals’ right to know and right to choose in automated decision-making, prevent and regulate the abuse of artificial intelligence technology to infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of the people, and promote artificial intelligence for the benefit of the people and for good.

research.titleEn: Reading a Legal Question Word by Word: Embedding Trajectories of 2,144 Vietnamese Legal Headlines
research.titleZh: 逐词阅读法律问题：2,144条越南法律标题的嵌入轨迹
research.abstractEn: A dense retriever encodes a question as one vector, but the question arrives one word at a time. We read 2,144 held-out headlines from Thu Vien Phap Luat (Vietnamese legal library) word by word with Nemotron-3-Embed 8B/1B and Qwen3-Embedding 8B/0.6B, encoding 65,444 prefixes against 20,034 articles, plus every prefix of 3,438 sub-questions from 1,112 multi-question headlines and of 168 answers. (i) The gold article becomes rank 1 after a median of 6-7 content words in every encoder, before the interrogative frame is read, and stays there to the end in 78-85% of cases. (ii) In a multi-question headline the lock is inside the first sub-question 94-98% of the time; the second leaves rank unchanged in 89-95%; encoded alone, the second reaches rank 1 in 42-58% vs 91-96% for the first, at the same lock word (95-97% identical). (iii) Numbers, dates and instrument identifiers move the embedding twice as far as content words and four times as far as interrogative words; 72-78% of steps move toward the gold article, and the closing interrogative frame moves against that direction in 95-99% of headlines. (iv) Rank/cosine clustering yields six archetypes (instant, typical, unstable, late, never-locking) that differ by legal area and form (chi-squared p < 1e-8): real-estate and litigation headlines never lock on a number; environmental and accounting headlines do so a third of the time. (v) An answer read word by word retrieves its article after 8-16 words and addresses the sub-questions in order asked in 83-89% of cases. (vi) A word's step keeps a consistent direction across headlines (cosine 0.25-0.33; 0.44-0.60 for numbers); a preceding question rotates that step by about 60 degrees and a greeting by about 30 degrees; steps shrink as i^{-0.8}; and a two-question headline is within 12-17 degrees of a linear mix of its two questions. We call this a context-modulated additive walk.
research.abstractZh: 稠密检索器将问题编码为一个向量，但问题是一个词一个词地到来的。我们使用Nemotron-3-Embed 8B/1B和Qwen3-Embedding 8B/0.6B，逐词阅读了来自Thu Vien Phap Luat（越南法律图书馆）的2,144条留出标题，将65,444个前缀与20,034篇文章进行编码，此外还编码了来自1,112条多问题标题的3,438个子问题的每个前缀以及168个答案的每个前缀。(i) 在每个编码器中，金标文章在阅读了中位数为6-7个内容词后成为排名第1，此时疑问框架尚未被阅读，并且在78-85%的情况下一直保持到结束。(ii) 在多问题标题中，锁定在94-98%的情况下发生在第一个子问题内；第二个子问题在89-95%的情况下使排名保持不变；单独编码时，第二个子问题在42-58%的情况下达到排名第1，而第一个子问题在91-96%的情况下达到排名第1，且锁定词相同（95-97%一致）。(iii) 数字、日期和文书标识符使嵌入移动的距离是内容词的两倍，是疑问词的四倍；72-78%的步骤朝向金标文章移动，而结尾的疑问框架在95-99%的标题中逆该方向移动。(iv) 排名/余弦聚类产生了六种原型（即时、典型、不稳定、晚期、从不锁定），它们因法律领域和形式而异（卡方检验p < 1e-8）：房地产和诉讼标题从不锁定在数字上；环境和会计标题则有三分之一的时间这样做。(v) 逐词阅读答案时，在8-16个词后检索到其文章，并在83-89%的情况下按提问顺序处理子问题。(vi) 一个词的步骤在标题间保持一致的方向（余弦0.25-0.33；数字为0.44-0.60）；前面的问题将该步骤旋转约60度，问候语旋转约30度；步骤以i^{-0.8}缩小；两个问题的标题与其两个问题的线性混合相差在12-17度以内。我们称之为上下文调制的加性行走。

research.titleEn: VeriScene: Reconstructing Crime Scenes from Legal Evidence via World-Model Agent
research.titleZh: VeriScene：通过世界模型智能体从法律证据重建犯罪现场
research.abstractEn: World models take multimodal inputs like text, photos, and diagrams to generate dynamic scenes in accordance with the laws of physics, thus opening a compelling application: fusing multimodal legal evidence to re-create a crime scene and re-enact how an offence could have been committed. However, feeding the raw, unorganized evidence into a world model fails in forensic use: it silently drops evidence, glosses over contradictory testimony, and produces motion that violates the evidentiary record. This paper presents VeriScene, an agent that orchestrates the world model: it reconstructs crime scenes from forensic photographs and witness statements of varying reliability, keeping every claim traceable to evidence and every motion physically plausible. VeriScene iteratively fuses the evidence into a cited narrative under an auditing loop, verifies the hypothesized dynamics via probe rollouts in the world model with corrective constraint injection, and renders the offence as a re-enactment video from a fused keyframe. On a benchmark of 25 crime scenarios across 7 physically-driven case types (139 forensic-style photographs and 65 statements with planted unreliability), VeriScene attains 0.9014 evidence coverage and 0.7217 factual consistency (0-1 scale) on the 20 test scenes, outperforming an end-to-end multimodal-LLM baseline by 20.35% in factual consistency and 34.88% in temporal coherence, while generalizing across four LLM orchestration backends at USD 1.82 per scene.
research.abstractZh: 世界模型接收文本、照片和图表等多模态输入，根据物理定律生成动态场景，从而开启了一个引人注目的应用：融合多模态法律证据来重建犯罪现场，并重新演绎犯罪可能发生的过程。然而，将原始、无组织的证据直接输入世界模型在法医应用中会失败：它会静默丢弃证据，掩盖相互矛盾的证词，并产生违反证据记录的运动。本文提出了 VeriScene，一个协调世界模型的智能体：它从法医照片和可靠性不一的证人陈述中重建犯罪现场，确保每一项主张都可追溯到证据，每一个动作在物理上都是合理的。VeriScene 在审计循环下迭代地将证据融合为带有引用的叙述，通过在世界模型中进行探测性推演并注入纠正性约束来验证假设的动态，并从融合的关键帧将犯罪渲染为重演视频。在涵盖 7 种物理驱动案件类型的 25 个犯罪场景基准（139 张法医风格照片和 65 份植入不可靠性的陈述）上，VeriScene 在 20 个测试场景中达到了 0.9014 的证据覆盖率和 0.7217 的事实一致性（0-1 量表），在事实一致性上比端到端多模态 LLM 基线高出 20.35%，在时间连贯性上高出 34.88%，同时在四个 LLM 编排后端上泛化，每个场景成本为 1.82 美元。

research.titleEn: Cassette: Case-to-Case Structural Distillation for Efficient Legal Case Retrieval
research.titleZh: Cassette：面向高效法律案例检索的案例到案例结构蒸馏
research.abstractEn: Legal case retrieval (LCR) is an essential tool for not only assisting legal practitioners to efficiently retrieve precedents but also enabling ordinary individuals to find valuable legal case information without relying on expensive professional legal services. Our previous work CaseLink demonstrated the effectiveness of using case to case graph structures to improve retrieval accuracy. However, its high computational cost during inference on large-scale legal databases limits its practical use in real-world settings. The main inefficiency comes from constructing test time graphs and computing pairwise term frequency similarities of cases. This process has O(n^2) complexity for n legal cases, making the runtime prohibitive as the number of candidates grows. For example, the retrieval time for one query on a database (COLIEE2022) with 1,563 candidate cases is more than 500 milliseconds, while the runtime would increase drastically to more than 3,500 seconds for a database (LeCaRDv2) with 55,192 candidate cases. To further enhance the retrieval performance while achieving a significant speed-up, in this extension paper, Cassette framework is proposed with a distillation strategy involving ranking objective and eigen-matching objective for an effective transfer of knowledge from a powerful and well-trained heavy teacher retriever to a lightweight and efficient hybrid student dual encoder. Specifically, the student query encoder is implemented as a multilayer perceptron model designed for fast online processing, whereas the student candidate encoder adopts a GNN architecture, suitable for an offline manner within the case database. Extensive experiments are conducted on three benchmark datasets, and the results verify the effectiveness of the ranking distillation while achieving high efficiency. The code has been released on https://github.com/yanran-tang/Cassette/.
research.abstractZh: 法律案例检索（LCR）不仅是一项帮助法律从业者高效检索先例的重要工具，也能让普通个人无需依赖昂贵的专业法律服务即可找到有价值的法律案例信息。我们之前的工作CaseLink证明了使用案例到案例图结构来提高检索准确率的有效性。然而，其在大规模法律数据库上进行推理时的高计算成本限制了其在现实场景中的实际应用。主要的低效源于构建测试时图以及计算案例之间的成对词频相似度。对于n个法律案例，该过程具有O(n^2)的复杂度，使得随着候选案例数量的增长，运行时间变得难以承受。例如，在一个包含1,563个候选案例的数据库（COLIEE2022）上，一次查询的检索时间超过500毫秒，而对于一个包含55,192个候选案例的数据库（LeCaRDv2），运行时间将急剧增加至超过3,500秒。为了在实现显著加速的同时进一步提升检索性能，在本扩展论文中，我们提出了Cassette框架，该框架采用了一种包含排序目标和特征匹配目标的蒸馏策略，以有效地将一个强大且训练有素的重型教师检索器的知识迁移到一个轻量且高效的混合学生双编码器。具体而言，学生查询编码器实现为多层感知机模型，旨在实现快速的在线处理；而学生候选编码器采用GNN架构，适合在案例数据库中以离线方式运行。我们在三个基准数据集上进行了大量实验，结果验证了排序蒸馏的有效性，同时实现了高效率。代码已在https://github.com/yanran-tang/Cassette/上发布。

policy.titleEn: 以人为本智能向善 ——聚焦《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》
policy.titleZh: 以人为本智能向善 ——聚焦《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》
policy.summaryZh: 9月7日，最高人民法院发布《关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》，以坚持以人为本、支持创新发展、筑牢安全底线为基本原则，聚焦群众关切、回应人工智能产业发展的法治需求。在侵权责任方面，《意见》明确，利用人工智能侵害民事权益，法律未规定适用无过错责任或过错推定责任的，适用过错责任原则；未经同意生成可识别自然人的虚拟数字形象、合成可识别声音，或操控虚拟形象、合成声音侵害名誉权的，依法追究侵权责任；为模型训练在合理范围内处理已合法公开且个人未明确拒绝的个人信息，一般不认定为侵权，但对个人权益有重大影响的应依法取得同意；生成式人工智能服务提供者经权利人通知未及时采取必要措施的，应承担侵权责任；依法规制大数据杀熟、仿冒名人带货，构成欺诈的可支持惩罚性赔偿；并对人格权侵害禁令、人工智能产品责任、自动驾驶汽车交通事故赔偿责任等作出规定。在知识产权方面，《意见》第三部分就侵权责任认定、开源软件相关方法律责任、专利授权确权、技术合同履行及数据使用规范作出规定，明确人工智能生成内容侵害著作权的责任认定考量因素，开源软件以综合考量、适当豁免为裁判思路，并明确涉人工智能发明创造的专利保护客体及发明人认定规则。
policy.bodyText:
“AI换脸拟声”真假难辨如何规制？生成式人工智能自动生成内容侵权，服务提供者责任如何认定？涉人工智能开源软件相关方的法律责任如何划分？
人工智能技术日新月异，在深刻改变生产生活方式的同时，也带来了一系列亟待回应的法律问题与治理挑战。
习近平总书记在2026世界人工智能大会暨人工智能全球治理高级别会议开幕式上的主旨讲话中强调：“人工智能技术发展越是一日千里，向上向善、造福人类的方向越要正确锚定，监管治理的尺度越要精准把握，防范失控的措施越要及时完善。”
在这一时代背景下，9月7日，《最高人民法院关于依法审理涉人工智能纠纷案件的意见》（以下简称《意见》）正式发布。《意见》以坚持以人为本、支持创新发展、筑牢安全底线为三项基本原则，聚焦人民群众关切、回应人工智能产业发展的法治需求，为相关纠纷依法审理和行业规范发展指明了方向。
维护权益：依法规制利用人工智能的侵权行为
人工智能技术在应用中引发的侵权纠纷日益增多，对民事主体合法权益保护提出新挑战。《意见》将“维护民事主体合法权益”摆在突出位置，明确依法妥善审理涉人工智能侵权案件，准确界定各方责任，切实保障人民群众合法权益，让技术进步始终在法治轨道上运行。
准确把握涉人工智能侵权责任的归责原则，是依法妥善处理此类纠纷、切实维护民事主体合法权益的关键。《意见》明确，利用人工智能侵害民事权益产生的法律责任，法律没有明确规定适用无过错责任或者过错推定责任的，应当适用过错责任原则。
当前，“AI换脸拟声”“AI复活逝者”“网络开盒”“人肉搜索”等违法行为时有发生，社会各界高度关切。为此，《意见》对利用人工智能侵害肖像权、名誉权、隐私权、声音权益等行为的责任追究作出了明确规范：未经同意利用人工智能处理自然人的姓名、肖像等，生成可识别该自然人的虚拟数字形象并使用、公开的，构成对姓名权、肖像权等人格权益的侵害；未经同意使用自然人声音作为训练语料，模仿其音色、语调和发音风格生成可识别的合成人声的，构成对声音权益的侵害；操控虚拟形象、合成声音实施不当行为或者发表不实言论、降低他人社会评价的，构成对名誉权的侵害，依法追究行为人的侵权责任。
人工智能发展高度依赖大规模训练数据，其中不可避免包含已合法公开的个人信息。为平衡保护个人信息权益与促进人工智能产业发展，《意见》明确，为人工智能模型训练，在合理范围内处理已合法公开的个人信息，且个人未明确拒绝的，一般不认定为侵权。但是，对个人权益有重大影响的，应当依照法律规定取得个人同意。
民法典第一千一百九十五条规定了“通知删除规则”，也就是人们常说的“避风港规则”。在《意见》中，这一规则同样可以参照适用。生成式人工智能自动生成的内容侵害他人名誉权、隐私权等人格权益，经权利人通知，生成式人工智能服务提供者未及时采取停止生成侵权内容等必要措施的，应当对造成的损害依法承担侵权责任。
算法“看人下菜”，AI“以假乱真”，消费者的公平交易权与知情权正在被悄然蚕食。《意见》依法规制“大数据杀熟”“仿冒名人带货”等侵害消费者权益的行为：经营者利用算法在交易价格等交易条件上实行不合理的差别待遇，侵害他人合法权益造成损害的，人民法院应当依法认定其承担相应的侵权责任；利用人工智能实施“仿冒名人带货”且构成欺诈的，可予支持惩罚性赔偿。
另外，《意见》对人格权侵害禁令制度、人工智能产品责任、涉自动驾驶汽车和具备辅助驾驶功能汽车交通事故的赔偿责任等作出了明确规定。
《意见》以司法之力为民事主体合法权益筑起坚实屏障。技术向善，终须以人为本。让人民群众在人工智能发展中有实实在在的安全感，是法治维护权益的应有之义。
保障发展：依法审理涉人工智能知识产权纠纷案件
人工智能深度参与创作与研发，使生成内容的权利归属、合同履行的违约责任以及人工智能模型训练数据使用等涉知识产权问题日益凸显。如何在保护创作者权益与激励技术创新之间寻求平衡，成为人工智能治理的重要课题。
《意见》第三部分对涉人工智能知识产权纠纷案件的审理作出专门规定，涉及侵权责任认定、开源软件相关方的法律责任、专利授权确权、技术合同履行以及数据使用规范五个方面。
《意见》依法规制涉人工智能侵害知识产权的行为。明确规定，人工智能生成内容侵害他人著作权的，人民法院应当综合考量人工智能服务类型、行业特点、训练数据来源、各方参与度、采取的必要措施以及获利情况等因素，依法合理认定人工智能开发者、提供者、使用者的责任。利用人工智能实施侵权假冒、虚假宣传、刷量刷单等行为，侵害他人权利或者构成不正当竞争的，依法承担相应责任。
在开源软件相关方的法律责任方面，《意见》以“综合考量、适当豁免”为裁判思路。认定侵权责任时，结合开源许可协议类型、权利限制、安全合规举措与信息披露程度等因素综合判断，并依法给予适当责任豁免；对以免费开源方式提供代码模块并已公开说明功能和安全风险的，可认定不承担侵权责任，为开源创新提供明确预期。
实践中，涉人工智能发明创造的专利确权，关键在于厘清“何种客体受专利法保护”与“谁为发明人”。《意见》明确，涉人工智能发明创造采用遵循自然规律的技术手段，解决了技术问题，实现了符合自然规律的技术效果的，人民法院应当依法认定其为专利法所保护的客体。自然人使用人工智能完成的发明创造，该自然人对发明创造的实质性特点作出了创造性贡献的，应当认定该自然人为发明人。
《意见》在鼓励人工智能技术创新与维护权利人合法权益之间寻求平衡，旗帜鲜明支持和保障人工智能技术和产业创新发展，既严格保护合法权利，又为技术研发和产业发展留出必要空间，实现激励创新与规范秩序的有机统一。
最高人民法院研究室主任周加海表示：“《意见》一方面强调，对于故意利用人工智能实施的危害国家安全、侵犯公民权益、扰乱社会秩序等犯罪行为，坚决依法严惩；另一方面要求，对于在人工智能研发、应用中的创新性行为，要依法审慎处理，恪守罪刑法定、罪责刑相适应原则。”
完善机制：探索完善审理规则和工作机制
人工智能的影响是全领域的，审判活动同样面临新的风险挑战。涉人工智能纠纷案件具有技术性、专业性强等特点，事实认定与证据审查的难度显著增加。《意见》紧扣审理程序规则这一关键环节，完善涉人工智能纠纷中证据审查、事实查明等机制，依法惩治利用生成式人工智能妨害司法秩序的行为，并加大审判指导力度，以程序正义守护司法公正。
《意见》第四部分聚焦涉人工智能纠纷案件审理程序规则，在维护司法秩序方面，《意见》对利用人工智能妨害诉讼、伪造证据、进行虚假诉讼等行为依法予以规制，并根据情节轻重采取强制措施乃至追究刑事责任。对使用人工智能生成诉讼材料的情形，要求如实说明并确保内容真实准确。同时，对利用人工智能实施诈骗、侮辱、诽谤、侵犯公民个人信息等犯罪，以及规避辅助驾驶监测致害等行为，明确依法惩治，坚决维护司法权威和公共安全。
面对人工智能带来的系统性挑战，事后追责与个案规制仅是其中一环，健全审判指导与工作机制、推动源头治理同样关键。
在健全完善工作机制方面，《意见》强调发挥多元解纷机制作用，推动与行业主管部门、调解组织及专家学者协同联动，做实先行调解，并通过庭审公开、以案释法等方式发挥示范引领作用，促进纠纷源头预防和及时化解。同时，规范适用提级管辖，对涉及重大利益、规则确立意义或需统一法律适用标准的案件，由上级法院提级审理，依托案例库加强指导，推动裁判尺度统一和治理规则完善。
人工智能技术应用场景仍在快速拓展，司法实践中的新情况新问题不断涌现，部分问题的法律定性和裁判规则尚需在实践中逐步检验。坚持问题导向和场景应用，对于目前难以形成共识的问题，《意见》做了留白处理，待进一步积累经验，条件成熟时再通过适当方式作出明确。
最高人民法院民三庭庭长李剑表示：“当前，人工智能技术发展一日千里，新情况新问题不断涌现，下一步，我们将继续密切关注人工智能等新兴领域的知识产权保护问题，在实践中不断认识和把握规律，不断总结审判经验，完善裁判规则，努力推动形成共识。”
人工智能新浪潮奔涌向前，法治是不可偏离的航道。人民法院将继续坚持发展和安全并重，把握人工智能发展趋势和规律，充分发挥司法裁判规范、引领作用，促进人工智能技术以人为本、智能向善，为在法治轨道上推进中国式现代化贡献司法力量。
（ 见习记者 刘新源 ）

news.titleEn: Why AI Isn’t Increasing Law Firm Revenue
news.titleZh: 为什么AI没有增加律所收入
news.summaryZh: 71%的独立律师正在使用AI，其中约三分之一收入高于以往。但数据揭示了一个关键差距：约十分之一的律所报告AI带来收入改善，而在广泛使用AI的律所中，69%报告了显著的积极收入影响。今年更多律所使用通用AI工具而非法律专用工具，这意味着AI正从法律实践转向律所运营。AI最被低估的营销功能是记忆：例如在离婚案件中，十年后子女接近成年时，AI能读取现有案件上下文，浮现里程碑并提醒律师。速度也可成为竞争优势，有律师在机场安检排队时用移动应用生成策略提案，35分钟内从冷电话到提案，客户签约。关于计费，弗吉尼亚州律师协会伦理意见指出，任务耗时只是衡量价值的一种方式，若收费五千美元，耗时减少并不自动使费用不合理，只需能解释合理性。Clio研究显示法律服务价格弹性比多数律师假设的更大，客户首先问的是回复速度和是否处理过类似案件。57%的独立律师和55%的小型律所没有AI政策或不知道是否存在，而超过70%的客户想知道律所是否使用AI。新泽西最高法院已发布示范政策，Clio博客有模板。Joshua建议积极拥抱并保持透明，发布AI政策。
news.bodyHtml:
Seventy-one percent of solo attorneys are using AI. Roughly a third of them are earning more than they were before.

That gap is the most important number in legal technology right now, and most firms are drawing the wrong conclusion from it. The instinct is to assume the tools are overhyped, or that the benefit will arrive eventually, or that law is simply different. None of those is what the data says.

I put the question to Joshua Lenon, Lawyer in Residence at Clio and the person behind the Legal Trends Report. His answer was more useful than I expected in this week’s episode of Counsel Cast, Why Isn’t AI Making Your Firm Money?

The variable is breadth, not quality

Joshua Lenon described a flip in the data. For years, most firms reported using legal-specific AI. Research tools. Contract analysis. Task-shaped software that does one job extremely well and touches nothing else in the business.

This year, more firms reported using general AI tools than legal-specific ones. That sounds like a downgrade. It isn’t. It means AI has started moving out of the practice of law and into the operation of the firm, and the operation of the firm is where money is made or lost.

The numbers back it up. About one in ten firms report improved revenue from AI. But among firms that describe themselves as widely using AI across their business, 69% report significant positive revenue impact.

Same technology. Different surface area. Completely different result.

So the honest question is not whether your firm uses AI. It’s how much of your firm it actually touches.

AI’s most underrated marketing function is memory

The clearest example Joshua gave had nothing to do with drafting.

Think about a divorce matter with minor children. Ten years later those children approach the age of majority, and that milestone carries consequences. Tax implications. Support obligations. Whatever the separation agreement said about college. Insurance coverage that shifts.

You knew all of that when you closed the file. Then a decade passed.

No reminder system survives ten years reliably. But AI can read the context inside your existing matters, surface the milestone, and bring it to your attention at the moment it becomes relevant. Joshua’s phrase for it was a research librarian raising things over your morning coffee.

From the client’s side, this reads as a lawyer who remembered. From the firm’s side, it’s a marketing message that is consistent, timely, and grounded in something real.

Speed as a competitive position

Joshua told a story about a lawyer who received a prospect call while standing in an airport security line. He said he would take a look and get back to them shortly. He opened the mobile app, pointed it at files already in the system, asked for a strategy proposal based on the firm’s templates, and by the time he reached his gate he had something to send.

Thirty-five minutes from cold call to proposal. The client signed.

I asked the obvious follow-up. If five lawyers all have the same tools and the same documents, what makes any of them different?

Joshua’s answer: it’s not the tool, it’s the person.

Tools converge fast. What does not converge is judgment. Which cases you take. What kind of practice you are building. Whether you know the client’s history. I have clients going into their second decade with me, and when one came back last year I pulled our notes from the original brand build ten years earlier. That conversation was different from the one any other agency could have had, and no software created that advantage.

The pricing problem has an answer already

Every conversation about AI efficiency eventually hits billing. If you bill hourly and the work takes a fifth of the time, you have handed your client a discount they never asked for.

Most firms know this. Very few have changed anything.

Joshua pointed to a Virginia State Bar ethics opinion that says something firms should have been told louder and sooner. Time spent on a task is only one possible way of measuring value. If you charge five thousand dollars for a matter, the fact that it took less time than it used to does not automatically make that fee unreasonable. You just have to be able to explain why it’s reasonable, and expertise, systems, and tool selection are all legitimate parts of that explanation.

The rules already allowed this. Firms have been waiting for permission that was already on the books.

I spent years as a travel agent before this career, in a job where every minute was measured. I was routinely two to three times faster than my colleagues. When I was five minutes late one morning, my manager wanted a word. I asked whether it mattered, given that I was taking three times the calls. Should I slow down?

That’s the hourly model. It punishes your best performer and rewards the slowest one. Every other industry sorted this out. Law is still deciding.

Your pricing is a marketing decision

Joshua shared something from Clio’s current research: there is more price elasticity in legal services than most lawyers assume. Price is not the first question clients ask. They ask how quickly you will get back to them, and whether you have handled this kind of matter before.

But price is a hurdle, and hurdles matter.

When a prospect can find a flat fee or even a clear range before the consultation, the hurdle is gone before the call starts. The wrong-fit clients screen themselves out. The right ones arrive already comfortable. The conversation shifts from negotiating an hourly rate to discussing what they need and what you provide.

Clients want predictability. They are having one of the worst weeks of their lives. Nobody wants an unknown number attached to it.

The AI policy nobody has written

Here is where I think there is real, immediate opportunity.

Fifty-seven percent of solos and 55% of small firms either have no AI policy or don’t know if one exists. Those are the same thing.

Meanwhile, more than 70% of clients say they want to know whether their firm uses AI. Up from the year before.

That’s a gap you can close this month. Joshua has worked with the Virginia and New Jersey state bar associations on this, and the New Jersey Supreme Court has published a model policy. Clio has a template on its blog.

Frame it correctly and it stops being a compliance document. A public AI policy tells clients how you use technology to serve them better. It gives clients guidance on their own AI use, which matters more than firms realize, because clients are already turning to consumer AI tools whether you address it or not.

Writing the policy also forces a conversation inside the firm about which tools are approved and where the limits are. Without that, you get shadow IT. Staff quietly using whatever makes their day easier, with no parameters and no oversight.

And from a marketing standpoint: if half your competitors have nothing, publishing yours makes you one of the few firms in your market that has answered a question your prospects are already thinking about.

Where the human stops

Joshua’s book pick was Co-Intelligence by Ethan Mollick, and the argument fits the whole conversation. AI is not a replacement for people. It’s an extension of them.

We landed on a metaphor I’ll keep using. Terminator or Iron Man. One is fully automated with no human left inside. The other is a person, amplified. Efficiency for its own sake takes you toward the first one, and that is where firms lose the thing clients actually hire them for.

My own line is specific. I outline first. I write the substance. AI comes in afterward to refine, catch what I missed, and check how it will perform in search. The order is not negotiable.

What to do this week

Audit how widely AI actually touches your firm. If it’s one tool doing one job, that’s your answer on revenue.

Pick one matter type and price it on value instead of hours. Document your reasoning.

Publish an AI policy. Use the New Jersey model as a starting point.

Joshua’s closing advice was to lean in and be transparent. That is right, and I’d add one more word. Publish. Transparency your clients can’t find isn’t doing anything for you.

news.titleEn: Beyond the Law Firm Pyramid: Manuel Deó on Ambar, Fractional Legal Talent, and the Future of Legal Delivery
news.titleZh: 超越律所金字塔：Manuel Deó谈Ambar、灵活法律人才与法律服务的未来
news.summaryZh: 本期The Geek in Review播客对话Ambar Partners联合创始人兼联合首席执行官Manuel Deó。Ambar近期在Chambers获评欧洲替代性法律服务提供商Band One。Ambar并非要取代大型律所，而是填补企业永久内部招聘与传统外部律师之间的空白。Ambar模式让律师自主决定客户、项目、费用和时间安排，同时让客户对成本及具体服务律师有更高可见度。Deó介绍Ambar所称的“法律操作系统”，围绕归属感、业务、运营支撑和认证构建，为独立律师和精品所提供社区、业务拓展、合规、合同、计费、技术及机构信誉支持。其共享技术环境包含Harvey、Microsoft Copilot、Legora等法律技术产品。Deó认为法律知识正日益普及，判断力愈发宝贵，Ambar通过“专家孪生”将经律师批准的知识、既往工作、操作手册和经验形成可信层，用于AI辅助工作。他预计法律部门将围绕具体事务动态组合内部律师、传统律所、独立专家、精品所、管理服务及AI代理，未来属于能够统筹能力的法律部门。
news.bodyHtml:
What happens when you separate elite legal talent from the traditional law firm structure? This week on The Geek in Review, we talk with Manuel Deó, co-founder and co-CEO of Ambar Partners, about a model designed around senior independent lawyers, flexible capacity, enterprise technology, and client choice. Deó explains why he and co-founder Rosa Espín did not set out to replace Big Law, but instead to address a gap between permanent in-house hiring and traditional outside counsel.

At the center of Ambar’s model is a simple idea: legal demand comes in different shapes, and the delivery model should match the problem. Deó describes how Ambar gives lawyers control over the clients, projects, fees, and schedules they take on, while giving clients greater visibility into cost and the individual lawyers doing the work. He also discusses Ambar’s recent Chambers recognition and argues that the term “alternative” is starting to lose some of its usefulness as clients grow more comfortable assembling legal services from a wider range of providers.

Deó walks through what Ambar calls its legal operating system, built around belonging, business, backbone, and badge. The model combines a professional community with business development, compliance, contracting, billing, technology, and institutional credibility for independent lawyers and specialist boutiques. Ambar’s public materials describe a shared technology environment that includes tools such as Harvey, Microsoft Copilot, Legora, and other legal technology products. The goal, according to Deó, is to give independent lawyers access to the infrastructure associated with a large firm without requiring them to give up professional independence.

The conversation also turns to AI, knowledge, and professional judgment. Deó argues that legal knowledge is becoming more abundant while judgment grows more valuable. He describes Ambar’s work on “expert twins,” where approved knowledge, prior work, playbooks, and experience associated with an individual lawyer form a trusted layer for AI-assisted work. That emphasis on institutional knowledge and permissions echoes a broader trend across legal AI, where vendors are increasingly focused on connecting AI systems to trusted internal work product and organizational context.

Finally, Deó offers a broader view of where legal delivery is heading. He sees legal departments assembling teams dynamically from in-house lawyers, traditional firms, independent specialists, boutiques, managed services, and AI agents based on the needs of a particular matter. Instead of asking which firm to hire, clients increasingly have reason to ask what combination of people, technology, expertise, and risk structure best fits the work. For Deó, the future belongs less to a single dominant delivery model and more to legal departments acting as orchestrators of capability.

[Special Thanks to ⁠⁠Legal Technology Hub⁠⁠ for their sponsoring this episode.]

: geekinreviewpodcast@gmail.com

Music: Jerry David DeCicca

  • Ambar Partners
  • Ambar Community
  • Ambar Hauss Membership Plans
  • Dr. No Newsletter

Transcript

Greg Lambert (00:01)

Hey everyone, I’m Greg Lambert, and this week on The Geek in Review, we have with us Manuel Deó from Ambar Partners. But first, let’s get some insights from our friends at Legal Technology Hub.

Marlene Gebauer (00:14)

Hi, I’m Marlene Gebauer from The Geek in Review. I have Sam Moore here from Legal Technology Hub. He’s going to tell us about AI governance from the advisory side.

Sam Moore (00:23)

Thank you. Good to see you again. Well, in the advisory team at Legal Technology Hub, we’ve been having a lot of conversations with clients about AI governance. Now, most law firms and departments have at least an AI policy of some kind, and there are some broad standards which are starting to emerge. A trend we’re seeing at the moment is a shift away from policies written in 2023 and 2024, which largely stated what you couldn’t do, and towards a more informative approach which defines different risk categories and makes distinctions between routine, low-risk use of AI and other more substantial use cases. I think that’s appropriate for where we are. It’s also what clients are coming to expect from their advisors. But one of the bigger challenges we’re seeing right now is, how do you express an AI use policy in such a way that any member of your legal team could explain it to a client? I think that’s still a big challenge for the industry.

Marlene Gebauer (00:41)

Okay.

Sam Moore (01:21)

I don’t think clients are all that happy if their attorney says, “I’ll have to get back to you about that,” because the attorney is using AI day-to-day. So they should be able to explain the policy themselves. How else do you know they’re complying with it? We’re doing some interesting work at the moment helping law firms and law departments take those first-version AI use policies that are very much “thou shalt not” and turn them into more easily readable, appropriate governance positions that inform the conversation with clients. If anyone wants to find out more about our advisory services, they can find me or Cheryl Wilson Griffin on LinkedIn, or they can visit legaltechnologyhub.com.

Marlene Gebauer (02:05)

Thank you, Sam. I mean, it is important to have AI policy in plain language so people understand it.

Sam Moore (02:11)

Absolutely.

Marlene Gebauer (02:19)

Welcome to The Geek in Review, the podcast focused on innovative and creative ideas in the legal industry. I’m Marlene Gebauer.

Greg Lambert (02:26)

And I’m Greg Lambert, and today we are examining the complete deconstruction of the traditional law firm. For decades, the legal industry was defined by centralization, kind of bringing the talent, the technology, the overhead, and the clients under one structured, highly leveraged roof and partnership pyramid. But a new model is proving you can unbundle law firms, keeping the elite talent and the enterprise technology while stripping away the rigid hierarchy.

Marlene Gebauer (02:56)

Our guest today is operating at the absolute forefront of this shift in the European and Latin American markets. Manuel Deó is the co-founder and co-CEO of Ambar Partners, which recently secured a Band One ranking in Chambers as a leading alternative legal service provider. Before launching Ambar, Manuel was the youngest Spanish lawyer to make partner at Latham & Watkins, eventually leading their corporate and M&A practice in Spain.

Greg Lambert (03:25)

And Manuel and his co-founder, Rosa Espín, have built what they describe as a legal operating system. It’s a digital platform called Ambar Haus that connects a highly vetted, curated community of over 400 senior independent lawyers with multinational enterprise clients. They are deploying enterprise tools like Harvey AI at scale, across borders, and completely rethinking how legal capacity is consumed and built.

Marlene Gebauer (03:55)

Manuel, welcome to The Geek in Review.

Manuel Deó (03:57)

Thank you, Marlene. Thank you, Greg, for having me. It’s a true pleasure. Thank you.

Marlene Gebauer (04:03)

So Manuel, you went from leading corporate and private equity at Latham & Watkins in Spain to co-founding Ambar. What did you see in the traditional legal market that convinced you to build a different kind of legal business?

Manuel Deó (04:18)

First, I should say that I loved Big Law, right? I always consider myself a son of the old model, and I’m a grateful son for many different reasons. Latham, in particular, where I was a partner, taught me what excellence, intensity, and global execution look like.

I did not build Ambar because I believed traditional law firms were broken. This is something people sometimes ask me. I built it with Rosa because no single institution is optimized for every type of legal need. We kept seeing two false choices when we were back at Big Law.

On one side, you had outstanding lawyers who had to choose between institutional prestige and professional autonomy. On the other side, you had clients who had to choose between adding permanent headcount to their teams or engaging a traditional law firm, usually through a narrow model, an hourly-rate basis.

But a significant part of corporate legal demand is neither permanent nor junior. It is senior, important, urgent, and variable. The market has never been short of talent. I think quite the opposite. What it’s been short of is an architecture capable of deploying that talent differently.

We wanted to separate expertise from real estate in specific offices on specific streets, seniority from hierarchy, and value from time. I think the traditional legal market had two gears. One is hire a lawyer, or hire a law firm. What we built is a gearbox. I think that’s the broader opportunity we’re building here. Not to replace law firms or internal legal departments, but to give clients a more intelligent, flexible way of building legal capacity around the problem they have.

So that’s what we’re doing and why we went from Big Law to building Ambar.

Greg Lambert (06:38)

As you were building this with Rosa, how were you thinking of structuring it in a way that was both enticing for the lawyers you wanted to recruit and also for the clients to understand what the business model was and what you were offering?

Manuel Deó (07:02)

Right. I think for lawyers the most important part of our model is freedom. We give lawyers freedom. Freedom to decide which projects they are engaged on, for which clients, for what fees, on what terms, and at what moment of the year they want to work. They have full control to decide which type of projects they are a part of. That’s the main value proposition for lawyers.

On the other side, for clients, it’s twofold. One is having full control. Full control over the cost, and also over the specific lawyer delivering the legal service. When you’re part of other, more traditional models, you hire a firm, but you don’t always have full control over who’s doing the job, right? Who’s doing the legal work? Because they have a number of people there doing the legal delivery.

So from one specific point, that’s full control over cost and delivery. And second, access to highly vetted lawyers where you have full control over the talent, expertise, and knowledge of the lawyer, who is highly vetted by third parties, not only by us, but by other clients, other colleagues, and, obviously, traditional firms.

Marlene Gebauer (08:17)

See, this is interesting. When we talk about value, we’re usually talking about value to the client, but I think you’re talking about it going both ways. What does the lawyer find valuable to work on, as well as delivering value to the client?

Manuel Deó (08:29)

Yeah, absolutely.

Greg Lambert (08:32)

Marlene mentioned this in the intro, but congratulations on Ambar’s recent Chambers recognition as Band One for ALSPs in Europe. Both you and Rosa were also named individually in Band One as well. The Chambers submissions, I know outside of legal no one knows what those are, but it’s a big deal inside legal. So what does that recognition tell you about the legal market’s acceptance of the type of model you’re providing?

Manuel Deó (09:07)

Right. The recognition is specifically for what they call NewLaw, or alternative legal service firms. What that tells me is that the word “alternative,” which is a buzzword used in the sector for many years, is approaching its expiration date.

We’re grateful for a prestigious institution like Chambers recognizing Ambar as Band One with other global companies, but clients validated the model before Chambers did. Chambers has made visible something that was already happening.

I think the true thing is that sophisticated clients are increasingly indifferent to labels and brands. They care about quality, speed, accountability, commercial understanding, and value. The general counsel, which is the name given to the most senior person in the legal department at big corporations and S&P 500 companies, are sophisticated people with a lot of pressure in their companies. They’re typically trusted advisors to the CEO and have a lot of pressure to deliver more value with less.

This recognition demonstrates that top-tier standards exist outside the traditional partnership pyramid. Independence, which is part of our value for lawyers because they are independent lawyers, does not have to mean fragmentation. Flexibility, which is something we provide to our clients, does not have to mean lower quality. Quite the opposite.

A lawyer does not have to sit inside a large institution for that lawyer’s expertise to be institutional-grade, relevant, and appealing to a big client. We are proud of that recognition. But the ranking is a mirror, it’s not a moat. The question is no longer whether clients will accept these models. I think they already do.

The hard question for me is who will scale the model without diluting trust, quality, or accountability.

Marlene Gebauer (11:33)

So I want to dig in a little bit at how the platform works.

Manuel Deó (11:38)

Sure.

Marlene Gebauer (11:39)

Ambar describes itself as a global platform of independent senior legal talent and as an operating system for flexible, borderless legal work. So walk us through what that operating system provides to lawyers and clients.

Manuel Deó (11:55)

Sure. I sometimes regret using the word “platform,” although people sometimes refer to us like that, because people picture a database of lawyers with better typography, basically. We’re not putting lawyers on a website and calling it innovation, right? It’s a totally different thing.

Traditionally, a law firm bundled several things together. The talent, the brand, the clients, the technology, compliance, operations, and professional community. When a great lawyer became independent, that lawyer did not lose their expertise, but they often lost access to that entire institutional bundle.

What Ambar is doing is rebuilding those capabilities as a shared infrastructure without asking the lawyer or boutique law firm to give up their independence, their economics, brand, or professional identity.

For independent lawyers and specialist boutiques, which are the types of lawyers who are part of Ambar, we think about an operating system through four Bs.

One is belonging. You are an independent lawyer, but you’re also part of something bigger. Independence is professionally liberating when people leave certain institutions, but it also becomes lonely. We provide a curated professional community, practice groups, city chapters, trusted peers, knowledge-sharing spaces, and opportunities to collaborate with other exceptional lawyers. That’s the first one, belonging.

The second one is business. We provide access to sophisticated referrals among the different lawyers, cross-selling opportunities, team formation, and the infrastructure required to transform expertise into a sustainable legal business. Many outstanding lawyers do not want to spend half their lives becoming salespeople. That’s typically something lawyers don’t like to do, or chasing invoices, or learning digital marketing, or whatever. They want to practice law at the highest level. We help create those conditions around them to make that possible. So that’s the second B, business.

The third one is backbone. That’s the operational machinery around legal work. The intake, the proposals for the client, building the proposal with your scope, your fees, the contractual engagement letter, the specific conflict processes, KYC, anti-money laundering, insurance, invoicing, collections, all the red tape around sophisticated legal service delivery. We take care of that. The lawyer remains independent but no longer has to rebuild an entire institution alone with all the compliance and KYC around that. So that’s the third part, backbone.

The fourth one is the badge. That’s certification of your expertise, reputation, positioning, and institutional credibility, which is important in our sector and, obviously, in any professional service. We give independent experts and boutiques the ability to compete for sophisticated legal work that was historically reserved for larger organizations while preserving their own identity.

We are also building that with AI. AI is becoming more important in any profession, but obviously in legal. There are many players, frontier models building legal verticals, and AI legal-specific companies building legal tools. We have agreements with certain legal AI tools to deliver that legal AI expertise and those tools for our lawyers.

Greg Lambert (16:08)

Let me point at that last, almost like a fifth level here on the tech stack. How do you set up the attorneys on the technology stack so they have access to the tools, but then they also understand, say, how to use the tools, the interoperability between them, and all of that? How do you look at your tech stack?

Marlene Gebauer (16:28)

Responsibly.

Manuel Deó (16:34)

Right. I think we’re moving into a moment in which knowledge will be a commodity. That’s something hard for a lawyer because we’ve been, and I still consider myself a lawyer, tested for our knowledge of specific verticals, specific cases, specific contracts. But that’s a commodity.

I think the key here is that lawyers need to move from that sort of mantra where knowledge was key to a mantra where judgment will be the key driver of sophisticated legal services moving forward.

That’s our focus. Giving lawyers the ability to control, train, and use these tools, have full knowledge of the different AI tools available, and know that certain tools are available and helpful for specific needs while others are better for other needs. And second, providing judgment to that sort of legal service delivery.

The technology we’re building with other partners is allowing that judgment to develop memory, speed, and consistency, which are likely the three things clients are asking for.

Memory in terms of, “I want all my proprietary data, all my proprietary information to be stored. I want the AI to learn from my prior experience and from my knowledge.” Speed in terms of efficiency and time of delivery. And consistency. “I want to control that all my answers, all my legal advice, are consistent with my prior advice.”

That’s what we’re building. We’re building it with training, obviously, with different dedicated people in the different AI companies we’re partnering with. It’s not a one-shot process. It’s long.

We have more than 300 lawyers in our community currently from different backgrounds, different seniorities, and different geographies. I think sophisticated lawyers are typically tech savvy, but obviously not all of them have the same appetite to learn and the same ability to be aware of what AI is and what AI delivers to them.

Marlene Gebauer (18:59)

It’s interesting. You distinguish between knowledge as a commodity versus judgment, where I think a lot of firms would say their internal knowledge of things is kind of their IP. So how do you distinguish the two?

Manuel Deó (19:17)

There’s been a great debate around that topic lately in Big Law, basically because many firms have realized that if you hire an AI frontier model or AI legal solution, and you upload certain documentation to that AI tool, you might lose control over that information and not even know where that knowledge will end up.

So we’re building what we call the expert twins, which is a specific layer of information and documentation for each and every lawyer who is part of our community.

That’s basically a controlled, evolving system built so that the specific expert has approved knowledge. Knowledge that they approve, which is valid, which is dedicated. Picture a contract, picture a court case, something they’ve been validly involved in and they know that knowledge is valid. It’s been certified by them, with playbooks and experience specifically uploaded by that lawyer, and building a second layer of information validated by that lawyer.

That helps the lawyer trust the information being used by the AI tool.

Greg Lambert (20:46)

I want to switch over and look at Ambar from your clients’ perspective. I know a lot of them are looking at adding internal headcount or engaging with a traditional law firm for their legal needs. So how do you approach your clients and kind of sell to them what your platform at Ambar provides instead of these traditional methods?

Manuel Deó (21:15)

Sure. We use a simple rule. Fixed demand deserves fixed cost. Variable demand deserves variable capacity. Rare expertise deserves access and not ownership.

What I mean by that is that a company should hire internally, as an FTE, as a full-time employee, when the work is permanent, predictable, and central to its institutional knowledge, even typically sensitive core strategic information or knowledge in that organization.

But it should engage a traditional law firm when it needs institutional firepower, a highly leveraged team, court representation, a regulated local structure, or the resources required for a bet-the-company matter. M&A, capital markets, all those major, important transactions in the life of a company.

But Ambar sits between those two options when the need is important but variable, when they require senior expertise quickly, or when they need someone operating close to the business without making a permanent addition to the organization.

So you might have a fractional lawyer working 10, 20, 30 hours a week. It might be a leave of absence of one of your colleagues, post-acquisition integration, an internal expansion, a specialist regulatory problem, an investigation, litigation support for a specific period of time, or additional capacity during a peak of work.

In 2025, we handled approximately 300 projects, 293 projects, for 140 clients. More than 70% of that work was fractional counsel work, which is an external lawyer dedicated to your team as a natural extension of your in-house team.

This is important because fractional work is not simply a short secondment. The lawyer in a fractional project becomes part of the client’s operating rhythm, but the capacity remains adjustable. The client gains seniority, continuity, and business context without automatically adding permanent fixed cost.

Sometimes the problem is urgent, but that doesn’t mean the organization chart should become permanent. Clients do not always need another lawyer. They need the right expertise at the precise moment when that expertise becomes valuable.

More especially now, we’re in an uncertain moment where people don’t know, from a macroeconomic perspective, what’s going to happen. In many verticals and industries, there’s a lot of uncertainty. Of course, AI is bringing even more uncertainty in the legal sector.

Many clients, many general counsel, look at the fractional model as a quick, efficient, and flexible manner of accessing capacity without adding permanent headcount.

Marlene Gebauer (24:46)

So operating across jurisdictions with hundreds of independent lawyers, I picture, creates difficult questions around conflicts, privilege, professional ethics, data security, and AI use.

Greg Lambert (24:55)

A little bit.

Marlene Gebauer (24:59)

So how are all those responsibilities allocated and managed, and who’s ultimately accountable to the client?

Manuel Deó (25:11)

Sure. Independence must never mean ambiguity. In fact, a distributed model like ours only works when responsibility is more explicit, not less.

The allocation is clear. The lawyer remains professionally responsible for legal judgment, conflict checks, privilege, and all the ethical obligations applicable in the relevant jurisdiction in which they are barred or qualified.

Ambar is accountable for the operating environment we control. The certification of that lawyer, the selection, the contracting, the insurance we provide to our clients, the cybersecurity standards, governance, process, compliance, anti-money laundering, monitoring, and escalation.

In particular, one of the things you’ve mentioned is conflicts, conflict checks, which are a critical part of our business. Those are assessed in relation to the individual lawyer and the particular engagement.

We do not create one central environment in which independent lawyers access confidential information belonging to the clients of other lawyers in the community. We would never do that.

Each professional, each lawyer, retains responsibility for their own practice and professional obligations, supported by our engagement processes and infrastructure.

Privilege is addressed through the structure of the engagement and the rules of the relevant jurisdiction applicable to that engagement. It’s never something we simply assume because technology is involved.

AI use is also governed by clear principles of client requirements, approved tools, defined data boundaries, confidentiality, and human review. As you might expect, we have B2B enterprise clients who are sophisticated. They all have AI governance and data privacy policies which we need to comply with and be audited against.

Where local rules require work to be delivered through a regulated law firm or a particular professional structure, the engagement must reflect that.

So that’s what we do. We’re careful to do that and do not use the independence of those lawyers as a liability escape hatch.

We think distributed delivery should distribute capability, not responsibility. The client should never have to guess who owns the risk. We’re clear. The engagement letter covers that.

We have an engagement letter where the client, the lawyer, and Ambar are parties to the same relationship because we believe in transparency and each party knowing who owns what and who’s responsible for each part of the legal delivery.

Greg Lambert (28:21)

Well, I think this ties in nicely with the next question. I want to talk to you about Ambar’s community, its culture, and some of the interesting things I’ve seen.

As I was driving into work this morning, I was listening to something and someone mentioned culture at an organization. They defined it in a way that makes sense, but I hadn’t heard it quite this way before. Culture is a set of rules and guidelines on how a person should perform and act in the environment in order to succeed within this community.

When you have a distributed network of independent lawyers, let me ask you up front, how do you prevent this independent contractor from feeling like a transactional database of freelance attorneys? Let me start with that.

Manuel Deó (29:30)

Sure. It’s a long process. One is the right selection of the lawyers, so the vetting of that lawyer, being super demanding on the type of lawyer who is part of the community. We’re picky on that.

I hate to say that, but 95% of the lawyers who request being admitted to Ambar are not able to do it. So we have less than a 4% admission rate right now.

We require those lawyers to come from, or to have expertise in, a closed-ended list of law firms or in-house departments, which gives us certainty on the type of lawyer, the type of culture, and the work ethic around that lawyer.

We take that certification and admission process seriously. We’re part of it through the vetting of that lawyer with third-party references, but also with an in-person meeting with my co-founder, Rosa, who sits with each and every lawyer who’s part of Ambar and wants to be part of it. So we’re careful with that.

That’s one thing. Second, we have a clear code of practice. Obviously, when you’re talking about sophisticated lawyers, these lawyers come from specific backgrounds. They are subject to the ethical standards of their jurisdictions. This is a small market, and there’s tremendous ownership of each person’s reputation and brand.

We’ve never had any issue with that. We’re careful with it. We always have to be listening to our clients regarding the feedback we get on our lawyers in connection with our projects.

We’ve been disruptive there, too, because we’ve been proactively asking for feedback, which is something that’s not common in this sector, and getting the client to verbalize the feedback they have on their lawyers, put that on the record, and make that transparent to the lawyer.

So we’re careful about that. Obviously, it’s a distributed model. Ambar is accountable for the system and the lawyer is accountable for the legal judgment and the legal delivery. That’s clear. I think that’s something that’s also been clear for our clients.

Greg Lambert (32:24)

There’s one more thing you do in community that’s interesting to me, and that’s your communications with your clients.

You’ve put out a newsletter that I think you call Dr. No, and it’s read by thousands of general counsel. But instead of talking about case law updates and changes in regulation, you write about leadership, legal operations, and strategy.

How do your clients respond to a different approach like this?

Manuel Deó (33:10)

Sure. Dr. No, and by the way, the name comes from how certain in-house lawyers are described in their companies because they’re always saying no.

What we try to say there is that we need to put our clients at the center of the conversation, which is something that’s not common in the legal sector.

We’ve always been talking about the rainmakers in this law firm. We talked about Chambers before. Chambers has a lot of rankings, but they’ve always concentrated on law firms and not on in-house lawyers and general counsel.

What we’re trying to suggest here is that we should change the conversation, put the general counsel in the middle of the conversation, and offer different tools those lawyers in those companies need.

I’m not going to teach law to a general counsel or a senior lawyer in an important company. I would never intend to do that. But we talk about things they need to become more influential in their companies, to become more central.

Think about HR managers 20 years ago, who became influential people in their companies through many different changes. One of them is a change of name, which changed to Chief People Officer or Chief Talent Officer, and they became senior and influential people on the board.

Or CFOs, who went from being financial analysts or controllers to becoming influential people in their companies.

What we’re trying to provide are those tools for general counsel to become as influential as a Chief Legal Officer, someone who’s talking about metrics, return on investment, how much savings the department provides to the company, and treating a legal department as another separate business unit of a company.

Greg Lambert (35:25)

All right, well, we are at the end. We want to have you look back before we ask you our crystal ball question. So Manuel, what is something that’s different today, or wasn’t necessarily true a year ago?

Manuel Deó (35:48)

I don’t want to talk about AI because it would be too obvious. Obviously, every week we have a new development in AI.

Marlene Gebauer (35:59)

So boring, AI.

Manuel Deó (36:01)

Right. So it’s something I would avoid mentioning. It’s a difficult question, but I think we’ve run through a process where general counsel don’t want to be seen as a cost center in their companies and want to be seen as something different.

That’s changing the conversation, and it’s changing the type of solutions we as legal suppliers need to provide our clients.

Because it’s not a matter of an hourly rate or, “I’m the best expert in this specific industry.” It’s a matter of how much value did I provide to my client? Because I need to help that client explain to their CEO, their CFO, the value they’re bringing.

That’s something we’re starting to see now that we didn’t see a year, a year and a half ago. How important value contribution is, and being a true investment as a legal department in a company, is changing the mindset of many general counsel.

Marlene Gebauer (37:11)

Well, if that question was hard, this one might be a little harder.

Greg Lambert (37:14)

Yeah.

Marlene Gebauer (37:15)

This time we’re going to ask you to look into the future.

Manuel Deó (37:17)

Wow.

Marlene Gebauer (37:18)

Our crystal ball question is, what’s the single biggest change you see coming for how firms operate and interact with their clients?

Manuel Deó (37:29)

That’s also a hard one, yeah. I think the single biggest change will be that traditional firms will stop being the only meaningful unit of legal delivery.

Law firms will be important, but they will become more porous. The future legal team will combine small strategic in-house core teams. They will engage traditional firms when they need them, but they will also engage independent senior specialists, specialist boutiques, managed services, and AI agents to deliver legal solutions appropriate to the specifics of that legal need.

Those capabilities will be assembled by each legal department in a dynamic manner around each problem.

I think clients will move from asking, “Which firm should we hire?” to, “What is the best configuration of people, technology, knowledge, and risk for this particular matter?”

The traditional pyramid was designed for a world in which legal knowledge was scarce and coordination was expensive. That will be totally different.

AI makes information, as I said before, increasingly abundant and truly a commodity, in my opinion. Technology makes coordination much cheaper. I think that will change the geometry of the industry.

I think we’ll be seeing legal departments more as trusted orchestrators of capabilities. That’s how I see the future going forward. AI, boring matter, but I know it’s something we always…

Greg Lambert (39:26)

Well, I think you handled both of those questions well.

Marlene Gebauer (39:27)

Yeah, I think you did a great job.

Manuel Deó (39:28)

Yeah.

Greg Lambert (39:30)

Well, Manuel Deó, thank you so much for taking time out of your day to talk to us. This has been great.

Marlene Gebauer (39:37)

Thank you.

Manuel Deó (39:37)

Thank you. Thanks for having me.

Marlene Gebauer (39:40)

And thanks to all of you for listening. And don’t forget to like and subscribe on Substack, YouTube, and LinkedIn.

Greg Lambert (39:48)

And Manuel, where’s the best place for people to follow your content and to learn more about Ambar?

Manuel Deó (39:54)

Well, the best place to follow me is LinkedIn. I write regularly about the business of law, leadership, innovation, entrepreneurship, and AI.

I also publish a daily newsletter called Dr. No for legal leaders who want to be more innovative, about mental models, about cool stories. Less than a one-minute read each and every day.

Many clients tell me they resend it and forward it to their teams to send specific messages.

And that’s pretty much it. You can find Dr. No on our webpage, ambarpartners.com, under Dr. No.

Marlene Gebauer (40:38)

And as always, the music here is from Jerry David DeCicca. Thank you, Jerry, and bye, everybody.
news.bodyText:
What happens when you separate elite legal talent from the traditional law firm structure? This week on The Geek in Review , we talk with Manuel Deó , co-founder and co-CEO of Ambar Partners , about a model designed around senior independent lawyers, flexible capacity, enterprise technology, and client choice. Deó explains why he and co-founder Rosa Espín did not set out to replace Big Law, but instead to address a gap between permanent in-house hiring and traditional outside counsel.

At the center of Ambar’s model is a simple idea: legal demand comes in different shapes, and the delivery model should match the problem. Deó describes how Ambar gives lawyers control over the clients, projects, fees, and schedules they take on, while giving clients greater visibility into cost and the individual lawyers doing the work. He also discusses Ambar’s recent Chambers recognition and argues that the term “alternative” is starting to lose some of its usefulness as clients grow more comfortable assembling legal services from a wider range of providers.

Deó walks through what Ambar calls its legal operating system, built around belonging, business, backbone, and badge. The model combines a professional community with business development, compliance, contracting, billing, technology, and institutional credibility for independent lawyers and specialist boutiques. Ambar’s public materials describe a shared technology environment that includes tools such as Harvey, Microsoft Copilot, Legora, and other legal technology products. The goal, according to Deó, is to give independent lawyers access to the infrastructure associated with a large firm without requiring them to give up professional independence.

The conversation also turns to AI, knowledge, and professional judgment. Deó argues that legal knowledge is becoming more abundant while judgment grows more valuable. He describes Ambar’s work on “expert twins,” where approved knowledge, prior work, playbooks, and experience associated with an individual lawyer form a trusted layer for AI-assisted work. That emphasis on institutional knowledge and permissions echoes a broader trend across legal AI, where vendors are increasingly focused on connecting AI systems to trusted internal work product and organizational context.

Finally, Deó offers a broader view of where legal delivery is heading. He sees legal departments assembling teams dynamically from in-house lawyers, traditional firms, independent specialists, boutiques, managed services, and AI agents based on the needs of a particular matter. Instead of asking which firm to hire, clients increasingly have reason to ask what combination of people, technology, expertise, and risk structure best fits the work. For Deó, the future belongs less to a single dominant delivery model and more to legal departments acting as orchestrators of capability.
