: geekinreviewpodcast@gmail.com

Hey everyone, I’m Greg Lambert, and this week on The Geek in Review, we have with us Manuel Deó from Ambar Partners. But first, let’s get some insights from our friends at Legal Technology Hub.

Hi, I’m Marlene Gebauer from The Geek in Review. I have Sam Moore here from Legal Technology Hub. He’s going to tell us about AI governance from the advisory side.

Thank you. Good to see you again. Well, in the advisory team at Legal Technology Hub, we’ve been having a lot of conversations with clients about AI governance. Now, most law firms and departments have at least an AI policy of some kind, and there are some broad standards which are starting to emerge. A trend we’re seeing at the moment is a shift away from policies written in 2023 and 2024, which largely stated what you couldn’t do, and towards a more informative approach which defines different risk categories and makes distinctions between routine, low-risk use of AI and other more substantial use cases. I think that’s appropriate for where we are. It’s also what clients are coming to expect from their advisors. But one of the bigger challenges we’re seeing right now is, how do you express an AI use policy in such a way that any member of your legal team could explain it to a client? I think that’s still a big challenge for the industry.

I don’t think clients are all that happy if their attorney says, “I’ll have to get back to you about that,” because the attorney is using AI day-to-day. So they should be able to explain the policy themselves. How else do you know they’re complying with it? We’re doing some interesting work at the moment helping law firms and law departments take those first-version AI use policies that are very much “thou shalt not” and turn them into more easily readable, appropriate governance positions that inform the conversation with clients. If anyone wants to find out more about our advisory services, they can find me or Cheryl Wilson Griffin on LinkedIn, or they can visit legaltechnologyhub.com.

Thank you, Sam. I mean, it is important to have AI policy in plain language so people understand it.

Welcome to The Geek in Review, the podcast focused on innovative and creative ideas in the legal industry. I’m Marlene Gebauer.

And I’m Greg Lambert, and today we are examining the complete deconstruction of the traditional law firm. For decades, the legal industry was defined by centralization, kind of bringing the talent, the technology, the overhead, and the clients under one structured, highly leveraged roof and partnership pyramid. But a new model is proving you can unbundle law firms, keeping the elite talent and the enterprise technology while stripping away the rigid hierarchy.

Our guest today is operating at the absolute forefront of this shift in the European and Latin American markets. Manuel Deó is the co-founder and co-CEO of Ambar Partners, which recently secured a Band One ranking in Chambers as a leading alternative legal service provider. Before launching Ambar, Manuel was the youngest Spanish lawyer to make partner at Latham & Watkins, eventually leading their corporate and M&A practice in Spain.

And Manuel and his co-founder, Rosa Espín, have built what they describe as a legal operating system. It’s a digital platform called Ambar Haus that connects a highly vetted, curated community of over 400 senior independent lawyers with multinational enterprise clients. They are deploying enterprise tools like Harvey AI at scale, across borders, and completely rethinking how legal capacity is consumed and built.

Manuel, welcome to The Geek in Review.

Thank you, Marlene. Thank you, Greg, for having me. It’s a true pleasure. Thank you.

So Manuel, you went from leading corporate and private equity at Latham & Watkins in Spain to co-founding Ambar. What did you see in the traditional legal market that convinced you to build a different kind of legal business?

First, I should say that I loved Big Law, right? I always consider myself a son of the old model, and I’m a grateful son for many different reasons. Latham, in particular, where I was a partner, taught me what excellence, intensity, and global execution look like.

I did not build Ambar because I believed traditional law firms were broken. This is something people sometimes ask me. I built it with Rosa because no single institution is optimized for every type of legal need. We kept seeing two false choices when we were back at Big Law.

On one side, you had outstanding lawyers who had to choose between institutional prestige and professional autonomy. On the other side, you had clients who had to choose between adding permanent headcount to their teams or engaging a traditional law firm, usually through a narrow model, an hourly-rate basis.

But a significant part of corporate legal demand is neither permanent nor junior. It is senior, important, urgent, and variable. The market has never been short of talent. I think quite the opposite. What it’s been short of is an architecture capable of deploying that talent differently.

We wanted to separate expertise from real estate in specific offices on specific streets, seniority from hierarchy, and value from time. I think the traditional legal market had two gears. One is hire a lawyer, or hire a law firm. What we built is a gearbox. I think that’s the broader opportunity we’re building here. Not to replace law firms or internal legal departments, but to give clients a more intelligent, flexible way of building legal capacity around the problem they have.

So that’s what we’re doing and why we went from Big Law to building Ambar.

As you were building this with Rosa, how were you thinking of structuring it in a way that was both enticing for the lawyers you wanted to recruit and also for the clients to understand what the business model was and what you were offering?

Right. I think for lawyers the most important part of our model is freedom. We give lawyers freedom. Freedom to decide which projects they are engaged on, for which clients, for what fees, on what terms, and at what moment of the year they want to work. They have full control to decide which type of projects they are a part of. That’s the main value proposition for lawyers.

On the other side, for clients, it’s twofold. One is having full control. Full control over the cost, and also over the specific lawyer delivering the legal service. When you’re part of other, more traditional models, you hire a firm, but you don’t always have full control over who’s doing the job, right? Who’s doing the legal work? Because they have a number of people there doing the legal delivery.

So from one specific point, that’s full control over cost and delivery. And second, access to highly vetted lawyers where you have full control over the talent, expertise, and knowledge of the lawyer, who is highly vetted by third parties, not only by us, but by other clients, other colleagues, and, obviously, traditional firms.

See, this is interesting. When we talk about value, we’re usually talking about value to the client, but I think you’re talking about it going both ways. What does the lawyer find valuable to work on, as well as delivering value to the client?

Marlene mentioned this in the intro, but congratulations on Ambar’s recent Chambers recognition as Band One for ALSPs in Europe. Both you and Rosa were also named individually in Band One as well. The Chambers submissions, I know outside of legal no one knows what those are, but it’s a big deal inside legal. So what does that recognition tell you about the legal market’s acceptance of the type of model you’re providing?

Right. The recognition is specifically for what they call NewLaw, or alternative legal service firms. What that tells me is that the word “alternative,” which is a buzzword used in the sector for many years, is approaching its expiration date.

We’re grateful for a prestigious institution like Chambers recognizing Ambar as Band One with other global companies, but clients validated the model before Chambers did. Chambers has made visible something that was already happening.

I think the true thing is that sophisticated clients are increasingly indifferent to labels and brands. They care about quality, speed, accountability, commercial understanding, and value. The general counsel, which is the name given to the most senior person in the legal department at big corporations and S&P 500 companies, are sophisticated people with a lot of pressure in their companies. They’re typically trusted advisors to the CEO and have a lot of pressure to deliver more value with less.

This recognition demonstrates that top-tier standards exist outside the traditional partnership pyramid. Independence, which is part of our value for lawyers because they are independent lawyers, does not have to mean fragmentation. Flexibility, which is something we provide to our clients, does not have to mean lower quality. Quite the opposite.

A lawyer does not have to sit inside a large institution for that lawyer’s expertise to be institutional-grade, relevant, and appealing to a big client. We are proud of that recognition. But the ranking is a mirror, it’s not a moat. The question is no longer whether clients will accept these models. I think they already do.

The hard question for me is who will scale the model without diluting trust, quality, or accountability.

So I want to dig in a little bit at how the platform works.

Ambar describes itself as a global platform of independent senior legal talent and as an operating system for flexible, borderless legal work. So walk us through what that operating system provides to lawyers and clients.

Sure. I sometimes regret using the word “platform,” although people sometimes refer to us like that, because people picture a database of lawyers with better typography, basically. We’re not putting lawyers on a website and calling it innovation, right? It’s a totally different thing.

Traditionally, a law firm bundled several things together. The talent, the brand, the clients, the technology, compliance, operations, and professional community. When a great lawyer became independent, that lawyer did not lose their expertise, but they often lost access to that entire institutional bundle.

What Ambar is doing is rebuilding those capabilities as a shared infrastructure without asking the lawyer or boutique law firm to give up their independence, their economics, brand, or professional identity.

For independent lawyers and specialist boutiques, which are the types of lawyers who are part of Ambar, we think about an operating system through four Bs.

One is belonging. You are an independent lawyer, but you’re also part of something bigger. Independence is professionally liberating when people leave certain institutions, but it also becomes lonely. We provide a curated professional community, practice groups, city chapters, trusted peers, knowledge-sharing spaces, and opportunities to collaborate with other exceptional lawyers. That’s the first one, belonging.

The second one is business. We provide access to sophisticated referrals among the different lawyers, cross-selling opportunities, team formation, and the infrastructure required to transform expertise into a sustainable legal business. Many outstanding lawyers do not want to spend half their lives becoming salespeople. That’s typically something lawyers don’t like to do, or chasing invoices, or learning digital marketing, or whatever. They want to practice law at the highest level. We help create those conditions around them to make that possible. So that’s the second B, business.

The third one is backbone. That’s the operational machinery around legal work. The intake, the proposals for the client, building the proposal with your scope, your fees, the contractual engagement letter, the specific conflict processes, KYC, anti-money laundering, insurance, invoicing, collections, all the red tape around sophisticated legal service delivery. We take care of that. The lawyer remains independent but no longer has to rebuild an entire institution alone with all the compliance and KYC around that. So that’s the third part, backbone.

The fourth one is the badge. That’s certification of your expertise, reputation, positioning, and institutional credibility, which is important in our sector and, obviously, in any professional service. We give independent experts and boutiques the ability to compete for sophisticated legal work that was historically reserved for larger organizations while preserving their own identity.

We are also building that with AI. AI is becoming more important in any profession, but obviously in legal. There are many players, frontier models building legal verticals, and AI legal-specific companies building legal tools. We have agreements with certain legal AI tools to deliver that legal AI expertise and those tools for our lawyers.

Let me point at that last, almost like a fifth level here on the tech stack. How do you set up the attorneys on the technology stack so they have access to the tools, but then they also understand, say, how to use the tools, the interoperability between them, and all of that? How do you look at your tech stack?

Right. I think we’re moving into a moment in which knowledge will be a commodity. That’s something hard for a lawyer because we’ve been, and I still consider myself a lawyer, tested for our knowledge of specific verticals, specific cases, specific contracts. But that’s a commodity.

I think the key here is that lawyers need to move from that sort of mantra where knowledge was key to a mantra where judgment will be the key driver of sophisticated legal services moving forward.

That’s our focus. Giving lawyers the ability to control, train, and use these tools, have full knowledge of the different AI tools available, and know that certain tools are available and helpful for specific needs while others are better for other needs. And second, providing judgment to that sort of legal service delivery.

The technology we’re building with other partners is allowing that judgment to develop memory, speed, and consistency, which are likely the three things clients are asking for.

Memory in terms of, “I want all my proprietary data, all my proprietary information to be stored. I want the AI to learn from my prior experience and from my knowledge.” Speed in terms of efficiency and time of delivery. And consistency. “I want to control that all my answers, all my legal advice, are consistent with my prior advice.”

That’s what we’re building. We’re building it with training, obviously, with different dedicated people in the different AI companies we’re partnering with. It’s not a one-shot process. It’s long.

We have more than 300 lawyers in our community currently from different backgrounds, different seniorities, and different geographies. I think sophisticated lawyers are typically tech savvy, but obviously not all of them have the same appetite to learn and the same ability to be aware of what AI is and what AI delivers to them.

It’s interesting. You distinguish between knowledge as a commodity versus judgment, where I think a lot of firms would say their internal knowledge of things is kind of their IP. So how do you distinguish the two?

There’s been a great debate around that topic lately in Big Law, basically because many firms have realized that if you hire an AI frontier model or AI legal solution, and you upload certain documentation to that AI tool, you might lose control over that information and not even know where that knowledge will end up.

So we’re building what we call the expert twins, which is a specific layer of information and documentation for each and every lawyer who is part of our community.

That’s basically a controlled, evolving system built so that the specific expert has approved knowledge. Knowledge that they approve, which is valid, which is dedicated. Picture a contract, picture a court case, something they’ve been validly involved in and they know that knowledge is valid. It’s been certified by them, with playbooks and experience specifically uploaded by that lawyer, and building a second layer of information validated by that lawyer.

That helps the lawyer trust the information being used by the AI tool.

I want to switch over and look at Ambar from your clients’ perspective. I know a lot of them are looking at adding internal headcount or engaging with a traditional law firm for their legal needs. So how do you approach your clients and kind of sell to them what your platform at Ambar provides instead of these traditional methods?

Sure. We use a simple rule. Fixed demand deserves fixed cost. Variable demand deserves variable capacity. Rare expertise deserves access and not ownership.

What I mean by that is that a company should hire internally, as an FTE, as a full-time employee, when the work is permanent, predictable, and central to its institutional knowledge, even typically sensitive core strategic information or knowledge in that organization.

But it should engage a traditional law firm when it needs institutional firepower, a highly leveraged team, court representation, a regulated local structure, or the resources required for a bet-the-company matter. M&A, capital markets, all those major, important transactions in the life of a company.

But Ambar sits between those two options when the need is important but variable, when they require senior expertise quickly, or when they need someone operating close to the business without making a permanent addition to the organization.

So you might have a fractional lawyer working 10, 20, 30 hours a week. It might be a leave of absence of one of your colleagues, post-acquisition integration, an internal expansion, a specialist regulatory problem, an investigation, litigation support for a specific period of time, or additional capacity during a peak of work.

In 2025, we handled approximately 300 projects, 293 projects, for 140 clients. More than 70% of that work was fractional counsel work, which is an external lawyer dedicated to your team as a natural extension of your in-house team.

This is important because fractional work is not simply a short secondment. The lawyer in a fractional project becomes part of the client’s operating rhythm, but the capacity remains adjustable. The client gains seniority, continuity, and business context without automatically adding permanent fixed cost.

Sometimes the problem is urgent, but that doesn’t mean the organization chart should become permanent. Clients do not always need another lawyer. They need the right expertise at the precise moment when that expertise becomes valuable.

More especially now, we’re in an uncertain moment where people don’t know, from a macroeconomic perspective, what’s going to happen. In many verticals and industries, there’s a lot of uncertainty. Of course, AI is bringing even more uncertainty in the legal sector.

Many clients, many general counsel, look at the fractional model as a quick, efficient, and flexible manner of accessing capacity without adding permanent headcount.

So operating across jurisdictions with hundreds of independent lawyers, I picture, creates difficult questions around conflicts, privilege, professional ethics, data security, and AI use.

So how are all those responsibilities allocated and managed, and who’s ultimately accountable to the client?

Sure. Independence must never mean ambiguity. In fact, a distributed model like ours only works when responsibility is more explicit, not less.

The allocation is clear. The lawyer remains professionally responsible for legal judgment, conflict checks, privilege, and all the ethical obligations applicable in the relevant jurisdiction in which they are barred or qualified.

Ambar is accountable for the operating environment we control. The certification of that lawyer, the selection, the contracting, the insurance we provide to our clients, the cybersecurity standards, governance, process, compliance, anti-money laundering, monitoring, and escalation.

In particular, one of the things you’ve mentioned is conflicts, conflict checks, which are a critical part of our business. Those are assessed in relation to the individual lawyer and the particular engagement.

We do not create one central environment in which independent lawyers access confidential information belonging to the clients of other lawyers in the community. We would never do that.

Each professional, each lawyer, retains responsibility for their own practice and professional obligations, supported by our engagement processes and infrastructure.

Privilege is addressed through the structure of the engagement and the rules of the relevant jurisdiction applicable to that engagement. It’s never something we simply assume because technology is involved.

AI use is also governed by clear principles of client requirements, approved tools, defined data boundaries, confidentiality, and human review. As you might expect, we have B2B enterprise clients who are sophisticated. They all have AI governance and data privacy policies which we need to comply with and be audited against.

Where local rules require work to be delivered through a regulated law firm or a particular professional structure, the engagement must reflect that.

So that’s what we do. We’re careful to do that and do not use the independence of those lawyers as a liability escape hatch.

We think distributed delivery should distribute capability, not responsibility. The client should never have to guess who owns the risk. We’re clear. The engagement letter covers that.

We have an engagement letter where the client, the lawyer, and Ambar are parties to the same relationship because we believe in transparency and each party knowing who owns what and who’s responsible for each part of the legal delivery.

Well, I think this ties in nicely with the next question. I want to talk to you about Ambar’s community, its culture, and some of the interesting things I’ve seen.

As I was driving into work this morning, I was listening to something and someone mentioned culture at an organization. They defined it in a way that makes sense, but I hadn’t heard it quite this way before. Culture is a set of rules and guidelines on how a person should perform and act in the environment in order to succeed within this community.

When you have a distributed network of independent lawyers, let me ask you up front, how do you prevent this independent contractor from feeling like a transactional database of freelance attorneys? Let me start with that.

Sure. It’s a long process. One is the right selection of the lawyers, so the vetting of that lawyer, being super demanding on the type of lawyer who is part of the community. We’re picky on that.

I hate to say that, but 95% of the lawyers who request being admitted to Ambar are not able to do it. So we have less than a 4% admission rate right now.

We require those lawyers to come from, or to have expertise in, a closed-ended list of law firms or in-house departments, which gives us certainty on the type of lawyer, the type of culture, and the work ethic around that lawyer.

We take that certification and admission process seriously. We’re part of it through the vetting of that lawyer with third-party references, but also with an in-person meeting with my co-founder, Rosa, who sits with each and every lawyer who’s part of Ambar and wants to be part of it. So we’re careful with that.

That’s one thing. Second, we have a clear code of practice. Obviously, when you’re talking about sophisticated lawyers, these lawyers come from specific backgrounds. They are subject to the ethical standards of their jurisdictions. This is a small market, and there’s tremendous ownership of each person’s reputation and brand.

We’ve never had any issue with that. We’re careful with it. We always have to be listening to our clients regarding the feedback we get on our lawyers in connection with our projects.

We’ve been disruptive there, too, because we’ve been proactively asking for feedback, which is something that’s not common in this sector, and getting the client to verbalize the feedback they have on their lawyers, put that on the record, and make that transparent to the lawyer.

So we’re careful about that. Obviously, it’s a distributed model. Ambar is accountable for the system and the lawyer is accountable for the legal judgment and the legal delivery. That’s clear. I think that’s something that’s also been clear for our clients.

There’s one more thing you do in community that’s interesting to me, and that’s your communications with your clients.

You’ve put out a newsletter that I think you call Dr. No, and it’s read by thousands of general counsel. But instead of talking about case law updates and changes in regulation, you write about leadership, legal operations, and strategy.

How do your clients respond to a different approach like this?

Sure. Dr. No, and by the way, the name comes from how certain in-house lawyers are described in their companies because they’re always saying no.

What we try to say there is that we need to put our clients at the center of the conversation, which is something that’s not common in the legal sector.

We’ve always been talking about the rainmakers in this law firm. We talked about Chambers before. Chambers has a lot of rankings, but they’ve always concentrated on law firms and not on in-house lawyers and general counsel.

What we’re trying to suggest here is that we should change the conversation, put the general counsel in the middle of the conversation, and offer different tools those lawyers in those companies need.

I’m not going to teach law to a general counsel or a senior lawyer in an important company. I would never intend to do that. But we talk about things they need to become more influential in their companies, to become more central.

Think about HR managers 20 years ago, who became influential people in their companies through many different changes. One of them is a change of name, which changed to Chief People Officer or Chief Talent Officer, and they became senior and influential people on the board.

Or CFOs, who went from being financial analysts or controllers to becoming influential people in their companies.

What we’re trying to provide are those tools for general counsel to become as influential as a Chief Legal Officer, someone who’s talking about metrics, return on investment, how much savings the department provides to the company, and treating a legal department as another separate business unit of a company.

All right, well, we are at the end. We want to have you look back before we ask you our crystal ball question. So Manuel, what is something that’s different today, or wasn’t necessarily true a year ago?

I don’t want to talk about AI because it would be too obvious. Obviously, every week we have a new development in AI.

Right. So it’s something I would avoid mentioning. It’s a difficult question, but I think we’ve run through a process where general counsel don’t want to be seen as a cost center in their companies and want to be seen as something different.

That’s changing the conversation, and it’s changing the type of solutions we as legal suppliers need to provide our clients.

Because it’s not a matter of an hourly rate or, “I’m the best expert in this specific industry.” It’s a matter of how much value did I provide to my client? Because I need to help that client explain to their CEO, their CFO, the value they’re bringing.

That’s something we’re starting to see now that we didn’t see a year, a year and a half ago. How important value contribution is, and being a true investment as a legal department in a company, is changing the mindset of many general counsel.

Well, if that question was hard, this one might be a little harder.

This time we’re going to ask you to look into the future.

Our crystal ball question is, what’s the single biggest change you see coming for how firms operate and interact with their clients?

That’s also a hard one, yeah. I think the single biggest change will be that traditional firms will stop being the only meaningful unit of legal delivery.

Law firms will be important, but they will become more porous. The future legal team will combine small strategic in-house core teams. They will engage traditional firms when they need them, but they will also engage independent senior specialists, specialist boutiques, managed services, and AI agents to deliver legal solutions appropriate to the specifics of that legal need.

Those capabilities will be assembled by each legal department in a dynamic manner around each problem.

I think clients will move from asking, “Which firm should we hire?” to, “What is the best configuration of people, technology, knowledge, and risk for this particular matter?”

The traditional pyramid was designed for a world in which legal knowledge was scarce and coordination was expensive. That will be totally different.

AI makes information, as I said before, increasingly abundant and truly a commodity, in my opinion. Technology makes coordination much cheaper. I think that will change the geometry of the industry.

I think we’ll be seeing legal departments more as trusted orchestrators of capabilities. That’s how I see the future going forward. AI, boring matter, but I know it’s something we always…

Well, I think you handled both of those questions well.

Yeah, I think you did a great job.

Well, Manuel Deó, thank you so much for taking time out of your day to talk to us. This has been great.

Thank you. Thanks for having me.

And thanks to all of you for listening. And don’t forget to like and subscribe on Substack, YouTube, and LinkedIn.

And Manuel, where’s the best place for people to follow your content and to learn more about Ambar?

Well, the best place to follow me is LinkedIn. I write regularly about the business of law, leadership, innovation, entrepreneurship, and AI.

I also publish a daily newsletter called Dr. No for legal leaders who want to be more innovative, about mental models, about cool stories. Less than a one-minute read each and every day.

Many clients tell me they resend it and forward it to their teams to send specific messages.

And that’s pretty much it. You can find Dr. No on our webpage, ambarpartners.com, under Dr. No.

And as always, the music here is from Jerry David DeCicca. Thank you, Jerry, and bye, everybody.

research.titleEn: JudgmentLens: Human-AI Sensemaking of Complex Legal Judgments
research.titleZh: JudgmentLens：面向复杂法律判决的人机意义建构
research.abstractEn: Judicial judgments are increasingly available, yet dense language and distributed relationships among facts, evidence, reasoning, and rulings remain difficult for non-experts to interpret. Through a mixed-methods formative study with Chinese non-expert readers (survey N=34; interviews N=6), we identified structural, interpretive, verification, and action breakdowns. We developed JudgmentLens, an AI-augmented reading system combining persistent case representations, adaptive explanations, and traceable links from generated interpretations to judgment passages. In a counterbalanced within-subject evaluation (N=16), participants completed tasks faster with JudgmentLens than with conventional PDF reading and reported lower workload and greater self-reported decision understanding, while rubric-scored comprehension did not differ reliably. An exploratory PDF+DeepSeek probe suggested that conversational AI supported formulated questions while leaving question formulation, answer integration, and source checking largely to users. We contribute an empirical account of non-expert judgment sensemaking and design strategies for inspectable, source-grounded AI mediation.
research.abstractZh: 司法判决日益公开可及，然而其密集的语言以及事实、证据、推理与裁决之间分散的关系，仍令非专业读者难以解读。通过一项针对中国非专业读者的混合方法形成性研究（问卷调查 N=34；访谈 N=6），我们识别出结构、解释、验证与行动层面的障碍。我们开发了 JudgmentLens，一个AI增强的阅读系统，结合了持久案件表征、自适应解释，以及从生成解释到判决段落的可追溯链接。在一项平衡的被试内评估（N=16）中，参与者使用 JudgmentLens 完成任务的速度快于使用传统PDF阅读，并报告了更低的工作负荷和更高的自评决策理解，而评分量表所测的理解程度并无可靠差异。一项探索性的PDF+DeepSeek探测表明，对话式AI支持了已提出的问题，但在问题形成、答案整合与来源核查方面仍主要依赖用户自身。我们贡献了对非专业判决意义建构的实证描述，以及面向可审查、有来源依据的AI中介的设计策略。

news.titleZh: 华盛顿特区最高法院因四个虚假引注驳回诉讼文书，并称自身制裁权限不明
news.summaryZh: 哥伦比亚特区上诉法院于9月3日驳回了德意志银行受托人的一份诉讼文书，原因是其中引用的四个案例并不存在。该法院是华盛顿特区的终审法院，而非联邦哥伦比亚特区巡回上诉法院。签署该文书的每位律所律师均负有责任，但一位法官随即在同一文件中长篇主张对此作更狭义的解释。法院认为其制裁权限的整体范围尚不明确，并将该问题提交至规则委员会处理。现行规则中，第38条仅涉及 frivolous appeals 而非诉讼文书，第46条仅涉及律师执业准入，而固有权力需要恶意行为的认定，但本案记录不足以支持该认定。高级法官斯蒂芬·H·格利克曼单独撰文，主张对规则作更窄的解读，并指出现有规则似乎仅允许公开谴责和驳回文书。此外，命令中引用的供应商幻觉数据出现在两份已公布的判决中，但将数字归因于错误的产品，斯坦福研究的结果与之相反。该事件凸显了在受监管职能中构建AI治理时，需关注文书审查者、起草者的培训与监督等未解问题。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: A court of last resort struck an institutional litigant’s brief this month over four citations that did not exist. Its most quotable line, that “every firm attorney who signed the brief bears some responsibility,” is real. Senior Judge Stephen H. Glickman wrote separately to urge a narrower reading, and to argue that existing rules appear to leave the court little beyond a published admonishment and the strike itself. Rule 38 in the District reaches frivolous appeals, but not briefs; its Rule 46 covers only bar admission, and inherent authority needs a bad-faith finding this record would not support.

Practitioners who stop at that line will miss the qualification, and that gap is where compliance effort can get misdirected. Anyone building AI governance for a regulated function should read what the order leaves unanswered: who reviewed the brief, and how the drafter was trained and supervised.

Two things to carry. The panel called the full scope of its sanctions authority unclear and sent the question to its Rules Committee, where the answer will come from. And the vendor hallucination figures the order quotes, now in two published decisions, assign the numbers to the wrong products; the Stanford study says the reverse.

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat

D.C.’s highest court struck a brief over four fake citations and called its own sanctions authority unclear

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

The District of Columbia Court of Appeals struck a Deutsche Bank trustee’s brief on Sept. 3 after four cited cases turned out not to exist. The harder question took the rest of the order: how much more this court can actually do.

The order’s most quotable line, that “every firm attorney who signed the brief bears some responsibility,” is real, and it comes from the District’s local court of last resort, not the federal D.C. Circuit. One judge on that panel immediately urged a narrower reading of it, at length, in the same document.

The District of Columbia Court of Appeals struck a Deutsche Bank trustee’s brief on Sept. 3 after four cited cases turned out not to exist. The harder question took the rest of the order: how much more this court can actually do.

The order’s most quotable line, that “every firm attorney who signed the brief bears some responsibility,” is real, and it comes from the District’s local court of last resort, not the federal D.C. Circuit. One judge on that panel immediately urged a narrower reading of it, at length, in the same document.

research.titleEn: Ordinary, Reasonable Chatbots: Do AI Models Track Human Legal Judgments?
research.titleZh: 普通、合理的聊天机器人：AI模型能否追踪人类的法律判断？
research.abstractEn: As people increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI) for guidance in their own lives, scholars, lawyers, and even judges have begun to consider the role of AI in legal decision-making. As "silicon sampling" -- the use of generative AI models in social science research -- is now impacting academia, "silicon jurors" could make an appearance in courtrooms. This study joins an emerging line of research on generative AI models' ability to simulate human legal judgments. In particular, we study how large language model (LLM)-powered chatbots respond to series of questions about legal reasonableness. When the law needs to judge the appropriateness of a behavior, it most often asks whether the behavior was "reasonable." Yet despite the ubiquity of reasonableness judgments, they are the site of constant vexation for lawyers, judges, and lay people. Reasonableness seems inherently vague and unpredictable, since it relies on variable context and implicit conceptual schemas. Moreover, many scholars caution that reasonableness judgments may vary along demographic lines. We compare the answers of human participants to those of twenty-six LLMs across twenty-five different legally relevant reasonableness judgments. Overall, our findings suggest that chatbot responses generally track those of human participants. Nonetheless, we find some suggestive -- and potentially concerning -- results. Compared to humans, LLMs generate more homogeneous responses and occasionally treat a variable standard as an invariant rule. And, compared to humans, LLMs tend to generate answers that are more favorable to the government and to corporations. Finally, our results indicate that LLMs' responses tend to align more closely with those of respondents who are white, male, older, and more educated. More systematic research is needed to confirm or reject these initial findings.
research.abstractZh: 随着人们越来越依赖人工智能（AI）为自己的生活提供指导，学者、律师甚至法官已开始考虑AI在法律决策中的作用。随着“硅基抽样”——在社会科学研究中使用生成式AI模型——正在影响学术界，“硅基陪审员”可能会出现在法庭上。本研究加入了关于生成式AI模型模拟人类法律判断能力的新兴研究行列。具体而言，我们研究由大型语言模型（LLM）驱动的聊天机器人如何回应一系列关于法律合理性的问题。当法律需要判断某一行为的适当性时，最常问的是该行为是否“合理”。然而，尽管合理性判断无处不在，它们却是律师、法官和普通人持续感到困扰的根源。合理性似乎本质上是模糊且不可预测的，因为它依赖于可变的语境和隐含的概念图式。此外，许多学者警告说，合理性判断可能因人口统计特征而异。我们将人类参与者的回答与26个LLM在25个不同的法律相关合理性判断上的回答进行了比较。总体而言，我们的发现表明，聊天机器人的回答通常与人类参与者的回答一致。尽管如此，我们发现了一些具有提示性——且可能令人担忧——的结果。与人类相比，LLM生成的回答更加同质化，并且偶尔将可变标准视为不变规则。而且，与人类相比，LLM倾向于生成对政府和公司更有利的回答。最后，我们的结果表明，LLM的回答往往更接近那些白人、男性、年长和受教育程度更高的受访者。需要更系统的研究来证实或否定这些初步发现。

research.titleEn: Formalising and Implementing Grassroots Social Contracts: From Legal Text to Grassroots Platforms (Full Version)
research.titleZh: 形式化与实现草根社会契约：从法律文本到草根平台（完整版）
research.abstractEn: Two centuries ago Pierre-Joseph Proudhon envisioned a social contract that is (1) an agreement of man with man; (2) reciprocal; (3) imposing no obligation upon the parties except that which results from their personal promise; (4) subject to no external authority; (5) freely accepted and signed by all the participants; (6) of the nature of a contract of exchange. He also envisioned a property of social contracts, analogous to a property of digital platforms we term grassroots: that one could "make a contract with all, as ... with some"; digitally, that a grassroots platform can have multiple instances, which may coalesce by mutual consent. We define grassroots social contracts as social contracts meeting these conditions and that (7) people are free to deal with each other; and (8) there is no external register of people. We show that a grassroots social contract can be transformed into a working grassroots platform through an abstraction cascade, from the contract text to formal act schemas, verified syntactically to be grassroots, and then to volition-guarded multiagent atomic transactions. Act schemas are a formal language for the acts the contract describes, each naming the parties' roles, which of them must will the act, and its precondition and effect at each role. Any contract written in this language meets the eight conditions, provided it is syntactically grassroots, satisfying three decidable conditions, Introduction, Provenance and Volition. We prove that the protocol realising a syntactically grassroots contract is grassroots, and volitionally so. Clauses of a grassroots social contract are of three legal types: a breach of an enforced clause is impossible with a correct implementation; a breach of an attested or undertaken clause can be taken to court, with signed evidence for an attested clause. We illustrate them with a grassroots social graph and grassroots currencies.
research.abstractZh: 两个世纪前，皮埃尔-约瑟夫·蒲鲁东设想了一种社会契约，它（1）是人与人之间的协议；（2）是互惠的；（3）除当事人个人承诺所产生的义务外，不施加任何其他义务；（4）不受任何外部权威的约束；（5）由所有参与者自由接受并签署；（6）具有交换合同的性质。他还设想了一种社会契约的属性，类似于我们称之为“草根”的数字平台的一种属性：一个人可以“与所有人订立契约，正如……与某些人订立契约一样”；在数字上，草根平台可以有多个实例，这些实例可以通过相互同意而合并。我们将草根社会契约定义为满足这些条件的社会契约，并且（7）人们可以自由地相互交易；（8）不存在外部的人员登记册。我们表明，通过一个抽象级联，草根社会契约可以转化为一个可运行的草根平台：从契约文本到形式化的行为模式，在语法上验证为草根，然后到意愿守护的多智能体原子事务。行为模式是一种形式语言，用于描述契约所描述的行为，每个行为都命名了当事人的角色、其中哪些角色必须意愿该行为，以及该行为在每个角色上的前置条件和效果。任何用这种语言编写的契约都满足这八个条件，只要它在语法上是草根的，即满足三个可判定条件：引入、来源和意愿。我们证明，实现语法上草根契约的协议是草根的，并且在意愿上也是如此。草根社会契约的条款有三种法律类型：对于强制执行的条款，在正确实现下违约是不可能的；对于经证明或承诺的条款，违约可以诉诸法院，对于经证明的条款，有签名的证据。我们用草根社交图谱和草根货币来说明这些。

news.titleEn: ILTACON News Round-Up Part 4, The Business of Law: Litera, Aderant, Oddr, TRĒ AI, Intapp
news.titleZh: ILTACON新闻汇总第四部分，法律业务领域：Litera、Aderant、Oddr、TRĒ AI、Intapp
news.summaryZh: 上周ILTACON年会带来可能是该会议史上最繁忙的新闻周期，大量产品公告以代理式AI和模型上下文协议（MCP）为主题。本文为第四部分，聚焦法律业务领域。Litera在七月围绕单一AI代理Lito进行品牌重塑后，宣布推出Firm AI Search和业务发展智能功能，通过Lito让律师以自然语言查询事务所的事务、客户和专业知识数据，并连接Foundation、事务系统和专业知识数据库。Litera还宣布与视频法律培训公司Hotshot签署谅解备忘录，计划通过其CE Manager平台提供Hotshot订阅和培训库，预计今年第四季度上线。发票到现金平台Oddr发布三项公告：AI驱动的收款能力（包括AI起草的收款邮件和自动跟进序列）、即将推出的Oddr Collections Agent（可监控应收账款组合并建议行动）、现金预测功能早期访问，以及MCP服务器，允许管理合伙人和财务负责人通过兼容AI平台用自然语言查询实时数据。Intapp为首批集成合作伙伴，Oddr与Intapp Time和Billstream with Celeste连接，打造端到端发票到现金解决方案。TRĒ AI推出TRĒ-D Signals，据称是首个业务发展信号引擎，可在事务所财务系统内证明新事务投资回报率，提供高精度信号提醒、一键行动、AI代理自动处理外联和跟进，以及ROI报告。Aderant在ILTACON新闻发布会上宣布其Agent Center进入早期访问，该框架基于Stridyn平台和MADDI AI层，现包含七个任务专用代理：上诉代理、收款代理、人才代理、时间代理、合规代理、总账预测代理和费率代理。Intapp与Legora宣布战略合作，涵盖三个领域：Legora集成Intapp Walls for AI以尊重道德墙和保密义务；时间捕获集成自动生成Intapp Time条目；以及联合创新代理工作流，结合Legora Agent与Celeste，初始版本允许客户在Legora内触发Celeste功能。
news.bodyHtml:
Last week’s ILTACON, the annual conference of the International Legal Technology Association, brought what may have been the busiest news cycle I can remember for this conference, with a torrent of product announcements dominated by two themes: agentic AI and the Model Context Protocol.

I have already covered the conference and several of the week’s biggest stories – including LexisNexis’s Legal Intelligence Engine, Thomson Reuters’ launch of its Thomson LLM, and Clio’s hiring of Pablo Arredondo to lead a new judiciary initiative. Now, as I dig out from a hectic week, I am rounding up here other notable announcements from the conference.

I’ll do this in four parts:

  • Part 1: E-Discovery.
  • Part 2: Litigation.
  • Part 3: Documents, Data and AI.
  • Part 4: The Business of Law

This is part 4, the business of law.

Note: I used Claude to assist in creating the summaries.

Litera Announces Firm AI Search and Business Development Intelligence

Litera, fresh off its July relaunch around a single AI agent, which I covered at the time, announced Firm AI Search and business development Intelligence, which it says turn siloed firm data into new revenue opportunities by giving lawyers natural language access to firm knowledge.

Firm AI Search is accessed through Lito, Litera’s legal AI agent, letting lawyers query their firm’s matter, client and expertise data directly in the tools they already use.

Firm AI Search connects the data that already lives across Foundation, matter systems and expertise databases into a single conversational interface, the company says. With Lito Lookups, a simple @mention surfaces matter, client and people records without leaving the chat.

Litera also announced new growth intelligence capabilities that surface proactive business development signals with monetary value directly inside Foundation 365.

Separately, Litera announced a memorandum of understanding to work towards a collaboration with Hotshot, the video-based legal training company, under which lawyers and firms will be able to access Hotshot subscriptions and its training library through Litera CE Manager, the company’s learning management and CLE compliance platform.

Lawyers will be able to discover and take Hotshot courses, as well as track their completion and eligible credits, all within CE Manager.

The integration is expected to be available by the fourth quarter of this year.

Read more:

  • Litera Delivers Firm AI Search and Business Development Intelligence, Turning Siloed Data into New Revenue Opportunities.
  • Hotshot Collaborates with Litera on Legal Training as Firms Rethink Talent Development in the Age of AI.

Oddr Rolls Out a Trio of Announcements: MCP Server, Agentic Collections, Cash Flow Forecasting

Invoice-to-cash platform Oddr made three announcements across the week.

First, it announced AI-powered collections capabilities, including AI-drafted, context-aware collections emails with tone controls, and automated follow-up sequences.

Coming soon is the Oddr Collections Agent, an agentic capability that will continuously monitor a firm’s AR portfolio, surface the accounts with the greatest impact on cash flow, and prepare the recommended action — a drafted email, a call brief, or a note to the attorney — while finance teams retain control of every decision.

The agent launches in early access ahead of general availability later this year.

Second, it announced early access to Cash Flow Forecasting, moving the platform from reactive reporting to predictive intelligence.

Third, it launched its MCP Server, which lets managing partners and finance leaders ask plain-language questions — current DSO, past-due clients, 90-day cash flow — through any compatible AI platform and get answers drawn from Oddr’s live billing, collections, payments, and forecasting data.

Intapp is among the first integration partners. Through a formal partnership, Oddr now connects with Intapp Time and Billstream with Celeste, which the companies describe as creating the first end-to-end invoice-to-cash solution for law firms.

“Law firm finance leaders have been asking for a smarter way to understand their revenue cycle without having to dig through multiple systems,” said Milan Bobde, cofounder and CEO. “The Oddr MCP Server changes that. Ask a question, get an answer, take action. It is that simple.”

TRĒ AI Launches TRĒ-D Signals for Business Development

TRĒ AI launched TRĒ-D Signals, which it describes as the first business development signal engine built to prove new-matter ROI within a firm’s own financial systems.

“Combining precision BD intelligence and automated AI activation, TRĒ-D Signals delivers targeted opportunities to individual attorneys, enabling them to launch high-potential BD actions with only one click,” the company said in its announcement. “AI agents automatically interact with the opportunity to translate it into new matters with minimal effort from the attorney.”

According to the company, the product delivers:

  • High-precision, attorney-specific BD signal alerts drawn from TRĒ AI’s relationship intelligence engine.
  • One-click opportunity actions that require no manual data entry or CRM maintenance from attorneys.
  • AI agents that automatically handle outreach, follow-up, and scheduling on behalf of attorneys.
  • ROI reporting designed to connect signal actions to resulting matters in the firm’s financial management system.

“TRĒ-D Signals brings relevant opportunities to attorneys, drafts communications, and automatically handles the resulting interaction, follow-up, and scheduling with one click,” said CEO Todd Miller. “TRĒ-D Signals is designed to generate more matters and revenue with a fraction of the time and effort required by CRM and coaching.”

Aderant Moves Agent Center Into Early Access

Aderant used a press conference at ILTACON to announce early access availability of its Agent Center, the framework for deploying AI agents across law firm financial and operational workflows that it first unveiled at its Momentum Global conference in May.

The Agent Center, built on the company’s Stridyn platform and powered by its MADDI AI layer, has expanded to include seven task-specific agents:

  • Appeals Agent. Identifies and prioritizes high-value appeal opportunities and drafting supporting rationale for review.
  • Collections Agent. Helps accelerate cash collection by prioritizing accounts, surfacing aging trends and payment risk, and recommending next-best actions and outreach.
  • Talent Agent. Gives managers a complete, evidence-based view of associate performance.
  • Time Agent. Helps timekeepers create clearer, more compliant time entries by improving narratives, flagging billing risk, and recommending codes.
  • Compliance Agent. Helps firms interpret and operationalize outside counsel guidelines.
  • General Ledger Forecasting Agent. Anticipates future performance by combining forward-looking GL forecasts with recent actuals, confidence ranges, and variance analysis across accounts, offices, and departments.
  • Rates Agent. Shows firms which billing rates apply, why they apply, and how they have changed.

“Agent Center reflects a shift we’re seeing across the industry, from isolated automation to intelligent systems that coordinate work across the business,” said Lisa Erickson, SVP of product management and AI at Aderant. “These agents are purpose-built for legal operations, not general-purpose AI bolted onto a firm’s workflows.”

Intapp and Legora Announce Strategic Partnership

Intapp and Legora announced a strategic partnership to deliver governed, AI-native workflows for law firms, spanning three areas.

Legora will integrate with Intapp Walls for AI so that AI-powered work in Legora respects a firm’s ethical walls, confidentiality obligations, and regulatory requirements.

A time-capture integration will automatically capture structured usage data from work done in Legora and generate entries in Intapp Time.

And the companies will co-innovate on agentic workflows combining the Legora Agent with Celeste, Intapp’s AI coworker for the business of the firm, with an initial version letting mutual customers trigger Celeste capabilities within Legora and vice versa.

Legora co-founder and CEO Max Junestrand said firms want to deploy AI broadly without compromising the controls their clients rely on.

Intapp chairman and CEO John Hall said the partnership pairs Legora’s practice-of-law capabilities with Celeste’s business-of-law solutions. The integrations will be delivered in phases.

news.titleEn: After the Hype? Legal tech leaders reflect on the real lessons of ILTACON 2026
news.titleZh: 热潮过后？法律科技领袖反思ILTACON 2026的真正经验
news.summaryZh: 法律科技媒体Legal IT Insider报道，在今年的ILTACON大会上，高级领导者的关注焦点及展台内外的热门话题已浮出水面。过去一周，该媒体通过视频采访了16位首席信息官、供应商代表及ILTA负责人，探讨这场为期四天、吸引5700人参加的会议所带来的关键启示。受访者的见解各异，但存在一致的主题：今年终端用户之间的对话成熟度显著提升，他们正讨论以受控方式实施人工智能，并深入探讨防护措施、代币成本以及为实现这些领域正确结果而持续开展的数据工作。总体而言，行业正从人工智能实验阶段迈向运营化阶段。这些访谈内容可在YouTube和Spotify上集中收听，也可通过每位嘉宾姓名旁附带的链接单独收听。文章总结了会议中体现的进展领域与尚存挑战，强调行业正在经历从实验到实际部署的关键转变，而数据基础与成本控制成为当前讨论的核心议题。
news.bodyHtml:
What were senior leaders focusing on at ILTACON this year and what were the burning topics of conversation at the stands and behind the scenes? In the past week we’ve chatted on camera to 16 CIOs, vendors, and ILTA heads about the key takeaways from a conference that saw 5,700 people join over four days.

The insights are varied but there are consistent themes: this year saw a huge uptick in the maturity of conversations among end users, who are talking about implementing AI in a controlled way, with deep dives into guardrails, token costs, and the continuing data work required behind the scenes to achieve the right outcomes in both those areas.

news.titleEn: LEGALFLY launches Contract Intelligence to become a system of record
news.titleZh: LEGALFLY推出合同智能，成为记录系统
news.summaryZh: LEGALFLY于9月4日宣布推出Contract Intelligence，这家比利时成立的法律操作系统由此覆盖合同签署前与签署后的全生命周期，使法律团队能够统一查看风险所在及下一步优先事项。LEGALFLY的第一个前沿是让法律工作更快，下一个前沿是解决更困难的问题：让法律和企业团队在不得不询问之前就知道什么需要关注，因此推出了Contract Intelligence。LEGALFLY已是法律团队的工作系统，现在增加合同记录系统，并在其上叠加持续智能层。Contract Intelligence不是简单地在签署后存储协议，而是持续理解协议内容、变化、风险所在、即将到来的义务以及下一步需要关注的事项。LEGALFLY成立于2023年，与包括欧盟委员会、博世、毕马威和SAP在内的企业法律团队合作。从业务角度看，公司获得了速度、一致性和信心，商业团队更快获得法律意见，有助于更快完成交易，风险管理得到改善，公司总体上更有能力支持增长雄心。简而言之，LEGALFLY帮助公司将法律转变为真正的业务赋能者和主动的业务伙伴。
news.bodyHtml:
LEGALFLY today (4 September) announced the launch of Contract Intelligence, meaning that the Belgian-founded legal operating system now covers the pre and post signature contract lifecycle, giving legal teams one view of where risk sits and what to prioritise next.

Ruben Miessen, CEO of LEGALFLY, said: “The first frontier for LEGALFLY was making legal work faster. The next frontier is solving a far harder problem: enabling legal and enterprise teams to know what needs their attention, before they have to ask. That’s why we’ve launched Contract Intelligence. Already a system of work for legal teams, LEGALFLY is now adding a system of record for contracts, with a continuous intelligence layer on top. Rather than simply storing agreements after signature, Contract Intelligence continuously understands what’s in them, what has changed, where risk sits, what obligations are approaching and what requires attention next.”

Advertisement

LEGALFLY, founded in 2023, works with legal teams at enterprises including the European Commission, Bosch, KPMG and SAP.

Speaking about the results his company has achieved using LEGALFLY, Gilles Buchmann, CLO at Duvel Moortgat, said: “From a business perspective we’ve gained speed, consistency and confidence. Commercial teams get their legal input faster, which helps them close deals more quickly. Risk management has improved and we are generally better positioned to support the company’s growth ambitions. In short, LEGALFLY has helped us to turn Legal into a true business enabler and proactive business partner.”

news.titleEn: A lawyer fed AI citations to his own regulator, and the tribunal struck him off
news.titleZh: 律师向监管机构提交AI生成的引注，被审裁庭除名
news.summaryZh: 英格兰和威尔士律师纪律审裁庭将一名律师从外国律师名册中除名，原因是该律师在自我辩护中使用了由生成式人工智能编造的判例引注。该律师名为Abhishek Kumar，其辩护对象正是起诉他的监管机构。当监管机构律师指出错误后，Kumar通过电子邮件回应，而这封邮件同样由生成式AI起草，并包含新的虚假材料。审裁庭于9月3日公布案件记录，称这是该法庭首次审理律师在法律程序中使用人工智能的案件。这是律师在诉讼中使用AI或大语言模型首次在该法庭被诉。案件于7月29日开庭审理，判决日期为8月25日。审裁庭在评估时既考虑了Kumar最初如何使用AI，也考虑了他在错误被发现后的行为，并对其重复行为给予了非常重大的权重。这一区分与事件响应实践中的原则一致，即缺陷的处理方式与缺陷本身被分别评判。此外，大西洋两岸的法院曾将AI引注失败案件移交监管机构，但Kumar案并非由法院移交，而是英国律师监管局（SRA）已在起诉他。在截至2026年7月的一年中，收到42起潜在AI滥用报告，相关调查正在进行中。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: A disciplinary tribunal in London has removed a lawyer from the register of foreign lawyers over legal authorities that generative AI invented, and those authorities sat in his defense against the regulator prosecuting him. When the regulator’s counsel flagged the errors, he answered with an email he had also drafted using AI, and that email carried further false material. The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal says this is the first time a lawyer’s use of AI in legal proceedings has been litigated before it.

Professionals in cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery should read the culpability findings rather than the headline. The tribunal weighed both how Kumar began using AI and what he did once the errors were identified, and it gave very substantial weight to the repetition. The same distinction runs through incident-response practice, where the handling of a defect is judged separately from the defect.

Watch the referral route. Courts on both sides of the Atlantic have referred AI citation failures to regulators, though no court referred Kumar; the SRA was already prosecuting him. The Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) said it received 42 reports of potential AI misuse in the year to July 2026, with investigations underway.

News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat

A lawyer fed AI citations to his own regulator, and the tribunal struck him off

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

The Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal for England and Wales has struck a lawyer from the register of foreign lawyers over AI-fabricated authorities, which he filed in his own defense against the regulator prosecuting him. When the regulator’s counsel flagged the errors, Abhishek Kumar answered by email. He had drafted that email with generative artificial intelligence as well, and it carried fresh false material.

The tribunal published its record of the case on Sept. 3, and it is the first of its kind in that forum. “This was the first time that a lawyer’s use of artificial intelligence or large language models in legal proceedings had been litigated before the Tribunal,” the tribunal said in its published case summary. The panel heard the matter on July 29 and dated its judgment Aug. 25.

For anyone running an eDiscovery workflow, an information governance program, or a security function that leans on machine output, the decision matters less for its novelty than for what the tribunal refused to accept as an excuse.

news.titleEn: AI Acqui-Hires and Antitrust: When Is Hiring Talent a Merger?
news.titleZh: AI“反向收购式招聘”与反垄断：何时招聘人才等同于合并？
news.summaryZh: 人工智能领域出现一场新兴反垄断辩论：某些招聘交易是否实为变相合并。争议焦点并非大型科技公司是否收购了初创企业——在这类交易中并未发生收购，而是公司是否挖走了使初创企业具有价值的人才、专有技术、技术访问权和战略能力，从而获取收购的诸多好处却无需承担正式合并的负担。David T. Wong在《耶鲁法律杂志》评论中主张，更恰当的问题是经济上重要的资产是否易手，相关资产可能是人力资本。他将这种结构称为“反向收购式招聘”：大型科技公司从AI初创企业挖走关键高管、研究人员或工程师，向初创企业支付巨额费用，并通常获得非独占技术许可或其他战略利益；初创企业在法律上保持独立，未发生正式收购，但使其具有价值的资产已转移他处。《克莱顿法》第7条禁止可能实质性减少竞争或趋向形成垄断的资产收购。Wong写道，如果人力资本属于资产，那么挖走初创企业的领导层和核心技术团队即使未收购初创企业本身，也可能需要反垄断审查。谷歌2025年与Windsurf的安排即为例证：据报道，谷歌同意向AI编程初创企业Windsurf支付24亿美元以获得非独占技术许可，同时将Windsurf的CEO、联合创始人及数名AI研究人员招入Google DeepMind，但未收购Windsurf，也未持有其股份。形式上这不是合并，经济现实则更为复杂。类似结构已出现在微软与Inflection AI、亚马逊与Adept、谷歌与Character.AI以及Meta与Scale AI的交易中，共同点并非所有权，而是对人才、技术和战略能力的获取。传统合并分析通常从所有权入手：谁收购。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! An emerging antitrust debate in artificial intelligence asks whether some hiring deals are mergers in disguise. The issue is not whether a large technology company bought a startup. In these deals, it did not. The question is whether the company hired away the people, know-how, technology access, and strategic capabilities that made the startup valuable—capturing many of the benefits of an acquisition without the baggage of a formal merger. David T. Wong, author of the Yale Law Journal Comment An Acquisition by Another Name: Reverse Acquihires Under the Clayton Act, argues that the better question is whether economically significant assets changed hands. In his view, the relevant asset may be human capital. Wong calls the structure a “reverse acquihire.” A large technology company hires key executives, researchers, or engineers from an AI startup, pays the startup a substantial fee, and often receives a nonexclusive technology license or other strategic benefit. The startup remains legally independent. No formal acquisition occurs. But the assets that made the startup valuable have moved elsewhere. Section 7 of the Clayton Act prohibits acquisitions of assets where the effect may be substantially to lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly. If human capital is an asset, then hiring a startup’s leadership and core technical team may warrant antitrust scrutiny, Wong writes, even when the startup itself is not acquired. Google’s 2025 arrangement with Windsurf illustrates the problem. Google reportedly agreed to pay $2.4 billion to AI coding startup Windsurf for a nonexclusive technology license while hiring Windsurf’s CEO, cofounder, and several AI researchers to join Google DeepMind. Google did not acquire Windsurf or take an ownership stake in the company. Formally, that is not a merger. The economic reality is more complicated. Similar structures have appeared in transactions involving Microsoft and Inflection AI, Amazon and Adept, Google and Character.AI, and Meta and Scale AI. The common thread is not ownership. It is access to talent, technology, and strategic capabilities. Traditional merger analysis often begins with ownership: who bought whom, what assets changed hands, and how the transaction changes market structure. The AI economy is built differently. Many AI startups derive much of their value from scarce human talent, proprietary know-how, software development techniques, data expertise, and accumulated research experience. In some cases, founders and engineering teams may be the company’s most valuable assets.

research.titleEn: LexFlip: A Dissociation Diagnostic for Legal Meaning Preservation Metrics
research.titleZh: LexFlip：法律意义保留度量的解离诊断
research.abstractEn: Does a simplified legal clause still say what the original said? The checks in current use cannot establish that it does: requiring an identical pair to score highest and an unrelated pair lowest moves lexical overlap and legal force together, so any monotone function of token overlap satisfies both. Our remedy is a dissociation, an item holding surface form fixed while legal force moves. We release LexFlip, 373 minimal perturbations of Quebec statutory French that reverse legal force while preserving 0.93 of the tokens, with a harness scoring metrics, regressors and prompted judges alike. The seven embedding and BERTScore metrics we test spend only 0.022 to 0.039 of their identical-to-unrelated range on such an edit, against 0.670 for bidirectional NLI, the one family the identical-pair check would disqualify. On FrJudge, against a measured human ceiling of r=0.597, a bare length feature outscores every semantic metric and has the lowest margin we measure.
research.abstractZh: 简化后的法律条款是否仍然表达了原条款的含义？当前使用的检查方法无法确定这一点：要求完全相同的配对得分最高、不相关的配对得分最低，这会使词汇重叠和法律效力同步变化，因此任何基于词元重叠的单调函数都能满足这两个条件。我们的补救措施是一种解离，即一个保持表面形式不变而法律效力发生变化的项目。我们发布了 LexFlip，这是对魁北克成文法法语进行的 373 个最小扰动，它们在保留 0.93 词元的同时逆转了法律效力，并附带一个对度量、回归器和提示法官进行评分的测试框架。我们测试的七个嵌入和 BERTScore 度量在此类编辑上仅花费了其相同到不相关范围的 0.022 至 0.039，而双向 NLI 为 0.670，后者是唯一会被相同配对检查取消资格的家族。在 FrJudge 上，相对于测得的人类上限 r=0.597，一个裸长度特征得分超过了所有语义度量，并且具有我们测得的最低裕度。

news.titleEn: ‘Beyond CRM’: Wilson Sonsini and Salesforce talk AI-driven intelligence
news.titleZh: “超越CRM”：Wilson Sonsini与Salesforce探讨AI驱动的智能
news.summaryZh: 美国律所Wilson Sonsini在ILTACON与Salesforce同台，介绍为代理式AI时代所做的准备，Salesforce称“客户关系管理已经不够”。会议由该所CIO Jeffrey Lolley与Salesforce全球客户总监兼法律行业负责人Kiel Parker主持。双方合作始于如何武器化并制度化数据；Salesforce用于推介、提供客户业务背景与新客户接触点，所有RFP均输入其中，已成为整体推介管理平台，带来一致性、速度并投入大量精力。该所数据分散在NetDocuments和G-Suite，永远不会集中一处，因此需要数据湖仓、治理层及与LLM无关的治理，确保遵守客户义务，这是与Salesforce合作的技术栈，也是首选提供的第一组数据，用于更快响应RFP和推介。该所文化鼓励创新，但须在创新与安全交付间平衡。最难的是数据：数据到处都是，必须围绕它构建；关键是从人脑中提取数据，自动化是关键，获得干净数据是最大挑战，数据必须先行。用户信任随成功案例提升，律师因获得原本没有的信息而愿意再用，许可逐步增长。代理式AI的近期价值是更快做好工作，使其成为律所DNA；该所不想新建数据环境，而要构建能为律师决策的引擎。会议还演示了Salesforce Data Cloud的“协调引擎”，即元数据摄取与映射。Legal IT Insider现场笔记，引文或与记录略有差异。
news.bodyHtml:
US multinational law firm Wilson Sonsini at ILTACON this year took to the stage with Salesforce to detail the work the pair are doing together to prepare for the agentic AI era, with Salesforce saying that “client relationship management isn’t enough.” 

One of the first public glimpses of the work being done behind the scenes, this session was led by Wilson Sonsini’s CIO Jeffrey Lolley and Salesforce’s global account director and legal industry lead Kiel Parker. 

Advertisement

Lolley pointed to Wilson Sonsini’s long relationship with Salesforce, which is also a client. “It started around how we weaponise data and institutionalise it,” he observed. 

At Wilson Sonsini, Salesforce is used for pitches and providing context around the current business with the client, and who might have touchpoints with a new client. All RFPs are fed in and it has become an overarching pitch management platform. Lolley says: “It started with a box we knew could do great things, and letting individuals know they can rely on it every day to grow their business. We use it for consistency, speed, pitches, RFPs and a lot of effort went into that.” 

Advertisement

Wilson Sonsini talks about the creation of an engine and Lolley says: “It started out by us saying we need a data lake house across all our data. We are unique in Silicon Valley. We have data in NetDocuments and G-Suite and we are never going to get to a stage where it’s in one place, and we need to embrace that, it’s the culture of the firm. So we needed a data layer and had to decide how to govern it. How do we make sure we comply with our client obligations? So we needed a governance layer that is LLM agnostic that we can provide to users. That is the stack I associate with what we do with Salesforce. That was the first set of data we chose to provide, and that interface is how we set out to deliver to clients and make the way we respond to RFPs and do pitches even faster. The foundation of knowledge is there. All those years of putting data in had to be a part of our ecosystem as we thought about our AI journey.” 

Wilson Sonsini is one of the leading advisors to the tech industry and Lolley described a culture at the firm where partners push hard on new ideas “but we need to balance being super innovative with how we deliver work in a safe and secure way.” He says: “At partner retreats we talk about it over a glass of wine and discuss what the balance should be, they really understand it and what is driving us forward at the same time.” 

The hardest part is the data, and Lolley says: “When we started out, our data was all over the place and we had to build around it. We’ll never get to a place where our data is all in one place.” 

He adds: “With Salesforce it’s how to extract data from people’s heads and so automation is key. Getting people to understand the value of and getting data that was clean was the biggest challenge. You hear about people who went out and bought the first thing and sat it on top of data that wasn’t clean. But the data needs to be the first part.”  

In a fireside chat on stage, Parker asked Lolley about trust – how did users come to trust Salesforce and understand that it meant no more extra admin work? Lolley said that adoption has risen over time thanks to success stories, commenting simply: “Going into meetings, lawyers had information they wouldn’t have had, so wanted to use it again.” The licensing grew incrementally. 

Perhaps most interestingly, when it comes to the clearest near-term value for agentic AI, Lolley said: “By embracing these technologies we do can great work for people quicker. It’s not how will it flip our world up but how will we make it part of our DNA and structure the firm round it in terms of our thought processes and engagement.” Wilson Sonsini didn’t want to build a new data environment and Lolley says: “We wanted to build an engine that could make decisions for our lawyers that takes decision making out of their hands. Associates want to know if they can do this or that in an AI platform and our system does that for you.” 

A demo during the session looked at Salesforce’s ‘harmonisation engine’ which refers to the metadata ingestion and mapping within the Salesforce Data Cloud.  

Please note, Legal IT Insider took notes during the live session at ILTACON and so quotes may slightly differ to the transcript of the session, which we will share when it becomes available.

That was the first set of data we chose to provide, and that interface is how we set out to deliver to clients and make the way we respond to RFPs and do pitches even faster. The foundation of knowledge is there. All those years of putting data in had to be a part of our ecosystem as we thought about our AI journey.”

Wilson Sonsini is one of the leading advisors to the tech industry and Lolley described a culture at the firm where partners push hard on new ideas “but we need to balance being super innovative with how we deliver work in a safe and secure way.” He says: “At partner retreats we talk about it over a glass of wine and discuss what the balance should be, they really understand it and what is driving us forward at the same time.”

The hardest part is the data, and Lolley says: “When we started out, our data was all over the place and we had to build around it. We’ll never get to a place where our data is all in one place.”

He adds: “With Salesforce it’s how to extract data from people’s heads and so automation is key. Getting people to understand the value of and getting data that was clean was the biggest challenge. You hear about people who went out and bought the first thing and sat it on top of data that wasn’t clean. But the data needs to be the first part.”

In a fireside chat on stage, Parker asked Lolley about trust – how did users come to trust Salesforce and understand that it meant no more extra admin work? Lolley said that adoption has risen over time thanks to success stories, commenting simply: “Going into meetings, lawyers had information they wouldn’t have had, so wanted to use it again.” The licensing grew incrementally.

Perhaps most interestingly, when it comes to the clearest near-term value for agentic AI, Lolley said: “By embracing these technologies we do can great work for people quicker. It’s not how will it flip our world up but how will we make it part of our DNA and structure the firm round it in terms of our thought processes and engagement.” Wilson Sonsini didn’t want to build a new data environment and Lolley says: “We wanted to build an engine that could make decisions for our lawyers that takes decision making out of their hands. Associates want to know if they can do this or that in an AI platform and our system does that for you.”

A demo during the session looked at Salesforce’s ‘harmonisation engine’ which refers to the metadata ingestion and mapping within the Salesforce Data Cloud.

Please note, Legal IT Insider took notes during the live session at ILTACON and so quotes may slightly differ to the transcript of the session, which we will share when it becomes available.

news.titleEn: Querious Announces Integration with 8am MyCase, Bringing Legal Conversational Intelligence™ Into the Practice Management Workflow
news.titleZh: Querious宣布与8am MyCase集成，将法律对话智能引入执业管理工作流程
news.summaryZh: 2026年9月3日，总部位于北卡罗来纳州罗利的Querious公司宣布，其专为律师打造的法律对话智能平台现已与8am MyCase实现集成，将客户对话直接连接到律所的执业管理工作流程中。此次集成使律师能够将Querious对话与MyCase案件关联，在对话中引入相关案件背景，并在会议结束后将对话内容转化为结构化的法律工作成果。执业管理软件已改变了客户会议前后的工作方式，而下一前沿是充分利用对话本身。通过连接Querious与MyCase，律师可以带着已有背景进入对话，在Querious协助下全神贯注于客户，随后将对话转化为有用的案件笔记和计费条目，无需从头开始。与主要生成转录和摘要的通用AI记录工具不同，Querious专为法律对话的隐私、安全和道德要求而设计。集成后，律师可提前准备，将即将进行的对话与相关MyCase案件关联；对话期间，Querious实时捕捉关键事实，并提示相关问题与后续提问建议；对话结束后，自动起草详细笔记、摘要邮件和计费条目供律师审阅；保存至客户案件的笔记和邮件可成为案件工作流程的一部分，为下次客户互动提供背景。Querious与8am在法律技术上理念一致，即必须为专业人士量身定制，以实用性和保密性为核心。此次合作旨在缩小客户对话与案件之间的差距，减少行政工作，让律所更多时间服务客户。Querious由律师为律师设计，以隐私、安全和负责任的人工智能为核心，帮助律所从客户对话这一历史上数字化程度最低的重要环节中获取更大价值。
news.bodyHtml:
New integration connects client conversations with matter context so that attorneys have more productive interactions and get more value from 8am MyCase.

RALEIGH, N.C. — September 3, 2026 — Querious®, the Legal Conversational Intelligence™ platform purpose-built for attorneys, today announced a new integration with8am™ MyCase, connecting the client conversation directly to the law firm’s practice management workflow.

The integration allows attorneys to associate a Querious conversation with a MyCase matter, bring relevant matter context into the conversation, and turn what happens during the meeting into structured legal work product afterward.

“Practice management software has transformed what happens before and after a client meeting. We believe the next frontier is making the most of the conversation itself,” said Hilary Bowman, Founder and CEO of Querious. “By connecting Querious with MyCase, attorneys can bring the context they already have into the conversation, give clients their full attention while Querious works alongside them, and then turn that conversation into useful matter notes and billing entries without starting from scratch.”

From matter context to client conversation and back again

Unlike generic AI notetakers built primarily to create transcripts and summaries, Querious is designed specifically for the privacy, security, and ethical demands of legal conversations.

With the MyCase integration, attorneys can:

  • Start prepared. Associate an upcoming conversation with the relevant MyCase matter so existing matter information can help attorneys quickly understand the context of the conversation. 
  • Stay focused on the client. During the conversation, Querious captures key facts as they emerge while surfacing relevant issues and suggested follow-up questions in real time. 
  • Create valuable work product. Afterward, Querious automatically drafts detailed notes, a summary email, and billing entries for attorney review, reducing the administrative work required after client meetings. 
  • Preserve context for what comes next. Notes and emails created by Querious and saved to a client matter can become part of the matter workflow so attorneys have better context available when preparing for the next client interaction. 

More than an AI notetaker

Querious was built around the premise that attorneys need more from AI than a record of what was said. Client conversations are where attorneys gather facts, develop strategy, advise clients, and build trust.

Querious helps attorneys remain engaged in those conversations while capturing information accurately and completely, organizing it around the legal matter, and producing usable work product when the conversation ends.

“Integrating conversational intelligence with practice management creates a continuous loop,” Bowman added. “The matter helps inform the conversation, the conversation creates new matter knowledge, and that knowledge is available to make the next conversation better.”

Built for the requirements of legal practice

Querious is designed by attorneys for attorneys, with privacy, security and responsible AI use incorporated into the platform. Rather than adapting a generic meeting assistant to legal work, Querious is purpose-built around the confidentiality, professional responsibility and workflow requirements associated with attorney-client conversations.

The integration with MyCase extends that approach into the systems law firms already use to manage their matters, helping create a more connected workflow between the client conversation and the matter record.

“Querious and 8am share a similar philosophy on legal technology: it must be purpose-built for professionals, with practicality and confidentiality embedded at the core,” said Chris Setcos, Senior Vice President of Partnerships, 8am. “By bringing Querious’ real-time conversational intelligence together with MyCase, we’re closing the gap between client conversations and matters so firms can spend less time on administrative work and more time with their clients. Firms do their best work when their tools work together seamlessly, and we’re proud to partner with Querious to bring that connectivity to customers.”

 

About Querious

Querious® is a Legal Conversational Intelligence™ platform designed specifically for attorneys. Querious works alongside attorneys during client conversations to capture key facts and context, surface relevant issues and suggested questions in real time, and transform conversations into valuable work product including detailed matter notes and billing entries.

Designed by attorneys with privacy, security and responsible AI at its core, Querious helps law firms get more value from one of the most important and historically under-digitized parts of legal practice: the client conversation.

To learn more, visit www.querious.ai/8am. 

 

Media Contact

Querious, Inc.
Hilary Bowman
hilary@querious.ai
