news.titleEn: ILTACON News Round-Up Part 2, Litigation: LawToolBox, Opus 2, Clarra, Eve
news.titleZh: ILTACON新闻综述第二部分，诉讼领域：LawToolBox、Opus 2、Clarra、Eve
news.summaryZh: 上周举行的ILTACON（国际法律技术协会年会）带来了可能是该会议记忆中最繁忙的新闻周期，大量产品公告以代理式AI和模型上下文协议（MCP）为主题。此前已报道了LexisNexis的法律智能引擎、汤森路透的Thomson LLM以及Clio聘请Pablo Arredondo领导新的司法计划。本文为第二部分，涵盖其他重要公告。Opus 2推出了其代理式AI框架Ingenuity，该框架内置于其诉讼平台中，并非新产品，而是AI识别和理解案件上下文方式的演进。平台每月自动生成近1100万条洞察，为AI层和专业代理提供基础。AI的有效性取决于其能理解的信息。LawToolBox推出了面向Microsoft 365和Claude的MCP，连接M365 Copilot、CoCounsel、Harvey、Legora、Protégé、Claude和ChatGPT等AI工具与Matter Containers中的案件上下文。该MCP连接器包含70个工具，利用M365数据、法律法规和团队战略分析。Clarra推出了面向Claude的案件管理MCP服务器，使AI工具能访问案件信息，支持生成诉讼简报、分析证词、制定策略、创建仪表板等。法律团队不应为每项任务购买不同的AI应用。Eve宣布其Analyst和Atlas功能全面上市。Analyst允许律所领导用自然语言提问并获得即时答案，并提供保存的仪表板。Atlas实时结构化所有记录、账单和通信，确保数据实时性，目前适用于人身伤害律所。
news.bodyHtml:
Last week’s ILTACON, the annual conference of the International Legal Technology Association, brought what may have been the busiest news cycle I can remember for this conference, with a torrent of product announcements dominated by two themes: agentic AI and the Model Context Protocol.

I have already covered the conference and several of the week’s biggest stories – including LexisNexis’s Legal Intelligence Engine, Thomson Reuters’ launch of its Thomson LLM, and Clio’s hiring of Pablo Arredondo to lead a new judiciary initiative. Now, as I dig out from a hectic week, I am rounding up here other notable announcements from the conference.

I’ll do this in four parts:

  • Part 1: E-Discovery.
  • Part 2: Litigation.
  • Part 3: Documents, Data and AI.
  • Part 4: The Business of Law.

This is part 2, litigation.

Note: I used Claude to assist in creating the summaries.

Opus 2 Introduces Ingenuity, Its Agentic AI Framework

 Opus 2 introduced Opus 2 Ingenuity, an agentic AI framework built into its litigation platform.

The company stresses that Ingenuity is not a new product but rather an evolution of how its AI recognizes and understands the context of a matter based on how legal teams interact with documents, define relationships between information, and manage workflows.

These insights — nearly 11 million of them created across the platform each month, the company says — are generated automatically as teams build case strategy in Opus 2, and give Ingenuity’s AI layers and specialty agents a stronger foundation for surfacing and acting on intelligence across workflows from case assessment through hearing.

“AI is only as effective as the information it can understand,” said Greg Blackman, CEO of Opus 2. “Ingenuity unlocks AI through a deeper understanding of the insights inside our platform – delivering productivity, cost-efficiency, quality, security, and other valuable benefits across any law firm.”

The company says that the matter intelligence powering Ingenuity results in higher quality AI outputs that are more accurate, making AI-driven work more dependable, reducing risks associated with unsupported conclusions, enabling teams to spend more time on strategy and less time on validation, and more efficiently balancing AI compute, potentially lowering costs.

Read more: Opus 2 Ingenuity™ delivers the next AI advantage to the legal industry: better AI outcomes from less AI effort.

For a recent walk-through of Opus 2, see this video:

LawToolBox Launches MCP Connecting Legal AI to Matter Data in Microsoft 365

LawToolBox announced LawToolBox MCP for Microsoft 365 and Claude, which connects the legal AI tools customers already use — including M365 Copilot, CoCounsel, Harvey, Legora, Protégé, Claude, and ChatGPT — to the matter-specific context that LawToolBox organizes in Matter Containers within Microsoft 365.

LawToolBox is a legal SaaS platform that lives inside each legal organization’s M365 account and transforms Outlook, Word, SharePoint and M365 Teams into a legal solution.

Its MCP connector includes 70 tools that leverage the M365 data in the LawToolBox matter containers, the applicable laws and regulations, and the legal team’s strategic analysis, all amplified with LLMs and saved to containers.

LawToolBox uses each organization’s CRM, DMS or homegrown database as the system of record to create AI-ready client matter data containers in their M365 that adhere to data governance and ethical walls.

To learn more, read this article on LawNext or watch this video.

Clarra Introduces Case Management MCP Server for Claude

Litigation case management company Clarra introduced what it calls the most comprehensive legal case management MCP server for Claude, giving AI tools meaningful access to case information without creating another disconnected system.

Through the integration, the company said, legal teams can:

  • Generate litigation briefs, matter summaries, chronologies, and demand letters.
  • Analyze deposition transcripts, medical records, and other case materials.
  • Prepare case strategies, deposition outlines, and litigation analyses.
  • Create staffing, budgeting and billing dashboards, and board reporting using live matter data.
  • Update matters, create tasks, and configure workflows using agentic AI.

“Legal teams shouldn’t have to purchase a different AI application for every task,” said Keao Caindec, CEO of Clarra. “By connecting Claude directly to Clarra, organizations can leverage one of the world’s most capable AI platforms to generate insights, draft legal work product, and automate operational tasks without leaving the platform.”

Eve Brings Analyst and Atlas to General Availability

Eve, the AI platform for plaintiff firms valued at more than $1 billion after its Series B, announced the general availability of two capabilities.

Analyst lets firm leaders ask any performance question — such as why Q3 settlement pace is behind — in plain English and get an instant answer.

Law firms also get a saved dashboard they can visit at any time that shows analytics such as settlement pacing, case loads, attorney performance, and more.

Atlas makes a law firm’s data all real-time by structuring every record, bill and communication the moment it hits the firm, so Analyst is never working from stale data, the company says.

Atlas automatically extracts records, bills and communications into a live case file, so the numbers Analyst reports come from work Eve already did, not data someone had to enter twice.

Atlas is available now for personal injury firms, with the same foundation extending to more practice areas as it matures.

news.titleEn: Descrybe Brings Legal Research and Intelligence to Microsoft 365 Copilot
news.titleZh: Descrybe将法律研究与智能引入Microsoft 365 Copilot
news.summaryZh:
2026年9月2日，Descrybe宣布Descrybe Legal Engine已在Microsoft 365 Copilot生态系统中可用，使组织能将专业法律研究与智能引入团队已在使用的AI工具。微软在2026年8月31日的Copilot新功能公告中将其列为六项新法律服务之一，与iManage Work、Boardwise、Harvey、Relativity和Everlaw并列。微软在Microsoft-built连接器库中列出Descrybe Legal Engine，发布者为微软。作为微软发布的联合连接器，除非管理员禁用，Descrybe默认对Microsoft 365租户启用。用户可在Copilot的Sources菜单中找到Descrybe并直接连接，无需手动配置MCP连接。

Descrybe Legal Engine还可与Microsoft Copilot Cowork配合使用，使用户能在单一Microsoft 365工作流中从法律研究转向工作成果：Cowork可使用Descrybe进行法律研究，然后利用结果创建Microsoft Word文档以供审阅。Descrybe Legal Engine使AI系统直接访问Descrybe的法律研究基础设施，该基础设施结合广泛的美国初级法律覆盖与结构化法律智能，旨在帮助识别不仅存在哪些权威，而且哪些权威对当前问题重要。Descrybe不是将法律信息视为无差别的文本体，而是结构化案件、引证、处理、法院和法律问题之间的关系，使AI系统能更智能、高效地检索和处理法律权威。该集成推进了Descrybe让其法律智能在整个AI生态系统中可用的战略，而非要求法律专业人士采用单一专有AI界面。Descrybe Legal Engine还可通过其他主要AI平台的集成和连接器使用，包括Claude、ChatGPT和Perplexity。Descrybe是一家法律技术公司，为专业人士、机构和AI系统构建可访问的法律研究和法律智能基础设施。
news.bodyHtml:
Descrybe’s expansion into Microsoft 365 Copilot further advances its strategy to make legal intelligence available wherever people work

BOSTON, September 2, 2026 — Descrybe today announced that Descrybe Legal Engine is available within the Microsoft 365 Copilot ecosystem, giving organizations a new way to bring specialized legal research and intelligence directly into the AI tools their teams already use.

Microsoft highlighted Descrybe Legal Engine in its August 31, 2026 What’s New in Microsoft Copilotannouncement as one of six new Legal Services offerings, alongside iManage Work, Boardwise, Harvey, Relativity and Everlaw. The announcement was part of Microsoft’s continued expansion of the Copilot ecosystem with connectors and plugins that bring domain-specific knowledge and business data into everyday AI workflows.

Microsoft lists Descrybe Legal Engine in its Microsoft-built connectors gallery, with Microsoft as the publisher. As a Microsoft-published federated connector, Descrybe is enabled by default for Microsoft 365 tenants unless administrators disable it. Users can find Descrybe directly in Copilot’s Sources menu and connect without manually configuring an MCP connection.

Descrybe Legal Engine also works with Microsoft Copilot Cowork, enabling users to move from legal research to work product within a single Microsoft 365 workflow. Cowork can conduct legal research using Descrybe Legal Engine and then use the results to create a Microsoft Word document for review.

“This is where the integration gets particularly interesting,” said Richard DiBona, co-founder and CTO of Descrybe. “Copilot Cowork can use Descrybe to conduct legal research and then turn the results into a Word document, all within the same workflow. That’s exactly why we built the Legal Engine as infrastructure: specialized legal intelligence can become part of the work people are already doing, rather than requiring them to move into another system.”

“For legal professionals, the question is increasingly not whether they will use AI, but whether the AI tools they already use can access the specialized intelligence required for serious legal work,” said Kara Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Descrybe. “Our goal has always been to make high-quality legal research available wherever people choose to work. Bringing Descrybe directly into Microsoft 365 Copilot is another important step toward that future.”

Descrybe Legal Engine gives AI systems direct access to Descrybe’s legal research infrastructure, which combines extensive U.S. primary-law coverage with structured legal intelligence designed to help identify not simply what authority exists, but which authority matters for the question at hand.

That distinction is central to Descrybe’s approach to AI-enabled legal research. Rather than treating legal information as an undifferentiated body of text, Descrybe structures relationships among cases, citations, treatments, courts and legal issues so AI systems can retrieve and work with legal authority more intelligently and efficiently.

“General-purpose AI is becoming extraordinarily capable, but legal work still requires trusted legal data, specialized retrieval and an understanding of authority,” Peterson said. “We believe the strongest legal AI ecosystem will combine increasingly powerful models with purpose-built legal intelligence. Microsoft’s approach to extending Copilot through specialized connectors is very much aligned with how we believe this market will develop.”

The Microsoft 365 Copilot integration advances Descrybe’s strategy of making its legal intelligence available across the AI ecosystem rather than requiring legal professionals to adopt a single proprietary AI interface. Descrybe Legal Engine is also available through integrations and connectors for other major AI platforms, including Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity, enabling users and organizations to bring the same underlying legal research capabilities into multiple workflows.

news.summaryZh: 本期《We Get AI》播客中，Jackson Lewis律所AI团队负责人Eric Felsberg与Joe Lazzarotti讨论了美国各州AI立法的最新进展及其对跨州雇主的影响。各州AI法律日益碎片化，使得多州雇主在维持一致的招聘实践、满足通知、透明度和治理要求方面面临更大挑战。近期最显著的发展是科罗拉多州对其先前全面而广泛的AI法律进行了大幅缩减，但雇主仍需履行某些义务。与此同时，康涅狄格州通过了新的法律，涵盖就业、伴侣机器人、聊天机器人、涉及儿童的问题等多个领域。过去一年中，纽约市、伊利诺伊州、科罗拉多州、加利福尼亚州和康涅狄格州等司法辖区相继出台AI相关法规，纽约市作为地方司法辖区，在就业领域AI使用监管方面被视为先行者，其要求包括偏见审计和发布相关通知。各司法辖区虽然关注相似主题，但具体做法有所不同。早期如科罗拉多州等地曾侧重于分析就业工具输出中的偏见证据，而当前各州立法呈现多样化趋势，雇主需密切关注并适应这一不断演变的监管环境。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The growing patchwork of AI laws makes maintaining consistent hiring practices and complying with notice, transparency and governance requirements more challenging for multi-state employers. In this episode, We Get AI co-hosts Eric Felsberg and Joe Lazzarotti address how the latest AI laws in Colorado and Connecticut fit into the broader employment regulatory landscape. Eric FelsbergPrincipal, Long Island Welcome to the We Get AI podcast. My name is Eric Felsberg, and I'm joined by my colleague Joe Lazzarotti. Joe and I are the leaders of the AI group at Jackson Lewis. We're happy to be with you as we try to demystify a lot of the AI developments that we're all experiencing; this is a rapidly moving area. The goal of this podcast is to ensure that we take some of those developments and break them down into easy-to-understand segments. If it goes well, offer you some practical tips on how to navigate this evolving area. Joe LazzarottiPrincipal, Tampa Hey, good to be with you, Eric. Today we want to try to touch on some recent developments. There was a significant change in Colorado. They had come out with a comprehensive, expansive AI law that required developers and deployers to take several steps, and it looks like that's been pretty scaled back, although there are still some things that have to be done. Connecticut more recently passed its own law that touched on a whole range of areas, obviously including employment, but also companion bots, chat bots, AI with children, issues with children, and a whole range of other issues. A good place to start is to touch on the Connecticut law and tell us what the key issues are and what businesses should be thinking about. Felsberg Those have been the two most recent developments. It's helpful to provide some context to the landscape of AI laws that are now joined by this updated Colorado law, as you mentioned, of course, Connecticut. We have seen laws pop up pretty consistently over the last year or so in different jurisdictions. We have New York City, of course, Illinois, Colorado, you mentioned, Joe, and you're going to cover. Colorado has this take two, if you will. California and Connecticut – these states are all popping up. In the case of New York, New York City as a local jurisdiction is coming up with its own methods for enforcing AI. It's challenging for employers because each of these jurisdictions is getting at the same themes. They're just going about it a little bit differently. The other thing that I find interesting is New York City, at least with respect to regulating use of AI in the employment context, has been seen as the leader here. You may recall New York City has a bias audit requirement. There's a publication requirement of the bias, or of course there's a notice piece. For a while, in places like Colorado, there seemed to be an emphasis on analyzing the output from some of these tools that we use in the employment context for evidence of bias. That seemed to be the emphasis early on.

news.summaryZh:
SpaceX于2026年6月与开源AI初创公司Reflection AI达成协议。据CNBC和TechCrunch报道，Reflection每月将支付约1.5亿美元，到2029年总额约63亿美元，以获取托管在SpaceX旗下Colossus 2数据中心的高性能英伟达GB300芯片及相关基础设施的使用权。该合同使Reflection立即获得稀缺的下一代训练算力。英伟达是Reflection的投资方之一，英伟达据报在投资该公司的同时，Reflection正付费获取由SpaceX收购并运营的英伟达硬件，这使英伟达既是该AI开发商的财务支持者，也是其增长所依赖的稀缺芯片的间接供应方。

该交易并非孤立事件。据CNBC报道，SpaceX今年早些时候完成与埃隆·马斯克旗下人工智能公司xAI的合并，合并后企业估值约1.25万亿美元，将发射能力、卫星基础设施与AI模型开发整合于同一公司架构。Colossus数据中心最初为支持内部AI业务而建，如今日益向包括谷歌和Anthropic在内的外部客户开放。该协议表明SpaceX正将大规模算力基础设施这一资本密集型能力转化为经常性收入来源，也反映出AI生态系统中先进模型开发对高端GPU等专用硬件的依赖及供应限制。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The agreement shows how control over frontier compute, data centers, chips, and related infrastructure may shape which AI developers can compete at scale. SpaceX’s June 2026 agreement with open-source AI startup Reflection AI underscores a broader shift Mogin Law has tracked in prior analysis of AI chokepoint deals: control is moving down the stack, from models to compute. According to CNBC and TechCrunch, Reflection will pay approximately $150 million per month—up to roughly $6.3 billion through 2029—for access to high-performance Nvidia GB300 chips and related infrastructure housed in SpaceX’s Colossus 2 data center. The contract gives Reflection immediate access to scarce, next-generation training capacity, a constraint that increasingly defines the frontier of AI development. The Nvidia connection adds another layer to the competitive picture. Later reporting described Reflection as having Nvidia among its backers, and noted that Nvidia reportedly invested in the company while Reflection is now paying for access to Nvidia hardware acquired and operated by SpaceX. That structure makes Nvidia both a financial supporter of the AI developer and an indirect supplier of the scarce chips on which the developer’s growth depends. The deal is not an isolated transaction. It reflects a deliberate effort by SpaceX to position itself as a central supplier of AI compute capacity, not merely as a participant in model development. Earlier this year, SpaceX completed its merger with Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI in a transaction that valued the combined enterprise at approximately $1.25 trillion, according to CNBC reporting. That deal consolidated launch capability, satellite infrastructure, and AI model development within a single corporate structure. The Reflection agreement shows how SpaceX is now monetizing a key byproduct of that integration: large-scale compute infrastructure. This fits reporting on AI infrastructure transactions. Capital is flowing into the physical and operational layers needed for AI systems to scale. Originally built to support internal AI efforts, the Colossus data centers are increasingly being opened to outside customers, including major AI developers such as Google and Anthropic. That model also echoes the competitive questions raised by major AI compute and cloud arrangements, including Mogin Law’s analysis of the AWS–OpenAI deal. This strategy resembles earlier platform shifts in technology markets. Control over critical infrastructure—whether operating systems, cloud platforms, or semiconductor fabrication—has often solidified durable competitive advantages. Here, the relevant input is not software distribution or chip design, but access to the compute resources required to train and run large language models. (Control over infrastructure is even into literal power itself, as big deals are being cut for electricty generation.) The importance of the Reflection deal lies less in its size and more in what it signals about constraints in the AI ecosystem. Advanced AI development depends on access to specialized hardware, particularly high-end GPUs. Supply remains limited, and the costs associated with building and operating large-scale data centers—including power, cooling, and real estate—are substantial. By aggregating these resources at scale, SpaceX is effectively converting a capital-intensive capability into a recurring revenue stream.

research.titleEn: KhatianDoc: A Human-Verified Benchmark Diagnosing Multimodal LLM Failure on Bengali Legal Land Records
research.titleZh: KhatianDoc：一个人类验证的基准，用于诊断多模态大语言模型在孟加拉法律土地记录上的失败
research.abstractEn: Land ownership in Bangladesh is recorded in Ana-Ganda-Kora-Kranti-Til, a base-16 positional fraction system with dedicated Unicode glyphs, no mainstream font, and no coverage in any OCR pipeline or tokenizer. The handwritten records that carry these fractions, RS Khatians, are the authoritative title record for millions of parcels and a frequent subject of civil litigation, yet no benchmark has asked whether a machine can read one. We introduce KhatianDoc, a four-task benchmark built from 107 real RS Khatian records from the Vumi (land) Office of Munshiganj, Bangladesh: symbol recognition, base-16-to-decimal conversion, structured field extraction, and legal document question answering over 1,634 QA pairs. Ground truth was transcribed by hand, verified by a land-law practitioner to full agreement, and anonymized through positional tokens that keep the referential distinctions multi-hop questions depend on. We evaluate six multimodal LLMs (8B to 72B+, open and closed) under a fixed zero-shot protocol. Five QA categories, 39.3% of our stratified set, return zero correct answers from every model; on the arithmetic task, every model that emits a number does worse than a constant-mean baseline, with exact- and near-match scores coinciding: decorrelation, not approximation. Auditing our own metrics surfaced two artifacts in opposite directions: we correct a refusal-scoring bug and report the fixed scores beside the originals, and flag an inflated metadata metric as an upper bound. KhatianDoc documents not a performance gap but the absence of a capability, with verified ground truth for future systems. Code and data, with a redacted image release, are publicly available.
research.abstractZh: 孟加拉国的土地所有权记录在Ana-Ganda-Kora-Kranti-Til中，这是一种基数为16的位置分数系统，拥有专用的Unicode字形，没有主流字体，且在任何OCR流程或分词器中均无覆盖。承载这些分数的手写记录，即RS Khatians，是数百万地块的权威所有权记录，也是民事诉讼的常见主题，然而尚无基准测试询问机器是否能读取其中一份。我们引入了KhatianDoc，一个由孟加拉国Munshiganj的Vumi（土地）办公室的107份真实RS Khatian记录构建的四任务基准：符号识别、基16到十进制转换、结构化字段提取，以及针对1,634个问答对的法律文档问答。真实标签由手工转录，经土地法律从业者验证完全一致，并通过位置标记进行匿名化，这些标记保留了多跳问题所依赖的指代区分。我们在固定的零样本协议下评估了六个多模态大语言模型（8B至72B+，开源和闭源）。五个问答类别，占我们分层集的39.3%，从所有模型返回零正确答案；在算术任务上，每个输出数字的模型都比常数均值基线表现更差，精确匹配和近似匹配分数重合：去相关，而非近似。审计我们自己的指标发现了两个方向相反的伪影：我们修正了一个拒绝评分错误，并在原始分数旁报告修正后的分数，同时将一个虚高的元数据指标标记为上限。KhatianDoc记录的不是性能差距，而是能力的缺失，并为未来系统提供了经过验证的真实标签。代码和数据，以及经过脱敏的图像发布，均已公开可用。

news.titleEn: Filevine Takes On Shepard’s and KeyCite With Its Own AI Case Law Citator and Hallucination Checker
news.titleZh: Filevine推出自有AI判例引证工具及幻觉检测功能，对标Shepard's与KeyCite
news.summaryZh: 法律科技公司Filevine在LOIS平台推出AI原生引证工具及配套简报审查工具，性能媲美或优于LexisNexis和Thomson Reuters的领先产品。引证工具可检查简报中的幻觉引用、篡改引文和错误描述权威，并允许用户高亮判决段落以验证其是否仍为有效法律。反幻觉工具本周首次发布。传统黄金标准Shepard's和KeyCite常对案件有效性意见不一，引用研究显示三者一致率仅15%，失败率分别为33%、38%和72%；Westlaw和Lexis的重叠率仅约三分之一。简报审查工具提取分析引用后，报告命题、系统发现、状态及严重程度。演示中，工具识别出简报错误引用“100%治愈”保单和Knight案中的引文问题。引证工具通过遍历引证图和语义相似性搜索，发现隐性冲突，并生成综合论文。评估显示，在2,073条引用中，LOIS验证61.8%，标记38.2%供审查，8.4%为严重，包括捏造案例、错误引文和错误描述权威。Filevine使用CourtListener库，计划添加法规。Anderson承认工具不能完全替代人工审查。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal technology company Filevine has launched an AI-native citator and a companion brief-checking tool inside LOIS, its Legal Operating Intelligence System AI platform, that its CEO says perform as well as or better than the leading legal citators from LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters.

The citator has two core features. One checks a filed or draft brief for hallucinated citations, altered quotations, and mischaracterized authority. The other checks whether a proposition is still good law by letting a lawyer highlight a specific passage in an opinion and find out whether later courts have undercut the holding expressed in the passage.

Although Filevine had previously announced the citator in June as part of its new LOIS Legal Research offering, which provides access to millions of opinions from U.S. federal and state courts, CEO Ryan Anderson, in a briefing this week, told me the company had not heavily promoted the citator until it believed the product was fully ready for customers to use.

The company had not previously announced the anti-hallucination tool, which is being released for the first time this week.

As Filevine described the citator in its June release: “While legal verification tools rely on explicit citation relationships and apply treatment signals to entire opinions, LOIS Legal Research operates at the user-selected passage level.” This enables legal professionals to verify the exact rule they plan to rely on in their argument.

The Challenge Of Citators

I have previously written that developing a strong citator tool is the Holy Grail of a legal research platform. Among companies to have succeeded in developing their own in recent years were vLex and Paxton, Descrybe, and Midpage, and if you read those linked articles, you will see that each of them took distinct approaches to the problem. (My Midpage article only teased its forthcoming citator, which it has since released.)

But it is not an easy task. In fact, in my briefing with Filevine this week, John Rizner, the product manager who led the development of the citator, pointed out something that most law librarians will know but that may be news to almost everyone else, which is that the two citators lawyers have long considered to be the gold standard routinely disagree with each other about whether a case is still good law.

He pointed to a 2018 study in the Law Library Journal by Paul Hellyer, a librarian at William & Mary Law School, who reviewed 357 citing relationships that at least one of Shepard’s, KeyCite or BCite had labeled negative.

All three citators agreed that the treatment was negative only 53 times, meaning that in 85% of the relationships in Hellyer’s sample, the three citators did not agree that a negative treatment had occurred.

Hellyer also examined whether the flags that did appear were correct. Counting relationships the citators omitted or mislabeled as positive or neutral, together with those labeled negative but incorrectly described, he found overall failure rates of 33% for Shepard’s, 38% for KeyCite and 72% for BCite.

Rizner also cited a second line of research, from Susan Nevelow Mart, the former director of the law library at the University of Colorado, whose 2013 examinations of digest and citator results found that the overlap between the Westlaw and Lexis citator systems on relevant results was small – only about a third.

As the abstract of Mart’s article put it: “Neither algorithm is doing a very good job of finding all the relevant results; the overlap between the two citator systems is not that large.”

Ahead of our briefing, Rizner ran his own test. He pulled Freedom Mortgage Corp. v. Engel on both platforms and filtered each down to negative treatment in reported opinions. Westlaw found 28 and Lexis found 13. The overlap between the two sets, by his count, was about 41%.

“If my law firm happens to have Lexis, I might be missing opinions because I don’t have Westlaw, or vice versa,” Rizner said.

What that means, Anderson said, is that even though the legacy citators have been best in class up until now, that does not mean that they do not make mistakes.

Citators As An Essential Tool

At this point, you may be thinking: “Sure, but what does this all have to do with Filevine, which is not a legal research platform?”

In my opinion, it has everything to do with Filevine and every other legal platform in which legal professionals are using AI to draft legal documents that rely on legal citations.

Thanks to concerns about AI accuracy and rampant hallucinations, the role – or maybe I should say the place – of the citator is evolving.

For most of their history, citators were legal research products – the last step before you wrapped up your research. But, as Anderson argued in our briefing, citation validation is now a required step in any legal workflow that produces a document relying on case law.

“Usually you’re taking facts, applying them to law and drafting,” he said. “That is the day-to-day shoe leather work of a lawyer.”

Filevine already held the facts, he said, but the missing pieces were a case law corpus and a way to confirm that what the corpus returns is still good law.

“And I think now there’s another step,” he said, “which is make sure nothing you’ve looked at is hallucinated.”

Earlier this year, at a meeting of roughly 20 large firms that Filevine convened, Anderson heard the same anxiety about hallucinations expressed repeatedly. One litigator said his top-10 firm now requires three separate sign-offs before any filing goes out, with the briefing associate required to attest that the associate had checked every citation and every holding.

Filevine’s Answer to This Need

So what is Filevine’s answer to this need? In our briefing this week, Anderson and Rizner demonstrated how the brief auditor and citator work.

For the brief auditor, after It ingests a document, it extracts and analyzes every citation, and then reports four things in a side-by-side chart:

  • The proposition the brief says the authority supports.
  • The citation given.
  • What the system found in the opinion.
  • The status, which can be verified, unverified, suspect, ambiguous, mischaracterized or wrong case name.

Using briefs pulled from PACER in matters where courts had already found problems, Anderson showed me examples. In one, a brief asserted that the 11th Circuit had squarely held that “100% healed” policies violate the ADA. The tool reported that the phrase appears in the opinion only in the plaintiff’s own request to return to full duty.

In another, drawn from Knight v. Baptist Hospital of Miami, the brief cited a passage for the proposition that disparate discipline of similarly situated employees is evidence of pretext. The tool flagged that the quoted sentence does not appear in the opinion and that the court’s reasoning runs the other way, having found the comparator not similarly situated.

“It’s really quite remarkable how subtle these hallucinations can be even when the case itself is not hallucinated,” he said. He noted that fabricated support often turns up in a dissent or in a recitation of case history rather than in the holding.

The citator works differently from a traditional one. Rather than starting from a case and examining its citation graph, the user highlights the specific language at issue.

Filevine then runs two passes – a traversal of the citation graph and a semantic similarity search – across its corpus for opinions using comparable reasoning. Opinions that come up as likely candidates are handed to LLMs, which distill the conflicts.

The output is a report keyed to the highlighted passage, with a severity rating and a written treatment for each authority.

In the results, a second tab generates what Rizner described as a synthetic treatise – a narrative discussion of the doctrinal tension, structured like a secondary source but built around the specific issue the user selected.

Because the semantic pass does not depend on one court citing another, Rizner said, it surfaces sub silentio conflicts, such as, for example, a 1985 decision and a 2005 decision that squarely contradict each other but never cite each other. This would be invisible to any citator built on a citation graph alone.

Evaluating the Results

Filevine gave me access to an as-yet unpublished paper evaluating its anti-hallucination tool.

According to the paper, Filevine’s evaluation team started with a database of 1,314 actual matters in which a judge had identified potentially hallucinated citations tied to admitted or suspected use of gen AI. It narrowed that pool to federal filings and then to filings submitted by attorneys rather than pro se litigants. That left 103 cases, of which 68 had records available for full analysis.

For each of the 68 matters, Filevine pulled the court’s order and the offending brief, ran the brief through LOIS using an identical prompt, and compared the output against the order. LOIS worked only from its own case law corpus, blocking general web search to keep it from finding news coverage or blog abouts about the cases.

Across 2,073 citations, LOIS verified 61.8%, flagged 38.2% for attorney review, and marked 8.4% as severe, meaning they were mischaracterized holdings or citations pointing to the wrong or a non-existent case. Every document in the sample produced at least one flag. Among the highest-citation filings, the cleanest still had roughly 9% of its citations flagged, while the worst had 76%.

Specifically, LOIS was instructed to look for three categories of hallucinated cases: fabricated case law, false or misattributed quotations, and mischaracterized authority.

For fabricated case law, LOIS found them in multiple matters. The report gave the example of Renschler v. Yosh, 909 F. Supp. 2d 1197, a citation LOIS flagged because no case by that name appeared anywhere in the reporter database.

For altered quotations, it also found multiple examples. The paper points to a Rule 37 sanctions argument that quoted the 2nd Circuit case of Shcherbakovskiy v. Da Capo Al Fine, Ltd. as requiring fault “of the sanctioned party,” when the court actually wrote “of the deponent.”

Filevine said the third category, mischaracterized authority, yielded “the exercise’s most critical observation,” which was the high number of instances when the citation appeared legitimate, but it did not stand for the proposition asserted, did not contain the argument attributed to it, or contained citations that LOIS could not access to confirm the authority.

In one filing, a brief cited Watson v. State of California for the proposition that California Government Code § 845.6 imposes an affirmative duty to summon medical care, when the opinion holds the statute confers broad immunity and the Watson plaintiff lost.

In another, Nai v. National Asset Mortgage, LLC, in the Western District of Michigan, counsel quoted RESPA’s limitations provision, 12 U.S.C. § 2614, as running from the “first” occurrence of the violation. The word “first” is not in the statute, meaning its insertion converted an occurrence-based trigger into a first-occurrence trigger, which counsel used to argue two tax years of claims were time-barred.

Notably, the report says, in matters where the bad citation had already been flagged by a court, LOIS caught the same defect, and it identified authorities cited for propositions that contradicted the underlying argument.

A Few Other Notes

As I noted above, the citator bases its analysis on the text highlighted by the user. Given that, I asked Rizner whether it was possible that a lawyer who validates one holding in a long, multi-issue opinion would not necessarily learn that the case was reversed on an unrelated holding.

He confirmed that is possible, though he said the system’s severity ratings are designed to explain when a citing case engaged with the opinion but not with the issue at hand. Anderson suggested that a direct query, or highlighting the full opinion, would likely catch it, but acknowledged the company had not tested that.

As for the source of Filevine’s case law corpus, it is using the CourtListener library, supplemented by licensed material that provides reporter citations and pagination for cases where they are lacking from the CourtListener collection.

The collection does not currently include statutes or regulations, although Filevine plans to add them in the future.

Bottom Line

I have not yet directly tested Filevine’s citator and anti-hallucination tools, although I hope to do that soon.

However, I think that this will prove to be of significant value to Filevine’s customers, many of whom are law firms with significant litigation practices.

By integrating within its AI platform both a corpus of case law and the ability to check citations against that corpus, Filevine is providing customers with an important safety check against hallucinations.

Of course, as Anderson pointed out, none of that replaces the need for lawyers and legal professionals to validate their own work.

“I don’t think it completely solves the problem,” he said. “A human still has to take a look. But at least we’re going to point you in the right direction.”

news.titleEn: 15% of Large Firm Lawyers ‘Now Dependent on AI’
news.titleZh: 调查：大型律所15%律师“现在依赖AI”
news.summaryZh: LexisNexis在英国开展的一项调查发现，大型律所中15%的律师“现在依赖AI”完成工作，企业内部律师的这一依赖比例也达到13%，表明法律AI已真正嵌入整个行业，且这些数字只会继续上升。在500多名受访律师中，34%表示每天使用AI工具处理法律工作，32%表示每周使用多次，约三分之二的律师频繁使用AI。调查显示，排名前三的使用场景为起草、法律研究和文件审阅。绝大多数受访者仍担忧AI工具可能产生幻觉和错误，许多人青睐能围绕准确性和使用经过验证的来源提供保障的AI系统，而大型法律数据提供商可以做到这一点。调查还发现，多数人认为AI的使用正导致公众及其自身客户对法律问题产生错误理解。调查表明，法律AI已成为许多律师生活中的关键部分，相当数量的律师离开它便无法工作。这些数字只会上升，意味着法律人才可能流向支持高水平AI使用的律所。这对法律AI公司而言也是天赐良机，其客户不会流失，且还会增多；尽管控制市场份额的竞争可能激烈，但市场似乎只会更广更深。大量使用AI的一个副作用是token成本，该领域仍在变化，但显然总得有人为token使用付费；这或许并非致命问题，而是市场成熟的标志。总体而言，这对法律AI领域非常有利，尽管有些人可能会担忧越来越多律师不愿在没有AI辅助的情况下工作，另一些人则可能认为这在意料之中，就像许多律师需要Microsoft Word、电脑、桌子和椅子一样。
news.bodyHtml:
15% of lawyers at large law firms are ‘now dependent on AI’ to do their job, a survey by LexisNexis in the UK has found. For inhouse this dependency also stood at a notable 13% – indicating that legal AI has well and truly become embedded now across the profession. Plus, those numbers will only increase.

Moreover, 34% of the 500-plus lawyers surveyed said that they used AI tools for legal work every day, and 32% ‘multiple times per week’. So, around two-thirds of lawyers are really using AI frequently.

They also surfaced that the top three use cases are: drafting, legal research, and document review, which is to be expected.

Understandably, the vast majority were still concerned about a potential risk for hallucinations and errors from AI tools, and equally understandably many favoured AI systems that could provide reassurance around accuracy and the use of verified sources – something that the major legal data providers can do.

One other survey finding was that the majority also felt that AI use is leading to the general public, and their own clients, getting an incorrect understanding of legal issues – something that connects to yesterday’s survey by Justice about the wider use of chatbots.

What does this tell us?

It shows – especially on the usage and dependence points – that legal AI has become a critical part of many lawyers’ lives, in fact so much so that a notable number could not do their work without it.

Those numbers will only rise, meaning that legal talent will likely gravitate to those firms that support high levels of AI usage.

It also is manna from heaven for the legal AI companies, i.e. their customers are not going anywhere – and there will be more of them. There may be intense competition to control market share, but that market is only growing wider and deeper, it appears.

One side effect of heavy AI use is token costs. This area is still in flux, but quite clearly someone, somewhere has to pay for the token usage. Although, this is perhaps not a killer problem – and is a sign of a maturing market.

Overall, all very promising for the field of legal AI – although some may of course be concerned that an increasing number of lawyers would not want to do their work without AI in a supporting role. Others may say that this is to be expected, the same as many lawyers would want to have Microsoft Word, a computer, a desk and a chair….! Technology moves on, and so do expectations of what is normal to have.

You can find the LexisNexis survey and report here.

—

Come and join us in London this November 4th + 5th at Legal Innovators! The conference at the intersection of legal AI and the business of law. Day One: law firms, Day Two: inhouse.

Legal Innovators UK – London, Nov 4 and 5

news.titleEn: Compliance used to be a cost center. The best firms are running it like a competitive advantage.
news.titleZh: 合规曾是成本中心，顶尖律所正将其转化为竞争优势
news.summaryZh:
客户会注意到律所受理新业务的速度差异：三小时与三天的差距并非人员配置问题，而是流程问题，并已成为竞争问题。过去二十年，合规与业务受理被视为必要但令人暗自抵触的职能，冲突分析师埋首搜索结果、受理请求停滞在队列中、聘用函来回往复，每家律所都面临同样的摩擦，却无人寻求更优方案。如今这一假设不再成立。AmLaw 100律所需管理复杂的外部律师指南，要求记录冲突审查流程、依据特定义务审核聘用条款，并在工作开始前配置道德墙。手动、大规模、不增加人手地满足这些要求，问题不会自行解决，反而随客户关系复杂化和监管预期收紧而恶化。行动最快的律所并未通过招聘解决，而是重建了该职能。

文章解释“代理式AI”的具体变化：新业务进入时，完整受理工作流自动运行，包括冲突检索与分类、外部律师指南匹配与例外审查、聘用条款起草、道德墙配置。合规专业人员看到业务时，常规工作已完成，呈递的是真正需要人类判断的例外。代理完成工作后交由专业人员决策，合规团队未被取代，而是被释放以专注于最重要案件。速度是可见收益，更不可见的是长期积累：每笔业务强化冲突检索逻辑、优化指南匹配、增加可搜索的机构知识，形成竞争对手无法构建的竞争护城河。文章警告，运行本地基础设施的律所面临风险，每季度停留在遗留系统，云端原生律所就在机构知识上扩大领先。
news.bodyHtml:
There is a firm in your market that accepted a new matter in three hours. Yours took three days. The client noticed and filed that away.

That gap is not a staffing problem. It’s a process problem. And it’s now a competitive one.

The first three pieces in this series made the case for why the firms pulling ahead are running the business side of law with the same rigor they bring to the practice side: growing on better relationship intelligence, protecting revenue before it disappears at billing. This is where that argument lands. Because none of it compounds the way it should if the front door is slow. A firm that wins the relationship but takes three days to onboard the matter is losing ground to a firm that closes in three hours.

Compliance and business acceptance aren’t separate from growth and revenue protection. They’re the function that either accelerates both or quietly constrains them.

For most of the last two decades, compliance and business acceptance were functions firms managed around. Necessary, respected in principle, quietly resented in practice. The conflicts analyst buried in search results. The intake request stalled in someone’s queue. The engagement letter going back and forth while the client waited to get started. Every firm dealt with the same friction. Nobody had a better option, so nobody asked whether there was one.

That assumption no longer holds.

The cost of slow intake

The economics of business acceptance have always been straightforward. A matter your firm can’t onboard in time is a matter your competitor onboards instead. What’s changed is the speed at which clients form that comparison and how quickly a pattern of slow intake compounds into a structural relationship disadvantage.

AmLaw 100 firms manage complex outside counsel guidelines that require documented conflict-check processes, engagement terms reviewed against specific obligations, and ethical walls configured before work begins. Meeting those requirements manually, at volume, without adding headcount, is not a problem that works itself out. It’s a problem that gets worse as client relationships grow more complex and regulatory expectations keep tightening.

The firms moving fastest have not found a way to hire their way out of it. They’ve rebuilt the function.

What agentic compliance actually means

The phrase “agentic AI” earns skepticism in most firms, and rightly so. A decade of technology promises has taught legal and compliance leaders to tune out the abstractions and ask what, specifically, changes.

Here is what specifically changes. This isn’t another technology layer on top of the work; it’s a fundamental shift in how the work gets done and who does it.

The moment a new matter comes in, the full acceptance workflow runs automatically. Conflicts are searched and triaged. Outside counsel guidelines are pulled, matched against the specific matter, and reviewed for exceptions. Engagement terms are drafted. Ethical walls are configured where required. By the time a compliance professional sees the matter, the routine work is done. What lands on their desk is the exception that genuinely needs them: the complex conflict, the unusual OCG requirement, the high-risk engagement that warrants human judgment.

Agents do the work and bring it back to your professionals for the decisions that actually require them. The compliance team isn’t displaced; they’re freed to focus on the cases that matter most, at scale.

Speed is the visible benefit. The less visible one compounds over a longer horizon.

Every matter that flows through an agentic system strengthens the conflict-check logic, refines OCG matching, and adds to searchable institutional knowledge that competitors running manual processes cannot build. That accumulated intelligence becomes the firm’s competitive moat. The gap it creates is structural and doesn’t close.

The firms most at risk are the ones currently running on-premises infrastructure and treating migration as a future-year decision. On-premises technology is a competitive problem. Every quarter spent on legacy systems is a quarter the cloud-native firms are extending their lead on the institutional knowledge that only accumulates in the cloud.

Intapp Celeste is the AI platform purpose-built for the work that runs a professional firm, on your own data, under your own rules. Compliance with Celeste deploys agents across conflicts clearance, new business intake, and client obligations management: the three functions that together determine how fast and how cleanly a firm can onboard new business.

An agent that creates and prepopulates intake forms using emails shared by requestors, validates data before submission, and flags enhancements before the request goes through. An agent that ingests outside counsel guideline documents, matches them to client records, and auto-populates key information into a central repository that enforces compliance in downstream systems.

Compliance with Celeste doesn’t replace the compliance professional. It removes the work that should never have required one.

A firm whose compliance team spends its time on genuine risk decisions retains better talent and makes better calls than one where analysts are absorbed in search logistics.

The window to close that gap is narrowing. Every quarter spent on legacy systems is a quarter the cloud-native firms are extending a lead that doesn’t shrink on its own.

research.titleEn: OBJECTION! Lawyer Agents Mitigate Guilty Bias in Legal Judgment Prediction
research.titleZh: 异议！律师代理缓解法律判决预测中的有罪偏见
research.abstractEn: Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) models are typically trained on documents that describe facts from a prosecutorial perspective. Existing datasets further exhibit severe label imbalance toward guilty outcomes. Consequently, these models suffer from "Guilty Bias", blindly accepting the prosecution's narrative as objective truth. Previous studies employing three-step reasoning structures or training on synthetically generated innocence data improve overall accuracy, but they still fail to mitigate bias at inference time.   In this paper, we introduce OBJECTION, an inference-time pipeline that integrates an Adversarial Lawyer Agent into each 3-step reasoning of offense, unlawfulness, and culpability. Unlike generic critics, our agent actively challenges the model's presumptions of guilt by injecting legal defense arguments at each reasoning stage. To thoroughly evaluate this, we present a new "Natural Innocent" dataset including 3.4k real-world cases, overcoming the limitations of synthetic innocence benchmarks. Test results show that OBJECTION drastically reduces the False Guilty Rate (FGR) from 82.93% (SOTA baseline) to 16.69%, proving its capability to perform substantive legal reasoning. This work denotes a key progress toward aligning Legal AI with the presumption of innocence.
research.abstractZh: 法律判决预测（LJP）模型通常基于从起诉方视角描述事实的文档进行训练。现有数据集进一步表现出对有罪结果的严重标签不平衡。因此，这些模型遭受“有罪偏见”，盲目地将起诉方的叙述接受为客观事实。先前采用三步推理结构或在合成生成的无罪数据上训练的研究提高了整体准确率，但在推理时仍未能缓解偏见。在本文中，我们引入了OBJECTION，这是一个推理时管道，将对抗性律师代理集成到犯罪、违法性和有责性的每个三步推理中。与一般的批评者不同，我们的代理通过在每个推理阶段注入法律辩护论点，主动挑战模型的有罪推定。为了全面评估这一点，我们提出了一个新的“自然无罪”数据集，包含3.4k个真实世界案例，克服了合成无罪基准的局限性。测试结果表明，OBJECTION将错误有罪率（FGR）从82.93%（SOTA基线）大幅降低至16.69%，证明了其进行实质性法律推理的能力。这项工作标志着在法律AI与无罪推定对齐方面迈出了关键一步。

research.titleEn: LexIssue: Benchmarking Legal Issue Identification in Chinese Civil Litigation
research.titleZh: LexIssue：中国民事诉讼中法律争点识别的基准测试
research.abstractEn: Identifying the issues disputed between litigating parties is a crucial component of real-world litigation. However, legal issues remain comparatively underexplored in legal AI research. In this work, we study the computational modelling of legal issue identification in litigation. We introduce a legally grounded hierarchical schema that represents legal issues through both free-form issue descriptions and structured legal categories, and formulate legal issue identification as two complementary tasks: legal issue generation and legal issue classification. Based on this formulation, we construct LexIssue, a benchmark containing 430 real-world Chinese civil litigation cases and 1,303 expert-annotated disputed legal issues. We further develop an issue-centric legal knowledge base spanning 27 causes of action and 441 candidate legal issue entries to support retrieval-augmented reasoning. Experimental results across a diverse set of models show that retrieval-augmented generation using the constructed legal issue knowledge base consistently improves performance in identifying disputed legal issues and their corresponding legal attributes.
research.abstractZh: 识别诉讼当事人之间争议的问题（争点）是现实诉讼中的关键环节。然而，法律争点在法律人工智能研究中相对而言仍未得到充分探索。在本研究中，我们探讨了诉讼中法律争点识别的计算建模。我们引入了一个基于法律的分层模式，通过自由形式的争点描述和结构化的法律类别来表示法律争点，并将法律争点识别表述为两个互补的任务：法律争点生成和法律争点分类。基于这一表述，我们构建了LexIssue，一个包含430个真实中国民事诉讼案件和1,303个专家标注的争议法律争点的基准。我们进一步开发了一个以争点为中心的法律知识库，涵盖27个案由和441个候选法律争点条目，以支持检索增强推理。在多种模型上的实验结果表明，使用所构建的法律争点知识库进行检索增强生成，能够持续提升识别争议法律争点及其相应法律属性的性能。

news.titleEn: Partner Spotlight | Philips SpeechLive
news.titleZh: 合作伙伴聚焦 | Philips SpeechLive
news.summaryZh:
Philips SpeechLive 是一款云端语音转文字与法律口述解决方案，帮助各类规模律所更快创建文档，减少行政工作并提升效率。其与 Actionstep 合作，源于后者现代化、云原生的法律实践管理方式，双方共享通过互联技术提升律所效率的愿景。Actionstep 的开放生态系统让律所连接 SpeechLive 等一流方案，灵活构建符合自身工作方式的流程。

该集成解决法律专业人士耗费大量时间创建笔记、信函和文档的问题：律师可通过移动应用、桌面应用或浏览器随时随地口述，录音经 AI 语音识别或专业转录服务安全转录，并纳入 Actionstep 文档工作流，实现转录、委派与案件分配。许多律所报告文档创建时间显著节省、行政负担减少、客户沟通加快，口述笔记和信函能更快转化为可用案件内容。AI 正将重复性工作移出日常工作流，帮助律师和支持人员更快捕捉、转录、起草、总结和路由工作。现代律所日益寻求云端集成技术，以减少复杂性、支持混合工作、提升安全性并自动化重复任务，同时重视用户体验。Philips SpeechLive 期待继续帮助 Actionstep 律所现代化文档创建工作流，利用 AI 语音识别进步，共同简化运营、提升生产力。
news.bodyHtml:
We caught up with the team at Philips SpeechLive to talk about bringing voice productivity into the legal workflow, and how their integration with Actionstep is helping firms turn dictation into delegated, trackable work. 

Can you briefly introduce your organization and the types of law firms you typically work with? 

Philips SpeechLive is a cloud-based speech-to-text and legal dictation solution that helps law firms create documentation faster and more efficiently. We work with firms of all sizes, from boutique practices to large, multi-office firms, helping legal professionals reduce administrative work, improve productivity, and spend more time focusing on their clients. 

What attracted you to Actionstep’s product initially? 

We partnered with Actionstep because of its modern, cloud-native approach to legal practice management. Actionstep shares our vision of helping firms work more efficiently through connected technology, making it a natural fit for integrating voice productivity into legal workflows. 

What excites you most about working with Actionstep’s platform and community of law firms? 

We’re excited to work alongside a platform that’s committed to innovation and helping law firms embrace smarter ways of working. Actionstep’s open ecosystem enables firms to connect best-in-class solutions like SpeechLive, giving lawyers the flexibility to build workflows that match how they work while improving productivity across the firm. 

What problem does your integration solve for Actionstep firms, and how did the idea come about? 

Legal professionals spend a significant amount of time creating notes, correspondence, and legal documents. Our integration allows them to capture their thoughts naturally using their voice and have those recordings securely transcribed, delegated, and made available within their workflow. The partnership was driven by a shared goal of reducing administrative burden while making document creation faster and more accurate. 

Can you walk us through how your integration works alongside Actionstep in a firm’s daily workflow? 

Lawyers can dictate from wherever they work — whether they’re in the office, at court, or meeting with clients — using the SpeechLive mobile app, desktop application, or browser. Recordings are securely transcribed using AI speech recognition or professional transcription services and can then be incorporated into the firm’s document workflows within Actionstep, helping teams complete work more efficiently without disrupting existing processes. 

What kind of results or efficiencies have firms seen after adding your integration to their Actionstep setup? 

Many firms report significant time savings in document creation, reduced administrative workload, and faster turnaround on client communications. By replacing manual typing with voice, lawyers can complete documentation more efficiently while maintaining high levels of accuracy, allowing support staff to focus on higher-value work. 

What benefits do your clients see most from implementing Actionstep or adopting your integration? 

Clients see the biggest benefit in turning dictated notes and correspondence into usable matter content faster. Instead of dictations, transcriptions, and follow-up tasks being spread across email inboxes, devices, or separate systems, everything can be kept in one place and quickly assigned to the relevant matter in Actionstep. 

Lawyers can capture information by voice immediately after a meeting, call, or court appearance, while support teams can access the recording or transcript, delegate the next step, and move work forward without chasing files or instructions. This creates a clearer workflow for delegation, speeds up client communication, and helps firms keep matters moving with less manual administration. 

How are you seeing AI reshape the way law firms operate, and where do you think it’s headed? 

AI is reshaping law firm operations by taking repetitive work out of the day-to-day workflow. Instead of manually typing attendance notes, drafting first versions of routine correspondence, or searching through scattered information, lawyers and support staff can use AI to capture, transcribe, draft, summarize, and route work faster. In practice, this means a dictated note can become a transcript, be assigned to the right matter, and give the team a clear next step much more quickly. 

What trends are you seeing in how modern law firms think about operations and technology? 

Law firms are increasingly looking for cloud-based, integrated technology that reduces complexity rather than adding to it. They want solutions that connect seamlessly, support hybrid work, improve security, and automate repetitive tasks. Firms are also placing greater emphasis on user experience, recognizing that technology adoption is just as important as technology capability. 

What are you most looking forward to in your continued partnership with Actionstep? 

We’re excited to continue helping Actionstep firms modernize their document creation workflows and take advantage of advances in AI-powered speech recognition. Together, we can help firms streamline operations, improve productivity, and deliver an even better experience for both legal professionals and their clients. 

Ready to bring voice productivity into your firm’s workflow? 

The Philips SpeechLive integration with Actionstep helps lawyers turn dictation into delegated, trackable work — cutting administrative time and speeding up client communication. Get in touch to see how Philips SpeechLive can fit into your firm’s daily workflow. 

The post Partner Spotlight | Philips SpeechLive appeared first on Actionstep.

news.titleZh: Practus LLP 部署 Intapp 代理式 AI 解决方案，驱动创新与增长
news.summaryZh:
Intapp（纳斯达克代码：INTA）于2026年9月1日宣布，法律服务公司Practus, LLP及其后台服务提供商Auxana Administrative Services已选择Intapp作为核心技术合作伙伴，以简化法律和业务运营。Intapp的集成应用及其原生代理式AI能力将帮助Practus和Auxana提升从客户受理、利益冲突、工时到客户关系管理的效率。Practus由John Lively于2018年创立，是一家虚拟律师事务所，结合顶级法律专长与灵活、技术先行的运营模式。Auxana为律师事务所提供后台运营、技术和行政基础设施，通过其平台和战略技术领导力，Practus选择Intapp实施统一的企业级解决方案，以增强客户受理、改善数据可见性并简化全所运营效率。

过去两年，Practus和Auxana使用Intapp Conflicts评估新业务，识别并处理道德、商业和主题利益冲突，同时利用Intapp Walls维护信息屏障。现新增Intapp Intake自动化客户入职流程，捕获合规所需关键数据。Intapp Time将为律师提供灵活工时记录方法和AI能力，防止计费时间流失。业务发展方面，将部署Intapp DealCloud with Celeste，Celeste作为专家AI协作者，支持自然语言提问并综合关系历史、互动活动和管道背景提供答案，通过文档摄取和对话式记录更新消除手动数据录入，快速生成会前简报、管道摘要和关系情报。DealCloud提供集中平台，零录入数据能力帮助构建客户、潜在客户和联系人关系的全面视图，利用专有和第三方数据提供客户趋势和行业发展的可操作洞察。Auxana将与Intapp实施服务团队及Intapp合作伙伴Epiq和Nidaan Systems合作，以迭代、以用户为中心的方法完成部署。
news.bodyHtml:
From conflicts and intake to relationship intelligence, a next-generation virtual law firm is building its operational backbone on Intapp’s governed AI platform

PALO ALTO, Calif. — September 1, 2026 — Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA), the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries, today announced that legal services firm Practus, LLP, and its back-office services provider, Auxana Administrative Services, have chosen Intapp as a core technology partner to streamline their legal and business operations. Intapp’s integrated applications, including its native agentic AI capabilities, will help Practus and Auxana improve efficiency across intake, conflicts, time, and client relationship management.

Practus is a next-generation law firm founded in 2018 by John Lively to modernize the delivery of legal services. The virtual firm combines top-tier legal expertise with a flexible, technology-forward operating model. Central to Practus’ continued growth is Auxana Administrative Services, an integrated legal services organization that provides back-office operations, technology, and administrative infrastructure for law firms and other professional services organizations. Through Auxana’s platform and strategic technology leadership, Practus selected Intapp to implement a unified, enterprise-grade solution that enhances client intake, improves data visibility, and streamlines firmwide operational efficiency.

Technology is central to the identity and operational model of Practus and Auxana. They continually evaluate technology investments to ensure they meet the evolving needs of their lawyers and clients. Through a strategic approach to technology adoption, Auxana turned to Intapp to create a connected ecosystem of AI-enabled solutions designed to simplify workflows, strengthen connectivity across its virtual environment, and enhance client relationships.

Delivering elevated legal services

For the past two years, Practus and Auxana have used Intapp Conflicts to quickly and thoroughly evaluate new business. The solution helps them identify and address ethical, business, and subject-matter conflicts of interest, while Intapp Walls maintains information barriers that protect sensitive information across the firms. The organizations have now added Intapp Intake to automate client onboarding processes by capturing critical data needed to manage compliance with industry regulations. This enables partners to focus on delivering exceptional client service rather than manual data capture and entry.

With Intapp Time, Practus and Auxana will give their lawyers flexible timekeeping methods, AI capabilities, and an easy, modern way to record their time and prevent losing billable hours. The solution will also help them easily see how they’re allocating their time, and better understand the value delivered across each matter.

Empowering lawyers with data and AI

For business development, Practus and Auxana will deploy Intapp DealCloud with Celeste. Celeste is the expert AI coworker that transforms how professionals interact with DealCloud. Rather than navigating records or pulling reports, lawyers and business-development professionals can ask questions in plain language and receive synthesized answers drawn across relationship history, engagement activity, and pipeline context. Celeste also eliminates manual data entry through document ingestion and conversational record updates, helping keep firm intelligence current without interrupting the flow of work. Pre-meeting briefs, pipeline summaries, and relationship intelligence that would otherwise require hours of research can be surfaced in seconds. This helps business-development teams identify the warmest path to a contact, prioritize outreach, and engage clients and prospects with the full weight of the firm’s collective knowledge behind every interaction.

With DealCloud, Practus and Auxana will have a centralized platform where lawyers and business professionals can find and reference communications, workflows, and other data relating to client relationships, outreach, and engagements. Zero-entry data capabilities will help the firm build and manage a comprehensive view of its relationships with clients, prospects, and other contacts. Access to collective firm intelligence will help teams use AI to strengthen relationships, accurately track and forecast work, accelerate execution, and identify opportunities to expand relationships across other business units. Leveraging proprietary and third-party data will also provide actionable insights into client trends and industry developments.

Software delivery

To facilitate a successful deployment of Intapp Intake, Time, and DealCloud, Auxana will work closely with the Intapp Implementation Services team, as well as Epiq and Nidaan Systems — both Intapp partners. These implementation specialists will take an iterative, user-centric approach aligned with Auxana’s unique business needs.

Supporting quotes

Valerie Spengler, Chief Innovation and Strategy Officer, Practus, LLP
“From the start, Practus was built to run without the overhead a traditional firm carries. Our people collaborate seamlessly regardless of location. Intapp gives us one connected system for the business of running the firm, so conflicts, intake, and time don’t pull our lawyers away from the sophisticated work clients hire them for.”

Laura Saklad, Vice President, Legal Industry, Intapp
“Choosing Intapp for conflicts, intake, and time management aligns directly with Auxana’s ‘intelligent use of resources’ strategy — letting them achieve optimal outcomes while easing the administrative burden on their professionals. It will also allow Auxana to better collect and use institutional knowledge to make more informed decisions for their own businesses and their clients’ businesses alike.”

Chris Raymond, Practice Group Leader, Intapp
“As Auxana and Practus grow, DealCloud will help them expand their offerings in alignment with their clients’ needs. Access to centralized data will also let each professional make better use of firmwide intelligence across the client lifecycle to build their books of business.”

Additional resources

  • Learn about Intapp Celeste 
  • Learn about Intapp Conflicts 
  • Learn about Intapp DealCloud  
  • Learn about Intapp Intake 
  • Learn about Intapp Time 
  • Learn about Intapp Walls for AI 

Connect with Intapp

  • Learn more at Intapp 
  • Get more news in the Intapp newsroom 
  • Follow Intapp on LinkedIn 

Forward-looking statements

This press release contains express and implied “forward-looking statements” within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including statements regarding Intapp’s products and services and the expected results or benefits from use of our products and services. By their nature, these statements are subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including factors beyond our control, that could cause actual results, performance, or achievement to differ materially and adversely from those anticipated or implied in the statements. Additional risks and uncertainties that could cause actual outcomes and results to differ materially from those contemplated by the forward-looking statements are included under the caption “Risk Factors” and elsewhere in our Annual Report on Form 10-K, our Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q, and any subsequent public filings. Forward-looking statements speak only as of the date the statements are made and are based on information available to us at the time those statements are made and/or management’s good faith belief as of that time with respect to future events. We assume no obligation to update forward-looking statements to reflect events or circumstances after the date they were made, except as required by law. Any unreleased services, features, or functions referenced in this document, our website, or other press releases or public statements that are not currently available are subject to change at Intapp’s discretion and may not be delivered as planned or at all.

About Intapp

Intapp (NASDAQ: INTA) is the governed AI platform for professional firms in highly regulated industries. Intapp’s vertically tailored agentic solutions are built for the specialized workflows, complex relationship networks, and professional compliance requirements of accounting, consulting, investment banking, law, private capital, and real assets firms. By applying Firm AI to core processes and data, Intapp helps partners, dealmakers, and advisors drive firm growth, manage compliance, and improve profitability. Learn why the world’s top firms trust Intapp’s industry-specific enterprise solutions at intapp.com.

Contact
Emily Martinez
Global Media and Communications Director

news.titleEn: Your analyst isn’t the bottleneck. Your process is.
news.titleZh: 你的分析师不是瓶颈，流程才是。
news.summaryZh: 在律所中，AI利益冲突清理本应成为竞争优势，但中型律所的分析师却需花费数小时手动重建公司树、追查intake表格、交叉核对可能未反映客户最新修订的外部律师指南电子表格。每一步流程都必不可少，问题在于由谁或什么来完成：重建公司树是数据组装，追查intake是项目协调，交叉核对电子表格是版本控制，而分析师本应负责发现不明显的问题、权衡风险并做出判断。通用AI模型不了解利益冲突检查、公司关联方与冲突方的区别、道德墙要求或案件关系，更快的结果若基于不完整的领域知识会带来实际后果。欧盟《人工智能法案》是全球首个全面监管AI的独立立法，其他司法管辖区也在响应，如澳大利亚隐私法改革将于2026年12月生效，要求律所披露AI在影响个人的决策中做出或实质性协助的情况。无论在哪里运营，责任都在部署AI的律所。通用AI能帮助个人分析师更快工作，但无法强制执行道德墙、管辖规则和跨业务治理义务。MIT 2025年研究发现95%的企业AI计划零可衡量回报。领先的合规领导者已做出特定架构选择：AI在受治理环境中处理组装，人类在完整背景下处理判断。Intapp Compliance with Celeste基于此设计，AI代理在intake、利益冲突清理和客户义务管理中运行，使用专为律所案件、关系和风险结构构建的数据模型，融入现有工作流。
news.bodyHtml:
For law firms, AI conflicts clearance should be a competitive advantage. Instead, a conflicts analyst at a mid-size firm spends hours clearing a single matter. She reconstructs the corporate tree by hand. She chases intake forms. She cross-references Outside Counsel Guideline (OCG) spreadsheets that may or may not reflect the latest client amendments. By the time the matter is cleared, the firm has done the work correctly. The client has been waiting since Monday.

Across town, a competitor cleared the same matter before lunch.

The analyst didn’t do anything wrong.

The job that got rewritten

Every step of that process needs to happen. The question is who, or what, does it.

Reconstructing a corporate tree is data assembly. Chasing intake completions is project coordination. Cross-referencing spreadsheets against outside counsel guidelines is version control. The analyst was hired to find the thing that isn’t obvious, weigh the risk, and make the call. Somewhere along the way, the platform’s limitations rewrote the job description. And because every firm’s platform had the same limitations, the industry normalised it.

Why layering generic AI makes it worse

A general-purpose model doesn’t know what a conflict check is. It doesn’t understand the difference between a corporate affiliate and a conflicting party, what an ethical wall requires, or how matter relationships sit inside a law firm. It moves faster, and faster results built on incomplete domain knowledge carry real consequences.

The EU AI Act is the first and most comprehensive standalone legislation specifically governing AI and regulatory development in AI governance globally. Other jurisdictions are watching it and responding in their own way: some are developing dedicated frameworks, others are slotting AI obligations into existing legislation. Australia is a case in point, its Privacy Act reforms, coming into effect December 2026, will require firms to disclose where AI makes or substantially assists in decisions that affect individuals. The instruments differ. The direction doesn’t. Wherever you operate, the accountability sits with the firm deploying the AI.

There is also the difference between personal productivity and firm productivity. A general-purpose AI can help an individual analyst work faster. It cannot enforce the ethical walls, jurisdictional rules, and cross-practice governance obligations that a conflicts decision requires, particularly for firms operating across regions or practice groups where those obligations differ.

Most firms discover this after the pilot. MIT’s 2025 research found 95% of enterprise AI initiatives deliver zero measurable return. S&P Global puts the abandonment rate at 42% of all AI projects in 2025, more than double the year before. The firms that stalled didn’t fail because the technology let them down. They entered production without the foundation it requires: governance that maps to how the firm actually operates, and a data model that understands what a matter, an ethical wall, and a cross-practice conflict actually mean.

What the shift actually looks like

The compliance leaders pulling ahead have made a specific architectural choice: AI handles the assembly in a governed environment, humans handle the judgment with full context.

By the time a question reaches the analyst, the corporate tree is already mapped, the search has already run, and results are triaged by relationship type and risk level. What used to take a morning takes minutes, not because the analyst works faster, but because the preparation is done before they open the matter.

Client obligations follow the same logic. Instead of manually cataloguing OCGs against a spreadsheet that lags every client update by weeks, obligations are surfaced automatically and tracked consistently across matters.

This is also the answer to the question every compliance leader eventually asks: what happens when the AI gets it wrong? For intake, conflicts, and terms, full autonomy isn’t the right model. The right design keeps humans accountable for decisions while removing the manual preparation that was making those decisions slow.

Intapp Compliance with Celeste is built on that design. AI agents run across intake, conflicts clearance, and client obligations management using a data model built specifically for how law firms structure matters, relationships, and risk, inside existing workflows, so the firm doesn’t have to choose between modernising and keeping the team operational while it does.

What C-level conversations on this tell me

The compliance leader who makes this case internally needs language their managing partner will act on. When I sit with managing partners and COOs, the conversation usually moves quickly from “does it work” to three bigger questions.

Speed and capacity move together. Faster clearance means more matters through the same window. But the more durable gain is that analysts shift from data preparation to judgment work. The firm gets both: throughput goes up, and the quality of the analysis improves because the analyst is doing what they were actually hired to do.

Intake quality compounds downstream. When AI handles intake follow-up automatically, flagging incomplete submissions before they hit the queue, searches run on cleaner data. Fewer matters reopened. Fewer escalations. Fewer write-offs. Fewer billing disputes. That downstream effect often exceeds the speed gain and it’s where the hard savings show up.

When compliance runs cleanly, the firm has a platform to grow from, not a queue to manage. Compliance teams currently absorb demand spikes by stretching permanent staff or bringing in temporary cover. When the platform handles the preparation work, that pressure has somewhere to go. And when compliance data is reliable and real-time, managing partners can see which practice groups have capacity, where intake is creating friction, and where the firm has room to grow without adding risk. Managing partners who run compliance on a modern platform stop asking how to manage demand. They start asking how much more the firm can take on.

The transition is the real test

The concern most compliance leaders carry into this conversation isn’t whether the technology works. It’s whether the people and the data will move with it.

Data migration is the visible risk. Conflicts systems carry years of matter history and obligation records, a migration that loses fidelity, even briefly, creates the exposure it was meant to prevent. What runs in parallel, what the rollback plan looks like. These are the questions a production-ready platform should answer without hesitation.

Change management is equally high on the list. Analysts adopt a new platform when it fits how they actually work and feels more intuitive to use. The firms that get this right map both analysts’ and firm workflow, demonstrate where the friction disappears, and build the transition around that. Intapp Compliance with Celeste is built to answer all of this before the migration begins.

The compounding cost of waiting

The capability gap between firms running AI-native compliance and firms still on legacy platforms widens every quarter. A competitor clearing the same matter in hours rather than days doesn’t just win that matter faster. Over time, they accept more work, deepen client relationships, and make the case to their own managing partners that compliance is a growth function, not a cost centre.

See how Intapp Compliance with Celeste helps your firm accept more business, faster — without adding headcount or compromising risk.

Schedule a demo

news.titleEn: 1/4 of Young People Use AI For Their Legal Needs
news.titleZh: 四分之一年轻人使用AI满足法律需求
news.summaryZh: 一项针对3200多人的新调查发现，18至24岁人群中略超四分之一（26%）在遇到法律问题时求助于AI，55至64岁人群该比例为10%。AI系统提供的情感支持往往是使用因素之一。调查发现，人们“常要求聊天机器人解释法律术语、核查律师建议、起草投诉和邮件，并提供情感安慰”。数据由英国法律慈善机构Justice与行政公平实验室收集，时间跨度为去年年底至2026年1月。许多人在主要不属于法律援助范围的常见法律问题上寻求AI帮助，如住房、就业、债务、消费者问题和家庭法。参与者描述了对法庭诉讼的恐惧、对失业的担忧，以及对持续纠纷不确定性的不堪重负。然而，在向这些聊天机器人寻求情感和法律支持时，用户可能无意中让自己获得不太可靠的建议。证据表明，将聊天机器人设计得友好温暖会使它们更可能强化错误信念，而听起来最脆弱的人得到的回答最不准确。”Justice副法律总监Ellen Lefley评论：“问题不在于AI是否成为人们法律旅程的一部分——它已经是了。这项研究提供了关于谁在使用以及如何使用的独特见解。现在的挑战是确保人们获得可靠支持，同时解决最初驱使一些人转向AI的未满足法律需求。”行政公平实验室联合主任Jed Meers博士补充：“法院和法庭系统需求上升有一系列复杂驱动因素。我们的研究表明，人们在遇到各种法律问题时正在使用这些工具，且数量已相当可观。随着这些工具的使用增长，它们将成为更重要的因素。
news.bodyHtml:
A new survey of over 3,200 people has found that just over one quarter (26%) of 18 to 24 year olds have turned to AI when they had a legal problem. For those between 55 and 64 it was 10%. Emotional support from the AI systems was often a factor in their use.

People ‘commonly asked chatbots to explain legal jargon, check advice from lawyers, draft complaints and emails, and provide emotional reassurance’, the survey found.

And it must be a bit galling for some lawyers when they find out that their clients are using ChatGPT to check their advice….! I.e. they’d rather trust the AI than the lawyer.

The data from UK legal charity Justice, and the Administrative Fairness Lab, was collected between the end of last year and January 2026. It shows just how far AI is having an impact on the wider legal world, although AL has to say, this site would have assumed the vast majority of people of any age would use AI to help with a legal issue these days.

But, Google will tell you that only around 15 million people in the UK use, or have used, a tool such as ChatGPT – which is just under one quarter of the population. So, perhaps what this data really shows is this: if you regularly use AI tools, then you are likely to use LLMs to help with any legal issues you may have.

For example, an individual may use AI to help with general information about a landlord issue, but they may equally perform speculative legal research in relation to employment law.

The survey authors commented that: ‘Many sought AI help on common legal problems that largely fall outside the scope of legal aid, such as housing, employment, debt, consumer issues, and family law.‘

In short, society is turning to AI to do what regular human lawyers are there to provide – and it’s important to note the emotional reassurance point.

Now…..is that advice correct? Is it useful? Does it confuse the user?

As Justice put it: ‘Participants described feeling frightened about court proceedings, worried about losing their job, and overwhelmed by the uncertainty of ongoing disputes, for example. 

‘However, in seeking emotional as well as legal support from these chatbots, users may unwittingly be setting themselves up to receive less reliable advice. Evidence suggests designing chatbots to be friendly and warm makes them more likely to reinforce false beliefs, with the most vulnerable-sounding people eliciting the least accurate responses.’

And this goes to a very real problem we have now. AI has widened access to justice, at least in informational terms, and yet those outputs are not regulated.

This free support can also lead to companies and courts becoming overwhelmed with legal demands, some of which judges may see as ‘vexatious’ or simply invalid – and at a time when the courts face major backlogs and a lack of funding. (Note: LegalOn and AL will be holding a webinar that connects to this ‘legal flooding’ challenge for corporates: see here.)

On the flipside, more people now have a chance to get at least somewhere with a legal issue, where before they may have been stuck. It’s a finely balanced change to society’s fabric.

Ellen Lefley, Deputy Legal Director at Justice, commented: ‘The question is not whether AI becomes part of people’s legal journeys – it already is. This research provides a unique insight into who is using it and how. The challenge now is ensuring people receive reliable support, while addressing the unmet legal needs that drive some towards AI in the first place.’

And Dr Jed Meers, Administrative Fairness Lab co-director, added: ‘Rising demand across the courts and tribunals system has a complex set of drivers. What our research shows is that people are using these tools when they run into all kinds of legal problems and are already doing so in significant numbers. As the use of these tools grows, they’ll become an even more important part of the picture.’

Overall, we have entered a new world, and there is no going back.

More about the survey here.

—

Come and join us in London this November 4th + 5th at Legal Innovators! The conference at the intersection of legal AI and the business of law. Day One: law firms, Day Two: inhouse.

Legal Innovators UK – London, Nov 4 and 5
