news.titleEn: Aderant launches iTimekeep integration with Harvey
news.titleZh: Aderant 推出 iTimekeep 与 Harvey 的集成
news.summaryZh: 8月17日，Aderant 宣布其 iTimekeep 与 Harvey 的集成正式全面可用。使用 Harvey 和 Aderant iTimekeep 的律师事务所可以将两个解决方案连接起来，使 Harvey 中捕获的工作（从起草、研究到审查和分析）直接流入草拟的时间条目，并包含事项背景、时长和 AI 生成的描述。律师随后在 iTimekeep 中审查、编辑并提交该草稿，遵循各事务所自身的审批流程。Harvey 已经了解客户律师的日常工作，将该知识直接集成到 iTimekeep 中可为事务所创建更互联的生态系统，使用户无需更改计费流程即可实现更准确的时间捕获。对于律师而言，该集成减少了在一天结束时重建时间的行政负担。这种集成正是他在执业时所希望拥有的互联体验，录入时间很痛苦，这是解决该问题的第一步。
news.bodyHtml:
Aderant today (17 August) announced the general availability of its iTimekeep integration with Harvey.

Firms using Harvey and Aderant’s iTimekeep can connect the two solutions so that work captured in Harvey, from drafting and research to review and analysis, flows directly into a draft time entry, complete with matter context, duration, and an AI-generated narrative. Lawyers then review, edit, and submit that draft in iTimekeep, following each firm’s own approval process.

Advertisement

“Harvey already understands the work our clients’ attorneys are doing every day,” said Lisa Erickson, SVP of product management and AI at Aderant. “Integrating that knowledge directly into iTimekeep creates a more connected ecosystem for firms, enabling users to achieve more accurate time capture without requiring any changes to their billing process.”

For lawyers, the integration reduces the administrative burden of reconstructing their time at the end of the day.

Advertisement

“This integration is exactly the kind of connected experience that I would have loved when I was practicing; entering time is painful, and this is the first step towards solving that pain,” said Matthew Guillod, senior product manager at Harvey.
news.bodyText:
Aderant today (17 August) announced the general availability of its iTimekeep integration with Harvey .

Firms using Harvey and Aderant’s iTimekeep can connect the two solutions so that work captured in Harvey, from drafting and research to review and analysis, flows directly into a draft time entry, complete with matter context, duration, and an AI-generated narrative. Lawyers then review, edit, and submit that draft in iTimekeep, following each firm’s own approval process.

“Harvey already understands the work our clients’ attorneys are doing every day,” said Lisa Erickson, SVP of product management and AI at Aderant. “Integrating that knowledge directly into iTimekeep creates a more connected ecosystem for firms, enabling users to achieve more accurate time capture without requiring any changes to their billing process.”

For lawyers, the integration reduces the administrative burden of reconstructing their time at the end of the day.

“This integration is exactly the kind of connected experience that I would have loved when I was practicing; entering time is painful, and this is the first step towards solving that pain,” said Matthew Guillod, senior product manager at Harvey.

news.titleEn: Is Someone Recording? Managing the Workplace Risks of Portable AI Notetakers
news.titleZh: 有人在录音吗？管理便携式AI笔记工具的工作场所风险
news.summaryZh: AI笔记工具正在改变工作方式，例如可吸附在手机背面的“AI助手”能即时完成会议记录、摘要和跟进事项，减轻行政负担并让员工专注对话。此前虚拟笔记工具会作为参会者出现在视频会议中，便于批准或移除，组织也可限制公司设备上的应用安装或连接公司系统。但便携式AI笔记工具可录制面对面谈话和电话通话，离线存储后同步生成文字记录、摘要和行动项，部分小到可放入口袋或附着手机，无需加入虚拟会议、运行于组织网络或安装在公司电脑上。员工控制的设备可能在组织不知情下录制会议室讨论、面试、电话或非正式对话，并将信息发送给第三方AI服务。这虽有益处，却带来隐私、安全、雇佣和诉讼风险。联邦和州法律可能限制录制电话和其他通信：多数州只需一方同意，其他州通常要求所有各方同意，参与者跨州或跨国时分析尤为复杂。便携设备还扩大了问题场景，包括求职面试、客户通话、工作场所调查、便利安排会议及涉及患者或访客的对话。即使参与者同意被录制，该同意未必授权将录制及信息分享给第三方AI供应商，参与者可能不了解服务会接收其声音和陈述，用于创建文字记录、识别说话者、总结讨论并生成额外记录。许多组织已实施控制措施，如阻止AI会议机器人、限制浏览器扩展、阻止软件安装或限制公司设备访问公共AI平台，但便携式AI录音设备可绕过这些控制。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! AI notetakers illustrate how artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing how people work. For example, there are now “AI Assistants” that snap onto the back of cell phones like a wireless battery pack. Instead of taking detailed notes during a meeting, preparing a summary, and identifying follow-up items, employees can use an AI notetaker to complete these tasks almost instantly. These tools can reduce administrative burdens, improve follow-up, and allow employees to focus on a conversation rather than on taking notes. An assistant, wrapped in a small, inconspicuous package. Until recently, many AI notetakers were relatively easy to identify. A virtual notetaker, for example, might appear as a participant in a videoconference, which gives the meeting organizer and other attendees an opportunity to approve its use or remove it from the meeting. Organizations could also restrict which applications employees installed on company devices or connected to company systems. But what if the AI notetaker does not appear on the meeting’s participant list? What if it is already sitting on the conference-room table, or in an employee’s pocket? Portable AI notetakers can record in-person conversations and telephone calls, store recordings while offline, and later synchronize the recordings to generate searchable transcripts, summaries, action items, and other AI-enabled content. Some are small enough to fit in a pocket or attach to a cell phone. As a result, an AI notetaker no longer needs to join a virtual meeting, operate on an organization’s network, or be installed on an organization-issued computer. An employee-controlled device may be able to record a conference-room discussion, interview, telephone call, or informal workplace conversation and later send that information to a third-party AI service without the organization’s knowledge. While portable AI notetakers may provide meaningful benefits, they can also expose organizations to significant privacy, security, employment, and litigation risks. Federal and state laws may restrict the recording of telephone calls and other communications. In most states, the consent of one party to the conversation is sufficient. Other states generally require the consent of all parties. The analysis can become particularly complicated when participants are located in different states or countries. Additionally, portable devices expand the settings where the issue may arise, including job interviews, customer calls, workplace investigations, accommodation meetings, and conversations involving patients or visitors. Even when participants consent to being recorded, that consent alone may not authorize the recording and associated information to be shared with a third-party AI vendor. Participants may not understand that the service will receive their voices and statements and use that information to create a transcript, identify speakers, summarize the discussion, and generate additional records. Many organizations have implemented controls to prevent employees from using unapproved AI tools on their systems. An organization might block AI meeting bots, restrict browser extensions, prevent software installations, or limit access to public AI platforms from company devices. Portable AI recorders can bypass these controls. An employee may be able to record a workplace conversation without installing software on an organization’s computer or connecting the recorder to its network, then upload the recording through a personal device or account. This is a practice known as “shadow AI”: technology used without organizational approval or oversight. The organization may not know which tools are being used, what information is collected, where it is sent, which third parties process it, or how long it is retained. Workplace conversations frequently include information that should not be disclosed outside the organization. A discussion may concern an employee’s medical condition, a workplace complaint, customer or patient data, business strategy, or trade secrets. A portable recorder may capture incidental information that would never appear in formal meeting notes, such as an employee discussing a family member’s health, a trip to a place of worship, or another personal matter unrelated to the purpose of the meeting.

news.titleEn: INVITED PARTICIPANT OR THIRD-PARTY EAVESDROPPER?- Court Holds That Otter.ai Is A Third-Party Eavesdropper Because It Uses The Recordings For Its Own Benefit
news.titleZh: 受邀参与者还是第三方窃听者？法院裁定Otter.ai因将录音用于自身利益而构成第三方窃听者
news.summaryZh: 美国加州北区联邦地区法院在In Re Otter.AI Priv. Litig.案中部分批准、部分驳回Otter的驳回动议。法院认定，Otter的AI会议助手“Otter Notetaker”作为“沉默参与者”加入虚拟会议，实时录制并转录所有发言，且保留录音、转录文本和声纹，用于训练其自动语音识别和机器学习模型。因此，Otter独立收集、保留并将通信用于自身商业目的，构成《加州侵犯隐私法》第631条下的第三方窃听者，而非会议主持人的“受邀参与者”或录音工具。法院还认定，仅称通信“私密”或“敏感”而不提供具体事实细节，不足以根据第632条主张机密通信。七名来自加州、伊利诺伊州和华盛顿州的原告提出CIPA、ECPA、BIPA、不当得利和UCL等索赔。法院支持原告的Article III standing，并将本案与Popa v. Microsoft Corp.区分，认为录制与医疗和金融专业人士的私人通信内容不同于记录宠物用品网站上的鼠标移动等会话回放技术。CIPA、ECPA、BIPA、不当得利和UCL索赔全部存活；CFAA、CDAFA和华盛顿隐私法索赔以及除一名原告外的普通法隐私索赔被驳回。Otter不仅转录对话，还保留录音并用于训练自身模型，因此“扩展理论”不能使其免责。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Ever wondered how CIPA applies to the AI Notetakers that now show up uninvited in all the meetings on your calendar? In In Re Otter.AI Priv. Litig., No. 25-CV-06911-EKL, 2026 WL 2351237 (N.D. Cal. Aug.13,2026) United States District Court for the Northern District of California granted in part and denied in part Otter’s motion to dismiss. The CIPA, ECPA BIPA, unjust enrichment, the UCL claims survived in full. The CFAA, CDAFA, and the Washington Privacy Act claims were dismissed, as well as the common law privacy claims of every plaintiff except one. The Court holds that (1) Otter is a third-party eavesdropper under Section 631 because Otter independently collects, retains, and uses communications for its own commercial purposes and that (2) it is not enough to call your communication “private” or “sensitive” without giving additional factual detail regarding the substance of those communications to plausibly allege confidential communications under Section 632. The situation is familiar to anyone who has ever sat through a Zoom or Microsoft Teams call. Seven plaintiffs from California, Illinois, and Washington allege that Otter’s AI meeting assistant, the “Otter Notetaker,” joins virtual meetings as a “silent participant” and records and transcribes everything said in real time without the consent of all participants. The Plaintiffs allege that Otter then keeps the recordings, including transcripts and voiceprints, and uses that material to train its automatic speech recognition and machine-learning models. The conversations allegedly included communications with a doctor regarding “deeply personal and private medical information”, calls with financial professionals, sensitive business discussions, strategic planning sessions, confidential project meetings, performance reviews, discussions with clients and finally professional opportunities discussions. On Article III standing the Court distinguishes Popa v. Microsoft Corp., 153 F.4th 784 (9th Cir. 2025) on which Otter principally relies, saying that using sessionreplay technology to record a user’s interactions with a pet supply website, including information such as computer mouse movements, clicks, keystrokes, and pages visited is similar to “a store clerk’s observing shoppers”. Recording the content of the private communications with medical and financial professionals is completely different. The Court said the alleged conduct is closer to concrete injury alleged in Campbell where private Facebook messages were intercepted. So, Plaintiffs do have standing. Now CIPA claims: Otter’s main defense to the Section 631(a) claim was that the Notetaker is an “invited participant” and functions as the meeting host’s own recording tool, which would make it a party rather than an eavesdropper. That works under Graham v. Noom, Inc., 533 F. Supp. 3d 823 (N.D. Cal. 2021), where a software provider that acts only as an extension of its client is not a third-party interceptor, because a party to a communication may record it. However, Otter does not just participate in meetings, it retains the recordings of the conversations and uses them to improve its own machine-learning models and services. The Court held that Otter is a third-party eavesdropper who collects, retains and uses communications for its own commercial purposes. That is the main difference: Otter is not just a tool that transcribes the conversation and hands it back to the participants, but an independent party who uses the recordings to train its models for its own benefit. On Section 632 the Court held that Plaintiff Theus plausibly alleged confidential communication because he alleged a call with a medical professional involving “deeply personal medical information”. Plaintiffs Brewer and Ryan, by contrast, alleged only that their conversations were “private” or “sensitive,” saying nothing about the substance. Those labels were held “conclusory and insufficient”. For the same reason Brewer’s and Ryan’s intrusion upon seclusion and California constitutional privacy claims were dismissed. Washington plaintiff’s claims failed as well. As for pen register theory, the plaintiffs withdrew their Section 635 and Section 638.51 claims. On the ECPA claim, Otter unsuccessfully argued the party exception under 18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d). The Plaintiffs invoked the tortious purpose, alleging that Otter used their conversations to train its systems for its own pecuniary gain. Otter’s response was that its purpose was commercial. The Court said that “committing a tort and seeking a profit are not mutually exclusive.” Otter had no chance with BIPA. Voiceprints are biometric identifiers, and the plaintiffs alleged enough about Otter’s speaker tagging and speaker identification profiles to support an inference that the voiceprints can identify them. Otter’s reading of Zellmer v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 104 F.4th 1117 (9th Cir. 2024), was rejected as too broad. Because a Section 15(b) violation was plausibly alleged, standing followed for the Section 15(a). The extraterritoriality defense was rejected, since the plaintiffs alleged they were Illinois residents and they were physically located in Illinois when Otter collected their data during the meetings. Despite all, Otter had success with CFAA theories. The allegation that Otter accesses participants’ computers was conclusory under Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021), with no facts about how the Notetaker reaches any file, folder, or database. The Section 1030(a)(4) claim failed for want of a cognizable loss, since lost data value and emotional distress fall outside the statute’s narrow definition. See Andrews v. Sirius XM Radio Inc., 932 F.3d 1253 (9th Cir. 2019). The CDAFA claim went the same way under Cottle v. Plaid Inc., 536 F. Supp. 3d 461 (N.D. Cal. 2021). The important takeaway here is that the party status of an AI tool under Section 631 depends more on what the tool does with the recorded information. Companies using meeting assistants should ask their vendors only one question: does the vendor retain and reuse customer conversation content for model training? If the answer is yes, the “extension theory” will not save them. Big lesson for Plaintiffs is that vague pleading can cost you claims. Conclusory pleadings like “private” and “sensitive” are not enough to allege confidential communications.

news.titleEn: AI in Hiring- A Regulated Employment Practice, Not Just a Technology Purchase
news.titleZh: 招聘中的人工智能——受监管的雇佣实践，而非单纯的技术采购
news.summaryZh: 人工智能在雇主招聘流程中日益主流化，筛选简历、分析视频面试、预测候选人成功率及优化排班的工具已成为HR技术供应商的常见产品。但快速采用可能忽视相关法律框架。雇主应将AI招聘工具视为受监管的雇佣实践，而非单纯的技术采购，其带来诉讼风险。AI招聘工具易引发联邦和州反歧视法下的差别影响索赔，即使微小算法偏见也可能产生系统性不利影响。历史训练数据可能复制或放大先前歧视性招聘模式。Mobley诉Workday案和EEOC与iTutorGroup的和解表明，AI相关就业歧视索赔正被积极诉讼和执法。根据ADA，雇主仍需确保第三方AI工具不非法筛除残疾人，依赖供应商“ADA合规”保证不免除独立法律义务。许多AI工具是专有“黑箱”，决策逻辑透明度有限，但雇主而非供应商对歧视性结果负责。供应商保证不足，雇主需获取验证研究、不利影响分析和审计文档，并能解释招聘决定。联邦、州和地方各自独立监管AI招聘，要求零散且联邦统一指南不确定，雇主须监控自身使用并关注法律更新。使用或考虑AI招聘工具的雇主应考虑实际合规步骤。AI招聘工具的效率便利收益真实，法律暴露风险亦然。最安全使用结合可解释性、监督和文档。雇主通过理解工具运作、建立治理结构并将合规视为设计要求，可捕获效率收益并管理诉讼风险。将AI招聘视为采购决策而非受监管举措者，可能面临执法行动或集体索赔。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! What Employers Need to Know as Legal Requirements Try to Catch Up with Algorithmic Hiring Tools. Artificial intelligence is becoming more mainstream in employers’ hiring workflows. Tools that screen resumes, analyze video interviews, predict candidate success, and optimize scheduling are often standard offerings from HR technology vendors. But rapid adoption of these tools can overlook the legal frameworks governing them. Employers should approach AI-powered hiring tools not as just technology purchases but as regulated employment practices that carry litigation risks, including the following. Disparate Impact and Algorithmic Bias. AI hiring tools are susceptible to disparate impact claims under federal and state anti-discrimination laws. Even small algorithmic biases arising from biased training data, flawed model design, or so-called “proxy” variables like zip code, educational institution, or commute distance can produce selection ratios that may systematically disadvantage protected groups without any discriminatory intent on the part of the employer or tool developer. Historical data used to train the AI tool may replicate or amplify prior discriminatory hiring patterns, making bias a systemic rather than incidental risk. As we have previously written, cases like Mobley v. Workday and the EEOC’s settlement with iTutorGroup demonstrate that AI-related employment discrimination claims are actively being litigated and enforced. Disability Accommodation. Under the ADA, employers remain responsible for ensuring that third-party AI tools do not unlawfully screen out individuals with disabilities. When an AI assessment method disadvantages applicants with disabilities, employers may need to provide alternative assessment methods. Reliance on a vendor’s assurance that the tool is “ADA-compliant” does not relieve the employer of its independent legal obligations. Black-Box and Vendor Issues. Many AI hiring tools operate as proprietary “black boxes” with limited transparency into their decision-making logic. Yet employers, not vendors, bear responsibility when these tools produce discriminatory outcomes. Vendor assurances alone are insufficient; employers need access to validation studies, adverse impact analyses, and audit documentation. Ultimately, if a hiring decision is challenged, employers should be able to explain why they made it. Patchwork Federal, State, and Local Requirements. Federal, state, and local jurisdictions are each moving independently to regulate AI hiring, as we have previously written about. Given the patchwork of requirements and uncertainty regarding uniform federal guidelines, employers must both monitor their own usage of AI in hiring and stay apprised of updates to federal, state, and local laws and regulations. Practical Compliance Checklist for Employers. Employers using or contemplating AI hiring tools should consider the following steps: While the efficiency and convenience gains of AI hiring tools may be genuine, so are the legal exposure risks. The safest use of AI in hiring combines explainability, oversight, and documentation. Employers will be positioned to capture the efficiency benefits of AI while managing litigation risk by understanding how their tools work, building governance structures around them, and treating compliance as a design requirement for them. Those that treat AI hiring as a procurement decision rather than a regulated initiative may find themselves on the wrong end of an enforcement action or class claim. More Upcoming Events

news.titleEn: Claude’s Watermarks and their Legal Sector Impact
news.titleZh: Claude水印及其法律行业影响
news.summaryZh: Anthropic公司推出的Claude模型将采用一种新型水印技术，该技术通过在文本生成过程中嵌入隐蔽标记，使AI生成内容可被识别。根据欧盟《人工智能法案》要求，所有在欧盟运营的大语言模型提供商必须提供某种形式的标识，以告知用户和当局输出内容是否由AI生成。Anthropic作为OpenAI的竞争对手，已迅速明确其立场并保持高度透明。其水印机制并非传统意义上的可见水印，而是将信号伪装成页面上的正常词汇。大语言模型逐词生成文本，每次选择下一个词时，会从候选词列表中挑选最合理或最可能的选项。例如，在句子“今天天气寒冷且”中，下一个词不太可能是“甜的”，但很可能是“阴天”或“灰色”。在多数情况下，读者对模型选择哪个词并不敏感，句子含义基本相同，此时选择由随机数决定。水印技术利用这些低风险选择，在生成的文本中留下模式，该模式对读者不可见，但持有密钥的人可以检测。当启用水印时，选择仍是随机的，但随机源不同，使用密钥和前面的几个词来决定模型应选择的词。因此，Claude选择的词仍是随机的，但可以检查词序列是否与使用密钥时Claude的选择一致，从而判断文本是否由Claude生成。该方法基于Google DeepMind在2024年论文中提出的SynthID-Text方法。将很快提供水印检测API，目前正在制定实施细节。
news.bodyText: How will Claude’s watermarks work and how will they impact the legal world? Artificial Lawyer explores. Anthropic – and all other LLM makers operating within the EU – will have to provide some form of identification that tells a user and authorities whether an output is AI-generated. This is because of the EU AI Act. The rival to OpenAI has been both quick to set out its stall and has been very transparent. First, how they work. Essentially what Claude will do is insert certain words where there is a choice of options, in a way that it matches a key designed to reveal whether text is AI-manufactured or not. I.e. there is no actual ‘watermark’ as such, at least in the document, rather one could say the signal is ‘camouflaged’ as part of the normal words on the page. Claude gives a great explanation: ‘Large language models like Claude work by generating one word at a time. Each time the model decides on the next word, it chooses among a list of potential candidates, ultimately selecting the most sensible or likely based on the preceding text. ‘Take the sentence “The weather today was cold and…”. The next word is very unlikely to be “sugary.” But it is quite likely to be “overcast” or “grey.” ‘Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses, the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number…. ‘Watermarking uses low-stakes choices…., which occur many times over a piece of generated text, to leave a pattern in Claude’s responses. That pattern is undetectable to the reader, but is detectable to anyone who has a key that encodes it. ‘When watermarking is used, choices are still made at random, but the source of the randomness is different. Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick. ‘That is, the words that Claude picks are still random, but now, one can check the sequence of words and see if it’s consistent with the choices Claude would make if it was using the key. If it is, one can assign a probability that the text was generated by Claude.’ It truly is ingenious and builds upon the SynthID-Text approach published by Google DeepMind in a paper in 2024. They added that: They also noted that: ‘We will soon be offering a watermark detection API. We’re in the process of working out the details of its implementation.’

news.titleEn: Culture Still Eats AI For Breakfast – Workday Survey
news.titleZh: 文化仍比AI更“难吃”——Workday调查揭示法律AI落地困境
news.summaryZh: Workday对10个国家7000名律师及企业员工进行的一项大型调查显示，合同管理混乱问题依然普遍存在，仅有37%的企业内部律师认为“自己负责商业协议的签署后管理”。此外，超过半数受访者表示，他们仍然缺乏集中化的合同管理系统。调查表明，企业文化仍是阻碍法律AI充分发挥效益的主要因素。尽管这一结果可能令人意外，但Artificial Lawyer指出，十多年来类似统计数据屡见不鲜，说明尽管技术有所进步，核心的人类行为和企业文化并未发生太大变化。调查还显示，即便在律师群体中，也只有37%的人认为追踪合同是“自己的责任”，而企业其他员工中仅25%认为这是律师的工作。更令人担忧的是，26%的员工认为合同应由“最相关的”团队负责，这种模糊的归属感导致合同管理缺乏明确责任人。调查还发现，到2026年，情况依然令人惊讶。总体而言，当前面临的挑战与十年前相同，即使AI承诺带来巨大改进，合同仍“散落各处”，缺乏集中控制和监控，“所有权”似乎属于当天觉得最重要的人。法律AI若无法解决合同可见性和责任归属问题，便难以帮助企业全面掌握义务、加快流程或降低风险。
news.bodyText: A major survey by Workday of 7,000 lawyers and other enterprise staff across 10 countries has found that contract chaos persists, with only 37% of inhouse lawyers believing ‘they are responsible for post-signature management’ of business agreements. Moreover, over half of those surveyed said that they still lack a centralized contract system. In short, corporate culture is still dominant in preventing the full benefits of legal AI. While this may sound surprising, the reality is that Artificial Lawyer has been hearing statistics like this for over a decade – indicating that although the tech has improved, core human behaviours and enterprise culture has not changed that much. Moreover, despite the promise of legal AI tools, if most large companies are not even sure who is responsible for contract management, nor have moved to implement some form of cross-business contract system, then there is only a little that can be done to improve things. As the table below shows: Even among lawyers only 37% felt it was ‘their responsibility’ to track contracts, while for the rest of the staff in an enterprise only 25% thought it was the lawyers’ job. And that perhaps would not be a problem if at least someone did claim that role. However, the survey shows that 26% of staff felt contracts should belong to whichever team seemed to be ‘most relevant’. And then they also found that: And that amazingly in 2026: Plus they also found: In short, the overall challenge today is the same as it was 10 years ago, even if AI promises great improvements. Contracts are literally ‘all over the place’; there is little central control and monitoring; and ‘ownership’ seems to belong to whoever feels it matters most to them on the day. How is legal AI meant to make a dent in this? How can AI help a business to be on top of all of its obligations and help to speed things along, or reduce risk, if the contracts themselves are out of sight and out of mind, as it were, for many of the key people – and AI systems – that might be relevant?

news.titleEn: The real cost of building your own compliance
news.titleZh: 自建合规平台的真实成本
news.summaryZh: 多数律所并非有意自建合规平台，而是从通用AI工具、脚本和电子表格起步，直到人员离职、脚本失效才暴露问题。通用AI缺乏律所合规所需的数据模型，无法编码真实利益冲突、案件受理逻辑、客户义务及跨司法辖区规则，直接使用只会产生无审计轨迹、不可辩护的输出。将律所术语、义务和方法编码到通用代理中需从零开始数年，而Intapp已基于AmLaw 100中97家律所、二十年积累完成这一工作。自建还面临持续维护负担：客户指南变更、新AI模型发布、律师协会规则更新，均需内部人员更新、测试、验证并记录理由，形成永久开销。治理风险不体现在项目预算中：通用AI供应商无法回答如何尊重道德墙、避免幻觉、不暴露错误数据并生成可辩护的审计轨迹。通用AI保留文档内容却剥离元数据，而元数据正是合规态势所在——哪些合伙人被隔离、哪个交易团队掌握MNPI、哪些文档处于诉讼保留，剥离标签等于制造泄露。此外，通用AI将文档复制到律所保留规则和访问控制之外的新存储，可能面临取证请求却无保留计划。目前33%的律所已全所使用AI，高于2025年的17%，但76%的专业人员仍使用未经批准的工具，自建工具反而扩大这一差距。机会成本是决定性因素：Intapp Compliance with Celeste部署代理起草受理请求、构建冲突搜索策略、匹配公司树并摄取外部律师指南，吸收常规工作。律所每花一个季度自建，竞争对手就扩大一个季度差距，并损失自上线之日起累积的能力优势。
news.bodyHtml:
Most law firms don’t set out to build a compliance platform. It starts with a general-purpose AI tool pointed at conflicts, a script someone wrote to help with intake, a spreadsheet that tracks outside counsel guidelines. None of it feels like a platform decision. Until two years pass and a senior analyst leaves, the script breaks, and nobody is sure who owns fixing it.

General-purpose AI doesn’t know what a true conflict is

Conflicts clearance, matter intake, and client obligations management run on a data model that general-purpose AI doesn’t have. That model encodes what counts as a true conflict for your firm, why a matter was passed, which relationships carry institutional weight, and how your rules apply when a new matter touches three jurisdictions and a prior lateral hire. A general-purpose model has none of that context. Pointing it at your compliance data doesn’t give it the legal compliance model — it gives you confident-sounding output with no audit trail and nothing defensible underneath it. Encoding a firm’s vocabulary, obligations, and methods into a general agent is years of work from scratch. That work is already done.

research.titleEn: Can LLMs Reason in a Legally Meaningful Manner? A Small-scale Study on European Court of Human Rights Cases
research.titleZh: LLM能否以具有法律意义的方式进行推理？一项关于欧洲人权法院案件的小规模研究
research.abstractEn: Reasoning has become a standard technique and feature for contemporary LLMs; however, its application and quality in the context of demanding legal-oriented tasks, such as legal case forecasting, remain under explored. We investigate how LLMs reason in the context of legal case forecasting, using legal cases from the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) as a testbed. We evaluate OpenAI GPT 5.4, a recent top-tier LLM, by exploring alternative prompting strategies that are more or less suggestive of what counts as legally meaningful reasoning in the context of ECtHR jurisprudence. We present our findings derived from assessing the model's responses with both human and LLM evaluation. We find that the examined model scores far from ideal in legal reasoning, the model produces structurally complete but substantively shallow analyses, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators are internally consistent yet align only weakly with our trained annotators, i.e., reliable but not a valid substitute for human evaluation. Overall, the expert-curated prompt leads to more comprehensive reasoning, which does not result in more accurate predictions compared to the other examined settings. Based on our findings, we urge the community not to rely solely on automated LLM-based evaluation and to avoid using task accuracy as an appropriate proxy for reasoning quality.
research.abstractZh: 推理已成为当代LLM的标准技术和特征；然而，在诸如法律案件预测等要求较高的法律导向任务中，其应用和质量仍未得到充分探索。我们以欧洲人权法院（ECtHR）的法律案件为测试平台，研究LLM在法律案件预测背景下的推理方式。我们评估了OpenAI GPT 5.4（一款最新的顶级LLM），通过探索在ECtHR判例背景下，哪些提示策略或多或少地暗示了具有法律意义的推理。我们通过人工和LLM评估来评估模型的响应，并展示了我们的发现。我们发现，所检查的模型在法律推理方面得分远非理想，模型产生的分析结构完整但实质浅薄，并且LLM作为评审者的评估在内部一致，但与我们的训练有素的标注者仅弱对齐，即可靠但并非人工评估的有效替代品。总体而言，专家策划的提示导致更全面的推理，但与其他检查设置相比，并未导致更准确的预测。基于我们的发现，我们敦促社区不要仅依赖基于LLM的自动化评估，并避免将任务准确性作为推理质量的适当代理。

research.titleEn: Gated Against One Model, Open to the Next: Option-Only Solvability in Legal Multiple-Choice Benchmarks
research.titleZh: 对一种模型设防，对下一种模型敞开：法律多项选择基准中的仅选项可解性
research.abstractEn: Multiple-choice benchmarks are graded on whether a model picks the right option, not on whether it needed the question. Measuring that gap takes care: a model answering A to most items scores above chance wherever the key sits at A, and reads as recognition when it is not. We measure it on UA-JudgeExam: 11,990 four-option items with official keys, published by Ukraine's Higher Qualification Commission of Judges.   Shown the options and no question, Claude Haiku 4.5 scores 0.383 against chance, and the leak is concentrated: 11.8% of items are answered blind on all eight option orders, against 0.2 items expected by chance. It is not quotation: search over 280,059 editions of Ukrainian legislation recovers 0.128. Gating those out retains 8,128 items, on which the gating model itself now scores 0.204, and GPT-5.6, which took no part in the selection, still answers 0.515 of them with the question hidden. Scoring twelve held-out models on the whole set and subtracting each one's answer-position habit, only two keep an excess: GPT-5.6 at +0.265, Sonnet 4.6 at +0.081. Without it the ranking misleads: Llama 3.1 8B scores 0.292 blind, above every model but those two, purely by answering A to 92% of items.   The gate does select something real: on the items it rejected, eleven of twelve models score 0.518-0.789, every interval clear of what the same model scores on the items it kept. But that signal is one model's, and filtering on it does not transfer upward. Neither is visible on a 400-item sample, where nine models read as "statistically at chance". Rewriting distractors instead overshoots to 0.168, below chance and as exploitable. The same probe on LEXam returns chance: every option there points into the stem, none longer than 33 characters. Item format decides whether the problem can arise; capability decides how much is extracted. We release the corpus, the predictions and the harness.
research.abstractZh: 多项选择基准的评分依据是模型是否选择了正确的选项，而非其是否需要问题。衡量这一差距需要谨慎：一个对大多数题目回答A的模型，在正确答案位于A的情况下，其得分会高于随机水平，而当并非如此时，则会被视为识别。我们在UA-JudgeExam上对此进行了测量：该基准包含由乌克兰法官最高资格委员会发布的11,990道四选项题目，并附有官方答案。在仅显示选项而无问题的情况下，Claude Haiku 4.5的得分为0.383（随机水平之上），且泄漏集中：11.8%的题目在所有八种选项顺序下均被盲答，而随机预期仅为0.2题。这并非引用：对280,059个乌克兰立法版本进行搜索，仅恢复0.128。将这些题目排除后，保留8,128题，此时筛选模型本身的得分为0.204，而GPT-5.6（未参与筛选）在隐藏问题的情况下仍能答对其中0.515的题目。对十二个保留模型在整个集合上进行评分，并减去每个模型的答案位置习惯后，仅有两个模型保持超额：GPT-5.6为+0.265，Sonnet 4.6为+0.081。若无此调整，排名将产生误导：Llama 3.1 8B的盲测得分为0.292，高于除这两个模型外的所有模型，这纯粹是因为它对92%的题目回答了A。该筛选确实选择了某种真实的东西：在被其拒绝的题目上，十二个模型中有十一个的得分在0.518至0.789之间，每个区间都明显高于同一模型在保留题目上的得分。但该信号仅属于一个模型，基于此进行筛选并不能向上迁移。在400题的样本上，两者均不可见，其中九个模型被统计为“处于随机水平”。改写干扰项反而过度，达到0.168，低于随机水平且同样可利用。同样的探针在LEXam上返回随机水平：那里的每个选项都指向题干，且长度均不超过33个字符。题目格式决定了问题是否可能出现；能力决定了能提取多少。我们发布了语料库、预测结果和测试工具。

research.titleEn: Time as Structure: Temporal Dependency Graphs for Verifiable Deadline Computation over Legal Documents
research.titleZh: 时间即结构：用于法律文件可验证截止日期计算的时间依赖图
research.abstractEn: Miss a filing deadline by one day and the claim is barred, however strong the case. Computing that deadline is rarely simple: the period runs from a triggering event, is counted by a statutory convention, and may be suspended by a mandatory conciliation window. We ask whether a language model should answer such questions directly, or read the document and leave the arithmetic to code. We extract dated facts and their dependencies into a temporal dependency graph and compute deadlines from it with a calendar-correct engine. On UK Employment Appeal Tribunal judgments the engine reproduces six of seven timeliness rulings, and matches the judges' own dates to the day. The strongest of four language models, asked the same cases, gets the arithmetic right and the answer wrong: in six of twenty-one responses its stated verdict contradicts its own thinking, and every contradiction runs the same way, calling a late claim timely. To test the systems at scale we move the dismissal date across the statutory boundary, generating 427 cases whose answers are computed rather than annotated. On the cases both systems answer, the pipeline is right 90.2% of the time against 61.2% for direct answering. The limit is extraction: on contracts the errors are almost never in the arithmetic, but in choosing which event the period starts from.
research.abstractZh: 错过提交截止日期一天，无论案件多么有力，索赔即被禁止。计算该截止日期通常并不简单：期限从触发事件开始计算，按法定惯例计数，并可能因强制调解窗口而中止。我们探讨语言模型是否应直接回答此类问题，还是阅读文件并将计算留给代码。我们将带日期的事实及其依赖关系提取到时间依赖图中，并使用日历正确的引擎从中计算截止日期。在英国就业上诉法庭的判决中，该引擎再现了七项时效裁定中的六项，并与法官自己的日期精确到日。四个语言模型中最强的一个，在回答相同案件时，算术正确但答案错误：在二十一个回答中，有六个其陈述的裁决与其自身推理相矛盾，且每个矛盾都以相同方式出现，即将迟交的索赔称为及时。为了大规模测试系统，我们将解雇日期移至法定边界，生成427个案例，其答案由计算而非注释得出。在两个系统都回答的案例中，流水线在90.2%的情况下正确，而直接回答为61.2%。限制在于提取：在合同上，错误几乎不在算术，而在于选择期限从哪个事件开始。

news.titleEn: DeepJudge, DISCO, Spellbook and Korbyt unveil new capabilities ahead of ILTACON
news.titleZh: DeepJudge、DISCO、Spellbook与Korbyt在ILTACON前发布新功能
news.summaryZh: 在纳什维尔ILTACON倒计时之际，DeepJudge、DISCO、Spellbook及工作场所技术提供商Korbyt本周发布一系列公告。瑞士法律AI公司DeepJudge推出Agent Handoff Protocol（AHP），该开放协议旨在让用户在不同AI平台间切换时不丢失工作上下文。MCP等协议虽能实现系统间信息交换，但律师切换AI工具时常丢失宝贵上下文，被迫重建提示、重新上传文档并重新分析。新协议不仅传输信息，还传输目标、对话历史和支持材料。Harvey是首批实施该协议的供应商之一，测试版集成将于本月推出，Thomson Reuters也宣布支持。这反映出法律技术市场日益普遍的观点：没有单一AI平台能主导法律工作的所有方面，需要专业系统间更强的互操作性。诉讼技术提供商DISCO全面推出新的Advanced Research能力。该代理式AI工具通过多步推理处理复杂事实调查和证据分析，自动审查自身发现、识别缺口并启动额外搜索以优化结果。DISCO称该工具可帮助诉讼团队从大量证据集中快速生成时间线、调查备忘录和证言提纲。早期用户报告显著生产力提升，早期访问计划期间客户参与度增加一倍以上。这标志着eDiscovery提供商正从传统文档搜索转向日益自主的调查工作流。Spellbook在其Associate平台内推出AI文档编辑器，将Word体验引入Associate，允许律师在不切换应用的情况下审阅、修改和定稿文档。供应商称用户可指示Spellbook从一个地方对多个相关文档进行数百处更改，然后手动审阅和优化结果。Korbyt表示将AI引入其工作场所和会议室管理平台。
news.bodyHtml:
A series of announcements this week from DeepJudge, DISCO, Spellbook and workplace technology provider Korbyt is worth noting as things start to heat up in the countdown to ILTACON in Nashville.

Perhaps the most strategically significant announcement comes from Swiss legal AI company DeepJudge, which has introduced the Agent Handoff Protocol (AHP), an open protocol designed to allow users to move between AI platforms without losing the context of their work. While protocols such as MCP enable systems to exchange information, DeepJudge says lawyers frequently lose valuable context when switching between AI tools, forcing them to rebuild prompts, re-upload documents and recreate analysis.

Advertisement

The new protocol aims to solve that problem by enabling AI systems to transfer not only information but also objectives, conversation history and supporting materials. DeepJudge says Harvey is among the first vendors to implement the protocol, with a beta integration launching this month, while Thomson Reuters has also announced support. The move reflects an increasingly common view in the legal technology market that no single AI platform will dominate every aspect of legal work, requiring greater interoperability between specialist systems.

Elsewhere, litigation technology provider DISCO has made its new Advanced Research capability generally available. The agentic AI tool is designed to tackle complex fact investigations and evidence analysis through multi-step reasoning, automatically reviewing its own findings, identifying gaps and launching additional searches to refine results.

Advertisement

DISCO says the tool can help litigation teams rapidly develop timelines, investigation memos and deposition outlines from large evidence collections. Early users report significant productivity gains, with customer engagement more than doubling during the early access programme. The launch is another example of eDiscovery providers moving beyond traditional document search towards increasingly autonomous investigative workflows.

Also this week, Spellbook launched an AI document editor within its Associate platform. The new functionality brings the Word experience into Associate, allowing lawyers to review, amend and finalise documents without switching between applications. The vendor says users can instruct Spellbook to make hundreds of changes across multiple related documents from one place, before manually reviewing and refining the results.

Last but not least, Korbyt this week said it is bringing AI to its workplace and meeting room management platform. Ahead of ILTACON, the company unveiled new booking capabilities including ConciergeAI, a natural language assistant that enables lawyers and staff to reserve desks and meeting rooms through Microsoft Teams, Outlook or the Korbyt platform. Korbyt says the system automatically applies firm booking rules and availability constraints before presenting options, with the goal of reducing administrative friction and helping firms better utilise office space.

news.titleEn: Powerful Tool, but Not an Attorney: Massachusetts Court Rejects Work Product Protection for AI-Generated Documents
news.titleZh: 强大工具但非律师：马萨诸塞州法院拒绝为AI生成文件提供工作成果保护
news.summaryZh: 马萨诸塞州高等法院商业诉讼庭在首例裁决中认定，AI工具生成的材料不受工作成果原则保护，除非为律师或应律师指示而准备。在Shealy诉Seaside Investments案中，法院指出向非律师（包括AI工具）披露的信息可能面临开示风险。该案源于2025年1月购买协议和本票引发的商业投资纠纷。2025年5月，Earl Wade Shealy, Jr.收到Seaside关于潜在违约的函件后，将函件及交易文件发给恋爱对象Debbi Fields，让其用ChatGPT分析并准备回复。Fields上传文件及提示词，并将AI输出发回Shealy。尽管Shealy在交易中有律师代理，但二人均未咨询律师。诉讼后，Shealy提交经编辑的通信并主张工作成果保护。法院驳回，理由为：Fields和ChatGPT均不符合工作成果原则中“代表”的定义，马萨诸塞州不承认恋爱对象为“代表”，ChatGPT工具本身也不是Shealy的“代表”。法院区分了Morgan诉V2X和Warner诉Gilbarco等联邦案例，这些案例将保护扩展至无律师代理当事人使用AI生成的输出和提示词，因其反映当事人思维印象；但Shealy有律师代理且未按律师指示行事，故不适用。法院强调AI是工具而非人，ChatGPT生成内容不披露律师或其他代表的思维印象、结论、意见或法律理论，因此不能获得意见工作成果的高度保护。法院还类比2026年2月United States诉Heppner案，该案中受律师代理的刑事被告自行使用AI工具，不受特权或工作成果保护。裁决表明，实体和个人不能将AI查询外包给非律师并期望结果免于开示；要使AI工具使用受保护，必须由律师指示，否则AI输出及提示词可能成为开示对象。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! In a decision of first impression in Massachusetts, a judge in the Business Litigation Session of the Superior Court ruled that material generated by an artificial intelligence tool, or “AI output,” is not protected under the work product doctrine unless performed for or at the direction of counsel. Shealy v. Seaside Investments, LLC, serves as a cautionary example of courts analyzing AI-generated materials through the lens of established attorney-client privilege and work product frameworks and deciding that information disclosed to a non-attorney, including an AI-powered tool, potentially exposes those materials to discovery. The underlying dispute in Shealy v. Seaside Investments, LLC developed from a commercial investment relationship between sophisticated partners who executed a purchase agreement and promissory note in January 2025. After receiving correspondence from Seaside in May 2025 concerning a potential default under the promissory note, Earl Wade Shealy, Jr. sent Seaside’s correspondence and related transaction documents to his romantic partner, Debbi Fields, to have ChatGPT analyze and prepare a response letter. Fields then uploaded the documents to ChatGPT along with instructions or “prompts” and sent the AI-generated output back to Shealy. Notably, neither Shealy nor Fields consulted with an attorney during this process even though Shealy was represented by counsel in the transaction at issue. When the dispute escalated to litigation, Shealy produced redacted correspondence between himself and Fields, claiming that the correspondence and resulting AI output was protected as work product. Work product protection shields from discovery the mental impressions, conclusions, and legal theories that an attorney or representative prepares in anticipation of litigation. In ruling on Seaside’s motion to compel unredacted communications, the court rejected Shealy’s contention that the AI-generated materials were protected by the work product doctrine on multiple grounds. First, the court determined that neither Fields nor Chat-GPT qualified as a “representative” within the meaning of the work product doctrine, which protects materials prepared by or for certain representatives, including attorneys, consultants, agents, and insurers. Massachusetts does not recognize romantic partners as “representatives” for purposes of work product protection, and the trial court declined to extend the doctrine to include them in this instance, ultimately concluding that exchanges between Shealy and Fields were subject to disclosure. The court further determined that the ChatGPT tool itself was not Shealy’s “representative” for purposes of extending the work product protections to the AI output. In reaching this conclusion, the court distinguished recently-decided cases around the U.S. where certain courts have held that material prepared by ChatGPT and similar AI programs was protected as work product. For example, in Morgan v. V2X, Inc. and Warner v. Gilbarco, Inc., federal courts in Colorado and Michigan extended the work product doctrine to shield AI-generated output and prompts utilized by pro se litigants as such material reflected the mental impressions, opinions, and theories of the pro se litigants acting in the role of counsel. The Morgan court specifically noted the policy interest of leveling the playing field between represented and unrepresented parties. However, in Shealy, the Court found those cases inapposite because Shealy was represented by counsel at the time he and Fields utilized ChatGPT to generate the output, and acted without counsel’s direction. Shealy decided entirely on his own initiative to use AI through a non-attorney third party, without consulting counsel about how the tool would be used. The court further emphasized a critical consideration underlying its analysis, and stated: “[n]or does the output from ChatGPT constitute opinion work product. AI is a tool not a person. Nothing about what ChatGPT produces discloses the ‘mental impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal theories of an attorney or other representative of a party concerning the litigation.’” (emphasis added). Absent attorney direction or input, the AI-generated output did not reflect an attorney’s or qualified representative’s strategic thinking or mental impressions. Consequently, the output cannot qualify for the heightened protection afforded to opinion work product. The Massachusetts trial court analogized the case to the February 2026 decision in United States v. Heppner, where a represented criminal defendant’s independent use of an AI tool without counsel’s direction fell outside the scope of privilege or work product protection and was subject to disclosure to the opposing party. The decision in Shealy v. Seaside Investments provides important guidance as AI tools become increasingly prevalent across commercial operations and decision-making, including those related to litigation. Entities and individuals, including those represented by counsel, cannot simply outsource AI queries to non-attorneys and expect the results to be shielded from discovery. For AI tool use to receive protection, counsel must direct it; otherwise, the AI output and the prompts used to generate it may be fair game for discovery. This ruling reflects a growing trend in which courts apply traditional privilege doctrines to AI-generated materials without modification, holding that the technology itself does not warrant departing from established frameworks. The takeaway is clear: once litigation becomes anticipated, involving counsel in any analytical work, AI-assisted or otherwise, is essential to shield a party’s mental impressions, theories, and strategies from discovery.

research.titleEn: How Much Do Legal RAG Systems Still Hallucinate?
research.titleZh: 法律RAG系统仍然会产生多少幻觉？
research.abstractEn: Hallucination is a major challenge for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in the legal domain, where ungrounded answers can lead to serious consequences. To better understand this problem, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of hallucination behavior in eight legal RAG systems across two legal corpora, the GDPR (in English) and a national civil law (in French). Using claim-level and answer-level evaluation, we report on hallucination density and severity, analyze performance across question categories and user personas, and validate our findings on an independent set of 142 legal-expert-authored questions. Our results show that hallucinations remain pervasive, ranging from less than 10% of responses for the best-performing systems to nearly half in the worst case. We further find that false-premise questions, containing incorrect assumptions that must be rejected, produce high hallucination rates on the manually-drafted questions.
research.abstractZh: 幻觉是法律领域检索增强生成（RAG）系统面临的主要挑战，因为无根据的答案可能导致严重后果。为了更好地理解这一问题，我们对两个法律语料库（英文的GDPR和法文的国家民法）中的八个法律RAG系统进行了细粒度的幻觉行为分析。通过声明级和答案级评估，我们报告了幻觉密度和严重程度，分析了不同问题类别和用户角色的表现，并在142个由法律专家撰写的问题的独立集上验证了我们的发现。结果表明，幻觉仍然普遍存在，从表现最好的系统中不到10%的回答到最差情况下近一半的回答。我们进一步发现，包含必须拒绝的错误假设的虚假前提问题，在手工起草的问题上产生了较高的幻觉率。

news.titleEn: CosmoLex Launches AI Intake, a Breakthrough Feature That Automates Client Onboarding for Law Firms From First Click to First Consultation
news.titleZh: CosmoLex推出AI Intake突破性功能，实现律所从首次点击到首次咨询的客户引导自动化
news.summaryZh:
CosmoLex于2026年8月13日宣布推出以AI Intake为首的一系列AI功能。AI Intake利用人工智能即时生成定制引导表单，并将现有PDF和Word旧表单转换为可提交的数字化在线表单。表单提交后，CosmoLex自动将数据映射至正确的联系人和潜在客户记录，消除手动重新录入并降低错误风险。提交后自动化工作流随即触发，自动处理文件交付、咨询预约和后续沟通，使新客户提交表单后关键的24小时无需人工分诊。该功能解决每家律所都熟知的问题，即新线索进入后24小时内的混乱，通过自动生成正确表单、首次即正确映射数据并在提交时启动跟进，律所可将引导流程转变为优势。

该发布还包含更广泛的AI功能：AI引导表单构建器允许律所提供描述所需信息、格式、分区和必填字段的书面提示，AI完成约95%的工作，生成可审查、调整和发布的表单，无需CosmoLex更强大的CRM附加组件；文档摘要内置于原生文档存储中，可快速了解文档内容、呈现关键数据点并生成要点大纲；AI驱动的自然语言过滤允许用户直接输入自然语言查找所需内容。上述功能自2026年8月13日起向CosmoLex客户提供。CosmoLex是面向北美中小型律所的端到端法律实践管理解决方案，隶属于ProfitSolv。
news.bodyHtml:
New suite of AI-powered capabilities, including AI Intake, document summarization, and natural-language search, eliminates manual data entry and gives firms back the first 24 hours of every new client relationship

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. —Aug 13, 2026 — CosmoLex, a leading cloud-based legal practice management platform, today announced a new set of AI-powered features headlined by AI Intake, a transformational capability that captures clean client data and automatically moves every intake forward without anyone touching it. 

Client intake is the first, and often most costly bottleneck in a law firm’s client relationship. Manually built forms, re-keyed data, and disconnected follow-up processes routinely delay a firm’s response to new leads and create the risk of losing prospective clients in the shuffle. CosmoLex’s AI Intake is designed to remove that friction entirely, turning what has historically been a time-consuming, error-prone manual process into a seamless, connected experience, all within a single platform and without the need for a separate, third-party intake tool.

AI Intake: The Premiere Feature of the Release

At the center of the launch is AI Intake, which uses artificial intelligence to instantly generate custom intake forms and convert existing legacy PDF and Word forms into digitally intuitive online forms that users can submit. Once a form is submitted, CosmoLex automatically maps the data to the correct contact and lead records, eliminating the need for manual re-keying and reducing the risk of costly errors.

From there, CosmoLex’s automated post-submission workflows take over. Triggered the moment a form is submitted, the platform can automatically handle document delivery, consultation booking, and follow-up communications, often the critical first 24 hours after a prospective client submits an intake form runs without anyone needing to manually triage it.

“AI Intake is the feature we’re most excited to bring to market, because it solves a problem every single law firm knows intimately: the chaos of the first 24 hours after a new lead comes in,” said Kelley Castell, CEO at CosmoLex. “By automatically generating the right forms, mapping the data correctly the first time, and kicking off follow-up the moment a form is submitted, firms can finally treat intake as a strength rather than a source of lost time and lost clients.”

A Full Suite of AI-Powered Capabilities

AI Intake is joined by a broader set of AI features designed to reduce administrative work across the firm, including:

AI Intake Form Builder — Building the right intake form for each case type has traditionally been an overwhelming task, even though the right questions are critical to reducing back-and-forth and administrative follow-up. With CosmoLex’s new AI builder, firms can simply provide a written prompt describing the information they want to collect, along with formatting, sections, and required fields. The AI form builder does approximately 95% of the work, generating a ready-to-use form that firms can review, adjust, and publish — all without requiring CosmoLex’s more robust CRM add-on.

Document Summarization — Built directly into CosmoLex’s native document storage, this feature allows users to quickly understand what a document is about, surface key data points, and generate a bulleted outline — a highlight reel for even the longest documents. For document-heavy firms, this capability can eliminate hours of administrative review time.

AI-Powered Natural-Language Filtering — Rather than manually scouring through filters to find what they need, users can simply type in natural language what they’re looking for and let CosmoLex’s AI do the work of surfacing the right results.

“Firms already come to CosmoLex because they want one login and one connected view of their matters, billing, and accounting,” added Kelley Castell. “These AI features extend that same philosophy to the front end of the client relationship and to the everyday administrative work inside the platform, so firms spend less time on data entry and searching, and more time practicing law.”

Availability

AI Intake, the AI Intake Form Builder, Document Summarization, and AI-powered natural-language filtering will be available to CosmoLex customers beginning August 13, 2026. 

About CosmoLex

CosmoLex is a leading end-to-end legal practice management solution trusted by thousands of small to mid-sized law firms across North America. CosmoLex connects intake, calendaring and tasks, document management, billing, trust accounting, and firm accounting in one modern, compliant platform, giving firms a single login and a complete view of their matter and firm data, and reducing the need for additional tools and integrations. CosmoLex is part of ProfitSolv, a collection of best-in-class software solutions for professional services firms. For more information, visit www.cosmolex.com.

Media Contact

Karen Dixon/CMO

Email: PR@ProfitSolv.com

news.titleEn: DeepJudge Releases an Open Protocol for Passing Users – and Their Context – Between AI Products, with Harvey and Thomson Reuters On Board
news.titleZh: DeepJudge发布开放协议，实现用户及其工作上下文在AI产品间无缝传递，Harvey与汤森路透已加入支持
news.summaryZh: 总部位于苏黎世的企业搜索公司DeepJudge近日推出“Agent Handoff Protocol”（AHP）开放协议，旨在让用户能够在不同AI产品之间切换时保留完整的工作上下文。Harvey已宣布正在构建集成该协议的方案，并计划于本月进入测试阶段；汤森路透则表示将在其法律产品CoCounsel for Legal中支持该协议，但具体实施细节和时间尚未公布。DeepJudge开发AHP是为了解决用户在不同AI产品间切换时需重建上下文的问题。现有协议如Anthropic开发的Model Context Protocol（MCP）虽能实现系统间信息交换和操作执行，但无法将工作目标、支持材料、对话历史及已完成的分析等更广泛的上下文随用户迁移。AHP则允许AI平台将用户及其继续工作所需的上下文从一个系统传递至另一个系统。律师在DeepJudge中研究先例问题后，可直接带着相关上下文进入Harvey，无需重新上传材料或重建分析。该协议的技术文档已发布在agenthandoffprotocol.org，用户操作仅需点击一个按钮。协议规定传递的上下文内容由实施方自行决定，例如Harvey可能传递对话历史，而DeepJudge作为搜索引擎更可能传递用户找到的文档。AHP基于MCP构建，并非替代MCP，而是提供不同的用户体验。DeepJudge发布的是协议规范而非实现代码，无许可费用，旨在鼓励其他厂商采用。该协议不限于法律领域，DeepJudge希望其他垂直行业也能采纳。
news.bodyHtml:
DeepJudge, the Zurich-based enterprise search company that describes itself as the institutional intelligence platform for legal AI, today introduced the Agent Handoff Protocol, an open protocol designed to let users move from one AI product into another – and, in some cases, back again – while retaining the full context of their work.

Harvey has already announced that it is building an integration implementing the protocol, which will enter beta this month, and Thomson Reuters says it will support it in CoCounsel for Legal, with details on its implementation and timing still to come.

“The most capable legal workflows will draw on more than one specialized system,” said Siva Gurumurthy, chief technology officer at Harvey. “Agent Handoff Protocol lets a user move from Harvey into a partner’s product and back without losing the thread of their work, while leveraging both products to their full potential.”

DeepJudge developed AHP to address the increasingly common problem of having to move between different AI products and experiences – such as from Harvey to DeepJudge – to get work done.

While existing protocols such as the Model Context Protocol developed by Anthropic let systems exchange information and perform discrete actions, they do not allow the broader context of the work – the objective, the supporting materials, the conversation history, the analysis already done – to travel with the user from one product to another.

“The Agent Handoff Protocol addresses this challenge by enabling AI platforms to transfer the user and the context needed to continue work from one system to another,” DeepJudge says. “Rather than rebuilding context each time they switch products, users can move between AI experiences while preserving the information and progress that led to the current point.”

In its announcement, DeepJudge gives the example of a lawyer researching a precedent question in DeepJudge, who can then move into Harvey with the relevant context already in place, without re-uploading materials, recreating prompts, or rebuilding prior analysis.

“No single AI experience will be the right one for every task,” Yannic Kilcher, DeepJudge’s CTO and co-founder, said in the announcement. “People should be able to use the AI tool that’s best for what they need to do and take their context with them.”

How It Works

For those wanting to dive in deeper, the technical documentation for the protocol can be found at agenthandoffprotocol.org. But in an interview yesterday, Kilcher told me that, for users, the actual mechanism of the handoff is a simple button. The user clicks it and says, in effect, I want to continue this work in this other application.

“In the background we take care of bringing that context along,” Kilcher said. “There’s multiple things that have to happen in the background. We have to authenticate you, so the whole transfer is secure and scoped to you as a user.”

The GitHub page describes it this way: “AHP gives two independently operated agent applications one shared action: Continue this user’s task over there, with this objective, this selected conversation context, and these resources.”

In terms of what context gets carried over, the protocol leaves that open so it is up to the vendor implementing the protocol to make that decision.

“The protocol itself has no opinion on that,” Kilcher said. “We feel it is the job of the individual partners in the ecosystem to decide what an appropriate context is.”

Harvey might decide the user’s conversation history is the right thing to pass, for example, whereas DeepJudge, as a search engine, is more likely to pass back the documents the user found.

As currently written, the specification describes one application handing off to another, and then the other possibly handing back.

Kilcher said the hand-back is optional for developers to adopt. A user who starts in DeepJudge, collects documents, and moves into CoCounsel to finish a drafting workflow may have no particular reason to return, he noted.

Handoffs among multiple applications are conceivable but not specified, Kilcher said. “We’re just trying to keep it really simple for now.”

Not an MCP Replacement

When asked how AHP differs from MCP, Kilcher said AHP is built on top of MCP and is not intended to replace it.

For simple retrieval, MCP works well, he said. For example, a lawyer using a firm’s Claude Enterprise deployment who asks whether the firm has done a particular kind of deal before can get an answer from DeepJudge through MCP without ever needing to leave Claude.

But for more complex tasks, it is sometimes preferable to work directly within the connected application’s full user interface.

“There is a reason products have different user interfaces, because we built these products to serve very particular needs,” Kilcher said. “There was no good way of delivering that via MCP, because all you get is basically the bit of text you send back and forth.”

The GitHub page puts it this way:

MCP connects an LLM application to external context and capabilities. Its core architecture has hosts, clients, and servers; servers expose resources, prompts, and tools through JSON-RPC over transports such as stdio and Streamable HTTP. A host can use those capabilities while keeping the user in the host application.

AHP connects two complete, independently operated agent applications. It transfers an explicit objective, a selected conversation sample, resources, and continuity identifiers, then returns a URL for a prepared experience in the receiving application. The user and the task cross the product boundary; tools, credentials, and execution privileges do not.

AHP reuses a good deal of MCP’s machinery, including how messages are structured. “It’s really about providing a different user experience than MCP, but it’s compatible and complementary to MCP,” Kilcher said. “This is not a replacement.”

He notes that MCP connectors often come with restrictions. A vendor will allow you to connect to its MCP server, but it may allow you to do only limited functions.

“With this, we’re voluntarily passing the user to the other product,” Kilcher said. “Philosophically, this is an ecosystem. The different players fulfill different roles, and if we make the user experience great, everyone profits.”

An Open Protocol

DeepJudge is publishing the specification, not an implementation. There is no license fee and no reference code, and Kilcher said the point of releasing it openly is to remove any question about whether other vendors can build on it.

“We wanted to make it so that there is no danger of us being like, ‘Hey, this is ours,’” he said. “We’re not releasing the implementation anyway. This would be useless today – you can just give this protocol spec that we released to an LLM. It will do a fine job at implementing it.”

The spec covers what each side of the handoff must implement – message structure, transfer mechanism, how resources are represented – and Kilcher said it documents what DeepJudge has already built with its partners, so it is not aspirational.

“This is a full description of what we have implemented with our partners. So we know that this works.”

Nothing about the protocol is legal-specific, and Kilcher said DeepJudge would be happy to see it picked up in other verticals. Asked whether anything comparable already exists, he said the team found individual projects but no standard.

“Professionals will increasingly work across specialized AI experiences, and those systems need to work together without sacrificing the context, trust, and expertise required for high-stakes work,” said Joel Hron, chief technology officer at Thomson Reuters. “Open standards like Agent Handoff Protocol can help enable that interoperability.”

To my mind, the premise of AHP makes perfect sense. There are some things you can do well via an MCP connector to an application and some things you can do well only by directing engaging with the application and its full user experience. But you do not want that context switching to lose the context of your work.

As for whether AHP becomes a widely used standard, time will tell. Kilcher is modest about that. “This is how we’re doing it,” he said. “It’s a suggestion from us to the industry.”

Its core architecture has hosts, clients, and servers; servers expose resources, prompts, and tools through JSON-RPC over transports such as stdio and Streamable HTTP. A host can use those capabilities while keeping the user in the host application.

AHP connects two complete, independently operated agent applications. It transfers an explicit objective, a selected conversation sample, resources, and continuity identifiers, then returns a URL for a prepared experience in the receiving application. The user and the task cross the product boundary; tools, credentials, and execution privileges do not.

AHP reuses a good deal of MCP’s machinery, including how messages are structured. “It’s really about providing a different user experience than MCP, but it’s compatible and complementary to MCP,” Kilcher said. “This is not a replacement.”

He notes that MCP connectors often come with restrictions. A vendor will allow you to connect to its MCP server, but it may allow you to do only limited functions.

“With this, we’re voluntarily passing the user to the other product,” Kilcher said. “Philosophically, this is an ecosystem. The different players fulfill different roles, and if we make the user experience great, everyone profits.”

DeepJudge is publishing the specification, not an implementation. There is no license fee and no reference code, and Kilcher said the point of releasing it openly is to remove any question about whether other vendors can build on it.

“We wanted to make it so that there is no danger of us being like, ‘Hey, this is ours,’” he said. “We’re not releasing the implementation anyway. This would be useless today – you can just give this protocol spec that we released to an LLM. It will do a fine job at implementing it.”

The spec covers what each side of the handoff must implement – message structure, transfer mechanism, how resources are represented – and Kilcher said it documents what DeepJudge has already built with its partners, so it is not aspirational.

“This is a full description of what we have implemented with our partners. So we know that this works.”

Nothing about the protocol is legal-specific, and Kilcher said DeepJudge would be happy to see it picked up in other verticals. Asked whether anything comparable already exists, he said the team found individual projects but no standard.

“Professionals will increasingly work across specialized AI experiences, and those systems need to work together without sacrificing the context, trust, and expertise required for high-stakes work,” said Joel Hron, chief technology officer at Thomson Reuters. “Open standards like Agent Handoff Protocol can help enable that interoperability.”

To my mind, the premise of AHP makes perfect sense. There are some things you can do well via an MCP connector to an application and some things you can do well only by directing engaging with the application and its full user experience. But you do not want that context switching to lose the context of your work.

As for whether AHP becomes a widely used standard, time will tell. Kilcher is modest about that. “This is how we’re doing it,” he said. “It’s a suggestion from us to the industry.”

news.titleEn: FTC Issues Proposed Policy Statement on AI Accuracy and Output Steering
news.titleZh: FTC发布关于AI准确性与输出引导的拟议政策声明
news.summaryZh:
2026年7月1日，美国联邦贸易委员会（FTC）发布拟议政策声明，聚焦将AI输出导向未披露意识形态目标的做法，认为其可能损害准确性并违背消费者合理预期。该声明紧随第14365号行政令，该命令要求FTC澄清《FTC法》第5条如何适用于AI模型及各州新兴AI监管法律。

消费者通常期望AI力求准确并忠实执行请求，但开发者可能暗中“引导”输出以推进意识形态、回避争议或限制法律风险等目标。声明特别提及科罗拉多州《人工智能法》，该法规定企业可能因客户使用其产品产生的歧视性输出而担责；企业为遵守该法及其他州类似法律也可能损害准确性，若未充分披露，可能违反第5条。声明对披露设定高标准：不能埋在服务条款中，一次性披露后藏于细则也不够，必须清晰显著地消除系统旨在给出最佳答案的观念。遵守州要求不自动消除联邦欺骗担忧，州法律强制修改输出有时可能与联邦消费者保护原则冲突。声明未提供正式优先规则，但反映当前政府推动更统一国家AI监管框架的兴趣，并为FTC未来分析AI治理、透明度和内容控制提供初步路线图。利益相关者应审查营销传播和公开声明，评估AI训练与内容审核治理流程，并处理州AI与隐私法律及国际法律（如欧盟AI法案）与FTC立场之间的潜在脱节。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On July 1, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued a proposed policy statement focusing on AI models that steer outcomes toward undisclosed ideological objectives. According to the FTC, this practice may compromise accuracy and be contrary to reasonable consumer expectations about how AI models work. The proposed policy statement follows Executive Order 14365, which specifically directs the agency to clarify how § 5 of the FTC Act applies to both AI models and emerging state laws that regulate those models. According to the proposed policy statement, consumers generally expect AI systems to strive for accurate responses and faithfully carry out consumer requests, subject to ordinary technological limitations. These expectations are reasonable, the FTC contends, due to the inherent nature of AI systems and explicit or implied representations that companies have espoused for years about those systems. Unbeknownst to consumers, however, AI developers may engage in “steering” the output, the FTC says, by deliberately configuring AI systems to advance objectives other than accuracy (e.g., achieving ideological goals, avoiding controversial topics, or attempting to limit legal exposure). To illustrate this point, the proposed policy statement specifically points to Colorado’s recently enacted Artificial Intelligence Act, which provides, among other requirements, that companies can be held liable for discriminatory AI model outputs resulting from customers’ use of those products. The FTC asserts that even a company’s efforts to comply with this statute (and similar laws in other states) could compromise accuracy and be contrary to consumers’ reasonable expectations about how AI models work. In the FTC’s view, failure to sufficiently disclose this to consumers may violate § 5 because deception under the FTC Act includes “implied misrepresentations, half-truths, and instances where only a ‘significant minority’ of consumers are misled.” The proposed policy statement appears to set a high bar as to what constitutes an adequate disclosure on outcome steering, noting that the disclosure cannot be buried in the terms of service, and a one-time disclosure “subsequently hidden away in fine print” is unlikely to suffice. Instead, the disclosure must “clearly and conspicuously dispel the notion that the system is designed to give the best answer possible.” Additionally, the FTC clarifies that the more the disclosure cuts against the reasonable expectations that users would take away from other contexts, the more persistent and prominent the disclosure would need to be. In the proposed policy statement, the FTC considers how emerging state laws on AI, including the Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act, may require AI developers to alter, constrain, or otherwise influence AI outputs to achieve particular public policy objectives. The FTC takes the position that compliance with a state requirement does not automatically eliminate potential federal deception concerns if consumers are not adequately informed about how those requirements affect outputs. The proposed policy statement also suggests that state laws compelling modifications to AI outputs could, in some instances, conflict with federal consumer protection principles. Although the proposed policy statement does not provide a formal preemption rule, its discussion of emerging states AI laws seems to reflect the current administration’s interest in promoting a more uniform national framework for AI regulation. The proposed policy statement provides a tentative roadmap to how the FTC may analyze questions involving AI governance, transparency, and content controls in the future. Stakeholders should consider reviewing the content of their marketing communications and other public-facing statements — not only for explicit claims about AI products, but also for implied representations or potentially relevant information that has been omitted. Companies should consider assessing governance processes for AI model training and content moderation, given the FTC’s apparent scrutiny of intentional design choices. They should also consider how to address the potential disconnect between state AI and privacy laws (and international laws, such as the EU AI Act, where relevant) and the FTC’s position. news.titleEn: Neota Rolls Out New AI Governance Strategy
news.titleZh: Neota推出全新AI治理策略
news.summaryZh: Neota Logic以“法律团队的AI治理层”为定位，推出AI编排能力，允许律师将自选大语言模型引入受治理的工作流：每次调用均被记录、对照团队规则检查并路由至人工签核。该公司起源于2010年，曾是首批“无代码”法律工作流自动化公司之一，如今聚焦生成式AI，尤其是内部团队和合规团队的应用。新治理产品是其多项AI能力中的第一项，均遵循同一标准：法律团队应以AI速度推进工作，同时不丧失为工作辩护的能力。该编排将模型置于工作流内，仅用于提取、摘要、分类等擅长任务，规则、路由和人工签核仍由团队控制。工作流决定输出处理：合同可由模型读取，依据公司自身操作手册评估后自动路由，低风险事项直接通过，重大事项升级给相应律师。调用可链式进行，在下一步前检查上一模型输出，置信度下降时立即升级人工审查。每次运行产生完整审计追踪：AI被问及什么、返回什么、运行了哪个模型及谁签核。模型集中审批，默认不调用任何模型，团队通过自有账户与Anthropic、OpenAI、Azure OpenAI、Google、开源及AWS Bedrock等已用提供商合作。公司重申人工将检查最终输出。客户在AI上投入更多，但不想失去使法律和合规流程运作的规则与控制，希望将已选模型引入可信赖的工作流。随着LLM兴起，全球“无代码”规则型工作流自动化公司都面临重大挑战，因为简单自然语言提示即可执行复杂文本任务，而LLM中的代理和推理能力只会加剧这一点。
news.bodyText: Neota Logic, which is now going to market as ‘the AI governance layer for legal teams’, has launched an AI orchestration capability which lets lawyers bring their own choice of large language models into governed AI workflows. This means that ‘every AI call [to an LLM] is logged, checked against the team’s own rules, and routed for human sign-off’. This is a big change from what many of you will remember Neota doing in the past, which was one of the first ‘no code’ legal workflow automation companies. Neota, which can trace its roots back to 2010, is now very much focused on generative AI use, and in particular how inhouse teams and compliance groups are using the technology. They added that the new AI governance offering is ‘the first of several AI capabilities the company is bringing to market, all built to a single standard: legal teams should be able to move at the speed of AI without giving up the ability to defend the work’. But, back to the governance part. How does it work? This is how they explain it: ‘Calling a large language model is straightforward, and most tools stop at that: they return an answer and leave the user to catch what is wrong. Neota Logic’s AI orchestration places the model inside a workflow instead. It is called only for the tasks it does well, such as extraction, summarization, and classification, while the rules, the routing, and the human sign-off around it stay under the team’s control. ‘The workflow decides what happens to the model’s output. A contract can be read by the model, assessed against the firm’s own playbook, then routed automatically: low-risk matters cleared, anything material escalated to the right lawyer before it moves. Calls can be chained so one model’s output is checked before the next step runs, and a workflow can escalate to human review the moment confidence drops. ‘Every run produces a full audit trail: what the AI was asked, what it returned, which model ran, and who signed off. Models are approved centrally, no model is ever invoked by default, and legal teams work with the providers they already use, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Google, Open Source and AWS Bedrock, through their own accounts.’ And they reiterated that they are working on the basis that a human will check the final output. Vinay Varma, Chief Customer Officer at Neota Logic, commented: ‘Our customers are investing more in AI, but they do not want to lose the rules and controls that make their legal and compliance processes work. They want to bring the models they have already chosen into workflows they can trust and stand behind.’ Is this a big deal? Well, all of the ‘no code’ rules-based workflow automation companies across the world faced a major challenge once LLMs took off. This was because you easily could ask such AI systems to perform complex text-based tasks with just a simple, natural language prompt. Agents and better reasoning within LLMs only accentuated this.

news.titleEn: DeepJudge Launches Agent Handoff Protocol, Harvey + TR Adopt
news.titleZh: DeepJudge推出Agent Handoff Protocol，Harvey与汤森路透采纳
news.summaryZh: 知识管理先驱DeepJudge推出“Agent Handoff Protocol”（AHP），这是一个开放系统，使用户能够在不同AI平台之间切换而无需从头开始，并携带继续工作所需的上下文。Harvey和汤森路透均已决定参与。最强大的法律工作流将利用多个专业系统，AHP让用户从Harvey进入合作伙伴产品再返回，不会丢失工作线索，同时充分发挥两个产品的潜力。人们应该能够使用最适合其需求的AI工具，并随身携带上下文。专业人士将越来越多地跨专业AI体验工作，这些系统需要协同工作，而不牺牲高风险工作所需的上下文、信任和专业知识；AHP等开放标准有助于实现这种互操作性。DeepJudge解释，随着更多律师在不同AI产品之间切换，尽管已有MCP（模型上下文协议）允许系统交换信息和执行特定操作，但其灵活性不足以满足当今需求。律师工作需要更广泛的上下文来继续任务，包括目标、支持材料、对话历史和先前工作。AHP通过使AI平台能够将用户和继续工作所需的上下文从一个系统转移到另一个系统来解决这一挑战。例如，律师在DeepJudge中研究先例问题后，可以进入Harvey，相关上下文已就位，无需重新上传材料、重新创建提示或重建先前分析。Harvey宣布将于本月以测试版推出AHP。汤森路透也支持AHP，有关其实施和时间的更多细节将在未来公告中公布。
news.bodyText: KM pioneer DeepJudge has launched an ‘Agent Handoff Protocol’ or AHP, which is an open system that ‘enables users to move between AI platforms without starting fresh, carrying the context needed to continue their work’ – which is handy. Thomson Reuters and Harvey have both decided to get involved. Siva Gurumurthy, Chief Technology Officer at Harvey, commented: ‘The most capable legal workflows will draw on more than one specialized system. Agent Handoff Protocol lets a user move from Harvey into a partner’s product and back without losing the thread of their work, while leveraging both products to their full potential. We’re glad to be among the first to implement it.’ While Yannic Kilcher, CTO and Co-Founder of DeepJudge, added: ‘People should be able to use the AI tool that’s best for what they need to do and take their context with them. That is the experience we built Agent Handoff Protocol to enable.’ And Joel Hron, Chief Technology Officer at TR, concluded: ‘Professionals will increasingly work across specialized AI experiences, and those systems need to work together without sacrificing the context, trust, and expertise required for high-stakes work. Open standards like Agent Handoff Protocol can help enable that interoperability, which is why Thomson Reuters is excited to support this effort and help shape what comes next.’ All well and good, but why do this? DeepJudge explained that as more lawyers move ‘between different AI products and experiences to complete their work’ that although we have MCP (the Model Context Protocol) that allows systems to exchange information and perform specific actions, that it’s not sufficiently flexible to meet today’s needs. They underlined that in a lawyer’s work ‘a broader context [is] required to continue a task—including objectives, supporting materials, conversation history, and prior work’. The AHP addresses this challenge by ‘enabling AI platforms to transfer the user and the context needed to continue work from one system to another. Rather than rebuilding context each time they switch products, users can move between AI experiences while preserving the information and progress that led to the current point’. For example, they noted that a lawyer researching a precedent question in DeepJudge can now move into Harvey with the relevant context already in place, allowing the work to continue without re-uploading materials, recreating prompts, or rebuilding prior analysis. In terms of their legal tech peers, Harvey has announced it will roll out AHP in beta this month. While Thomson Reuters is also supporting AHP, with additional details on their implementation and timing to follow in future announcements. Overall, a nice move, and one that makes a lot of sense. In particular this is quite a coup for DeepJudge, given that they appear to be leading on this. The Agent Handoff Protocol specification and implementation resources are here.
