news.bodyHtml:
LexisNexis Legal & Professional today (4 August) announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City – describing it as a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped.  

Within the Lab, legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI collaborators like OpenAI and Amazon Web Services will “build side by side”, solving workflow pain points with prototypes “in hours”. 

Advertisement

The Lab launches with around 30 people, made up of engineers, AR scientists and productivity UX specialists, of which 20 are fully dedicated to the Lab. They have been hired in as well as moved internally, with the anticipation that LexisNexis will also cycle through its other 4,000 engineers and technologists.  

Speaking to Legal IT Insider about the Lab, LexisNexis executive vice president and chief technology officer Greg Dickason said that it is a reflection of the speed of change, observing: “What was done in months and years in the past is now being done in weeks.” 

Advertisement

With model providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI releasing models every six weeks to eight weeks, Dickason observed that “what we’re really seeing is that our customers are struggling with how do they absorb all of this AI, not just from the model providers, but also across the board from all the different vendors out there.” 

The idea of the Lab is to bring LexisNexis engineers closer to the customer, with “none of this middle layer.” It is hoped that this will help customers to get a handle on how to cut through the noise as well as help to build products live. 

Dickason says: “We did one this week, which I was pretty excited about. The customer gave us feedback, we iterated, they gave us more feedback, reiterated, and essentially in one hour, we had changed the product three times.  

“For me, that’s the real sort of signal of how the Lab can work, is that we can [not only] understand customer problems, but put them right with the people who can build the solution, which is the engineers.” 

Much of the development will focus on legal AI assistant LexisNexis Protégé, and asked how LexisNexis will streamline customer demands, Dickason said that “when you get that feedback from one customer, that doesn’t immediately become a product. It gives us really good ideas as to where we should be going. And then we can test it with a second set of customers and a third set. But very quickly, within a week or so, we would have tested it with, say, 10 or 20 different customers and got real ideas to what’s going to make a difference for them.” 

He adds: “The Lab’s really helping us crystallise what’s most important.”  

 LexisNexis via the Lab is already engaging with associates and CIOs and technology leaders. It is already working with a few of the Am Law top 50 firms and a couple of the Am Law top 10 firms. 

Examples of ideas that have come to fruition include an advanced, customer-managed Protégé Vault for analysing complex multimedia materials. Legal professionals will be able to store and analyse documents, videos, images, audio files, and other matter materials. A lawyer could, for example, analyse a two-hour deposition in minutes with Protégé, pinpoint the exact moments when key facts emerge, and trace findings directly to the timestamps and source materials. 

Interestingly, as we enter a period in which a lot of the largest law firms are looking at leveraging their own ecosystem rather than buying a product off the shelf, and even training their own models, Dickason says the Lab helps “because it helps them conceptualise.”

“I see it as educational,” he says. “So it’s not just about coming and us getting all the benefit of it. It’s also for them to get other benefits to come in, understand how we think about fine tuning, where we see fine tuning models make sense and where you should still be using foundation models. We use a blend of models across all the major vendors, but also fine tune our own. And I think it really comes down to what’s the right use case for your particular need , what you need to do.”  

While the Lab is currently a physical space in New York, LexisNexis will also be looking at rolling out in other major centers around the world.  

Dickason says: “I think you get so much more when people are in one room and they can actually see and interact. You get far more when people can see the response. And say ‘okay, that worked. That didn’t work.’ You don’t get that over Teams, et cetera.”  

“Congratulations to LexisNexis on the launch of its Customer Innovation Lab,” said Scott Liska, VP AWSI, Amazon Web Services in a statement. “Bringing trusted AI into professional work requires both rapid innovation and a strong technology foundation. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with LexisNexis as it advances secure, authoritative AI capabilities for legal professionals.”

LexisNexis Legal & Professional today (4 August) announced the opening of its Customer Innovation Lab in New York City – describing it as a new model for how legal AI gets built and shipped.

Within the Lab, legal professionals, LexisNexis engineers, and AI collaborators like OpenAI and Amazon Web Services will “build side by side”, solving workflow pain points with prototypes “in hours”.

The Lab launches with around 30 people, made up of engineers, AR scientists and productivity UX specialists, of which 20 are fully dedicated to the Lab. They have been hired in as well as moved internally, with the anticipation that LexisNexis will also cycle through its other 4,000 engineers and technologists.

news.summaryZh: LawSHIFT于7月1日推出迷你书《预受理问题：当受伤者寻找答案时，人身伤害律师缺席对话》，由Nick Kringas和Lydia Flocchini合著。书中将“预受理问题™”定义为受伤者在与法律顾问交谈前，试图了解发生了什么、自身权利及下一步行动的阶段。随着人们使用消费者AI平台提出法律问题、评估潜在索赔并决定信任哪些律师，AI在这一窗口期的影响力日益增强。人身伤害律所数十年来在搜索、电话或表单提交后竞争可见度，但最重要的决定越来越多地在受理前、律师与受伤者交谈前就已形成；第一次法律对话不再总是与律师进行，而越来越多是与AI进行。行业大量投资于改善受理后的流程，却较少关注人们仍在理解自身处境并决定信任谁的时期。LawSHIFT确立了“Pre-Intake AI for PI™”类别，并开发“AI for PI Index™”，追踪领先AI平台在美国数百个市场中如何解释、引用和推荐人身伤害律所。基于256个市场超过1500家律所的数据，覆盖约20000家律所，公司每周发布洞察，研究AI如何重塑法律可见度、权威和客户获取。客户旅程已经改变，律所声誉过去存在于市场中，现在还必须对机器可读，权威必须转化为AI能识别、信任和推荐的信号，这是新法律推荐经济的开始；AI不会取代人身伤害律师，但日益塑造受伤者的信念、提出的问题以及首先考虑的律师。该书现已在LawSHIFT的Substack上发布。LawSHIFT成立于2013年，总部纽约，拥有超过50年人身伤害营销、法律技术、类别设计和增长策略的综合经验，其技术包括AI for PI Index™、CASETIMATOR™和专有AI Authority Protocol™。
news.bodyHtml:
New mini-book examines how AI is influencing injured people before they ever speak with an attorney

NEW YORK — July 2026 — LawSHIFT, the Pre-Intake AI for PI™ company, announced the launch of The Pre-Intake Problem: When Injured People Are Searching for Answers, Personal Injury Attorneys Are Missing From the Conversation. This new mini-book co-authored by Nick Kringas and Lydia Flocchini examines how artificial intelligence is changing the earliest stage of the legal client journey.

Published July 1, the book defines the Pre-Intake Problem™ as the period when injured people are trying to understand what happened, what their rights may be, and what to do next before speaking with legal counsel. LawSHIFT argues that AI is becoming increasingly influential during this window as people use consumer AI platforms to ask legal questions, evaluate potential claims, and decide which attorneys they may trust.

“Personal injury firms have spent decades competing for visibility after someone searches, calls, or fills out a form,” said Nick Kringas, Founder and CEO of LawSHIFT. “The most important decisions are increasingly being shaped before intake and before a lawyer ever speaks with the injured person. That is the pre-intake problem.”

Law firms have traditionally built client acquisition strategies around referrals, advertising, reputation, and search visibility. Those channels remain important, but LawSHIFT believes the client journey is being rerouted as injured people increasingly seek AI-generated guidance before contacting a firm.

“The first legal conversation is no longer always with a lawyer. Increasingly, it is with AI,” Kringas said. “The legal industry has invested heavily in improving intake once someone reaches a firm, while paying far less attention to the period when that person is still trying to understand their situation and decide whom to trust.”

LawSHIFT was built around the question of what happens before an injured person ever calls an attorney. The company has established Pre-Intake AI for PI™ as a category focused on that previously difficult-to-measure stage and has developed the AI for PI Index™, an ongoing research initiative tracking how leading AI platforms interpret, cite, and recommend personal injury firms across hundreds of U.S. markets. Drawing on data from more than 1,500 firms across 256 markets, with visibility into approximately 20,000 firms, the company publishes weekly insights examining how AI is reshaping legal visibility, authority, and client acquisition.

 

Lydia Flocchini, Partner and Legal Category Designer at LawSHIFT, said, “The client journey has already changed. A law firm’s reputation used to live in the market. Now it must also be legible to machines. Authority has to be translated into signals AI can recognize, trust, and recommend. This is the beginning of a new legal referral economy.”

“AI is not replacing personal injury attorneys, but it is increasingly shaping what injured people believe, which questions they ask, and which attorneys they consider first,” Flocchini said. “Our mission is to help close the distance between that early search for answers and trusted legal counsel.”

The Pre-Intake Problem: When Injured People Are Searching for Answers, Personal Injury Attorneys Are Missing From the Conversation is available now on LawSHIFT’s Substack.

 

About LawSHIFT

LawSHIFT is the Pre-Intake AI for PI™ company, building AI systems, visibility infrastructure, and pre-intake tools for the personal injury legal market. Founded in 2013 and headquartered in New York, the company brings together more than 50 years of combined experience across personal injury marketing, legal technology, category design, and growth strategy. LawSHIFT’s technology includes the AI for PI Index™, CASETIMATOR™, and its proprietary AI Authority Protocol™, all developed around its mission to help injured people move from early questions and AI-assisted research toward trusted legal counsel.

Media Contact
Name: Lydia Flocchini
Email: lydia@lawshift.ai

news.titleEn: When 'Agentic AI' Meets Data Protection Laws: A Fundamental Mismatch?
news.titleZh: 当“代理式AI”遇上数据保护法：根本性错配？
news.summaryZh: 代理式AI是自主、目标导向的系统，能追求开放式目标、自行创建工作流并在有限人类监督下实时适应，已在金融、医疗、物流和机器人等行业获得关注，主要AI开发商提供预构建工作流模板以加速这一转变。该技术对现代隐私与数据保护法构成根本性挑战，后者依赖同意、目的限制以及个人与非个人数据区分等假设。文章主张代理式AI要求重新思考隐私法，并邀请政策制定者、监管机构与科技公司考虑数据保护规则应如何为日益自主的AI系统演进。代理式AI违背GDPR和CCPA等法规的基本假设，体现在两个系统性挑战：个人与非个人数据的刚性二分法在AI介导的交互中瓦解；同意与目的限制等核心原则在自主代理流动、不确定的意图无法事前确定时功能上过时。GDPR建立在“同意与控制”框架上，依赖静态数据处理模型，要求控制者在收集时明确阐述具体目的，但该假设在AI时代不再成立。自主系统缺乏固定操作路径，使传统目的限制规则失去意义；AI代理遵循开放式目标并动态生成中间步骤、工作流和数据收集策略，其实际意图与行动轨迹无法事前知晓或预测。代理式爬虫基于广泛目标自主导航，动态决定路径，控制者无法事前知晓是否会摄取个人数据。AI代理持续重新利用数据，例如从健身追踪器生物识别数据推断心理健康状况，可能构成GDPR旨在防止的未经授权“进一步处理”。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! Agentic AI represents a seismic shift toward autonomous, goal-directed systems that can pursue open-ended objectives, create their own workflows, and adapt in real time with limited human oversight. This development poses fundamental challenges to modern privacy and data protection laws, which depend on assumptions about consent, purpose limitation, and the distinction between personal and non-personal data. This post argues that agentic AI requires a rethinking of privacy law and invites policymakers, regulators, and technology companies to consider how data protection rules should evolve for a world of increasingly autonomous AI systems. Modern agentic AI introduces a distinct paradigm shift in data protection. Agentic AI refers to autonomous, goal-seeking systems capable of pursuing open-ended objectives and adapting continuously without persistent human direction. From a cognitive perspective, AI agents are capable of learning dynamically from their environment, revising their own goals, and making decisions with minimal human oversight and control. Adaptive AI agents are already gaining traction across sectors as diverse as finance, healthcare, logistics, and robotics. To accelerate this transition, major AI developers are providing pre-built workflow templates that automate complex sequences or empower users to build custom-designed agentic architectures. However, the rise of agentic AI reveals a profound and growing mismatch between the realities of machine autonomy and the well-established legal frameworks designed to govern digital systems and protect personal privacy. Crucially, agentic AI defies the foundational assumptions underpinning data protection regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). This tension is best illustrated by two systemic challenges. First, the rigid dichotomy between personal and non-personal data (a distinction central to regulatory scope) collapses within context-hungry, AI-mediated interactions. Second, core principles governing data processing, such as consent and purpose limitation, become functionally obsolete when the fluid, indeterminate, and unpredictable intent of an autonomous agent cannot be determined ex ante. Europe’s flagship data protection regulation, the GDPR, is built on an ambition to restrain the unchecked exploitation of data. The EU aimed to empower individual consumers and curb the surveillance-capitalism models that defined the commercialized Internet. The GDPR mandates a lawful basis for processing personal data while establishing robust safeguards for data subjects such as explicit consent, lawful basis, and purpose limitation. Under this “consent and control” framework, data subjects “relinquish” absolute privacy in exchange for an enforceable regime of “data protection.” This framework relies on a fundamentally static model of data processing, wherein a human data controller pre-determines what data is collected, how it will be utilized, and when it will be deleted. As such, the GDPR operates on the assumption that controllers can clearly articulate these discrete purposes to data subjects at the point of data collection. That assumption no longer holds in the age of AI. Agentic AI systems undermine these well-established legal principles. First, autonomous systems lack a fixed, pre-programmed operational path, rendering traditional purpose-limitation rules meaningless. AI agents follow open-ended objectives and dynamically generate their own intermediary steps, workflows, and data-gathering strategies. Simply put, the actual intent and action trajectory of an AI agent cannot be known or predicted ex ante, and this characteristic of the technology is by design. This systemic unpredictability of intent can be illustrated by modern automated web intelligence, or data scraping, practices. Unlike legacy scrapers that execute deterministic scripts targeting specific data fields, an agentic crawler operates autonomously in a browser based on broad goals, such as “map regional market sentiment” or “find the top 10 trending items on Amazon.” It independently navigates the web, uses adaptive machine learning to overcome operational frictions, and dynamically decides which pathways or unindexed forums to harvest. Because its retrieval logic evolves in real time, the controller cannot know ex ante whether it will ingest personal data or cross-reference anonymous profiles. In this setting, ex ante declarations of data access intent risk becoming a legal fiction because the agent itself determines relevance and collection scope mid-execution. Second, AI agents continuously repurpose data. Their core utility lies in reapplying ingested knowledge across fluid, evolving contexts. For example, an agent with access to an individual’s biometric data from a fitness tracker might begin by monitoring step counts, but later infer a user’s mental health status, burnout levels, or cardiac conditions. Neither the developer nor the user could have predicted this outcome ex ante. Although such synthesis may be an engineering breakthrough, it may constitute an unauthorized “further processing” the GDPR was designed to prevent. Because an autonomous agent reasons non-linearly and in real time, it cannot pause mid-execution to conduct an Article 6(4) compatibility assessment before shifting the purpose of its processing.

阿拉巴马州律师协会加入越来越多提供律师使用人工智能正式指导的司法管辖区行列。第2026-01号正式意见《人工智能使用：现行职业行为规则下的最佳实践》并未创设新的伦理义务，而是解释《职业行为规则》下的长期义务在律师于执业中使用生成式AI和新兴代理式AI工具时如何适用。该意见认识到AI已迅速从实验性技术转变为日常工具，用于起草文件、总结证据、开展研究、分析合同及与客户沟通。阿拉巴马州律师协会未等待纪律问题出现，而是主动解释现行职业行为规则如何管辖这些技术。

news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The Alabama State Bar has joined a growing number of jurisdictions providing formal guidance on lawyers’ use of artificial intelligence. Formal Opinion 2026-01, Artificial Intelligence Use: Best Practices Under Existing Professional Conduct Rules, does not create new ethical obligations. Instead, it explains how longstanding duties under the Rules of Professional Conduct apply when lawyers use generative AI and emerging agentic AI tools in practice. Below are answers to some of the most important questions for law firms and legal departments. The opinion recognizes that AI has rapidly moved from an experimental technology to an everyday tool used to draft documents, summarize evidence, conduct research, analyze contracts, and communicate with clients. Rather than waiting for disciplinary issues to arise, the Alabama State Bar sought to explain how existing professional conduct rules govern these technologies. Importantly, the opinion emphasizes that AI does not create new ethical duties. Instead, it “recontextualizes” existing duties—including competence, confidentiality, supervision, communication, candor, and reasonable fees—in light of AI-assisted legal practice. No. To the contrary, the opinion recognizes AI’s potential to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and expand access to legal services. Alabama acknowledges that AI is becoming an ordinary component of modern legal practice and that lawyers should understand both its benefits and its limitations. The opinion also notes that as AI becomes more integrated into legal education and practice, technological competence increasingly includes understanding AI tools. The opinion consistently returns to one central principle: Lawyers remain responsible for the final work product—even when AI assisted in creating it. Among the practical expectations discussed are: The opinion explains that competent representation now includes understanding how AI works sufficiently to appreciate both its capabilities and its risks.

news.summaryZh: 在Schulte诉LinkedIn公司案中，美国加利福尼亚北区联邦治安法官Laurel Beeler签署了一项12页的命令，驳回了原告针对LinkedIn的Relativity aiR工作流程提出的全部三项要求。法官将该工具视为技术辅助审查的一种形式，并依据双方已有的证据开示协议进行处理。该命令于2026年6月30日签署，次日录入案件目录。它不构成对其他法院有约束力的先例，仅基于特定案件记录解决了一项协议争议，而非普遍认可生成式人工智能审查。评论认为此案的克制态度是新闻点。退休的美国治安法官Andrew Peck及其DLA Piper同事Reema Holz将Schulte案描述为第一个接受生成式人工智能在证据开示中做出最终响应性判断的联邦决定。该案本身是一起反垄断集体诉讼，而非技术争议。原告于2022年1月起诉LinkedIn，指控其垄断专业社交网络市场并向高级订阅用户超额收费。命令还一并解决了另外两项未引发评论的请求，即拒绝将内部律师添加为保管人以及拒绝提供短信的要求。
news.bodyHtml:
Editor’s Note: A federal magistrate judge has given litigators their first close look at how a court handles generative artificial intelligence making final responsiveness calls, and the answer required no new law. In Schulte v. LinkedIn Corp., the court denied three plaintiff demands aimed at LinkedIn’s Relativity aiR workflow and treated the tool as a form of technology-assisted review under the case’s existing ESI order. The order is nonprecedential and tied to its record, which is exactly why the commentary matters: retired Magistrate Judge Andrew Peck, whose Da Silva Moore opinion opened the TAR era, describes it with DLA Piper colleague Reema Holz as the first federal decision to accept generative AI in that role.

Compliance, security and information governance teams should note what mattered: custodial volume materially influenced the proportionality decision, disclosure obligations began and ended with the protocol, and validation metrics were not compelled absent a specific deficiency. Watch the search-string conference the order required, the diverging AI confidentiality rulings, and the protocol language crossing your desk this quarter.

The rules held. The expectations moved.

Industry News – Artificial Intelligence Beat

Federal magistrate judge treats LinkedIn’s Relativity aiR workflow as TAR

ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff

A federal magistrate judge has looked at LinkedIn’s plan to let a generative artificial intelligence tool make final responsiveness calls and found nothing that required new rules.

In a 12-page order in Schulte v. LinkedIn Corp., U.S. Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler of the Northern District of California denied all three plaintiff demands aimed at the Relativity aiR workflow, treating the tool as a form of technology-assisted review, or TAR, under the discovery protocol the parties already had.

Beeler signed the order June 30, 2026, and it entered the docket the next day. It creates no precedent that binds another court, and it resolves one protocol fight on one record rather than blessing generative AI review at large. What it does is meet a closely watched test with the machinery that already exists: reasonableness, proportionality and the disfavored status of discovery on discovery.

The commentary treated that restraint as the news. Retired U.S. Magistrate Judge Andrew Peck, who wrote the 2012 opinion in Da Silva Moore v. Publicis Groupe that first approved technology-assisted review, and his DLA Piper colleague Reema Holz describe Schulte as the first federal decision to accept generative AI making the final responsiveness call in discovery. At least eight law firms and eDiscovery providers published analyses within a month of the order.

The underlying case is an antitrust class action, not a technology dispute. Todd Crowder, Kevin Schulte and Garrick Vance sued LinkedIn in January 2022, alleging the company monopolized the professional social networking market and overcharged Premium subscribers. The operative complaint, as the discovery order summarizes it, alleges LinkedIn offered potential rivals access to its private user data through application programming interfaces unavailable to others, on the condition that they not compete with LinkedIn, and tied its user data to parent company Microsoft’s Azure cloud product. U.S. District Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. dismissed an earlier version of the complaint with leave to amend in 2023, then allowed the amended complaint to proceed in March 2024. A proposed class settlement failed to win preliminary approval in 2025, Reuters reported, returning the parties to litigation and to the custodial document discovery that produced this dispute in case number 22-cv-00237. Court records opened the matter as Crowder v. LinkedIn Corporation; the discovery order and the commentary around it carry Schulte’s name. The order itself resolved three discovery letter briefs at once, and the two that drew no commentary, a denied request to add an in-house attorney as a custodian and a denied demand for text message production, are a reminder that the aiR fight was one dispute among several.

research.titleEn: LegalPincite: Multi-level Legal Information Retrieval Dataset
research.titleZh: LegalPincite：多层级法律信息检索数据集
research.abstractEn: A common task in legal Information Retrieval (IR) is to find relevant legal sources from case-law collections. While legal practice often requires pinpoint citations (pincites) to specific case paragraphs, most existing public legal IR datasets lack paragraph-level citation annotations. Yet, publicly available datasets with such information contain data leakage in the query text and exclude paragraphs that are neither citing nor cited from the corpora, creating an unrealistic and oversimplified retrieval setting, potentially leading to inflated performance. To address these limitations, we contribute a large-scale legal IR dataset constructed from Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) judgments. The dataset contains: (i) masked case/paragraph queries, with removed citation information; (ii) a corpus that includes all paragraphs; and (iii) case- and paragraph-level ground-truth citations, with partial human expert validation. Our dataset supports both the development and rigorous evaluation of legal IR methods, at multiple query-document levels (case-to-case, paragraph-to-case, and paragraph-to-paragraph retrieval). Link to dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite
research.abstractZh: 法律信息检索（IR）中的一个常见任务是从判例法集合中查找相关的法律来源。虽然法律实践通常需要针对特定案件段落的精确引用（pincites），但大多数现有的公开法律IR数据集缺乏段落级别的引用标注。然而，具有此类信息的公开数据集在查询文本中存在数据泄漏，并且从语料库中排除了既未引用也未引用的段落，从而造成不现实且过度简化的检索环境，可能导致性能虚高。为解决这些局限性，我们构建了一个基于欧盟法院（CJEU）判决的大规模法律IR数据集。该数据集包含：（i）掩码的案件/段落查询，移除了引用信息；（ii）包含所有段落的语料库；以及（iii）案件级和段落级的地面真值引用，并经过部分人类专家验证。我们的数据集支持法律IR方法在多个查询-文档层级（案件到案件、段落到案件、段落到段落检索）上的开发和严格评估。数据集链接：https://huggingface.co/datasets/theresiavr/legalpincite

news.titleEn: As AI Legal Research Tools Race to Give Answers, This New Product Gives Only Cases — And That’s the Point
news.titleZh: 当AI法律研究工具竞相给出答案时，这款新产品只提供案例——而这正是其用意
news.summaryZh: 诉讼技术公司Align发布Align Research，接收自然语言研究问题，运行数小时后返回相关法院判决并高亮关键段落，不提供备忘录、摘要或答案，公司称其“检索而非生成”。设计既为应对生成式AI的幻觉问题，也为回归诉讼律师最常需要的任务：不是“回答问题”，而是“给我案例”。多数AI法律研究产品采用相反模式，提问后返回经过研究和验证的答案。他在LinkedIn列出理念，包括“不要委托你应该学习的内容”和“AI应该展示而非告知”。该产品是代理式流水线：模型分别分析问题、决定搜索、阅读分类案例、判断相关性并决定高亮段落，完成后邮件通知用户。案例以活页夹格式显示，高亮可点击，可下载PDF。产品仅返回实际判决并高亮相关文本，最坏是遗漏或高亮不准，但不会捏造引证。目前无法对话式跟进，需运行新任务或下载到其他AI工具分析。覆盖美国联邦和州判例法，来自CourtListener数据库，Align正构建自有数据库并计划回馈。定价无订阅，免费层每月三次且不过期，之后每任务100美元。Align自筹资金，每次搜索消耗真实AI代币成本，认为按任务定价是行业必然趋势，当前无限订阅反映供应商补贴代币以建立用户基础，律所会将费用转嫁客户。他并非针对Westlaw或Lexis，但认为该工具可在寻找初始案例集方面节省大量时间和律师工时。
news.bodyHtml:
At a time when virtually every major AI legal research product is moving toward delivering a single, synthesized answer to your research question, a new product launching today is based on the premise that many litigators want something that sounds almost old school – just the cases.

Align Research, released to general availability this morning by the litigation technology company Align, takes a research question in plain language, goes off for a few hours, and comes back with a set of relevant court opinions, with the key passages highlighted, and nothing else.

There is no memo, no summary, no answer. As the company’s press release puts it, the product “retrieves rather than generates.”

Align founder and CEO Sam Davidoff, a former litigation partner at Williams & Connolly, said the product’s design is in part an answer to the hallucination problem that has plagued the use of generative AI in law, and in part a return to what he believes is the actual task litigators most often want done.

“It’s not telling you anything, it’s just showing you,” Davidoff told me in an interview about the launch on my LawNext PR podcast. “If all the AI is doing is essentially pointing you to pre-existing things, as opposed to writing some narrative for you, it actually can’t hallucinate. It could miss something, it could highlight something that you don’t agree with, but it can’t make something up.”

‘Get Me the Cases’

Davidoff said he had long resisted entering the legal research market, which he considered well saturated. What changed his mind was a gap he perceived in the current crop of AI research tools, rooted in his own years of practice.

The research task he most often performed as an associate, and most often assigned as a partner, was not, “Answer this question,” he said, but, “Get me the cases. Find me every district court that has ever ruled this way on a motion to dismiss.”

Most AI legal research products these days are built around the opposite model, where you ask a question and get back a researched and validated answer. “That’s a little different than what, at least a lot of times, litigators want,” Davidoff said.

When I observed that this sounds, in a way, old school – closer to how we used to do research – he readily agreed. “There’s no secret where I get my ideas from. I was practicing law and this is how we used to do it, and there’s a little part of me that says, ‘Hey, some of our old tricks still kind of work.’”

In a LinkedIn post ahead of today’s launch, Davidoff listed some of the ideas that went into the product relating to the proper division of labor between lawyers and AI. Among them are, “Don’t delegate what you should learn,” and, “AI should show, not tell.”

Give the AI the uninteresting work of churning through thousands of cases, he said, and keep the interesting work of reading and analyzing the few dozen that matter for the lawyer to do.

“If you give to AI the job of actually reading the cases and distilling the final analysis, it means you’re not doing it,” he told me. “That’s both sometimes the fun of being a lawyer, but also sometimes the strategic advantage of being a lawyer – that I’ve read the cases and I see a new angle for how we could argue this in front of this judge.”

How It Works

As Davidoff describes it, Align Research is an agentic pipeline. One model analyzes the question and breaks out the legal research issues. Another decides what searches to run. Others read the retrieved cases, classify them, make relevance decisions, and determine whether more searching is needed. A final stage decides which passages to highlight.

That is why a research job in Align can run for a few hours before returning a result. Rather than work like a chatbot, Davidoff said, the product works more like a researcher on your staff. You submit a question, go do other work, and the system emails you when the results are ready.

The cases then appear on the website in a binder-like format, with highlights you can click through, and can be downloaded as PDFs.

While it is still possible that the product “may, under the hood, hallucinate,” Davidoff said, it does not matter, because the product returns only actual court opinions with relevant text highlighted. The worst that can happen, he said, is a missed case or an off-target highlight, but not a fabricated citation.

For now, a user has no ability to follow-up in a conversational way with a research result. If the results raise a new question, you run another job. Alternatively, Davidoff suggested, you can download the cases and load them into some other AI tool for further interrogation.

Coverage spans U.S. federal and state case law, drawn from the Free Law Project’s CourtListener database. Align is building out additional case law databases of its own, but Davidoff said the company intends to contribute those cases back to the CourtListener opinion database, reflecting his view that the underlying case law corpus should not be the differentiator among legal tech companies.

Pricing Based on Use

Another way Align Research departs from the market norm is pricing. There is no subscription. A free tier provides three research jobs per month, with no expiration. Beyond that, the company charges a flat $100 per job.

Part of the rationale for that is practical. Align is bootstrapped and self-funded, Davidoff said, and every search costs the company real money in AI tokens.

But he also believes that per-job pricing is an inevitability for the industry at large, arguing that the all-you-can-eat subscription pricing now common in legal AI reflects vendors subsidizing token costs to build user bases.

“I don’t think it can last,” he said. “These token costs are real. The amount of money that every legal tech AI provider has to pay to Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini – that’s real money and it’s per token.”

He sees law firms passing this fee through to their clients. The math should be easy to explain to them, he said. A research task that once consumed a couple of associate hours at a couple hundred dollars or more per hour becomes a $100 flat fee.

In developing this product, Davidoff told me, he is not gunning for Westlaw or Lexis: “They have amazing databases that they’ve built up. But I think that our tool can save you a lot of time and attorney hours in terms of finding those initial sets of cases.”

But Align Research is clearly staking out an approach at odds with where most of the market is heading.

Davidoff invites the argument. Whether users like the product or not, he said, he wants to hear from them: “No one’s going to be annoying me by sending me their suggestions.”

[Disclosure: The LawNext PR interview cited in this article is a paid product for which Align paid LawNext an advertising fee.]

news.titleEn: The Difference Between Using AI and Becoming an AI-Native Law Firm
news.titleZh: 使用AI与成为AI原生律所之间的区别
news.summaryZh:
多数律所将AI采用视为一次采购，但成为AI原生律所并非单一事件，而是一段漫长旅程，多数律所仅处于起点。法律行业正同时朝两个方向发展：律师个人持续使用ChatGPT、Claude等AI工具，律所则在平台层面重建标准化数据基础。目前几乎所有人只关注其中一个维度，同时聚焦两者的律所将获得真正的AI优势。随着个人AI使用普及与平台围绕AI重建，日常法律工作开始转变，常规打字和研究由工具处理，律师得以将更多时间用于咨询客户、行使判断和建立关系。

AI需要上下文才能有用，上下文要求访问律所全部数据。外挂式工具通常连接单一系统，只做好一件窄事；原生AI层位于完整实践管理系统之上，无论用户在哪工作，AI都能看到事项、客户历史和律所政策。原生AI在规模应用下可将不可计费时间推向零，并提升每个计费小时的价值，使律所更盈利、客户法律服务更便宜。原生还关乎安全：通过AI原生层使用ChatGPT等工具，可继承相同的治理和护栏，避免野蛮生长。中型律所通常无法像大所那样大量投资工具和人才，雇佣一人领导AI战略很脆弱，应通过平台合作伙伴而非内部招聘。投资AI原生工具的中型律所可为新律师提供更好日常工作、更少琐碎工作、现代工具和生活质量差异，从而吸引人才。律所需先整合数据、上云并结构化，但不要一次解决所有问题，先选一个对工作者影响最大的问题解决，早期胜利建立势头。这一切需要领导层自上而下真正推动。
news.bodyHtml:
Most firms talk about AI adoption like it’s a purchase. Buy the tool, turn it on, done. I push back on that idea every chance I get. Becoming an AI-native law firm isn’t a single event. It’s a longer journey, and most firms are only at the start of it. 

Actionstep’s Chief Product Officer, Triona Buckley covered the shift from the practice of law to the business of law in an earlier piece, “AI for Law Firms: Myths and Realities Explained.” Something law firms need to keep in mind over the next few years, is why the difference between bolted on AI and native AI matters so much, and why mid-market firms may be better positioned for this shift than people assume. 

Becoming AI native is a journey, not a purchase 

The legal industry heading toward two things happening at once. On one side, lawyers will keep using AI tools personally, the same way people across every industry now lean on tools like ChatGPT and Claude for their own work. On the other side, firms will be retooling at the platform level, building the standardized data foundation that AI needs to be useful. 

Right now, almost everyone is focused on only one of those two dimensions, either the personal productivity side or the platform side, rarely both. The firms that focus on both will have the real AI advantage. As individual AI use becomes more common in law firms, and firms rebuild their platforms around AI at the same time, those two threads start to come together, and the day-to-day work of a lawyer begins to shift. Routine typing and research get handled by the tools, which frees lawyers to spend more of their time advising clients, exercising judgment, and building relationships. That shift undercuts the doom and gloom predictions about law firms disappearing. Five years from now, those predictions will look less like a real outcome and more like a trivia question nobody thought to ask twice. 

The difference between bolted on AI and native AI 

One of the points we keep coming back to is that AI needs context to be useful, and context requires access to the firm’s full data, not just one part of it. A bolted-on tool typically connects to a single system and does one narrow thing well. A native AI layer sits on top of the complete practice management system, so AI has visibility into a matter, a client’s history, and firm policy no matter where someone is working. 

That difference has a direct financial effect. When AI operates with complete context, it can recommend or even execute work based on what’s worked for the firm in the past, or how the firm set up work to get done, then explain its reasoning for review. My honest expectation is that, done at scale, native AI pushes the unbillable hour toward zero and increases the value of each billable hour. Firms get more done per hour of work. If that plays out the way I think it will, it’s a rare case where both sides win: firms get more profitable, and legal services get less expensive for clients. 

Native also matters for a reason that has nothing to do with productivity: safety. One of the advantages of a native AI layer is that you can use AI against it from outside the system too. Someone can go use a tool like ChatGPT, and if it’s working through an AI-native layer, it inherits the same governance and guardrails Triona talked about, so your people can use these tools safely rather than operating in the wild west. That’s a big part of why AI needs to be built in at the base level of the platform, not added on the side. A bolt-on might let you do one thing well, but it also leaves you exposed everywhere it doesn’t reach, and stuck in your old ways everywhere else. 

Why mid-market firms need a partner, not a hire 

Large firms can often brute force their way into AI adoption by investing heavily in tools and specialized talent. Mid-market firms usually can’t. Hiring one person to lead an AI strategy is fragile. If that person leaves, the firm is back to square one. 

The path forward for mid-market firms is to run through platform partners rather than internal hires. A modern, AI-capable platform can carry more of that weight than a solo internal expert ever could, and a growing network of consultants is already emerging to help mid-market firms put these tools to work.This shouldn’t be thought of as a disadvantage. It’s simply a different, and often easier, path than the one larger law firms are on. 

There’s also an upside here that doesn’t get enough attention and that’s talent. A mid-market firm that invests in AI-native tools now and can offer new associates a genuinely better day-to-day with less of the mundane work, access to modern tools, and a real quality-of-life difference. It is going to look progressive to the next generation of graduates. That gives mid-market firms a real shot at attracting talent away from big firms, where the tooling and the competition for attention can be a lot less favorable. 

Start with one problem, not everything at once 

Firms need their data consolidated, cloud-based, and structured well enough for AI to come in and use it properly, and no matter which AI tool firms adopt, a patchwork of disconnected, on-premises tools will hold them back from becoming AI-native. 

So first, get your data house in order first because there’s no way around it. 

But don’t try to fix all of it at once. Pick one problem that would make the biggest difference to the people doing the work and solve that first. The early win builds momentum, and the next opportunity tends to become obvious. 

None of this happens without leadership driving it from the top, with real commitment, not as a side project for whoever happens to be curious. 

That same thinking shapes how we build AI into the Actionstep platform. We’re not interested in sprinkling in isolated features. We’re building one layer that connects the work a firm has already done to the work still ahead of it, all within Actionstep so firms don’t have to choose between moving fast and moving carefully. 

See what’s possible when AI works with your firm’s expert judgment, not in place of it. Talk to our team to learn how Actionstep can help you prepare for the future of law. 

The post The Difference Between Using AI and Becoming an AI-Native Law Firm  appeared first on Actionstep.

news.titleEn: Client Alert- Illinois Raises the Bar for Frontier AI Governance
news.titleZh: 客户警示——伊利诺伊州提高前沿人工智能治理门槛
news.summaryZh: 2026年7月6日，州长JB·普利兹克签署参议院第315号法案《人工智能安全措施法案》，伊利诺伊州成为继加州和纽约州之后美国第三个对最强大人工智能系统开发者施加全面安全与透明度要求的州。义务仅适用于少数超大型人工智能开发者，而非普通商业用户，但下游影响显著：新的披露文件、强制审计、事件报告时限和举报人保护将重塑供应商合同、采购尽职调查和企业事件响应规划。伊利诺伊州与加州（SB 53，2025年9月签署）和纽约州（RAISE法案，2025年12月签署）共同构建州级前沿人工智能监管框架，并在一个关键方面走得更远：它是首个要求对受涵盖开发者的安全实践进行年度独立第三方审计的州。该法案在州议会获得两党支持，并得到人工智能安全倡导者和行业利益相关者的支持。这些前沿人工智能法律不同于针对算法决策的更广泛的州级立法浪潮。科罗拉多州人工智能法案（SB 24-205）于2024年5月签署，是美国首部全面人工智能治理法，但采取不同路径：不是基于计算阈值监管最大模型开发者，而是对用于影响消费者的重大决策（就业、住房、信贷、保险和教育）的“高风险人工智能系统”开发者和部署者施加义务。商业领袖应同时关注前沿人工智能治理（伊利诺伊州、加州、纽约州）以及算法公平与透明度（科罗拉多州，预计更多州将跟进）两条监管轨道。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! On July 6, 2026, Governor JB Pritzker signed Senate Bill 315, the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (the "Act"), into law. Illinois is now the third U.S. state, after California and New York, to impose comprehensive safety and transparency requirements on developers of the most powerful AI systems. The Act's obligations fall on a narrow set of very large AI developers, not ordinary business users. But the downstream effects will be significant: new disclosure documents, mandatory audits, incident-reporting timelines, and whistleblower protections will reshape vendor contracts, procurement due diligence, and enterprise incident-response planning. Illinois joins California (SB 53, signed September 2025) and New York (the RAISE Act, signed December 2025) [1] in building a state-level regulatory framework for frontier AI. Illinois goes further than its peers in one critical respect: it is the first state to require annual independent third-party audits of covered developers' safety practices. The Act passed the General Assembly with bipartisan support and drew backing from both AI safety advocates and industry stakeholders. These frontier AI laws are distinct from the broader wave of state AI legislation targeting algorithmic decision-making. Colorado's AI Act (SB 24-205), signed in May 2024, was the first comprehensive AI governance law in the U.S., but it takes a different approach. Rather than regulating the largest model developers based on compute thresholds, Colorado imposes obligations on developers and deployers of "high-risk AI systems" used in consequential decisions affecting consumers (employment, housing, credit, insurance, and education). Business leaders should track both regulatory tracks: frontier AI governance (Illinois, California, New York) and algorithmic fairness and transparency (Colorado and likely more states to follow).[2] The Act targets a narrow class of AI companies: Bottom line: Today, this likely covers only a handful of the largest foundation-model developers. But as computing costs decline and models scale, the thresholds may capture additional players. Enforcement: The Illinois Attorney General has exclusive civil enforcement authority; there is no private right of action. Penalties reach up to $1 million for initial violations and $3 million for subsequent violations. Even if your organization is not a frontier developer, the Act will reshape AI procurement and governance:

news.titleEn: The Government’s Attempted Anthropic Ban- What Government Contractors Should Be Doing Now
news.titleZh: 政府试图禁用Anthropic：政府承包商现在应采取的应对措施
news.summaryZh:
联邦政府试图禁止使用Anthropic的人工智能技术，给依赖AI支持合同履行和内部运营的政府承包商带来重大不确定性。尽管联邦法院已暂时阻止该指令关键部分执行，但诉讼表明，当政府针对特定技术供应商时，合规环境可能迅速变化。使用Anthropic的Claude模型或其嵌入的软件与云服务的承包商，不应等待最终裁决，而应立即查明Anthropic技术的使用位置，评估其是否支持联邦合同履行，并制定应对策略。

承包商应首先全面清点Anthropic技术的使用情况，包括直接订阅以及嵌入Claude的第三方软件、云服务和企业平台，随后确定这些使用是否与联邦合同履行相关，例如用于开发交付物、分析政府数据、准备提案、支持软件开发或处理合同相关信息，并评估是否涉及受控非机密信息、政府专有信息、来源选择信息等敏感数据。承包商还应与IT人员和关键供应商合作，确认现有软件环境中是否嵌入Anthropic技术，以及能否禁用Claude或切换至其他支持的AI模型。尽管诉讼仍在进行，承包商不应假设初步禁令已永久解决问题，而应制定书面应急计划，明确替代方案及工作流程切换速度。同时，应密切关注招标、合同修改、机构备忘录、类别偏离和客户通信中关于Anthropic或商用AI技术限制的引用，并审查新招标是否纳入AI特定陈述、认证、披露要求或合同条款。此外，应评估内部政策是否充分涵盖Anthropic产品和服务的使用，建立明确程序规范审批、信息输入、AI生成工作成果审查及合同履行期间政府要求变。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The federal government’s attempt to prohibit the use of Anthropic’s artificial intelligence technology has created significant uncertainty for government contractors that rely on AI to support contract performance and internal business operations. Although a federal court has temporarily blocked enforcement of key portions of the government’s directive, the litigation underscores how quickly the compliance landscape can shift when the government targets a specific technology provider. Contractors that use Anthropic’s Claude models — or software and cloud services that incorporate them — should not wait for a final court decision before evaluating how the government’s actions could affect their operations. Instead, now is the time to identify where Anthropic technology is being used, assess whether it supports federal contract performance, and develop a strategy for responding if restrictions are ultimately reinstated or modified. While the legal battle has understandably focused on whether the government has the authority to restrict Anthropic’s technology, contractors should focus on a different question: How would their business be affected if the government’s restrictions ultimately take effect? Many government contractors have integrated Anthropic’s Claude models into their day-to-day operations. Some use Claude to assist with software development, proposal drafting, technical documentation, data analysis, research, or administrative functions. Others may not even realize they are relying on Anthropic because Claude’s capabilities are embedded in third-party software, cloud services, or enterprise platforms. Whether the government’s attempted ban ultimately survives judicial review or not, the litigation demonstrates that agencies are willing to take extraordinary procurement actions affecting commercial AI providers. Contractors should use this opportunity to better understand their reliance on Anthropic and prepare for the possibility that future restrictions could require swift operational changes. The first priority should be understanding whether, and to what extent, Anthropic technology is being used throughout the organization. For many companies, AI adoption has occurred organically, with different business units independently adopting AI-powered tools. Employees may access Claude directly through Anthropic’s platform, while others may use applications that rely on Claude behind the scenes. Contractors should identify not only direct subscriptions but also enterprise software and cloud-based services that incorporate Anthropic models. Without a clear inventory, responding to future government requirements could become both time-consuming and disruptive. After identifying where Anthropic products are being used, contractors should determine whether those uses are connected to federal contract performance. For example, organizations should evaluate whether Claude is being used to develop deliverables, analyze government data, prepare proposals, support software development, or process information associated with federal contracts. Contractors should also assess whether Anthropic products are used in connection with Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), proprietary government information, source selection information, or other sensitive data that may be subject to contractual or regulatory requirements. Understanding the role Anthropic plays in contract performance will help contractors evaluate both operational and contractual risks if restrictions are ultimately implemented. Not every contractor uses Anthropic products directly. Many commercial software products and cloud platforms incorporate Claude as one of several available large language models. Contractors should therefore work with information technology personnel and key vendors to determine whether Anthropic technology is embedded within existing software environments. Organizations should also understand whether those platforms allow users to disable Claude functionality or transition to another supported AI model if necessary. Identifying these options now can help minimize disruption if government requirements change. Although the litigation remains pending, contractors should avoid assuming that the preliminary injunction resolves the issue permanently. Organizations that depend heavily on Anthropic technology should consider how critical business functions would continue if future government guidance prohibited or restricted its use. This does not necessarily require abandoning Anthropic today, but it does mean understanding what alternatives are available and how quickly workflows could be transitioned if necessary. Having a documented contingency plan will allow contractors to respond far more efficiently than attempting to identify replacement technologies after new requirements take effect. The Anthropic litigation continues to evolve, and agencies may issue additional guidance while the case proceeds. Contractors should closely monitor solicitations, contract modifications, agency memoranda, class deviations, and customer communications for any references to Anthropic or restrictions affecting the use of commercial AI technologies. Companies should also review new solicitations carefully to determine whether agencies begin incorporating AI-specific representations, certifications, disclosure requirements, or contract clauses. Remaining informed will enable contractors to identify compliance obligations before they become performance issues. The government’s attempted ban also provides an opportunity for contractors to evaluate whether existing internal policies adequately address the use of Anthropic’s products and services. Organizations should establish clear procedures governing who may approve the use of Claude for government contract work, what types of information may be entered into Anthropic’s systems, how AI-generated work product is reviewed, and how the organization will respond if government requirements change during contract performance. Even if contractors ultimately continue using Anthropic, establishing clear governance now will reduce compliance risks and improve consistency across the organization.

research.titleEn: Does the Competitive Component of Adversarial Self-Play Improve Legal Reasoning? A Controlled Negative Result
research.titleZh: 对抗性自我对弈的竞争成分能否提高法律推理能力？一项受控的阴性结果
research.abstractEn: Adversarial self-play is an appealing recipe for legal reasoning: have a student model draft an argument, have an adversary attack it, and reward the student when its argument survives the attack. We designed exactly such a training signal -- a verifiable "survival" reward in which both the student's cited authorities and the adversary's counter-authorities are checked by a citation verifier, so that survival is decided on verified grounds rather than rhetoric, and fabricated citations are automatically neutralized. We then asked a narrow but important question: does the competitive component itself -- the adversary and the survival reward -- add anything on top of an otherwise identical non-competitive training run? Across four independent tests -- a bootstrap comparison, a two-seed replication, a paired per-case adversarial-robustness comparison, and a blinded head-to-head judgment of generated arguments, plus a follow-up pilot with a deliberately strengthened self-play adversary -- the competitive component produced no reliable benefit. The blinded judgment gave a 49% win rate (binomial p approx. 1.000); the strengthened-adversary pilot gave a 50% win rate (32:32, p approx. 1.000). An early apparent +29% advantage reversed and proved to be a small-sample artifact. We report this as an honest negative result. The value of the paper is reproducibility and the sharing of concrete pitfalls: an initially promising metric that inverted on more data, and an adversarial-robustness metric that silently collapsed to plain recall once the adversary stopped citing the same authorities as the gold answer. This null is consistent with, and reconfirms in the legal domain, the conclusion of the companion coding-domain study (Kim, 2026, arXiv:2607.08255) that the value of multi-teacher curricula arises from constructing a verifiable environment rather than from competition itself.
research.abstractZh: 对抗性自我对弈是法律推理的一种有吸引力的方法：让学生模型起草论点，让对手攻击它，当学生的论点在攻击中幸存时给予奖励。我们设计了这样一个训练信号——一个可验证的“生存”奖励，其中学生引用的权威和对手的反权威都由引文验证器检查，因此生存是基于验证的事实而非修辞，捏造的引文会被自动中和。然后我们提出了一个狭窄但重要的问题：竞争成分本身——对手和生存奖励——是否在原本相同的非竞争性训练运行之上增加了任何价值？在四项独立测试中——自举比较、双种子复制、逐案例的成对对抗鲁棒性比较，以及生成论点的盲法头对头判断，外加一项故意加强自我对弈对手的后续试点——竞争成分没有产生可靠的收益。盲法判断的胜率为49%（二项式p约1.000）；加强对手的试点胜率为50%（32:32，p约1.000）。早期表面上的+29%优势逆转了，并被证明是小样本伪影。我们将其报告为诚实的阴性结果。本文的价值在于可重复性和具体陷阱的分享：一个最初有希望的指标在更多数据上反转，以及一个对抗鲁棒性指标在对手停止引用与黄金答案相同的权威后悄然退化为纯召回率。这一零结果与配套的编码领域研究（Kim, 2026, arXiv:2607.08255）的结论一致，并在法律领域再次确认：多教师课程的价值源于构建可验证的环境，而非竞争本身。

research.titleEn: CrossLex: A Source-Grounded Benchmark for Cross-Jurisdictional Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models
research.titleZh: CrossLex：面向大语言模型跨法域法律推理的源基基准
research.abstractEn: Legal reasoning is inherently jurisdiction-dependent: the same facts can call for different legal rules and yield different conclusions across legal systems. Yet existing benchmarks rarely evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize such jurisdiction-specific variation, especially when identical fact patterns lead to divergent legal outcomes.We introduce CrossLex, a same-fact, legal-source-grounded benchmark for evaluating cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning in LLMs across three jurisdictions: China, California, and Germany. Built from authoritative legal sources, CrossLex aligns 55 legal issues spanning contract, consumer, criminal, family, and labor law, and constructs jurisdiction-aligned questions paired with answers and supporting citations. In total, CrossLex contains 6,149 instances organized into 385 fact groups, with all legal issues, answers, and cited authorities reviewed by legal professionals.To disentangle basic legal knowledge from cross-jurisdictional reasoning, CrossLex defines three complementary tasks: single-jurisdiction reasoning (T1), joint cross-jurisdictional comparison (T2), and fine-grained cross-jurisdictional evaluation (T3). We further propose Grounded Joint, a metric that jointly assesses answer correctness and legal-source grounding, and provide a unified evaluation for streamlined benchmarking. Extensive experiments on representative LLMs show that, although current models can often answer legal questions correctly, they struggle to provide accurate cross-jurisdictional legal citations.We hope that CrossLex will facilitate future research on source-grounded cross-jurisdictional legal reasoning.
research.abstractZh: 法律推理本质上依赖于法域：相同的事实可能在不同法律体系中引发不同的法律规则并产生不同的结论。然而，现有基准很少评估大语言模型（LLM）是否能够识别这种特定于法域的差异，尤其是在相同事实模式导致不同法律结果的情况下。我们引入了CrossLex，一个基于相同事实、以法律来源为依据的基准，用于评估LLM在中国、加利福尼亚和德国三个法域的跨法域法律推理能力。CrossLex基于权威法律来源构建，涵盖了合同、消费者、刑事、家庭和劳动法领域的55个法律问题，并构建了与法域对齐的问题，配有答案和支持性引文。总计，CrossLex包含6,149个实例，组织成385个事实组，所有法律问题、答案和引用的权威来源均由法律专业人士审查。为了区分基本法律知识与跨法域推理，CrossLex定义了三个互补任务：单法域推理（T1）、联合跨法域比较（T2）和细粒度跨法域评估（T3）。我们进一步提出了Grounded Joint，一种联合评估答案正确性和法律来源依据的指标，并提供了统一评估以简化基准测试。对代表性LLM的大量实验表明，尽管当前模型通常能正确回答法律问题，但它们在提供准确的跨法域法律引文方面存在困难。我们希望CrossLex能够促进未来关于基于来源的跨法域法律推理的研究。

research.titleEn: Exploring Usability and Legal Practice: Insights from German Judicial Users of Digital Forensics
research.titleZh: 探索可用性与法律实践：来自德国司法数字取证用户的见解
research.abstractEn: Digital forensics has become an integral part of modern criminal proceedings, yet its effective integration remains challenging because of increasing data volumes, evolving technologies, and complex interactions between technical and legal stakeholders. Although prior work has focused primarily on digital forensic tools and methods, its broader procedural and organizational context has received limited attention. Building on emerging perspectives inspired by usability research and human-centered security, we conceptualize digital forensics as part of a socio-technical system within criminal proceedings. We consequently investigate this perspective through a survey of 101 practitioners from the judiciary of the German federal state of North Rhine-Westphalia, including public prosecutors, judges, and digital forensic experts. The results indicate a strong demand for improved integration of digital forensics into workflows, enhanced cross-domain communication, and a closer alignment of stakeholder expectations. They also uncover great potential for the improvement of digital forensics usability, e.g., through stronger interdisciplinary cooperation, easier and faster access to evidential data and results, or improvement of stakeholder training and education.
research.abstractZh: 数字取证已成为现代刑事诉讼中不可或缺的一部分，然而，由于数据量的不断增加、技术的不断演进以及技术和法律利益相关者之间复杂的互动，其有效整合仍然具有挑战性。尽管先前的工作主要关注数字取证工具和方法，但其更广泛的程序性和组织性背景受到的关注有限。基于可用性研究和以人为本的安全所启发的新兴视角，我们将数字取证概念化为刑事诉讼中社会技术系统的一部分。因此，我们通过对德国北莱茵-威斯特法伦州司法机构的101名从业者（包括检察官、法官和数字取证专家）进行调查来研究这一视角。结果表明，对于将数字取证更好地整合到工作流程中、增强跨领域沟通以及更紧密地协调利益相关者期望的需求强烈。他们还揭示了改进数字取证可用性的巨大潜力，例如通过加强跨学科合作、更轻松快速地访问证据数据和结果，或改进利益相关者的培训和教育。

news.titleEn: Startup Corner: Caddi targets law firm operations with an ‘agent that build agents’
news.titleZh: 创业公司角：Caddi以“构建代理的代理”瞄准律所运营
news.summaryZh: Caddi为专业服务公司构建后台运营代理，涵盖客户接待、冲突检查、文件归档、账单准备和CRM更新。其核心特点是Caddi本身是一个构建这些代理的代理：用户只需通过屏幕共享展示工作流程，Caddi即可构建出执行任务的代理，并随时间持续改进，无需IT项目。Caddi Agent是一个自我改进的代理，能将演示的工作流程转化为可用的运营代理，并在运行中优化，且跨律所现有工具工作。公司CEO兼联合创始人为Alejandro Castellano，CTO兼联合创始人为Aditya Sastry。目标客户为约50人及以上的专业服务公司，核心聚焦律所和RIA，同时服务银行、信用合作社、抵押贷款公司和保险公司等受监管领域，重点覆盖中小型公司。一家AmLaw 50律所目前通过Caddi每天自动化数百次冲突检查；一家Top-10 RIA在收购其他公司时无需考虑运营人员编制，因为工作可扩展而团队无需扩展。公司获得Ubiquity的500万美元种子轮融资。自成立以来，公司从面向所有专业服务转向聚焦律所和RIA。市场挑战在于突破噪音，许多律所被多方推销AI和自动化，但过去承诺的自动化效益往往需要大量IT投入才能实现，因此需快速具体地展示代理能自行构建自动化。Caddi起源于AI2 Incubator，该孵化器隶属于Paul Allen创立的Allen Institute for AI。
news.bodyHtml:
An AmLaw 50 firm is now automating hundreds of conflict checks a day through Caddi. We find out more about the ‘agent that builds agents’ to help you run the back office, including client intake and conflicts checks.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Caddi builds agents that run the back-office work at professional services firms, like client intake, conflict checks, filing documents, prepping bills, and updating the CRM. The twist is that Caddi is an agent that builds those agents for you. Automating this stuff used to mean a big IT project. Now you just chat with Caddi and show it your workflow over a screenshare, the way you’d onboard a new hire, and it builds the agent that does the job. It also keeps getting better over time.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

Caddi Agent is a self-improving agent that builds back-office operations agents for professional services. Instead of architecting an automation yourself, wrestling a drag-and-drop builder, vibe-coding, standing up backend servers, and wiring integrations, you show Caddi your work on a screenshare and it builds the agent for you. The interesting part is the “build without IT” mechanism: an agent that turns a demonstrated workflow into working operations agents, then improves them as it runs, all across the tools your firm already uses.

When were you founded?

2024

Advertisement
By who?

Alejandro Castellano

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Alejandro Castellano, CEO & co-founder

Aditya Sastry, CTO & co-founder

Who are your target clients?

Professional services firms of roughly 50 employees and up, with our core focus on law firms and RIAs (wealth and finance). We also serve adjacent regulated segments like banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, and insurance carriers. A big part of who we serve is the small and mid-sized firm: Big Law, big RIAs, and big insurance can afford the IT lift to roll out AI teams, which leaves smaller firms at risk of getting swallowed. Caddi removes that lift so those firms can stand up a digital workforce and compete.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Outbound sales, inbound seo, events, partnerships.

Key achievements?

An AmLaw 50 firm is now automating hundreds of conflict checks a day through Caddi. And a Top-10 RIA has been able to acquire other firms without having to think about operational headcount, because the work scales without the team having to.

Have you received investment?

Yes, a $5M seed round from Ubiquity.

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

Yes. We started out aimed at all professional services and have since narrowed our focus to law firms and RIAs.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Cutting through the noise. Every firm is being pitched “AI” and “automation” from a dozen directions right now, and law firms in particular have been promised automation benefits for years that never quite materialized without heavy IT lift. So a big part of the challenge is showing, quickly and concretely, that an agent can now build the automation for you rather than you building it.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company? 

Caddi got its start inside the AI2 Incubator, part of the Allen Institute for AI that Paul Allen founded, so the company’s roots run straight back to a Microsoft co-founder’s bet on AI research.

news.titleEn: Foot Anstey selects iManage Cloud supported by Tiger Eye
news.titleZh: Foot Anstey选择iManage Cloud，由Tiger Eye提供支持
news.summaryZh:
英国国家律师事务所Foot Anstey宣布选择iManage Cloud知识工作平台，该平台将由iManage Cloud合作伙伴Tiger Eye负责实施、支持和构建。Tiger Eye将于今年晚些时候将该律所4500万份文档、电子邮件和知识从本地iManage环境迁移至iManage Cloud。迁移完成后，Tiger Eye还将为iManage提供持续的主动平台支持，并启用和优化一系列附加组件。作为项目的一部分，Foot Anstey还将采用Tiger Eye Administrate——Tiger Eye针对iManage的模块化数据管理解决方案。

Foot Anstey选择iManage Cloud平台是其全所数字化转型战略的一部分，该战略包括从私有云环境转向软件即服务（SaaS）平台，以获得更高的安全性、敏捷性和成本效益。在评估现有文档管理系统后，iManage Cloud因能降低本地解决方案的管理开销，同时为员工提供市场领先的协作功能而被选中，这些功能包括共同创作、iManage与Microsoft Teams集成以及Ask iManage——内置于DMS中的强大自然语言助手。Tiger Eye凭借其声誉、对iManage的专注以及为AMPA、Gateley和Mills & Reeve等国家组织完成类似大规模iManage Cloud迁移的经验，被Foot Anstey选为iManage Cloud迁移提供商和长期iManage合作伙伴。Foot Anstey是一家总部位于英格兰西南部的英国百强律师事务所，拥有11个办公室网络，700多名员工作为一个国家团队协同工作，为区域、国家和国际客户提供专业法律咨询和服务。该律所的iManage Cloud迁移将于2026年第三季度完成。
news.bodyHtml:
This in today (31 July) – from the press release:

Leading national law firm Foot Anstey has announced its selection of the iManage Cloud knowledge work platform, which will be implemented, supported and built upon by iManage Cloud Partner Tiger Eye.

Advertisement

Tiger Eye will migrate the group’s 45 million documents, emails and knowledge to the iManage Cloud later this year from the firm’s on premises iManage environment. Once in the Cloud, Tiger Eye will also provide ongoing Proactive Platform Support for iManage and enable and optimise a range of add-ons. As part of the project, Foot Anstey will also adopt Tiger Eye Administrate, Tiger Eye’s modular data management solution for iManage.

Foot Anstey’s selection of the iManage Cloud platform is part of a firmwide digital transformation strategy, which includes a move away from private cloud environments towards software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms for greater security, agility and cost-efficiency. After reviewing available document management systems, iManage Cloud was selected to reduce the overheads of an on-premise solution while empowering employees with market-leading collaboration features such as Co-Authoring, the iManage and Microsoft Teams integration and Ask iManage: a powerful natural language assistant built within the DMS.

Advertisement

Tiger Eye was chosen by Foot Anstey as the firm’s iManage Cloud migration provider and ongoing iManage Partner given the vendor’s reputation, dedicated iManage focus and experience with similar large-scale iManage Cloud migrations for national organisations such as AMPA, Gateley and Mills & Reeve.

Foot Anstey is a UK Top 100 law firm headquartered in the South-West of England. The firm has a network of eleven offices, with over 700 staff working together as one national team to provide specialist legal advice and services to regional, national and international clients, including both businesses and individuals. The firm’s iManage Cloud migration will be completed in Q3 2026.

Sara Wilson, Chief Technology and Transformation Officer at Foot Anstey, commented:

“The firm adopted iManage over a decade ago, however the platform wasn’t delivering the strategic enablement required to meet the firm’s growth ambitions. While iManage Cloud will deliver the scalable and secure platform we need with access to new capabilities, we also recognised the need to invest in a responsive partner with deep domain knowledge and expertise in whom we could have a high degree of confidence. Tiger Eye came highly recommended and from our market review we identified that they were the right iManage Partner to not only migrate us to iManage Cloud quickly and securely, but also drive iManage adoption through training, support and best practices.”

Sam Hudson, Chief Growth Officer at Tiger Eye, added:

“With a national footprint, large team and multi-office set-up, Foot Anstey needed a secure, scalable document and email management platform to underpin its work. The iManage Cloud is the perfect fit for the firm’s IT strategy, delivering agility, need-to-know security and best-of-breed features for collaboration and governance. Through our team’s expertise, the platform will be perfectly tailored to support user workflows. It is always rewarding to collaborate with innovative, ambitious firms, and so it has been a pleasure working with Sara and the wider technology team to achieve their transformation objectives with iManage.”

news.titleEn: iManage and VXT launch AI notetaking integration for attorneys
news.titleZh: iManage与VXT推出面向律师的AI笔记集成功能
news.summaryZh: 为律所打造的AI笔记工具VXT宣布与云端文档管理系统iManage集成，将通话和会议对话转化为结构化文件笔记，直接保存至iManage中正确的案件事项下。案件建立在对话之上，但通话、会议和往来沟通中的内容几乎从未进入文件，该集成旨在弥合这一差距，把通话或会议中所说和决定的内容直接放入案件事项中。律师可在VXT中拨打和接听电话，来电时即可查看客户信息，VXT记录通话并在通话和会议中充当AI笔记工具。对iManage而言，这是唯一此类集成，可将法律对话中的重要细节直接保存至正确的案件事项。与VXT现有的实践管理系统（如Actionstep）集成配合使用时，这一功能更加有用。Actionstep和iManage等工具中的AI效果取决于所输入的信息，而目前大量信息根本未到达这些系统，因为通话和会议中讨论的许多内容都存在于文件之外，导致AI仅凭部分信息处理案件。通过将通话和会议笔记纳入记录，该集成为法律AI提供了缺失的那部分故事——所说的内容，而不仅仅是键入的内容。该集成是VXT法律科技解决方案生态系统的最新成员，加入了与Clio、8am MyCase和Smokeball等法律软件近30个现有集成。美国、加拿大、英国、澳大利亚和新西兰的律所依赖VXT跟踪时间、做笔记和管理通话。尚未使用VXT的律师可通过预约演示了解该集成如何增强律所的文档管理。
news.bodyHtml: VXT, the AI notetaker built for law firms, has announced an integration with iManage, one of the most widely used cloud-based document management systems for legal teams. The integration takes conversations from calls and meetings and turns them into structured file notes that can be saved directly to the correct matter in iManage. | Jul 31, 2026
news.bodyText:
VXT , the AI notetaker built for law firms, has announced an integration with iManage , one of the most widely used cloud-based document management systems for legal teams.

The integration takes conversations from calls and meetings and turns them into structured file notes that can be saved directly to the correct matter in iManage.

Luke Campbell, CEO and Co-Founder of VXT, says important parts of a matter happen in conversations that rarely ever make it into the file and sees this integration as a way to change that.

"A matter is really built on conversations," Campbell says.

“On calls, in meetings, in the back-and-forth that never gets written down.

"The problem is that almost none of it reaches the file.

“It's in a recording somewhere, or a set of scribbled notes, or just in someone’s head.

"So the actual thinking behind a matter ends up living apart from the matter itself.

"This integration closes that gap…it takes what was said and decided on a call or in a meeting and puts it straight into the matter in iManage, alongside everything else.”

Attorneys can make and take calls in VXT and see client information the moment a call comes in. VXT records those calls and acts as an AI notetaker across calls and meetings.

For iManage, this is the only integration of its kind that works by saving the important details from legal conversations directly to the correct matter.

This becomes even more useful when paired with VXT's existing integrations with a firm's practice management system, like Actionstep .

With the AI features being rolled out across many platforms, Campbell says getting what happens on calls and in meetings into a firm’s document and practice management systems matters now more than ever.

"The AI in tools like Actionstep and iManage are only as good as the information they’re fed," Campbell says.

"And right now, a huge amount never reaches it at all, because so much of what's discussed on calls and in meetings sits outside the file.

"So the AI is working on a matter with only part of the picture.

"By bringing calls and meeting notes into that record, the integration gives your legal AI the side of the story it's been missing — what was spoken, not just what was typed.”

The VXT–iManage integration is the latest addition to VXT’s growing ecosystem of legal tech solutions, joining almost 30 existing integrations with legal software like Clio , 8am MyCase and Smokeball .

Law firms across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and New Zealand rely on VXT to track time, take notes, and manage calls.

For attorneys not yet using VXT, booking a demo is the quickest way to see how the VXT-iManage integration can enhance document management at your firm.

‍

About VXT VXT is the AI notetaker and phone system built for law firms.

Attorneys use VXT to make phone calls, and it automates the paperwork that follows, turning calls and meetings into structured file notes that save directly into a firm's legal software.

Founded in 2018 in Christchurch, New Zealand, VXT supports more than 12,000 attorneys across 2,000+ firms globally and has managed over 27 million calls.

‍

About iManage Built for mid-sized and large enterprise law firms, iManage is a top-rated, highly secure document and email management platform.

It centralizes all case-related files and emails into smart, digital workspaces, helping firms secure sensitive data, automate organization, and find critical information instantly.

Over one million professionals at more than 4,000 organizations across 65+ countries — including 2,500+ law firms and 1,200+ corporate legal departments — rely on iManage to deliver client and corporate work.

Want to see the integration in action? Get a free demo

news.titleEn: EU Digital Omnibus on AI Enters Into Force
news.titleZh: 欧盟数字综合法案中的人工智能条款生效
news.summaryZh: 欧盟通过《人工智能法案》首个实质性修正案，即《人工智能综合法案》（Regulation (EU) 2026/1744），于2026年7月24日刊登官方公报，7月27日生效。该法案推迟了部分合规时间表，但并非欧洲AI监管的广泛暂停。最显著变化是推迟许多高风险AI系统义务：附件III下独立高风险系统（用于就业、教育、信用评估、执法和关键基础设施）的适用日期从2026年8月2日移至2027年12月2日；嵌入已受欧盟产品安全立法约束产品（如医疗器械、机械和玩具）的AI系统合规推迟至2028年8月2日。许多重要要求仍按原时间表执行，尤其是通用人工智能（GPAI）模型条款继续适用，包括对最大模型的透明度、报告和系统性风险义务。法案新增两项禁止的AI实践，针对生成或操纵逼真亲密图像或儿童性虐待材料的系统，自2026年12月2日起适用，反映欧盟对AI助长危害的关注，并将提供直接监管执法依据。法案显著加强欧洲AI办公室作用，赋予其对某些基于GPAI模型的AI系统及集成到受《数字服务法》监管的超大型在线平台和搜索引擎的AI系统的独家监管责任，权力类似欧洲竞争监管机构，包括启动调查、强制提供信息、检查、接受有约束力承诺，以及对持续违规处以最高日均营业额5%的定期罚款。组织不应被“延迟”头条误导：延迟不延伸至大部分透明度义务，从2026年8月2日起仍须继续遵守相关要求。
news.bodyText: Find Your Next Job ! The EU has adopted its first substantive amendment to the AI Act. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, commonly referred to as the AI Omnibus, was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. While the legislation postpones certain aspects of the AI Act’s compliance timetable, it would be a mistake for organisations to view the Omnibus as a broad pause on AI regulation in Europe. The most significant change is the deferral of obligations applying to many high-risk AI systems. The application date for stand-alone high-risk systems under Annex III, including AI used in employment, education, credit assessment, law enforcement and critical infrastructure, moves from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027. For AI systems embedded in products already subject to EU product safety legislation, such as medical devices, machinery and toys, compliance is deferred further, until 2 August 2028. Many important requirements remain on their original timetable. Most notably, the AI Act’s provisions governing general-purpose AI (GPAI) models continue to apply as planned, including transparency, reporting and systemic risk obligations for the largest models. The Omnibus also introduces two new prohibited AI practices, targeting systems designed to generate or manipulate realistic intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material. These prohibitions apply from 2 December 2026 and reflect the EU’s increasing focus on AI-enabled harms. While other legal regimes already address such conduct, the AI Act will soon provide a direct regulatory basis for enforcement. The Omnibus significantly strengthens the role of the European AI Office. The AI Office now has exclusive supervisory responsibility for certain AI systems built on general-purpose AI models and for AI systems integrated into very large online platforms and search engines regulated under the Digital Services Act. The new provisions give the AI Office powers closely resembling those exercised by European competition regulators. These include the ability to launch investigations, compel the production of information, carry out inspections, accept binding commitments and impose periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily turnover for continuing infringements. Organisations should not be misled by headlines that say “delayed”: delay does not extend to most of the AI Act’s transparency obligations. research.titleEn: Semantics of Subterfuge: Benchmarking Legal Deception Detection Against General-domain State-of-the-Art
research.titleZh: 欺骗的语义：法律欺骗检测与通用领域最新技术的基准测试
research.abstractEn: Deception detection has critical implications for legal proceedings, law enforcement, and online security. Although human judgment is limited in accuracy and scalability, Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a data-driven alternative. We present a survey and comparative analysis of NLP-based Automatic Deception Detection (ADD) focusing on the legal domain, reviewing the evolution from feature-based machine learning to Large Language Model (LLM) approaches. We conduct a unified empirical evaluation across seven datasets (two legal, five general-domain), comparing six fine-tuned transformer models and seven LLMs under four prompting strategies. The results show strong domain sensitivity, with fine-tuned models excelling in data-rich general domains and few-shot LLMs remaining competitive in low-resource legal settings. Chain-of-Thought prompting often underperforms direct classification. These findings highlight the need for domain adaptation and interpretable systems in high-stakes legal contexts.
research.abstractZh: 欺骗检测对法律诉讼、执法和在线安全具有关键意义。尽管人类判断在准确性和可扩展性方面存在局限，自然语言处理（NLP）提供了一种数据驱动的替代方案。我们提出了一项针对法律领域的基于NLP的自动欺骗检测（ADD）的综述和比较分析，回顾了从基于特征的机器学习到大型语言模型（LLM）方法的演变。我们在七个数据集（两个法律领域，五个通用领域）上进行了统一的实证评估，比较了六种微调的Transformer模型和七种LLM在四种提示策略下的表现。结果显示强烈的领域敏感性，微调模型在数据丰富的通用领域表现出色，而少样本LLM在资源匮乏的法律环境中保持竞争力。思维链提示通常不如直接分类。这些发现强调了在高风险法律环境中进行领域适应和可解释系统的必要性。

news.titleEn: Casepoint launches MCP server
news.titleZh: Casepoint推出MCP服务器
news.summaryZh: 美国电子发现提供商Casepoint于7月30日宣布推出Casepoint模型上下文协议（MCP）服务器，使组织能够将其AI模型、代理和AI生态系统与Casepoint平台连接，应用于电子发现、法律保留、调查、信息自由法（FOIA）以及其他法律和合规工作流程。该MCP基于开放的MCP标准构建，在外部AI代理与Casepoint平台之间提供安全、标准化的集成层。每个MCP请求都使用经过认证用户的现有权限执行，确保AI代理永远不会访问超出该权限的材料。未来不是围墙花园的方式，除了在平台内提供一套强大的AI功能外，他们还为客户提供灵活性，使用他们信任的模型和生态系统构建自己的代理。他们致力于提供安全、基于标准的基础，使这些代理能够与Casepoint交互，同时保持治理、权限和客户控制。未来的版本将继续扩展MCP服务器功能库，增加更多功能，使客户能够更深入地将AI集成到法律、监管、调查和合规工作流程中。如需演示，请访问www.casepoint.com。
news.bodyHtml:
US eDiscovery provider Casepoint today(30 July) announced the launch of the Casepoint Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server, enabling organizations to connect their AI models, agents and AI ecosystems with the Casepoint platform across eDiscovery, legal hold, investigations, FOIA, and other legal and compliance workflows.

Built on the open MCP standard, Casepoint’s MCP provides a secure, standardized integration layer between external AI agents and the Casepoint platform. Every MCP request executes using the authenticated user’s existing permissions, ensuring AI agents never gain access to material beyond that.

Advertisement

Chief product officer Pete Feinberg said: “The future isn’t a walled garden approach. In addition to delivering a suite of powerful AI capabilities within our platform, we are also giving customers the flexibility to build their own agents using the models and ecosystems they trust.

“We are committed to providing a secure, standards-based foundation that allows those agents to interact with Casepoint while preserving governance, permissions, and customer control.”

Advertisement

We’re told that future releases will continue expanding the MCP Server function library with additional capabilities, enabling customers to integrate AI more deeply across legal, regulatory, investigative, and compliance workflows.

To see a demo, visit www.casepoint.com.
