news.titleEn: Intapp bets on ‘firm AI’ with general release of Celeste
news.titleZh: Intapp全面发布Celeste，押注“律所AI”
news.summaryZh: Intapp本月宣布，其代理式“AI同事”Celeste在2月预览后已全面上市，定位为“律所AI”新类别，专注提升律所整体绩效而非个体律师生产力。Celeste立足Intapp长期运营的法律业务领域，帮助律所进行交易筛选、利益冲突清理、业务拓展和横向招聘。市场充斥各类AI，律师起草、审阅文件和合同的速度加快，但律所并未增长更快，因为为执业构建的AI只让个体更快，个体生产力不等于律所生产力。他指出正出现三类AI：通用助手AI如Claude或Copilot，执业AI如Harvey和Legora，以及为法律业务服务的律所AI，后者几乎无人构建，因其最难。Celeste聚焦律所核心工作流，Jampol称这些关键工作流多年未变：赢得客户、扩展关系、横向招聘、经历伦理财务战略步骤引入客户、配备团队、交付工作并确保计时开票收款，端到端客户事项生命周期依然成立。过去工作流、BPM、RPA等技术多绕开问题实质，关乎信息路由、审批、报告和审计日志；现在AI和代理可开始解决日常决策和判断挑战。Celeste将吸引看重Intapp资历及其执行护栏的律所。Jampol称市场反应极为积极，但大家用相同模型，已成基本门槛，律所未见财务绩效或竞争优势改善。将横向招聘等流程用于AI审查、冲突检查和整合管理是重大突破。另一早期用例是intake和冲突侧，这是每家律所必须做的流程，介于赢得客户与开始工作和计费之间，任何能缩短并减轻合伙人繁重工作的方法都受欢迎。Baker Hostetler是Celeste发布客户之一，Hg是另一早期采用者，其数据、技术和AI战略负责人Shirin Veeran表示，智能属于自己而非通用应用，Celeste根据实际mandate筛选。
news.bodyHtml:
Intapp this month announced that its agentic ‘AI coworker’ Celeste, previewed in February, is now generally available. The listed company positions Celeste as part of a new category of ‘firm AI’, focused on improving law firm performance rather than individual lawyer productivity.

Celeste sits in the business of law space that Intapp has operated in since its inception, helping firms with deal screening and conflicts clearance, to business development and lateral hiring.  

Advertisement

Speaking with Legal IT Insider, co-founder and chief product officer Thad Jampol said: “Every desk, every lawyer is using some form of AI. It’s flooded the market. And I think it is having some beneficial effect that lawyers are drafting faster, they’re reviewing documents faster, they’re working on contracts faster, certainly more than they did a year ago or two years ago. But the question everyone’s asking is, is the firm growing any faster?  

“For most of these organizations, the answer is not yet. And it’s really because AI built for the practice makes individuals faster, but it’s not converting into growth for the firm. So, the headline is that individual productivity is just not equal to firm productivity.”  

Advertisement

Jampol says that almost every tool up to this point in the generative AI, agentic AI wave has been built for the individuals and not for the firm. He points out that there are three ‘categories’ of AI emerging: generalist assistant AI such as Claude or Copilot (“that we think every firm is going to have and is really good for everyday work”); then the practice of AI, such as Harvey and Legora (that “have had a lot of oxygen in the industry first wave”); and a third category that is firm AI for the business of law (“and no-one, almost no-one, is building that right now because it’s the hard one to do.”) 

Celeste focuses on core workflows or value chains that Jampol describes as “the beating heart of the firm as an organization.” 

He says: “In a really interesting way, those key workflows have not changed over the years. Firms have to go win clients. They have to expand their relationship with those clients. They pursue laterals. They have to go through a lot of very onerous, ethical, financial, strategic steps to onboard those clients, upholding their duties of loyalty and their ethical obligations. They have to staff the team. They have to then go deliver the work, but also get time out and ensure that it is invoiced and collected. And that end-to-end client matter lifecycle, we believe, still holds.  

“Now, it may begin to be re-engineered as from a process standpoint to really take advantage of the agents and the new technology. But we’re really bringing, I think, a totally new set of capabilities to those same important workflows. A lot of the past technology generations, like if you think about when workflow and BPM came out and then like robotic process automation and RPA and there’s a lot of these technologies that certainly helped and Intapp used, but a lot of times they worked around the real substance of the problem. They were really about the routing of information and then the approvals and the reporting of that and the audit logs. Now with AI and agents, we can really begin to solve more of the day-to-day decision-making and judgment part of the challenges that I think are really going to take this to a totally new level.” 

It will appeal to firms that Intapp’s pedigree is in Walls, and that Celeste enforces your guardrails. 

Jampol says that the market reaction to Celeste has been extremely positive, observing that, while everyone is talking about AI in the practice of law, “everyone has the same thing. Everyone is using the same models. It’s kind of become table stakes. The firm isn’t seeing an improvement in financial performance or competitive advantage.” 

 The ability to take processes such as bringing on lateral hires and use AI for vetting, conflicts checks and managing the integration is, Jampol says, “a really big needle mover.” 

Another early use case is on the intake and conflict side. Jampol says: “It’s the process that every firm has to do that stands between winning a client and then being able to start doing the work for them and billing for that time. And anything you can do to both shrink that as well as take off a lot of the onerous work that the partner themselves has to do instead of spending time with that client, they love it.” 

Baker Hostetler is one of Intapp’s Celeste launch clients. “That is the use case that they really grabbed onto,” says Jampol. Hg is another named early adopter. Shirin Veeran, head of data, tech & AI strategy at Hg, says: “The intelligence is ours, not something generic applied to our firm. Celeste screens against our actual mandate, drawing on knowledge we have built across the firm over two decades. Having a clear, always-current view of deal progress and pipeline speed — without the usual reporting lift — is genuinely valuable to any deal team.” 

In terms of whether this is a new category, Litera has long focused its AI developments on the business and practice of law and with its recent relaunch, undoubtedly focuses on the ‘firm AI’ category. 

As margins come under pressure, however, it’s undeniable that there will be more focus, from different lenses, on firm-wide efficiency. Many law firms find that their business services resources are stretched, and anything that can truly enable them to augment overstretched teams is likely to prove attractive.

news.titleEn: Bringing Home The Bacon: Clio Launches ‘Clio Work’ AI In Its Home Country Of Canada
news.titleZh: Clio在加拿大本土推出Clio Work AI，携加拿大法律数据回家
news.summaryZh: Clio于2025年10月推出Clio Work AI产品，称其是公司18年历史上采用最快的产品，但该产品此前未在Clio的创立地和总部所在地加拿大提供。Clio于6月收购了总部位于多伦多的法律AI和数据公司Jurisage，约六周后，Clio Work于7月23日在加拿大上线，由Jurisage提供的超过47万件加拿大案例语料库支持。Clio当时表示Clio Work将在“今年晚些时候”进入加拿大，实际落地快于这一表述。Jurisage收购为Clio Work在加拿大推出铺平了道路，没有其他AI能同时理解律所具体案件和加拿大法律本身。Clio Work是一款“案件感知”AI工具，Clio称其理解案件、背景和法律，从案件档案中已有的文件、任务、截止日期、客户沟通和笔记中提取信息，再结合法律权威。加拿大用户可用其总结案件并呈现关键事实、主张、风险和日期；研究加拿大法律并将结果链接回来源；在承诺前压力测试策略的优缺点；起草和修订工作成果。用户可将多步骤任务委托给产品的代理能力，按顺序规划和执行，并在每个阶段为律师提供可见性和控制。背后的Jurisage数据库覆盖40多个法院的超过47万件加拿大判决，每日更新。早期用户反应是如释重负，称他们首次拥有真正了解其工作的AI，感觉更像可依赖的同事而非需管理的工具。根据Clio的加拿大律所法律趋势报告，95%的加拿大法律专业人士现在以某种形式使用AI，但大多数使用的是并非为法律工作设计的通用工具，更不用说加拿大法律工作。在此公告之前，Clio Work已在美国、英国、爱尔兰、新西兰、新加坡和香港提供。
news.bodyHtml:
Since launching its Clio Work AI product in October 2025, Clio says it has been the fastest-adopted product in the company’s 18-year history. But there was one place where Clio Work was not available — Canada, the country where Clio was founded and is headquartered.

Now Clio has brought home the bacon, so to speak, launching Clio Work in Canada — and doing it roughly six weeks after acquiring the Canadian legal data company that made the launch possible.

Clio Work went live in Canada on July 23, enabled by a corpus of more than 470,000 Canadian cases drawn from Jurisage, the Toronto-based legal AI and data company Clio acquired in June.

At the time of that deal, Clio said Clio Work would reach Canada “later this year.” It got there faster than that language might have suggested.

“The Jurisage acquisition paved the way for the Canadian launch of Clio Work,” said Jack Newton, Clio’s CEO and founder. “No other AI understands both the specifics of a firm’s matters and Canadian law itself. That’s a powerful combination, and we believe it’s going to fuel the future of legal work in Canada.”

What Clio Work Does

Clio Work is a “matter-aware” AI tool that Clio says “understands your cases, their context and the law. It pulls from the documents, tasks, deadlines, client communications and notes already sitting in the matter file, and then combines that context with legal authority.

Clio says Canadian users can use it to summarize a matter and surface key facts, claims, risks and dates; research Canadian law with results linked back to source; stress-test a strategy’s strengths and weaknesses before committing to it; and draft and revise work product.

Users can delegate multi-step tasks to the product’s agentic capabilities, which plan and execute in sequence while providing the lawyer visibility and control at each stage.

The Jurisage database behind it covers more than 470,000 Canadian decisions across 40-plus courts and is updated daily.

‘Relief’ Among Canadian Customers

Luke Slan, Clio’s general manager for Canada, said the reaction from early users has been relief.

“For the first time, they have an AI that actually knows their work,” Slan said. “It feels less like a tool they have to manage and more like a colleague they can rely on for real client work.”

According to Clio’s Legal Trends for Canadian Law Firms Report, 95% of Canadian legal professionals now use AI in some form. However, most of that use is generic tools that were not designed for legal work, let alone Canadian legal work.

Prio to this announcement, Clio Work had been available in the United States, the United Kingdom, Ireland, New Zealand, Singapore and Hong Kong.

Now, Clio has brought home the bacon to its native soil, and, thanks to the Jurisage acquisition, that bacon is Canadian.

Luke Slan, Clio’s general manager for Canada, said the reaction from early users has been relief.

“For the first time, they have an AI that actually knows their work,” Slan said. “It feels less like a tool they have to manage and more like a colleague they can rely on for real client work.”

According to Clio’s Legal Trends for Canadian Law Firms Report , 95% of Canadian legal professionals now use AI in some form. However, most of that use is generic tools that were not designed for legal work, let alone Canadian legal work.

Prio to this announcement, Clio Work had been available in the United States, the United Kingdom, Ireland, New Zealand, Singapore and Hong Kong.

Now, Clio has brought home the bacon to its native soil, and, thanks to the Jurisage acquisition, that bacon is Canadian.

news.titleEn: LawNext: From Product to Practice – Why Casetext’s Former CTO Founded General Legal, An AI Native Law Firm
news.titleZh: LawNext：从产品到实践——Casetext前CTO为何创立AI原生律所General Legal
news.summaryZh:

Mohler，曾任Casetext LLM工程师，现任首席产品官兼管理合伙人。他们的最终目标是让General Legal成为全球最大的法律服务提供商，并在此过程中打破使法律帮助无法触及需要之人的稀缺模式。
news.bodyHtml:
As chief technology officer at Casetext, Ryan Walker helped build CoCounsel, one of the first and most consequential generative AI legal assistants — a product so significant it led to the company’s $650 million acquisition by Thomson Reuters. But Walker came away unsatisfied. Although the legal tech tools kept getting better, he believed, clients were seeing no benefit. Billing rates kept climbing and the efficiency gains never reached them.

That spurred him to pivot from building products to forming a practice — General Legal, an AI-native law firm he cofounded and leads as CEO, built on the premise that the fastest path to transforming legal services is not retrofitting AI onto traditional firms, but rebuilding the law firm from the ground up on an AI-forward foundation. Just six months out of Y Combinator, the firm has some 400 clients, a newly launched venture financing practice, and, in what may be a first for a law firm, an MCP server that lets clients’ AI agents engage the firm directly.

In this episode of LawNext, Walker — not a lawyer but a PhD mathematician — tells host Bob Ambrogi why he believes AI can now automate 95% of routine legal work, how the management services organization structure allows an investable technology company to operate alongside a law firm, and why an AI-native firm paradoxically depends on hiring highly experienced lawyers rather than supercharging junior ones. He also explains the “second brain” approach that lets the firm’s work product reflect each client’s strategy, what earlier failed innovators like Atrium and Clearspire got wrong, and why he thinks the real reckoning will come when major clients simply refuse to pay for work AI can do.

Walker cofounded the firm along with two other Casetext colleagues, Javed Qadrud-Din, who was head of AI at Casetext and is now General Legal’s chief technology officer, and J.P. Mohler, who was an LLM engineer at Casetext and is now chief product officer and managing partner. Their ultimate ambition, Walker says, is to make General Legal the biggest provider of legal services in the world and, along the way, to break the scarcity model that keeps legal help out of reach for the people and companies who need it.

  • Briefpoint, eliminating routine discovery response and request drafting tasks so you can focus on drafting what matters (or just make it home for dinner).

news.bodyHtml:
Descrybe Open Connector gives legal organizations the freedom to combine their own expertise and processes with Descrybe’s legal intelligence.

BOSTON, July 27, 2026 — Descrybe, the legal technology company building trusted legal research and intelligence for wherever legal work happens, today announced the Descrybe Open Connector, a new initiative that enables law firms and legal organizations to build, customize and control their own AI-powered legal research tools and workflows on top of the Descrybe Legal Engine.

The initiative allows organizations to combine their own expertise, processes and institutional knowledge with Descrybe’s legal intelligence, creating applications and workflows that reflect how they actually work and can evolve alongside the AI technologies they choose to use. 

“Firms can begin to separate the legal intelligence they need from the workflows and applications that make their organizations distinctive,” said Kara Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Descrybe. “They can maintain control over how they work, preserve their institutional knowledge, choose the AI environments that make sense for them and still have trusted legal intelligence underneath it all. It also creates a powerful ecosystem model for Descrybe. As firms and legal builders create new tools and experiences, they create new ways for people to use Descrybe. That is a fundamentally different model for legal technology.”

The announcement marks a significant expansion of Descrybe’s strategy to make trusted legal intelligence available wherever people work, moving from bringing that intelligence into the tools people already use to enabling organizations to build entirely new tools and workflows around it.

The Descrybe Legal Engine gives applications and AI systems access to structured U.S. primary law, legal-specific research and retrieval capabilities, citation and treatment intelligence, source verification and other tools built specifically for legal research.

The Descrybe Open Connector includes two open-source releases designed to make that intelligence easier to build around. The Descrybe Legal Engine Python SDK provides the technical foundation for connecting custom applications to the Legal Engine, while Descrybe Legal Research Workflows offers reusable research processes that organizations can use, modify or extend to reflect their own needs.

Users can explore the Resource Guide for documentation, demonstrations and additional resources to help them get started.

Initial workflows support tasks including developing research roadmaps, identifying supporting and competing authority, and auditing legal citations and quoted language. Organizations can use them as a starting point or create entirely new processes around their own practices and expertise.

AI-assisted development is also expanding who can build technology inside legal organizations. Lawyers, legal technologists and emerging “legal quants” can increasingly turn their own ideas into working applications and workflows.

“The people closest to the work often have the best ideas about how that work should evolve,” said Richard DiBona, co-founder and CTO of Descrybe. “The rise of legal builders and legal quants means more of those people can now create the tools they have always wished existed. We want to give them a serious legal intelligence layer to build with so they can focus on what is uniquely valuable about their organization and their ideas.”

Descrybe has spent years building the infrastructure behind that intelligence layer. Before an AI model receives a user’s question, the company has already performed extensive legal-specific processing across its corpus, including structuring courts and jurisdictions, mapping citation relationships, analyzing legal treatment, classifying legal materials and preparing information for targeted search, retrieval and verification.

Making those capabilities available as building blocks allows legal organizations to create sophisticated tools without independently recreating the same foundational research infrastructure. Providing models with targeted, structured legal information before AI reasoning begins can also reduce unnecessary processing, context and token consumption, allowing firms and legal builders to focus their resources on the expertise and ideas that are unique to them.

“What Descrybe is enabling here has the potential to reshape how legal organizations think about innovation,” said Ken Friedman, advisor to Descrybe and former Deputy General Counsel at LegalZoom. “When sophisticated legal intelligence can serve as a foundation rather than a fixed experience, firms have much more room to experiment, adapt and build around the way they actually practice. That can move innovation closer to the people and organizations doing the work.”

That flexibility also reflects Descrybe’s longstanding approach to creating practical, accessible and user-friendly legal technology designed around real needs.

Descrybe has structured the Open Connector to encourage internal innovation and experimentation while protecting the legal intelligence infrastructure at the core of its business. The open-source code is available under the Apache 2.0 license, while access to the hosted Descrybe Legal Engine is governed separately by the Descrybe Terms of Service.

Individual users of applications connected to the Legal Engine require their own Descrybe license unless another arrangement has been established. Legal builders interested in using the Descrybe service to develop commercial applications can also work with Descrybe on separate arrangements.

The Descrybe Legal Engine Python SDK and Descrybe Legal Research Workflows are available now on GitHub. To see what can be built with the Descrybe Open Connector, watch the demo or learn more about building with Descrybe.

###

About Descrybe

Descrybe is a Boston-based legal technology company building trusted legal research and intelligence designed to work wherever legal work happens. Its technology combines comprehensive U.S. primary law with structured legal data, proprietary research and citation intelligence, and AI-powered workflows available through the Descrybe platform and integrations with AI assistants. Descrybe was also an official launch partner for Claude for Legal, bringing the Descrybe Legal Engine directly into Anthropic’s AI environment for legal professionals.

Founded in 2023 by Kara Peterson and Richard DiBona, Descrybe is focused on making sophisticated legal research more accessible without compromising the reliability, transparency and source grounding that legal work demands.

For more information, visit Descrybe.com.

news.titleEn: Theorem targets in-house legal RFP inefficiencies with expanded procurement platform
news.titleZh: Theorem推出扩展采购平台，瞄准企业内部法律RFP效率痛点
news.summaryZh: Theorem Legal本月推出全新市场平台，帮助企业法务部门管理法律科技与外部律师采购全生命周期，涵盖供应商发现、产品比较、RFP创建及供应商选择。公司原以法律科技目录闻名，现称平台已发展为更广泛工具，针对法务部门碎片化、劳动密集的采购流程。平台由律师Josh Maley于2019年联合创立，对内部法律顾问和法律运营人员免费，通过供应商和律所订阅层级创收。战略总监Moustafa Abdel-Kader于11月从ACC加入，他表示其他平台向法律团队收费，而Theorem由供应商付费，依曝光度和RFP机会访问量分不同订阅级别。内部团队可管理供应商、搜索、比较，并更新自身法律科技栈以查看匹配情况。用户可在发起RFP前并排比较产品，买方指定需求、优先级、时间线和能力，匹配供应商会收到提醒。外部律师事务方面，可邀请现有面板律所或向市场开放机会。Theorem重点减少传统RFP响应行政负担，尤其是邮件和电子表格分发的RFP。Maley称平台AI生成类别特定模板，将需求转化为结构化请求并邀请合适供应商投标，更快、更透明且集中一处。律所和供应商可预载常见问题答案并在未来提交中复用，以应对日益增多的AI相关尽职调查和采购问题，提供更一致的信息收集和评估框架。该市场已通过为CLOC和ACC等组织创建的品牌部署使用，作为会员福利。Theorem押注，随着法务部门面临压力证明支出合理性并更高效决策，集成平台可消除当前法律RFP流程中的大量摩擦。
news.bodyHtml:
Theorem Legal this month unveiled a newly designed marketplace to help corporate legal departments manage the full lifecycle of procuring legal technology and outside counsel, from supplier discovery and product comparison through to RFP creation and vendor selection. 

While the company was originally known for its legal technology directory, Theorem says the platform has grown into something much broader, aimed at addressing the often fragmented and labour-intensive procurement processes used by many legal departments today. 

Advertisement

The platform, co-founded in 2019 by attorney Josh Maley, is free for in-house counsel and legal operations professionals, with Theorem generating revenue through subscription tiers for participating vendors and law firms seeking greater visibility and access to RFP opportunities. 

Speaking with Legal IT Insider, Moustafa Abdel-Kader, strategic director of growth and partnerships at Theorem, who joined from Association of Corporate Counsel in November, said: “Other platforms charge legal team but for us its vendors that pay, depending on how much visibility they want and how much access to RFP opportunities, so there are different subscription levels.” 

Advertisement

In-house legal teams are able to go from a discovery and research process to submitting RFPs for legal tech and also law firm matters. Abdel-Kader says: “They can literally do everything. They can manage suppliers through the marketplace. They can search through it. They can do comparisons. They can update their own legal tech stack on their profile so that they’re able to see what is going to work within their tech stack as they’re searching through. So it’s a really great end-to-end procurement process for them.” 

Users can compare tech products side by side before initiating an RFP process. Buyers can specify business requirements, purchasing priorities, timelines and desired capabilities, while vendors that match the relevant search criteria are alerted to opportunities. 

For outside counsel engagements, corporate legal teams can either invite firms from existing panel arrangements or open opportunities more broadly to the market. 

A key focus for Theorem is reducing the administrative burden traditionally associated with responding to RFPs, particularly those circulated through email and spreadsheets. 

“What we’re trying to do from a law firm perspective and for a legal tech perspective is really simplify the way that they are able to view these opportunities, but also respond to these opportunities,” Abdel-Kader said.  

Maley added: “An RFP can sound like a large, formal exercise, but our platform AI generates category-specific templates to turn a team’s requirements into a structured request and invite the right providers to bid. That means it’s faster, more transparent, and all in one place.”

Often RFPs involve looking at data held in multiple spreadsheets and reinventing the wheel in the responses. To address that challenge, law firms and vendors can preload responses to frequently asked questions and reuse them across future submissions. 

Standardisation point is particularly relevant at a time when legal departments and vendors alike are attempting to navigate a growing volume of AI-related due diligence and procurement questions. Rather than requiring suppliers to repeatedly answer different versions of substantially similar questionnaires, Theorem’s approach aims to provide a more consistent framework for information gathering and evaluation.  

The marketplace is already being utilised through branded deployments created for industry organisations including CLOC and the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC), which offer access to members as part of their benefits programmes.  

Theorem’s bet is that as corporate legal departments face increasing pressure to justify legal spend and make technology purchasing decisions more efficiently, an integrated marketplace and procurement platform could remove much of the friction that continues to characterise legal RFP processes today.  

To find out more, head to https://www.theoremlegal.com/

Users can compare tech products side by side before initiating an RFP process. Buyers can specify business requirements, purchasing priorities, timelines and desired capabilities, while vendors that match the relevant search criteria are alerted to opportunities.

For outside counsel engagements, corporate legal teams can either invite firms from existing panel arrangements or open opportunities more broadly to the market.

A key focus for Theorem is reducing the administrative burden traditionally associated with responding to RFPs, particularly those circulated through email and spreadsheets.

“What we’re trying to do from a law firm perspective and for a legal tech perspective is really simplify the way that they are able to view these opportunities, but also respond to these opportunities,” Abdel-Kader said.

Maley added: “An RFP can sound like a large, formal exercise, but our platform AI generates category-specific templates to turn a team’s requirements into a structured request and invite the right providers to bid. That means it’s faster, more transparent, and all in one place.”

Often RFPs involve looking at data held in multiple spreadsheets and reinventing the wheel in the responses. To address that challenge, law firms and vendors can preload responses to frequently asked questions and reuse them across future submissions.

Standardisation point is particularly relevant at a time when legal departments and vendors alike are attempting to navigate a growing volume of AI-related due diligence and procurement questions. Rather than requiring suppliers to repeatedly answer different versions of substantially similar questionnaires, Theorem’s approach aims to provide a more consistent framework for information gathering and evaluation.

The marketplace is already being utilised through branded deployments created for industry organisations including CLOC and the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC), which offer access to members as part of their benefits programmes.

Theorem’s bet is that as corporate legal departments face increasing pressure to justify legal spend and make technology purchasing decisions more efficiently, an integrated marketplace and procurement platform could remove much of the friction that continues to characterise legal RFP processes today.

To find out more, head to https://www.theoremlegal.com/

news.bodyText:
Fresh from AALL in Cleveland, Greg reflects on a conference filled with legal information professionals who understand how technology performs under real working conditions. These librarians purchase products, train users, support law schools and courts, and often serve as internal advocates for legal technology. Their expertise makes vendor engagement especially valuable, yet major product announcements were scarce. Marlene balances Greg’s conference report with stories from her hiking trip through Zion and Bryce Canyon, plus a brief comparison of Ohio and Utah karaoke culture.

The conversation turns to the rapid growth of innovation attorney positions across law firms and legal organizations. Greg and Marlene describe these professionals as translators who connect legal practice, technology, workflow design, and organizational change. Firms are searching beyond traditional legal career paths for people who combine technical fluency with strong interpersonal skills. For law students and junior lawyers facing uncertainty around AI, these emerging roles offer broader career options beyond the familiar associate track.

Marlene explores the growing use of AI personas and simulations for professional development. Deposition witnesses, opposing counsel, negotiation partners, and drafting reviewers now appear as interactive characters with distinct goals and behaviors. Lawyers receive a place to practice, make decisions, and receive feedback before working with clients or appearing in court. Greg connects simulation-based learning with legal fiction, including his _Beyond the Model_ series, which uses a fictional law firm to explain AI systems, business pressures, and changes in legal work.

The discussion takes a serious turn with a reported AI benchmarking incident involving an agentic model, a breached sandbox, and unauthorized access to Hugging Face resources in search of an answer key. Greg and Marlene examine the episode as a warning about containment, accountability, and excessive faith in technical guardrails. From there, they consider the renewed importance of knowledge management and security as AI systems gain access to documents, financial information, client data, and institutional expertise. Greg predicts growing attention around AI harnesses, structured software layers designed to guide model behavior and produce predictable outputs.

Marlene closes with examples of AI moving into client intake, business qualification, and workflow decisions, including an AI legal receptionist designed for smaller firms. The larger shift involves moving beyond simple tool adoption toward redesigned workflows, staffing models, pricing structures, and client service. Token costs are creating immediate budget pressure, while clients are questioning which AI expenses belong on their bills. Greg and Marlene argue firms must connect AI spending with legal judgment, measurable value, and responsible delivery, rather than treating consumption as a proxy for progress.

Here is a chronological list of the substantive topics and sources referenced in the episode:

- **00:25:**The Arithmetic of AI: Tokens and Claude in Legal Work, Legal Technology Hub’s series on token usage and prompting habits.

- **00:25:**Legora’s consumption-based pricing for Agent Pro, including matter-level usage tracking and spending controls.

- **02:22:**AALL 2026 Annual Meeting and Conference, held in Cleveland for legal information professionals.

- **08:35:**“The Hottest Job at Big Law Firms Is Becoming Difficult to Fill”, Bloomberg Law’s report on demand for legal AI and innovation professionals.

- **11:29:**Ai4 2026, the cross-industry artificial intelligence conference at The Venetian in Las Vegas.

- **12:49:**AltaClaro and Verbit’s DepoSim, an AI simulation platform for deposition training.

- **13:31:**Stanford CodeX, including its work on AI personas and legal education.

- **13:56:**Vorys’ AI lawyer personas, modeled on 19 firm partners for training and knowledge transfer.

- **16:33:**Stanford CodeX and Flatiron’s M&A Negotiation Simulator, led by Megan Ma.

- **16:48:**Beyond the Model, Greg’s fictional series explaining legal AI technology, workflows, governance, and law-firm economics.

- **17:24:**Richard Tromans and Artificial Lawyer, including his use of fictional storytelling to examine legal innovation.

- **17:24:**Jennifer Leonard’s work with the Practising Law Institute, using characters and narrative to explain professional change.

- **18:06:**How Tech Workers Are Feeling in 2026, the survey Greg adapted for a fictional law firm workforce.

- **22:55:**Retrieval-Augmented Generation and why legal AI research improved, explored through the first part of _Beyond the Model_.

- **23:52:**Microsoft CELA’s adoption of Harvey, covering Microsoft’s use of Harvey across legal and compliance operations.

- **26:42:**OpenAI and Hugging Face’s security incident, involving an agent escaping a testing sandbox and accessing Hugging Face systems.

- **29:01:**Simon Willison’s analysis of the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, including ExploitGym, disabled guardrails, containment failures, and Hugging Face’s use of GLM-5.2 for forensic analysis.

- **30:48:**NetDocuments Smart Answers and AI connectivity, focused on institutional knowledge and governed access.

- **30:48:**iManage’s AI and knowledge-platform developments, including AI controls, agent monitoring, and permission-aware access.

- **32:01:**ClearPeople’s Atlas knowledge-management platform, creating a structured knowledge layer across Microsoft 365.

- **32:01:**Atlas AI and private legal knowledge graphs, discussed during the earlier TGIR interview with Stephen Costigan.

- **32:29:**Knowledge security, permissions, and need-to-know access in iManage, including inherited document-management controls for AI tools.

- **33:52:**Claire Vo’s custom AI harness demonstration, showing how software around an AI agent creates repeatable workflows, controlled permissions, and structured outputs.

- **36:44:**LexiDesk, an AI receptionist and intake system for smaller and consumer-facing law firms.

- **37:50:**Simon Willison’s conversation with Anthropic’s Claude Code team, which inspired the question, “What is true today that wasn’t true a year ago?”

Token cost moved into the spotlight recently as tools like Claude gained traction in legal, because most plans come with token limits, as well as the ability to request limit increases, which has resulted in tales of astronomical bills for some users. Recently, Legora also announced that it’s moving its Agent Pro offering to consumption-based pricing, which means it’s billing by what the agent does rather than by a flat seat license. research.titleEn: LLM-Assisted Ontology Engineering and Construction of a French Legal Knowledge Graph
research.titleZh: 基于LLM辅助的本体工程与法语法律知识图谱构建
research.abstractEn: Maintenance regulations are complex legal texts that are difficult to exploit when addressing a specific case and challenging to integrate into operational systems. This paper presents a two-stage LLM-assisted workflow for French maintenance regulations: ontology engineering from a SEMLEG-based core ontology, followed by construction of an ontology-grounded French legal knowledge graph. The first stage consists in the open extraction of typed entities and triples from a stratified corpus sample, the normalization of labels through embedding-based fusion, and the induction of candidate object properties with their signature (domain and range). The second stage uses the resulting ontology to guide the closed extraction of triples and RDF graph construction over the full corpus. Experiments with GPT-4.1 and mistral-large-2512 show robust structured outputs, near-complete class alignment, and a substantial reduction of duplicated entities and predicates after fusion. Fewer than 20% of triples introduce unseen properties, while lower exact signature compliance reveals new domain-range combinations for existing predicates. These results point to predicate normalization and the validation of newly observed relation signatures as key refinement steps for industrial maintenance settings.
research.abstractZh: 维护法规是复杂的法律文本，在处理特定案例时难以利用，并且难以集成到操作系统中。本文提出了一种针对法语维护法规的两阶段LLM辅助工作流程：从基于SEMLEG的核心本体进行本体工程，然后构建基于本体的法语法律知识图谱。第一阶段包括从分层语料库样本中开放提取类型化实体和三元组，通过基于嵌入的融合进行标签归一化，以及归纳候选对象属性及其签名（定义域和值域）。第二阶段利用生成的本体指导全语料库上的封闭三元组提取和RDF图构建。使用GPT-4.1和mistral-large-2512的实验显示出稳健的结构化输出、近乎完整的类对齐，以及融合后重复实体和谓词的显著减少。少于20%的三元组引入了未见过的属性，而较低的精确签名符合性揭示了现有谓词的新定义域-值域组合。这些结果表明，谓词归一化和对新观察到的关系签名的验证是工业维护环境中的关键细化步骤。

research.titleEn: Do Small Models Use the Law You Give Them? Context-Injected Fine-Tuning for Legal QA in Bangladesh
research.titleZh: 小模型会使用你提供的法律吗？孟加拉国法律问答中的上下文注入微调
research.abstractEn: A small language model can receive the governing statutory provision and still answer incorrectly. We test whether fine-tuning on examples containing relevant law improves later use of retrieved law. We curate 2{,}165 bilingual QA records from six Bangladeshi acts and three schedules, then fine-tune Qwen3.5 at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B. Evaluation uses the 2022 and 2023 Bangladesh Bar Council exams in Bangla and machine-translated English, with no retrieval, BM25, or FAISS, scored by strict consistency over three seeded runs. At 0.8B, fine-tuning raises the 2022 English FAISS score from 2 to 34 of 100. Gains at 0.8B and 2B survive paired testing, but the 4B model has no detectable net gain: Bangla improves while several English conditions regress. Fine-tuning also reduces answers that drift from Bangla into mostly English from 44.0--53.2\% to 0.2--0.7\%, with adjusted $p<.001$ at every scale. Retrieval quality is therefore not the only bottleneck. Small bilingual legal models also differ in how they use supplied law and whether they answer in the requested language. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/momahadi/bangladesh-legal-qa-dataset.
research.abstractZh: 一个小型语言模型可以接收到适用的法定条款，但仍然会给出错误的答案。我们测试了在包含相关法律的示例上进行微调是否能改善后续对检索到的法律的使用。我们从六部孟加拉国法案和三个附表中整理了2,165条双语问答记录，然后对Qwen3.5的0.8B、2B和4B版本进行微调。评估使用2022年和2023年孟加拉国律师协会考试（孟加拉语和机器翻译的英语），不进行检索、BM25或FAISS，通过三次种子运行的严格一致性进行评分。在0.8B规模下，微调将2022年英语FAISS分数从2分提高到34分（满分100分）。0.8B和2B规模的提升在配对检验中仍然显著，但4B模型没有可检测到的净收益：孟加拉语有所改善，而几个英语条件则出现退步。微调还将从孟加拉语漂移到主要使用英语的答案比例从44.0%–53.2%降低到0.2%–0.7%，在每个规模下调整后的p<.001。因此，检索质量并不是唯一的瓶颈。小型双语法律模型在如何使用提供的法律以及是否以所要求的语言回答方面也存在差异。该数据集公开可用，网址为https://huggingface.co/datasets/momahadi/bangladesh-legal-qa-dataset。

news.titleEn: Alabama Bar Draws a Clear Ethics Line on Lawyers’ AI Use
news.titleZh: 阿拉巴马州律师协会就律师使用AI划定明确道德界限
news.summaryZh:
阿拉巴马州律师协会发布正式道德指导意见，明确AI对律所而言不仅是技术问题，更是职业责任问题。意见聚焦计费与客户沟通：警告律师不得就AI辅助完成的工作收取虚高费用，并应坦诚告知客户AI的使用方式。意见将AI定位为须在胜任、合理、诚实和监督等长期义务框架内使用的工具，而非禁止性工具。

该意见影响超出阿拉巴马州。律师协会意见常成为法院、纪律机构、职业责任保险商及律所风险委员会的实践路线图。在正式规则尚未完全跟上技术发展之际，道德指导意见正日益塑造评判律师的标准，等待上诉判决或纪律案例再行动的律所可能已经落后。对诉讼律师而言，若AI减少研究、起草或文件审查时间而时间记录未反映效率提升，传统计费小时模式将更难辩护；同时律师不能将判断外包给聊天机器人，人工审查仍不可或缺，尤其考虑到对虚构判例、不准确摘要和过度自信输出的持续担忧。对内部法律顾问，该意见强化了向外聘律所直接询问AI政策的必要性：使用哪些工具、如何保护机密信息、AI辅助工作如何审查及如何计费。合规与风险团队也应注意，正式指导意见可迅速影响内部培训、委托书、网络安全协议和记录管理实践；已允许使用AI的律所可能需要更精确的书面规则，涵盖披露、监督和计费纪律。更广泛的结论是，法律道德监管机构行动速度快于许多人的预期。阿拉巴马州的意见强调了一个简单而有力。

Alabama Bar Draws a Clear Ethics Line on Lawyers’ AI Use

by Bruno Queiroz

The Alabama State Bar has issued formal ethics guidance on lawyers’ use of artificial intelligence, offering one of the clearest signals yet that AI is no longer just a technology issue for law firms — it is a professional responsibility issue.

The opinion reportedly focuses on two especially sensitive areas: billing and client communication. Lawyers are warned not to charge inflated fees for work performed with the assistance of AI, and they are expected to be candid with clients about how AI is being used in legal services. That combination is important. It frames AI not as a prohibited tool, but as one that must be used within long-standing duties of competence, reasonableness, honesty, and supervision.

For legal professionals, the significance goes beyond Alabama. Bar opinions often become practical roadmaps for courts, disciplinary authorities, malpractice carriers, and law firm risk committees. In an area where formal rules have not fully caught up to the technology, ethics guidance is increasingly shaping the standards attorneys will be judged by. That means firms waiting for appellate decisions or disciplinary cases before acting may already be behind.

For litigators, the billing point is particularly consequential. If AI reduces the time required for research, drafting, or document review, the traditional billable-hour model becomes harder to defend if time entries do not reflect that efficiency. At the same time, lawyers cannot outsource judgment to a chatbot. Human review remains essential, especially given continuing concerns about hallucinated authorities, inaccurate summaries, and overconfident outputs.

For in-house counsel, the opinion reinforces the value of asking outside firms direct questions about AI policies: What tools are being used? How is confidential information protected? How is AI-assisted work reviewed? How is that work billed? Those questions are becoming part of ordinary vendor-management and outside-counsel oversight.

Compliance and risk teams should also take note. Formal bar guidance can quickly influence internal training, engagement letters, cybersecurity protocols, and records-management practices. Firms that already permit AI use may now need more precise written rules on disclosure, supervision, and billing discipline.

The broader takeaway is that legal ethics regulators are moving faster than many expected. Alabama’s opinion underscores a simple but powerful principle: AI may change how legal work is done, but it does not change the lawyer’s duty to deliver accurate work, charge fairly, and communicate honestly with the client.

news.titleZh: 创业角：Lexidesk，律所的人工智能接待员
news.summaryZh: Lexidesk是一家快速成长的法律AI初创公司，致力于解决中小型律所持续面临的挑战：获取并筛选新业务。该公司由Ivan Tryskyba于2025年6月创立，结合对话式AI、语音技术和法律专用接案工作流，全天候接听电话和网络咨询。公司瞄准人身伤害、家庭、移民、刑事辩护和遗产规划等高业务量领域，定位为专为法律服务打造的AI接待员，而非通用语音助手。其平台整合语音AI、电话基础设施和LLM驱动的资格筛选逻辑，并具备原生CRM集成和针对每家律所及业务领域调优的提示架构。公司已在美国和英国签约50多家律所，推出基于对话的定价模式，上线多个CRM市场集成，并推出外呼功能。公司从Caseguru（与Vadym Baranivsky共同创立的律师市场）转型至当前的AI接案方向。市场挑战包括：律所技术采用缓慢，对涉及客户沟通的技术持风险规避态度；信任和准确性（不产生幻觉法律建议、正确的范围/冲突检查）至关重要；市场充斥着不理解法律接案细微差别的通用AI语音代理。公司首名客户通过ChatGPT找到他们，现已成为公司顾问。
news.bodyHtml:
In this week’s Startup Corner is Lexidesk, a fast-growing legal AI startup tackling one of the most persistent challenges facing smaller law firms: capturing and qualifying new business. Founded in June 2025 by Ivan Tryskyba, Lexidesk combines conversational AI, voice technology and legal-specific intake workflows to answer calls and web enquiries around the clock.

Targeting high-volume practice areas such as personal injury, family, immigration, criminal defence and estate planning, the company is positioning itself as an AI receptionist built specifically for legal services rather than a general-purpose voice assistant. Having already signed more than 50 law firms across the UK and US, launched multiple CRM integrations and expanded into outbound calling, the bootstrapped startup is seeking to differentiate itself through deep legal intake expertise at a time when the market is becoming increasingly crowded with AI voice solutions.

Advertisement

We caught up with Tryskyba and CTO Vadim Baranivsky to hear their origin story, how the company pivoted, its strategy, and a fact no-one else knows.

How would you describe your company to a friend?

Lexidesk is an AI receptionist for law firms. It answers the phone and website chat 24/7, figures out if a caller has a real case, and books them straight into a consultation — so firms stop losing leads to voicemail.

Advertisement
And to a techy?

Lexidesk is a conversational AI intake platform combining voice AI, telephony infrastructure, and LLM-driven qualification logic, with native CRM integrations and a state-of-the-art prompt architecture tuned per firm and practice area.

When were you founded?

June 2025

By who?

Ivan Tryskyba 

Who are your key managers/senior execs?

Ivan Tryskyba CEO, Vadim Baranivsky CTO

Who are your target clients?

Small-to-mid-size US and UK law firms — personal injury, family, immigration, criminal defense, and estate planning practices — that get high call/lead volume and can’t staff round-the-clock intake.

What is your plan (growth strategy)?

Direct sales plus CRM marketplace distribution, content/SEO via our Knowledge Hub, and expanding product surface area (outbound calling, referral network, agent memory) to increase seat value and reduce churn.

Key achievements?

50+ law firm clients live across the US and UK; conversation-based pricing model shipped; multiple CRM marketplace integrations live; outbound calling feature launched.

Have you received investment?

We are bootstrapping

Have there been any key changes in direction since you were founded?

Pivoted from Caseguru (a lawyer marketplace, co-founded with Vadym Baranivsky) to Lexidesk’s current AI intake focus.

What are the key challenges in your market?

Law firms are slow tech adopters and risk-averse about anything touching client communication; trust and accuracy (no hallucinated legal advice, correct scope/conflict checks) are non-negotiable; and the market is getting noisy with general-purpose AI voice agents that don’t understand legal intake nuance.

Tell us something people don’t already know about the company?

Our first customer found us through ChatGPT — and is now an advisor to the company.

research.titleEn: Legal Nugget Extraction for Granular Retrieval over Long Jurisprudential Texts
research.titleZh: 面向长篇幅法学文本的细粒度检索的法律要点提取
research.abstractEn: Legal retrieval over jurisprudential collections is challenging because court decisions are long, heterogeneous documents whose relevant legal thesis may occupy only a small portion of the text. This paper asks whether legal nuggets, defined as short and self-contained legal theses extracted from source documents, can improve dense retrieval over Brazilian legal collections. We propose a pipeline that extracts nuggets from each document, indexes them with embeddings, retrieves nugget-level evidence, and aggregates the retrieved nuggets back to document-level rankings. We evaluate this approach on four Portuguese legal retrieval benchmarks from the JUA ecosystem, reporting NDCG@10, MAP@10, and MRR@10. Nugget retrieval substantially improves the two jurisprudential datasets: on JUA-Juris, NDCG@10 increases from 0.10265 to 0.20461, and on JurisTCU from 0.20898 to 0.32696. However, it underperforms full-document retrieval on NormasTCU and BR-TaxQA, and an embedding-model ablation shows that strong domain-adapted retrievers can remain better in the full-document setting. The results demonstrate that legal nuggets can be useful for jurisprudence search, especially when queries are formulated as legal theses, but they may not transfer equally well to other legal retrieval scenarios.
research.abstractZh: 法律检索在判例集合中具有挑战性，因为法院判决是长篇幅、异构的文档，其相关的法律论点可能仅占文本的一小部分。本文探讨了法律要点（定义为从源文档中提取的简短且自包含的法律论点）是否能够改进巴西法律集合的密集检索。我们提出了一种流水线，从每个文档中提取要点，用嵌入向量对其进行索引，检索要点级别的证据，并将检索到的要点聚合回文档级别的排名。我们在JUA生态系统的四个葡萄牙语法律检索基准上评估了该方法，报告了NDCG@10、MAP@10和MRR@10。要点检索显著改善了这两个判例数据集：在JUA-Juris上，NDCG@10从0.10265提高到0.20461；在JurisTCU上，从0.20898提高到0.32696。然而，在NormasTCU和BR-TaxQA上，其表现不如全文检索，并且嵌入模型消融实验表明，强大的领域自适应检索器在全文设置中可能仍然更好。结果表明，法律要点对于判例搜索可能是有用的，特别是当查询以法律论点的形式提出时，但它们可能无法同样地迁移到其他法律检索场景。

news.titleEn: Microsoft’s Own Legal Department Will Use Harvey, As the Two Companies Deepen Their Alliance
news.titleZh: 微软法务部将采用Harvey平台，两家公司深化合作
news.summaryZh: 法律AI公司Harvey于今日宣布，微软的企业、外部及法律事务部门（CELA）将采用Harvey平台，以支持其法律与合规运营。CELA是微软内部约2000人的部门，涵盖公司律师与合规专业人员。与此同时，Harvey也宣布将扩大自身对微软365及微软365 Copilot的内部使用，称此举可让其团队与众多客户使用同一可信平台。微软产品是律师工作的基础，感谢与微软团队的深厚关系，并称此次公告是双方持续关系中的下一步。很高兴扩大与Harvey的合作，作为将AI引入运营的更广泛努力的一部分，该合作将帮助团队更高效地工作，专注于复杂且高影响力的工作。此次公告是双方多年合作的最新进展。Harvey运行于微软Azure基础设施上，2024年12月双方宣布整合Harvey与SharePoint、Word及微软365 Copilot。2025年3月，Harvey将其法律智能直接构建为微软365 Copilot中的代理，并于6月扩展至Copilot Cowork。微软采用第三方法律AI可能暗示Copilot无法独立处理专业法律工作，但更准确的理解是，微软一直将Copilot定位为横向平台，旨在承载专业垂直代理，Harvey正是理想候选。因此，微软法务部部署Harvey并非否定Copilot，而是产品生态系统按预期整合的体现。Harvey自豪于拥有超过1000个内部法律团队使用其平台，并致力于支持法律团队的全面需求，同时与组织合作实现更广泛的业务目标。
news.bodyHtml:
Microsoft’s legal department is becoming a Harvey customer.

The legal AI company Harvey announced today that Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization — the roughly 2,000-person unit that houses the company’s lawyers and compliance professionals — will use the Harvey platform to support its legal and compliance operations.

As part of the same announcement, Harvey said it will expand its own internal use of Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 Copilot, which the company said will put its teams “on the same trusted platform used by many of its customers.”

For Harvey, landing Microsoft’s legal department as a customer is a significant milestone, given that it is arguably one of the most closely watched in-house legal teams in the technology industry. However, as I discuss more below, it is not so much a customer win as it is a next step in an evolving relationship.

“Microsoft’s products are foundational to the work lawyers do, so we have always been grateful for our deep relationship with their team,” said Winston Weinberg, Harvey’s CEO, in a statement.

“Today’s announcement that Microsoft’s legal team will use Harvey’s platform and that Harvey associates will use more Microsoft products to support our global growth represents the next step in our ongoing relationship with their team, and we look forward to building on it.”

Antony Cook, corporate vice president and deputy general counsel at Microsoft, said the company is “pleased to expand our work with Harvey as part of our broader efforts to bring the benefits of AI into our operations,” adding that the collaboration “will help our teams work more efficiently and focus on the complex, high-impact work that matters most.”

A Developing Relationship

Today’s announcement is the latest step in a relationship that has been building for several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft’s Azure infrastructure, and in December 2024 the two companies announced integrations connecting Harvey with SharePoint, Word and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

In March, Harvey went further, building its legal intelligence directly into Microsoft 365 Copilot as an agent, and in June it extended that to Copilot Cowork.

Against that backdrop, today’s news is not so much a customer win as it is a next step in an expanding relationship, with Microsoft’s lawyers adopting Harvey, and Harvey standardizing on Microsoft.

Even so, some might read Microsoft’s adoption of a third-party legal AI as a tacit admission that Copilot alone cannot handle specialized legal work. After all, if Copilot fully met the needs of Microsoft’s own lawyers, then CELA presumably would not need Harvey.

But the reality is more nuanced. The fact of the matter is that Microsoft has consistently positioned Copilot as a horizontal platform designed to host specialized vertical agents, with Harvey as a perfect candidate.

For that reason, its legal department’s deployment of Harvey probably should not be seen as a repudiation of Copilot, but as a demonstration of this product ecosystem coming together as intended.

“Harvey is proud to have more than 1,000 in-house legal teams using our platform to make their work more effective and efficient,” said Katie Burke, chief operating officer at Harvey. “We are committed to supporting the comprehensive needs of legal teams while partnering with their organization to help achieve broader business goals.”
news.bodyText:
Microsoft’s legal department is becoming a Harvey customer.

The legal AI company Harvey announced today that Microsoft’s Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization — the roughly 2,000-person unit that houses the company’s lawyers and compliance professionals — will use the Harvey platform to support its legal and compliance operations.

As part of the same announcement, Harvey said it will expand its own internal use of Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 Copilot, which the company said will put its teams “on the same trusted platform used by many of its customers.”

For Harvey, landing Microsoft’s legal department as a customer is a significant milestone, given that it is arguably one of the most closely watched in-house legal teams in the technology industry. However, as I discuss more below, it is not so much a customer win as it is a next step in an evolving relationship.

“Microsoft’s products are foundational to the work lawyers do, so we have always been grateful for our deep relationship with their team,” said Winston Weinberg, Harvey’s CEO, in a statement.

“Today’s announcement that Microsoft’s legal team will use Harvey’s platform and that Harvey associates will use more Microsoft products to support our global growth represents the next step in our ongoing relationship with their team, and we look forward to building on it.”

Antony Cook, corporate vice president and deputy general counsel at Microsoft, said the company is “pleased to expand our work with Harvey as part of our broader efforts to bring the benefits of AI into our operations,” adding that the collaboration “will help our teams work more efficiently and focus on the complex, high-impact work that matters most.”

Today’s announcement is the latest step in a relationship that has been building for several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft’s Azure infrastructure , and in December 2024 the two companies announced integrations connecting Harvey with SharePoint, Word and Microsoft 365 Copilot.

In March, Harvey went further, building its legal intelligence directly into Microsoft 365 Copilot as an agent, and in June it extended that to Copilot Cowork .

Against that backdrop, today’s news is not so much a customer win as it is a next step in an expanding relationship, with Microsoft’s lawyers adopting Harvey, and Harvey standardizing on Microsoft.

Even so, some might read Microsoft’s adoption of a third-party legal AI as a tacit admission that Copilot alone cannot handle specialized legal work. After all, if Copilot fully met the needs of Microsoft’s own lawyers, then CELA presumably would not need Harvey.

But the reality is more nuanced. The fact of the matter is that Microsoft has consistently positioned Copilot as a horizontal platform designed to host specialized vertical agents, with Harvey as a perfect candidate.

For that reason, its legal department’s deployment of Harvey probably should not be seen as a repudiation of Copilot, but as a demonstration of this product ecosystem coming together as intended.

“Harvey is proud to have more than 1,000 in-house legal teams using our platform to make their work more effective and efficient,” said Katie Burke, chief operating officer at Harvey. “We are committed to supporting the comprehensive needs of legal teams while partnering with their organization to help achieve broader business goals.”

news.bodyHtml:
Entegrata has hired Andrew Baker as chief AI & data strategy officer, bringing on board one of the legal sector’s most experienced AI practitioners as it expands its ambitions beyond just data infrastructure and into AI enablement.

Baker joins from Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, where he served as director of applied AI and built a team of around 20 specialists focused on the firm’s AI and innovation strategy. During his time at the Am Law 10 firm, Baker helped drive the adoption of leading generative AI platforms including Harvey and DeepJudge and gained firsthand experience of the opportunities and limitations firms face as they scale AI across the enterprise.

Advertisement

Baker’s roles over the years include global director for legal product and technology at Seyfarth Shaw, director of legal transformation at Janders Dean, VP and global head of services at LexPredict, and a senior director at HBR.

This latest appointment coincides with Entegrata’s plans to launch a new AI enablement layer built on top of its existing data lakehouse platform. Rather than creating another legal AI application, the company says its focus is on helping firms establish the data foundations required to support multiple AI tools, models and internally developed applications.

Advertisement

Speaking to Legal IT Insider, Entegrata founder and chief executive Tom Baldwin said the market’s biggest challenge is no longer a shortage of AI tools.

“Firms don’t need another AI tool,” he said. “It is the layer beneath all these tools that gives firms more content, context, cost control and choice. Firms want more freedom to pick different models and not be locked into any one vendor as the market changes.”

According to Baldwin, law firms are increasingly concerned about preserving institutional knowledge and maintaining flexibility as AI models evolve rapidly. Entegrata’s new offering is designed to provide a single source of truth for firm knowledge that can sit underneath platforms such as Harvey, Legora, CoCounsel and future AI applications, allowing firms to switch between models without losing context, expertise or control over their data.

For Baker, the move reflects a broader shift taking place across the legal sector. After two years of intense experimentation with generative AI, firms are now turning their attention to what sits underneath the technology.

Baker said. “The question is how do you begin to capitalise on what’s happening across different platforms and bring it together in the right way.”

He argues that the industry is entering a new phase where data readiness, governance and software development capability will become just as important as selecting the right AI tools.

“We’re expecting to see a big swing toward custom development and much more software engineering in the market,” Baker said. “Regardless of how that happens, you need the right kind of data layer below that to support more creative uses of generative AI.”

That view reflects a growing trend among leading firms, many of which are now exploring whether competitive advantage will come not from deploying the same AI platforms as their peers, but from building proprietary workflows, products and client-facing solutions on top of them.

While legal AI vendors continue to compete aggressively, firms are increasingly aware that today’s leading products may not be tomorrow’s winners.

Baker says: “The economics of building and supporting custom software development have changed dramatically,” he said. “Every firm is looking for an experience beyond the four corners of Harvey, beyond the four corners of Legora. Right now there is a bit of a sea of sameness.”

Firms are looking to create differentiated experiences, whether for internal knowledge delivery, client service, pricing innovation or entirely new product offerings. But doing so requires access to well-governed, structured and unstructured data that can be reused consistently across multiple AI systems.

Entegrata’s answer is to provide what Entegrata’s founder Tom Baldwin describes as the “plumbing layer”, enabling firms to focus on building products and solutions rather than spending months assembling data infrastructure. The company says this will help firms accelerate AI initiatives while retaining greater control over costs, governance and model selection.

One area likely to become increasingly important is model routing, where firms direct different tasks to different AI models according to cost, capability and risk. Baker argues that making those decisions effectively requires deep contextual understanding of firm data and workflows.

Looking ahead, Baker’s role will encompass product architecture, advising firms on AI team development and supporting broader data strategy initiatives. More fundamentally, however, his appointment signals Entegrata’s belief that the next phase of legal AI will be won not by the firms with the most tools, but by those with the strongest foundations.

news.summaryZh: 法律数据公司Entegrata已聘请Andrew Baker担任其首任首席AI与数据战略官。Baker此前在Simpson Thacher & Bartlett领导应用AI与数据科学超过五年。他将负责开发一条专注于为律所提供AI赋能的新产品线。Entegrata的数据湖仓平台帮助律所将孤立数据整合为单一可信来源。签约前10家客户用了三年，而签约最近10家客户用了六个月，近期签约客户包括Cleary Gottlieb、Mayer Brown、Wilson Sonsini、Mintz、Kilpatrick Townsend和Winston Taylor等全球大型律所。Entegrata于2023年由Baldwin创立，去年获得450万美元种子轮融资。Baker的职责包括：架构新的AI赋能产品线；向正在建立应用AI团队的律所提供其经验作为服务；接管Baldwin此前领导的数据战略咨询工作。Baldwin将产品愿景概括为四个C：内容、上下文、成本控制和选择。公司正在构建法律数据本体论，基于已包含约5000个字段的模式，旨在捕捉律所内部关系网络，提供360度视图。公司不构建新的AI模型或产品，而是为现有工具（如Harvey、Legora和Deep Judge）提供更丰富的上下文和内容，并保留律所更换工具的灵活性。数据层已成为律所推进生成式AI部署的瓶颈，律所面临的挑战在于数据宽度，需要整合20到30个系统的数据。领先的法律AI平台虽有帮助，但存在硬边界，而Entegrata能更好地为分析、综合和创新准备数据结构。公司正为一家拥有2000名律师的律所构建AI工具，供三名高层领导使用，以回答战略方向性问题。Baker将于8月23日至27日在纳什维尔举行的ILTACON上与企业会面。
news.bodyHtml:
The legal data company Entegrata, whose data lakehouse platform helps law firms consolidate siloed data into a single source of truth, has hired Andrew Baker, who for more than five years led applied AI and data science at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, as its first chief AI and data strategy officer, where he will lead development of a new product line focused on AI enablement for law firms.

The appointment, announced today, comes at a time of rapid growth for the company, founder and CEO Tom Baldwin told me during an interview this week with him and Baker. “It took us three years to sign our first 10 customers,” Baldwin said. “It’s taken six months to sign the last 10.”

Among those recent signings are some of the largest firms in the world, including Cleary Gottlieb, Mayer Brown, Wilson Sonsini, Mintz, Kilpatrick Townsend, and Winston Taylor.

As I reported last year when Entegrata raised $4.5 million in seed funding, Baldwin — the former CIO or CKO at firms including Cadwalader, Reed Smith and Sheppard Mullin — founded the company in 2023 to address the fragmentation of law firm data across dozens of business systems, consolidating it within a purpose-built data lakehouse.

With Baker’s hire, the company is extending that mission from business intelligence into the data layer that underpins firm-wide AI.

A Reunion Two Decades in the Making

For Baldwin and Baker, the hire is something of a reunion. The two worked together at Reed Smith in the early 2010s, when Baldwin was running pricing, legal project management and other functions there and, as he tells it, went looking for “a unicorn in the form of a JD black belt” in process improvement, and found Baker’s profile on LinkedIn.

Baker later returned to Seyfarth Shaw, where he had previously worked, to help launch that firm’s innovation program. There, he founded what Entegrata says was the industry’s first legal technology innovations office and pioneered the legal solutions architect role.

He went on to co-lead the legal transformation and innovation practice at HBR Consulting (now Harbor) before joining Simpson Thacher, where he has spent the last five-and-a-half years advancing the firm’s use of data science and emerging technology. Along the way, he earned a master’s degree in applied data science.

“I’ve been hunkered down at this intersection of law, data, tech and strategy for quite some time,” Baker said.

So why leave what he called “probably one of the cooler jobs in a law firm that you could ask for” to join a vendor?

“It’s really about the opportunity to build something big and lasting in the industry,” Baker said. “I spent a lot of time in pretty much every vendor tool that’s out there, a lot of time working with teams to build custom solutions within our firm, and I feel like I have a pretty clear understanding of where the hard edges are on each of those. And we keep running into the same challenges over and over.”

Solving those challenges from inside a single firm is daunting, he said, but it is a different ballgame from the outside.

“When you think about where you want to put your time and energy if you’re doing technical work in a law firm, it’s not on the plumbing and the data ecosystem,” he said. “It’s building the cool, exciting, creative things.”

What ‘AI Enablement’ Means

In his new role, Baker will own Entegrata’s AI roadmap across engineering, product and customer experience, with his central focus on a new product line the company describes as AI enablement.

To date, Baker said, Entegrata has been adjacent to the AI story — its data could be put to creative use, but AI was one step removed from the core product.

“This next chapter in the book brings Entegrata straight to the coalface on everything AI-related,” he said. Whatever firms are pursuing — model routing, autonomous agents, custom development — “none of those can be executed very well without the right kind of content or context to make that happen.”

The goal, he said, is “providing a framework and layer to help people truly do that, and moving beyond theory into pragmatism.”

Baldwin says the product vision centers around what he calls the four Cs: content, context, cost control and choice. The idea is to give AI tools richer content and context drawn from across a firm’s systems, provide firms observability into AI costs, and preserve their ability to swap in new models and tools as the market shifts, without starting over each time.

“To be clear, we are not building yet another AI model or product,” Baldwin said. “We’re enabling deeper context and giving more content to the existing tools firms have” — he named Harvey, Legora and Deep Judge as examples — “and creating that downstream off-ramp to different tools as they become available.”

Central to the effort is an ontology for legal data that the company is currently building, layered on top of a schema that Baldwin said already contains some 5,000 fields. (When I wrote about the company last year, that schema had 3,500 fields.)

The ontology is designed to capture the full web of relationships within a firm — the “360-degree view” that connects a document to a timekeeper, the timekeeper to a matter, the matter to a client, and outward to industry, jurisdiction, judge and opposing counsel.

“You lose all of that context the minute you take a document out of the DMS and manually upload it into an AI tool,” Baldwin said. “We bring that all back and throw an ontology on top of it.”

He drew a comparison to the much-discussed partnership between Kirkland & Ellis and Palantir. “Long term, this is going to be an offering that’s going to feel very Kirkland-esque in terms of the capabilities, but at a fraction of the time and cost that it’ll take to implement something like Palantir.”

The Data Layer as the Bottleneck

Both men agree that the data layer has become the choke point for firms trying to move beyond their first wave of generative AI deployments.

In the early rush, Baldwin said, firms were under enormous pressure simply to get AI up and running, in part so they could say they were using it.

Now that firms have had time to settle into it, he said, the next stage of maturity is “moving beyond the disconnected download-documents-out-of-the-DM, upload-them-manually-into-an-AI-tool” workflow toward AI that can run on the firm’s full data estate. He said the last six firms Entegrata signed all characterized their moves as being about AI readiness and enablement.

The challenge for law firms, Baldwin said, differs from other industries. “The challenge isn’t in depth and speed. We don’t have petabytes of real-time streaming from one or two ERP sources. Our challenge is width. It’s stitching together data from 20 or 30 systems.”

“Right now, there are a number of solutions that are focused on retrieval, and some of them do a really good job,” Baker said. “But that next hop over — how do we analyze, synthesize and create anew — it’s hard to get the data in the right structure for that. And we think we can do that in a way that others really can’t.”

As an example of what this can mean for customers, Baldwin said that for one of its largest customers, a 2,000-lawyer firm, Entegrata is building an AI tool for just three people in firm leadership designed to answer the questions that, as he put it, the people who sign everyone’s checks care about.

“It’s the opposite of, ‘I’m a third-year associate grinding through this asset purchase agreement draft,'” he said. “It’s, ‘I’m the chair of the firm and I want to know directionally where the firm’s headed.'”

Baker’s Remit

Baldwin described Baker’s mandate as spanning three buckets. First and foremost is architecting the new AI enablement product line. Second, with law firms increasingly hiring for net-new data and AI leadership roles, Baker will offer his playbook as a service to firms just standing up applied AI functions — drawing on his consulting experience at Harbor in making what works at one firm portable to many. Third, he will take over much of the data strategy engagement work that Baldwin has been leading himself.

“Andrew has lived this problem from inside one of the most prestigious firms on the planet, so he knows what it takes to make AI dependable across a real practice,” Baldwin said.

“His mandate is simple: prepare firm data and context so any model or tool it chooses actually delivers. That is the layer most of the industry is still missing, and it is what Andrew will build for our clients.”

Baker will be at ILTACON in Nashville, Aug. 23-27, where he hopes to meet with firms to discuss the intersection of data strategy and AI.

The legal data company Entegrata , whose data lakehouse platform helps law firms consolidate siloed data into a single source of truth, has hired Andrew Baker , who for more than five years led applied AI and data science at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, as its first chief AI and data strategy officer, where he will lead development of a new product line focused on AI enablement for law firms.

The appointment, announced today, comes at a time of rapid growth for the company, founder and CEO Tom Baldwin told me during an interview this week with him and Baker. “It took us three years to sign our first 10 customers,” Baldwin said. “It’s taken six months to sign the last 10.”

Among those recent signings are some of the largest firms in the world, including Cleary Gottlieb, Mayer Brown, Wilson Sonsini, Mintz, Kilpatrick Townsend, and Winston Taylor.

As I reported last year when Entegrata raised $4.5 million in seed funding , Baldwin — the former CIO or CKO at firms including Cadwalader, Reed Smith and Sheppard Mullin — founded the company in 2023 to address the fragmentation of law firm data across dozens of business systems, consolidating it within a purpose-built data lakehouse.

With Baker’s hire, the company is extending that mission from business intelligence into the data layer that underpins firm-wide AI.

A Reunion Two Decades in the Making

For Baldwin and Baker, the hire is something of a reunion. The two worked together at Reed Smith in the early 2010s, when Baldwin was running pricing, legal project management and other functions there and, as he tells it, went looking for “a unicorn in the form of a JD black belt” in process improvement, and found Baker’s profile on LinkedIn.

Baker later returned to Seyfarth Shaw, where he had previously worked, to help launch that firm’s innovation program. There, he founded what Entegrata says was the industry’s first legal technology innovations office and pioneered the legal solutions architect role.

He went on to co-lead the legal transformation and innovation practice at HBR Consulting (now Harbor) before joining Simpson Thacher, where he has spent the last five-and-a-half years advancing the firm’s use of data science and emerging technology. Along the way, he earned a master’s degree in applied data science.

“I’ve been hunkered down at this intersection of law, data, tech and strategy for quite some time,” Baker said.

So why leave what he called “probably one of the cooler jobs in a law firm that you could ask for” to join a vendor?

“It’s really about the opportunity to build something big and lasting in the industry,” Baker said. “I spent a lot of time in pretty much every vendor tool that’s out there, a lot of time working with teams to build custom solutions within our firm, and I feel like I have a pretty clear understanding of where the hard edges are on each of those. And we keep running into the same challenges over and over.”

Solving those challenges from inside a single firm is daunting, he said, but it is a different ballgame from the outside.

“When you think about where you want to put your time and energy if you’re doing technical work in a law firm, it’s not on the plumbing and the data ecosystem,” he said. “It’s building the cool, exciting, creative things.”

In his new role, Baker will own Entegrata’s AI roadmap across engineering, product and customer experience, with his central focus on a new product line the company describes as AI enablement.

To date, Baker said, Entegrata has been adjacent to the AI story — its data could be put to creative use, but AI was one step removed from the core product.

“This next chapter in the book brings Entegrata straight to the coalface on everything AI-related,” he said. Whatever firms are pursuing — model routing, autonomous agents, custom development — “none of those can be executed very well without the right kind of content or context to make that happen.”

The goal, he said, is “providing a framework and layer to help people truly do that, and moving beyond theory into pragmatism.”

Baldwin says the product vision centers around what he calls the four Cs: content, context, cost control and choice. The idea is to give AI tools richer content and context drawn from across a firm’s systems, provide firms observability into AI costs, and preserve their ability to swap in new models and tools as the market shifts, without starting over each time.

Central to the effort is an ontology for legal data that the company is currently building, layered on top of a schema that Baldwin said already contains some 5,000 fields. (When I wrote about the company last year, that schema had 3,500 fields.)

The ontology is designed to capture the full web of relationships within a firm — the “360-degree view” that connects a document to a timekeeper, the timekeeper to a matter, the matter to a client, and outward to industry, jurisdiction, judge and opposing counsel.

“You lose all of that context the minute you take a document out of the DMS and manually upload it into an AI tool,” Baldwin said. “We bring that all back and throw an ontology on top of it.”

He drew a comparison to the much-discussed partnership between Kirkland & Ellis and Palantir. “Long term, this is going to be an offering that’s going to feel very Kirkland-esque in terms of the capabilities, but at a fraction of the time and cost that it’ll take to implement something like Palantir.”

The Data Layer as the Bottleneck

Both men agree that the data layer has become the choke point for firms trying to move beyond their first wave of generative AI deployments.
